author: Corey Larocque
title: Mounties took too long to get their man, judge says
content:
Two sex charges against an Iqaluit man will not proceed because the RCMP took more than four years after the charges were laid to arrest their suspect.




A 14-year-old girl had reported to police in August 2020 that Isaac Strickland has sexually assaulted her multiple times over a period of one year.




She was 13 and he was 19 the first time she was allegedly sexually assaulted, said Justice Mark Mossey in a decision handed down Wednesday. A court-ordered ban prevents the identification of the girl.




Strickland was charged Dec. 7, 2020, with one count of sexual assault and and one count of sexual interference, and RCMP obtained a warrant for his arrest.




But Strickland wasn’t arrested until Jan. 8, 2025, more than four years later, after the complainant told police where to find him.




Mossey called it a “troubling case” in a decision he gave Wednesday in response to an application from Strickland’s lawyer to have the charges stayed.




“The RCMP’s failure to act with reasonable diligence, or to act at all for almost 50 months … will necessarily result in serious allegations of sexual abuse against a child being unable to be tested at trial,” Mossey wrote in his decision.
















“Mr. Strickland would not have been difficult to find, had the RCMP taken any steps, at all, to locate him.”




Strickland has a Charter-protected right to be tried within a reasonable amount of time from when charges are laid, said Mossey in his decision. The Supreme Court has established that amount of time should be 30 months.




Curtis Mesher, Strickland’s lawyer, declined to comment on the case, saying his client had not given him instructions about talking to the media.




In the summer of 2020 Strickland was living in Iqaluit with his parents.




That September, RCMP looked for him at the Frobisher Inn, where he was a security guard. But a manager told police Strickland had moved to Ottawa.




That led police to Algonquin College, where they were told he was a student. It turned out he was not at the college but was enrolled at Nunavut Sivuniksavut instead.
















Police looked for him at an address they were given not far from Nunavut Sivuniksavut. But they had the wrong address. He was actually living in an apartment next door.




In April 2021, Strickland took a job at Inuuqatigiit Centre for Inuit Children, Youth and Families in Ottawa that required him to get a criminal record check. As part of this process, Strickland gave his address to police, said Mossey.




“The [criminal record check] came back clean, and at no point was Mr. Strickland told by police that he had outstanding criminal charges,” said Mossey in his decision.




In October 2023, Strickland moved to Pangnirtung for a job with Innguaq Association, and in 2024 took a job with the hamlet.




By November 2024, Strickland was back in Iqaluit working at Atiigo Media and staying in staff housing. He was arrested on Jan. 8, 2025, after the complainant led police to him.
















In the four years his arrest warrant was active, Strickland filed tax returns and got a Nunavut driver’s licence among other government-issued identification, Mossey said, referring to an affidavit Strickland filed as part of his application to have the charges stayed.




Strickland’s mother is a retired assistant deputy minister of Public Safety in Nunavut, he said in his affidavit, and was “regularly in contact with RCMP and other Justice stakeholders throughout her employment.”




In August 2020, around the time the complaint was made, Strickland was living with the son of an RCMP officer for a two-week period before going to Nunavut Sinuviksavut.




He was also highly visible on various social media platforms.




“On many of the platforms, where he posted under his own name, Mr. Strickland’s location was listed during livestreams,” Mossey said.




Crown lawyer Jennifer Althot-Savoie argued the delay was “an exceptional circumstance” that should have stopped the 30-month clock from ticking.




But the judge said exceptional circumstances are outside the Crown’s control because they are unforeseen and cannot be remedied.




“Mr. Strickland’s case is not such an instance,” Mossey wrote, adding none of the delays in arresting him were attributable to Strickland.




The Public Prosecution Service of Canada does not comment on judicial decisions, a spokesperson said by email on Thursday, but noted the service has a 30-day window to file an appeal in Nunavut.




The spokesperson for the Nunavut RCMP could not be reached for comment on the decision.

author: By Konstantinos Zilos, Contributor
title: Frontline Voices of Albania’s Gen Z Uprising
content:
Tirana, Albania — Gen Z is at the forefront of a new wave of social and political protests in different parts of the world, seeking to change the existing situation. From Nepal and Serbia to India and France, young people are taking to the streets demanding political change, transparency and a better future. Social media plays a crucial role in organizing and spreading these movements, creating new forms of collective action.




In Albania, young people are giving new momentum to the protest movement known as the “Flamingo Revolution,” which began as an 

environmental protest

 earlier this year and evolved into a broader anti-government movement. Youth are gathering across the country and demanding a different future. 




In Tirana, protesters Arlinda, Jesmina, Ani and Jurgen, along with many other young people, shared with Unicorn Riot the uncertainty they experience in a country where the rising cost of living, corruption scandals, the lack of professional opportunities, and distrust in political leadership have fueled the frustration of a generation that refuses to remain silent.
















Issues such as housing, the declining quality of education, unemployment, low wages, limited employment opportunities and social inequalities are among the main problems facing young people, who are no longer willing to tolerate impunity.







“

The rents are high. The education system is falling apart. And most of all, the corruption has gotten so out of hand.

“







The protests emerged as a result of all these social and economic inequalities. For the young people who have taken to the streets, demanding a dignified life is no longer simply a request, but an ongoing struggle.




The unity of young people is what has brought this struggle this far, and it is what will keep it going. Many of the young people we met want to have a future in their country, to stay there and contribute to its development. 







Youth lead protests against the government in Tirana, Albania in November 2026. Photo contributed by Konstantinos Zilos.







A large number of the young people taking part in the demonstrations believe they are living under a regime that restricts democratic freedoms. Kristina, in particular, described the situation in her country as a dictatorship.




One of the protesters’ main demands is the resignation of the country’s Prime Minister, Edi Rama, as they believe that the political promises he has made for the country have come to nothing. What they are demanding is a better future, with a government that cares about its people and its country.




There is widespread distrust of the country’s politicians and, for many, the challenge is to find an alternative political proposal that can put an end to the dilemma of “Rama or Berisha.”




On the one hand, Edi Rama calls for dialogue, while on the other, allegations of police violence remain at the center of the protests. At the same time, he announced a €2,500 bonus for each police officer on the front line of the demonstrations, as well as salary increases for police officers. 




Meanwhile, according to a testimony we received, plainclothes police officers visit the homes of families of young people identified as participants in the demonstrations and who have experienced police violence, in order to deliver fines to them.




The protesters believe that the government cares neither about their living conditions nor about the future they can have in their own country. This is closely linked to one of Albania’s biggest challenges: the emigration of young Albanians to other countries in search of greater opportunities and a better standard of living.







A protester walks through tear gas during youth-led protests against the government in Tirana, Albania in November 2026. Photo contributed by Konstantinos Zilos.







*The people we met and who spoke to us about the protests were between 20 and 33 years old.

 

Cover image contributed by Konstantinos Zilos.

title: Peyman Viyan: Women are no longer victims but pioneers of struggle
content:
Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK) Co-Chair Peyman Viyan said in an assessment marking 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, that violence against women in Iran was not limited to isolated incidents but was systematically perpetuated as a result of the state's male-dominated and gerontocratic mentality. Viyan emphasized that women must intensify their struggle against these policies on the basis of self-defense and self-organization.







 







Peyman Viyan said that the struggle against violence against women was not limited to 25 November: “The struggle waged through women is a struggle for society as a whole. Women's struggle against male violence extends to every day of the year because violence against women is also perpetrated in different forms every day.”




‘The regime's ideology seeks to destroy society through women’




Viyan said that women in Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat) and Iran were subjected to multiple forms of violence and drew attention to the ideological objectives behind this violence. She described Iran's system of governance as male-dominated and gerontocratic, saying: “The mentality underlying the Iranian system, based on male dominance and the rule of older men, is subjecting the whole of society to a spiral of annihilation. Women bear the brunt of this violence. The policies of the Islamic Republic seek to destroy society through women.”




The Jin, Jiyan, Azadî revolution dealt the greatest blow to this sexist and religious fundamentalist ideology




Viyan said that the Jin, Jiyan, Azadî (Woman, Life, Freedom) revolution, which developed under women's leadership, dealt a severe blow to the sexist and religious fundamentalist ideology of the Iranian regime: “The Jin, Jiyan, Azadî revolution dealt the greatest blow to this sexist and religious fundamentalist ideology. It dealt a major blow to the aging mentality that maintains its grip on power by every possible means and to the ideology of the Iranian regime. This struggle and quest continue within society today.”




Peyman Viyan said that the regime was attempting to hollow out the concept of Jin, Jiyan, Azadî and the revolution itself, adding that attacks against women were not limited to physical violence but also continued on psychological and intellectual levels. Viyan said: “This is systematic and premeditated violence against women. The mentality that established the system legitimizes this violence through Sharia and laws. It maintains its power through the domination it imposes on women.”




‘The male-dominated system grants men the right to kill women’




Viyan said that femicides and suicides in Iran were particularly prevalent in Kurdistan, where the strength of the women's struggle and the development of social consciousness enabled such incidents to become public more quickly. She said that numerous femicides in other parts of Iran went unreported: “Every day across Iran, women are murdered without anyone knowing or hearing about it. This is why I say that it is a systematic order. The system itself is governed through violence.”




Peyman Viyan emphasized that violence against women was rooted in a mentality that regarded women as men's property. She said that fathers, older brothers and husbands believed they had ownership rights over women and that the regime's policies legitimized this mentality.




Viyan said that policies of impunity for femicide in Iran also reinforced this mentality: “Even someone imprisoned in Iran for killing a woman is effectively rewarded and released after a short period. This is because men are granted ownership rights; fathers, older brothers and husbands regard women as their property. The policies of the Iranian regime legitimize this notion of ownership and grant the male-dominated mentality the right to kill women every day.”




Viyan said that eliminating women's leadership in society would also lead to the collapse of society itself: “A society in which women are neither leaders nor bearers of wisdom is a society that has collapsed, become hollow and lost its essence. It becomes a society stripped of its moral and political substance. However, women are resisting and fighting against this situation today.”




‘Women no longer define themselves as victims’




Peyman Viyan said that one of the reasons for the intensification of violence against women was their refusal to accept these policies and their struggle against the male-dominated mentality. She added that women could no longer be defined solely as victims of violence.




Viyan said: “Women no longer see themselves merely as victims. The reason women are subjected to such intense violence today is that they no longer accept this violence or these policies. They stand against the male-dominated mentality. This is truly a fatal blow to the system because women no longer define themselves as victims; they are taking the lead and fighting.”




Call for a collective response to the death of Sogend Seyadî




Viyan cited the death of high school student Sogend Seyadî in Kermanshah (Kirmaşan), saying that the young woman had thrown herself from an upper floor of her school building because of the violence inflicted on her by her father. Viyan said that Sogend's death was not merely the result of an individual act of violence but of a male-dominated mentality that had permeated different areas of society.




Viyan said: “What actually drove Sogend to throw herself from the school building was her father's violent mentality and the system itself.”




Peyman Viyan emphasized the importance of the response shown by young people and society following Sogend Seyadî's death and said that this response must be sustained. She said that violence against women targeted not only the individual subjected to violence but society as a whole: “The violence directed against Sogend today will tomorrow target all the students in that school, all young people in society and all women. Young people must therefore maintain their determined response and readiness to act.”




Viyan said that a collective response could curb the male-dominated mentality: “If people repeatedly respond in this way and stand against violence, men will no longer be able to pursue these policies, and limits will be placed on their dominance.”




‘Self-defense is not merely about protecting oneself with weapons’




Viyan emphasized that women needed a system of self-defense and organization, saying that self-defense should not be understood solely in terms of physical protection or armed struggle. Peyman Viyan said that self-defense encompassed a broad field of struggle, ranging from strengthening intellectual resolve to building social solidarity: “When we speak of self-defense, we do not simply mean taking up a weapon to protect oneself; it also means strengthening one's intellectual resolve. It means thousands of young people coming together to take a stand against a man who attacks a woman and against the mentality he represents. Young people taking to the streets in response to Sogend's death is also a form of self-defense.”




Viyan said that young people must develop an organized and determined collective stance against violence targeting women and drew attention to the importance of perpetrators facing social sanctions: “If a father kills his own daughter, the collective response must be so strong that he can no longer remain on that street or in that city and must face various forms of social sanctions. Young people must organize and assert their own will.”




Peyman Viyan said that young women must develop the consciousness and determination necessary to defend themselves against male domination within the family and against men who exercise power in society. She added that organization would expand the social struggle.




Viyan said: “Organizing means coming together: two people, ten people, twenty people, a hundred people... The more people come together, the stronger the collective stance becomes and the greater the struggle against this mentality.” She emphasized that every attack against young women must be regarded as an attack on the very existence of society.




‘Women's struggle must become global, and self-defense and organization must be strengthened’




Viyan said that the women's struggle was not limited to Iran and Kurdistan but must be waged on a global scale. She said that the male-dominated system and statist mentality targeted women through wars and conflicts in different parts of the world.




Peyman Viyan said: “A male-dominated system and a statist mentality prevail in the world today. Women are the primary victims of all the wars and conflicts being waged. The women's struggle against male violence must therefore become more radical in the current period, not only in Iran but globally.”




Viyan said that women must develop an awareness of self-defense that would enable them to protect themselves on the streets, at universities, in schools, in sports and in all areas of life. She concluded: “What we consider most important in this process is a system of self-defense and self-organization. Young people must know how to organize more effectively and use these methods to intensify the struggle in the coming period.”

title: Detention orders issued for 12 people in Halk TV Investigation
content:
A new wave of detentions targeting Halk TV has been launched as part of an investigation conducted by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office. Detention orders have been issued for 12 people, including Halk TV Programme Coordinator Kürşad Oğuz and presenters Ece Üner and Deniz Bayramoğlu.




Those facing detention orders include Halk TV employees, as well as executives and owners of various companies and two employees of Izmir Metropolitan Municipality.




The individuals named in the detention orders are:




-Halk TV presenters Özge Ece Bayramoğlu and Özgür Deniz Bayramoğlu




-Bustech executives Haydar Rüzgar and Ahmet Keçiyokuşu




-Ulaş Eroğlu, Head of the Machinery Supply, Maintenance and Repair Department at Izmir Metropolitan Municipality




-Aşkın Tahan, a municipal employee




-Ali Kemal Korgan, owner of Korganlar




-Hamza Okuyucu, owner of HMF Taşımacılık




-Halit Akın, Bustech Purchasing Manager




-Emre Kaya, owner of Esbakım




-Kürşad Oğuz, Halk TV News Coordinator




-Recep Ersü, an official at Repar




It was reported that Recep Ersü, who is among those named on the list, is already in pre-trial detention.

title: The prison regime's impasse in the Peace and Democratic Society Process
content:
Understanding the actual course of political crises and efforts to find a solution in Turkey requires more than examining speeches delivered in parliament or statements made behind the scenes of diplomatic negotiations. One of the most concrete indicators of this process is the treatment of political prisoners.




The Peace and Democratic Society Process, which began with the call made by Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) leader Devlet Bahçeli on 22 October 2024 and entered a new stage with Abdullah Öcalan's call on 27 February 2025, has entered a new phase with the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), steps towards disarmament and the publication of the framework law. However, the Turkish state's failure to introduce concrete measures despite the steps taken throughout the process reveals a significant contradiction. One of the areas where this contradiction is most apparent is the situation of political prisoners. Sentence enforcement practices, isolation and disciplinary punishments imposed on prisoners largely remain unchanged, while repression has intensified in some areas.




Explaining this situation in terms of "bureaucratic resistance" or "state habits" means overlooking the essence of the issue. Prison policies in Turkey have never been merely a technical matter administered by judicial or penal institutions. On the contrary, these policies have been one of the direct means through which the state exercises its power relations with the Kurdish Movement, maintains its bargaining capacity and implements its strategy of disciplining social opposition.




The fact that prison conditions remain unchanged and practices targeting political prisoners continue as the process advances is neither a matter of negligence nor delay. It is precisely a means of preserving political asymmetry on the ground.




Sentence enforcement under administrative tutelage




One of the primary demands of the Kurdish Movement and democratic circles since the beginning of the process has been the establishment of legal guarantees and the elimination of inequalities in sentence enforcement law. However, the reality on the ground points not only to the need for legal reform but also to a regime of administrative arbitrariness in which even the implementation of existing laws is suspended.




The release of hundreds of political prisoners who have completed their legally prescribed sentences is now being postponed not through court rulings but through assessments conducted by Administration and Observation Boards, composed of prison directors, prosecutors, psychologists and administrative personnel.




The crucial point here is the function of these boards. They operate as instruments for producing political outcomes without assuming political responsibility. The government and state institutions adopt the flexible and inclusive language required by the Peace and Democratic Society Process outside prisons, while prisoners' releases are postponed for periods of three or six months on vague grounds such as "lack of good conduct," "failure to demonstrate remorse" and "institutional security." These practices maintain psychological pressure on prisoners while also restricting the political movement's room for maneuver outside prisons.




The sentence enforcement regime is thus being detached from the legal principle of predictability and transformed into a "mechanism of bargaining and discipline" that can be activated or suspended according to political circumstances. The government's attempt to transfer responsibility to the bureaucracy by saying, "We are conducting the process; releases are at the discretion of the judiciary and the boards," points to a deliberate division of responsibilities.




Fragmenting collective memory through S- and Y-type prisons




Prisons have never been merely places of confinement in the political history of the Kurdish Freedom Movement. They have been spaces of resistance where collective consciousness, shared memory and political agency were constructed, from the military coup of 12 September 1980 to the 1990s, and from hunger strikes to defense statements. The model of S-type, Y-type and high-security closed prisons that the state has rapidly expanded in recent years must be understood as a spatial response to this historical memory.




This new generation of prisons, consisting of single-person or small-capacity cells, where even the view of the sky in exercise yards is restricted by wire mesh and opportunities for communal activities and social interaction have largely been eliminated, is designed not only to isolate prisoners from the outside world but also to sever their ties with their comrades and their collective will. The fact that this prison model has not been phased out during discussions on the Peace and Democratic Society Process, but has instead been expanded through new prisoner transfers, reveals a striking contradiction. The construction of the process is being discussed outside prisons, while even the most fundamental right of political prisoners to collective life is regarded as a security threat inside.




It is no coincidence that the systematic practices of absolute incommunicado detention and isolation imposed on Abdullah Öcalan in Imralı for years have evolved into a form of prison administration extending to all prisons in various forms. Arbitrary restrictions on Kurdish-language publications, letters destroyed or withheld for months on the grounds that they are deemed "objectionable," and visiting and telephone rights suspended through disciplinary punishments are all components of a comprehensive isolation strategy aimed at severing prisoners' ties with social transformation outside prisons.




Seriously ill prisoners and biological attrition




One of the areas where the unchanged prison policies have undoubtedly had the most severe consequences is the situation of seriously ill prisoners. The government approaches the process outside prisons in terms of "timelines, commissions, stages and legal regulations," while time becomes a matter of life and death for prisoners suffering from serious health conditions such as advanced-stage cancer, heart and respiratory failure and paralysis, or those unable to manage their daily lives independently.




The reports issued by the Forensic Medicine Institute, shaped by security-oriented considerations rather than medical assessments, and the rejection of requests for the suspension of sentences on the grounds that prisoners pose a "threat to public safety" demonstrate that what is at work here is not the law but a deliberate policy of punishment extended over time. Keeping a bedridden person in a single-person cell or issuing a release decision days after their funeral inflicts irreparable wounds on society's conscience.




15 prisoners died, 458 releases were blocked




Data from human rights organizations, legal associations and organizations representing prisoners' relatives, including the Human Rights Association (IHD), the Free Lawyers Association (ÖHD) and the Federation of Legal Solidarity Associations of Prisoners’ Families (TUHAD-FED), show that reports of rights violations, postponed releases and deaths in prisons have become increasingly frequent since Abdullah Öcalan's call on 27 February 2025:




Mehmet Sait Yıldırım: 

Yıldırım, who has not been released despite completing 30 consecutive years in prison, suffers from heart disease, hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Administration and Observation Board postponed his release for a second time on 25 November 2025 and subsequently for a third time on the grounds of the "possibility of establishing contact with the organization." Yıldırım's appeal was rejected by the Sentence Enforcement Judgeship on 3 September 2026, bringing the total period of his postponed release to 21 months.




Mehmet Edip Taşar: 

The 70-year-old seriously ill prisoner remained in prison despite his deteriorating health and his weight dropping to approximately 40 kilograms. Taşar, whose previous applications for release had also been unsuccessful, died on 24 March 2026. The Forensic Medicine Institute had previously issued a report stating that he was "fit to remain in prison."




Abdullah Tırpan: 

Tırpan, a sick prisoner who had been incarcerated for 31 years, had his release postponed for one year on 27 July 2026, just 14 days before his scheduled release. The 73-year-old prisoner, whose left leg was amputated below the knee due to advanced gangrene and who was intubated in intensive care, died on 26 October 2026.




Reports published by the ÖHD, IHD and Amed (Diyarbakır) Bar Association covering the 2025-2026 period indicate that at least 15 sick prisoners died in prisons between the beginning of the process and November 2026. The conditional release and release rights of a total of 458 prisoners were postponed through decisions by Administration and Observation Boards during the same period. The release of at least 116 of these prisoners was postponed in the first ten months of 2026.




The threshold of trust, political legitimacy and fragility




The impact of this rigidity behind prison walls on the process goes beyond humanitarian concerns and becomes a structural factor directly determining political balances and the sustainability of the process. The historical memory of the 2009-2015 experience remains fresh. A lasting solution, from the perspective of the Kurdish Movement, depends on reciprocal steps taken on the basis of legal guarantees. The Kurdish side has taken historic decisions and demonstrated its determination to disarm and strengthen the foundations of democratic politics. At such a critical juncture, the state's failure to normalize conditions even in prisons under its own administrative authority further exposes the absence of confidence-building measures.




The freedom of political prisoners constitutes the foundation of democratic politics' legitimacy. The continued imprisonment of long-standing political figures, mayors, journalists and cadres of the freedom struggle disrupts the stages of building the process outside prisons. Is the state keeping prison doors closed to confine politics outside prisons to a constant agenda of "expectations of release" and "rights advocacy," both emotionally and organizationally, thereby exhausting its constructive and transformative energy?




Prisons represent a living memory that reaches the doorstep of every family in Kurdish society. People's faith in the process is directly measured by improvements in the conditions of their imprisoned relatives. The discourse of peace struggles to gain social resonance in an atmosphere where arbitrary extensions of imprisonment, forced prison transfers and isolation practices continue.

title: Guerrillas celebrate the 48th anniversary of the founding of the PKK
content:
On the occasion of the 48th anniversary of the founding of the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK), members of the People’s Defense Forces (HPG) and Free Women’s Troops (YJA Star) held a commemorative and cultural event in the Qandil region. In addition to political speeches, the program featured musical and theatrical performances.




The event opened with a speech by HPG commander Seyîdxan Dersim, who extended his greetings on November 27 to PKK founder Abdullah Öcalan, the Kurdish people and the guerrilla forces, and commemorated PKK cadre Haki Karer and those fell in the freedom struggle in Kurdistan.




Seyîdxan Dersim addressed the historical significance of the founding date. He said that November 27 represented not merely the founding of a party but marked a historic transformation in the development of the Kurdish people’s political consciousness and resistance. In this context, he also commemorated figures from the PKK’s history, including Kemal Pir, Mahsum “Egîd” Korkmaz and Zeynep Kınacı (Zîlan).










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/79ccb789_20261127104611_2026-11-27-qendil-ozgurluk-gerillari-27-kasimi-buyuk-bir-cosku-ve-heyecanla-kutladi-1.mp4










Transition to a new historical phase




Seyîdxan Dersim stated that a new stage of social reconstruction and reorganization had now begun with the conclusion of the phase of national resistance

. 

He identified securing Abdullah Öcalan’s physical freedom as a central task.




Following the speech, guerrillas presented a cultural program featuring songs, theatrical performances and traditional circle dances. The music group Koma Awazê Çiya also performed at the event.




On the sidelines of the event, members of the HPG and YJA Star spoke about the significance of the PKK’s historical legacy and the prospects for the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process. They attributed the emergence of the process to Öcalan’s efforts, the sacrifices of the Kurdish movement and the PKK’s history of resistance.




The event concluded with songs, Govend dances and chants.

title: KCK: We will do our part to protect the gains of Southern Kurdistan
content:
On November 24, the government in Baghdad announced a series of decisions aimed at strengthening federal control over border crossings and the energy sector. These include closing officially unrecognized border crossings, transferring control of oil fields in territories disputed between Baghdad and Erbil to the federal Oil Ministry, and tightening oversight of oil transportation and exports.




The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) subsequently warned in a joint statement against interference with the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, describing any violation of those rights as a red line.




The Co-Presidency of the KCK (Kurdistan Communities Union) Executive Council released a statement regarding the latest developments in Southern Kurdistan (Northern Iraq), describing the Baghdad government’s decision as a restriction of fundamental aspects of life and a direct interference with the functioning of the Kurdish federation.




The KCK statement on Saturday includes the following:




“The Iraqi Prime Minister announced that a decision had been made to transfer the oil fields and customs crossings in Southern Kurdistan to the central government. He demanded that the oil fields and customs crossings in Southern Kurdistan be handed over to the central government. This means transferring all the financial resources of the Southern Kurdistan federation to the central government. When a society and political system are deprived of financial resources, they can be rendered completely dependent. Particularly today, financial resources play an important role in establishing and sustaining economic, social, cultural and political systems. In this respect, the Baghdad government’s decision amounts to restricting fundamental aspects of life and directly interfering with the functioning of the Southern Kurdistan federation.




'Southern Kurdistan struggled for decades to secure its fundamental national rights'




The fundamental reason for the problems arising today among different ethnic, religious and national communities is the persistence of the centralized model of governance of the 19th and 20th centuries. This inevitably creates problems in political and social life. Following the establishment of Iraq, the central government’s approach of exercising power and domination led to serious conflicts with the Kurds, who rejected these policies and resisted them. However, when the decision was made to keep Southern Kurdistan within Iraq following the 1924 report of the Mosul Commission established by the League of Nations, the same commission also adopted a decision recognizing the Kurds’ right to self-government and education in their mother tongue. Yet because the Iraqi government failed to implement this decision of the Mosul Commission, Southern Kurdistan struggled for decades to secure its fundamental national rights. In 2003, the hegemonic centralist regime was overthrown, and a new constitution was drafted. Under this constitution, a more democratic political system replaced the former centralized model of government, and the Southern Kurdistan federation was recognized as a constitutional entity.




‘The Iraqi government should abandon this misguided course’




The Iraqi government’s return to a centralist approach and its efforts to restrict the rights of the Southern Kurdistan federation amount to the reimposition of the old centralist model. Yet this approach led to serious conflicts between Iraq and the Kurds for decades. In this respect, the Iraqi government is taking a misguided step. This decision will also create serious problems for Iraq’s stability and democratic unity. It would be in the best interests of both Iraq as a whole and the Kurds for the Iraqi government to abandon this misguided course and act in a manner that strengthens Iraq’s democratic unity.




'What Southern Kurdistan needs is a democratic national unity government'




Democratic Kurdish unity is extremely important to prevent the Kurds from facing such situations. The Kurds, too, must abandon centralist approaches in politics and adopt democratic unity as their guiding principle. What Southern Kurdistan needs at present is a democratic national unity government that includes all political parties. A government representing all Kurdish political parties and social groups, rather than just one or two parties, would strengthen the Kurds and the Southern Kurdistan federation. The parties’ desire to dominate does not strengthen either the Kurds or the federation. Indeed, the failure to establish democratic Kurdish unity is the reason for the weakness that has persisted until now.




The Kurdish federation in Southern Kurdistan is an achievement secured through the struggle of the people of Southern Kurdistan and the entire Kurdish people. Our struggle over the past 54 years has also played a major role in securing these gains. In this respect, the entire Kurdish people and Kurdish political forces will defend the gains achieved in Southern Kurdistan. Our Freedom Movement will continue to do its part to protect these gains, just as it has done in the past.




‘The importance of Öcalan’s proposal and call is now better understood’




Recognizing the importance of democratic Kurdish unity at a time when new political balances are emerging in the Middle East, Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] has been proposing for the past two years the establishment of a democratic unity government in Southern Kurdistan with the participation of all Kurdish parties. He has also conveyed these calls directly to the KDP and PUK. Political forces in Southern Kurdistan must seek solutions to their problems through democratic unity. What will strengthen the Kurds is the democratic unity government proposed by Leader Apo. We have been making calls and assessments on this issue for months. The importance of Leader Apo’s proposal and call is now better understood than ever.




'Kurds should maintain democratic unity across all parts of Kurdistan'




Political approaches aimed at keeping the Kurds under domination in all four parts of Kurdistan and refusing to recognize their democratic national will still persist. In this respect, it is important for the Kurds to maintain democratic unity across all parts of Kurdistan. It is also important to mobilize all forces advocating democracy and freedom in the Middle East and around the world to support the Kurds’ struggle for freedom and democracy.




We call on Iraq to refrain from taking centralist and hegemonic steps and urge the Kurds to act in unity to protect their gains during such processes.”

title: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards reportedly preparing for an attack on Kurdish parties
content:
According to a statement by the Kurdistan Human Rights Organization, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is preparing to attack Kurdish parties from Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat).




The IRGC reportedly deployed large numbers of troops, along with drones and heavy weapons, to the cities of Sardasht, Marivan, Kamyaran, Ravansar and Javanrud in Rojhilat over the past week.




The statement noted a visible increase in the military activity of IRGC forces in these cities.




The main mission of these forces is reportedly to monitor the positions and forces of Kurdish opposition parties in the highlands of Sardasht, Marivan and Shaho and to attack these locations with artillery fire and drones.




The organization also reported an increase in military deployments following the recent deaths of numerous members of the Basij and IRGC forces.

title: 15 families of the disappeared contact IHD after the discovery of human remains in Silvan
content:
Following the discovery of numerous human remains in a cave in the Silvan district of Amed (Diyarbakır) province, 15 families of victims of enforced disappearance in the 1990s have so far contacted the Human Rights Association (IHD) in Amed. The relatives hope that DNA comparisons will make it possible to identify the deceased and finally provide them with certainty about the fate of their family members. The IHD expects more families to come forward.




During an investigation ordered by the public prosecutor’s office, nine intact skulls, 36 skull fragments and hundreds of other bone fragments were recovered on Tuesday from the three-level cave in the Qesra Fila area. The human remains were transferred to the state-run Forensic Medicine Institute (ATK) in Istanbul for forensic examination. The identities of the deceased, the age of the bones and the circumstances of their deaths remain unknown.




Given the numerous cases of enforced disappearance, unsolved murders and serious human rights violations in Silvan, particularly during the 1990s, the Human Rights Association (IHD), the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD) and the Amed Bar Association consider the discovery particularly significant for confronting the past. The organizations are calling for a comprehensive investigation that also examines how the cave was used in the past and any possible links to human rights violations committed by the state.




According to the IHD’s findings, there are at least 303 mass graves in Kurdistan that have yet to be opened. The recent discovery in Silvan is not included in this figure.

title: Arab guerrilla fighter: Leader Öcalan’s philosophy has given women great courage
content:
On the occasion of November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, millions of women took to the streets to condemn femicides and violence against women.




Speaking to ANF on the occasion, Nergêz Şawîş, an Arab member of the YJA Star guerrillas, said they regarded November 25 as a day of resistance:










https://video.anf-news2.com/live/firat/dd1b8384_20261125140215_2026-11-26-behdinan-nergez-sawis-gerilaya-yja-stare-ji-sideta-li-ser-jine-re-na-1.mp4










“Women are stronger than men because of their creative nature, and they have always proven themselves through their will and existence. The male-dominated mentality, however, oppresses women. This is why it attacks women’s legitimate rights every day. We are fighting against this denial of women’s rights. Our primary goal is to eliminate this dominant mentality. Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] also states that society cannot be liberated unless women are liberated.




Society as it exists today can organize itself thanks to the existence of women. This dominant mentality is particularly widespread in Arab society. Therefore, I call on our Arab community to join hands and stand in solidarity. If you want to understand society, you must first understand women and recognize the importance of their role within it. We do not want this situation to continue. We will carry on our struggle until the very end to put an end to it. Why are women so strong within the movement today? Because Leader Apo introduced the concept of the free woman to everyone and demonstrated how influential women’s power is in life. Leader Apo showed what kind of stance women should adopt in everything, from ideological work to military activities. Women’s resistance has also been highly effective in the mountains. Leader Apo’s philosophy has given women great courage and has always placed them at the forefront because he knows that only women can bring about success. Society’s liberation will be achieved through women.




Examples of this include Comrade Sara (Sakine Cansız), martyr Zilan, martyr Bêrîtan and thousands of heroic women who have been inspired by Leader Apo’s ideas. All of his efforts are aimed at empowering women, ensuring their participation in every sphere, enabling them to believe in themselves and act through their own strength. As an Arab woman, I was inspired by the comradeship within the movement. I was also deeply impressed by women’s participation in all areas of work.”




Şawîş also addressed Arab women. She said that the role of women in the movement’s activities and the solidarity she had witnessed had influenced her decision to join the movement.

title: Trump backs move to bring border crossings in KRI under Baghdad’s control
content:
US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that his administration supported Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s initiative to bring border crossings and certain oil fields in the Kurdistan Region under Baghdad’s control.




In a statement posted on his Truth Social account, Trump said: “We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state.”




Trump added that the US supported al-Zaidi’s “efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions.”




On Tuesday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi decided to place border crossings and certain oil fields in the Kurdistan Region under federal government control, citing the need to combat oil smuggling. On Wednesday, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court approved the deployment of federal forces along the borders of the Kurdistan Region.




The court stated that the federal government has the authority to secure all of Iraq’s borders with neighboring countries, control border crossings and deploy federal armed forces. The ruling also applies to territories administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government.




The court also ruled that the Iraqi Oil Ministry has the constitutional and legal authority to oversee activities and contracts related to the production, extraction, marketing and export of oil and natural gas.




The Kurdistan Regional Government reacted to the federal government’s decision, describing it as “a violation of the Constitution and an attack on the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region.”




The regional government opposed the measure, stating that the decision was a dangerous indication of a lack of confidence in the federal system.




The Iraqi government has yet to provide a detailed explanation of when and how the transfer of border crossings and oil fields to federal control will be implemented.

author: Rizomatica
title: Comunicado de Nelson Alonso Llempi, PPM caso Grollmus en huelga de hambre
content:
«Marri marri kom pu che, pu longko, pu machi, pu peñi, pu lamuen:




Inche Nelson Alonso Llempi, del lof Huape tuwun, padre e hijo de familia, junto a otros 10 peñi, hemos tomado la difícil decisión de iniciar una HUELGA DE HAMBRE EL DÍA 23 DE NOVIEMBRE, como medida de protesta frente a la condena desproporcionada que nos ha impuesto el Tribunal de Cañete, que en conjunto supera los 1.055 años de prisión.




Nos enfrentamos a un juicio que consideramos profundamente injusto, donde la Fiscalía sustentó sus acusaciones únicamente en cuatro supuestos testigos sin nombre ni rostro, sin una corroboración científica o técnica que respaldara sus declaraciones.




Ni nosotros ni nuestras defensas hemos tenido certeza sobre la identidad y existencia de estos supuestos testigos. 




¿Cómo se puede condenar a personas a semejantes cantidades de años de prisión sin que exista la posibilidad de conocer y cuestionar debidamente a quienes nos acusan?




Para nosotros, este proceso representa una persecución de carácter político, que busca castigarnos y silenciar nuestra lucha.




Hoy, frente a esta injusticia, hemos decidido llevar adelante esta huelga de hambre, entendiendo que es uno de los pocos medios de protesta que tenemos a nuestro alcance desde la prisión.




NUESTRA EXIGENCIA ES CLARA:




– La nulidad de este juicio que consideramos injusto.- El respeto a nuestro derecho a un debido proceso.







Justicia frente a las graves irregularidades que denunciamos.







– Nuestra libertad y el respeto a nuestra dignidad.No estamos tomando esta decisión por voluntad de sufrir. Lo hacemos porque sentimos que se han cerrado los caminos para ser escuchados y porque no estamos dispuestos a aceptar en silencio una condena que consideramos injusta.




Hago un llamado a la solidaridad frente a este proceso de persecución injusto e ilegal que tiene como único fin detener la justa lucha de nuestro pueblo mapuche. Que nuestra voz salga de estos muros. Que nuestra lucha llegue a cada territorio. Que la injusticia no quede en el silencio.




No pedimos privilegios, exigimos justicia. 




No buscamos compasión, exigimos que se respeten nuestros derechos y nuestra dignidad.




¡POR LA NULIDAD DEL JUICIO!¡POR LA JUSTICIA Y LA DIGNIDAD DEL PUEBLO MAPUCHE!




¡Marichiwew!




Nelson Alonso Lliempi, Cárcel de Concepción. Noviembre 27 de 2026.»







*ENVIADO A LA RADIO




Esta información se publicó en 

Radio Kurruf

.

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: A place to call home, but only for six months: Yellowknife Housing First secures temporary housing
content:
Marlena Francis and her boyfriend, Preston Beaulieu, spent nights in Yellowknife shelters, never knowing if they would be turned away.




Becoming Housing First residents brought some stability, but it did not end the uncertainty. A fire forced them out of their first apartment at Sunridge. After two weeks in a hotel, they moved into a unit in Norseman, where they stayed for a little more than a year before facing another displacement.




“They [YKWS] didn’t really have a place for us to go for a while and I was losing a lot of sleep,” Francis said. “I really thought that we were going to be back on the streets.”




This summer, six downtown apartment buildings were sold by property management giant Northview Residential REIT to Montreal-based Balto Capital Inc.

 

As part of the sale, Northview moved to evict tenants in all 23 units rented by Housing First clients by Oct. 31.




At the eleventh hour, the society reached an agreement with the new property owners, allowing Housing First residents to live together in one building at Dorset Apartments.




Francis and Beaulieu are among 20 clients now receiving services in one centralized location.




Francis said she has already started settling into the space.




“I actually got my creativity back, and I’m actually enjoying drawing,” Francis said. “I love cooking and I have a working oven again.”




But the new arrangement is guaranteed for only six months. The lease with Balto Capital ends April 30, 2027, leaving the society with another deadline to find somewhere for residents to live.




The limits of scattered housing




Becky Broderick Basil, executive director of Yellowknife Women’s Society (YKWS), says the previous model made it difficult to provide the consistent support the program was designed to offer.




For more than a decade, YKWS has delivered its Housing First program by renting individual units scattered across the city. The society was responsible for supporting residents but had limited control over the conditions in the buildings where they lived.




Residents described apartments with poor upkeep, longstanding repair requests, and disruptive conditions.




Beaulieu, who lived with Francis at Norseman, recalled a bathtub that was plugged and leaking for about two weeks.




“We couldn’t use the tub and it was leaking and plugged,” he said. “We had to sit there and scoop water and make sure it didn’t overflow, for like forever.”




Over the years, 

APTN News

 has

 

reported on tenant complaints about maintenance and safety in Northview buildings

, while reporting by

 

Cabin Radio has documented legal rulings

 involving basic upkeep and repairs.




Myles Nelson, another Housing First resident, described the noise and activity outside his former apartment at Fort Gary. He said he would watch from his balcony and see what he described as unsavoury foot traffic and drug deals.




“At Fort Gary, the doors would smash and crash just outside my apartment,” Nelson said. “You didn’t even pay attention anymore because it was just natural, but now we’re here [Dorset], you don’t hear anything.”







Myles Nelson, another Housing First resident, described the noise and activity outside his former apartment at Fort Gary. Photo: APTN News/Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs







When being housed doesn’t mean being treated like a tenant




For Housing First residents, the challenges of scattered-site housing went beyond maintenance. Broderick says residents also faced discrimination and scrutiny from people responsible for managing the buildings where they lived.




She says the stigma attached to homelessness and the Housing First label could follow residents into their homes, affecting how landlords, security personnel and contractors treated them.




“When you’re used to scattered market rent and you’re discriminated against and you face security and landlords and even contractors and mechanical people coming in and out of your unit like you’re not even there or being treated badly by security just trying to go home,” Broderick said.




Broderick says the society saw how that scrutiny played out through regular reports from private security contractors.







In 2022, Northview hired Equity Security to address complaints about unsafe conditions in and around its properties. Broderick says YKWS began receiving weekly reports from the company, known as “trouble tenant” reports.




Over time, the paperwork added up to more than 100 reports relating specifically to Housing First tenants, according to Broderick. The reports documented residents’ activities in writing and through photographs.







A ‘trouble tenant’ report prepared by the security company hired by Northview REIT for the building now owned by Balto Capital Inc. and leased to Housing First. Photo: APTN News/Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs







Some reports described visitors believed to be associated with a Housing First tenant pacing in a hallway or causing a disturbance. Others documented seemingly routine activity, such as a tenant leaving their apartment four times in an hour.




The reports offer a glimpse into how closely some residents’ daily activities were monitored. For people already facing the stigma of homelessness, that kind of scrutiny could reinforce the feeling that they were being treated as a problem rather than as tenants.




Broderick says the consequences of eviction notices can also be lost on the people issuing them.




“You think these evictions are just like pieces of paper handed out, but people forget about the people,” Broderick said. “That person, because of the evictions, has lost all hope.”




The effects can stay with residents even after they move. Having experienced repeated displacement, some are wary of trusting that their new housing will last.




Broderick says the overwhelming majority of Housing First clients are Indigenous and that the move into a shared building is also an adjustment for people who have spent years in precarious housing.




“When you have people who have been homeless and in such precarious situations for so long, you become so sensitive to those changes as a trauma response,” she said. “The lights are different, the doors sound different, it’s all changed.”







Inside the Balto Capital building leased to Housing First. Photo: APTN News/Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs







A different experience under one roof




The centralized model is intended to change residents’ relationship with the people supporting them.




Instead of having to reach workers across the city, residents can find someone in the building who knows them and understands their circumstances. The society has support staff on site 24 hours a day, rather than relying on the security personnel residents encountered in their previous buildings.




Broderick says the distinction is important. The organization still has boundaries and expectations, but its starting point is support.




“That’s what doesn’t happen here,” she said. “We’re staffed 24 hours a day with Housing First staff who know you, who care about you and who support you.”




The society is also working to establish programming and routines in a shared space, something Broderick says was missing from the scattered-site model.




Housing can make room for other changes




When Cindy Nitsiza and Louis Chartrand faced eviction, they were already living in a unit at Dorset.




Chartrand was away attending a treatment program in Ontario, while Nitsiza had to spend three weeks in hospital. They returned to see the building transform.




“We used to see a lot of street people in the stairway here and garbage all over and very noisy,” Nitsiza said. “Right now it’s totally different.”




Chartrand says he is grateful for the support he has received.




“This housing really helped change our lives,” Chartrand said. “I’ve been sober for a while and I’ve never been able to do that before.”




Nitsiza is awaiting treatment early next year and is almost a month sober. But the uncertainty around the lease remains on her mind.




“Housing First are doing a good job and they’re taking care of us,” Nitsiza said. “But after six months, what are we gonna do?”




Broderick says she cannot guarantee what comes after the lease ends. For now, she wants residents to have access to support, shared activities and opportunities to build connections.




The cost of keeping everyone together




Not every unit at Dorset was turn-key ready. The building is more than 50 years old and much of the interior remains dated and visibly worn.




Broderick says some units initially had no heat and some toilets were not functioning. The society has had to address repairs and make sure units are habitable as it takes on responsibility for operating the building.




The Dorset arrangement costs the society about $66,000 a month, according to Broderick.




The six-month agreement covers a 30-unit building, 26 one-bedroom and four two-bedroom.




YKWS is responsible for rent, utilities and the costs of operating the property. The society projects it will run an operational deficit of hundreds of thousands of dollars by the end of the agreement.




Broderick says the society does not intend to cut programming to cover the shortfall.




“because this is part of the basic human rights that people deserve, we’re not going to cut any of the programming,” she said.




The financial pressure comes as the society takes on a more centralized role in managing the building and supporting residents. Broderick says YKWS has the experience to operate the program but does not have the capital or resources to develop permanent housing infrastructure on its own.




Another move may be ahead




The agreement with Balto Capital gives the society time to demonstrate how a centralized Housing First model can work. But it does not give residents a permanent home.




Broderick says the society is exploring longer-term options, including finding a building owner willing to lease or sell a property.




Another possibility is a temporary drill camp on a downtown lot, using modular, skid-mounted or trailer-based units to provide housing for about two years. Broderick says the proposal would require municipal approvals and work to meet building and energy standards.




For residents, the uncertainty is familiar.




“I’ve started over so many times in my life that it’s just unbelievable,” Nelson said. “But you start right from the bottom and build yourself up again.”




Broderick says the agreement gives the society time to show what a centralized model can offer, but it is not a permanent solution.




“It buys us some time to show Yellowknife the goal, but also it’s not a solution,” Broderick said.




The post 

A place to call home, but only for six months: Yellowknife Housing First secures temporary housing

 appeared first on 

APTN News

author: Darío Aranda
title: El embrujo extractivista del progresismo uruguayo
content:
Por Raúl Zibechi




El gobierno de Yamandú Orsi parece empeñado en profundizar la carrera extractivista que inició Tabaré Vázquez con Botnia y continuó José Mujica con la minera Aratirí (que tuvo que detener por la amplia oposición que despertó). Ahora se están multiplicando los emprendimientos extractivos, entre los que destacan nueve barrios privados en la costa de Canelones, gobernado durante décadas por el Frente Amplio, que amenazan los últimos pulmones verdes de ese departamento. Puertos sobre ríos y sobre la costa atlántica, el lujoso barrio "+Colonia" frente a Buenos Aires y la desregulación ambiental, son algunos de los síntomas de este creciente contagio del progresismo de la cepa desarrollista que conocemos como extractivismo.




También se suman los centros de datos, uno en construcción por Google, y otro aprobado por el Presidente, que lo anunció el 14 de octubre en rueda de prensa como la “mayor inversión en la historia” del país, 5.700 millones de dólares para construir un campus de centros de datos por la española Solaria.




Abierto el grifo, se prevé un total de nueve centros de datos en los próximos años. Se trata de una iniciativa de la empresa española Solaria Energía y Medio Ambiente, que ya firmó con el gobierno y la empresa estatal de electricidad (UTE), para desarrollar el mega proyecto. Además del centro datos se construirá un hub tecnológico de hasta 500 Megavatios (MW) bajo el régimen de zona franca y un parque fotovoltaico para generar 350 MW de energía solar. Se instalarán en los departamentos de Canelones, San José y Florida y la promesa del gobierno es de crear 1.500 empleos permanentes.




Foto: Solaria




Solaria ya tiene dos plantas solares en Uruguay de 9,5 MW cada una. Ahora ocupará unas 700 hectáreas de UTE en régimen de comodato. El periodista y activista ambiental 

Enrique Amestoy

 asegura en el 

semanario Brecha

 que la empresa tiene un valor en bolsa de 2.080 millones de dólares, algo más de un tercio de la inversión anunciada, por lo que “grandes operadores internacionales de servicios en la nube financiarán el proyecto”, pero en realidad se trata de “inversores desconocidos”.







La planta consumirá una enorme cantidad de energía. Estima que llegará a 4.400 gigavatios al año, más que el consumo total de Montevideo donde habita la mitad de la población uruguaya

.







Amestoy recuerda que los centros de datos operan con unas 50 personas, por lo cual los datos sobre empleo suenan más a campaña publicitaria que a realidad Pero lo más significativoses que en este negocio “el país aporta energía, terrenos, conectividad y obras de red, mientras los servicios se venden al exterior”. Al operar en zona franca, está exenta de tributos.




Las críticas surgieron en el mismo momento en que se anunció el proyecto, y se multiplican, incluso entre aliados del progresismo gobernante. 

La Diaria

, periódico de claro cuño frenteamplista, recoge el análisis de la economista argentina Cecilia Rikap, quien advirtió que un espacio destinado a los centros de datos no equivale a un parque tecnológico y sostuvo que podría convertirse en “un cementerio en el cual Uruguay entierra sus posibilidades de desarrollo”.







“

U

n parque de centros de datos no es un parque tecnológico. La imagen de este

 

ú

ltimo son centros de I+D, empresas de base tecnológica. Nada de eso habita en un parque lleno de centros de datos

”

, sostuvo

 

Rikap

. Más aún,

 

consider

a que este tipo de emprendimientos profundiza la matriz extractiva ya imperante en el país.







“Abrirle los brazos a inversiones predatorias como esta es profundizar la dependencia, abrir más el espacio a las inversiones que cada vez más comunidades del mundo rechazan. Es cristalizar un rol subordinado en el capitalismo global en lugar de buscar un camino propio para el desarrollo”, dijo Rikap. Difunde la imagen del “cementerio” porque los centros de datos no sólo sobre utilizan el agua y la energía sino que generan contaminación auditiva, visual y del aire.




Foto: Google




El sociólogo Dani Pena se detiene en la resistencia popular a la empresa de celulosa UPM (ex Botnia), pero sobre todo a la impugnación del primer centro de datos en Uruguay. En 2022, Eleanor Applications SRL, subsidiaria de Google en el país, presentó un proyecto en el que se declaró confidencial el consumo de agua, energía y las aguas residuales. “Tuvimos que ganar un juicio en el Tribunal de lo Contencioso Administrativo contra el Ministerio de Ambiente para saber que Google pretendía evaporar 7,6 millones de litros de agua potable procedentes de la red pública por día para enfriar sus procesadores, que ocuparían unas 30 hectáreas”, recordó en el periódico Brecha en octubre pasado.




El primer centro de datos debió reformular su proyecto por uno de circuito cerrado, luego de las potentes 

movilizaciones por el agua en 2023, durante la seguía

. Aún así, consume tanta energía eléctrica como 200.000 hogares, medio millón de personas.




El 

Movimiento por un Uruguay Sustentable (Movus)

, que nació en 2011 en el marco de la oposición a la minera Aratirí, integrado por ambientalistas, productores rurales e investigadores, criticó el secretismo de las negociaciones . “Nadie sabe qué dice ese documento firmado a vista de todos. Está totalmente fuera de circulación”, afirmó Raúl Viñas. Dijo que el movimiento solicitó acceder a la documentación mediante el mecanismo de acceso a la información pública, ya que “un gobierno en serio que firmó algo que dice que es conveniente no debería tener ninguna razón para ocultarlo”.




La integrante de la organización 

Redes-Amigos de la Tierra

, Natalia Carrau, sostuvo en la 

revista Caras y Caretas

 que “este tipo de inversiones hay que vincularlas, como bien se dice, en el marco de una geopolítica concreta que también atraviesa los datos, con el uso que empresas trasnacionales de gran porte han hecho de esa información y el manejo de los algoritmos de las plataformas y las aplicaciones. No es el caso de esta empresa, sino de otras muy renombradas, el uso que han hecho en los países para modificar la toma de decisiones de los ciudadanos, de las ciudadanas, en contextos de elecciones u otros”.




Carrau recordó que este mismo año hubo denuncias sobre la injerencia de grandes firmas tecnológicas en procesos electorales y decisiones políticas soberanas. Más grave aún, es que “la digitalización, el mundo 5.0, el internet de las cosas, la inteligencia artificial, llegó sin que los Estados estuviesen preparados para recibir ese tipo de tecnología”.




El actual gobierno, el quinto del Frente Amplio, está lejos de ser progresista ya que presenta buena parte de los vicios del modelo neoliberal. La reciente instalación de un proyecto inmobiliariao en la franja costera de Canelones, de donde procede políticamente Orsi, que pretende fraccionar un extenso espacio verde contiguo a la playa para vender 101 lotes para viviendas lujo, sacó a la luz algo tan impopular en este país como la corrupción: “Entre los promotores y el equipo técnico del proyecto figuran ex jerarcas de la comuna (de Canelones) y aportantes en las últimas campañas electorales del Frente Amplio”, 

denunció el semanario Brecha

.







Foto: Presidencia Uruguay




La entrada 

El embrujo extractivista del progresismo uruguayo

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.
