author: Simon Childs
title: Bristol Bans Black Friday Ads From Council Spaces
content:
Bristol has become the first city in the UK to ban Black Friday and fast fashion from council-owned advertising spaces.




The ban is part of a wider crackdown on the advertising of environmentally damaging products and overconsumption.




Advertising for fossil fuel companies, SUVs, package holidays, airlines and cruise holidays is also banned. The ban applies to council-owned advertising spaces, such as at bus-stops. 




Privately owned advertising spaces are unaffected and businesses can still promote Black Friday events through their own social media and shop-fronts.




In 2021, Bristol became the first council outside of London to ban fast-food promotion and it also banned advertising pay-day-loans, gambling and alcohol.




Bristol deputy council leader Heather Mack 

told the Retail Gazette

, “We don’t want Bristol to be a billboard for polluters while we’re working hard to improve health, air quality and nature in the city.”




The move comes as part of a wider movement, as more than 20 councils have introduced limits on certain high-carbon advertising.

author: Ash Sarkar
title: Labour Wants to Have Its Oil and Burn It Too
content:
Andy Burnham’s biggest problem in office so far appears to have been a brainrot TikTokker posting content from Downing Street. But will mounting discontent over Rosebank have the PM yearning for the halcyon days of bomboclat wallahi?




The Guardian reports that 

nearly 100 Labour MPs

 – including at least four frontbenchers – have written to the prime minister expressing their opposition to drilling the biggest undeveloped oilfield in UK territorial waters. According to this morning’s Playbook, at least one frontbencher is considering resignation.




Unrelatedly, does Burnham stick by his 

2024 opinion

 that the whipping system should be scrapped?



















The Cortado

 





          Get your shot of political analysis from 

Ash Sarkar

 and 

Steven Methven

, every Monday and Friday morning.        






















Leave this field empty 













First name:













Email:













I agree to the 

Privacy Policy





















































      Sign up error: 

. Try again later.
    


























      Thanks for signing up.
    






















How come there are so many MPs opposed to developing new oilfields when we may have 

already breached a 2°C change

 in global heating? Beats me. Luckily the Times’ Aubrey Allegretti 

had sight of the rebels’ letter

 to Burnham. They warn of the risk of “permanently damaging” Labour’s climate credentials, the need to preserve “our ‘progressive’ electoral base”, and urged the prime minister to “show that Labour is on the side of the people experiencing climate change’s impacts, not those fuelling it”.




Maybe the naysayers are onto something. This summer, there were 

more than 5,000 excess heat-related deaths

 in England alone: twice the previous high of 2022. Climate change has, according to 

the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit

, compressed nearly 20 years of food price inflation into just over five years. And flood ‘n’ storm season is only just beginning. As I believe Bob Dylan once said, you don’t need a weatherman to determine the impact of climate change on the cost of living. Spoiler: it’s bad.




It’s not just fossil fuel magnates a la J.R. Ewing who want Rosebank opened up. Unite and GMB – Labour’s first and third largest trade union backers respectively – have piled the pressure on the government. Both unions cite the protection of existing jobs, energy security, and the lack of renewable energy jobs offering comparable pay as their reasons for backing the Rosebank development. 




Though there is grassroots organising against Rosebank in Unite, and dissensus within the trade union movement more broadly, general secretaries Sharon Graham and Gary Smith offer pro-worker cover to an anti-climate position. You can see how that would be tempting to a government trying to scrape together tax revenue any way it can.




So, what happens next? All eyes are on Miatta Fahnbulleh – the energy secretary, who before she was elected, 

publicly opposed drilling at Rosebank

. MPs don’t get a vote on Rosebank (just like they didn’t with Jackdaw), unless opposition parties force one. It’s Fahnbulleh who has the ultimate say-so. Though rumours that she’s been secretly organising a backbench rebellion have seemingly come to nought, her comments at COP31 saying that Rosebank development 

wouldn’t cut household bills

 give us a clue about what her private opinions might be. But private opinions, in politics, have as much value as the Italian lira. 




Will there be resignations? It’s worth noting that, for many MPs, they’ll be thinking about their own jobs more than the ones in the energy sector. A stable government means it’s less likely there’ll be an early election, and even with Burnham riding high in the polls, any election means it’s likely many Labour MPs will lose their seats. Rumblings of discontent there may be, but we’re still a long way from all-out rebellion.

title: Guerrillas: We will uphold the PKK's legacy no matter what
content:
The Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) was founded on 27 November 1978 in the village of Fis in the Lice district of Amed (Diyarbakır), in memory of martyr Haki Karer, based on the struggle for Kurdish identity and the vision of a free life. Throughout the PKK movement's history of resistance, major initiatives have continually been undertaken to keep the memory of fallen comrades alive. These initiatives contributed to the growth of the PKK movement over the years and enabled it to accumulate an invaluable legacy and experience. Abdullah Öcalan defines the PKK as the party of martyrs. People’s Defense Forces (HPG) and Free Women’s Units (YJA Star) guerrillas Şîlan Amara and Tîrêj Şêrîn spoke to ANF on the occasion of the 48th anniversary of the PKK's foundation.







 







YJA Star guerrilla Şîlan Amara said that the Kurdish people rose again with the foundation of the PKK: "Comrade Haki laid the foundations of our struggle and the establishment of our party, the PKK. This is a day of rebirth. Millions of people pursue this cause today, and this is the meaning we attach to this day. For us, the PKK represents the existence of a people. Today, the PKK has dissolved itself in accordance with the needs of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan) decided to dissolve the party in accordance with the conditions in the Middle East. Before the PKK was founded, our movement was an Apoist movement. It began as an Apoist group and later developed into the PKK movement. Above all, we are Apoists, and we wage our struggle on the basis of the Apoist legacy, thought and philosophy. Today, our people are in the streets, struggling and demanding their rights.




If we can speak about our rights in parliament today, it is thanks to the PKK. The PKK martyrs created a free life moment by moment and advanced their struggle through self-sacrifice. They wrote epics through their struggle and became the bearers of a free life. They struggled for years for a single purpose. They became the enduring and universal legacy of a genuine thought and philosophy. We have lost 35,000 martyrs, and these martyrs embody the values of this movement. We have reached this day by paying such a heavy price and have waged our struggle on this basis. Today, we need a stronger struggle than ever before. No matter what happens, we will uphold the legacy left behind by the PKK. Today, we continue our struggle as the Apoist movement. We will carry this legacy and keep this flag flying until the end. Our struggle will continue on this basis."




The PKK made the world recognize the existence of the Kurdish people







 







HPG guerrilla Tîrêj Şêrîn said that 27 November is a particularly significant date for the Kurdish people: "I congratulate all our people, the families of martyrs and Leader Apo on the 48th anniversary of the PKK. We are now in November, the month in which the PKK was founded. The PKK, through its foundation and its defense of the Kurdish people and Kurdistan, made the entire world recognize the existence of the Kurds and secured their existence through its struggle. Before the PKK, almost nothing remained in the name of the Kurdish people and Kurdistan, whose existence had been denied. The emergence and foundation of the PKK proclaimed the existence of the Kurdish people to the world. We therefore reiterate that the PKK represents a spirit, a life and a philosophy of life for us.




The Peace and Democratic Society Process is currently underway in Turkey. As part of this process, the PKK has dissolved itself as a party. Its mode of operation as an organization and its political status may have been dissolved. However, the Apoist group existed before the PKK movement. The PKK was founded and developed in this way. It has now dissolved itself as part of this process. However, we remain an Apoist movement and continue to act accordingly. The dissolution of the PKK does not mean that we have abandoned our Apoist struggle. We have our goals and objectives. A legacy was established through the PKK. We have our martyrs, 50,000 martyrs. There is a body of thought. Methods and forms change, but the struggle continues. As the Apoist movement, we will fulfill whatever responsibilities fall upon us during this process for the people of Kurdistan and the existence of Kurdistan. Martyrs are a bridge between human beings and truth, enabling them to attain a passion for life.




We have duties and responsibilities during this important process. Yes, the PKK has dissolved itself, but the struggle continues. Both as members of the Apoist movement and as the people of Kurdistan, we have responsibilities during this process. Our martyred comrades have entrusted us with these duties and responsibilities. The PKK was founded to keep the memory of the martyrs alive. Therefore, we will not forget the martyrs, and we will fulfill our duties and responsibilities to the best of our ability. For us, the martyrs represent a way of life and a philosophy. Leader Apo always said when referring to the martyrs, 'Forgetting is betrayal.' We will not forget either. We will do whatever is required of us. We will fulfill the promises we made to the martyrs and realize their objectives. We were also influenced by the existence and thought established by the PKK, which is why we joined the movement. We will therefore continue our struggle to commemorate and avenge the martyrs until Leader Apo's physical freedom is secured, our people in Kurdistan attain freedom and our mothers' tears come to an end."

title: The road to 27 November: The PKK founding Congress and its aftermath
content:
This article is compiled from a piece written by Duran Kalkan and published in a special edition of

 Serxwebûn 

marking the 30th anniversary of the founding of the PKK.




For a period, an ideological grouping developed in Ankara among university students around a form of communal life. Through Leader Apo’s [Abdullah Öcalan] understanding of freedom, equality, democracy, sharing, and his way of life and political stance, this grouping acquired a sense of consciousness and organization and was subsequently carried to Kurdistan.




The ideological grouping established among the student youths in Ankara developed, during 1976–77, into a dynamic youth organization in Kurdistan, based primarily on secondary-school students.




Secondary-school young people are generally less experienced and younger, and they require more education. In terms of organizational life, they are also less mature and tend to be closer to their families and family-oriented characteristics. University students, by contrast, represent a more advanced position in these areas.




Indeed, the fact that the first ideological grouping was established among university students served two purposes for the PKK: it helped identify potential cadres capable of educating and training all segments of youth and developing their experience and strength; at the same time, it made it possible to establish the communal way of life, to which university students were more receptive, as the dominant approach within all forms of youth organization.




On the road to the PKK founding Congress




Almost every city and town in Northern Kurdistan, and virtually every place with schools, had such a youth organization and a communal youth life.




In particular, following the martyrdom of Haki Karer on May 18, 1977, the process of developing youth organization and transforming the movement into a party led to a more advanced and mature level of activity and organization.




As the PKK moved toward its Founding Congress, unorganized youth environments, especially among students, had become almost nonexistent.




At the same time, significant progress had been made in discussions about the party and the organization in preparation for the congress.




Leader Apo repeatedly stated that, following the killing of Comrade Haki Karer, he had decided to establish a party as a way of honoring his memory and had prepared a draft party program on this basis.




In short, beginning in the summer of 1977, the process of party formation became an issue on the agenda of the Freedom Movement. Everywhere, the questions of "How should we organize?" and "What should the party look like?" began to be discussed in all their aspects.




The preparation of a draft program and its presentation to the cadres inevitably made these discussions more organized and systematic.




The decision to form a party and the first issue of 

Serxwebûn




On this basis, in November 1977, during the Eid al-Adha period, a meeting of cadres was held in Amed (Diyarbakır) to discuss the question: "How should we organize and form a party?"




The discussions at this meeting were undoubtedly interesting.




In response to Leader Apo’s position, which placed great importance on the organization and, within it, the formation of a party, and which brought these issues onto the agenda for discussion, Şahin Dönmez displayed an unwillingness to form a party and adopted an approach that sought to postpone the process.




Such a debate took place, and the majority of the cadres attending the meeting, particularly Mazlum Doğan, supported Leader Apo’s idea of forming a party.




This meeting did not result in any organizational decision. However, it brought the discussion process, particularly the question of "What kind of organization and party should we have?", more seriously and comprehensively onto the agenda of the youth movement.




Later, in the spring of 1978, a similar meeting was held in Elazığ. The agenda was the same: "What kind of organization and party should we have?"




Similar discussions took place there as well. Unlike the meeting in Amed, however, this gathering marked a step toward a certain organizational differentiation and development, and decisions were taken to make this possible. Thus, following this meeting, youth organization was developed on the one hand to carry out all kinds of practical and organizational activities. On the other hand, a decision was made to organize publishing activities and develop press and publication work in order to advance theoretical work and ideological struggle.




A division of labor was established accordingly, and organizational responsibilities were assigned. As a result, the 

Manifesto of the Revolution in Kurdistan

 was produced and prepared. Both the program and the manifesto were printed and distributed to the widest possible circles, and publication of the 

Serxwebûn

 journal began in October 1978. Undoubtedly, all these activities were of enormous importance in preparing for the PKK Founding Congress.




A third important aspect of the preparations for the congress was the development of practical and tactical approaches and the conduct of the struggle. It is particularly well known that the massacre of May 18, 1977, marked a turning point for the PKK in this regard. Leader Apo also clearly expressed this reality in his defense statements.




The Antep massacre confronted the Apocu youth grouping with the following reality: even propaganda activities for national identity and freedom in Kurdistan had to be conducted on the basis of legitimate self-defense. A movement that cannot defend itself has no chance of surviving or succeeding. This was a lesson that the Antep massacre clearly revealed and taught. On this basis, new systems and measures gradually emerged in working methods and organizational operations, creating a more cautious and controlled level of activity.




A movement that could defend itself, withstand attacks without being defeated, remain standing, hold its attackers accountable and, so to speak, demonstrate its capacity for revenge gradually took shape.




First and foremost, revenge was taken for the Antep massacre. Subsequently, active defense was adopted against attacks targeting youth cadres in various locations, carried out by fascist, reactionary, feudal, and social-chauvinist groups.




This gradually led the Apocu movement toward a tactical understanding based on the use of violence against structures, individuals, and institutions that had become collaborators or agents.




In particular, the killing of Comrade Halil Çavgun on May 19, 1978, through the cooperation of feudal gangs, fascists, and the police, made the need to conduct the struggle on the basis of such a tactical approach unmistakably clear.




On this basis, while the Hilvan resistance was being organized, particularly to avenge this attack, this tactical understanding spread to every area experiencing reactionary and fascist attacks, as well as attacks by the police and social-chauvinist groups.




Thus, during the summer of 1978, an increasingly widespread and intense armed resistance developed throughout Kurdistan, particularly in Hilvan, against fascists, police attacks, and armed assaults by reactionary and social-chauvinist circles.




This defensive resistance spread across all areas of Kurdistan, reached considerable intensity, and increasingly began to influence the political environment and various social groups more deeply.




As a result, the movement expanded beyond the youth and reached other segments of society, including women, workers, and peasants. As the PKK Founding Congress approached, the Apocu movement had moved beyond being merely a youth movement and had reached the level of a popular movement, particularly in the central regions of Kurdistan: Urfa, Mardin, Diyarbakır, and Batman, as well as along the Bingöl-Dersim and Serhat corridors.




Congress preparations were carried out secretly




These are some points we can make about the general situation of the Apocu movement as it approached the PKK Founding Congress. Of course, other activities were also carried out in preparation for the congress. For example, there was a search for a suitable location to hold the congress. Eventually, the house of Comrade Seyfettin Zoğurlu in the village of Fis, in the Lice district, was deemed suitable.




It was a house we already knew. Comrade Seyfettin had joined the movement from the Teachers' Training School in Dersim and was working as a full-time revolutionary. One reason for choosing this location was that one side of the house was close to the paved road, making it possible for people to enter and leave without attracting much attention and while maintaining secrecy. The fact that the family were sympathizers was, of course, another important factor in resolving other practical difficulties. At the end of November, Amed was already rainy and shrouded in fog. For this reason, the location was chosen partly to help preserve secrecy. In a period when the struggle had become so intense, it was naturally important to maintain secrecy and organize activities in a way that would evade police surveillance. Indeed, November 26, 1978, was an extremely rainy and foggy day. The cadres invited from different areas first arrived in Amed and gathered at designated addresses in various locations. Using an organized vehicle, the comrades were transported in groups to the Fis plain throughout the night of November 25, continuing until morning.




The vehicles did not turn off their headlights, and the passengers got out and entered the house before the vehicles had even come to a complete stop. In this way, no opportunity was given for anyone to notice that people were getting out of the vehicles.




The vehicles continued along the road and turned back only after reaching a certain distance.




Particular care was taken to avoid attracting attention. At the time, one of our sympathizers, Comrade Alaattin, who was also a military deserter, kept constant watch. Comrade Seyfettin’s father continuously monitored and checked the comings and goings at the tea house and restaurant located there. The women of the household took care of preparing food and carrying out other domestic tasks. The family members not only raised no objections but carried out their duties with enthusiasm and excitement. They truly fulfilled a historic responsibility. Along with selecting the location, the process of determining which cadres would be invited was organized by Leader Apo.




Representatives working at a semi-official level in each region were asked to ensure that a sufficient number of delegates came from their respective areas. The number of delegates was determined. In some places, their names were also decided in advance, while in others, the selection was left to the discretion of the comrades working there. Thus, the number of delegates invited was—if I remember correctly—25. Three of those selected were unable to attend. With the participation of 22 delegates, the PKK Founding Congress was held on November 26 and 27 in the village of Fis, in the Lice district. The participants arrived at the meeting location during the night of November 25–26.




On the morning of November 26, Leader Apo and the comrades accompanying him arrived as the final group. The proceedings began on November 26. The participants stayed overnight in the house on the night of November 26–27, and the work continued on November 27. The congress concluded that evening. On the evening of November 27, the delegates were transported from the village back to Amed using the same method. From there, they dispersed, and the necessary organizational arrangements were put in place.




The victory in Hilvan merged with the excitement of the Congress




The Hilvan-Siverek group was unable to attend the congress. The group was led by Comrade Mehmet Karasungur. They had requested not to attend the meeting, explaining that the Hilvan resistance had reached a critical stage and was now approaching its conclusion, and that their departure could turn the situation against us. Leader Apo considered their request reasonable and gave them permission to stay away.




As it turned out, this assessment was confirmed in practice: on the very day the congress concluded, the Hilvan resistance also came to a successful end. The Süleymanlar tribal-feudal group was brought to surrender, thereby ensuring the victory of the Hilvan resistance.




In this way, at the end of November, our movement celebrated two victories simultaneously: on the one hand, the Founding Congress, and on the other, the triumph of the Hilvan resistance. In addition to these developments, preparations for the congress also included drafting the manifesto and program and giving them their final form. These documents were distributed to all regions, where meetings were held by regional organizations to discuss them. Each region prepared its views on the manifesto and its proposed amendments, which were then brought to the congress by its delegates. Leader Apo also prepared a draft organizational statute consisting of nine articles. Thus, the materials that a party founding congress needed to adopt in order to formally establish the party had been prepared in advance and discussed. The views of all regions had been gathered, and the congress was convened on this basis.




The Congress agenda 




The meeting lasted two days, November 26 and 27. Decisions were adopted on the evening of November 27, and the meeting came to an end. The agenda was established at the outset. These documents are preserved in the archives. The agenda included evaluating practical organizational activities; discussing the program, statute, and manifesto; addressing organizational problems; planning the new period; and electing an official central leadership. These items followed the familiar framework of congress' agendas.




The presidium of the meeting consisted of one comrade. Comrade Hayri served as the chair of the meeting. Leader Apo stated that he intended to participate more actively in the meeting and take part in the discussions. He therefore felt that it would not be appropriate for him to chair the proceedings and that it would be better for another comrade to do so. On this basis, Comrade Hayri was appointed to the presidium. Nobody raised any objection to his appointment.




In any case, the circumstances did not require the presidium to play a particularly extensive role. A culture of meetings had already developed within the Apocu movement through its activities at the time. There was an environment in which meetings could be conducted naturally, without requiring extensive intervention from a formal chairing body.




The main agenda item was an assessment of the existing political, military, and organizational situation, as well as the activities being carried out. Leader Apo presented a comprehensive analysis of the current situation. Alongside this, there was some discussion of our practical and organizational situation and our ongoing work.




Since the movement was already in the process of being formally established, the main question was whether its overall development and preparations were sufficient to proceed with the establishment of an organization. Some limited criticisms were raised, but the main emphasis was placed on adopting decisions for the new period.




Adoption of the program and statute




Two issues came to the forefront in the process of reaching these decisions. The first was the discussion and adoption of the manifesto, program, and statute. On this matter, various regions presented the views and proposals they had developed during their earlier meetings. These were discussed, proposed amendments considered appropriate were incorporated, and those deemed unsuitable were rejected. Ultimately, the manifesto, program, and statute were adopted by the congress delegates. Thus, the Apocu movement had now become a formal organization operating according to an established manifesto, program, and statute.




The second major organizational issue was understanding what the establishment of a party organization actually meant and what would change by declaring ourselves an organization through the adoption of a program, statute, and manifesto. There was a certain weakness and inadequacy in the general outlook of the cadres regarding this matter. This caused Leader Apo some concern.




On this issue, Leader Apo delivered extensive and strongly cautionary assessments, explaining what it meant to become an organization and form a party, and what it meant to enter a formal working structure governed by a manifesto, program, and statute.




He provided detailed explanations of the difference between voluntary work and formal organizational work. He also explained how our organizations would function in the process ahead and how cadres would need to approach their responsibilities.




The debate over the formation of the party 




At the congress, Leader Apo presented the following justification for forming a party: "We have now become a popular movement. In the past, we were an ideological group, and later we became a youth movement. One person could assume responsibility for such a group and youth organization, and until now I have carried out these duties and responsibilities on my own. However, our movement has now expanded. It has gone beyond the youth and spread to women, peasants, workers, and laborers. Armed violence has also become part of the struggle. We have become a popular movement. It is neither possible nor right or sufficient for one person to assume and carry out the responsibility for such a popular movement.




Only a well-organized party structure can carry out such a task. Only a party can bear this responsibility. Only a party organization based on collective functioning and a collectively working leadership can fulfill the tasks and responsibilities of leading such a popular movement. Therefore, it is no longer possible to manage and develop the movement through individual responsibility alone. It is essential that we organize ourselves, become a party, establish a collectively functioning leadership, and assume responsibility together."




On this basis, he argued that we needed to organize ourselves, form a party, and adopt a decision to establish the party at the congress.




Since these issues had already been discussed over the preceding one or two years, and the necessary criticisms had been made during that period, nobody openly expressed opposition to these views or made statements contradicting them at this meeting. The reasons Leader Apo put forward for organizing and forming a party were accepted.




Secondly, after the decision to form a party had been made, Leader Apo explained the difference between voluntary work and formal, professional organizational work. He made particularly instructive and cautionary explanations on this subject. He explained the principles underlying voluntary work, what it was based on, and how it involved no obligation, coercion, or system of accountability. Everyone participated as they wished.




However, once the decision had been made to become a formal organization, voluntary participation was no longer sufficient. Everyone would now be obliged to work in accordance with the provisions of the program and statute. On this basis, official responsibilities would be assigned, and accountability would be established according to the results of the work carried out. Everyone would be required to live and work on a daily basis according to the principles of the party program and statute, rather than simply acting as they pleased. He expressed all these points in particularly striking terms. Leader Apo's explanations and efforts at the congress demonstrate that there was an inadequacy and weakness among the cadres. There were weaknesses in their understanding, approach, and overall attitude, and this concerned him. Indeed, Leader Apo also had concerns about whether the party should be established at all.




He repeatedly warned the cadres about this issue: "We may decide to establish a party and give ourselves the name of a party. But if we cannot fulfill the requirements of being a party and carry out its enormous responsibilities in practice, we will become guilty before history. History will laugh at us."




For this reason, he sought to develop an awareness of how prepared the cadres actually were to become a party, how unprepared they might be, and how they could be brought to the necessary level of readiness. He tried to encourage them to question themselves on this matter. Such an approach demonstrates just how much importance Leader Apo attached to the party. According to Leader Apo, a party must necessarily create something new, transform social life, and achieve success.




He consistently criticized and condemned organizations that called themselves parties but were incapable of accomplishing anything, as well as approaches that diluted the meaning of a party and behaved in ways unworthy of its name. From the very beginning, he approached the question of the party with great seriousness. At the congress, he sought to develop a process of party formation based on this seriousness and to instill the same awareness and attitude in all cadres. This was because the PKK was not going to be like other parties. The party that was to be established would take the lead in social development, play a leading role, enter into a major confrontation, and transform the organizational stance and way of life of Kurdish society. It would truly be a vanguard party worthy of its name.




To become such a party required the appropriate consciousness, determination, willpower, and capacity for organized work. Leader Apo sought to create these qualities. The reason he placed so much emphasis on party organization was that he recognized that the cadres were not yet fully prepared for the standards and mindset required of a formal, professional party. He never concealed this concern and consistently kept it on the agenda.




All the documents were prepared on the basis of establishing a party, and the congress decided to establish an organization. Nevertheless, Leader Apo continued to raise the question and explore the possibility of whether the movement should immediately call itself a party or instead organize and work as a different form of collective structure for a while longer. In other words, he continued to discuss whether it might be better to develop the organizational system on this basis, train and consolidate the cadres, and only then take the step of formally becoming a party and adopting that name.




The PKK name and the election of the central committee




On this basis, the congress decided to establish a party, but it did not give the party a name. A decision was made that "we had become an organization," and the party program and statute were adopted. However, the party was not even given an official name at that point. This issue was discussed over the following three months, and a founding declaration was prepared. In April 1979, the Central Committee convened and decided to establish the 

Partiya Karkerên Kurdistan

 (Kurdistan Workers' Party), or PKK.




The decision to name the party the PKK was therefore made at the Central Committee meeting in April 1979. Until then, Leader Apo had discussed various possible organizational names internally, and some discussions had also taken place within the central leadership. Ultimately, the name PKK was agreed upon through the decision and collective will of the Central Committee. Another important task of the Founding Congress was to hold elections and elect a Central Committee—in other words, to establish a central leadership. Until that time, Leader Apo had been the sole person responsible for organizing and coordinating the movement's activities.




Considerable discussion also took place regarding the elections. Indeed, everyone nominated people they knew, resulting in a large number of candidates. Leader Apo spoke individually with those who had been nominated, trying to understand how willing and prepared they were to take on and carry out these responsibilities. His conversation with Comrade Mazlum Doğan was particularly instructive.




When Leader Apo asked Mazlum, "You have not made much preparation. How will you carry out this responsibility? Why did you become a candidate?" Mazlum replied: "I did not nominate myself. The other comrades considered me suitable for this responsibility and nominated me. If I am to become a member of the party, I must be prepared to accept any assignment. The important thing is whether I am capable of becoming a member of the PKK. Anyone who is a member of the party must also be capable of carrying out Central Committee responsibilities. To become a member, I must be ready to undertake any kind of duty. For this reason, I am obliged to carry out whatever task this congress assigns to me. I must approach the matter with this understanding. The comrades nominated me. Therefore, whatever the congress decides, I will work accordingly."




This example was highly meaningful and instructive in demonstrating both how party cadres should approach duties and responsibilities and the level of party consciousness among the cadres attending the congress. In the leadership elections, nobody nominated themselves except for one person. The only person who put forward their own candidacy was Şahin Dönmez. This was met with some amusement, but his candidacy was not rejected simply because he had nominated himself and made an effort to pursue it. Ultimately, the congress did not elect the seven-member Central Committee it had initially envisaged. Instead, it decided to establish a three-member Central Executive Committee, consisting of Leader Apo, Mehmet Karasungur, and Şahin Dönmez.




Leader Apo was designated as the party's General Secretary, while Comrade Mehmet Karasungur and Şahin Dönmez were appointed as his two deputies. Leader Apo was then entrusted and authorized to select the remaining four members of the Central Committee. He was given the authority to choose whoever he wished to work with and whoever he considered suitable, thereby completing the Central Committee. Subsequently, Leader Apo selected Comrade Mazlum, Comrade Hayri, Comrade Cuma, and Baki. Thus, the first Central Committee consisted of these seven individuals.




At the first meeting of the Central Committee, Comrade Mehmet Karasungur proposed that he was not suitable for membership of the Central Executive Committee because he was responsible for the military committee and was engaged in military activities. Following this proposal, a change was made, and Comrade Cuma was included in the Central Executive Committee instead. Comrade Mehmet Karasungur continued his work as the person responsible for the military committee.

my stance on left unity is statecomms/socdems can do sick anarchist shit w me if they want but im not gonna waste my time doing lame statecomm/socdem shit w them

yesssss

my other stance on left unity is that my activism can be intersectional as fuck, and if the statecomms/socdems claim it’s ‘too woke’ or 'not focussed enough on class struggle’, then they’re the one ruining the left unity by deciding that some minorities are expendable.

Sometimes your belief systems are wrong, dead wrong. You need to be open to that possibility

I don’t think we’re going to agree any time of which of our belief systems is wrong (it’s yours), but that was not the point of this post at all. The point was “under what conditions can we work together to fight capitalism despite disagreeing on some key issues?”

“We can join together when we want to but we have no obligation to join each other’s actions when we don’t see the point”

I do feel that ancomms and their ilk often do things that are actively counterproductive to both of our objectives (idc about socdems) like constantly falling for strategy of tension subversion and doing adventurist activism which only brings the ire of the state on us collectively. so like maybe they should stop doing that. please 🥺

title: Those tags make no sense. ‘Modern society’ did not start in the early 2000s. If this graph showed…
content:
wrenchinator-central

:

zolltraak

:




Those tags make no sense. ‘Modern society’ did not start in the early 2000s. If this graph showed the loss of community in modern society (it does not), we would see a continuous development since the 1950s at least and probably long before that. 

We would also see 'work’ and 'through family’ being less effected because capitalism has maintained these two social spheres. We do see 'work’ rising as a place to meet a spouse in the 1950s to 1980s, coinciding with a growth in the percentage of women in the workplace. But it would be ridiculous to argue that the dominance of work in our life has declined since then, and yet meeting your spouse at work also took a nosedive in the 2000s. 

Instead, the decline we’re seeing can be completely, easily explained by the fact that since the 2000s online dating became an easy way to meet people and allowed people to explore, reject and select far more potential partners than ever before. Which says absolutely nothing about the state of community. 

It does open up interesting questions. If over 50% of couples meet outside their existing social circles, does that reduce societal segregation along lines like ethnicity and class? Are people more likely to meet a partner outside their own home town and travel to be with them? Does the lower reliance on meeting friends through existing social circles make it easier for isolated individuals to find partners? The data doesn’t show us this but it would be interesting to explore.

Finally, note that this data was presented in this manner by Marriage Pact, a creepy matchmaking organization committed to pushing US college students to get married. It is worth asking where an organization that sees marriage as one of the highest goals in life stand politically and what it seeks to gain by presenting this data?

title: Soma ve Kangal termik santrallerinde üretim durdu: İşçiler alacakları için Konya'da eylem yaptı
content:
Konya — Soma B Termik Santrali’nin üretiminin durması ve kamuya devredilmesinin ardından yaklaşık bin 100 çalışanın maaş ve kıdem tazminatı alacakları gündemdeki yerini korurken, Sivas Kangal Termik Santrali’nde de kömür tedarikinin kesilmesiyle üretim durdu. Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şubesi ile TES-İş’in öncülüğünde Konya’da bir araya gelen maden ve enerji işçileri, milyarlarca liralık alacaklarının ödenmesini istedi. İşçiler, kamulaştırma ve üretimin yeniden başlaması çağrısı yaptı.

Manisa’nın Soma ilçesinde yıllarca kömür üreten maden işletmelerinin, termik santral işçilerinin ve kent ekonomisinin geleceğini etkileyen sorun, bu kez Konya’da Torku ve Konya Şeker’in önünde verilen mücadeleyle gündeme geldi. Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şubesi temsilcileri ile Soma B ve Sivas Kangal termik santrallerinin işçileri, ödenmeyen alacakları ve iş güvencesi talepleri için şirketin merkezi önünde bir araya geldi.

TES-İş Sendikası Genel Merkezi öncülüğünde, Soma ve Sivas şubelerinin koordinasyonuyla gerçekleştirilen eyleme, Soma’daki maden işçileri de destek verdi. İşçiler, yalnızca bireysel ücret ve tazminat alacaklarının değil, işletmeler arasındaki birikmiş borçların ve üretimin durmasının yarattığı ekonomik sonuçların da çözülmesini istedi.

Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şubesi İş Yeri Temsilcisi Emin Kara, eylem alanında yaptığı açıklamada, maden işletmelerinin milyarlarca liralık alacakları bulunduğunu belirterek Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’a, İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi ve Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanı Murat Kurum'a çağrıda bulunarak, “Memleketinizdeyiz. Devletin gücünü iliklerimize kadar burada hissettik; aynı gücün, aynı iradenin masada da Torku'ya karşı verilmesini istiyoruz" dedi.

Eyleme katılan maden işçileri, Soma’daki üretim zincirinin yalnızca termik santralde çalışanlardan oluşmadığını, santrale kömür sağlayan işletmelerin de yaşanan krizden etkilendiğini dile getirdi.

Maden işçileri, “İşletmemizin 1,4 milyar alacağı var. Hakkımızı almadan buradan dönmeyeceğiz” sözleriyle taleplerini dile getirdi. İşçiler, alacakları için Konya’ya geldiklerini belirterek, maaş ve özlük haklarında yaşanan aksamaların çalışanları mağdur ettiğini söyledi. İşçiler, haklarının bir an önce ödenmesini talep etti.

Türkiye Maden-İş Sendikası Ege Bölge Şube Başkan Yardımcısı Turgay Aydoğdu da TES-İş Sendikası’nın başlattığı direnişe destek verdiklerini belirtti. Konya Torku Şeker önündeki eylemin sürdüğünü ifade eden Aydoğdu, işçilerin yaşadığı ekonomik sıkıntıları aileleri üzerinden anlatarak, “Konya Torku Şeker müdürlerinin çocukları okul harçlığı almadan gidebiliyorlar mı? Çocuklara cep harçlığı vermeden çocukları okula gönderebiliyorlar mı? Onlar, bir babanın çocuğunun gözünün içine bakamayacak duruma düşmesini bilebiliyorlar mı” ifadelerini kullandı.

İşçilerin yaşadığı mağduriyete dikkat çeken Aydoğdu, eylem sırasında polisin orantısız güç kullandığını ileri sürdü. Devletin güvenlik güçleri aracılığıyla gösterdiği iradenin işçilerin taleplerinin çözümü için de ortaya konulması gerektiğini savunan Aydoğdu, işçilerin hak arayışını sürdüreceğini belirtti.

TES-İş Sendikası Teşkilatlanma ve Örgütlenmeden Sorumlu Genel Başkan Yardımcısı Fatih Erçelik, Konya’daki açıklamasında Soma ve Kangal termik santrallerinde yaşananları değerlendirdi. Erçelik, şirket yönetimini yeterli yatırım yapmamak, borçlarını ödememek ve işçileri mağdur etmekle eleştirdi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: İran: ABD'nin el koyduğu İran'a ait iki petrol tankeri, düzenlenen operasyonla geri alındı
content:
İran Ordusu Deniz Kuvvetleri Komutanı Tuğamiral Şehram İrani, ABD’nin İran’a ait iki petrol tankerine el koyduğunu ancak daha sonra İran Ordusu Deniz Kuvvetleri’nin ABD’lilerin uyuduğu bir sırada düzenlediği operasyonla söz konusu iki tankeri geri aldığını iddia etti.

Yarı resmi Fars Haber Ajansı’na göre, İrani, gündeme ilişkin açıklamalarda bulundu.

ABD’nin tüm araçları kullanarak Hürmüz Boğazı’ndan gemi geçirmeye çalıştığını ancak bunun bir hayalden ibaret olduğunu ve boğazın kapalı olduğunu belirten İrani, ABD’nin İran’a ait iki petrol tankerine el koyduğunu ancak daha sonra İran Ordusu Deniz Kuvvetleri’nin ABD’lilerin uyuduğu bir sırada düzenlediği operasyonla söz konusu iki tankeri geri aldığını öne sürdü.

İrani ayrıca, ABD’nin, Hürmüz Boğazı’ndan geçmek isteyen gemilerden para aldığını ancak gemilerin saldırıya uğraması halinde sorumluluğu üstlenmediğini ve parayı da iade etmediğini söyledi.

title: Habaş patlamasına ilişkin haberlere sahte erişim engeli kararları gönderildi
content:
İzmir’in Aliağa ilçesindeki Habaş Demir Çelik Fabrikası’nda 9 Kasım günü meydana gelen patlamada 19 işçi hayatını kaybetti. Patlamanın ardından fabrikaya ve hayatını kaybeden işçilere ilişkin yayımlanan haberlerin sahte mahkeme kararlarıyla kaldırılmaya çalışıldığı ortaya çıktı.

Gazete Pencere’nin haberine göre, Bilgi Teknolojileri ve İletişim Kurumu (BTK) adına açılan sahte bir e-posta adresinden gazeteye 13 Kasım’da iki bildirim gönderildi. Bildirimlerde, “HABAŞ patlamasında 19 işçinin hikayesi yürekleri burktu” ve “HABAŞ’ın kurucusu da fabrika inşaatı sırasında ölmüş” başlıklı haberlere erişim engeli getirildiği ileri sürülerek haberlerin yayından kaldırılması istendi.

E-postaların ekinde Aliağa Sulh Ceza Hâkimliğine ait olduğu öne sürülen sahte mahkeme kararlarının da yer aldığı belirtildi. Aynı e-posta adresinden daha sonra yeni bir bildirim gönderilerek HABAŞ’ın kurucusuna ilişkin haberin erişime engellendiği iddiası tekrarlandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Win Or Lose, What Comes After the “Ocean Current”?
content:
TAIWAN WILL GO to the polls tomorrow to vote for a series of nine different government positions, hence the name nine-in-one elections. Most focus is on city/county councilor elections, as well as mayoral elections.

The predominant theme of the elections is local governance. This became the case after the meteoric rise of Puma Shen as a DPP mayoral candidate in Taipei. Before the rise of Shen, in what came to be termed the “Ocean Current” phenomenon, the election was one that seemed characterized by familiar, stale issues, in which there was seemingly no real difference between the two parties except for their stance on cross-strait issues.

Taiwanese politics has long faced the issue that both major parties largely agree on what the issues facing Taiwanese society are–that young people are paid low salaries, work long hours, and Taiwan’s population is increasingly elderly. Both parties do not fundamentally differ on any of the solutions that they offer, in that no party is willing to make structural changes to Taiwanese society, for fear of offending big business interests. That being the case, the two political parties largely only differ on their position on cross-strait politics.

The “Ocean Current” phenomenon represents a desire for alternatives, especially from the youth. This is especially visible in the backlash against the KMT, given that Shen is up against Chiang Wan-an, who is increasingly perceived as someone who comes from a powerful political family and may be handsome, but who has little concrete knowledge of policy and has stumbled his way to a high political office.

Nevertheless, before the rise of Shen, the DPP, too, was struggling. Shen is of the political generation that entered politics after the 2014 Sunflower Movement and if someone as young as him manages to become Taipei mayor, that represents another benchmark in this generation’s ascent up the political ladder. But even if the youthful politicians who entered electoral politics after 2014 were fresh faces, many have simply entered the DPP’s familiar rotation of cast members every election–whose main asset is that they are not aging or geriatric, as the DPP’s political leadership is.

What explains the rise of Shen, then, was his ability to project competency in offering policy that was formulated based on assessing and consulting the needs of the citizenry, and grasping social reality through data analytics. This sharply differed from the familiar cycle of the DPP and KMT simply seeking to one-up each other in terms of the policy they offer, but without any true difference in the kind of policies that were put forth.

But Shen was not a data analytics technocrat either, instead emphasizing how formulation of policy should be an open, transparent process. Through the survey results he collected and analyzed in the course of his campaign, he was also able to identify policy needs that were not previously recognized–for example, Taipei residents’ concern with the declining amount of greenery in Taipei. In this sense, Shen has excited the public because he seems to offer the promise of participatory decision-making that would restore agency to the citizenry.

Yet, in spite of the frequent comparisons to New York’s Zohran Mamdani, Shen is not exactly Mamdani because he has not called for structural changes to society. A message of good governance can be sufficient for addressing issues of decaying urban infrastructure, perhaps, but still proves insufficient to address deeply-rooted socioeconomic inequalities.

And if the DPP and KMT have proven reluctant to rock the boat, for fear of offending big business interests, it is to be seen whether Shen would be able to if elected mayor. If so, Shen would face opposition not only from the KMT but also from elements of his own party.

After all, one notes how in the wake of the Sunflower Movement, activists desired alternatives from the DPP and KMT alike–with the view that the DPP had become equally corrupt to the KMT in the course of its many years in office. It was fears of a split vote leading to a KMT victory that led many activists to join the DPP after the 2018 elections.

In 2018, the KMT proved unexpectedly resurgent, with the KMT unexpectedly making inroads into the DPP’s heartland in southern Taiwan through Han Kuo-yu’s victory in Kaohsiung. Han’s victory was seen as marking the ascendancy of the “Han wave” phenomenon, later propelling him to become the KMT’s presidential candidate in 2020. But, in this sense, with many activists joining the DPP in panic after the rise of the “Han wave”, this proved the death knell of the “Third Force” that had emerged after the Sunflower Movement, allowing for the rise of Ko Wen-je’s TPP as a party that frames itself as an alternative to the DPP and KMT but has in reality hewed very close to the KMT’s political trajectory.

Eight years later, it is now Puma Shen’s “Ocean Current” that electrifies the public. And the emergence of the phenomenon represents the desire of the Taiwanese public for alternatives to traditional two-party DPP-KMT governance. Except that, with no “Third Force,” it is a DPP candidate who has seized public momentum.

Indeed, it would be a mistake to interpret the elections as a referendum on cross-strait relations. Taiwanese local elections are, after all, primarily about local issues. Cross-strait relations lurk as a dimension in the background, but as one factor among many. But the rise of the “Ocean Current”, as well as of the “Third Force” before it, shows that another factor that one increasingly has to contend with in Taiwanese politics is the desire for alternatives to traditional establishment politics. Win or lose, that is something that one needs to increasingly understand about Taiwanese politics in the wake of the “Ocean Current”.
