 that the Italian parliament had just voted to approve a law proposed by pseudo-patriotic prime minister Georgia Meloni’s government that formally incorporates the operational definition of anti-semitism drawn up by the zionist International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).










Erika Guevara Rosas, senior director of campaigns and research at Amnesty, said: “The new law is based on a definition that has long raised serious concerns because it confuses anti-semitism with legitimate criticism of Israel, increasing the risk of widespread forms of censorship and self-censorship.




“Its application in schools, universities, social media platforms, and other settings risks creating an intimidating climate that discourages people from exercising their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly”.




She warned that it risked “removing the policies and practices of the Israeli state from the legitimate control of public opinion and public debate” by stigmatising “criticism of the brutal Israeli occupation, the apartheid system imposed by Israel, and the ongoing genocide against the Palestinian population in Gaza” as some kind of hate crime.




UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese (

pictured

) 

remarked

: “For the Italian parliament, on the 1137th day of genocide, to have found nothing better to do than ban its denunciation is a scandal of historic proportions”.










Journalist Roberto Vivaldelli 

wrote

: “The law establishes a National Coordinator for the fight against antisemitism at the Presidency of the Council, a three-year national strategy, and a database on episodes of antisemitism and hate crimes.




“However, the problem is not the penal code. It is the definition, which becomes the criterion by which the facts will be read. Among the IHRA’s examples [of anti-semitism] are the comparison between contemporary Israeli politics and that of the Nazis, the thesis that the existence of the State of Israel is a racist enterprise, and the application of ‘double standards’ to Israel.




“Once enshrined in a state law, these examples become the framework with which schools, universities, police headquarters, prefectures, social platforms, and magistrates can classify a conference, a protest sign, a lesson, or a post as anti-semitic. And the national database will collect those ‘episodes'”.




Another journalist, Alberto Negri, 

commented

 on 

X

: “From today, we are less free… It is the most freedom-destroying and repressive law in the 80 years of the republic. I and anyone who follows this page have been warned: no more criticism of Israel and Zionism. Never in my life would I have thought I would have to write something like this”.




Giorgio Bianchi 

pointed to

 a sinister propagandistic and brainwashing aspect to the new law that many had overlooked.




“Anti-semitism prevention is to be incorporated into school curricula. The topics include: the history of Judaism and Jewish communities; the history of the Holocaust; the historical development of anti-semitism; hate speech and stereotypes; conspiracy theories and disinformation, including on social media…




“Training and professional development initiatives are also planned specifically for: the police and other law enforcement agencies; the armed forces; prefectural staff and judges and prosecutors. For law enforcement agencies, the text also provides for training on correctly identifying and recording anti-Semitic incidents… Extraordinary, isn’t it?”










Others expressed both disgust and defiance in the face of this odious assault on free speech. Sabrina 

observed

: “While they talk to us about the risk of Islamization, they foist Israelization on us”.




Geppo Erfolle 

said

: “It wasn’t a real vote; when they need to push through ‘unconstitutional things’, they agree beforehand on how to get the numbers and pretend there are parties opposed to it”.




And ‘il Surfista’ 

added

: “The anti-Semitism bill simply serves to remind you that voting is absolutely pointless because decisions are made elsewhere anyway”.




Noting that the 

IHRA

 version of “anti-semitism” includes any suggestion of “a world Jewish conspiracy or of Jews controlling the media, economy, government or other societal institutions”, Giammarco Desideri 

remarked

: “Imagine that from today on, it is forbidden to state that the Earth orbits the Sun. The Holy Inquisition were amateurs by comparison”.




Savino Balzano 

said

: “Instead of imposing sanctions on Israel, a threat to the entire world, we kneel before its corrupt ruling class. Imagine if, in 1942, the British had passed a law preventing criticism of Berlin, on the pretext of protecting Germans from racism. History will not forgive you, and above all, we will never let you silence us”.




And Giuseppe Salamone 

declared

: “We are not afraid of your gag laws, and we will shout the truth ever louder”.










Meanwhile, in Britain, anti-zionist academic 

David Miller

 went on 

UK Column News

 on November 18 to 

expose

 a bid to reverse the protected status of anti-zionist beliefs that his own legal efforts have secured.




This has come in the form of a “

report

” submitted to the government by the zionist freemasonic entity B’nai B’rith. On November 17 zio-Labour MP Luke Akehurst submitted a written 

question

 asking “if the Government will recognise antizionism as an extremist ideology, as recommended in Dr Jeremy Havardi’s report for B’nai B’rith UK, 

Antizionism: The New Face of Anti-Jewish Extremism

“.




As Miller’s 

Powerbase

 website 

explains

, this spurious document argues that anti-zionism should be “understood as an extremist movement which demonises and delegitimises the movement for Jewish national self-determination”, that its “roots” lie in “Nazi, Soviet and Islamist ideology”, and that it has become “the predominant expression of today’s obsessive antisemitism”.




It sets out eleven policy recommendations, including that the UK government identify anti-zionism as an extremist ideology and condemn political parties, NGOs and civil society organisations that promote it; that all public bodies adopt the (absurd) IHRA definition of anti-semitism; and that limits be imposed on “antizionist marches”.










Similar moves are being made across the world. In August 2026 

The Jewish Chronicle

 

reported

 that 46 national governments have adopted the IHRA definition, along with dozens of US states and more than 1,000 global entities.




It added: “Just last year, 67 entities worldwide adopted the IHRA definition, a 97 per cent increase from the 34 adoptions recorded the previous year, according to the Combat Antisemitism Movement”.




The zionist newspaper celebrated the fact that the Dominican Republic would be joining them, despite the fact that in a country with a population of nearly 12 million, “estimates vary on the number of Jews living in the Dominican Republic from 100 to 3,000”.




It said a source put the move down to “the efforts of the Combat Antisemitism Movement, along with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Yehuda Kaploun, a rabbi and the State Department’s special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism”.




Argentina holds the sole IHRA full member status in Latin America, while six other Latin American countries have previously adopted the definition, those being Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Panama and Uruguay.




The Latin American and Caribbean Parliament, a consultative assembly made up of national parliamentarians representing 23 countries, has also adopted it.










The article revealed that “the Trump administration in Washington is working closely with the government of Argentina to bring more Latin American countries into the IHRA fold… progress is expected to be made public soon”.




Part of this accelerating programme of judeo-supremacist totalitarianism is the appearance just about everywhere of people termed “anti-semitism czars”, with a variety of specific job titles.




Czars?

 Did we ever consent to such people playing a role in our supposedly democratic societies?




The USA’s “czar against global anti-semitism”, officially “Special Envoy and Ambassador at Large to Combat Global Antisemitism”, the aformentioned Kaploun, was appointed by his 

old buddy

 Donald Trump in December 2025.




The UK equivalent is 

John Mann

 (“Baron” Mann), the former Labour MP who played a leading role in ousting Jeremy Corbyn from the party leadership on the basis of concocted “anti-semitism” smears.




The proud recipient of an award from the American Jewish Committee “for fighting antisemitism in all of its forms”, Mann once confronted former Mayor of London Ken Livingstone in front of a news camera crew, ridiculously calling him a “Nazi apologist” and a “f**king disgrace” for having pointed out Adolf Hitler’s 

very real

 links to zionism.










I 

mentioned

 recently how Australia’s “antisemitism envoy” Jillian Segal (

pictured

) has claimed that “far-left activists” have been harnessing public outrage at the Gaza Holocaust “to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest”.




Red Pill Poet

 commented that “Jillian Segal would appear to be quite the piece of work” and 

pointed to

 this 

information

 from 

Wikipedia

: “In July 2025, Segal recommended she become a monitor of media organisations, with the ability to ‘readily terminate’ funding for public institutions, such as universities, festivals and public broadcasters, if they fail to combat antisemitism…




“In October 2026, Segal suggested that visitors to Australia should be screened for the ‘risk of holding anti-Semitic views’… Her report further asked that public arts organisations should be empowered to impose ‘enforceable conditions’ on artists and revoke grants if they promoted what they deemed ‘anti-Semitic'”.




Cities and regions within nations are also having these characters imposed on them – I see, from a quick search, that 

New York

 and the 

Brandenburg

 area of Germany both have their own “czars”.




And the new infrastructure of zio-control also extends to the supranational level, as we saw with Latin America.










I 

wrote

 nearly three years ago about Katharina von Schnurbein (

pictured

), who was appointed the first “European Commission Coordinator on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life” in December 2015.




Her great achievement seems to have been to have whipped up the spectre of “anti-semitism” stalking Europe without much in the way of evidence.




In a 2019 piece singing her praises, the 

Jewish Telegraphic Agency

 

enthused

: “Some of the most shocking headlines about anti-Semitism in Europe since 2015 came from work promoted by von Schnurbein, who began working at the European Union in 2002 as a press officer”.




Von Schnurbein has also been trying to identify – or rather invent! – “new forms” of anti-semitism involving anything to do with noticing conspiracies, such as during the Covid scam, 

announcing

: “Where conspiracy grows, antisemitism has already grown”.




She has been 

quoted

 as saying that bake sales by EU staff to raise funds for humanitarian relief, including Red Cross activity in Gaza, fuelled “ambient antisemitism”.




And in 2025 she claimed that anti-zionism is “anti-semitic” because holding Jews collectively responsible for the actions of Israel is anti-semitic – obscuring the actual reality that 

only zionists

 equate Israel and its actions with 

all

 Jewish people!










Von Schnurbein is also heavily involved at the global level of the zionist “anti-semitism” agenda, in the shape of the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Network run by the World Jewish Congress (WJC).




The WJC website 

states

 that SECCA “brings together government-appointed officials, Jewish community leaders, and international partners, including European Commission, the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (

UNESCO

), to coordinate responses to antisemitism and strengthen protections for Jewish life worldwide”.




It was 

launched

 in Bucharest, the Romanian capital, in 2019 at an event “held to coincide with the WJC’s 6th National Community Directors forum, an annual gathering of the top representatives of WJC’s affiliated communities aimed at discussing the key issues facing Jewish communities today”.




We learn: “After a private meeting of the special envoys and coordinators, the two forums reconvened to exchange ideas and experiences. In his address to the joint session, WJC CEO and Executive Vice President Robert Singer said: ‘I know that this extraordinary gathering will be an important watershed moment in our common struggle to help eliminate antisemitism, whether openly expressed or masked behind the façade of anti-Zionism'”.




The 

seventh

 SECCA meeting in three years was in Jerusalem in 2022 and “held in cooperation with the ministry of foreign affairs of Israel and the European Commission”. 










In May 2026, as world opinion of genocidal Israel sank still further, SECCA 

summoned to Geneva

 “32 Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism from more than two dozen countries and international organizations”.




A joint statement was issued, “signed by representatives from the United States, European nations, Israel, Australia, Canada, the Organization of American States, OSCE [Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe], European Commission, the Council of Europe and others”.




This claimed that “antisemitism is no longer a marginal phenomenon, but an escalating global threat targeting Jewish communities, democratic values, and the foundations of free societies” and called for “strengthened security for Jewish communities, prosecution of antisemitic offenders, expanded Holocaust education, and coordinated international action to combat the spread of antisemitic hatred online and offline”.




SECCA’s most recent meeting was in Dublin on October 14 2026. The website 

tells us

: “The gathering, which included visits to the European headquarters of Tik Tok and Meta, brought dozens of representatives of WJC-affiliated Jewish communities and organizations together with 39 government delegates from 28 countries and representatives from seven multilateral institutions”.










Noah Shack (

pictured

), CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (CIJA) in Canada, “outlined recent government measures to address the escalating threat, including new criminal legislation targeting hate-motivated offenses and intimidation, increased funding for Jewish communal security, strengthened reporting and accountability mechanisms, and greater recognition of antisemitism expressed through anti-Zionist rhetoric.




“While acknowledging these developments as important steps, he emphasized the need to translate legislative and political commitments into effective enforcement and lasting protections”.




Rather tellingly, regarding the UK, the zionist Anti-Defamation League’s Nicole Mutchnik “briefed participants on the J7’s recent work, including its conversations with the UK’s Foreign Secretary on Monday. Michael Wegier, CEO of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, shared that the group would hold further discussions at Downing Street and at the BBC upon their return to London following the Forum”.




In case you were wondering, the J7 

describes itself

 as “The Large Communities’ Task Force Against Antisemitism” and is “comprised of the seven largest Diaspora Jewish communities”, those being in the USA, Canada, Argentina, the UK, France, Germany and Australia.










Although in Dublin “the bulk of the Forum was held under Chatham House rules” – for more on that secretive body I would refer readers to my 

2024 investigation

 – we are told that the SECCA event had “a focus on AI and on the regulation of online platforms”.




This, of course, is nothing to do with silencing critics of Israel and the global zio-imperialist system, but all about countering “extremist political movements”, “the broader threat that antisemitism poses to democratic societies” and protecting “Jewish life globally”.




I found it very interesting that SECCA’s logo incorporates a “globe” symbol which, particularly in the WJC context, I would say obviously depicts two seven-branched Jewish menorahs.










Is it anti-semitic conspiracy theory regarding worldwide Jewish control of the financial system to observe that the similar World Bank logo also has seven branches (four vertical and three horizontal)?










We should be quite clear that ZIM’s domination represents a 

grave existential threat

 to 99.8% of humankind living today and to all our descendants to come.




It is 

essential

 that we all continue speaking out and standing firm against its tyranny, despite all the repression and censorship it is rolling out.




The struggle against ZIM is a struggle against genocide, war, exploitation, environmental destruction, usury, propaganda, authoritarianism, child trafficking, paedocriminality and arrogant supremacism.




And it is a struggle 

for

 truth, nature, beauty, decency, freedom and life!

author: Muximba da Silva
title: ‘Essas queimadas destroem os sonhos da gente’: O Amapá sob incêndios e o El Niño
content:
Era 6 de outubro de 2026. O dia estava mais quente que o normal. Maria Tavares havia viajado do município de Tartarugalzinho, estado do Amapá, para votar no 1.º turno das eleições de 2026 na capital, Macapá. Cerca de 228 km percorridos. Quando saiu de casa, deixou o esposo e os filhos cuidando da roça da família. No local, plantações de limão, caju, ameixa, macaxeira e outros frutos da terra que são divididos entre subsistência e fonte de renda para a comunidade de Ponta do Socorro, zona no entorno da Reserva Biológica do Lago Piratuba. Aí vieram as queimadas.




Foi através de uma mensagem no celular que Maria recebeu a notícia. “Um vizinho veio avisar meu esposo que o fogo estava vindo e que ia passar, atravessar a estrada. Aí os meninos foram pra lá [a roça da família], meus filhos, e quando chegaram lá já estava pegando fogo”, relata. O esposo, Paulo Brito, é da família que fundou a comunidade e, junto de Maria e dos filhos, fazem parte da Associação de Agricultores da comunidade.




O que as 57 famílias de Ponta do Socorro estão vivendo faz parte de um aumento expressivo nos incêndios no Amapá.

 Dados do BDQueimadas, do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), revelam que entre 1º de agosto e 16 de novembro de 2026, foram registrados 2.152 focos de calor, quase quatro vezes o que foi medido no mesmo período de 2025, com 569 focos. O levantamento considera as detecções do satélite de referência utilizado pelo programa. Um foco de calor é o registro feito por satélites de um ponto na superfície com temperatura muito alta, que indica um incêndio.




“É uma sensação de impotência saber que tudo que a gente lutou anos para construir, agora ver queimado, destruído, é muito triste.

 “Foi a primeira vez que queimou tudo assim, eu fiquei muito triste, até chorei porque é doloroso a gente ter as coisas da gente, lutar pra ter, e acontecer isso, né?! Essas queimadas destroem os sonhos da gente também”, diz Tavares.




O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo

O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo

O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo

O que sobrou da roça da família Tavares após a passagem do fogo




Os números colocam o Amapá como o estado com o maior aumento percentual de focos de calor entre os nove estados da Amazônia Legal.

 Tartarugalzinho, no período analisado, teve 227 focos, quase o dobro em relação a 2025.




Dados do Núcleo de Hidrometeorologia e Energia Renováveis (NHMET-Iepa) revelam que, em setembro, o Amapá atingiu uma média de temperaturas acima de 34 ºC, sendo a maior dos últimos 58 anos. 

“No mês de outubro foram registrados picos de elevações de temperatura ultrapassando os 38 °C, juntamente com a umidade relativa que ficou abaixo dos 30%, que é considerada uma umidade de climas desérticos.

 Isso se deve à intensidade do El Niño, que está intensificando o período de estiagem na nossa região”, comenta o meteorologista Jefferson Vilhena, pesquisador do NHMET-Iepa.




Segundo o quinto boletim do Painel El Niño, publicado pelo Inmet, entre novembro de 2026 e janeiro de 2027, o fenômeno pode levar a temperaturas acima da média em quase todo o país e chuvas abaixo da média em grande parte da Região Norte. O episódio pode ser o mais intenso desde 1950.




Agravados pelo El Niño, incêndios estão ligados à ação humana




Renato Hilário, professor e pesquisador da Universidade Federal do Amapá, explica que esse cenário é propício para o aumento das queimadas no estado. 

“O fenômeno pode favorecer condições ambientais que facilitam a propagação do fogo. Isso acontece porque o El Niño intensifica a estação seca em diferentes regiões da Amazônia, reduzindo a umidade da vegetação.

 Com a vegetação mais seca, o fogo consegue se espalhar com maior facilidade, fazendo com que os incêndios atinjam áreas maiores e se tornem mais difíceis de controlar”, explica.




No entanto, Hilário explica que o fogo não deve ser colocado apenas na conta do El Niño. “Embora possam ocorrer incêndios de origem natural na Amazônia, provocados principalmente por raios, esses eventos são relativamente raros. A grande maioria dos incêndios que observamos na região tem origem em atividades humanas. Nesse sentido, o El Niño não é o principal responsável pelo início dos incêndios, já que a origem do fogo está predominantemente relacionada à ação humana”.




Segundo dados enviados pelo Ibama à reportagem, a distribuição dos focos de calor mostra que 650 registros ocorreram em áreas ocupadas por propriedades privadas, o equivalente a 29,5% do total.

 Outros 411 foram identificados em terras públicas federais sem destinação (18,6%), 282 em projetos de assentamento (12,8%), 273 em unidades de conservação federais (12,4%) e 260 em terras indígenas (11,8%).
















No Oiapoque, o fogo também atingiu grandes áreas, como as terras indígenas Uaça e Jumniã




A superintendente do Ibama no Amapá, Débora Thomaz, explica que 

parte das queimadas está relacionada ao uso do fogo para preparar áreas de cultivo, uma prática tradicional na região.

 A atividade, porém, precisa de autorização municipal e acompanhamento das brigadas para evitar que as chamas se espalhem. “Quando nós não somos chamados é muito complicado, porque a força do vento precisa ser monitorada, a direção do vento precisa ser monitorada, o combustível precisa ser analisado”, afirma.




Thomaz também alerta para casos em que responsáveis por áreas autorizadas a desmatar ultrapassam os limites permitidos. “A gente pede para que os empreendedores não tentem fazer esse esticamento, essa coisinha de ‘vou mais umas duas árvores, mais três árvores’. Isso está sendo acompanhado em tempo real e serão responsabilizados, sim, aqueles que cometerem esse tipo de infração”.




Alerta de emergência no Amapá




Em 16 de outubro de 2026, o governo do Amapá decretou situação de emergência em todo o estado, por 180 dias, em razão da estiagem.

 A medida ocorreu após a suspensão do uso do fogo em áreas rurais e urbanas, estabelecida em 1º de setembro e válida até 30 de novembro, com exceções previstas para determinadas atividades, como práticas agrícolas de subsistência de povos e comunidades tradicionais, desde que autorizadas e supervisionadas. 

Quatro dias depois, o governo federal também reconheceu a situação de emergência em 14 municípios amapaenses.




O decreto de situação de emergência permite que o Estado receba auxílio para agir no combate aos focos de incêndio 




Já em 19 de outubro, o Ministério da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional autorizou R$ 4,1 milhões para ações de resposta à estiagem no Amapá. Desse total, mais de R$ 3 milhões foram destinados ao governo estadual e quase R$ 1 milhão à Prefeitura de Tartarugalzinho. Segundo a 

Secretaria de Estado do Meio Ambiente

 (Sema), a Região dos Lagos, que abrange Tartarugalzinho, Amapá e Pracuúba, historicamente apresenta maior incidência de focos de incêndio durante o período de estiagem, em razão das altas temperaturas e da redução dos níveis dos rios.




No distrito do Aporema, localizado no município, uma escola da rede estadual precisou fechar as portas e mandar os alunos para casa. 

O cheiro da fumaça tem invadido as salas de aula e os espaços onde os alunos se alimentam, provocando tosses, espirros e crises de asma nas crianças.

 “A mesa, que a gente limpava de vez em quando, agora de minutos em minutos a gente está limpando, porque é um pó misturado com poeira, com resto de fuligem que vem das queimadas”, conta a moradora.




A fumaça é uma das preocupações da Vigilância em Saúde do Amapá. Mas os efeitos da estiagem agravada pelo El Niño também afetam o abastecimento de água. Solange Sacramento, gerente do Centro de Informações Estratégicas e Respostas em Vigilância em Saúde do Estado (CIEVS-AP), chama atenção: “Pode aumentar os riscos de doenças diarreicas e outros problemas relacionados ao consumo de água imprópria”, afirma.




Sacramento destaca que comunidades ribeirinhas, indígenas, quilombolas e rurais merecem atenção especial, sobretudo quando enfrentam dificuldades de abastecimento de água ou de deslocamento até os serviços de saúde.

 “Entre os grupos mais vulneráveis estão crianças, idosos, gestantes, pessoas com asma, doenças pulmonares crônicas e problemas cardiovasculares”, ressalta.




A reportagem procurou a Defesa Civil estadual e a Prefeitura de Tartarugalzinho para saber como os recursos estão sendo aplicados, quais comunidades estão sendo atendidas e se os valores são suficientes diante da dimensão dos impactos, mas não obteve resposta. A Secretaria Municipal de Saúde do município também foi procurada, mas não deu retorno até a publicação.




Uma estiagem diferente da esperada




O calor não costuma surpreender quem vive no Amapá. Com a chegada do segundo semestre, os sinais da estiagem já são conhecidos: o preço do açaí sobe, o suor escorre pela testa de quem enfrenta o sol nas ruas das cidades e as sombras das árvores se tornam ainda mais valiosas. 

É um período ao qual os amapaenses já estão acostumados. Mas, nos últimos anos, até aquilo que parecia previsível tem dado sinais de mudança.




No estado, o período de estiagem costuma começar em agosto e se estender até novembro. É a época que interrompe a estação chuvosa e reforça a seca. 

Segundo o meteorologista Jefferson Vilhena, setembro e outubro são os meses mais secos, quando os acumulados de chuva podem chegar perto de zero. Mas em 2026, as previsões apontam que os sinais de chuva chegarão mais tarde.

 “Os modelos meteorológicos e climáticos já estão apontando que o período chuvoso deve ocorrer somente no mês de dezembro, o que normalmente aconteceria já no mês de novembro”, diz.
















“Não tem nem 1 metro de água aí. Você olha assim, mas não tem nem 1 metro de água de tão seco. E no fundo dá pra ver a fumaça”, diz Maria Tavares, sobre o Igarapé Terra Firme




Para Talita Tavares, bióloga e filha de Maria Tavares, da comunidade de Ponta do Socorro, a estiagem deste ano está sendo mais severa para os povos amazônidas devido à interação com a crise climática e as mudanças no fenômeno El Niño. “Nas nossas comunidades na Amazônia, aquelas que dependem diretamente dos rios e da floresta, significa que toda a condição básica de sobrevivência daquele território está comprometida, porque quando os rios baixam, o acesso dessas comunidades fica mais difícil, o deslocamento para chegar é mais caro, é mais demorado e o acesso à água é comprometido”, reforça.




Tavares também chama a atenção para a sobrevivência de comunidades que dependem dos rios. “Comunidades pesqueiras, por exemplo, além da perda do transporte, essas pessoas também perdem a principal fonte de alimento que elas possuem, que é onde está o peixe, onde elas vão conseguir se alimentar. Então a gente encontra um desafio de abastecimento, de alimento mesmo, que produz prejuízos econômicos e uma extrema insegurança alimentar”, diz.




A bióloga é diretora administrativa do Instituto Mapinguari, organização amapaense que atua para promover a conservação da Amazônia. O Instituto representou a sociedade civil amapaense na COP31, levando experiências do estado e propostas para o debate internacional sobre adaptação climática.




Na conferência, a organização pautou a necessidade de que decisões internacionais reconheçam o papel dos governos locais, garantam participação social e ampliem o acesso ao financiamento climático. “A Amazônia não pode ser o território onde o mundo decide o que o que vai ser feito, como vai ser feito. A gente, como a Amazônia, precisa ser protagonista nessas decisões”, aponta Tavares.




A partir de janeiro de 2027, a responsabilidade sobre a adaptação climática no Amapá estará sob a gestão de Dr. Furlan (PSD), eleito governador em outubro. 

Contudo, 

no plano de governo

 apresentado para o mandato de 2027 a 2030, não aparecem, entre as propostas, ações diretas para a crise climática e para a redução dos focos de calor.




Uma busca por palavras no documento revela que “clima”, “crise climática” e “El Niño” não são mencionados, enquanto “queimada” também não aparece. A palavra “incêndio” é citada uma vez em referência a causa do apagão de 2020 e a palavra “calor”, também única, é citada para relatar a sensação de afeto que o político sentiu quando se mudou para o estado. Em contraste, “petróleo” aparece 25 vezes no plano.




No eixo dedicado ao meio ambiente e à bioeconomia, a proposta de Furlan é que a política ambiental deixe de ser vista como um órgão de fiscalização e punição e passe a atuar como “uma engrenagem de desenvolvimento econômico”. O documento também prevê acelerar a emissão de licenças ambientais e autorizações para supressão vegetal.




A cidade do petróleo, os territórios preservados e o aumento fora da curva nos focos de calor




O “cuidado” dado ao petróleo no plano de gestão de Furlan está relacionado à expectativa que já movimenta Oiapoque, a cidade mais próxima da área de exploração na Foz do Amazonas.




Uma apuração feita pelo veículo 

Seles Nafes

 aponta que pelo menos sete novos bairros foram criados na cidade nos últimos dois anos. Dados da Sema, publicados no Diário Oficial em 11 de fevereiro de 2025, indicam que 98,96% do território de Oiapoque está abrangido por unidades de conservação e terras indígenas. Dos 23 mil km² de área municipal considerados no levantamento, 22,7 mil km² correspondem a áreas protegidas.




Durante sobrevoos em Oiapoque, equipes do Ibama identificaram grandes manchas de queimadas próximas às Terras Indígenas Juminã e Uaçá. Uma delas foi estimada em cerca de 7 mil hectares. “Essas comunidades vivem da flora e da fauna. E no momento que a gente tem esse tamanho de devastação, a gente tem uma perda muito grande não só ambiental, mas também social”, afirma a superintendente.




Durante inspeção, equipe do Ibama flagra uma grande queimada nas proximidades das Terras Indígenas Juminã e Uaçá




A situação em Oiapoque acendeu um alerta por fugir do padrão histórico de ocorrências no estado. “Geralmente, quem chama mais a atenção é a região dos Lagos, Amapá e Tartarugalzinho. Mas, nas últimas duas semanas, Oiapoque se destacou negativamente pelo número exponencial de focos de calor e de incêndio”, afirma Helder Souza, chefe do Centro de Comunicação Social do Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Amapá. Segundo ele, o aumento das ocorrências levou à instalação de uma sala de situação com participação de diferentes órgãos para coordenar o combate aos incêndios e reduzir os impactos da fumaça sobre a população. O Ibama também montou uma estrutura de monitoramento na comunidade do Manga, para coordenar as ações da Operação Manga, e deslocou 30 dos seus 60 brigadistas para o município.




A Amazônia em chamas enquanto a COP31 acontecia




A 31ª edição da COP aconteceu em Antalya, na Turquia, neste mês de novembro. O evento reuniu diferentes países para debater o avanço das políticas climáticas e dar continuidade aos acordos feitos no ano passado em Belém, na COP30. 

No entanto, o evento terminou sem um consenso político e sem a aprovação do Pacto de Antalya, documento que deveria reunir os principais encaminhamentos das negociações e apontar caminhos para o enfrentamento da crise climática.
















Anália Barreto, diretora executiva do Instituto Mapinguari, esteve em Antalya, na Turquia para acompanhar a 31ª edição da COP




“Estamos falando de uma contradição muito profunda. A ciência demonstra que precisamos reduzir rapidamente as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, mas os países continuam enfrentando enormes dificuldades para estabelecer caminhos concretos para abandonar os combustíveis fósseis, que são os principais responsáveis pelo aquecimento global”, comenta a jornalista Anália Barreto, diretora executiva do Instituto Mapinguari.




O aumento exponencial de focos de calor na Amazônia também está relacionado com a queima de combustíveis fósseis, uma vez que a queima contribui para o aquecimento global que, por sua vez, interferem em fenômenos naturais, como o El Niño. “O problema é que esse fenômeno acontece hoje em um planeta que já está significativamente mais quente em consequência das atividades humanas, especialmente da queima de combustíveis fósseis e do desmatamento. Isso significa que os efeitos de uma estiagem podem ser muito mais graves, porque temperaturas elevadas aumentam a evaporação da água e intensificam o ressecamento da vegetação e do solo”, explica Barreto.




Na COP30, o Instituto publicou um manifesto que aponta um distanciamento entre o que é decidido internacionalmente e o que é aplicado nos territórios. “No Brasil, essa contradição aparece de maneira muito evidente. Ao mesmo tempo em que o país busca exercer uma liderança internacional na agenda climática, seguimos discutindo a ampliação da exploração de petróleo, inclusive na Margem Equatorial, e acompanhamos movimentos de flexibilização da legislação ambiental”, conclui Barreto.

title: Résistances au Colonialisme Vert
content:
Mardi 8 décembre de 19h à 21h, table Ronde avec Verónica Chávez, Beatriz Perea et Oriana Mora. À la Bourse du Travail - 3 rue du Château d'eau - Paris 10

e




 

 

 

 




Le 8 décembre 2026, nous avons l'honneur d'accueillir Verónica Chávez, figure majeure de la lutte des peuples autochtones, ainsi que Beatriz Perea et Oriana Mora, trois défenseuses des territoires venues d'Argentine et du Chili, qui partageront les réalités difficiles auxquelles leurs communautés sont confrontées, mais aussi la dignité de leurs luttes et de leurs résistances.




Elles viennent en Europe pour porter la lutte qu'elles mènent dans ce que l'on appelle le triangle du lithium, entre l'Argentine, le Chili et la Bolivie, où se déroule une nouvelle offensive coloniale sur les territoires des peuples autochtones.




Cette offensive se présente sous les habits de la transition énergétique, au service d'une économie qui prétend devenir «

 

verte

 

» sans pour autant renoncer au pillage.




Les territoires autochtones de cette région sont une fois de plus transformés en zones de sacrifice, où l'eau qui fait vivre les populations, la mémoire ancestrale et l'avenir de communautés entières sont subordonnés aux intérêts de ceux qui ne voient dans ces terres que des minerais stratégiques pour la transition énergétique.




La justice globale ne naît pas des discours des puissants, mais de la rencontre entre les peuples qui résistent.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Aesthetics, Technology, and Politics in the 2026 Local Elections
content:
THE 2026 LOCAL ELECTIONS have been marked by distinctive and innovative campaigning by the DPP, mostly related to the “Ocean Current” phenomenon. In many ways, the “Ocean Current” phenomenon and the aesthetic and political experimentation it entailed carried out the logical development of aesthetic and political tendencies that date back to the Sunflower Movement. But in the vast amount of aesthetic and cultural references it included, one can also point to how the “Ocean Current” phenomenon reflects contemporary Taiwanese identity trends–as well as its incorporation of data analytics into its political aesthetic.

The most distinctive feature of the “Ocean Current” is perhaps the distinctive ribbon associated with Puma Shen supporters. Many design variations of this ribbon exist, which are released periodically and available openly for supporters to make variations on.

Craze around such ribbons is such that Shen supporters will crowd for hours at DPP city councilor offices, cafes, and other places where limited-edition designs will be released. Especially popular variations are those which involve animal designs, rainbows, or other prominent symbols.

A post shared by Sheena Wu (@nanawuco)

Indeed, the term “Ocean Current” originates with two designers, Ken and Hsu Chia-lun. A poster made by the two designers for Shen gained attention on social media, leading the DPP to seek permission to use the name for the two designers. But, in this sense, many designers have contributed their own poster designs to the “Ocean Current” phenomenon, printing them out and distributing them personally, or distributing them at rallies.

The distinctive “merch” of the “Ocean Current,” then, perhaps takes advantage of the craze of contemporary Taiwanese for merch. Craze for anime collectibles is such that even convenience stores sell and distribute limited-edition anime merchandise. And election collectibles were already a feature of the political landscape, dating back to democratization. The craze about election collectibles is such that Shen will even have areas set up in his political rallies for supporters to trade campaign merch. Nevertheless, from this, one can observe the open, participatory, and tactile nature of the “Ocean Current” phenomenon.

Indeed, Puma Shen emphasized a campaign that, in some form, emphasized expertise, in that Shen often brandished his academic expertise as a researcher in analyzing data to formulate policy. Yet often the focus was on collecting data and opinions from members of the citizenry and communicating them in an open and transparent manner.

Shen used his campaign website in order to collect opinions and what issues the public cared about through the “Mayor, Listen to Me!” platform. This at times led to surprising conclusions, such as discovering that members of the Taipei public were concerned with the decreasing amount of greenery in the urban landscape. Shen collected over 70,000 responses, which were organized according to local area, allowing Shen to come up with specifically tailored policy proposals. The website was gamified and featured interactive cartoon animal characters.

Shen’s campaign website, then, was used to publicize the platforms he came up with. The “Heart Island” website, which resembled Animal Crossing or similar online games and contained detailed policy briefs, was in itself interactive and engaging, as a presentation of policy platforms within a microcosm depicting the city itself. Shen can be found wandering the depiction himself–reportedly along with competitor Chiang Wan-an.

Likewise, one notes the emergence of several websites that compiled lists and maps of stores in Taipei considered pro-Taiwan, pan-Green, or supportive of the “Ocean Current”, such as a store tracker that centered the Shen campaign, and another with a more pro-Taiwan theme.

To this extent, in line with the tactile nature of the “Ocean Current”’s merch, well-designed print publications detailing these policy platforms were distributed by Shen at campaign stops in the form of campaign newspapers. What’s more, however, was that this was not merely a newsletter. Zine versions of the same policy platforms were also rolled out, incorporating the work of writers, artists, designers, and other creatives. An online music contest was also held by the Shen campaign to gather fan-made anthems, similar to past online music contests held by Tsai Ing-wen.

Campaign rallies by Shen, then, have sought to emphasize this participatory nature of policymaking–interestingly enough, seeing as Shen is a politician who emerged in the wake of the 2014 Sunflower Movement, such rallies drew together many of the threads of the 2014 Sunflower Movement when it came to experimentation with street-level direct democracy. Shen has often taken direct questions from the public, for example, and responded at length with detailed local policy proposals–taking advantage of his now well-known strengths in public speaking. To show that this is not scripted, Shen not only takes questions from an online QR code system, but also through paper Q-and-A ballots drawn from a box.

Indeed, there were a number of post-Sunflower politicians that rejected the empty sloganeering of traditional campaigning, in which a political ad might simply have a slogan and no detail about policy. If there were efforts to have more speeches that incorporated discussion of policy proposals, or to put QR codes with links to full policy platforms on campaign ads, this often bored members of the public. But through his strong public speaking skills and the dynamic showmanship of his rallies, Shen has managed to make what would otherwise be dry policy appealing and engaging to members of the public.

And as with other post-Sunflower electoral rallies, one has often seen costumes and musical performances at Shen rallies. These have often involved various pro-Taiwan, youth-oriented bands. Apart from costumes such as, say, sheep costumes riffing off of the last character in Shen’s name, Shen has also termed his supporters–members of the “Ocean Current”–to be “Little Droplets.” This is not so different than how Ko Wen-je of the TPP created an identity for his supporters by terming them “Little Grass.”

But more broadly speaking, the “Ocean Current” phenomenon has had an oceanic and maritime theme. Shen has frequently dressed in cosplay as a captain, then holding various maritime props on-stage. A frequent sound effect at his rallies is the sound of a ship’s bullhorn as it pulls into harbor.

The suggestion is that Shen is a candidate leading Taiwan to a better future. The Japanese anime One Piece, about youthful, freedom-loving pirates fighting against a tyrannical world government, is a frequent point of allusion along with this maritime theme, as well as because Shen has been open about his love of anime.

Shen is not the first Taiwanese political candidate to play off of anime references as a means of making themselves more relatable to the public. One recalls former legislator Lai Pin-yu, for example, who was open about her love of cosplay, and would appear at campaign events in cosplay. Like Lai, Shen has alluded to many times to his love of postmodern mecha anime Neon Genesis Evangelion.

Unsurprisingly, then, one has seen the incorporation of anime props into rallies. Apart from that, senior DPP figures have gifted him maritime props, such as a telescope used for maritime navigation, to signal support; President Lai Ching-te would gift Shen an anime-style European hero’s sword. Shen and other DPP candidates also wear Japanese-style Happi coats during rallies, highlighting their festive, carnivalesque nature. At times, the use of anime-inspired campaigning props has led pan-Blue media to lash out at the DPP with the accusation that they remain culturally beholden to Japanese colonialism.

Insofar as it is the “Ocean Current” phenomenon that truly defined the current election cycle, other DPP candidates have been buoyed by Shen’s popularity. Shen has, consequently, been called on to make campaign stops to back them across Taiwan.

But, in this sense, other DPP candidates have largely drawn from the aesthetic tropes set by the “Ocean Current” phenomenon. A campaign ad featuring DPP New Taipei mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui, who was already running a competitive race and for whom the “Ocean Current” phenomenon may push to victory, is designed to be viewed on two iPhones next to each other, with one ad featuring Su and another featuring Shen. The ad depicts Su and Shen as parallels who studied in graduate school in the US at the same time but gave up comfortable lives there in order to benefit Taiwan.

Though not necessarily drawing from the same aesthetic tropes, another distinctive ad, featuring Kaohsiung DPP mayoral candidate Lai Jui-lung, highlights Lai as an everyman who could be anyone in the city–depicting Lai as members of the citizenry interrogating him about his policy.

By contrast, the KMT has struggled when it comes to aesthetic innovation in the present election cycle. In an examination of messaging from the KMT, there is a reliance on historical photos referencing Sun Yat-sen and AI-generated images. This is not surprising in consideration of the fact that it is the DPP that has clearly set the tone for the present election cycle.

Certainly, the Shen campaign has probably benefited from the significant extent to which the KMT has outraged creatives in past years. Through gutting cultural funding and dismissing artists, designers, musicians, and other creatives as “beggars”, the KMT has turned an industry of people whose jobs are to communicate ideas against them. The strength of the Shen campaign’s design aesthetics may be, in this sense, roosters coming home to nest.

But, more broadly, one observes how the Shen campaign has expanded and built on themes seen in election campaigning after the Sunflower Movement–while also incorporating digital technologies to allow for transparency, openness, and participatory governance. This shows how the “Ocean Current” phenomenon does not occur apropos of nothing, but is the culmination of the past decade of repeated movements and elections in Taiwan.

This is reflected, too, in its aesthetics and its use of technology. The unity of aesthetics and technology as part of a campaign whose political message has been to call for transparency, accountability, and good governance dovetails with the civic hacker communities that Shen is linked to as g0v. Organizations he founded, such as the Doublethink Lab and Kuma Academy, as Taiwan’s premier disinformation research organization and civil defense organization, originate from the primordial soup of communities as g0v. It may not be surprising to see this reflected in Shen’s campaign aesthetics, then.

author: By Osiris Castañeda, Contributor
title: Line 5 Reroute Threatens the Wetlands of the Bad River Watershed
content:
Ashland County, Wisconsin — April Stone walks along a stretch of the highly controversial and dangerous 

Line 5 reroute

. “This is the Line 5 reroute,” she says. “It’s a 41-mile swath of cut land going around the whole Reservation.”




The Enbridge Line 5 is a 645-mile pipeline that pumps crude oil and natural gas from Superior, Wisconsin into Ontario, Canada. This recent reroute cuts through forests, wetlands, and swamps surrounding the Bad River Reservation in northern Wisconsin.




Stone, an Ojibwe Black Ash basket weaver and member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, has witnessed the loss of Black Ash harvesting areas along the Line 5 reroute. She walks into a wetland where standing water pools beneath the trees with the exposed pipeline corridor.




“There’s a small creek that’s running here,” she explains. “It’s a saturated area. It has more standing water than the uplands all around.”
















It’s in these wetlands, adjacent to Lake Superior, where one can find Black Ash trees thriving.




Indigenous peoples throughout the Great Lakes have harvested Black Ash to create traditional baskets, pack frames, fishing gear, and storage containers. Stone harvests her own trees from these swamps.




“That’s where the Black Ash trees were growing,” she says. “Where I have harvested trees in the past for my baskets.”




Today, many of those trees are gone. “When they took this swath in here … they cut through the Ash swamp as well,” Stone says. She points toward Black Ash trees tagged in pink. “There are still some standing Ash trees, but many of them are cut down.”




Stone is recognized as one of the foremost Black Ash basket makers in the Great Lakes area.




She began teaching herself basketry after discovering that there weren’t any practicing Black Ash basket weavers left in her own tribal community. Stone is one of the last Black Ash basket weavers of the Bad River Band, making her work central to preserving a cultural tradition that had nearly disappeared.




Stone’s baskets embody ecological knowledge, harvesting practices, language, ceremony, and a relationship with wetlands that can not exist without healthy forests. That relationship now faces a huge threat.




The proposed Line 5 re-route was designed after the Bad River Band went to court against Enbridge for criminally trespassing on tribal land. The giant oil company’s lease had expired and was not being renewed. As a response to the court loss and despite the environmental dangers, Enbridge began constructing 41 miles of new pipeline — surrounding most of the Bad River Reservation.




Although the reroute technically avoids reservation boundaries, it remains inside the Bad River watershed and covers almost three-quarters of the Reservation boundaries. According to environmental permitting documents processed by the Army Corps of Engineers, construction of the pipeline re-route would cross 186 streams, rivers, and other waterways, covering more than 100 acres of wetlands.




The corridor also requires clearing forests through numerous wetlands where Black Ash trees grow.




Line 5 Pipeline Reroute Endangers Maple Trees and Native Lifeways




Stone says those impacts cannot be separated from what happens downstream.




Describing how water connects the entire watershed, Stone continued, “The Reservation itself makes up the lower-third portion of the entire watershed. All the water that flows from the lakes, from the streams, from the rivers… eventually all of it goes into Bad River… eventually all of it goes through the Reservation… out into Lake Superior.”




Although this wetland nourishes one of the largest freshwater ecosystems on Earth, for the Bad River Band, the watershed is not simply geography. It is home to one of the Ojibwe’s most important cultural relations — Manoomin (wild rice).




Wild rice thrives on the clean fresh lake water and is a precious food source that is inextricably tied to Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) origin stories and prophecies. The rice is legally and culturally seen as a spiritual “relative” and a foundational gift from the Creator that ensured their survival.




“Line 5 has split this swamp in two,” Stone says. But she isn’t only talking about wetlands.




“Not just here, but everywhere else along the 41-mile span where swamps exist.”




To Stone, the pipeline corridor divides more than the natural habitat. These are places where people have harvested together and passed on traditional ecological knowledge for generations.




When the swamp is cut apart, cultural and intergenerational learning risks being lost as well.




The Black Ash, the wetlands, and the water are all connected. What happens to one affects the others.




When a leak from Line 5 reaches the watershed, there is nowhere for that contamination to simply stop. Water carries it toward Bad River and eventually toward Lake Superior.




Protecting the watershed means protecting the future of Bad River itself.

author: Renfrey Clarke
title: Palestine activists protest Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce lunch
content:
Sixty members and supporters of the Palestinian community protested outside the Australia-Israel Chamber of Commerce (AICC) business luncheon on November 27 demanding that Israel end its genocide on Gaza.

The AICC is deeply embedded in Australian collaboration with Israel on arms production, much of which is centred in this city.

Organisations taking part included Adelaide University Students for Palestine. The university was a sponsor of the event and its Vice Chancellor was the guest speaker.

AICC promotes business with Israel’s military-industrial complex, including Elbit Systems and Rafael, and corporations involved in weapons, surveillance and illegal settlements.

The protesters demanded an end to the normalising of war crimes; an end to Adelaide University sponsorship of AICC; and an end to apartheid.

author: Wendy Bacon
title: CAMouflage: Antisemitism conference for councils
content:
Several hundred people gathered at Martin Place on November 24 to oppose this week’s national Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM) Local Government Summit that will urge councils to impose the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism on communities.

The protest was organised by a number of pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist Jewish groups, including Palestine Justice Movement and Jews Against the Occupation ‘48 (JAO48), who defiantly vowed to continue fighting against Israel’s genocidal war and apartheid.

If the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition is enforced, the six speakers would face allegations of antisemitism. Those holding banners stating “Globalise the Intifada” and “Readers and Writers against Genocide” could be arrested if proposed laws, that CAM supports, are passed. All the speakers rejected CAM’s claim that anti-Zionism is antisemitism.

The protest included an absurdist theatre performance — CAM-ou FLAGE — created by the JAO ‘48. It effectively called out CAM, which purports to be about building social cohesion but which is more likely to add to social division, censorship and hierarchies of social discrimination.

By contrast, the conference itself quietly kicked off with welcome drinks and speeches at Bondi Surf Club, not far from the site of the Bondi massacre.

The first speaker was Sheina Gutnick, whose father, Reuven Morrison, was killed by the gunmen. Not long after the massacre, CAM appointed her as its public affairs officer.

Other opening night speakers included Tahli Blicblau, former director of strategic intelligence and capabilities at the NSW Crime Commission, now CEO of the Dor Foundation, which was established by ex-Liberal Treasurer Josh Frydenberg.

Another was David Solsky, who organised a hugely successful memorial Paddle Out after the massacre. He also spoke at last week’s Jerusalem Post Summit, encouraging investment in Israel.

The opening attracted about the same numbers as those who attended the protest. The conference organisers seem to have gone out of their way to avoid attention by keeping its locations secret, or perhaps to amplify the sense of threat. The newly-formed Armed Response Command attended.

Whereas the protesters issued a media release, which was ignored by mainstream media, CAM issued no such thing in the lead-up to its conference.

The silence stands in stark contrast to last year’s conference. That was organised in collaboration with PR agency Agenda C, which boasted that it achieved 972 media mentions.

This year’s media strategy was executed around Gutnick’s story, about turning the loss of her father into a constructive purpose. Gutnick told the Daily Telegraph: “If anyone were actually open to having a conversation with us, understand the work that we’re doing and what we are trying to achieve against the background of the horrific antisemitism that has exploded, unfortunately, within Australia.”

She also attacked lawyer Nick Hanna who, in a video, drew attention to CAM’s association with the extremist pro-Israel and Trump supporter Congressman Randy Fine for spreading “disinformation”. He responded with a second video.

In rejecting Hanna’s focus on CAM’s global connections, Gutnick failed to mention that her work for the conference included a trip to New York, where she consulted with two Zionist members of New York City Council, who are opponents of the Muslim Mayor Zoran Mandami.

Gutnick was quoted as saying: “We find ways to come together and address [challenges] with unity and strength. CAM offers an amazing and unique international platform.”

The protest groups, including JAO48, Palestine Justice Movement, Coalition of Women for Justice and Peace, initiated a letter-writing campaign to councils and promoted this week’s protest.

CAM’s CEO in Tel Aviv, Sacha Roytman, sprang into action with an open letter calling on councillors to attend. Roytman, who was busy in the United States meeting with 150 leaders to launch a tracker to monitor CAM progress, didn’t see the contradiction in arguing that critics are unfair, while highlighting his past IDF connections and/or the activities of the Zionist lobby.

He went further, suggesting: “To me, some of the rhetoric around this campaign echoes narratives I have seen promoted internationally by actors in Iran, Qatar, China, and Russia. That resemblance is not evidence that any of those governments organised or paid for this campaign. I am asking Australian authorities to examine credible reports of intimidation against councillors, council staff, and participants. If they find evidence of organised harassment or unlawful interference, they should establish who coordinated it, who financed it, and whether anyone abroad played a role.”

Australia’s representatives on CAM’s global board include businessman David Gonski, who is chairing the conference, as well as the Special Envoy for Antisemitism Jillian Segal’s Education Taskforce.

The other three are Orna Triguboff, the daughter of Australia’s second richest person, Harry Triguboff; Charmaine Roth, the widow of the widow of pro-Israel champion and Advance donor Stanley Roth; and Maroubra dentist Ron Weiner.

Roytman insisted that these people, who live on the Eastern fringe of Sydney, need no help. “They know their communities. They need no one abroad to tell them what is at stake.”Can the CAM committee really claim to know what is at stake for communities in other parts of Australia?

According to MWM research, even an offer of 50 free places has not persuaded anyone to attend from Cumberland or Parramatta councils in Western Sydney which, between them, contain more than half a million people. Only one person is attending from Sydney’s largest LGA, Blacktown, which has almost half a million people.

By contrast, Waverley Council, which is co-hosting the conference, and Randwick and Woollahra Councils together represent about 275,000 people. They will be represented by at least 10 councillors.

Councillor Ahmed Ouf from Cumberland Council urged people at the protest to keep up the pressure on councils to pass boycott, divestment and sanctions motions to increase pressure on Israel to end its brutal occupation of Palestine. He strongly believes that believers of every faith must be free to practice their religion, and accused those attending the conference of providing cover for Zionists sanitising Israel’s genocide.

Greens Inner West Councillor Liz Atkins, another speaker at the protest, called on mayors and councillors not to attend the conference. They said it was “not a conference aimed at promoting social cohesion. It is not a conference about anti-racism. Put simply, it is a conference which lends support to Israel and to a definition of antisemitism, that aims to prevent criticism of Israel and Zionism.

“Australia has a racism problem and elevating antisemitism above all other forms of racism, including racism against First Nations people and Islamophobia is wrong.”

Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne is one of a few Labor councillors on the program. Byrne’s contribution was billed as a presentation by “Two mayors who have led their communities through real tension, on public space, protest, intimidation and local leadership under pressure.”

This is not the first time that Byrne has alleged that some Inner West residents who oppose Israel’s genocide are guilty of intimidation.

Atkins said protests for Palestine in the Inner West “have always been respectful ,despite what the mayor has said in the past. It may have been loud, it may have been angry, it may have been passionate, but it has never been hateful or antisemitic. Councillors who attend this conference will be lending support to CAM’s pro-Israel agenda and its efforts to smear the Palestine movement and attack free speech.”

Bryne has kept a low profile, unlike attendees from other councils. He did not raise the matter at council meeting or answer letters requesting him not to attend.

The conference ends on November 27, after a visit to a bakery and synagogue where Chabad Rabbis will introduce participants to Noah’s seven universal principles. These include a prohibition on adultery and a prohibition on stealing. Adherence to a legal system is mentioned, but there is no reference to human rights, equality or justice.

We assume Israel’s theft of Palestinian land, including daily attacks on the West Bank, is not included.

After lunch, the Governor General Sam Mostyn will lead a moment of reflection. There will be an affirmation of CAM’s local government agenda, including denying public spaces to those judged to be antisemitic. Councils will be required to report on what they have achieved next year.

CAM has not yet succeeded in getting most councils on board. Working with grassroots is proving much harder than working with politicians and bureaucrats. Councillors who are aware that there is solid support for Palestine or negative attitudes to Israel are understandably going to resist adopting the IHRA definition.

If they are disappointed with this year’s results, CAM may opt to push their proposal for a “National Local Government Partnership Against Antisemitism and for Social Cohesion,” delivered through the Australian Local Government Association (ALGA). In other words, it may try to impose the IHRA definition from above.

This option is canvassed in its submission to the Royal Commission on antisemiticism and social cohesion.

This is similar to the approach being used to force curriculum changes on schools, impose the IHRA or Universities Australia definition of antisemitism on universities, and adding the IHRA definition as a regulatory tool for health workers. We will see if the royal commission lends its weight to this top-down approach.

[Wendy Bacon is an investigative journalist and writes for Michael West Media, where this article was first published.]

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Inquest jury calls for more mental health support for families of police shooting victims
content:
Jury members of the inquest into 21-year-old Trey Angootealuk’s death recommended that Nunavut provide more support for the families whose loved ones have been killed by police.




The jury delivered its verdict following a four-day inquest that heard testimony from the RCMP officers who fatally shot Angootealuk in Rankin Inlet on Nov. 7, 2021, after an extended standoff with four officers in the outskirts of town.




Jurors ruled he died from a gunshot wound to the chest, and that his death was a homicide.




“Nunavut has some of the highest rates of police shootings in the country,” said Nikolai Sittmann, counsel for the Angootealuk family. “In light of this reality, it’s important that families and loved ones affected in these situations get the services and support they need.”




The jury said Nunavut’s Health Department should be responsible for creating the counselling program, with specialized trauma counsellors.




The inquest by Nunavut chief coroner Marianna Cervantes began Monday at the Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet. The jury made its recommendations Thursday afternoon.




Coroner’s inquests are mandatory in Nunavut for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. Juries do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved.
















The jury was asked to rule on the cause of his death, to provide recommendations for how to prevent deaths of similar circumstance, and to make recommendations for how police can respond in similar incidents.

 




It also recommended that Nunavut RCMP have access to Inuktitut-speaking negotiators at all times and for the territorial government and Inuit organizations to better inform citizens about the safe firearm storage.




Technical recommendations included that infrared devices be incorporated into each RCMP detachment to improve visibility in the night, as well as the introduction of modern drones.




Visibility was a challenge the morning Angootealuk was killed, officers testified, and they couldn’t use their drone to deliver a message during the standoff because it was being used to light up the truck that Angootealuk was in.




The jury also recommended that coroner’s inquests into fatal police shootings be completed within two years of the incident.




The recommendations were largely based on those provided by lawyers for the Angootealuk family, coroner and the RCMP. All three parties were in agreement.
















“In these particular circumstances, there may not have been anything exactly more that could have been done, given the danger present and the reality of the situation the ground,” said coroner’s counsel Jessi Casebeer when sharing her recommendations.




“While the recommendations may not go directly to preventing similar deaths, they will go to minimizing the harm of these types of deaths.”

title: Hesekê Asayish Command: Two of our members killed in bomb attack
content:
A security centre belonging to the Internal Security Forces, located in the Mişêrfê neighbourhood of Hesekê, was targeted in an attack involving a bomb-laden motorcycle.




In a statement on the attack, the Internal Security Forces (Asayish) Command said that ISIS cells had targeted the security centre using three motorcycles rigged with explosives.




The Asayish Command confirmed that two of its members had been killed, and five others wounded in the attack.
