author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Grieving her daughter, a Manitoba mother’s fight for answers from police continues: ‘I want transparency’
content:
Crystal Delvenne takes to Winnipeg’s streets to draw attention to her daughter Cassie’s arrest and death nine days later, after she was left with unanswered questions by police and investigators. She has kept a sacred fire burning by the provincial legislature for nearly 90 days. 

Photo by Crystal Greene




This story was updated on Friday, November 27 to add details from a press conference with the family.




Content warning: This story details violence towards an Indigenous woman. Please read with care and look after your spirit.







Manitoba’s attorney general is asking the province’s chief medical examiner to call an inquest into the death of a young Indigenous woman who passed away nine days after being arrested by the Brandon Police Service.




Matt Wiebe, who is also justice minister, wrote a letter to John Younes asking him to initiate a probe into the circumstances of Cassity (Cassie) Marie Delvenne under the Fatality Inquiries Act. The letter was provided to Delvenne’s family and obtained by IndigiNews.




At a press conference on Friday, Cassie’s mother Crystal Delvenne closed a sacred fire she had been tending outside the Manitoba legislature for 87 days — saying although the fire is no longer burning, she won’t stop fighting for answers. 




“I will continue speaking her name and seeking truth and accountability, justice for Cassie,” Delvenne said.




“I’m just glad that we finally got something, some progress.”




As Cassie’s family took questions from reporters, an eagle flew overhead — and it was mentioned that Cassie was of the eagle clan.  Cassie was a member of Shoal Lake 40 First Nation, with ties to Wuskwi Sipihk First Nation and “Barrows,” Manitoba.




Delvenne said the family “came to an agreement” to let the sacred fire go out after they met with premier Wab Kinew on Nov. 6 where he assured them that an inquest would be requested. A poplar tree sapling will eventually be planted in the same spot as Cassie’s fire, according to her family.




(Left to right) Donna Delvenne, Patrick Neilan, Barb Guimond, and Crystal Delvenne, were among 20 people who gathered for a closing ceremony of Cassie Delvenne’s sacred fire on Friday, November 27. Photo by Crystal Greene 




Crystal tended to the fire for nearly three months. As the seasons shifted from summer to autumn, and the year’s first snowfall blanketed the grounds, supporters brought firewood, warm meals, and condolences.




The 24-year-old died on June 21 — nine days after her violent arrest by the Brandon Police Service, which her mother alleges left Cassie with severe injuries. She said an autopsy and toxicology results found a “long list” of 16 or 17 injuries. 




After Brandon Police Service (BPS) received the medical examiner’s report and toxicology results, the force issued a 

Nov. 6 press release

 that her death was “non-suspicious in nature with no evidence of foul play.” 




But they did not publicly disclose its details, citing “respect for the family” and privacy provisions of the province’s Personal Health Information Act. 




The BPS said its “investigation into this matter is now concluded.”




But Cassie’s mother has not stopped pushing for answers about the chain of events leading to her daughter’s death.




“They’re not investigating properly, they’re covering it up,” Delvenne alleged. In an interview with IndigiNews, she spoke of what she perceives as a lack of willingness for the province’s police watchdog and the BPS to investigate further.




In Wiebe’s letter asking for an inquest, he acknowledged “family members still have unanswered questions about what happened in the days, hours minutes leading up to [Cassie’s] death” and said the probe would “hopefully provide clarity for her family” as well as provide recommendations.




‘She was full of life and full of love’




A Facebook profile photo of Cassity (Cassie) Marie Delvenne, 24, was posted only a few weeks before her June 21 death. She was a member of Shoal Lake 40 First Nation, with ties to Wuskwi Sipihk First Nation. 

Photo courtesy Cassie Delvenne/Facebook




Cassie, who was nicknamed Sunshine, was set to enter her final year of studying psychiatric nursing at Brandon University. She was a mother of a young girl, Zoelille.




“She was an amazing mom,” Delvenne said. “She loved her little girl, and she just cared about everybody around her. She was full of life and full of love.”




Delvenne said Zoelille “misses her lots,” and “knows her mom’s in heaven.”




“She’s a hard worker; she cared about people so much,” she added, pausing as a tear ran down her cheek. 




“She was an amazing writer ever since she was little. She just loved to write and read — she was so smart.” 




Delvenne said the loss has been felt widely, including at her university — where one of her instructors emailed to say they’d donated to the school to support a bursary in her memory. Cassie wrote a winning essay on truth and reconciliation, Delvenne said.




Her daughter also made an impression throughout her education, according to her friend Hailey Flett.




“She was the first person that came up to me to be my friend,” said Flett, who recalled the day she met Cassie at Assiniboine Community College. Flett spoke at the protest outside the BPS building.




“She would have done so many great things,” she said. “She wanted to help people with addictions — people that are struggling.




“Now her little girl will never see her mom ever again.”







“She would have done so many great things … Now her little girl will never see her mom ever again.”

— Hailey Flett, friend of Cassie







‘She went to emergency right after’




Just over a week before Cassie died, Brandon police received a call at 1:30 a.m. about a vehicle speeding “into oncoming traffic,” and that its driver may have been “impaired as it was swerving,” according to a June 12 

media release

.




Police found the vehicle parked on the 1900 block of Patricia Avenue, and charged the female driver, 24, with impaired driving, resisting arrest, and failing to provide a breath sample; her male passenger, 23, was charged with assaulting and obstructing a police officer. 




The release said both occupants left the vehicle and “tried to walk away” after police told them “multiple times” to stay inside. 




The officer at the scene tried to “gain physical control of both subjects,” BPS stated, and “one of the occupants began pushing the officer interfering with the apprehension of the other occupant.”




Although police at the time did not identify the two accused, on Sept.11 the force confirmed the driver charged was Cassie.




A witness — who Delvenne said recorded a 45-second video of the incident — posted footage online that appears to show part of the arrest. Delvenne said the video was filmed from inside a nearby apartment. 




The low-resolution, poorly-lit video clip appears to show a barefooted woman being pinned to the ground by two officers in a dark parking lot. An officer’s arm appears to repeatedly strike down on the woman, and loud cracking sounds can be heard several times as well as screams from the woman.




Her family believes the cracking sounds on that video were an officer’s taser, which police have denied using during the incident. 




IndigiNews reviewed the short video closely, but cannot confirm what happened before or after what was filmed, nor could we independently verify the video’s authenticity or circumstances. 




Brandon’s police chief disputed that officers used a taser, and refuted that and other allegations swirling around the case online.




“The information circulating publicly has generated a false, misleading narrative to the June 12 incident and arrest of Cassie Delvenne,” said police chief Tyler Bates on Sept. 11.




He added that while Brandon officers do carry tasers, pepper spray and batons,“none of these were ever used in this interaction” leading up to Cassie’s detention. 




Delvenne does not accept that version of events, continuing to allege officers did used a taser.




She also alleged her daughter had pleaded for medical attention after she was detained, describing several injuries including bruised ribs, bleeding ears, hearing loss, a chipped tooth, scrapes, and missing toenail.




“She went to emergency right after,” she said.




BPS deputy chief Greg Hebert took a complaint from Cassie and first made a phone call to the acting civilian director of Manitoba’s police watchdog, the Independent Investigation Unit (IIU).




Delvenne said her daughter filed a complaint before being released from custody.




Under the 

Police Services Act,

 the IIU “must be immediately notified by the police service” if there is evidence or a complaint that “a police officer may have caused the death of a person” or “a serious injury.”




Delvenne alleges Cassie’s original complaint was not investigated until after the 45-second video “was already all over” social media.




In a September meeting with the BPS police chief and the force’s executive team — except for Hebert — Delvenne brought up the injuries she said Cassie had filed her complaint about. 




She shared a Facebook video of the meeting, at which she asked questions about how the BPS conducted Cassie’s arrest.




“She was 112 pounds,” she said in the video, “a little person.




“Even if she was resisting, that shouldn’t have happened to her.”




In a video recording of the meeting — which Delvenne shared to Facebook — BPS Insp. Jason Dupuis said Cassie’s injuries “could have happened prior, we don’t know that.”




Content warning: 

This 45-second video features a violent police interaction and swearing. It was filmed by a civilian witness of Cassie Delvenne’s arrest by the Brandon Police Service on June 12. IndigiNews has not been able to verify what happened before or after the clip, nor its authenticity. 

Video courtesy of Crystal Delvenne




In another, later meeting she recorded with the IIU’s civilian director, viewed by IndigiNews, he confirmed that BPS sent him photos taken during Cassie’s detention “soon after the incident.”




“I reviewed the photos,” he said. “I was advised of the situation at that point in time. There was nothing of concern.




“Once I reviewed those I said, based on what you’ve provided me so far, there’s no serious injury to this individual.”




Nine days after Cassie’s arrest on June 21 at 9:11 p.m., emergency responders were called to Cassie’s apartment, where they found her “unconscious and not breathing,” according to a BPS media release. 




“Neither police nor the Chief Medical Examiner’s office have identified any indicators of foul play,” the release noted.




However, Delvenne raised concerns that police never secured the apartment as a potential crime scene.




When she later entered the home after Cassie’s death, she alleged she found “blood all over the bathroom, there’s holes in the walls” — and believes the 24-year-old had been frightened for her safety before she died.




In a publicly shared Facebook video of Delvenne’s Sept. 2 meeting with BPS’ leaders, Delvenne questioned his force’s investigative methods.




During the recorded meeting, police chief Bates told her he could “not even fathom” the family’s grief after their loss.




“I can’t imagine how difficult it is to not have answers, to not know what contributed to your loved one’s death,” he said in the video. 




“If I were in your situation, I would want answers too. We should be providing those answers, but we don’t have them yet … I wish we didn’t have so many unknowns.” 




Delvenne claimed a camera was filming inside the apartment, which she alleged showed officers leaving after less than seven minutes.




“Six-and-a-half minutes and you’re ruling it an overdose?” she asked Bates. (IndigiNews could not independently verify the video or duration officers were present).




In response, Bates spoke about the importance of attending officers “holding a scene” to preserve evidence and prevent interference.




“Far be it from me to question the investigator that specifically attended the scene,” he replied. “But you better be confident that there is no foul play — no suspicious element to the death — if you’re not holding the scene.




“Because at the end of the day, you only get one chance to hold a scene. They were convinced that there was no foul play involved. Rightly or wrongly, that’s the determination that they made, and that’s why the scene wasn’t held.”




Bates said that the cause of death remained “unexplained,” and that the Chief Medical Examiner had “found no bodily injury contributed to her death.”




“We don’t know why your daughter died,” Bates said. “In this case, we were provided very little other than to say it’s unexplained and further toxicology examinations are required to establish what caused her death.”




But the police chief confirmed officers had previously responded to calls related to “conflict” at the apartment where she died.




“It’s clear from the calls and whatnot that relate to conflict at that address … certainly there was conflict and arguments taking place,” Bates said. “There had been calls for service to that location, calls that were attended.




“There was just not evidence of assaultive behaviour that took place that night.”




While live-streaming video, Crystal Delvenne (left) meets with senior leaders of Brandon Police Service in September, including Insp. Dana McCallum (centre left), Insp. Jason Dupuis (centre right), and police chief Tyler Bates (right). 

Photo by Barb Guimond




In a video she recorded of a meeting she attended with the police department’s chief and senior leaders, Delvenne asked officials why she had been forced to interview witnesses, gather footage and seek medical evidence herself.




“No mom should have to investigate her own daughter’s death,” she told BPS top brass on Sept. 2. 




“This is your guys’ job. I shouldn’t have had to do this. I shouldn’t have interviewed people, I shouldn’t have had to do any of this, and I want to know why.”




The latest development comes after months of waiting for autopsy and toxicology reports, and live-streaming meetings with the police and government officials, which were shared on social media.




At an August protest outside the BPS headquarters, Delvenne spoke passionately into a megaphone — criticizing investigators for ruling out foul play.




“The apartment was not protected like a possible crime scene,” she told supporters.




“Assumptions were made — her death was treated as an overdose.”




What caused Cassie’s death remains uncertain. But Delvenne asserted that “Cassie’s toxicology testing did not detect any illegal drugs. As her mom, I want to know what evidence deputy chief Hebert based that account on.” IndigiNews was not able to independently verify the toxicology results.




Delvenne alleged police told her Cassie died after she “injected her boyfriend with fentanyl, then injected herself,” she wrote in a 

Nov. 6

 Facebook post.




Asked to verify what Hebert told her, a force spokesperson said it could not provide “further commentary” due to an “ongoing investigative process.”




Complaint to police watchdog hits a wall




Supporters of Camp Cassie protest in Winnipeg for justice in the later 24-year-old Shoal Lake 40 First Nation member’s death. 

Photo by Crystal Greene




Under the province’s 

Police Services Act

, police chiefs have a duty to report serious injuries or death of civilians involving their officers — or if officers may have committed a crime — 

to the IIU.

  




The threshold of 

serious injuries

 that fall under the IIU’s mandate include fractured bones, the loss of a body part; vision or hearing loss; injuries that require a hospital stay; any wounds from a gunshot, not including an impact munition or other non-lethal munition. 




Police chief Bates said in the Sept. 2 recording that once BPS notified the IIU, the watchdog then  “declined it and said that it didn’t meet their mandate.”




Delvenne, along with supporter Barb Guimond and Cassie’s grandmother Donna Delvenne, livestreamed a meeting with the IIU’s acting civilian director, Bruce Sychuk, an experienced Crown attorney.




He told the women that he originally reviewed photos related to the incident, and later received police paperwork with additional material, including the 45-second witness video, as well as witnesses’ audio tapes, and footage from the police vehicle’s WatchGuard camera. 




Delvenne alleged that BPS deputy police chief Hebert told her that the dashcam wasn’t working the night of Cassie’s arrest.  




Sychuk emphasized his legal mandate only allowed him to investigate based on what police provided him, but said if there was documentation about broken ribs it would meet his “serious injury” threshold.




“How do you know she didn’t have broken ribs? She went to an X-ray,” Donna replied, asking Sychuk if he would review Cassie’s medical records or later autopsy.




“I’m not reviewing the autopsy,” he said. “It’s not come to me; it’s not foul play, it wouldn’t come to me.”




The IIU was never given her medical records, only what the BPS submitted.




Delvenne told him that Cassie “was crying for medical attention in her cell … because her ears were ringing,” saying she “couldn’t hear out of one ear” and “blood was coming from her ears, draining out.” 




“If you provide me with that medical information, [that] there was total hearing loss, it would meet my mandatory investigation,” Sychuk said.




Her grandmother also accused police of not giving her requested medical attention in custody, even though Cassie said “she could not breathe.” Delvenne alleged her daughter’s lungs were “a pound heavier than they should have been” — and when she was released she “went straight to the hospital.” 




“They sent her for an X-ray on her ribs and her ribs were quite bruised,” Donna said, stating the family would try to obtain those records themselves.




“If there is medical evidence that suggests she had a fractured rib, it would meet my mandatory investigation, it would,” Sychuk said. 




“I would strongly suggest you wait until the autopsy report and the toxicology reports come back. If the situation after the autopsy report comes back suggests foul play, clearly it has to be investigated.”




Delvenne complained that police “get to pick and choose” what evidence they submit to the IIU. 




Cassity (Cassie) Marie Delvenne, age 24. 

Photo courtesy Cassie Delvenne/Facebook




Sychuk said that if the police were to not provide him “a fulsome disclosure on purpose, that would be extremely concerning and it would definitely cause some ramifications.”




In Delvenne’s recording of the meeting, Sychuk promised he would be “happy to take this matter on” were he given new evidence that meets the IIU mandate.




Donna said she thought it was “pretty darn serious” BPS did not send the IIU information about officers’ alleged use of a taser on Cassie, which she said the video shows, despite police denials.




“If there is actual evidence of a taser, that would be a concern,” Sychuk said. “I don’t have anything from them.




“We’ve declined jurisdiction on this matter. So, we have no duty to investigate anything. Based on the information I have been provided it would not meet the public interest to investigate this matter any further.”




Delvenne said she wants officers involved to be held accountable — and to learn the full truth of what happened to her daughter between her violent arrest and her death nine days later.




“I want transparency,” she said. “I want them to quit lying …  they shouldn’t be allowed to get away with this.”




“The IIU should be helping, but they only have a two per cent rate” of recommending charges for officers involved in civilians’ deaths, she added, citing a 

recent Investigative Journalism Foundation report

.




Her concerns echo the conclusions of a 

2021 report

 by Legal Aid Manitoba’s Public Interest Law Centre.




“There is currently no way for the IIU to know how often a police service fails to notify the agency of an incident within its mandate,” the report stated. 




“This ‘good faith’ procedural standard for notification has proven insufficient and a major loophole obfuscating reporting between the police service and chief to notify the IIU as required.” 




Crystal Delvenne (centre) displays a ‘Justice for Cassie’ banner at Manito Ahbee powwow in October, alongside supporters Patrick Ritchot (left) and Patrick Neilan (right). 

Photo courtesy Barb Guimond




A quest for justice continues — like many before in province




Cassie’s story — and her mom’s months-long quest for justice — has resonated with a growing number of supporters in the province, many of whom have regularly attended demonstrations in both Brandon and Winnipeg, and supplied her with firewood, food and tobacco offerings for her sacred fire outside the provincial legislature.




Firekeeper Patrick Neilan said that the sacred fire was put up because “it was the right thing to do to get their attention.” He gave examples of sacred fires for Morgan Harris and Marcedes Myran as drawing attention to fights for justice. 




Manitoba’s justice system has come under fire for decades for its treatment of Indigenous people. In 1988, the province held an Aboriginal Justice Inquiry (AJI) after the high-profile deaths of Helen Betty Osborne and J.J. Harper.




It issued numerous 

recommendations

, including creating a “special investigations unit, or … a special investigations team for a particular incident, able to take control of the investigation immediately,” and that “police forces in the province be required to provide all available assistance and co-operation.”




The province states on its website that 

ultimately

 drove “changes to address systemic racism in Manitoba’s criminal justice system.” Yet there would be no such investigative unit until after a 2008 provincial 

inquiry

 into an off-duty cop’s killing of mother-of-three Crystal Taman in a hit-and-run.




That inquiry called for “a provincial special investigation union independent of all police enforcement agencies” — finally resulting in the IIU’s formation seven years later, and 

disbanding

 the East St. Paul, Man., police department.




Since then, the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls echoed many of the same grievances and recommendations from the previous decades’ inquiries.




It called for a new dedicated investigation unit to examine “incidents of failures to investigate, police misconduct, and all forms of discriminatory practices and mistreatment of Indigenous Peoples” — and provide reports to Indigenous communities directly.




Since Delvenne set up camp outside the provincial legislature, she has sought meetings with officials such as justice minister Wiebe.




(Left to right) Firekeeper Patrick Neilan, Crystal Delvenne, and Barb Guimond spoke to reporters on Friday, after the sacred fire went out for Crystal’s daughter Cassie Delvenne. Photo by Crystal Greene




Under the Police Services Act, Wiebe has the power to determine if a “police service has failed to provide adequate and effective” policing, and ultimately to “suspend” a department entirely, as happened in the Taman case.




As she fights for answers, Delvenne 

fundraised

 more than $3,100 for legal representation, eventually retaining the same law firm involved in a public inquest into the 2020 police shooting of 16-year-old 

Eishia Hudson

.




”Having a lawyer can help with making an impact at an inquest,” explained 

Bronwyn Dobchuk-Land

, a University of Winnipeg criminal justice associate professor, in an email.




“At an inquest, Crown counsel is supposed to neutrally represent the interests of the public, and that is often legally assumed to include the interests of the family, however that is not always the case in practice.”




A lawyer can also help victims’ families file civil lawsuits against police, she added, but she is unaware of any such suits against the IIU.




“Officials work to pin the blame for a death in custody on the person who died,” she said. “This is devastating and dehumanizing.”




“We don’t trust the Brandon police,” Delvenne told IndigiNews by her sacred fire. “That’s what we’re trying to get — is for them to be held accountable.”




She previously told IndigiNews that she was hoping to winterize Camp Cassie, to keep the fire burning, during what she is aware will be a slow, bureaucratic process. 




But after months of waiting, meeting officials, and praying, she decided to wind down the sacred fire. 




The firepit with grandfather rocks placed in the shape of a turtle will remain. Eventually, a poplar tree sapling is set to be planted in it’s spot. Photo by Crystal Greene




But that in no way means she or her supporters are abandoning their fight for justice — and for all other families who believe justice was not done.




“This is for everyone, I’m sure we’re not ones that this is happening to,” Barbara Guimond, who’s been at Delvenne’s side since summer, agreed. 




“This affects all races — not only our people, but predominantly us though, in Manitoba.”




Delvenne said on Friday that she plans to start a non-profit organization called Cassie’s Legacy which would support families calling for police accountability. Cassie’s family hopes that following a potential inquest there will be changes to the IIU’s mandate on how they look into cases of police violence and deaths to civilians.  She also wants the Brandon Police Service to be held accountable for how they did their investigation. 




“It helps me,” she said, “being surrounded by support.”







The post 

Grieving her daughter, a Manitoba mother’s fight for answers from police continues: ‘I want transparency’

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Father of man killed by police testifies at inquest
content:
The father of the 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man shot and killed by police five years ago testified at the coroner’s inquest into his son’s death on Thursday.




Thomas Angootealuk was emotional as he took to the witness stand for about 10 minutes.




“He was my son,” Thomas Angootealuk said with tears in his eyes, as he held a photo of Trey Angootealuk.




On Nov. 7, 2021, police fatally shot Trey Angootealuk after a standoff

 with

 four RCMP officers in the outskirts of town.




A day earlier, Trey Angootealuk hijacked a truck and shot at police officers before parking and remaining in it for several hours. The standoff ended after police launched a canister through the truck’s rear window and then shot him.




The inquest by Nunavut chief coroner Marianna Cervantes began Monday at the Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet. The jury made its recommendations Thursday afternoon.




Coroner’s inquests are mandatory in Nunavut for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved.
















The jury has been asked to rule on the cause of his death, to provide recommendations for how to prevent deaths of similar circumstance, and to make recommendations for how police can respond in similar incidents.

 




Thomas Angootealuk told the jury that he always tried to be a good role model for his son. He was training him to operate heavy equipment.




Thomas Angootealuk, a school bus driver, found his son a job as a school bus monitor. They worked together, with Trey Angootealuk making sure kids stayed put in their seats.




“I couldn’t work after losing my son,” Thomas Angootealuk said.




When he did try to return to work, a child asked where his son had gone. Thomas Angootealuk said he broke down.

 




“How am I supposed to answer an eight-year-old boy, who doesn’t know anything about that?”
















Two of Angootealuk’s siblings also testified Thursday, sharing fond memories, such as the time he gave caribou meat to elders.

 




“Me and my brother had a bond I’ll never be able to explain to anybody else,” his sister Rosalie Angoshadluk said. “We didn’t need a plan, we just needed to be out together laughing until our stomach hurt and acting like we had all the time we wanted in the world.”

author: By Darren Thompson, Unicorn Riot
title: 10th Annual Walk Against Uranium Brings Hundreds to White Mesa Ute Community
content:
Ute Mountain Ute Reservation — On Saturday, October 17, hundreds joined the White Mesa Ute community in an annual rally and spiritual walk against a uranium mill that is central to the country’s domestic uranium supply chain. Ute Mountain Ute tribal members say that the White Mesa Mill facility located in Blanding, Utah, threatens their environment and pledge to continue their opposition against the operation. 




Event organizer and White Mesa community member Yolanda Badback spoke to a crowd of several hundred, welcoming them to the Ute Mountain Ute Reservation in southeastern Utah. She explained the purpose of the event, what the intention was and what people could expect. “Thank you for coming to White Mesa to help us in our opposition against the uranium mill,” she told the crowd who gathered at the White Mesa Community Center at the beginning of the rally. 







“This mill is contaminating our land, our water, and our people and it must be stopped.” 




Yolanda Badback, White Mesa community member, event organizer




The White Mesa Mill is owned and operated by Denver-based Energy Fuels and is the only conventional and fully-licensed uranium mill in the country. The mill sits five miles away from the Ute Mountain Ute reservation in southeastern Utah and has the capacity to produce up to eight million pounds of uranium per year. Last year, the mill produced more than 1,000,000 million pounds of uranium, according to the 

company’s website

. 







Aerial view of the White Mesa Mill in Blanding, Utah. Photo contributed by Darren Thompson.







The mill has been licensed since 1980, where it processed natural uranium ore into yellowcake (U₃O₈) for nuclear energy. Today, the mill processes “alternate feeds” including radioactive residues from Superfund and Manhattan Project sites and produces vanadium and light rare earth elements. 




The company 

announced in July 2026

 that the mill is expanding. Energy Fuels says the expansion will enable large-scale production of heavy rare earth oxides, which are planned to be used to produce rare earth metals, alloys and magnets essential to the automotive, robotics, data center, energy and defense industries. 




The planned expansion is two-fold and its first phase is expected to be completed by the end of 2027 and the second phase to be completed by the end of 2028. 




Currently, multiple semi-truck loads are seen arriving at the White Mesa Mill on a daily basis and they’re transporting uranium ore from the 

Pinyon Plain Mine

 via two routes in northern Arizona through the Navajo Nation. 




The mine is an active uranium mine near Red Butte Mesa, a sacred site to the Havasupai Tribe, and is owned and operated by Energy Fuels. 




Since transportation began in 2025, there have been two reported accidents involving the transportation of the mineral on the Navajo Nation.




There are approximately 1,629,000 pounds of U₃O₈ at Pinyon Plain Mine, contained in 82,800 tons at an average grade of 0.98% U₃O₈. It is one of the highest grades of U₃O₈ in the world and the mine’s operations are in the Baaj Nwaavjo I’tah Kukveni – Ancestral Footprints of the Grand Canyon National Monument. 




Related – May 2026: 

Indigenous Grand Canyon National Monument Designation Wins in Appeals Court




The National Monument was established by President Joe Biden on August 8, 2023 and led by a coalition of tribes including the Havasupai, Hopi, Hualapai, Navajo Nation, Paiute bands, and Pueblo of Zuni. The Havasupai and other tribes have opposed the uranium mine since the mine’s beginning in 1980 and its leaders continue to voice their opposition to the mine’s operations. 




“We came up here and saw all these mining trucks and it really broke our hearts, but that’s not going to stop us” said Havasupai tribal citizen Carletta Tilousi during the rally. “We are the water people and we came here to support the White Mesa community and all of you, because this issue doesn’t just affect this community.” 




The Havasupai have been monitoring the operations of the Pinyon Plain Mine and they have voiced several concerns regarding the permit’s request to raise the minimum arsenic levels in three groundwater wells at the mining operation.




Related – June 2026: 

Anti-Uranium Summit Sheds Light on Toxic Industry




Recently, the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality denied the tribe’s appeal that amended the mining permit to raise the minimum arsenic level 10%, from 0.05 to 0.055 milligrams. 




Several representatives from other Tribal Nations participated in the day’s event including representatives from the Quechan Indian Tribe, the Navajo Nation, the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, and speakers from other tribes were included. Other organizations supported the annual event including Greenaction for Health & Environmental Justice, Bears Ears Inter-Tribal Coalition, Gila River Alliance for a Clean Environment, Indigenous Environmental Network, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, and dozens more. 







Participants marched along Utah Highway 191 for six miles to the White Mesa Mill in Blanding, Utah on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Photo contributed by Darren Thompson.







The concern of the mill’s operations isn’t just land contamination, it’s also about protecting sacred lands, according to many speakers during the event. 




The mill sits miles from the Bears Ears National Monument, the first National Monument led by a coalition of Tribal Nations including the Navajo Nation, Hopi Tribe, Pueblo of Zuni, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, and Ute Indian Tribe. Together they formed the 

Bears Ears Inter-tribal Coalition

 to preserve and co-manage a landscape that is significant to their history and their culture. 




Since its national monument designation by President Barack Obama in 2016, the boundaries of Bears Ears National Monument have changed multiple times — reduced twice by President Donald Trump. Trump’s 2017 reduction was restored by President Joe Biden in 2021. Trump’s second reduction of the boundaries was earlier this year via 

executive order

. The area has since seen a resurgence of mining claims. 




Several conservation organizations joined in a 

lawsuit

 challenging Trump’s executive orders, citing the Antiquities Act and arguing that the law permits presidents to “declare” National Monuments and “reserve” land for their protection, but not to abolish them in whole or in part. 




“President Trump’s unlawful actions imperil these and other irreplaceable resources by opening the lands around them to hard rock mining; oil and gas leasing; and other destructive uses that the default federal land laws generally authorize,” the lawsuit states. “Indeed, mining companies located claims on the excised lands following the 2017 Dismantling Proclamation and have already done so again following the 2026 Dismantling Proclamation.”




On November 17, the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance (SUWA) launched a new campaign to restore two monuments in Utah — Grand Staircase-Escalante and Bears Ears National Monuments. Dubbed “Keep Utah Monumental,” its intended to hold Utah’s politicians accountable in the shrinking of the national monuments. 




Utah’s entire federal delegation including Senator 

Mike Lee

 and Representative 

Celeste Maloy

, Governor 

Spencer Cox

, Attorney General 

Derek Brown

, Speaker 

Mike Schultz

, and Senate President 

J. Stuart Adams

 supported or celebrated Trump’s 2026 executive order decreasing the size of Bears Ears National Monument. 




Prior to the executive order, the 

Government Accountability Office (GAO) announced

 that the 

Bears Ears National Monument land-use plan

 (finalized in 2025) is subject to the Congressional Review Act, giving Utah Senator Mike Lee an opportunity to introduce legislation that would topple Tribal collaborative management and speed up the destruction of the landscape. 




With the GAO opinion in hand, an opportunity is open to introduce a bill under the Congressional Review Act to undo the Bears Ears National Monument Management Plan. 




Senator Lee led an effort earlier this year with Representative Celeste Maloy (R-UT-02) attempting to dismantle the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument Management Plan. That effort was largely opposed by Tribal Nations and other conservationists and ultimately failed. 







Participants of the 10th annual White Mesa Walk & Rally stand atop of a hill along Utah Highway 191 to show their solidarity to traffic on the highway. Photo contributed by Darren Thompson.







The movement to oppose uranium and mining in general has ramped up in recent years, largely because efforts to fast track the permitting process on public state and federal lands as well as increased mining claims for minerals such as uranium and lithium. 




Faron Owl, a Qeuchan Tribal councilman from Fort Yuma, Arizona, said that his tribe, the Quechan Indian Tribe, is opposing several mining efforts in their historical lands in southern California and Nevada. 




“We’re basically going through the same situation that all of you are,” he said. “We’re fighting a gold mine, we’re fighting a transmission line and lithium mining — it’s just continuous.”




The six-mile walk from the community center took multiple hours with a line of participants and several vehicles that exceeded a half-mile on the side of Utah Highway 191, between the Ute Mountain Ute Reservation line and the White Mesa Mill. The event required permits, with walkers staying off the highway and not disrupting traffic. Along the walk, organizers led chants when music wasn’t being played for people to follow. 




At the conclusion of the walk, organizers mentioned this was the first year they noticed local law enforcement, including the Utah State Troopers and the San Juan County Sheriff’s Office, present throughout the walk. 




The officers monitored traffic and closed off the highway at the end of the walk so walkers could cross the highway safely to the roadway leading into the White Mesa Mill. 







Two San Juan County Sheriff’s Office deputies at the entrance of the White Mesa Mill in Blanding, Utah on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Photo contributed by Darren Thompson.







At the roadway to the mill, people offered speeches, prayers, and songs asking for continued support and unity against the operation. 




“Indigenous land across the so-called United States has long fed the insatiable appetite of the empire,” Sabrina Mathues Manygoats told Unicorn Riot. 







“Sacred sites such as Wii’i Gdwiisa, Tsoodził, Kwiyagatu Nukavachi, Pahá Sápa and Stluputqu are being raped in the name of ‘national security’ and ‘clean energy.’ We march today with our Nuuchu relatives to raise awareness and radicalize those who’ve turned a blind eye to this genocide in the name of progress.”




Sabrina Mathues Manygoats, Diné (Navajo)




Manygoats monitored the walk with a handheld radiation detector. Modern radiation detectors have the capability to sense and measure ionizing radiation — such as beta particles, gamma rays, and X-rays.




“Background radiation is notably higher in this territory due to Energy Fuel’s White Mesa Mill’s operations,” Manygoats said. “I witnessed levels range from 0.2-0.4 microsieverts per hour on the road and 1.6 microsieverts per hour at an elevation of 2400ft above the mill. These radiation readings are evident that we are in the final genocide of our Indigenous communities.”




Cover image contributed by Darren Thompson showing a group of several hundreds participants pose at the entrance road to the White Mesa Mill in Blanding, Utah showing their solidarity against uranium mining on Saturday, October 17, 2026. 







Darren Thompson is a multi-media journalist enrolled at the Lac du Flambeau Band of Lake Superior Chippewa in Northern Wisconsin, where he grew up. He covers breaking news, missing and murdered Indigenous people, environmental and social justice, tribal sovereignty, art, music, and film. He can be reached through his website, 

www.darrenthompson.net

.

title: Peoples’ Climate Summit: COP31 has failed to deliver climate justice
content:
The Peoples’ Climate Summit, held in Antalya from November 14 to 18, has published a statement on the outcomes of the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31). After more than two weeks of negotiations, the global climate conference ended without an overarching final agreement or a consensus on phasing out fossil fuels. The Peoples’ Climate Summit also sees this as a structural failure of the international climate regime and questions its democratic foundations.




Global power imbalances in climate policy




In the statement, the organizations criticized the lack of transparency in the decision-making processes at COP31, stating that the presentation of draft negotiating texts in the middle of the night made it difficult for participating countries to engage effectively in the deliberations. The Peoples’ Climate Summit highlighted an incident during the closing session as particularly revealing: “COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister, Murat Kurum, cut off Ghanaian Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who was speaking on behalf of 54 African countries. The fact that representatives of African peoples, who have contributed the least to causing the climate crisis but face its most severe consequences, are silenced reflects the power imbalances within the international climate regime. There can be no climate justice without democracy.”




False technological solutions serving the interests of the fossil fuel industry




The statement said: “While references to fossil fuels disappeared from the draft decisions over the course of the negotiations, the COP31 presidency maintained its targets for carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) technologies, despite opposition from a coalition of 126 countries. The Peoples’ Climate Summit views the political promotion of technologies whose viability on a large scale has yet to be demonstrated as a means for polluting corporations to evade their responsibility to reduce emissions.




“Forests and ecosystems must not be reduced to carbon credits that companies can purchase to continue polluting the environment. Technology cannot replace actual emissions reductions.”




Half a billion dollars to host COP31




According to the organizations, the demand by countries of the Global South to provide $120 billion annually by 2035 for adaptation to the impacts of the climate crisis went unmet in Antalya. The Peoples’ Climate Summit illustrated the priorities that were set instead by pointing to the costs of hosting COP31. Citing data from the Electronic Public Procurement Platform (EKAP), the organizations estimate that the total value of tenders awarded and contracts signed by Turkey as part of the summit preparations up to September 2026 exceeded 25 billion lira, equivalent to approximately $500 million. According to the statement, this contrasts with just $50.2 million in new funding pledges to the international Adaptation Fund.




The total value of contracts for preparing the UN Climate Change Conference was therefore approximately ten times the amount of new pledges to the Adaptation Fund. The Peoples’ Climate Summit demanded that the Turkish government provide a detailed disclosure of all expenditures.




The hypocrisy of fossil fuel policy




 




Among the fundamental contradictions of COP31 is the continued investment in fossil fuels by Turkey and Australia, which jointly assumed leadership of the UN Climate Change Conference. On November 9, the very day COP31 began, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced the discovery of two new oil fields in the Gabar region of Northern Kurdistan, with an estimated potential of 135 million barrels. “The fact that a government which, in its capacity as COP31 president, brings countries together in Antalya presents increased fossil fuel production as a success exposed the hypocrisy of its climate policy on the very first day,” the statement said.




Five concrete demands to the Turkish government




The Peoples’ Climate Summit expects concrete political action from Turkey, which will hold the COP presidency until COP32: “Coal-fired power plants must be shut down, and a binding timetable for phasing out coal must be presented. New oil, natural gas and coal projects must be halted, and fossil fuel subsidies must be abolished. Ecocide must be established as a criminal offense under national law; Turkey must accede to the Rome Statute and the Aarhus Convention. Legal provisions that leave nature at the mercy of capital’s interests, particularly the Mining Law and Law No. 7554, must be repealed. Just transition plans must be developed for workers and local communities in coal-producing regions, with the participation of trade unions.”




For a democratic international climate council




In view of the influence of fossil fuel corporations and lobbying groups representing polluting industries on the COP mechanism, the Peoples’ Climate Summit proposes an alternative institutional framework: a democratic International Climate Council should be established under the auspices of the United Nations, without veto privileges and with the authority to impose sanctions. The organizations from the environmental, trade union, women’s and youth movements that gathered in Antalya intend to further strengthen their cross-border solidarity and continue their joint struggle for climate justice, including at COP32, which will take place in the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, in 2027.

title: DEM Party Imrali delegation meets with MHP leader Devlet Bahçeli
content:
The Imrali delegation of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) met with Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) Chair Devlet Bahçeli in Ankara on Thursday.




The meeting, held in Bahçeli’s office in the MHP parliamentary group section of the Turkish Parliament, was attended by DEM Party deputies Pervin Buldan and Mithat Sancar, as well as lawyer Faik Özgür Erol. The meeting, which lasted approximately one hour, focused on the current state of the Peace and Democratic Society Process and the legal and political requirements of the present phase. The Imrali delegation had last met with Bahçeli on October 9.




The Imrali delegation had also held talks with Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek on Wednesday. According to the DEM Party’s press office, the meeting focused on the legal aspects of the ongoing process to resolve the Kurdish question, as well as conditions in prisons. Particular attention was given to the situation of sick prisoners and problems related to the execution of sentences.

title: Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court strengthens Baghdad’s control over the Kurdistan Region
content:
The dispute between the Iraqi central government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) over control of border crossings, energy resources and public revenues is intensifying. On Wednesday, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court issued a ruling on the constitutional division of powers between Baghdad and Hewlêr (Erbil), largely upholding the central government’s recent decisions. Meanwhile, Iraqi border guard forces have begun implementing the first measures.




On November 24, the government in Baghdad announced a series of decisions aimed at strengthening federal control over border crossings and the energy sector. These include closing officially unrecognized border crossings, transferring control of oil fields in territories disputed between Baghdad and Erbil to the federal Oil Ministry, and tightening oversight of oil transportation and exports.




The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) subsequently warned in a joint statement against interference with the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, describing any violation of those rights as a red line.




Baghdad rejects allegations of foreign interference




Amid the dispute, the media office of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi rejected allegations that the decisions had been made at the behest of other countries. It stated that all measures taken within Iraq’s internationally recognized borders were based on the country’s sovereign decision-making authority, constitutional powers and legal obligations.




“Our decisions are Iraq’s own, our will is national, and our points of reference are the Constitution and the law. Iraq’s overriding interests are the guiding principle for our positions and actions,” the Prime Minister’s office stated.




Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council also intervened in the dispute. It called on the central government, the regional government and all political forces to abide by the 2005 Constitution. At the same time, the council reiterated that the authority to interpret the Constitution rests exclusively with the Federal Supreme Court.




Regional government rejects the language of weapons and threats




The Kurdistan Regional Government discussed Baghdad’s decisions at a meeting. In a statement issued afterward, it emphasized its willingness to cooperate in combating corruption, oil smuggling and other illegal activities, but rejected the central government’s approach.




“We have always acted jointly and in coordination with the federal government to prevent and put an end to all illegal activities. However, we reject the language of weapons and threats,” the regional government stated.




the Kurdistan Regional Government stated that efforts to combat corruption and oil smuggling must extend across the entire territory of Iraq. At the same time, it announced legal action against individuals who undermine the constitutional status and interests of the Kurdistan Region and incite the population to conflict.




Federal Supreme Court reaffirms Baghdad’s extensive powers




In its ruling announced during a public session on November 25, the Federal Supreme Court clarified the constitutional powers of the central and regional governments in several key areas. The ruling is final and binding on all state institutions.




Citing Articles 109 and 110 of the Iraqi Constitution, the court ruled that the protection of international borders falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the central government. Accordingly, Baghdad has the authority to deploy federal security forces along the external borders of the Kurdistan Region and take appropriate security measures.




Furthermore, under Law No. 30 of 2016, federal authorities have extensive supervisory and regulatory powers over all border crossings in Iraq. However, customs inspections at border crossings in the Kurdistan Region must be carried out in coordination with the regional government. According to the court, the introduction of a unified nationwide electronic monitoring system for border crossings and customs offices also falls within Baghdad’s jurisdiction.




In customs and fiscal policy, the court also reaffirmed the central government’s authority to introduce uniform regulations nationwide, monitor compliance with them, and ensure that public revenues generated from taxes, fees and other non-oil sources are transferred to the state treasury.




Joint management of oil and natural gas resources




The ruling takes a more nuanced approach to the energy sector. Referring to Article 112 of the Constitution, the court ruled that the management of extracted oil and natural gas must be carried out jointly by the federal government, the Kurdistan Regional Government and the respective oil- and gas-producing provinces.




However, the federal Oil Ministry and the relevant regulatory authorities have supervisory and oversight powers covering all aspects of oil and natural gas production, marketing and export. These powers also extend to the relevant contracts and production processes.




At the same time, the court emphasized that the cooperation between the central and regional governments stipulated by the Constitution must not be interrupted or undermined.




Disputed territories remain a central issue of contention




The ruling on the territorial scope of the regional government’s jurisdiction is of particular political significance. In this context, the Federal Supreme Court referred to Article 53(A) of the Transitional Administrative Law and Article 143 of the Iraqi Constitution.




Accordingly, the relevant territories are those in the provinces of Duhok, Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Kirkuk, Diyala and Nineveh that were administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government up to March 19, 2003.




According to the court, the exercise of regional powers beyond these boundaries must be assessed in light of the constitutional provisions governing disputed territories. Outside the recognized jurisdiction of the Kurdistan Region, administrative and executive powers rest with the federal government. The court thus ruled that de facto administration by the regional government does not, in itself, establish constitutional rights or powers.




The ruling therefore also touches on the still-unresolved issue of the disputed territories, whose status is to be determined in accordance with Article 140 of the Iraqi Constitution.




Iraq begins closing border crossings




While the political and constitutional dispute continues, the implementation of Baghdad’s initial decisions has already begun. Mohammed Abdulwahab Said, Commander of the Iraqi Border Guard Forces, confirmed to Iraqi media that his units had begun closing officially unrecognized border crossings and implementing measures to combat oil smuggling.




According to Said, efforts are also underway to integrate the administrative structures of border crossings in the Kurdistan Region with those in the rest of Iraq. While securing the external borders falls under the responsibility of the border guard forces, the control and management of border crossings are the responsibility of the federal Border Crossings Authority.




The statements issued so far do not specify which border crossings have already been affected by the measures or to what extent the central government’s other decisions are being implemented.

title: Berlin: Rigaer94 verteidigen gegen Räumung 15.12.
content:
Wie wir letztes Jahr berichtet haben, sind die zwischen den alten Mietvertragsinhaber*innen und den selbsternannten Anwälten Bernau und Aretin des angeblichen Eigentümers (Leonid Medved) zwar nicht formell, aber faktisch, Räumungstitel. Diese kommen zu den zwei bereits aus den letzten Jahren existierenden Räumungstiteln hinzu, was bedeutet das es jetzt insgesamt acht Räumungstitel im Haus gibt. In den letzten Monaten haben unsere Gegner einige Räumungsklagen zurückgezogen, die für sie aussichtslos wirkten. Obwohl dadurch einige Individuen aus den Räumungsklagen raus sind, sind das für uns keine guten Neuigkeiten – vielmehr macht es ein Räumungsszenario wahrscheinlicher, da es bald keine offenen Klagen, sondern nur noch Räumungstitel geben wird.




Es ist mal wieder ernst. Noch diesen Sommer haben wir davon berichtet, dass einige Räumungstitel gegen Wohnungen in unserem Haus bestehen: (

here

)




Letzte Woche Mittwoch, am 11. November, gab es wieder einen Verhandlungstermin zu diesen Räumungsklagen. In der Verhandlung machte der Richter erneut deutlich, dass er keineswegs plant, die Lafone Investments Limited als rechtsfähig anzuerkennen. Noch während der Verhandlung zogen die Anwälte des vermeintlichen Eigentümers dann auch die letzten aussichtslosen Klagen gegen diejenigen Individuen zurück, die nicht in Verbindung mit Mietverträgen stehen. Das scheint ihre aktuelle Strategie zu sein: Den Weg für eine Teilräumung zu ebnen. Und heute sehen wir auch, was genau das bedeutet:




Innerhalb der letzten Tage haben wir vier Räumungsankündigungen erhalten. Drei davon resultieren aus den Deals der alten Mietvertragsinhaber*innen mit den selbsternannten Anwälten. Eine der Räumungsankündigungen basiert auf einem bereits länger existierenden Räumungstitel. Bisher wissen wir also sicher, dass es vier Wohnungen betrifft. Wir müssen aber davon ausgehen, dass zu den vier weiteren Wohnungen auch noch Räumungsankündigungen eintreffen werden.




Die Obergerichtsvollzieherin Frau Knop (Segelfliegerdamm 89 12487 Berlin, Tel.03091693556) hat sich für den 15.12.26 um 06:00 Uhr morgens

 angekündigt, um die ehemaligen Mietvertragsinhaber*innen aus den Wohnungen zu räumen und die vermeintlichen Eigentümer*innen in diese “einzuweisen”.




Was treiben die Behörden da?




Wir fragen uns, ob die Ankündigung der Gerichtsvollzieherin eine rein bürokratische Angelegenheit ist, oder ob Bullen und Politik von Anfang an ihre Finger mit im Spiel haben. Es könnte ja sein, dass Frau Knop mal einen Brief losgeschickt hat, weil es einfach der übliche Verwaltungsweg ist.- ohne sich der Konsequenzen bewusst zu sein. Oder saß sie bereits mit Bernau, Aretin, einem „Eigentümer“, den Bullen und dem Innensenat an einem Tisch? Wissen dann die Hundertschaften schon Bescheid, dass sie sich auf Überstunden und Kürzungen von Urlaubstagen kurz vor Weihnachten und Silvester einstellen müssen? Oder machen die das gerne ehrenamtlich?




Falls es so ist, dass Politiker:innen bereits Bescheid wissen: Kurz vorm Sommer schien es wahrscheinlicher (

All out for the defence of Rigaer94

), dass ein Angriff gegen unser Haus dem CDU-geführten Senat im Berliner Wahlkampf attraktiv erschien. Die CDU hätte ihr Wahlversprechen einhalten können und sich zusammen mit Innensenatorin Iris Spranger (SPD) als Hardliner gegen links verkaufen können. Ist es jetzt der letzte Versuch einer abgewählten Regierung dem neuen Senat zu schaden bzw. ihn zu zwingen, eine Räumung zu Ende zu führen, die allen Wahlversprechen der LINKEn entgegen steht? Oder ist es der konfrontative Kurs im Kampf gegen eine Bewegung von unten, der mehr und mehr auf der Tagesordnung steht und auf den sich alle Parteien einigen können? (

Andreas Geisel

, ehemaliger Innensenator, 

Juni 2021

). Auf rechtlicher Ebene hat sich seitdem nicht viel verändert.




Diese Fragen sind dringend. Sie zu beantworten überlassen wir anderen.




Für uns ist auf dieser Ebene aber klar, dass ein nicht legitimierter „Eigentümer“




 aufgrund eines daher unrechtmäßigen Deals mit Leuten,

 die eigentlich keinen Deal abschließen dürfen, weil sie

 weder im Besitz der Wohnungen sind,

 noch die Miete zahlen, die monatlich anfällt




kein Recht besitzt, eine Gerichtsvollzieherin zu beauftragen, die tatsächlichen Bewohner:innen dieser Wohnungen rauszuschmeißen.




Es ist eine bitterkalte Zeit…







Der Rausschmiss aus dem eigenem Zuhause ist die Realität vieler Menschen. Auch mitten im Winter. Weil die Miete unbezahlbar ist, weil es für Arbeit nur Brotkrumen gibt. Weil Milliarden in das Militär und Krieg gesteckt werden anstatt in Sozial- und Bildungspolitik. Neue Kriegstechnologien, entwickelt von imperialen Kräften, werden erst in militärischen Kriegsgebieten und an den tödlichen Grenzen getestet und später im sozialen Krieg gegen die eigene Gesellschaft angewendet. Der Genozid in Palästina geht weiter. Der israelische Staat und die USA werfen Bomben auf Gaza, Libanon, Iran und Yemen.




Doch seit Oktober hat sich ein gesellschaftlicher Aufstand ausgebreitet, ausgelöst von einer Jugend, die Straßen und Schulen blockiert. Die Menschen gehen auf die Straßen, gegen die unerträglichen Lebensbedingungen, gegen Armut und Wehrpflicht. Dagegen, dass die Bedeutung von Wahlen nur in der Wahl zwischen Ignoranz oder brutaler Repression der Machthabenden besteht. Sie stehen auf, für die Befreiung Palästinas als Bedingung der Freiheit aller, für das Recht auf Selbstbestimmung und ein freies, würdevolles Leben. In den Funken der letzten Wochen sehen wir das Überwinden von Lähmung und Perspektivlosigkeit. Von Hoffnung, die entsteht. Und hier sehen wir uns. Als kleiner Ort in einer Nachbarschaft Berlins, als ein Teil der vielfältigen Kämpfe im Herzen der Bestie. Die Rigaer94 ist ein Beispiel für eine gelebte Realität, in der Verweigerung gesellschaftlicher Zwänge möglich wird. Es ist ein Ort, an dem sowohl Selbstbestimmung und gemeinsame Fürsoge als auch Ungehorsam und Akte des Widerstands in alltäglicher Praxis Gestalt annehmen. Es zeigt klar und konkret, dass Selbstorganisation nicht nur eine politische Vorstellung ist, sondern eine greifbare Möglichkeit. Und es gehört allen, die Ideen der Autonomie zum Leben erwecken wollen.




…und die Zukunft bleibt ungewiss…




Was am 15. Dezember passieren wird, können wir nicht vorhersehen. Es könnte sein, dass die Gerichtsvollzieherin vor verschlossener Tür steht, ein paar Mal klingelt und wieder abzieht, um ein paar Tage oder Wochen später mit den Cops wieder zu kommen. Es könnte sein, dass sie direkt mit mehreren Hundertschaften anrückt, die in unser Haus einbrechen, einen Teil der Wohnungen versuchen zu räumen und dabei alles kurz und klein schlagen. Oder es wurde sich auf eine große Operation vorbereitet: Unsere Feinde versuchen Fakten zu schaffen, indem die Cops die besagten Wohnungen im 3. und 4. Stock des Hinterhauses räumen. Der angebliche Eigentümer quartiert Securitys ein, die die Wohnungen mit Gewalt vor einer Wiederbesetzung schützen sollen. Und um die Securitys zu schützen, belagern die Cops wochenlang das Haus und den Kiez. Auch wenn sich das surreal anfühlt, ist ein solches Szenario weder unrealistisch noch unmöglich.




Um zu erahnen, wie solche Aktionen enden können, lohnt sich ein Blick in die bereits erwähnte Vergangenheit: Sowohl 

2016

 als auch 

2021

 endeten Räumgsversuche in einem Desaster für Bullen, Politik und sogenanntem Eigentümer. Heute wie damals ist ihre juristische Grundlage bröckelig und die politische Situation aufgeheizt. Heute wie damals gibt es die Sorge, dass ihr Angriff reine Provokation ist, damit unser Widerstand ihnen eine Legitimation liefert, die Räumung bis zum bitteren Ende durchzuziehen. Aber heute wie damals ist klar – wir werden uns verteidigen.




… aber der Winter wird heiß und voller Möglichkeiten




Der angekündigte Angriff ist kein Grund alles stehen und liegen zu lassen und uns in die Defensive zurückzuziehen. Wir werden unsere Kämpfe weiterführen, offensiv und solidarisch. Wir werden heute und in den nächsten Wochen mit euch zusammen auf die Straße gehen, das Haus mit Leben füllen, Verbindungen vertiefen und unsere Ideen verteidigen. Wir sehen uns verbunden mit und als Teil von den vielfältigen Kämpfen für Befreiung und Autonomie weltweit. Und so sehen wir auch jeden Akt der Verteidigung dieser Ideen als gemeinsamen Weg, als Akt der Solidarität mit unserem Haus.




Wir werden uns vorbereiten und wir rufen euch auf, dasselbe zu tun. Lasst uns unseren Feinden in den nächsten Wochen zeigen, dass ein Angriff auf dieses Haus ein Spiel mit dem Feuer ist!




Wir grüßen unsere Gefährt*innen im Prosfygika in Athen, im Evagelismo in Heraklion, im CSA in Liège und an allen anderen Orten, an denen für ein selbstorganisiertes Leben, Kollektivität und ein solidarisches Miteinander gekämpft wird!




Wir grüßen unsere Gefährtinnen Marianna und Dimitra im Knast – wir ziehen Kraft aus eurer Entschlossenheit! Kyriakos unvergessen in unseren Kämpfen!




Love and rage, Rigaer94

title: Gesundheit im Ausschaffungsknast Bässlergut
content:
Neue Broschüre: Sedierung statt Behandlung




Katastrophale Unterversorgung in den Ausschaffungsgefängnissen Bässlergut und Kloten




«Wir sind seit 26 Tagen hier im Gefängnis, mein Bruder hat einen gebrochenen Arm und bis jetzt keine Behandlung bekommen. Er braucht eine Operation, ich brauche eine Operation. Aber sie sprechen nicht mit uns. Ich bin kein Hund. Wir machen weiter mit dem Hungerstreik bis sie mit uns reden, bis sie uns Antworten geben.»




Erzählt ein Gefangener des Ausschaffungsknasts Bässlergut in Basel bei einem Besuch im April 2026. In dieser Zeit traten darin fast die Hälfte der Gefangenen für mehrere Tage in den Hungerstreik. Zentral war dabei unter anderem die Forderung nach einer besseren Gesundheitsversorgung. Damals haben wir die Stimmen der Gefangenen gesammelt, die erklären, wieso sie Widerstand leisten. Dabei sind sowohl Erfahrungsberichte als auch Interviews entstanden, die wir durch Texte aus dem Ausschaffungsknast in Zürich (ZAA) und Recherchen zu an Ausschaffungen beteiligte Behörden und Firmen ergänzt haben.




Wir möchten mit dieser Broschüre einen Beitrag dazu leisten, die Anliegen und die Geschichten der Gefangenen im Bässlergut und in anderen Ausschaffungsknästen in der Schweiz aus den Knastmauern raus in eine breitere Öffentlichkeit zu tragen. Hungerstreik ist das äusserste Mittel, das Gefangene wählen können, um Veränderung einzufordern. Ihr Widerstand soll nicht umsonst sein – er muss gehört werden.

title: Armed Conflict Hinders Efforts to Contain Deadly Ebola Outbreak in the Congo
content:
The outbreak has killed more than 5,900 people, while fighting prevents health workers from reaching affected communities.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Three months after the United Nations senior Ebola coordinator warned that the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo was “growing exponentially,” government data showed Thursday that confirmed cases have topped 12,000 and left over 5,900 people dead.

The epidemic’s figures still rank behind the 2014-16 West African outbreak — which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 — but it is “the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll” from a decade ago, according to The Associated Press, which published a series of graphs demonstrating how fast-growing this crisis is.

Since the outbreak — caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus — was declared in May, it has spread to eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces. Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data recently revealed that just 15% of new cases come from contacts known to health authorities, and a Reuters analysis of satellite ⁠imagery found the death toll may be underestimated in two hard-hit areas.

Dozens of residents in eastern Congo say they have been unable to locate the bodies of relatives who died in the ongoing Ebola outbreak, while others say loved ones have been buried without their knowledge https://t.co/o5tKFPtRTS pic.twitter.com/PdCpb9Wa6R

The World Health Organization (WHO) said last Friday that “no new cases have been reported from Kenya or Nigeria; and no new country has reported confirmed cases,” but “the high-level transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo calls for continued need for readiness in the region, including cross-border surveillance, points of entry monitoring, timely case detection, and coordinated preparedness and response measures.”

The response in the DRC has been hindered by lack of community trust in authorities, poor infrastructure, and armed conflict, particularly between the army and the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) — one of dozens of militant groups in the resource-rich eastern part of the country, and led by Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted⁠ of conscripting child soldiers by the International Criminal Court in 2012.

Summarizing remarks from Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the WHO’s incident manager in the DRC, the AP reported Wednesday that “the fighting between the army and rebel groups has prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus, and left some treatment centers with fewer staff.”

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

“They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them,” Smallwood said.

WHO temporarily moved its Mongbwalu team and partner staff to Bunia after fighting disrupted road access, Smallwood said. Mongbwalu, a mining town northwest of Bunia, is where the outbreak was first detected in May.

The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO) said Wednesday that “the security situation has deteriorated significantly in several localities” due to clashes between DRC forces and the CRP, and Bangladeshi peacekeepers helped with that evacuation of health workers.

UN peacekeepers faced “significant logistical challenges,” including “difficult terrain, poor road conditions, and the fragile state of a wooden bridge,” before they reached the healthcare workers, who were evacuated by air to Bunia, MONUSCO noted.

“These healthcare workers, who are actively involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak, play a vital role in assisting communities already weakened by violence and displacement,” the mission said. “This intervention is part of MONUSCO’s support for Ebola response efforts, particularly through the protection of healthcare personnel and the facilitation of safe access to healthcare for populations affected by violence.”

.@WHO staff, @MinSanteRDC and other colleagues have been safely evacuated from the hospital in Akwe, Ituri Province, where they were sheltering amid fierce conflict for over three days. They have been brought to safety thanks to combined efforts across health, government and…

After the evacuation, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus thanked all those involved and stressed that “healthcare, health workers, Ebola responders, and humanitarian [aid] must be protected at all times!”
