author: Mark Blackburn
title: Resolutions at upcoming UCP convention calls land acknowledgements ‘humiliating’ and ‘politically compelled’
content:
As members of the ruling United Conservative Party (UCP) in Alberta get set to meet in Calgary, two resolutions dealing with land acknowledgements and land claims is getting pushback from the Blackfoot Confederacy.

According to the UCP resolution page, one resolution put forward by the riding associations in Highwood, Edmonton-Gold Bar, Innisfail-Sylvan Lake, Sherwood Park, CalgarySouth East, calls for the province to end land acknowledgements.

“Publicly funded institutions should promote approaches to shared history and civic unity that are inclusive of all Albertans and grounded in accuracy, respect, and common purpose,” resolution WG-2026-P-27 says.

“Many Albertans view these statements as performative, politically compelled, and unnecessarily humiliating, particularly when citizens are repeatedly reminded that they are “guests” or “settlers” in their own country regardless of how many generations their families have lived, worked, and contributed to Alberta.

The resolution adds that land acknowledgements also foster “resentment and social division.”

The second is listed as a “policy resolution” put forward by the Edmonton-Gold Bar riding association that “supports Alberta using all available legal avenues to challenge federal land claims, including Indigenous claims that may infringe on private property owners and their rights.

It calls for the province to resolve “disputes through the courts and constitutional processes to protect Alberta’s interests while ensuring clarity, stability, and accountability in land governance.

“Albertans must take a stand against the federal government’s plan to ‘protect’ thirty percent of land and water in the country. This is a direct threat to private land ownership,” it says.

On Thursday, the Blackfoot Confederacy issued a statement “expressing strong opposition” to the resolutions.

“Both resolutions raise significant concerns regarding Treaty recognition, the protection of First Nations rights and the government-to-government relationship between Blackfoot Nations and the Province of Alberta,” the statement said.

“Blackfoot Confederacy Chiefs reject efforts to characterize First Nations land claims as a threat to private property ownership. Many of these claims arise from the Crown’s failure to honour Treaty promises and fulfill its fiduciary obligations to First Nations. These claims seek to remedy historical injustices and address outstanding legal obligations of the Crown.”

Relations between First Nations in the province and the provincial government led by Premier Danielle Smith have been stone-cold since the province allowed a vote on sovereignty in Canada. The province is also asking the courts to quash a constitutional challenge launched by several First Nations over the sovereignty act.

The Siksikaitsitapi Blackfoot Confederacy is made up of Kainai, Siksika, Blackfoot, Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni Nations.

The UCP convention starts Nov. 27 and runs through the weekend.

Before moving to become the APTN News social media producer, Mark was the executive producer for the news in eastern Canada. Before starting with APTN in 2009, Mark worked at CBC Radio and Television in Newfoundland and Labrador and Ottawa.

author: Tareq S. Hajjaj
title: Genocide, Displacement and Malnutrition Threaten Pregnancies in Gaza
content:
Doctors in Gaza report rising congenital abnormalities as pregnant women face exposure to bombs and toxic substances.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Faiqa al-Arini, 33, gave birth to her first child on October 19 at Al-Awda Maternity Hospital in central Gaza. She was forced to deliver early, at the beginning of her ninth month of pregnancy, after developing high blood pressure.

Al-Arini gave birth to a baby girl through a cesarean section. They named her Nour. After the delivery, the new mother remained in the intensive care unit while the newborn was transferred to the neonatal ward. Al-Arini did not see her daughter at all that first day.

Whenever she asked, “Where is my baby?” the nurses and her family members reassured her that the infant was in the neonatal ward.

The following day, Al-Arini began to feel that something was wrong. She recalled not hearing her daughter cry when she was born. She started questioning her family and was determined to get up and look for the baby herself if the nurses did not bring her. Eventually, her husband, Muhammad Abdel Jawad, 37, confronted her with the news.

“You know it is better to hear this from us than from someone else,” he told her. “Our baby has a congenital deformity. She was born without hands.”

Abdel Jawad had seen his daughter immediately after her birth. When he had asked the doctors about the main factors that could cause such abnormalities in newborn babies, the doctors pointed to the dust from missiles, toxic chemicals, and the unhealthy environment where displaced people are forced to live across the Gaza Strip.

According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, the number of recorded congenital abnormalities among newborns has been increasing year after year. The ministry confirmed that 260 cases of congenital abnormalities had been recorded among newborns by the end of September 2026, compared with 184 cases in 2022. The number of recorded cases reached 322 in 2025, representing a 75% increase over a three year time period. However, the Ministry of Health says these figures alone do not establish the rate of congenital abnormalities among newborns or determine their causes.

Ashraf Qeshta, an obstetrics and gynecology specialist at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, says that the number of cases of miscarriage and congenital abnormalities among pregnant women has exceeded normal levels. He attributes this to several factors produced by the genocide, most notably the inhalation of toxic gases, exposure to missile remnants, living in an unhealthy environment, malnutrition, and other hardships imposed by war.

“We are seeing a significant number of congenital abnormalities. For example, babies are being born without skulls, others without limbs, and some with serious health problems, such as non-functioning or damaged kidneys, or heart defects,” Qeshta told Mondoweiss.

Even in cases where doctors believe that the congenital abnormality is caused by exposure to bombs and toxic substances, proving this requires advanced medical testing, sophisticated equipment, and qualified specialists. According to Qeshta, these are precisely the resources the Ministry of Health lacks, making it difficult to investigate and establish the different causes with scientific certainty.

Al-Arini said her pregnancy was extremely difficult. She was repeatedly displaced from one place to another and faced severe economic hardship, including famine, as her pregnancy began during the final months of the famine in 2025.

“Like all women in the Gaza Strip, we live under the same conditions,” al-Arini said. “We are displaced, we go hungry, we live in fear, and we narrowly escape death almost every day. Bombs and missiles explode beside us, and shrapnel flies over us. This is the reality for all women in Gaza.”

“But the effects of all these things are now beginning to show on us. I am happy that I gave birth to a girl, and I love her very much. I had indeed wished she would be born with limbs, but their absence does not make her any less my daughter, nor does it change anything about my feelings toward her. However, it makes me think deeply about the condition of our homeland, and about how even giving birth here has become fraught with danger. A baby can be born with congenital abnormalities because of the conditions we are living in,” she said.

A report published by Human Rights Watch on January 28, 2025, documented the grave health and humanitarian risks that pregnant women in the Gaza Strip are facing as a result of the siege, destruction of healthcare facilities, shortages of food, water, and medicine, and Israel’s genocidal war.

The report noted that pregnant women in Gaza face a severe shortage of medical care before, during, and after pregnancy, in addition to malnutrition, dehydration, and anemia. They also struggle to reach hospitals and obtain the medical examinations, vitamins, and supplements necessary for a healthy pregnancy.

The report added that the deterioration of maternity and childbirth services had increased the risks of complications, including bleeding, preeclampsia, and infections, amid shortages of incubators and medical supplies. These conditions threaten the lives of mothers, fetuses, and newborn babies alike.

In addition, a report issued by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) on August 7, 2026, presented the findings of a survey conducted between June 2 and June 16. The survey covered a sample of 1,335 children and found that 12.2% suffered from stunting relative to their age as a result of chronic malnutrition and inadequate access to sufficient food.

Farah Abu Mustafa, 25, lives in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis with her nine-month-old daughter, Zainab. Abu Mustafa’s pregnancy was fraught with unexpected hardships, repeated displacement, daily bombardment, witnessing people die, and exposure to gases and missile remnants.

Abu Mustafa says her daughter, Zainab, was born under difficult circumstances marked by deprivation of food and a lack of medical services during pregnancy. Since her birth, she has spent almost as much time in the hospital as she has in the tent of their displacement camp.

Zainab is suffering from malnutrition, brain atrophy, delayed neurological and muscular development, and recurrent seizures. When she’s in the hospital, her weight and health improve because of the care she receives. But as soon as the family returns to the tent in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, her condition deteriorates again.

Abu Mustafa says her daughter requires specialized medical care and strict adherence to medications and treatment. But in the tents, she can barely provide her with something to sleep on, let alone a clean and suitable place to recover.

“This is the life of displacement,” Abu Mustafa said. “Even the simplest things require a miracle for us to obtain them. Everything around us is crushing and grinding down displaced people.”

Abu Mustafa also points out that even preventive treatments intended to reduce the risk of congenital abnormalities are not available in pharmacies or easily accessible.

“Our Israeli occupier is waging war on the very air we breathe,” she said. “It is creating an environment conducive to diseases, congenital abnormalities, and miscarriages. Every woman I know has experienced a miscarriage, and I know many women who have given birth to babies with congenital abnormalities.”

“The occupation wants to eliminate generations, not just leave them with deformities,” she said.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Proteger el agua y celebrar la vida: "Somos el territorio, somos el cerro Famatina"
content:
Por Graciela Castañeda

*




Este libro es parte de la historia viva de un movimiento que traspasa los límites provinciales, recorre el país y se expande por el mundo, por cada lugar de nuestra Madre Tierra habitado por personas que trabajan, estudian y miran su entorno como algo más que una posesión material; personas amigadas con la naturaleza, que parten de la empatía, la solidaridad, la compasión y el amor. Comunidades conscientes que el territorio nos fue dado para vivir en armonía, honrando a la Pachamama.




Desde hace años que pensamos en publicar un libro que recogiera nuestra historia, un material colectivo, pleno de sensibilidad, dignidad y alegría. Un libro donde se pudieran leer las historias de quienes participaron de esta lucha, donde cada texto mantuviera la esencia, el sentir y el parecer de quien lo escribiera.




En el 2025, a punto de cumplir los 20 años en defensa de nuestro Cerro Famatina, decidimos poner manos a la obra y concretar este libro. Se invitó a los defensores y las defensoras del territorio a una construcción colectiva, popular, libre y abierta que rescatara la historia viva de esta pueblada, la invitación dirigida a las y los protagonistas era clara: plasmar sus vivencias, expresar su sentir y su hacer en estos años de lucha incansable y sostenida.




Fue una propuesta nacida del amor, la gratitud y la esperanza, guida por el deseo de unión comunitaria, que permitiera superar el individualismo y nos uniera detrás de objetivos comunes y propios: el agua para los pueblos desde la defensa del territorio que nos legaron nuestros antepasados

.

 Aquellas y aquellos que tan sabiamente comprendían que no eran dueños de la Tierra, que nuestro pasar es efímero pero la Pacha queda y tiene que seguir siendo el hogar de las nuevas generaciones.




Fue así que, convocadas las voces a la escritura, primero fue el silencio y luego, tímidamente, aparecieron los primeros escritos, hasta que los textos nos inundaron. Allí estaba la escritura hilada en relatos, en poesías y en cantares que hoy son parte de este libro: "Wamatinag madre del agua". Un escrito que nos trae las historias de todas y todos los que aceptaron el desafío de poner en palabras una parte significativa de sus vidas.




Aquí están las voces de quienes recuerdan sus infancias cuando partían con sus madres y sus padres a los cortes de rutas, a las asambleas; o cuando jugaban, cantaban y reían en los refugios creciendo juntos y hoy se reconocen en hermandad.




Están quienes con joven ímpetu sentían que algo tenían que aportar a esta causa, tal vez pensándolo solo como una aventura o con la típica rebeldía de la adolescencia, pero luego se dieron cuenta que estaban plantando los cimientos de algo más grande, que lejos estaba de pasar a ser una anécdota de juventud.




Los adultos, que traían consigo un amplio bagaje desde sus profesiones y haceres —agricultores, docentes, artesanos, profesionales, trabajadores— fueron abriendo camino, promoviendo las reuniones, leyendo e investigando mucho para informar a la comunidad también cuentan sus experiencias.




También están las historias de los mayores que, en forma individual o en escritura colectiva, rescatan sus vivencias. Sintieron el llamado de sus ancestros, de su cerro, del agua que da vida y es indispensable para proveer los frutos de la Madre Tierra. Al hacer oír sus voces sintieron que su lucha no fue en vano y renovaron su esperanza. Y, más aún, están también las historias de quienes ya partieron, pero dejaron sus huellas en acciones y en palabras.




Con esa infancia, esa juventud, acompañada por esos y esas adultas conscientes, nacieron las asambleas que también tienen su espacio en el libro. Contamos, además, con el aporte de investigadoras e investigadores que nos acercaron sus trabajos para que fueran parte del libro, nutriéndolo con el saber académico, ese que está a favor de la vida.




Al leer y releer cada página nos inunda la emoción, se renueva la esperanza pues somos conscientes de que, aunque en nuestro entorno parezca avanzar el caos, "el Famatina no se toca" es grito sagrado que nos congrega y nos hace fuertes.




A no dudarlo, el eco de "Wamatinag madre del agua" llegará lejos, se convertirá en sinónimo de nuestra frase insignia porque es canto de lucha esperanzada, amorosa voz que retumba en nuestros corazones al sentirnos comunidad y afianza nuestro sentir de que somos parte del territorio que habitamos.










*Integrante de las asambleas riojanas.




**Compilación realizada por la Asamblea por la vida Chilecito y Defensoras del Agua del Famatina. Se puede descargar desde 

la página de la Editorial Muchos Mundos

.




La entrada 

Proteger el agua y celebrar la vida: "Somos el territorio, somos el cerro Famatina"

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: Software Architektur im Stream
title: Fishbowl 'Friction is a Feature: Navigating the Inevitable Tensions of Software Architecture'
content:
Software architecture doesn’t live in diagrams – it’s forged in the gaps between teams, technologies, timelines, and trade-offs. Today, that landscape is shifting fast. LLMs and agentic workflows promise to erase friction – but often amplify it through toolchain sprawl, quality drift, and shifting accountability.




Yet friction is a signal. The most resilient teams channel it through shared understanding, recognizing that we’re shaping socio-technical systems – aligned through collaborative modelling woven into everyday decisions across architects, developers, QA, analysts, etc.




This fishbowl session confronts the reality behind the hype: how AI-generated code collides with architectural rigor, QA concerns, and production constraints. We’ll examine classic tensions (Conway’s Law, legacy vs. innovation, business urgency vs. technical debt) alongside new ones (toolchain sprawl, quality drift, over-reliance on generative AI).




As a conference attendee, you’re invited to step into the circle and challenge assumptions. Whether you’re an architect, engineer, QA lead, or system analyst, you’ll walk away with a refreshed perspective of timeless insights – and the courage to question them when it matters most.




This is a live stream from iSAQB Software Architecture Gathering.

author: Administrador
title: Gebet und Tanz für eine gute Reise.
content:
Gebet und Tanz für eine gute Reise.

In den zapatistischen Caracoles und Gemeinden – und auch in den Gemeinden der Partei-Anhänger*innen – haben die Tuneles [der anzestralen Spiritualität der Pueblos] und Katechet*innen [der katholischen Kirche von unten] zu einem Gebet zusammengerufen, um für die Delegation, die sich mit den Familien Sucherinnen in Mexiko-Statt treffen wird, [für eine gute Reise] zu bitten. Es wurde für deren Wohlergehen gebetet, sowie für das Wohlergehen der Familien, die diesen Schmerz und Jammer tragen, nichts mehr von einem geliebten Menschen zu wissen. Damit es ihnen im Herzen die Kraft gibt, nicht nachzulassen, bis sie ihn*sie gefunden haben.

Danach folgte das Tanzvergnügen mit Sonidero-Musik. Und in der Morgendämmerung fuhren dann die Fahrzeuge aus den 12 Caracoles zum CIDECI in San Cristóbal de las Casas los. Einige kamen nach bis zu 8 Stunden Fahrt – hin- und hergestoßen auf den Ladeflächen der Pritschenwagen und bei leichtem Regen, der den Weg säuberte und die Müdigkeit wegwischte – heute am 25. November gen Mittagszeit an.

Morgen, am 26. November, werden tausende Hände sticken, um zu versuchen, die Geschenke für die Mütter Sucherinnen zu vervollständigen. All das wegen des Capitán, der zuerst sagte, es geht um 100 Geschenke, dann 200, später auf 400 erhöhte und jetzt meint er, es sind [Geschenke für] mehr als 700 Familienangehörige Mexikos, die suchen [und mit denen sich getroffen wird]. Also geht es auf die Kappe des Capitán, falls die Geschenke nicht vollständig werden sollten.

Und tausende bereiten sich vor, um zuzuhören und zu umarmen.

Aus den Bergen des Südosten Mexikos.

Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés.

PS. Hier ein Video mit [Aufnahmen] einer Gebetszeremonie in einem Caracol, vom Tanz, der Ankunft im CIDECI sowie der gesamten Delegation im dortigen Auditorium. Diejenigen, die während des [Parole-]Rufens Misstöne verbreiten, sind die vom Comando Popcorn. Sie gehen nur bei Süßigkeiten und Schokolade koordiniert vor.

Zapatistische Tuneles, Katechet*innen, Keyboarder, Chauffeurologen, vollständige Delegation.

Musik: »Somos la fuerza – Wir sind die Kraft«, Mexikan Sound System.

author: Esperanza
title: PANGUIPULLI REÚNE A PUEBLOS INDÍGENAS DE AMÉRICA LATINA EN EL 2° CONGRESO INTERNACIONAL DE TERRITORIOS INDÍGENAS DE CONSERVACIÓN
content:
Por Comunicaciones Füta Mawiza




El encuentro, que se extenderá hasta el viernes 27 de noviembre, convoca a representantes de pueblos originarios, organizaciones territoriales y redes internacionales de conservación para compartir estrategias de gobernanza, defensa y conservación biocultural de los Territorios de Vida.




Comenzó en Panguipulli el 

2° Congreso Internacional de Territorios Indígenas de Conservación

, que se extenderá hasta el viernes 27 de noviembre bajo el lema 

“Estrategias y desafíos para el resguardo de los Territorios de Vida”

. Organizado por la Iniciativa Füta Mawiza, el encuentro reúne a representantes de pueblos indígenas, organizaciones territoriales, redes internacionales y experiencias comunitarias de conservación de distintos países de América Latina. Entre las articulaciones convocadas se encuentran la Red Territorios de Vida TICCA Latinoamérica, la Red de Mujeres Originarias por la Defensa del Mar (RDM), la Identidad Territorial Lafkenche (ITL) y la Federación por la Autodeterminación de los Pueblos Indígenas (FAPI), de Paraguay, junto a diversas organizaciones y experiencias locales impulsadas por pueblos originarios en lo que hoy conocemos como Chile y otros territorios de Abya Yala (América Latina).




Esta segunda versión da continuidad al proceso de articulación iniciado en septiembre de 2024 en Kurarewe, reafirmando el compromiso de fortalecer las estrategias de los pueblos indígenas y sus alianzas para el resguardo, la gobernanza y la conservación biocultural de los Territorios de Vida. 




El propósito es avanzar desde el ejercicio de los derechos colectivos, el reconocimiento de los conocimientos, las instituciones y las formas propias de relacionarse con la naturaleza. 




En este contexto, el congreso constituye un espacio de intercambio político y territorial frente a los desafíos que enfrentan los territorios, particularmente ante las presiones extractivas, la crisis climática y las distintas amenazas que afectan la continuidad de los sistemas de vida.




 Durante tres jornadas, el programa contempla paneles internacionales sobre derechos e incidencia política, gobernanza territorial, reconocimiento y registro de los Territorios de Vida, soberanía de datos, cartografía participativa y monitoreo biocultural. También se abordarán experiencias de mujeres indígenas defensoras de la vida, investigación propia, metodologías interculturales y transmisión intergeneracional de conocimientos. Entre las actividades destacan las salidas a terreno que se desarrollarán el jueves 26 para conocer experiencias de conservación y resguardo en el territorio mapuche de Panguipulli, además de muestras de cine indígena, espacios de conversación y actividades culturales.




La participación de representantes de Argentina, Paraguay, Guatemala, Panamá, México, El Salvador, Ecuador, Colombia, Nicaragua, Perú y Chile permitirá poner en diálogo distintas experiencias y fortalecer redes de colaboración entre pueblos y organizaciones de la región.
















2° Congreso Internacional de Territorios Indígenas de Conservación

. Panguipulli 2026.







Pero ¿qué entendemos por Territorios de Vida? Esta noción reconoce la estrecha relación que existe entre un pueblo indígena y un territorio, área o conjunto de bienes comunes, cuando a ese vínculo se suma una gobernanza local efectiva y la conservación de la naturaleza. No se trata únicamente de espacios naturales que requieren protección, sino de territorios habitados, construidos y cuidados a través de generaciones, donde se preservan memorias, conocimientos, normas propias y formas de organización. Desde esta perspectiva, los pueblos indígenas no son solamente actores vinculados a la conservación, sino protagonistas de su definición, gobernanza y continuidad. El congreso busca contribuir a visibilizar estas experiencias y proyectar acuerdos y estrategias conjuntas que fortalezcan el reconocimiento de los derechos colectivos y el protagonismo de los pueblos en el resguardo de la biodiversidad y la vida.




De lo que hoy es Chile están presentes personas y organizaciones de: 

Kawésqar Waes, Isla de las Guaitecas, Chonchi y Ancud en Chiloé, Walaywé, Cochamó, Purranque, Puyehue de Osorno a la cordillera, San Juan de la Costa, Lago Ranco, Valdivia, Kurarewe, Mehuín, Temuco, Trewako, Lago Budi, Lonquimay, Galvarino, Cañete, Quintero, Freirina, Caleta Chañaral de Aceituno, San Pedro de Atacama, Toconao y Arica.




De otros países y regiones están presentes de Puelmapu (Argentina) proveniente de Aluminé, Neuquén y San Martín de los Andes. Guatemala, Colombia, Madre de Dios en la Amazonía peruana, Paraguay, entre otros. También participa una representante del pueblo Aymara, en representación del Foro Internacional Indígena sobre Biodiversidad (FIIB). En total en estas tres jornadas en Panguipulli se reúnen cerca de 150 personas.










Esta información se publicó en 

Radio Kurruf

.

author: Julia Conley
title: The FCC Approves SpaceX’s Plan for 1 Million Space Satellites
content:
Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Environmental advocates warn that expanding satellites will impact “everyday lives as well as the future of our planet.”

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Federal Communications Commission’s approval on Wednesday of SpaceX’s plan to deploy one million orbital data center satellites into space by 2040 was not “just irresponsible,” said one environmental advocate.

“It’s reckless,” said Tim Whitehouse, executive director of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility. “The potential for these projects to degrade the atmosphere with pollution and debris and harm wildlife needs to be carefully considered before licensing these projects.”

Whitehouse was among the critics who noted that the approval had been granted without an environmental review, which is required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the deployment of one million “orbital space modules,” which SpaceX has said would form a new data center constellation called “Starmind,” would open “a bold new frontier” and allow the U.S. to lead “the world into the era of super intelligence.”

The satellites would process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth, according to SpaceX, the space exploration company led by Republican megadonor Elon Musk.

The environmental legal group Earthjustice said they also risk “changing our atmosphere, disrupting our daily activities that rely on satellites currently operating, disturbing wildlife, and fundamentally altering our night sky,” and denounced the commission for releasing the decision as families across the U.S. were preparing to celebrate Thanksgiving.

“Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.”

The number of satellites in space has already grown rapidly in the last several years, with 15,000 satellites in orbit in 2026 — up from 1,400 just over a decade ago.

Satellites cause emissions as they are placed in space through rocket launches, and other environmental impacts include debris from potential collisions — especially as the number of satellites grows — degradation of the ozone layer, and light pollution.

Astronomers spoke out against SpaceX’s plan earlier this year, saying it would prevent scientists from studying the night sky with modern telescopes, as well as disrupting ecosystems and humans’ biological clocks due to extreme light pollution.

On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s licensing of Musk’s plan.

“The proposed constellation would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” said the group. “The intended and unintended radio emissions from a constellation of such unprecedented size would imperil radio astronomy research, and the waste heat generated by the data centers would produce a thermal signature that would increase the infrared background of the sky and threaten the efficacy of sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research. In addition, atmospheric pollution from the launches and reentries of so many satellites, as well as increased collision risks in orbit, remain significant concerns; both of these factors threaten research astronomy.”

“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” the AAS added.

Earthjustice emphasized that the approval came as Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the permitting reform bill that would prevent future administrations from revoking licenses for projects including data centers and would block courts from enforcing environmental review laws for such projects if they had been violated previously.

“This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on Earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of [President Donald] Trump,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president of Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.”

author: Amy Goodman
title: After Nearly 50 Years in Prison, Leonard Peltier Says the Struggle Continues
content:
The longtime Indigenous activist discusses his conviction, childhood in boarding school and commitment to Indigenous sovereignty.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

In September 2025, Democracy Now! host Amy Goodman sat down with longtime political prisoner and Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier for his first extended television and radio broadcast interview since his release to home confinement in February 2025. Before his commutation by former President Joe Biden, the 82-year-old Peltier spent nearly 50 years behind bars. Peltier has always maintained his innocence for the 1975 killing of two FBI officers. He is expected to serve the remainder of his life sentences under house arrest at the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Nation in Belcourt, North Dakota. In a wide-ranging conversation, we spoke to Peltier about his case, his time in prison, his childhood spent at an American Indian boarding school and his later involvement in the American Indian Movement (AIM) and more.

“We still have to live under that, that fear of losing our identity, losing our culture, our religion,” Peltier says about his continued commitment to Indigenous rights. “The struggle still goes on for me. I’m not going to give up.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: In this special broadcast, we spend the hour with longtime Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier. Last February, he was released from a federal prison in Florida after spending nearly half a century behind bars for a crime he says he did not commit. President Biden, on his last day in office, commuted Peltier’s life sentence to home confinement. Biden’s decision followed mounting calls by tribal leaders and supporters around the world in a decadeslong, community-led campaign fighting for his freedom.

In the 1970s, Peltier was involved with the American Indian Movement, known as AIM. In 1975, two FBI agents and one young AIM activist were killed in a shootout on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. Two AIM members were later arrested for killing the agents. At the trial, the jury acquitted them. Leonard Peltier was arrested later, tried separately and convicted. Peltier has always maintained his innocence.

Notable supporters of Leonard Peltier over the years have included South African President Nelson Mandela, Pope Francis and Amnesty International. Supporters of Peltier say his trial was marked by gross FBI and federal prosecutorial misconduct, including the coercion of witnesses, fabricated testimony and suppressed exculpatory evidence.

After being released in February, Leonard Peltier returned home to live on the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Reservation in Belcourt, North Dakota. On September 12th, Leonard Peltier celebrated his 81st birthday. People gathered throughout the day, visiting him and calling from around the world to celebrate. That night and the next day, we spoke to Leonard Peltier in his living room in his first extended TV/radio broadcast interview since his release from prison.

AMY GOODMAN: Hi. I’m Amy Goodman, host of Democracy Now!, in the home of Leonard Peltier, just recently freed from prison after 49 years. LEONARD PELTIER: Plus two months. AMY GOODMAN: Plus two months. LEONARD PELTIER: Yeah. AMY GOODMAN: I’ve spoken to you so many times, Leonard, in prison, in various prisons, several of them supermax prisons. It is quite astonishing to be here with you in person. Tell us where we are. Where are we sitting? LEONARD PELTIER: We’re sitting in my home, that was given to me by my supporters. This was not given to me by the tribe, or the government had nothing to do with it. I was released by Biden under a commutation of my sentence and home confinement. Actually, what happened was, I was — I was taken out of one prison cell and really put into another type of prison. But this is my home now. This is my home. So it’s a million times better. AMY GOODMAN: Wait, what do you mean when you say you were taken out of your prison cell after more than 49 years, and you’re saying that you’re not completely free? LEONARD PELTIER: No, no, I’m on very restrictive restrictions. Even to go to the post office, I got to call my — I call her my handler. I have to call her to go to the post office. Then, when I get back, I have to call her and tell her I’m back. Or if I go anything, if I go shopping or whatever, I have to do that. If I have to go a hundred miles past the nation — I don’t call my place a “reservation,” either; we’re nations of people — I have to get a pass, usually from Washington, D.C., to go to medical, usually medical, or religious ceremonies on different nations, Indian Native nations. AMY GOODMAN: So, let’s go back to that moment when you were in that prison cell in Coleman, in Florida, and you got word that President Biden had commuted your sentence. It was just hours before he was leaving office? Can you tell us about that process, how it took place? LEONARD PELTIER: Well, as I went through the years filing for pardons and stuff, Ronald Reagan was the first one to promise to leave me — pardon me. Somebody in Washington stopped it. There’s only one organization that could have stopped it, and didn’t have the power to stop it, but still, somehow, were in power, enough to where they can override a president of the United States, our Congress. It’s the FBI. And Reagan promised to let me go. And the FBI intervened, and that was stopped. And Bill Clinton and Obama, and, finally, we get to Biden. And Biden, there was pressure put on him from all over the world. Almost every tribal nation here in the United States filed for my release, demanding my release. The United Nations — the United Nations did a full report on my case, and they demanded that I be released immediately and to be “paid,” quote-unquote. Hundreds of Congress and senators and millions of people — AMY GOODMAN: And the pope. LEONARD PELTIER: And the pope, two popes, the last pope and the current pope. AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

We’re continuing with our conversation with longtime Indigenous activist Leonard Peltier in Belcourt, North Dakota. I spoke to him there on his 81st birthday weekend on the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Cree Reservation. He was released from the federal prison in Florida after nearly half a century behind bars.

AMY GOODMAN: So, take us back in time. Introduce us to you, starting by saying your name, who your parents were, the nations they were a part of, your family, where you lived growing up. LEONARD PELTIER: OK. My name is — English name is Leonard Peltier. I’m 81 years old as of yesterday. My father is a Chippewa Cree, from this reservation, this nation right here. I keep saying “reservations,” because we was trained — we was taught from childhood that we are all reservations, we’re Indians. And we’re not Indians, and this is not a reservation. We made treaties with the United States government, and the Constitution says they shall only make treaties with sovereign nations. So we’re sovereign nations. We’re not — we’re not Indians, as they claim to be — they claim we are. And my mother is from Fort Totten. But again, that’s not the real name. The real name is Spirit Lake, and that’s of the Lakota/Dakota people. I was raised, majority of my life, here with my grandparents, which is usually the traditional way of my people. The grandparents will take the children and raise them. But when grandpa died, grandma had no way, no way to support us, so she went to the agency here to ask for help. And in retaliation, they took us and put us in a boarding school. AMY GOODMAN: What boarding school? LEONARD PELTIER: Wahpeton, North Dakota, 1953. I was there ’til — for three years, ’56. And it was extremely brutal conditions. AMY GOODMAN: How old were you? LEONARD PELTIER: I was 9 then, when I went. And — AMY GOODMAN: Talk about the point of these boarding schools. Was your hair cut? Did they stop you from speaking your language? LEONARD PELTIER: Of course. They did all — they did — that was the purpose of the schools, is to take the Indian out of the Indians, is what they literally — was the order. They took us to the boarding schools. The first thing they did was cut all our — buzz cut our hair, took it all off, and then put us and took us into the shower. We showered, and we come out of the shower, and we were poured all over our bodies DDT. As you know, that’s poisonous. AMY GOODMAN: They poured DDT over your body? LEONARD PELTIER: They poured DDT, with all the cans, on your head, the whole body. And then they gave us — issued clothes, bedding and assigned us to a bed. And that was the beginning of our treatment. It was an extremely, extremely strict school, and beatings were regular for any little violation of those rules. I might have been a little hot-headed, I don’t know. But when I first got there, there was a group. They called themselves the Resisters. And I immediately joined them, and I became part of the Resisters. So, we would sneak behind the gymnasium, and we would talk our language. We would sing some song, even do some prayers, yeah. And if we got caught, we got the [bleep] beat out of us. AMY GOODMAN: You wrote in your book, Prison Writings: My Life Is My Sun Dance, that you consider these boarding schools your first imprisonment. LEONARD PELTIER: Yes, it was. Was. We had to haul water. We had to haul wood. And we only had $55 to live on, which was my father’s World War II military benefits, and that’s what we had to live on. And we were facing the — we were facing the time of termination. The United States government wrote a bill, passed by Congress, signed by the president, of termination in 1956. It was supposed to be completed by 1985. And the first one to be terminated was the Menominee Indians of Wisconsin. They had millions of making — millions of prime land, timber and lakes to make hunting lodges and other things out there. It was beautiful, which they do today. They still — they got all those things out there today. But they came and took all that land from them. Then they come here in 1958. Was it ’58? Yeah, ’58. I was 13 years old then. LEONARD PELTIER: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Cree, yes. And my father and all of them and their generation, a lot of people left on relocation. They said, “It’s hopeless. You can’t come here and tell us that we got to leave and you’re going to just terminate us as a race of people and tell us that we no longer exist. Go [bleep] yourself. Come on. Let’s fight it out.” And literally, they were — I was proud of them. I was 13 years old. They stopped all provisions. One little girl died over here from malnutrition, and that’s what really got everybody angry. AMY GOODMAN: So they thought they would starve you out. LEONARD PELTIER: Yeah, they were making conditions so hard that we were accepting termination. We were leaving. LEONARD PELTIER: They reversed their decision and gave us $50 — AMY GOODMAN: Vouchers? LEONARD PELTIER: Vouchers to go buy groceries here in Rolla. Everybody got — the whole reservation got $50. AMY GOODMAN: And they didn’t disband the reservation? LEONARD PELTIER: No, they got the hell out of here, because we told them we’re going to fight them. AMY GOODMAN: So, this was really the beginning of the Red Power Movement and the founding of AIM, right? LEONARD PELTIER: Well, I guess so, in so many — yeah, in so many — yeah. AMY GOODMAN: The American Indian Movement. LEONARD PELTIER: Yeah. AMY GOODMAN: Which you want to rename the American — LEONARD PELTIER: But they were — but they were doing that for — I mean, my people have been fighting back for 500 years, Amy. AMY GOODMAN: But the modern day. LEONARD PELTIER: Yeah, the modern-day stuff. But no, we went to war with them. We went to all kinds of different levels of — AMY GOODMAN: Resistance? LEONARD PELTIER: Resistance, you know. AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about the founding of AIM, the American Indian Movement, which you today would like to rename the American Indigenous Movement. LEONARD PELTIER: Well, I was involved in a number of different organizations before I joined AIM. One of the treaties that we were pushing them days — actually, our people was — older people were pushing this, too, but they just passed. All of our knowledge came from traditionalists. That’s the policies, the American Indian Movement, we followed there. There. First of all, people got to understand, the American Indian Movement policy is they can’t come onto this reservation, start dictating their policy. They have to be invited by the traditionalists or a tribal government or what else. We can’t just go onto a reservation and say, “You’re going to do this, you’re going to do that.” No, we can’t do that, and we don’t do that. We have to be invited first. That was a big area that they really fought hard and got really — AMY GOODMAN: Fishing and hunting rights. LEONARD PELTIER: Yes, treaty rights. In fact, Marlon Brando got arrested with us in 1955. He got arrested on one of them lakes. I wasn’t there, but he was — he got arrested fishing and hunting with the Natives out there. AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about the occupation of the BIA offices in Washington, moving on to Wounded Knee and Pine Ridge. LEONARD PELTIER: Well, it just — our resistance became extremely popular. American Indian Movement was growing, and not just here in America — Canada, Central America. Said, “Wow! There are a lot of full bloods all through Central America,” more than people — more than here in the United States. And we were uniting with all of them, all those Natives across this country — across this whole continent, I mean. And we were uniting. We were pulling them together with the American Indian Movement. That’s why we became a threat to the government so. And later, later on, when I was arrested — after I got arrested, this one guy was telling me, he said, “You know, I just went down to Mexico someplace, one of them towns.” And he said they were organizing for resistance and stuff like this. He said, “I was down there, down there visiting them.” He said, “I went to this old — this guy told me he was the — he was some kind of medicine man or something. So I went down and visited him, and so I went into his place,” into his — he had kind of a hut-like home, I guess. And he said, “What do I see?” He said, “I see your poster on one of the walls.” That’s so far back. But I wasn’t. We went through all that stuff. And so, anyway — AMY GOODMAN: But especially for young people to understand, I mean, you’re talking about this critical moment of 1973, ’4 and ’5. LEONARD PELTIER: ’60s, actually. AMY GOODMAN: What’s that? LEONARD PELTIER: Started in the ’60s, really. AMY GOODMAN: And also the height of the antiwar movement. And the role and the effect of the antiwar movement on the Native American movement, and vice versa? If you can talk about those critical moments? LEONARD PELTIER: We were — I was, and others were, a lot of us Natives were — we were also involved in the peace marches and with the Blacks and the antiwar movements and things like that. We were involved in all that stuff, too. But we were working on trying to get their support, and they were working on trying to get our support. Then the hippies came out, and the hippies really helped us. The hippies did a lot to help us. They started dressing like Natives. They started doing things like Native people. And a lot of them came from very, very wealthy families. A lot of people hated them. That’s one of the reasons the government hated them, is because they were really pushing the Native issues, the culture and stuff like that. AMY GOODMAN: So, the Trail of Broken Treaties, that was 1972. Explain what it was, which was a takeoff on the Trail of — LEONARD PELTIER: Well, we knew that we had to get to — get the government to start honoring our treaties, because they never honored our treaties. And the only way we could do this is to go right straight to Washington. And so, we organized a group. We called it the Trail of Broken Treaties. And we all organized from all over the country. They sent representatives in old cars. We had all — nobody had new cars them days. And we all went to Washington. AMY GOODMAN: You went? LEONARD PELTIER: Of course, I did. Of course, I was there, too, yeah. AMY GOODMAN: This is, of course, a takeoff on the Trail of Tears. And most people, in our schools, and maybe less so especially now, will ever even know what the Trail of Tears was. LEONARD PELTIER: Right, right, right, precisely. That was all past — everything we did, we called it — well, like the Trail of Broken Treaties, that was done out of the Trail of Tears, and the Long Walk, all them other events like that that happened. It wasn’t just the Trail of Tears. That’s what people have to understand. It was — the Trail of Tears was just one of them that became so well known, because I think 10,000 people died on that, and just laying alongside the trails and stuff from dying from sickness, malnutrition, all that stuff, on the Trail of Tears. And that’s why it got so — AMY GOODMAN: This was President Andrew Jackson? LEONARD PELTIER: Yes, yeah. AMY GOODMAN: The president who President Trump reveres. LEONARD PELTIER: It was [bleep] order, yeah. He was a anti — he was a hater. And so, we were prevented. We organized. We organized under basically the same policies of exposing what was done in the past, what continued to be done. And we still find it’s still happening today, Amy. Ann Coulter had made a public statement that — about Native people, that we didn’t kill enough of them Indians. That’s a very dangerous thing to say about anybody, because there’s a bunch of nuts out there, like, you know, you take one of them haters and everything, he can end up killing a lot of innocent Natives for — just because those type of words. You got a president trying to do away with our treaties. If our treaties go, we go. This is the only thing to prove that we are a sovereign nation and a race of people. And if that goes, we go, as a race of people. So, it’s not — I mean, it’s not ending for us. We’re still in danger. Yeah, you see it happening in the streets, you know, I mean, right today. Look at what they’re doing in Palestine, killing women, children, babies, unborn babies. That’s what they did to us, man. And here it is still happening. AMY GOODMAN: So, 52 years ago, 1973, the start of the American Indian Movement’s 71-day occupation of the village of Wounded Knee on Pine Ridge Reservation, occupation helping draw international attention to the plight of Native Americans, the U.S. government responding to the occupation with a full military siege that included armored personnel carriers, F-4 Phantom jets, U.S. Marshals, FBI, state and local enforcement. It was about halfway through. Then I went, and I went up there, and I helped pack in stuff into Wounded Knee. And I stayed out there on the outside forces. After we made all those trips to Washington and all that stuff, all those other demonstrations, and all those promises, they were going to do this and do that. They were going to investigate everything, all of our acquisitions and all that stuff. And we soon found out — we knew anyway, but we soon found out that was all a lie. They weren’t going to investigate [bleep]. And they didn’t. And so, finally, the elders and the chiefs made the decision to go to Wounded Knee. AIM had no part in that decision. We cannot go anyplace in Indian Country and make policies. We can’t. That’s not — that is not us. We can’t do that. And we can’t go unless we’re invited by those people. And they just got fed up with so many more false promises and what was happening. They were being terrorized by a group organized by — a mercenary group, I might add. And the leader made that — admitted that on a national interview. So we know that’s all true. They tried to deny it at first, but they called themselves the Guardians of the Oglala Nation. Nixon ordered the 82nd Airborne to go and investigate what’s going on down there. See, that was all illegal. And that’s how we found out a lot of stuff about what they were doing there. And it was all illegal. But he didn’t, because, we heard, his wife stepped forward and said, “No, don’t you do that.” AMY GOODMAN: Now, still going back 50 years, what landed you in jail? Murders went uninvestigated by the FBI, which had jurisdiction. The period culminating in the June 26th shootout for which Leonard Peltier was imprisoned. LEONARD PELTIER: First of all, I don’t know who the shooter is, or shooters. And I don’t — I wouldn’t tell you if I did know, so I’m not going to tell you anything in that area. But I’ll tell you — I’ll speak on the other issues, because it’s public knowledge, and it’s been — it’s been our attempts to continue to expose that stuff. But there was a lot of Native people, traditionalists, whose homes were burned, whose houses were — was drive-by shootings. People were pulled over and beaten, and some shot, some killed. And those things are literally recordings on this. We got records of all this stuff now, so people can’t deny this stuff. The only ones that are denying this [bleep] is the United States government and the FBI and people like that. They were — and getting away with it, because they didn’t have — they had no fear of being prosecuted. AMY GOODMAN: So, take us back in time. Introduce us to you, starting by saying your name, who your parents were, the nations they were a part of, your family, where you lived growing up.

LEONARD PELTIER: OK. My name is — English name is Leonard Peltier. I’m 81 years old as of yesterday. My father is a Chippewa Cree, from this reservation, this nation right here.

I keep saying “reservations,” because we was trained — we was taught from childhood that we are all reservations, we’re Indians. And we’re not Indians, and this is not a reservation. We made treaties with the United States government, and the Constitution says they shall only make treaties with sovereign nations. So we’re sovereign nations. We’re not — we’re not Indians, as they claim to be — they claim we are.

And my mother is from Fort Totten. But again, that’s not the real name. The real name is Spirit Lake, and that’s of the Lakota/Dakota people.

I was raised, majority of my life, here with my grandparents, which is usually the traditional way of my people. The grandparents will take the children and raise them. But when grandpa died, grandma had no way, no way to support us, so she went to the agency here to ask for help. And in retaliation, they took us and put us in a boarding school.

AMY GOODMAN: What boarding school?

LEONARD PELTIER: Wahpeton, North Dakota, 1953. I was there ’til — for three years, ’56. And it was extremely brutal conditions.

LEONARD PELTIER: I was 9 then, when I went. And —

AMY GOODMAN: Talk about the point of these boarding schools. Was your hair cut? Did they stop you from speaking your language?

LEONARD PELTIER: Of course. They did all — they did — that was the purpose of the schools, is to take the Indian out of the Indians, is what they literally — was the order. They took us to the boarding schools. The first thing they did was cut all our — buzz cut our hair, took it all off, and then put us and took us into the shower. We showered, and we come out of the shower, and we were poured all over our bodies DDT. As you know, that’s poisonous.

AMY GOODMAN: They poured DDT over your body?

LEONARD PELTIER: They poured DDT, with all the cans, on your head, the whole body. And then they gave us — issued clothes, bedding and assigned us to a bed. And that was the beginning of our treatment. It was an extremely, extremely strict school, and beatings were regular for any little violation of those rules.

I might have been a little hot-headed, I don’t know. But when I first got there, there was a group. They called themselves the Resisters. And I immediately joined them, and I became part of the Resisters. So, we would sneak behind the gymnasium, and we would talk our language. We would sing some song, even do some prayers, yeah. And if we got caught, we got the [bleep] beat out of us.

AMY GOODMAN: You wrote in your book, Prison Writings: My Life Is My Sun Dance, that you consider these boarding schools your first imprisonment.

LEONARD PELTIER: Yes, it was. Was. I found the rules more restrictive than when I went — ended up in prison.

AMY GOODMAN: So, you go to this residential school with your cousin and sister for three years. Where do you come back to? And how did you maintain your language and your culture?

LEONARD PELTIER: Well, I came back here to live with my father. And they were still living in log cabins, no electricity, no running water. We had to haul water. We had to haul wood. And we only had $55 to live on, which was my father’s World War II military benefits, and that’s what we had to live on.

And we were facing the — we were facing the time of termination. The United States government wrote a bill, passed by Congress, signed by the president, of termination in 1956. It was supposed to be completed by 1985. And the first one to be terminated was the Menominee Indians of Wisconsin. They had millions of making — millions of prime land, timber and lakes to make hunting lodges and other things out there. It was beautiful, which they do today. They still — they got all those things out there today. But they came and took all that land from them. Then they come here in 1958. Was it ’58? Yeah, ’58. I was 13 years old then. And they came and told us we have been terminated, and we have to accept that. We were supposed to be the second reservation to be terminated.

AMY GOODMAN: The Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Cree.

LEONARD PELTIER: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Cree, yes. And my father and all of them and their generation, a lot of people left on relocation. They said, “It’s hopeless. We can’t fight these people. They’re too powerful. They got — they’re just too powerful. You know, maybe life will be better over there,” and stuff like this on this relocation. So they picked the city to go to. A lot of them went to Washington state and Oregon.

And it was a small group of us stayed here and said, “No, we’re not leaving.” So, my dad and his generation said, “Well, what do you mean, ‘been terminated’? You can’t come here and tell us that we got to leave and you’re going to just terminate us as a race of people and tell us that we no longer exist. Go [bleep] yourself. Come on. Let’s fight it out.” And literally, they were — I was proud of them. I was 13 years old.

They stopped all provisions. One little girl died over here from malnutrition, and that’s what really got everybody angry.

AMY GOODMAN: So they thought they would starve you out.

LEONARD PELTIER: Yeah, they were making conditions so hard that we were accepting termination. We were leaving. A lot of people took to say, “Well, at least my kids won’t starve to death.”

AMY GOODMAN: And the BIA reversed its decision?

LEONARD PELTIER: They reversed their decision and gave us $50 —

LEONARD PELTIER: Vouchers to go buy groceries here in Rolla. Everybody got — the whole reservation got $50.

AMY GOODMAN: And they didn’t disband the reservation?

LEONARD PELTIER: No, they got the hell out of here, because we told them we’re going to fight them.

AMY GOODMAN: So, this was really the beginning of the Red Power Movement and the founding of AIM, right?

LEONARD PELTIER: Well, I guess so, in so many — yeah, in so many — yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: The American Indian Movement.

AMY GOODMAN: Which you want to rename the American —

LEONARD PELTIER: But they were — but they were doing that for — I mean, my people have been fighting back for 500 years, Amy.

AMY GOODMAN: But the modern day.

LEONARD PELTIER: Yeah, the modern-day stuff. But no, we went to war with them. We went to all kinds of different levels of —

LEONARD PELTIER: Resistance, you know.

AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about the founding of AIM, the American Indian Movement, which you today would like to rename the American Indigenous Movement.

LEONARD PELTIER: Well, I was involved in a number of different organizations before I joined AIM. And one of the biggest ones that I was — I helped organize the United Tribes of All Indians in Washington state. And we took over Fort Lawton. One of the treaties that we were pushing them days — actually, our people was — older people were pushing this, too, but they just passed. All of our knowledge came from traditionalists. That’s the policies, the American Indian Movement, we followed there. There.

First of all, people got to understand, the American Indian Movement policy is they can’t come onto this reservation, start dictating their policy. They have to be invited by the traditionalists or a tribal government or what else. We can’t just go onto a reservation and say, “You’re going to do this, you’re going to do that.” No, we can’t do that, and we don’t do that. We have to be invited first.

So, anyway, this was before I joined the American Indian Movement. I was involved with the fishing and hunting struggles over there. That was a big area that they really fought hard and got really —

AMY GOODMAN: Fishing and hunting rights.

LEONARD PELTIER: Yes, treaty rights. In fact, Marlon Brando got arrested with us in 1955. He got arrested on one of them lakes. I wasn’t there, but he was — he got arrested fishing and hunting with the Natives out there.

AMY GOODMAN: So, talk about the occupation of the BIA offices in Washington, moving on to Wounded Knee and Pine Ridge.

LEONARD PELTIER: Well, it just — our resistance became extremely popular. American Indian Movement was growing, and not just here in America — Canada, Central America. Said, “Wow! There are a lot of full bloods all through Central America,” more than people — more than here in the United States. And we were uniting with all of them, all those Natives across this country — across this whole continent, I mean. And we were uniting. We were pulling them together with the American Indian Movement. That’s why we became a threat to the government so.

And later, later on, when I was arrested — after I got arrested, this one guy was telling me, he said, “You know, I just went down to Mexico someplace, one of them towns.” And he said they were organizing for resistance and stuff like this. He said, “I was down there, down there visiting them.” He said, “I went to this old — this guy told me he was the — he was some kind of medicine man or something. So I went down and visited him, and so I went into his place,” into his — he had kind of a hut-like home, I guess. And he said, “What do I see?” He said, “I see your poster on one of the walls.” That’s so far back. But I wasn’t. We went through all that stuff. And so, anyway —

AMY GOODMAN: But especially for young people to understand, I mean, you’re talking about this critical moment of 1973, ’4 and ’5.

LEONARD PELTIER: ’60s, actually.

LEONARD PELTIER: Started in the ’60s, really.

AMY GOODMAN: And also the height of the antiwar movement. And the role and the effect of the antiwar movement on the Native American movement, and vice versa? If you can talk about those critical moments?

LEONARD PELTIER: We were — I was, and others were, a lot of us Natives were — we were also involved in the peace marches and with the Blacks and the antiwar movements and things like that. We were involved in all that stuff, too. But we were working on trying to get their support, and they were working on trying to get our support. Then the hippies came out, and the hippies really helped us. The hippies did a lot to help us. They started dressing like Natives. They started doing things like Native people. And a lot of them came from very, very wealthy families. A lot of people hated them. That’s one of the reasons the government hated them, is because they were really pushing the Native issues, the culture and stuff like that.

AMY GOODMAN: So, the Trail of Broken Treaties, that was 1972. Explain what it was, which was a takeoff on the Trail of —

LEONARD PELTIER: Well, we knew that we had to get to — get the government to start honoring our treaties, because they never honored our treaties. And the only way we could do this is to go right straight to Washington. And so, we organized a group. We called it the Trail of Broken Treaties. And we all organized from all over the country. They sent representatives in old cars. We had all — nobody had new cars them days. And we all went to Washington.

LEONARD PELTIER: Of course, I did. Of course, I was there, too, yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: This is, of course, a takeoff on the Trail of Tears. And most people, in our schools, and maybe less so especially now, will ever even know what the Trail of Tears was.

LEONARD PELTIER: Right, right, right, precisely. That was all past — everything we did, we called it — well, like the Trail of Broken Treaties, that was done out of the Trail of Tears, and the Long Walk, all them other events like that that happened. It wasn’t just the Trail of Tears. That’s what people have to understand. It was — the Trail of Tears was just one of them that became so well known, because I think 10,000 people died on that, and just laying alongside the trails and stuff from dying from sickness, malnutrition, all that stuff, on the Trail of Tears. And that’s why it got so —

AMY GOODMAN: This was President Andrew Jackson?

AMY GOODMAN: The president who President Trump reveres.

LEONARD PELTIER: It was [bleep] order, yeah. He was a anti — he was a hater. And so, we were prevented. We organized. We organized under basically the same policies of exposing what was done in the past, what continued to be done.

And we still find it’s still happening today, Amy. Ann Coulter had made a public statement that — about Native people, that we didn’t kill enough of them Indians. That’s a very dangerous thing to say about anybody, because there’s a bunch of nuts out there, like, you know, you take one of them haters and everything, he can end up killing a lot of innocent Natives for — just because those type of words.

You got a president trying to do away with our treaties. If our treaties go, we go. This is the only thing to prove that we are a sovereign nation and a race of people. And if that goes, we go, as a race of people. So, it’s not — I mean, it’s not ending for us. We’re still in danger. Yeah, you see it happening in the streets, you know, I mean, right today. Look at what they’re doing in Palestine, killing women, children, babies, unborn babies. That’s what they did to us, man. And here it is still happening.

AMY GOODMAN: So, 52 years ago, 1973, the start of the American Indian Movement’s 71-day occupation of the village of Wounded Knee on Pine Ridge Reservation, occupation helping draw international attention to the plight of Native Americans, the U.S. government responding to the occupation with a full military siege that included armored personnel carriers, F-4 Phantom jets, U.S. Marshals, FBI, state and local enforcement. During the occupation, two Sioux men shot dead by federal agents, and a Black civil rights activist, Ray Robinson, went missing. The FBI confirmed in 2014, decades later, that Ray Robinson had been killed during the standoff. Most people don’t know about this history.

AMY GOODMAN: Maybe they’ve heard the book Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee. So, can you talk about Pine Ridge and Wounded Knee, especially for young people who don’t know the history?

LEONARD PELTIER: Well, I was in jail during the beginning of Wounded Knee, but I got out. It was about halfway through. Then I went, and I went up there, and I helped pack in stuff into Wounded Knee. And I stayed out there on the outside forces.

After we made all those trips to Washington and all that stuff, all those other demonstrations, and all those promises, they were going to do this and do that. They were going to investigate everything, all of our acquisitions and all that stuff. And we soon found out — we knew anyway, but we soon found out that was all a lie. They weren’t going to investigate [bleep]. And they didn’t.

And so, finally, the elders and the chiefs made the decision to go to Wounded Knee. AIM had no part in that decision. We cannot go anyplace in Indian Country and make policies. We can’t. That’s not — that is not us. We can’t do that. And we can’t go unless we’re invited by those people. And they just got fed up with so many more false promises and what was happening.

They were being terrorized by a group organized by — a mercenary group, I might add. They were provided with intelligence, armored person ammunition, sophisticated weapons, surveillance and stuff like this, automobiles and stuff. And the leader made that — admitted that on a national interview. So we know that’s all true. They tried to deny it at first, but they called themselves the Guardians of the Oglala Nation. And —

LEONARD PELTIER: The GOONs, yeah.

LEONARD PELTIER: Dick Wilson, all them. Nixon ordered the 82nd Airborne to go and investigate what’s going on down there. And if there was — if we were like the government was claiming, that we were communists and Marxists, and we were being financed by the communists, they were to go up there and wipe us out.

When Nixon got the 82nd Airborne involved in it, we filed a lawsuit. And it took us 10 years, but we got all this information out of the files that they had to turn over to us, right? And we found that they had went to the armory and checked out 250,000 rounds of various caliber ammunition, different sophisticated weaponry, armored personnel carriers, and finances and surveillance and stuff like that. See, that was all illegal. And that’s how we found out a lot of stuff about what they were doing there. And it was all illegal. If it would have been left to Nixon, he would have — he was going to wipe us out. But he didn’t, because, we heard, his wife stepped forward and said, “No, don’t you do that.”

AMY GOODMAN: Now, still going back 50 years, what landed you in jail? I want to go to the words in Democracy Now! in 2003. The occupation of Wounded Knee is considered the beginning of what Oglala people refer to as the Reign of Terror, from ’73 to ’76, over 60 residents killed in this period. Murders went uninvestigated by the FBI, which had jurisdiction. The period culminating in the June 26th shootout for which Leonard Peltier was imprisoned.

LEONARD PELTIER: First of all, I don’t know who the shooter is, or shooters. And I don’t — I wouldn’t tell you if I did know, so I’m not going to tell you anything in that area. But I’ll tell you — I’ll speak on the other issues, because it’s public knowledge, and it’s been — it’s been our attempts to continue to expose that stuff.

But there was a lot of Native people, traditionalists, whose homes were burned, whose houses were — was drive-by shootings. People were pulled over and beaten, and some shot, some killed. And those things are literally recordings on this. We got records of all this stuff now, so people can’t deny this stuff. The only ones that are denying this [bleep] is the United States government and the FBI and people like that.

But we faced a time called the Reign of Terror, when they were getting away with all this [bleep]. None of them were getting investigated. A lot of the older people that seen these people identified them, but the FBI still wouldn’t investigate. They were able to kill people at random. They were — and getting away with it, because they didn’t have — they had no fear of being prosecuted. The only fear they had was of us, the American Indian Movement, because we wouldn’t take their [bleep]. Every chance we got together, we got a confrontation with them. And that’s the only fear they had of anything, of any retaliations, any arrests or anything else.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re spending the hour with Indigenous elder Leonard Peltier. He was released in February from prison after nearly 50 years behind bars. Stay with us.

LEONARD PELTIER: I never knew her. Her father came to my — was going to come testify at my trial that she had a serious mental problem. And they were sitting there drinking, drinking beer, and they ran out of beer. And they were watching TV, she said, and they decided to make a run off the reservation, because it was a dry reservation. No alcohol was allowed there. And so, she says, to go buy some more beer, come back and watch some more TV. And they started driving down the road, and all of a sudden a bulletin came over the radio: a big shootout in Oglala between the Marshals, FBI, BIA cops, GOON squads against the American Indian Movement. So they were over 50 miles away. Finally, Myrtle admitted that she didn’t know me. AMY GOODMAN: But she — her testimony said that — LEONARD PELTIER: Her testimony in the grand jury is what got us all indicted. AMY GOODMAN: Said she was your girlfriend and she had seen — LEONARD PELTIER: She witnessed — oh god. AMY GOODMAN: Seen all of this. LEONARD PELTIER: When the lawyers came to me in Canada, they said, “Leonard” — they said, “Leonard, we got bad news for you.” And I said, “Yeah? LEONARD PELTIER: Well, OK, I think — I’ve been asked this question quite a bit, and it’s hard for me to answer. But I think that what really kept me strong was my anger. I was extremely angry about what they did to me and my people. And I’m still — still very, very [bleep] angry. And there was no way in hell I was going to get justice. I could have had — I had at least 14 constitutional issues that I should have been released on, at least that many, and I knew I wasn’t going to get it. You know, I found evidence of them meeting with Judge Heaney. And Judge Heaney became a strong advocate for my release. But we found evidence he worked with the FBI. And I just — I felt so much hate and anger, and what they — what they did to Native people in this country, this continent, and that kept me strong. And so, the fight for, the struggle still goes on for me. I’m not going to give up. I’m not going to — I have not surrendered. I don’t want to go back to prison, although I heard that Trump was going to try to take away all of Biden’s pardons and everything else like that.
