author: Emma Honeybun
title: Plan to decolonize Manitoba’s child welfare system is a big task that will take time, says minister
content:
The director of Manitoba’s child advocacy office says that improving the current child welfare system needs a new approach that places control back to First Nations families.

However, doing so while First Nations are also struggling with a lack of resources and community spaces for the kids to thrive presents its own set of challenges.

“Decolonization is a huge undertaking,” said Sherry Gott, a member of Sapotaweyak Cree Nation who has been working in child welfare education for more than 30 years. “That means we must dismantle systems that have continued to colonize our people.”

Gott is the executive director of Manitoba’s Advocate for Children and Youth (MACY), a non-partisan social work office funded by the province. On Nov. 18, it published its latest annual report, which, among other findings, indicated that 53 per cent of serious injuries involving youth (aged 0 to 20) that resulted in a report were caused by sexual assault.

She said her “dream” would be an outcome where a typical CFS wouldn’t be necessary, because First Nations would have the resources necessary to support children who may be in crisis, but that those resources are currently hard to come by.

“We have to believe that we have the knowledge to be able to look at the system in a way where it supports our families,” Gott said. “So we also have to believe that we have traditional knowledge that is valuable. We must believe that we have the answers to support our families to thrive.”

According to the latest report from MACY, the agency doesn’t have the resources to keep up with a growing number of children in crisis.

She said the resources MACY currently needs the most is adequate staffing, and that the shortage can be “really taxing on our mental health, when you look at what comes through the door.”

“Issues of sexual exploitation and abuse is a really, really difficult subject to deal with. And when you have a name behind that incident, then you start to know who the family is and who the children are, who’s involved, it gets even more personal,” Gott continued. “Because you have names attached to it, and communities, Nations, where these children come from. So it is really hard to work daily at that level … It’s hard on our staff. But we try our best to keep their mental health and well-being in check.”

According to the report, the office received 506 referrals from April 2025 to March 2026, but only 300 were able to be reviewed, according to the legal definition of a serious injury.

Because of the demand, only 135 of the 300 referrals legally eligible for review have ended with complete serious injury reports, as of writing. Only 99 were assessed for potential investigation, and 36 of those assessments were reviewed further.

According to the 2025-2026 annual report from the office of provincial Minister of Families Nahanni Fontaine, 80 per cent of children in care are First Nations.

Similarly, Gott said that approximately 80 per cent of children represented in MACY’s serious injury reports are Indigenous.

MACY also completed 60 child death reports in 2025-26, although there were 71 in scope for a review.

Sixty-eight per cent of the children in the completed reports were Indigenous, and 98 per cent of the reports were linked to CFS.

The most recent reported death in care is five-year-old Baileigh Berens in Winnipeg. Baileigh had autism and was non-verbal, but had no known health conditions and her cause of death has not been determined. She was found in a dryer.

The Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs (AMC), which represents all 63 First Nations in Manitoba, held a sacred fire for the child at her mother’s house Wednesday evening.

Following the release of MACY’s annual report, AMC Grand Chief Kyra Wilson stated that “these findings are deeply concerning, but they are not new warnings.”

“First Nations families and survivors have been raising these concerns for decades. When children are placed in systems intended to protect them but continue to experience violence, exploitation, and abuse, we must hold those systems accountable,” she continued.

The AMC had called on Canada to examine “child welfare, child protection, and children in care” as part of the National Inquiry into Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in 2018, a recommendation that made it into the final report.

However, AMC stated, “Despite these longstanding concerns, First Nations children remain disproportionately represented in Manitoba’s child welfare system,” and that the high number of First Nations children in that system, according to the province, is “underscoring the urgent need for prevention, family reunification, and culturally appropriate supports.”

AMC, along with its own First Nations Family Advocate Office (FNFAO), stated the province would need to work “directly with First Nations governments to develop a comprehensive, culturally grounded prevention and protection strategy that addresses sexual exploitation and human trafficking, strengthens placement oversight, and ensures accessible, trauma-informed supports for children, youth, and families.”

FNFAO is a province-wide advocacy office that helps families “fighting to have their children returned to their homes or First Nations,” according to its website.

Since opening in 2015, it has worked with more than 1,500 families and has continuously urged for a total reform of the system.

According to Fontaine, changes are on the way. However, she also noted that they have taken a “very long time.”

“This is all new for everybody. But what I can tell you 100 per cent … and in five years, 10 years, and certainly in 15 years from now, child welfare will look incredibly different than it does right now. And what you will see is a system where First Nations and Métis families, leaderships, matriarchs and Elders and communities are caring collectively for children.”

Even in the last year, she said there was over a 200 per cent increase in kinship and customary care agreements, which are “voluntary, out-of-court child welfare arrangements” between the parents, the child and the respective agency.

Manitoba introduced the agreements to provincial law in 2024, to help safely keep children in their home communities without officially entering the system, Fontaine said.

“That’s phenomenal,” she said. “But what folks also have to remember is that we’re trying to decolonize a system that’s been around for 500 years, just in different forms and iterations.

“In many different iterations, Indigenous children have been harmed and have been targeted. And decolonizing these systems are going to take many, many years, but we’re doing that work right now,” Fontaine said.

In July 2026, Fontaine announced that Manitoba would conduct an independent review of its child welfare system by the end of the year, with a tentative release planned for Summer 2027. She confirmed with APTN that the process was ongoing.

“We’ve been doing all of those reviews, working with the authorities to make sure that they’re working with their agencies to ensure that children have the supports that they need,” Fontaine said. “But that work didn’t occur for many, many years. And so we’re doing that work, we’re looking at the totality of the system.”

She added that while it examines the system, the province is also working to give First Nations governments the “ability to assert jurisdiction over child welfare” when it involves their communities, and by extension, the Nation’s own laws.

“Our people are going to have a different way of doing child welfare,” Fontaine said. “It’s a way of keeping children in their communities, among their kin, among their lands, among their people. That’s something across the country that traditionally, child welfare didn’t do.”

In 2019, Ottawa passed Bill C-92, also known as an Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis Children, Youth, and Families, that, according to the government, “recognizes a simple truth: one size does not fit all when it comes to Indigenous child and family services.”

Co-developed with First Nation partners, the bill “enables Indigenous groups and communities to transition toward exercising partial or full jurisdiction over child and family services at a pace that they choose.”

While navigating the process of shifting jurisdiction in Manitoba, Fontaine acknowledged that the middle province has “the most complicated child welfare system in the country.”

Currently, child welfare in Manitoba is governed by four authorities — General Child and Family Services Authority, First Nations of Northern Manitoba Child and Family Services Authority, Southern First Nations Network of Care, and Métis Child and Family Services Authority — that oversee agencies that fall under their jurisdiction.

Although Indigenous serving authorities provide oversight and training to these agencies, it is done in accordance with provincial law and not under the jurisdiction of any specific First Nations government.

Fontaine said she’s been in care twice in her life, and although it was “needed,” she was far away from her community.

“At the end of the day, kids want to be with their family,” she said. “They want to be with their parents. They want to be with their kin. And we’re on this path to ensure that more children are staying with their family and their communities.”

However, although Gott said that Nations often have a drive to help, there is still a lack of resources.

“It’s limited, the funding that’s available,” she said. “So they make do with what they have. And when we think about things like a place for children or youth to hang out, that space needs to be safe. And it needs to have people that understand kids and where they’re coming from.

“I think it would be really important to have those in place so we’re not always responding to crisis, after crisis, after crisis,” she said.

Ultimately, Gott said, “I think what needs to be at the forefront of everybody’s mind is that children are suffering in Manitoba and I think we need to do better.”

“I hope that someday our families can go back to what they used to do, and look after our own.”

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

author: Joshua Carroll & James Crump
title: Jewish Group Launches Bid to Lift UK’s Terror Ban on Hamas
content:
The Jewish Network for Palestine (JNP) has applied to the UK government to reverse the proscription of Hamas under the Terrorism Act.




The activist group filed the de-proscription application on Thursday under Section 4 of the act. 




JNP, which has about 600 members and supporters, argues the ban had been used by the government to “silence Jews”.




Under the act, expressing support for a proscribed organisation is a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison. But what constitutes an expression of support has been

 liberally interpreted

 by some police forces, especially since Palestine Action was banned under the same law last year.      




JNP’s chair, David Cannon, said the proscription of Hamas has made it difficult to discuss its 7 October 2023 attacks in Israel. He 

told Al Jazeera

 that JNP has avoided talking publicly about 

false Israeli narratives

 surrounding the attacks for fear of running afoul of the law. 




“Now, all of these things needed to be discussed, but the UK government’s proscription of the political wing of Hamas has made referring to such evidence risk the accusation of supporting Hamas, which is not what we’re saying. We’re saying that we want to discuss these issues,” Cannon said.




In 2024, JNP co-founder Haim Bresheeth, who is 80 and a British-Israeli anti-Zionist filmmaker, was arrested under the Terrorism Act after he said in a speech in London that Israel “cannot fight the resistance” and “cannot win against Hamas”.




The investigation against Bresheeth, who is the child of Holocaust survivors, was later dropped without charge.




Another JNP member, Tony Greenstein, 72, was charged under the act after he wrote “full support for the Gaza ghetto uprising” on social media in the wake of 7 October. In August this year he was found not guilty of inviting support for Hamas. 




Cannon told

 the National

: “Five years ago we were told this ban was needed to protect Jewish people. Instead, it has been used to raid the home of a Jewish writer whose family died at Treblinka, and to detain an 80-year-old son of Auschwitz survivors for political speech opposing a genocide.




“We do not support Hamas,” he added. “We are asking the Home Secretary to end a law that is being used to silence Jews who speak up for Palestinians.”

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Indigenous Sovereignty Is Under Attack Today in the Name of Permitting Reform
content:
A bill now moving through Congress would allow tech oligarchs to circumvent tribal opposition to their projects.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In March 1621, months before the meal Americans now call the first Thanksgiving, the Wampanoag leader Ousamequin sat down with the Plymouth colonists and negotiated a mutual-defense treaty. His people had every reason to keep their distance: An epidemic carried by European traders had totally emptied the village of Patuxet only a few years earlier. They came to the table anyway.

That’s what reciprocity asks of you: the understanding that relationships between people — and between nations — run on ongoing giving, receiving, and responsibility.

Four hundred and five years later, the federal government has left a long record of making that table optional through ignoring treaties with tribal nations. Now it is seeking to throw out the table altogether.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) now moving through Congress puts forth a series of changes that would fast-track federal approvals for projects like data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure. The bill would collapse Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act by narrowing what is considered an “undertaking” –– where federal funding was the prior baseline ––and shrinking the scope of an “adverse effect”; it places review deadlines on projects, and offers program alternatives to fast-track approvals; and sets a 150-day limit to court challenges. BAAJA would render public input limited and optional, narrow what is deemed historic property, and diminish requirements for federal agencies to consult with Native nations. Despite its innocuous framing as “permitting reform,” the bill would allow tech oligarchs to legally circumvent the communities and tribes that clearly oppose expensive and extractive projects on their land.

Treaties — the supreme law of the land, alongside the Constitution — require nation-to-nation relations for all projects impacting tribal nations. BAAJA virtually eliminates whatever parity remains in this relationship.

BAAJA’s own name claims the bill is about affordability, and many proponents say it will create jobs and advance clean energy infrastructure. But the oil industry-backed bill, with roughly a page per year since that first colonial meal, pushes aside the land, water, and people who gave the Pilgrims food. BAAJA is championed first and foremost by the GOP, but it’s become a bipartisan bill. Fifteen Democrats pushed it through the Senate the same week that Capitol Police arrested Indigenous activists protesting the bill like Krystal Two Bulls, executive director of Honor the Earth. Her organization advocates against the “green colonialism” this bill is attempting to legally codify.

The Native American Rights Fund (NARF), the largest legal advocacy organization for tribes in the U.S., issued a social media statement: “You may have recently heard from certain members of Congress that BAAJA would help clean energy without weakening environmental protections or Tribal rights,” it said. “NARF attorneys reviewed the bill and found a different story: fewer safeguards, less say for Tribal Nations and the public, and fewer ways to stop harmful projects.”

Meanwhile, media pundits like Jason Hayes, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation, promote the bill’s emphasis on expediting permitting, framing the bill as providing cost- and time-saving mechanisms, and suggesting their reversal would risk corporate resources. Ezra Klein, a self-described liberal commentator at The New York Times, backs the bill, but tramples tribes by omission, never saying “Native American,” “Indigenous,” or “tribes” as he lays out his public support.

Klein’s advocacy for permitting reform is unsurprising, considering that it is central to a bestselling book he co-wrote, Abundance. But it carries a colonial logic of unlimited extraction with a greenwashed veneer. “We need to build and invent more of what we need,” Klein says. But who is “We”? Here it’s a pronoun that excludes tribes, and refers abstractly to technology and infrastructure development without context or consequence for the builder and the alleged beneficiaries. Such framing of development is greenwashing: a marketing practice that presents a product, policy, or company as more environmentally friendly than it actually is.

This has been done before: In 2024, the SunZia power line, a massive wind energy project, crossed New Mexico and Arizona into California, and transversed the Tohono O’odham Nation by running over historical properties. The Nation sued the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), but the suit was thrown out in a Tucson court that said the Nation waited too long to file an injunction.

The cycle repeated in 2021 for the Thacker Pass lithium mine in Nevada, sold as essential for electric vehicle batteries. The Biden administration fueled the lithium rush further by funneling billions of public dollars into clean energy projects, including $2.26 billion for Thacker Pass. The BLM’s tribal consultation process was minimal: One email was sent to the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe while staff were on furlough during a government shutdown.

Some of the same politicians and pundits who are trying to make extraction look green also attempt to make Zionism look reasonable, and even lend that project, itself an instrument of American power, a progressive sheen. New York Sen. Chuck Schumer, who received a letter from the Karuk Tribe urging him to strip the bill’s historic preservation changes, voted to advance it without any sort of public comment on tribal consultation. Schumer is also known as one of the staunchest defenders of Israel in Congress. Meanwhile, BAAJA architect Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island has also said he is “ardently pro-Israel.”

Zionism itself treats Jews’ Levantine presence 2,500 years ago as a sound basis for Jewish supremacy in Palestine today, all while Native genocide — waged through violence, land theft, and cultural genocide for over 500 years, and which continues to this day — is framed, in its elision, as a foregone conclusion. Both Palestinian and Native perspectives are regularly silenced in mainstream media, which removes from them the option of changing the narratives surrounding their own erasure. Cable news shows fail to include Palestinians, even at the height of genocide. Meanwhile, I have not seen Klein host a Native guest on his popular eponymous podcast, referring only to tribalism in politics with non-Native guests and making passing historical mention of tribes’ land dispossession in conversation with them. The perceived entitlement to both Palestinian and Native land repeats a colonial logic compounded by the dialectical erasure perpetuated in tandem. The situation is a hat on a hat: Tribes are excluded from the conversation on the exclusion of tribes.

Some environmental organizations like the Center for Biological Diversity and others call tribal exclusion more broadly from climate activism a form of “greenwashing.” Tom BK Goldtooth (Diné and Dakota), executive director of the Indigenous Environmental Network, has in the past called carbon offsets and “nature-based solutions” greenwashing: “Corporations and governments must cut carbon emission at source, rather than use [nature-based solutions] for greenwashing.” Adding insult to injury, tribes are lumped together as a monolith in BAAJA.

The exclusion is all the more crucial because tribes are leading more reciprocal and sustainable solutions to climate change. Colusa Indian Energy comes to mind. Its approach has buy-in from over 50 tribes and involves small data centers that require a fraction of the water of those produced by tech oligarchs. “If you’re using combined heat and power with dry cooling, potentially you’re looking at less than 100,000 gallons of water a day,” Chief Operating Officer Ken Ahmann (Cachil DeHe Band of Wintun Indians) told The Architect’s Newspaper. In October, the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs endured a fire without recourse except for mutual aid offered by other tribes. In California, Yurok fire leader Elizabeth Azzuz proactively performs cultural burns that reduce risk of wildfires and promote biodiversity — a reciprocal modus operandi functioning opposite to the extractive projects promoted by BAAJA. Scientists say climate change is intensifying California’s now-annual wildfires; cultural burning reduces the fuel that feeds them.

As we await the House’s vote expected after Thanksgiving, by November 30, we have an opportunity to reflect on the fact that the Pilgrims violated the covenant that sanctified reciprocity with the Wampanoag and how that dynamic reverberates to this day. Attacks on Indigenous sovereignty are not a thing of the past. Today, they are being carried out in the name of clean energy modernization and permitting reform. Native leaders like Ahmann and Azzuz are building their own table, but bills like BAAJA threaten even the most optimistic and expansive strategies — and partnership — for land stewardship and climate change mitigation.

In Lakota, Mitákuye Oyás’iŋ means literally “we are all related.” In practice, it suggests that a person’s value lies in their daily acts of care for the whole community. Whether or not they realize it, BAAJA’s proponents have pitted Indigenous sovereignty against a clean energy future. We must reject the notion that trampling on the rights of some will ostensibly benefit us all.

Truthout is funded almost entirely by readers — that’s why we can speak truth to power and cut against the mainstream narrative. But independent journalists at Truthout face mounting political repression under Trump.

We rely on your support to survive McCarthyist censorship. Please make a tax-deductible one-time or monthly donation.

title: Lotta newsletter # 2
content:
// BULLETIN ANARCHISTE // 2 // AOUT 2026 // GRATUIT //




Bienvenue dans ce deuxième numéro du bulletin d'information LOTTA. Le numéro précédent a été très bien accueilli. Grâce à la collaboration de groupes issus de différentes régions du monde, la revue a été publiée non seulement en anglais, mais aussi en tchèque, hongrois, italien, français et espagnol. Ce vif intérêt a également permis à ce deuxième numéro de compter davantage de pages et, par conséquent, de contenir plus d'informations.




Dans ce numéro, nous mettons une nouvelle fois l'accent sur le soutien aux déserteurs, aux personnes qui échappent à la mobilisation ou qui sabotent la machine de guerre. Dans nos entretiens, nous donnons la parole à ceux qui ont fui la guerre, ainsi qu'à ceux qui apportent un soutien concret aux réfugiés. Un sujet connexe concerne la détérioration des conditions de vie des réfugiés ukrainiens et russes qui se sont enfuis vers les pays de l'UE pour échapper à la guerre et à la mobilisation. Cependant, nous ne nous concentrons pas uniquement sur les sujets liés à la guerre en Ukraine. Nous offrons également une tribune aux camarades d'Iran et à ceux qui s'engagent dans la résistance contre le sionisme et les massacres qui ont lieu à Gaza.




Si nous nous attachons à rendre compte d'actes spécifiques de résistance anti-guerre tels que la désertion, les émeutes et autres actions directes, nous ne souhaitons pas pour autant négliger l'analyse et la théorie. Car ce n'est qu'en ayant une bonne compréhension de la réalité, du contexte plus large et des processus à l'œuvre que nos actions concrètes peuvent être efficaces. Les analyses de ce numéro portent principalement sur la critique des illusions pacifistes et la critique du militarisme, masqué par la rhétorique anti-guerre. Nous analysons également le contexte géopolitique et l'escalade des tensions inter-impérialistes qui rapprochent le monde d'une Troisième Guerre mondiale.




Dans les guerres, les armées d'État cherchent à forcer l'autre camp à capituler ou à lui imposer les termes d'une paix formelle, ce qui implique toutefois toujours des préparatifs en vue du prochain cycle guerrier. Notre perspective ne se concentre donc pas seulement sur le sabotage de l'effort de guerre en temps de guerre, mais aussi sur le sabotage de la paix capitaliste, qui revient toujours à faire la guerre par d'autres moyens. En bref, le but de notre lutte est de transformer les guerres entre États — et leur « paix » — en une lutte de classe contre les États. Nous ne voulons pas d'un retour au statu quo d'avant-guerre, mais la destruction révolutionnaire de tous les États.

title: Türkei ist auch, wenn am „Tag gegen Gewalt an Frauen“ Hunderte Frauen festgenommen werden…
content:
Dossier




„

Trotz Verbot und einem massiven Polizeiaufgebot sind zahlreiche Frauen in Istanbul auf die Straße gegangen, um zum Tag gegen Gewalt an Frauen gegen Unterdrückung und für ein Leben in Freiheit zu demonstrieren. (…) Aufgerufen zu der Demonstration hatte das „Frauenbündnis 25. November“, protestiert wurde unter der Losung „Für unsere Freiheit sind wir laut und geben unser Leben nicht auf – Nein zu patriarchaler und staatlicher Gewalt“. author: rti_admin
title: Brutality and Caste: The Murder of Rohit Anil Pathare
content:
What does the recent brutal murder of Rohit Pathare by a dominant caste group show? Here, it is inevitable to know the caste identity of the victim. A young ‘Ambedkari’ man from Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, and his killing in a hospital after a mob of dominant caste group brutally wounded him, exposes a grim reality of the caste system in India. If we understood it just as an act of violence against an individual, we may miss the social and structural underlying causal factors behind the kind of brutality it witnessed. This is a disturbing reflection of how caste hatred is deeply embedded in the social structure of Indian society, which continues to resurface time and again. This hatred appears at times in the form of Dalit youth like Somanath Suryawanshi, who was subjected to custodial torture and death in police custody, and at other times through incidents such as Khairlanji (2006), Mirchpur (2010), Bhima-Koregaon (2018), and Hathras (2020), alongside countless other cases of caste-based violence that remain unreported.

When a person is dragged out from his own house, in a broad daylight pulled through the streets and brought across a public square; when his wife is kicked in the stomach; when mob directs casteist slurs at him on his caste; when he is tied to a tree in a nearby agriculture field and brutally beaten by an iron rod; when wounds are made on his body by a screwdriver; when stones are used to crush his legs; and when, writhing in agony, he begs for water, urine poured over his face — such an inhuman and barbaric crime cannot remain confined to the individual victim alone. It casts a stain on the claims of so-called civility made by Indian society, the moral foundations of democracy, and the values of humanity at a global level. It also constitutes a grave affront to the universal principles of human dignity and fundamental human rights.

What kind of social system produces such inhuman violence and grants one human being the power to exercise domination and supremacy over another? This question leads us to Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar’s critique of the caste system. In Ambedkar’s intellectual framework, the question of human dignity cannot be separated from the complete annihilation of caste. According to him, caste is not merely a system of social stratification; it is a hierarchical structure of social and institutional inequality based on birth that denies individuals equal social recognition, freedom, and human dignity. Within such a system, caste-based violence does not manifest itself merely through physical assaults. It continuously reproduces through the humiliation of individuals, their systematic exclusion from society, the persistence of different forms of untouchability, and the systematic denial of their equal humanity.

Caste Hierarchy and Relations of Power

The caste system regulates the distribution of human dignity, power, and social rights, creating a hierarchy in which the humanity and dignity of some are systematically subordinated to the social privileges of others. Within this hierarchical order, violence is not merely a form of punishment; it becomes an inhuman lesson intended to remind the oppressed of their supposedly assigned ‘place’ in society. More importantly, caste-based violence cannot be separated from misogyny. When Rohit’s wife was kicked in the stomach by members of the mob, it exposed how caste supremacy employs patriarchy as a weapon of domination. Within the caste system, the bodies of women belonging to marginalised communities are often treated as instruments through which the collective morale of an entire community can be crushed and its members are subjected to collective humiliation.

This hierarchy also exposes a deep contradiction between the equality promised by the Constitution of India and the social inequality of everyday life practices. As long as a marginalised or Dalit individual remains within the conventional social boundaries and silently endures injustice, society appears to have no objection. However, when that very individual takes education, begins to advance, becomes conscious of their rights, and starts questioning the existing social order, the established social mindset becomes deeply unsettled. At such moments, social inequality and casteist arrogance become active forces, attempting to undermine that individual’s confidence and reassert their supposedly assigned ‘place’ in society.

At the same time, this fundamental contradiction highlights the intense conflict between individual morality and caste-based morality, whose most visible expression can be witnessed in the institution of marriage. Here, caste pride, hierarchy, and collective prejudice are often accorded greater importance than another human being’s love, education, suffering, and moral responsibility. This brings to the surface the underlying tension between political democracy and social democracy that Dr. Ambedkar recalled at the constitutional assembly debate. The society that dehumanises its people through caste discrimination and silently tolerates such brutal violence, can it claim to be democratic and civilised? Can it guarantee the meaningful realisation of equal rights to its citizens?

What is the role of the Modern State?

If everyday social relations continue to be governed by hierarchical relations of caste domination and subordination, the political equality guaranteed by the Constitution remains merely formal, and the promise on paper never reaches real lives. If individuals cannot exercise their constitutional rights free from caste-based humiliation, fear, and violence, the constitutional recognition of those rights loses its substantive meaning. Under such circumstances, it becomes imperative to critically examine not only the social order itself but also the so-called welfare-oriented and democratic role of this modern state, which bears the responsibility of intervening in this social order to establish constitutional promises including equality and justice.

A critical assessment of the state cannot be undertaken just because an incident of caste-based violence has occurred. Rather, it must be based on questions such as whether the state took adequate measures to prevent such violence, whether the police acted impartially, whether the investigation was conducted in a timely and credible manner, whether the victims received adequate protection, and whether the perpetrators were effectively held accountable. In other words, the democratic commitment of the state must be evaluated not only through the constitutional provisions it upholds but through its actual institutional conduct in situations involving caste supremacy and violence. When the state falls under the sway of the same dominant ideologies that feed inequality and injustice, instead of confronting them, it stops being the sovereign guardian of every citizen’s equal rights. It runs the risk of becoming one more instrument for reproducing established structures of social domination.

An examination of the functioning of the modern state in the Indian context raises a fundamental question: Do the policies, administrative machinery, police, and institutional practices of the state challenge the caste hierarchy and the socio-ideological dominance of dominant castes, or do they reproduce these very structures in newer forms? This question is not limited to the state’s inaction; it concerns the ways in which different state institutions, their mechanisms, and their everyday practices sustain and legitimise established caste-based power relations. If these institutions had truly been impartial, Rohit’s mother would not have been compelled to pour petrol over herself inside the Vaijapur police station in her desperate pursuit of justice following her son’s death.

That is the grim reality. Despite the existence of the constitutional framework of the Indian Republic, the violent hierarchy of caste supremacy and a kind of violence continues to persist in society through various political, social, and other institutional arrangements, albeit in different forms. Beneath the veneer of constitutional democracy, a parallel, unwritten social law appears to remain operative and is becoming stronger. For thousands of years, this law has sustained caste hierarchies and social domination by continually creating conditions conducive to violence, impunity, misogyny, and institutional complicity. Therefore, the murder of Rohit Pathare must not be understood as an isolated or exceptional incident of violence, but rather as a grave manifestation of the deep-seated conflict between constitutional values and the lived realities of Indian society.

Harshvardhan Ashok Wankhede is a PhD research scholar at the Centre for Political Studies, JNU.

content:

 de novembre: jornada de vaga per l’emergència social




67 

detencions durant la jornada

persones empresonades




El passat dia 11 de novembre es va convocar una vaga per tal de denunciar la situació d’emergència social que viu el país i que s’ha tornat insostenible. L’accés a un habitatge digne i el cost de la vida s’han convertit en una cursa d’obstacles que expulsa el veïnat dels seus barris i pobles i condemna milers de famílies a la precarietat.




Les persones i col·lectius sotasignants volem fer públic, a través d’aquest manifest, la defensa del dret fonamental a la vaga com una eina irrenunciable de justícia social, dignitat laboral i democràcia real, i exigim el respecte absolut i la garantia del seu exercici lliure i efectiu, sense coaccions, amenaces ni represàlies.




Malauradament aquesta exigència torna a ser necessària a dia d’avui perquè durant la jornada de vaga hi va haver 67 detencions i tres persones estan empresonades als Països Catalans, donat que el vaguista empresonat de Castelló ja ha estat posat en llibertat.




En lloc d’oferir solucions reals a l’emergència social, les institucions i els poders econòmics responen amb multes, identificacions arbitràries, càrregues policials, processos judicials i campanyes d’estigmatització contra les persones que es manifesten.




Per tot això:










Exigim la llibertat immediata i sense càrrecs de totes les persones preses per participar en la vaga del dia 11 de novembre.










Expressem tot el suport a les famílies i l’entorn de les persones preses.










Reclamem l’anul·lació de les multes i l’arxivament dels processos judicials oberts contra activistes pel fet d’exercir el dret de protesta i de vaga.










Denunciem la persecució policial, judicial i mediàtica contra les persones que exerceixen el dret de vaga per exigir un sostre i unes condicions de vida dignes.










Reclamem el respecte efectiu del dret de vaga i de protesta i, sobretot, exigim solucions urgents a la crisi de l’habitatge i del cost de la vida.

author: anonerror
title: Vivir la fuerza. Simone Weil y la Columna Durruti
content:
Año publicación: 

2025

Autor / es: 

Xavier Artigas, traducción de Lorena Franco. - Prólogo de Myrtille Gimenóloga

Editorial: 

Pepitas

ISBN: 

ISBN 978-84-10476-32-5

Páginas: 

352

Tamaño del libro: 

14,5 x 21

Web: 

https://www.pepitas.net/libro/vivir-la-fuerza

Una excelente publicación, que no sólo recupera el diario de Simone Weil durante la revolución en España, sino que le da contexto destruyendo mitos sobre su presunto rechazo a la revolución, o sobre su presuntamente justificado rechazo a la revolución, aunque quizás al precio de dar peso a otro mito no menos consolador de almas bellas: el de una CNT que traicionó a la revolución por burocrática. Esperamos volver a ello en alasbarricadas.org (Super8).







 




«A medida que avanza, nuestro historiador aficionado contribuye a esbozar, paso a paso, una forma de relacionarse, de reflexionar y de actuar propias de la crítica social de los años treinta, cuando abundaba un intenso deseo de emancipación del capitalismo»

. —Del prólogo de Myrtille Gonzalbo




«Imagino varias lecturas (y lectores) posibles de este libro. Los amantes de la historia de la Guerra Civil pueden disfrutar de la reconstrucción rigurosa del encuentro, a la vez brevísimo e imperecedero, cargado de consecuencias, entre Simone Weil y la Columna Durruti. Los amantes de la filósofa francesa pueden saborear —por primera vez en muchos casos— los detalles de su viaje a España, los antecedentes que lo hicieron posible, los personajes con los que se cruzó, los paisajes que atravesó, las escenas que vivió y la idea que se hizo de ellas. En mi caso, deleitándome también con estas dos primeras lecturas, con el inmenso trabajo histórico-detectivesco de Xavier Artigas, me he dejado guiar por una tercera: la pregunta por el valor político del viaje de Simone Weil. ¿Qué busca Simone Weil en España?»

. —Del epílogo de Amador Fernández-Savater




Este libro aborda la figura de la filósofa francesa Simone Weil en su dimensión política, desmantelando el mito que ha dominado la proyección de su pensamiento durante décadas, y que describe a Weil como una pensadora trascendente y apolítica. Una rigurosa investigación histórica reconstruye la breve pero intensa participación de Weil en la Guerra Civil española y ofrece una nueva perspectiva que reivindica el compromiso revolucionario de la filósofa.


	 




Vivir la fuerza

 reconstruye con precisión la evolución política de Weil y documenta su recorrido desde el sindicalismo revolucionario francés hacia posiciones libertarias, lo que permite explicar de manera coherente su participación en la Guerra Civil. Esta experiencia fue decisiva para el desarrollo de su concepto de «la fuerza», que articularía posteriormente en uno de los textos más importantes de su trayectoria filosófica: 

La Ilíada o el poema de la fuerza

.




Vivir la fuerza

 no solo recupera la figura de Weil como pensadora política comprometida, sino que también aporta una mirada nueva sobre un momento histórico clave y contribuye a reimaginar las posibilidades de emancipación social.

23.90€

author: Dalia Abu Ramadan
title: In Gaza, We Have No Feasts to Give Thanks For
content:
As Americans feast on Thanksgiving, we are still facing widespread malnutrition and acute hunger in Gaza.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

I grew up believing that food was readily available, that having access to it was something ordinary and something I could always count on. I never imagined that one day I would be deprived of it, or that I would find myself wishing for a single loaf of bread despite having the money to buy one. Yet I, my family, and my people were deprived of food for prolonged periods throughout Israel’s war on Gaza. Although the war has publicly been declared over, we continue to suffer its consequences — only now they unfold away from the headlines, behind the scenes.

I had always heard that we were a people living under siege, but I never imagined that human cruelty could reach such depths. I thought the worst cruelty could bring was the use of weapons. It never crossed my mind that hunger itself could be turned into a weapon against us; that food, one of the most basic necessities of life, could become a means of deprivation and suffering. How can human beings strip others of their right to food with so little regard for their humanity?

No human being has the right to decide that another human being or an animal should be starved! How can we advance technologically while regressing as human beings?

Although famine conditions in Gaza have eased since the ceasefire, the consequences of the war have not. Many of these consequences remain hidden from the world. As of October 15, around 90 percent of Gaza’s population still relied on humanitarian food assistance amid the collapse of livelihoods and widespread loss of purchasing power, leaving families struggling to secure even their most basic needs. For many, food aid is no longer supplementary support; it has become a lifeline. Yet that very lifeline is now under threat, at a time when most people in Gaza remain unable to meet their own food needs.

On October 19, the World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut its food assistance in Gaza by around one-third, meaning that approximately 500,000 people would lose access to essential assistance. These cuts were not the result of declining humanitarian needs, but of a shortfall in international funding.

Since the ceasefire was announced in October 2025, the WFP had been providing assistance to approximately 1.6 million people in Gaza every month through food parcels, wheat flour, bread, hot meals, nutritional support, school snacks, and cash assistance. By October 2026, however, the food program had reduced the number of people it supported to 1.1 million.

The World Food Programme announced that 500,000 people would lose access to essential assistance.

The WFP’s acting executive director, Carl Skau, told Australia’s ABC News that traditional donors, including the United States and European countries, had reduced their contributions. He also pointed to multiple humanitarian crises competing for limited funding and what he described as “donor fatigue.” Skau stressed that the cuts were not due to an inability to bring food into Gaza or a decline in people’s needs, but rather to a lack of funding.

A single disruption, seemingly small in itself, can push an entire population closer to famine.

On October 20, 2026, flour became scarce across Gaza after the WFP could no longer fund the bakeries that had been supplying bread to the population. That day, my uncle went to the market to see what he could find to feed his family. He was stunned to discover that flour was nowhere to be found. Wherever it was available, it was being sold at exorbitant prices because of the shortage.

He called my father and said, “Can you imagine, Imad? There’s no flour, no chicken, no eggs, nothing. They told me flour has become incredibly expensive, and most of the other goods are spoiled.”

“There is nothing we can do. We are in the same position as everyone else,” my father replied. “We don’t know how much longer we will have to keep thinking about stockpiling flour and food in case of a sudden famine that could last for days. We simply don’t know what might happen, and we can no longer count on food remaining available.”

That was the hardest day we had faced in terms of food since the so-called ceasefire was declared. We felt a level of despair we had never experienced before. That single day was enough to bring back memories of the famine we endured during the war, along with the anguish of families whose loved ones were lost while trying to secure food for their families.

In February 2024, at least 112 Palestinians were killed and 760 others injured while waiting for food aid.

How could we ever forget what happened during the famine in February 2024, at the Nabulsi Roundabout? According to a statement by the UN Human Rights Office for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, at least 112 Palestinians were killed and 760 others injured while waiting for food aid. The statement reported that Israeli forces had opened fire, alongside incidents of crowd crush and people being trampled.

That day, my brother, my father, and my uncles had gone to collect aid. We waited for them until morning, convinced that we had lost them after hearing the horrifying reports of those killed and the tragic stories emerging from the scene.

On October 20, 2026, my friend Ghada sent me a message expressing her frustration with the reality we have been forced to live through:

I feel so frustrated. What kind of life are we living? How much longer will we have to struggle to secure flour and chase after things that should be readily available in the first place? I feel as though we have lost our future entirely, while all we can think about is flour and food.

The shortage did not last long; flour returned to the markets within two days. But one question continued to haunt us: If we cannot even feel secure about having food, what is left for us to live for?

Imagine the children growing up in Gaza today, many of whom can barely remember the taste of certain fruits after being deprived of them for more than two years. Imagine what this young generation is going through. A 10-year-old child is thinking about stockpiling food instead of concentrating on schoolwork, playing, or dreaming about the future. The fear of food disappearing has taken over his thoughts at an age when his mind should be occupied with the ordinary concerns of childhood, not with whether he will have something to eat tomorrow.

We see food as a blessing that God has bestowed upon all of us. Only those who have been deprived of it can truly understand its worth.

On November 14, 2026, I was at a shopping mall buying a few necessities when I saw that everything was available, despite the high prices. I could not hold back my tears. I thought of all those who had been killed while trying to obtain food. I thought of how my people had been forced to endure humiliation and risk their lives just to secure a single meal for their children and families.

I remember vividly the severe famine I experienced in northern Gaza in 2024, when we were receiving food aid dropped from planes operated by several different countries. Perhaps those countries believed they were providing us with a way to survive, but they failed to understand that, as we waited for those aid packages, we had no way of knowing where they would drift or where they would land. Hunger drove people to run after them, desperately trying to secure something to feed their families. But for some, the desperate attempt to reach that aid ended in drowning.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, at least 17 Palestinians were reported killed in two incidents directly linked to airdropped aid in March 2024. On March 8, five Palestinians were killed when humanitarian aid fell on them after its parachutes malfunctioned near the Al Fayrouz Towers in Gaza City. On March 25, 12 Palestinians drowned while trying to reach aid packages that had fallen into the sea off the coast of Beit Lahia.

In Gaza, we have been humiliated in every possible way just to obtain food. On November 26, Thanksgiving Day in the United States, families gather around dining tables to celebrate and spend time together. In Gaza, however, we are forced to endure humiliation and hardship just to find something to eat. We long for the simplest moments that should never have been taken for granted: sitting together as a family around one table. Many have lost members of their families, and some tables no longer include those who once gathered around them.

I do not want to draw a comparison. Everyone has the right to celebrate, and food is a right that belongs to everyone. I am writing about this day for one reason: to remind people that there are others who are suffering. While families gather around tables filled with food, families in Gaza are still struggling to obtain the most basic thing they need to stay alive.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.
