author: Comunizar
title: Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria
content:
¿Qué está pasando?




            En las últimas semanas hemos visto una serie de eventos que parecen abrir la esperanza de un cambio en la dirección de las luchas sociales. Estamos pensando en primer lugar en las protestas en las calles de Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países. También hemos visto la derrota de la derecha en una serie de elecciones: Hungría, Serbia, Brasil, Estados Unidos. Pero al mismo tiempo y, sobre todo, sigue el genocidio en Gaza. ¿Qué está pasando?




            ¿Cómo entender la serie de protestas de las últimas semanas en Francia, Italia, Portugal, Alemania, Albania, India y muchos otros países? ¿Hasta qué punto se está abriendo, sobre todo entre lxs jóvenes, una perspectiva o una forma de organización que va contra-y-más-allá del capitalismo? ¿Es la rabia -volcánica- la conexión entre todas esas luchas actuales y pasadas?




            ¿Cómo entender la derrota de la derecha en las elecciones? ¿Pensamos que hay una diferencia significativa entre un gobierno de extrema derecha y uno de centro-izquierda? ¿Pensamos que el descontento expresado en esas elecciones podría desbordar la forma-Estado?




            ¿Cómo entender las luchas actuales en el marco del genocidio en Gaza? ¿En la virulencia de las recientes protestas en varios países de Europa, no estará escondido también un grito de impotencia/desahogo por el genocidio impune de Gaza? ¿Hay una rabia que esté tratando de salir del encierro que este sistema genocida nos impone? ¿Es posible sostener la esperanza crítica de un mundo otro no capitalista en un mundo que no ha logrado impedir ni detener el genocidio en Gaza?










Call for Papers




What’s Going On?




           

 In recent weeks we’ve seen a series of events that seem to open hope for a change in the direction of social struggle. We are thinking in the first place of the protests in the streets of France, Italy, Portugal, Germany, Albania, India and many other countries. And we have also seen the defeat of the right in a series of elections: Hungary, Serbia, Brazil, the Unites States. But at the same time, and above all, the genocide continues in Gaza. What’s going on?




            How do we understand the protests in all these countries? To what extent can we see, especially amongst the young, a perspective that goes against-and-beyond capitalism? To what extent are these protests breaking with the state-form and creating communising or other forms of organisation? Is volcanic rage the connection between all these struggles of the present and the past?




            How do we understand the defeat of the right in the various elections? Do we think that there is a significant difference between a government of the extreme right and one of the centre-left? Do we think that the discontent expressed in these elections could overflow from the state-form?




            How do we understand these struggles in the context of the genocide in Gaza? Does the virulence of these protests reflect a scream of hopelessness or fury in the face of the unpunished genocide in Gaza? In the violence of these protests is there a rage that is trying to break the enclosure that this genocidal system imposes on us? Is it still possible to maintain the hope of a world beyond capitalism in a world that has not succeeded in stopping the genocide in Gaza? In this context, of what significance are the elections in the USA or the visit of the Pope to Argentina and other countries of South America?




The post 

Crítica Anticapitalista no. 7 – Convocatoria

 first appeared on 

Comunizar

.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Denuncia penal contra autoridades del INTA: contaminación,  censura y venenos en la sangre
content:
Por Anabel Pomar




Tras la 

exoneración de la investigadora del INTA

 Virginia Aparicio, las repercusiones en torno al 

censurado Proyecto Sprint

 suman un nuevo capítulo, esta vez en sede judicial. En carácter de ciudadano habitante del sudeste bonaerense, el abogado Mario Bolla (representante también de Aparicio), ingresó una denuncia ante tribunales federales. Solicitó se investigue a las autoridades jerárquicas del INTA por incumplimiento de los deberes de funcionario público y posible puesta en peligro de la salud de la población.




En la presentación ante el Ministerio Público Fiscal de Mar del Plata, el denunciante —que es acompañado en el escrito por 19 voluntarios del Proyecto Sprint en calidad de testigos— pide se investigue la posible comisión del delito contemplado en el artículo 249 del Código Penal Argentino.




Los funcionarios denunciados por el período 2023 (cuando se suspendió la participación del INTA en la investigación) son: Mariano Garmendia (presidente), Nacira Muñoz (vicepresidenta), Carlos Parera (director nacional) y Horacio Berger (director regional, que sigue en su cargo en la actualidad). Y los actuales: Presidente: Nicolás Bronzovich (presidente), Carlos Vera (vicepresidente) y Ariel Pereda (directo nacional).




La denuncia también pide que se evalué la participación del resto de los 

integrantes del Consejo Directivo

, que ocupan cargos como vocales (con derecho a voto en las decisiones institucionales) tanto del sector público (son funcionarios nacionales) como del sector privado. Allí se encuentran representantes del INTA, de la Secretaría de Agricultura, Facultades de Agronomía, Facultades de Ciencias Veterinarias (Universidades Nacionales), la Asociación Argentina de Consorcios Regionales de Experimentación Agrícola (Aacrea), Confederación Intercooperativa Confederaciones Agropecuaria (Coninagro), Confederaciones Rurales Argentinas (CRA), Federación Agraria Argentina (FAA) y de la Sociedad Rural Argentina (SRA), entre otros.




Foto: Naranja Ciencia y Técnica




Ciudadanos contaminados y “huérfanos” de asistencia




El escrito de la denuncia penal señala que, desde junio de 2023, fecha en que las autoridades del INTA 

decidieron suspender intempestivamente las actividades

 del Proyecto Sprint, hasta finalmente retirarse completamente en diciembre de ese año, y hasta la actualidad, los voluntarios participantes quedaron “huérfanos” de toda asistencia, contención, guía y asesoramiento oficial por parte del organismo que los convocó a participar.




El 

Proyecto Sprint

, representado por el INTA en Argentina (socio número 16 identificado como CSS11-Buenos Aires dentro del proyecto), convocó la participación de personas en carácter de voluntarios. Son habitantes de zonas rurales o ciudades bonaerenses, comprendiendo las localidades de Balcarce, Necochea, Tres Arroyos, Lobería, San Cayetano y Mar del Plata. Fueron un total de 73 personas de Argentina que se prestaron como voluntarios donantes para que se les analizara en sus cuerpos la presencia de agrotóxicos.







Como informó Tierra Viva

, todas las personas testeadas tenían glifosato en su cuerpo con rango de 6 a 13 plaguicidas en orina, de 2 a 10 plaguicidas en sangre y hasta 18 plaguicidas en materia fecal. En el momento de conocerse internamente los resultados, las autoridades del INTA aceleraron la salida del organismo de ese proyecto, y jamás dieron a conocer públicamente esos resultados. Tampoco los que señalaban presencia alarmante en alimento, aire, agua y suelo, que documentan la presencia de una mezcla de agrotóxicos de 20, 30 o hasta más de 80 plaguicidas según la matriz estudiada.







La presentación judicial señala que era obligación de un organismo estatal, una vez que tuvieron en su poder los resultados alarmantes del estudio, dar intervención a las áreas de Salud de la Nación, de las provincias (en el caso, autoridades sanitarias de Buenos Aires) y de cada comuna en la cual se llevaron a cabo los muestreos. Por el contrario, institucionalmente se decidió "guardar silencio" sobre el tema, ocultar a la opinión pública y, en particular, no informar a la mayoría de los "voluntarios" los resultados obtenidos respecto a su salud.




“Ante el hallazgo de contaminantes químicos, con efectos lesivos sanitarios y ambientales diversos, tanto en el agua de consumo, el aire, como en organismos humanos y animales, los funcionarios responsables de realizar acciones tendientes a revertir un problema de salud pública, decidieron censurar y ocultar deliberadamente”, destaca la denuncia.




En el escrito se mencionan y recorren diversas leyes, normas y antecedentes jurídicos, que señalan el deber del Estado de garantizar el derecho a un ambiente sano, equilibrado y apto para el desarrollo humano, con la obligación de preservarlo para las generaciones presentes y futuras, y el mandato de comunicar esa información por parte de autoridades de un organismo estatal, y el derecho de la ciudadanía a saber.




La denuncia ofrece también testigos profesionales idóneos, reconocidos en el ambiente científico, para que puedan ser consultados sobre las implicancias y los peligros de los agrotóxicos hallados en los muestreos.




Foto: Patricia Rosas




Agrotóxicos en el cuerpo




Si la intención de las autoridades del INTA era tapar los resultados de una investigación que documentó agrotóxicos en suelo, agua, aire, granos, plantas, animales y personas en Argentina, se puede asegurar que no han tenido éxito. Tras exonerar a Virginia Aparicio, el trabajo y los resultados se difunden como no había pasado en los más de tres años que llevan censurados. A la par, crecen las muestras de solidaridad con la investigadora despedida y las expresiones de repudio a esa medida disciplinaria extrema, por parte de 

gremios

, organizaciones, 

científicos

 y 

políticos

. Los voluntarios del proyecto no son la excepción. Así como prestaron sus cuerpos para permitir esos estudios, hoy levantan sus voces.




Claudio De Francesco es uno de ellos. Es biólogo, investigador del Conicet, profesor de la Universidad Nacional de Mar del Plata y vive en Villa Laguna Brava (partido de Balcarce), zona afectada por el agronegocio y sus plaguicidas. En su cuerpo encontraron una docena de agrotóxicos, entre otros, glifosato, su metabolito AMPA; 2,4-D, fipronil sulfona, bromoxinil, lambda-cihalotrina. Y en el entorno donde viven se detectó atrazina, fipronil, imidacloprid, metolacloro y butóxido de piperonilo, entre otros. Un cóctel de plaguicidas cancerígenos, disruptores endocrinos, mutogénicos, neurotóxicos y genotóxicos.




Sobre cómo le afecta tener esos resultados, explica: “Es una sensación extraña, un poco agridulce. Por un lado, valoro mucho haber podido conocer mis resultados, porque antes solo suponía que, por vivir donde vivo, estaba expuesto a plaguicidas. Ahora sé cuáles son y conozco sus concentraciones. Y creo que saber siempre es mejor que ignorar”. Pero, al mismo tiempo, comparte que ese conocimiento trae nuevas preocupaciones: “Inevitablemente me pregunto si esas sustancias podrían estar afectando mi salud de alguna manera. Por ejemplo, cada vez que aparece algún problema de salud, ya sea digestivo, una alergia o alguna afección de la piel, no puedo evitar preguntarme si tendrá alguna relación con alguno de esos plaguicidas o, por qué no, con la exposición a la mezcla de todos ellos. Es una pregunta que vuelve una y otra vez, una hipótesis que siempre está presente entre las posibles explicaciones de cada malestar o problema de salud que tengo. Es una incertidumbre con la que tengo que convivir.”




Las autoridades del INTA, al censurar y retirarse del proyecto, dejaron a los voluntarios sin asistencia, con el agravante de no haber solicitado a ningún otro organismo estatal la atención adecuada de seguimiento de aquellos que tienen venenos en su cuerpo. “La falta de seguimiento por parte del INTA nos dejó a los voluntarios con muchas preguntas sin responder”, resume De Francesco, quién admite sentir una profunda decepción por la falta de preocupación y empatía que mostró la institución.




“Genera la sensación de haber quedado a mitad de camino. En ciencia usualmente se distingue entre patrones y procesos. Sprint nos permitió identificar patrones de exposición a plaguicidas, pero todavía falta investigar los procesos que los explican: cómo llegan esas sustancias hasta nosotros, por qué encontramos determinadas concentraciones, cómo varían con el tiempo y, fundamentalmente, qué consecuencias puede tener esa exposición para nuestra salud”, señala.




Foto: Patricia Rosas




"Se optó por el oscurantismo"




Gabriela Hassan también es bióloga, docente universitaria e investigadora del Conicet. Tampoco dudó en prestarse como voluntaria. “Vivimos con mi pareja y nuestros dos gatos en una zona rural. Es un lugar que elegimos hace ya varios años buscando tranquilidad y contacto con la naturaleza, y por suerte encontramos exactamente eso”, le cuenta a Agencia Tierra Viva.




Más allá de todo lo lindo de una vida alejada de la ciudad, las experiencias cotidianas la fueron enfrentando a algunas cosas negativas, como estar expuestos a las posibles consecuencias de los plaguicidas de los campos cercanos. Por eso, cuando surgió la posibilidad de participar en Sprint, le pareció una buena oportunidad para tener un diagnóstico de cuál era la situación en el cuerpo y en la casa. Le encontraron en el organismo bromoxinil, fipronil sulfona, pirimicarb, glifosato; 2,4-D y lambdacialotrina, entre otros.




“En el momento del muestreo estábamos confinados por la pandemia del Covid y tenía una huerta hermosa, de la que sacábamos casi todos los vegetales que se comían en casa. Eso quizás me dio cierta seguridad de que mis resultados no iban a ser tan malos, pero me lleve una sorpresa. Descubrí que había una gran variedad de plaguicidas en mi cuerpo. Lo que más me sorprendió fue la alta concentración de glifosato en materia fecal, lo que me indicaba que a pesar del esfuerzo que hacía en consumir productos orgánicos, los plaguicidas estaban ingresando a mi cuerpo. Fue una gran decepción", reconoce Hassan, que es también compañera de vida de De Francesco.




Pero más allá de las sustancias individuales, lo que le parece importante es que los resultados ponen en evidencia la exposición a mezclas. En general, cuando se evalúan las concentraciones límite para estas sustancias, se las considera por separado, pero la vida cotidiana se está expuesto a varios agrotóxicos actuando simultáneamente. Y se sabe muy poco de las consecuencias para la salud de estas mezclas.




Desde ese muestreo y en todo el tiempo aparece una palabra: preocupación. La contaminación no sólo afecta a quienes utilizan agrotóxicos o viven cerca de lugar fumigados. “Fue realmente sorprendente ver que en algunos casos quienes vivían en la ciudad tenían más variedad y concentración de compuestos que yo, que vivo muy cerca de un campo. Evidentemente los alimentos que consumimos están contaminados y eso asusta. Sobre todo porque no se ven respuestas ni acciones por parte de quienes tienen que tomar decisiones en estos temas. La respuesta de las autoridades fue suspender el proyecto, ocultar los resultados y olvidarse de nosotros. Fue y sigue siendo muy frustrante”, asegura Gabriela.




 Tanto Claudio como Gabriela, y el resto de los participantes, siguen esperando ese acompañamiento que no existió, pero sobre todo buscan que se tomen medidas para detener esa contaminación para prevenir más daños.




“Sabemos que estuvimos y estamos todos expuestos a estas sustancias, pero no sabemos qué consecuencias puede tener esta exposición para nuestra salud”, afirma Hassan. “Tampoco sabemos con certeza cómo llegan hasta nosotros ni qué podemos hacer para reducir esa exposición. El Proyecto Sprint podría haber sido un punto de partida para despejar esas dudas a través de la investigación, y su suspensión es una clara señal de que en realidad no hay interés por saber. Y esto no afecta solamente a quienes participamos del proyecto. Se perdió una oportunidad de generar conocimientos para mejorar las políticas ambientales y sanitarias. En lugar de buscar respuestas, se optó por el oscurantismo”.










*Edición: Darío Aranda.




La entrada 

Denuncia penal contra autoridades del INTA: contaminación,  censura y venenos en la sangre

 se publicó primero en 

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

title: CONCEPCIÓN: REALIZAN CONCENTRACIÓN EN APOYO A LOS PPM DE CASO GROLLMUS EN HUELGA DE HAMBRE
content:
Durante la mañana de este miércoles 25 de noviembre, se realizó una concentración a las afueras del Cp Biobío en apoyo a los ppm condenados por el Caso Grollmus, quienes se encuentran en su tercer día de huelga de hambre, exigiendo la anulación del juicio racista y parcial que los condenó, sin pruebas materiales y en base a los relatos de testigos protegidos.

En el lugar se realizó un ayekan y se ingresó a la visita de los huelguistas, en la cual se pudo corroborar la inestable condición de salud de estos, considerando que varios de ellos tienen enfermedades base que agudizan el peligro de su movilización por la falta de alimentos. Así mismo, se pudo corroborar que su peso ha variado, disminuyendo casi en un kilo por día de huelga.

Los presos políticos mapuche en huelga de hambre son: Nelson Alonso Llempi, Rodrigo Valenzuela Canullan, Felipe Paineo Antiman, José Melgarejo Calbullanca, David Mariñan Millahual y Javier Mariñan Millahual, y dentro de los próximos días otros ppm se sumarán a la movilización.

Para los próximos días se esperan más movilizaciones por la anulación del juicio.-

title: Ephéméride des luttes : 26 novembre
content:
Humeur combative pour ce 26 novembre de l'éphéméride des luttes, aux quatre coins du globe. Il faut dire qu'on est bien déterminé-e-s à ne pas se laisser faire.




1920 :

 En Ukraine, les bolcheviks rompent leur seconde alliance avec Makhno, et l'armée rouge attaque Goulai-Polé, siège de la Maknovtchina, mais Makhno réussira à s'enfuir.




1927 :

 A Buenos Aires, l'anarchiste Italien Severino Di Giovanni fait sauter l'usine de cigarettes Combinados. Celle-ci avait lancé une nouvelle cigarette « pour ouvriers » qu'elle avait nommée la « Sacco et Vanzetti » (trois jours plus tôt, les deux anarchistes de Boston avaient été exécutés sur la chais électrique) afin de plaire tout de suite et d'économiser des frais d'électricité.




1970 :

 La Nouvelle Résistance Populaire (liée à la Gauche Prolétarienne) enlève le député Michel De Grailly, instigateur de nombreuses lois répressives et idéologue de la Cour de Sûreté de l'État.




1972 :

 A Dublin, probablement l'IRA fait sauter une bombe à l'extérieur du cinéma Film Centre vers 1h30 du matin.




1977 :

 A Paris, manifestation contre l'expulsion des squats du 14e arrondissement : 1000 


personnes dont 300 autonomes : un squat expulsé est démuré, le siège de la SEMIREP et un car de police sont incendiés.




1978 :

 A Belfast, Albert Miles, responsable de la prison de Crumlin Road, est abattu devant chez lui par l'IRA.




1981 :

 A Garac (Gers), le Mouvement d'action révolutionnaire antinucléaire (MARAN) fait sauter un relais hertzien des PTT.




1983 :

 A Toulouse, le CLODO (Comité Liquidant et Détournant les Ordinateurs), composé de 'travailleurs de l'informatique', incendie les locaux de Speery Univac Ordinateur.




1984 :

 A Bierset, près de Liège, les Cellules Communistes Combattantes (CCC) font sauter deux pylônes et leurs installations au sol d'un centre de télécommunications de la base aérienne, qui accueille les chasseurs-bombardiers de l'OTAN.




2010 :

 A Rio de Janeiro, plus de 21.000 policiers surarmés investissent plusieurs favelas de la ville dans le but de les "pacifier", accompagnés de véhicules blindés et de soldats. Au moins 49 personnes sont tuées par balles au cours des plusieurs jours que dure cette "opération".




2013 :

 A Tegucigalpa, capitale hondurienne, des affrontements violents éclatent dans le cadre d'une lutte étudiante contre des résultats électoraux falsifiés.




2014 :

 Au Chili, dans la province de Talagante près de Santiago, le 'Groupe Anarchiste Coordonné (GAC) - Bande Organisée Mauricio Morales / Cellule Incendiaire Sebastián Oversluij' bloque des voies ferrées avec de gros rochers et des pneus incendiés en solidarité avec les anarchistes Tamara Sol Farías et Sebastián Oversluij.




2015 :

 A Tlanepantla dans la province de Puebla au Mexique, une manifestation a lieu contre le maire et sa politique. Rapidement, la manifestation tourne à l'affrontement contre la police venue réprimer la grogne, des molotovs font leur apparition et plusieurs véhicules du maire sont incendiés.




 A Maracaibo au Venezuela, c'est un bus qui est brûlé par un groupe de manifestant-e-s masqué-e-s lors d'une protestation.




2019 :

 A Buenos Aires, des anarchistes incendient une patrouille de police en plein coeur de la nuit.




Voir également 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 26 novembre.

author: Jeremy Brecher, Alexandria Shaner
title: United States: ‘Now the real work begins’
content:
Voters have just delivered an overwhelming rejection of United States President Donald Trump, opening a real opportunity to limit his drive to lock the country further into oil, gas and coal.

Labour historian and organiser, Jeremy Brecher, argues that this is only a starting point. Even if the worst of Trump’s fossil fuel agenda is blocked, the US is still on course to become a “fossil fuel island”, paying more for energy and falling behind economically while much of the world shifts to cheap solar, wind and batteries.

In his new report, The Greentech Revolution, Brecher makes the case that avoiding that fate means embracing a just transition to a fossil free economy.

Brecher stresses that cheaper technology won’t get us there on its own. What decides the outcome is who owns and controls the energy system, what it’s for, and whether ordinary people get a say. That fight is already underway in city halls, statehouses, and neighbourhoods organising against data centres.

With the midterms behind us, the real work begins now. I asked Brecher what that work looks like, from policy fights to organising well beyond the ballot box.

The midterms are over, and you say limiting Trump won’t be enough. What’s the gap between blocking the worst and actually building the alternative? Who has to close it, and where, outside of Congress?

We are already experiencing climate catastrophe and if we stay on our current trajectory it will only get worse and worse. We are already experiencing historic inequality, and if we stay on our current trajectory it will only get worse and worse. The same is true for our health, education, housing and all the other necessities of life.

Even if we block new Trump depredations, we will face an American era similar to Russia’s “Yeltsin Era” following the fall of the Soviet Union, when the legal, educational, healthcare, manufacturing and other basic systems went into unending decline — marked, for example, by a six-year drop in male life expectancy.

To change that will take the kind of transformative reconstruction that was envisioned by the Green New Deal. But because conditions have changed and deteriorated so much, we need to update that to what I call a “Green New Deal 2.0”.

From the beginning, the Green New Deal was a convergence of progressives inside the political system and social movements based in civil society.

The defeat of Trumpism in the 2026 midterm elections was similarly a convergence of outside-the-system forces like the No Kings coalition and inside-the-system Democrats who cared about Gaza, war, climate, the Constitution and the wellbeing of ordinary people. Plus, the decision by ordinary people that they had to step forward, whether it was by protecting their immigrant neighbours against ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] or in voting en masse against Republicans. Those same forces need to take the lead in developing the alternative — the “Green New Deal 2.0”.

The report argues the technology is already cheaper and winning. So why isn’t the US just switching? Who is holding it back, and what does the “fossil fuel island” cost ordinary people?

While the rest of the world is racing to switch to fossil-free greentech energy production and consumption, the US is going in the opposite direction. This is due to two main factors.

The first is the power of the fossil fuel industry.

Even under Joe Biden’s “Build Back Better” program, supposedly “green” policies like carbon capture and hydrogen were coined into profits for fossil fuel developers while the US underwent its largest ever expansion of natural gas.

The second is a nationalist drive to use energy policy for geopolitical power.

The Biden administration put high tariffs on cheap Chinese solar and EV imports that could have revolutionised American energy use. The Trump administration put both of these dynamics on steroids. It has tried to destroy Greentech energy initiatives not only in the US but worldwide. And it has provided vast subsidies for fossil fuel expansion.

But this is a fool’s strategy. You can see the actual results for ordinary Americans in the price of gasoline, heating oil, diesel fuel and electricity. And you can see the long-term effects of fossil fuel domination in the devastating heat waves, floods, wildfires and other products of climate change.

Your report says technology never dictates the form or speed of social change. Why does that matter right now? The “free lunch” idea is easy to read as “the market will handle it”. What does it mean in your argument, and what doesn’t it mean?

Converting to “green energy” used to be seen as a burdensome, if necessary, cost of creating a climate-safe economy. But the Greentech revolution has reduced the cost of producing and using fossil-free energy so much that the “green transition” is now not an expense but a “free lunch”. But who is going to get to enjoy that lunch?

As we see with the hyperscale datacentre buildout, massive investment in solar and wind energy can simply be a way to increase profits for a few hyperscalers, while generating environmental destruction and higher energy bills for the rest of us. A Green New Deal 2.0 can become a vehicle for the massive opposition to data centres and destructive forms of energy development, even as the Elon Musks of the world use “green energy” to pursue their nefarious ends.

You write that the transition isn’t just swapping energy sources. It also means asking what gets produced, at what scale, for whose benefit, and under whose control. What would answering that look like in practice? Ann Arbor’s public Sustainable Energy Utility and Seattle’s community assemblies seem like early examples.

In my book The Green New Deal from Below, in my “Greentech Revolution” report, and in my current series of commentaries on the “Green New Deal 2.0”, I describe scores of examples of fossil free energy initiatives in communities, cities, and states around the country, including the Ann Arbor and Seattle examples you mention.

Part of what is important here is the creativity of these initiatives, the way they develop multiple new approaches that replace fossil fuel extraction and burning while meeting the pressing needs of their communities.

With the raft of more progressive city and state governments installed by the 2026 midterm elections, there is a great opportunity for such initiatives. They can show that the Green New Deal 2.0 is not just a pipe dream, let alone a threat to working people’s living standards, but a practical, achievable means to make our lives — and our climate — better and more affordable.

Fossil fuels and renewables are both growing right now. Why isn’t adding Greentech enough, and what does it take to actually shrink fossil fuel extraction and burning? How do “leave it in the ground” fights fit in?

Until fossil fuel extraction and burning are halted, the effects of global warming, already devastating, will continue to intensify. Adding more green energy won’t forestall more apocalyptic floods, fires, heatwaves and superstorms, unless it is combined with a rapid phasing out of fossil fuels.

“All the above” policies that promote both fossil fueled and fossil free energy just accelerate global warming and its consequences.

Hundreds of local campaigns against coal-fired power plants and fossil fuel pipelines have exposed the climate crisis, reduced significant amounts of greenhouse gas emissions, and shown that people are not powerless to affect climate destruction. Such actions are not only effective in themselves; they also lay the groundwork for insistence on government policies to halt fossil fuel extraction and burning.

The data centre rebellion is one of the more surprising stories in the report. What does it tell us about organising outside electoral channels? Does it point toward democratic control over major infrastructure decisions, as opposed to deciding by corporate investment plans?

As a historian of social movements, I find the “data centre rebellion” embodies the often disregarded capacity of ordinary people to organise themselves — and the unexpected ways their action can affect governments, corporations and other institutions.

The data centre rebellion is overwhelmingly centered in working-class communities. While it has received help from various quarters, its core is the self-organisation of urban and rural residents to fight a direct threat.

Dissolving divisions between red and blue constituencies, it has highlighted the question of whether a few billionaires should have the power to disrupt the lives of ordinary people. It has passed anti-datacentre laws in hundreds of jurisdictions. And it made a significant contribution to the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections.

Whether it can parlay its successes into fuller control of corporate decision-making now hangs in the balance.

If you could pick a few policy fights to win in the next year, which would they be, and what can’t be left to policy at all?

Stop Green New Deal “hushing” — the silencing or even trashing of Green New Deal advocacy in response to Trump’s denigration.

Instead, articulate a transformative vision of a Green New Deal 2.0 based on greentech energy combined with affordability, jobs and justice.

Start implementing that vision immediately in states, cities and communities, drawing on the scores of Green New Deal from Below initiatives already under way in communities, cities and states.

Promote a convergence of the Green New Deal 2.0 and the data centre rebellion. Focus on the need for democratic control of corporations and their technologies, and on the harmful energy and environmental effects of data centres.

[Reprinted from ZNetwork.org and The Labor Network for Sustainability. View or download the full report here. Jeremy Brecher is a co-founder of the Labor Network for Sustainability and is active in peace, labour, environmental and other social movements. He wrote Strike! and Global Village or Global Pillage and is an award-winning documentary maker. Alexandria Shaner is an editor of ZNetwork.org, a writer for Extinction Rebellion, and is active with the Democratic Socialists of America and Food Not Bombs.]

author: L214
title: Carnage à l’abattoir de Luxeuil : fermeture d’urgence !
content:
Entre juillet et novembre 2026, des caméras ont filmé ce qui se passe à l'abattoir de Luxeuil-les-Bains (Haute-Saône). Des chevaux reçoivent plusieurs coups de matador avant d'être vraiment étourdis. Des veaux sont poussés à coups d'aiguillon électrique. Des moutons, des chevaux et des bovins sont saignés et suspendus par une patte encore sensibles et conscients. Des truies et des cochons, mal étourdis, sont saignés au sol.

Les installations sont défaillantes : des moutons et des chèvres s'échappent des équipements censés les retenir et errent dans l'abattoir, les pattes dans le sang. Des bovins sont libérés du box avant d'avoir perdu conscience. Les services de l'État sont présents dans l'abattoir et n'ont pas fait cesser ces infractions.

L214 porte plainte pour sévices graves et mauvais traitements auprès du tribunal judiciaire de Vesoul. Nous demandons la fermeture d'urgence de l'abattoir à Annie Genevard, ministre de l'Agriculture et au préfet de la Haute-Saône.

Aujourd'hui, vous pouvez agir en une minute en signant la pétition pour demander la fermeture de cet enfer. Merci 🙏

Des images tournées entre juillet et novembre 2026 à l'abattoir de Luxeuil-les-Bains (Haute-Saône) montrent des chevaux, des moutons et des bovins saignés et suspendus par une patte alors qu'ils sont encore sensibles et conscients. Des veaux sont poussés à coups d'aiguillon électrique. Des moutons et des chèvres s'échappent des équipements censés les retenir et errent dans l'abattoir, les pattes dans le sang. Des truies et des cochons de réforme, mal étourdis, sont saignés au sol.

Ces faits se déroulent dans un abattoir où les services de l'État sont présents. L214 porte plainte pour sévices graves et mauvais traitements.

Luxeuil est la dixième vidéo tournée dans un abattoir que L214 publie en deux ans. Il n'y a pas eu d'audit général de tous les abattoirs depuis 2016.

Je vous demande de procéder à la fermeture d'urgence de l'abattoir de Luxeuil-les-Bains, par la suspension ou le retrait de son agrément sanitaire.

Je vous demande aussi de lancer un audit général de tous les abattoirs français, d'en publier les rapports d'inspection et d'instaurer un moratoire sur la construction de nouveaux abattoirs.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: ‘No other option’: former RCMP leader stands by tactics that led to Rankin Inlet man’s death
content:
The RCMP detachment commander who approved the plan that led to police fatally shooting a 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man says that police couldn’t have done any better.




On Wednesday, the third day of the coroner’s inquest into Trey Angootealuk’s death, coroner’s counsel Jessi Casebeer asked Robert Gallant, now retired from the RCMP, if he could have done anything differently




“There was no other option,” he said. “If I had to redo the scenario, I would do the same thing.”




On Nov. 6, 2021, Angootealuk hijacked a truck, drove it to the outskirts of town, shot at police officers, and began a standoff with police that lasted several hours, inquest jury members have heard. Two officers fatally shot him early the next morning, after a canister of tear gas was launched through the rear window of his truck, forcing him to exit the truck.




Gallant, who was working from a command post in Iqaluit to direct officers on the ground, said he approved the plan to launch the gas canister and to shoot if necessary.




Supt. Stephen Bergerman, the critical incident commander before Gallant took over on the morning of Nov. 7, also testified Wednesday.




The Angootealuk family’s lawyer Nikolai Sittman asked him if mental health professionals were contacted at any point in the lead up to Angootealuk’s death.
















Bergerman said he didn’t recall getting any mental health staff involved, though RCMP would have had access to hospital staff.




On Nov. 6, a 

negotiator

 managed to speak on the phone with Angootealuk, who told him he wanted to end his life before hanging up.




Throughout his testimony, Bergerman reiterated that it was not safe enough to allow anyone other than police to approach Angootealuk because he had rifle.




The inquest by Nunavut Chief Coroner Marianna Cervantes, which is taking place at the Siniktarvik Hotel, began Monday and is scheduled to end Friday. It will determine the circumstances surrounding Angootealuk’s death. The coroner’s office gave Nunatsiaq News a video link to cover the inquest remotely.




Coroner’s inquests are mandatory under Nunavut law for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved. The jury will be expected to make recommendations aimed at avoiding future deaths in similar situations.




On Tuesday, attendees heard from Clark Plaetinck and Const. Jordan Booth of the emergency response team, who testified to firing the fatal gunshots. Both described fearing for their lives when they pulled the trigger.
















The inquest will resume Thursday at 9:30 a.m. CT, with testimony from an expert on use of force.

author: By Camilla Conzelli, Contributor
title: Trans Teacher Fired, Then Held in Men’s Cell, as Turkey Escalates Crackdown on LGBTQIA+ People
content:
Istanbul, Turkey — Months after being fired, trans teacher Zoe Lila was detained at a Sept. 15 protest against the “My Family Is Safe” operation, Turkey’s crackdown on LGBTQIA+ people, and she was held in a men’s cell.




“I was a queer kid, I’ve been discriminated against since childhood, and I never felt included in the school system,” Zoe Lila said. “That’s why teaching isn’t just a job for me: it means being there as an educator, making sure no human being experiences any kind of discrimination.”




Lila is a young Turkish trans woman who has worked in education for 10 years. In 2021, she started teaching English at a private school, Açı Middle School in Istanbul. “It’s an international school that welcomes many minorities and bases its approach on human rights,” she explained. “So I felt like I had finally found my place.”







Zoe Lila







In 2024, when she began hormone replacement therapy, Lila told the school’s administration about her transition. “Their first reaction was, ‘It’s your right, we’ll support you,’” she recalled. Encouraged by that support, she decided to stay in Turkey, despite a long and complex process.




Reyda Ergün, an academic working on LGBTQIA+ rights, said the country is one of the worst examples of a medicalized model for gender affirmation.




Under the 

current legal framework

, vaginoplasty or phalloplasty is a binding prerequisite for legal recognition. The surgery can only be authorized by a court, and the person must have a diagnosis of “transsexualism” certifying that surgery is necessary for their mental health. After the operation, a second court proceeding begins in which a judge has the discretion to decide whether the procedure was “sufficient and appropriate” to change the person’s biological characteristics.




Since 2018, Ergün has co-authored an annual report published by 

Kaos GL

, an organization that monitors the employment conditions of LGBTQIA+ people in Turkey’s 

public

 and 

private

 sectors. 




Over the years, the data has revealed that 

concealing one’s identity

 is the primary means of self-defense workers adopt for fear of retaliation or dismissal.




In this context, trans people are especially vulnerable. “The long and complex nature of the affirmation and legal recognition process can expose people to further discrimination and job insecurity,” Ergün said. “When changes in official records and physical appearance become visible before legal recognition has been obtained, concealment strategies are no longer viable, and the risks that had been averted until then materialize.”




Zoe Lila’s story is a textbook example. In the summer of 2026, she completed the process leading to her gender-affirming surgery. In mid-June, she first came out to her colleagues and then, during a dedicated session led by a psychologist, to her 120 students. The reaction at school was initially warm and welcoming, but a few days later, everything fell apart.




A parent sent Lila’s photo and personal information to pro-government media, setting off a virulent hate campaign. Newspapers published her image with a cross over her face, revealing all of her personal data and the details of the school where she worked.




“It was horrible. It was the most unfair, unethical and unlawful article I’ve ever read in my life. And the person it was talking about was me,” Lila said. Soon she began receiving death threats and insults, including from her own family. Feeling unsafe, she left her apartment and moved in with a friend.




Meanwhile, Turkey’s Ministry of National Education intervened directly at the school. Under threat of sanctions and mass layoffs, school administrators caved to the political pressure. On June 24, 2026, just 10 hours before her long-scheduled vaginoplasty, the school told Lila it would not renew her contract.




“I was fired 10 hours before the surgery, and it was devastating,” she said. The operation went ahead as planned, but Lila suddenly found herself without a job, without income and at the center of a violent attack. She immediately turned to a lawyer to take legal action, but ran up against Turkish labor law: private school teachers are typically hired on renewable one-year contracts, which rules out a lawsuit for reinstatement.




Still, the fight continues through complaints filed with the relevant authorities and the creation of a 

solidarity network

. “We don’t want financial compensation,” Lila said. “We want this to be an act of defense for trans and LGBTQ+ people in the workplace. We want it to become an exemplary case for the future.”
















Family Values as State Policy




“Work is closely tied to other rights, like housing and health,” Reyda Ergün said. “If you don’t have access to social and economic rights, it becomes impossible to exercise your fundamental rights, too.” For trans people in particular, the researcher noted, sudden job loss means losing access to essential medical care and safe housing, and workplace abuse then becomes total social and material exclusion.




In this sense, the discrimination LGBTQIA+ people face at work in Turkey is a litmus test for a much broader, deeply rooted repressive climate. The latest reports on Turkey from 

Amnesty International

 and 

Human Rights Watch

 describe democratic spaces that are shrinking constantly and visibly.




Over the past decade, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s ideology and his ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) have shaped the 

dominant political discourse

, promoting a vision of society that fuses religious conservatism with nationalism and places the heterosexual, patriarchal family at its center. In this vision, anything that deviates from the “founding moral values” — from feminist demands to LGBTQIA+ identities and relationships — is increasingly portrayed as a threat to the survival of the Turkish nation.




It’s no coincidence that 2015, the year after Erdoğan’s election as 

president

, marked the start of an escalation against queer rights. The first official ban on 

Istanbul Pride

 was followed by systematic censorship and bans on community events, along with police operations and criminal investigations targeting anyone who defended LGBTQIA+ rights.




The real turning point came in 2021, when Turkey unilaterally withdrew from the 

Istanbul Convention

 on preventing violence against women. The presidency officially justified the decision by claiming the treaty was being used to “normalize homosexuality,” which was framed as a direct threat to national values.




Institutional hostility has only deepened since. In December 2022, the governing coalition introduced a 

proposed constitutional amendment

 defining marriage exclusively as the union of a man and a woman. The text was later withdrawn, but anti-LGBTQIA+ rhetoric remained a pillar of the political agenda and was formally written into strategic plans for protecting the family.




That course was fully codified when Erdoğan declared 2025 the “

Year of the Family

,” then named 2026–2035 the “

Decade of Family and Population

,” explicitly meant to shield the institution of the family from alleged “gender-neutralizing policies.”




Following this ideological blueprint, the government attempted between 

2025

 and 

2026

 to pass legislative packages aimed at criminalizing LGBTQIA+ visibility and advocacy. Each time, civil society mobilization led to the provisions being struck before final approval, but the government has implemented their contents anyway through informal channels.




Through ministerial circulars and administrative practices, authorities have severely restricted 

access to hormone replacement therapy

. They have also begun twisting existing criminal laws — above all the law on “

obscenity

” — to prosecute queer visibility, block online content and target organizations, activists and community members.




An Unprecedented Escalation




Since Sept. 12, 2026, Turkey has been gripped by one of the largest and most coordinated 

crackdowns

 of its recent history against the LGBTQIA+ community, in an operation aptly named “My Family Is Safe.”




Police have carried out raids and searches across the country, storming the offices of nine organizations, confiscating digital equipment and 

detaining more than 100 people, 82 of whom have been jailed pending trial

. The offensive came with a sweeping digital blackout that hit more than 180 social media accounts and websites belonging to associations, independent media and activists.




The Justice Ministry gave the operation its ideological cover with a 

directive

 sent to prosecutors’ offices in all 81 provinces. The document instructed prosecutors to urgently pursue any activity deemed capable of “harming families and children” and violating “public morality.”




“This wasn’t a legal police operation, it was a real witch hunt: they picked people up right off the streets and out of their homes,” said Yıldız Tar, editor-in-chief of Kaos GL, one of the hardest-hit organizations.




Tar pointed to the legal anomaly in the cases against activists still jailed awaiting indictment. “The people arrested are charged with obscenity, which, even at the maximum sentence, doesn’t carry prison time under the Turkish penal code, only fines or a suspended sentence. This pretrial detention is already an illegal punishment in itself, and it violates the rule of law.”




According to Tar, the creation of this moral panic answers a specific problem for the government. “Turkey is going through an enormous economic crisis, and families are paying the highest price. The government is trying to divert attention and cover up its own failures by using us as scapegoats, creating a narrative in which queer people are the cause of families’ ruin.”
















Held in a Men’s Cell




In this climate of terror, Zoe Lila’s story has once again collided with state repression.




On Sept. 15, 2026, she went to a peaceful sit-in outside the Çağlayan courthouse in Istanbul. “I wasn’t there to lead the protest. I was in no physical or mental condition to face detention after everything that had happened,” she said. “I just wanted to be present to show my solidarity.”




Within minutes, police surrounded the square and sealed off every exit, trapping the crowd in the middle before making more than 100 arbitrary arrests. With plastic zip ties pulled tight behind her back, Lila was loaded onto a bus and left in a parking lot for more than six hours, without food or water.




Despite repeated requests, officers refused to cut the ties, forcing her to use the bathroom while restrained. “They knew who I was because my story had been in the papers. I felt they specifically wanted to punish me and go after me,” she said.




Late at night, three plainclothes men without ID, in an unmarked civilian car, took Lila away from the group of women she had initially been placed with and drove her along isolated roads. “I was terrified. I thought they were abducting me to hurt me,” she said.




At the police station, authorities refused to recognize her gender identity, using as a pretext the fact that the gender marker on her documents had not been updated. Male officers searched her, and she was locked in a men’s cell with 14 other people. “I told them I’m biologically a woman, that I was at risk of violence and rape, but they wouldn’t listen,” she said.




Only the urgent intervention of her lawyer, who filed a written statement holding authorities directly responsible for any assault, forced police to move her to a separate cell, still inside the men’s section.




Lila was held for about 36 hours before her release. Her account captures the intersection of institutional transphobia and police brutality that defines the current political moment in Turkey, as in many other countries where populist and nationalist rhetoric and practice are choking off the few remaining openings for freedom.

title: YPJ: We will continue our struggle against all forms of violence every single day
content:
The General Command of the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) released a statement marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.




The YPJ statement on Wednesday includes the following:




“​On the occasion of November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, we affirm that violence against women is neither an individual issue, a family matter, nor a passing incident; rather, it is a systematic phenomenon fed by authoritarian mentalities, regressive traditions, and policies that deprive women of their right to make decisions freely, control their own bodies, and determine the course of their lives. At their core, these practices aim to silence women’s will, subjugate them, and destroy their identity. Guided by this reality, we assert that protecting women is a fundamental, non-negotiable duty—one that is not limited to the military sphere, but encompasses social, psychological, legal, and moral dimensions as well.




​Our struggle against violence perpetrated against women is rooted in the very essence of our existence and identity. This struggle manifests in protecting female survivors of domestic violence, opposing forced marriage, combating so-called honor crimes, and rescuing women abducted and enslaved by terrorist groups—alongside raising societal awareness, promoting women’s education, and working to build a system that empowers women to defend themselves, voice their demands, seek justice, and make their own decisions with freedom and independence. We do not view this struggle as a temporary duty tied to a specific phase; rather, we consider it a permanent covenant, sealed with the blood of female martyrs.




​We emphasize that violence is not confined to physical assault and murder alone, but also includes silencing women, restricting their freedoms, depriving them of education, work, and participation in social life, subjecting them to psychological pressure, and denying their will and right to self-determination. All forms of violence stem from a single mentality and strive toward a single goal; therefore, all of them must be confronted with the exact same resolve and responsibility. Silence in the face of violence is, in itself, part of the violence.




​We call upon all women to safeguard and fiercely defend their dignity, placing it above all else. A woman’s dignity and freedom are no less vital than water and food; indeed, a life in which a woman is stripped of her dignity and will can never be a free life. We urge women not to isolate themselves or remain silent in the face of violence, and to hold fast to their will and defend their rights. We also stress the necessity for women to unite in confronting the mentality that imposes violence and domination upon them, for only through women’s unity can we defeat this mindset and build a free and just society. Women’s strength lies in their unity and solidarity, and they must recognize this power and harness it to defend their freedom and dignity.




​At the same time, we call upon society as a whole, legal institutions, and all forces that believe in freedom and equality to shoulder their responsibilities in protecting women and defending their rights and dignity. A society in which women do not enjoy freedom can never be a free society, and a society in which women are subjected to violence is a society whose present and future are under threat.




​Finally, we declare that we will continue our struggle against all forms of violence perpetrated against women—not only on November 25, but every single day and in every moment of our lives, with determination, dedication, and faith in women’s freedom. This struggle will persist until the day arrives when no woman is subjected to violence simply for being a woman, and until all women are able to live in freedom, dignity, and safety, far removed from fear and oppression.

”

author: Unknown
title: MSD: Protecting women’s rights requires explicit constitutional and legal guarantees
content:
The Syrian Democratic Council (MSD) released a statement marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women as Syrian women look toward a future that ends decades of systemic abuse.




This moment calls for a new chapter built on justice, full equality, and human dignity, said the MSD statement on November 25, which included the following:




“Violence against women extends far beyond murder, abduction, exploitation, and overt discrimination. It includes systematic marginalization and exclusion from leadership roles. Denying women an active voice in political decision-making and public governance is a direct form of violence that must be confronted.




Despite the political transition following December 8, 2024, conditions for Syrian women have deteriorated due to ongoing discriminatory policies. The transitional government and society at large must urgently reassess their approach to women’s rights. We need genuine gender justice in practice—not merely symbolic gestures for the media.




Protecting and sustaining women’s rights requires explicit constitutional and legal guarantees. These frameworks must ensure full equality and safeguard the hard-won gains of Syrian women against any rollback, regardless of the pretext.




Achieving transitional justice is essential to delivering redress for women, who represent a disproportionate share of the Syrian conflict’s victims. This process requires uncovering the fate of abducted and forcibly disappeared women, holding perpetrators accountable, providing reparations, and guaranteeing non-recurrence.




The MSD reaffirms that building a democratic and just Syria is impossible without women serving as equal partners in shaping the nation’s future. Their active leadership is vital to national reconciliation and the reconstruction of both state institutions and society. Women are not merely beneficiaries of peace; they are essential partners in forging and sustaining it.”

author: Unknown
title: HPJ vows to continue their struggle for all women in Iran and the Middle East
content:
The East Kurdistan Women’s Defense Forces (HPJ) issued a written statement on the occasion of November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. Referring to attacks against women, the statement said that the patriarchal system aims to strip women of their identity and will and to keep them under oppression in every sphere of life.




In its statement on Wednesday, the HPJ Command said, “The state system, built on the denial and destruction of women, has turned every sphere of life into a genocide against women through a patriarchal mentality for 30,000 years. Women, who created language, culture, defense, and education, have been reduced to a state of voicelessness and defenselessness.”




‘Women are the first to be exploited for the interests of the system and capital’




The HPJ Command pointed out that the system of capitalist modernity is patriarchal and that women were the first gender to be exploited for the interests of the system and capital.




“In reality, the oppression of women means the oppression and subjugation of society and every individual within it. All forms of violence against women are carried out through an organized and ideological system targeting society. Within the three-tiered system, harassment, rape, and massacres of women in the workplace and family, which have been sanctified by men, have reached the level of genocide,” the statement said.




The statement said the 21st century has witnessed the rise of the women’s liberation revolution, noting that women’s struggle against systematic oppression and the attempts to strip them of their identity has spread to different parts of the world.




‘Women must organize and educate themselves’




HPPJ remarked that the struggle waged by women in East Kurdistan against executions, killings, imprisonment, and attacks on women’s bodies has become a source of inspiration for women around the world. Attacks on women’s will and ideas constitute the gravest forms of aggression, it added.




Emphasizing that the killing of women and the suppression of their will amount to the destruction of society and its collective will, the statement issued the following call:




“In response to the executions, imprisonment, and violence carried out in the prisons of the Iranian regime, women must organize and educate themselves and defend society’s will and identity through women’s unity, based on the Manifesto for Peace and Democratic Society and the philosophy of ‘Jin, Jiyan, Azadî’ (Woman, Life, Freedom). A woman who is united with her organization is a woman who has gained free will and the power of self-defense.”




‘All women will become a force of defense for themselves and society’




The HPJ declared that, as the defense force of women in East Kurdistan, they would continue their struggle not only for women in East Kurdistan but also for all women in Iran and the Middle East.




The statement concluded, “We will continue our struggle to achieve women’s freedom and free will on the basis of Leader Abdullah Öcalan’s philosophy and ideology. Through the example of the women of East Kurdistan, all women around the world will establish their own free communes based on free will, thought, and life, and become a force of defense for themselves and society.”

title: Gorran: The constitutional and shared responsibilities of KRI authorities must be recognized
content:
In an attempt to take control of border crossings and oil fields in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) and the disputed territories, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered on Tuesday that all border crossings in the Kurdistan region be placed under the authority of the federal border crossings agency and that Baghdad’s powers over oil production and the export of petroleum products be expanded.




According to Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the prime minister and commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces, the Kurdistan Regional Government will henceforth be required to process export permits for crude oil and petroleum products exclusively through the Federal Ministry of Oil. Baghdad is thus asserting greater control over the region’s oil trade.




The Gorran Movement issued a written statement regarding Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s decisions and emphasized that combating corruption and resolving problems must not be used as a justification for violating constitutional powers.




Stressing that the region’s constitutional powers must not be weakened and that the position of the Kurds in Iraq’s new political landscape must not be overlooked, the statement called on the Iraqi Federal Government to reconsider the decisions in full coordination with the Kurdistan Regional Government.




The statement noted that the constitution must serve as the basis for resolving disputes and emphasized that the constitutional and shared responsibilities of regional authorities must be recognized, particularly in the management of the energy, oil, and natural gas sectors.




The Gorran Movement stated that it would not accept the use of anti-corruption efforts as a justification for violating the constitutional rights of the people of Kurdistan, describing Baghdad’s recent steps as a warning.




“Baghdad’s actions are a warning bell. Internal divisions, the weakness of national institutions, and the absence of good governance have undermined the status of the Kurdistan Region and led to an erosion of constitutional rights,” the statement said.




The Gorran Movement called on political forces and parties in Kurdistan to come together as soon as possible and set aside secondary disputes. It emphasized the need to develop a unified national strategy to protect the constitutional rights of the people of Kurdistan through a common stance.

author: Unknown
title: Varisheh Moradi: No policy of attrition can shake the foundations of our commitment
content:
Kurdish political prisoner Varisheh Moradi, who has been sentenced to death in Iran for the second time and is held in Evin Prison, wrote a letter on the occasion of November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.




The letter penned by the Kurdish activist reads as follows:




“Systematic violence is an interconnected structure that begins within the home and extends into the public sphere. Yet, in its most blatant manifestation as state violence, it imposes itself through policies of elimination and denial, intimidation, censorship, repression, and detention, reaching its peak in execution. Meanwhile, through economic pressure, the shrinking of people’s means of subsistence, and under the shadow of war and its consequences, those in power have effectively placed a noose around the neck of society as a whole. Although the death sentence has been issued against me personally, this noose is tightening around everyone’s throat, casting the shadow of an imposed death over all of the society. I see the issuance of a death sentence for the second time as an attempt to turn time into an instrument of subjugation, replacing the “possibility of living” with the “anticipation of death.” Yet those in power fail to realize that the foundations of my commitment, and ours, to our historical and intellectual choices are so firmly established that no policy of attrition can shake them.




Against this backdrop, the shadow of war has significantly increased the number of suicides and killings of women across all regions of Iran. In a land whose historical memory is intertwined with narratives of goddesses and divine beings, how have we reached a point where women’s bodies and very existence have become objects of control, possession, and violation in the social sphere, while their independent will leads to their elimination in the political arena? Both have the same root: a patriarchal mentality sustained by the interconnected forces of power, hierarchy, and domination over women, which cannot tolerate the presence in politics of a woman who possesses her own will and has attained self-awareness. This system of thought fears women’s power and the truth of their existence because a conscious woman breaks free from the position of being possessed and objectified, questioning and challenging forms of authority and the foundations of domination.




For this reason, various labels are used to drive women out of social, political, and economic spheres. In politics, they call us “rebels” so that we may be sentenced to death, while in society, under the guise of tradition, they label crimes as “honor killings” to legitimize the same approach. Yet no force or system has the right to monopolize the power to define and name. By what standards and according to which moral values are these names and labels defined, and who has granted themselves such authority?




Nevertheless, the very fact that news of these crimes and femicides no longer remains hidden and shrouded in silence, as it once did, is itself a step forward and the result of years of struggle and perseverance. For years, attempts were made to portray violence against women as a private matter. But this violence is by no means a private matter. It always has psychological, physical, and structural dimensions and is not an individual problem but a collective one, a concern for society as a whole.




Confronting such a structure requires a continuous and comprehensive struggle against violence against women, one that extends from the home into the public sphere through breaking the silence, speaking out, criticizing and challenging mechanisms of domination, and seeking ways to resist them. This resistance is not the work of one individual or one woman, but the collective will and movement of all women.




For in the essence of “Woman, Life, Freedom,” “woman” is not a figure of submission and subordination, but the creative and liberating force of society. “Life,” in opposition to the culture of death and repression, means living with dignity and awareness. And “freedom” can only be achieved by dismantling every form of oppression and domination.




The struggle against violence against women is a defense of women themselves, a safeguarding of the meaning of life, and an opening of the path to freedom for society as a whole.




Jin, Jiyan, Azadî




Varisha Moradi – Women’s Ward, Evin Prison




November 25, 2026”

title: Kurdistan Regional Government: We reject the use of military rhetoric and threats
content:
Kurdistan Region’s Prime Minister Masrour Barzani chaired the KRG Council of Ministers’ meeting today. The meeting focused primarily on the KRG’s position regarding measures taken yesterday by the federal government of Iraq.




The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region is committed to fulfilling all its constitutional obligations and demands the full provision of its constitutional rights: “The KRG has consistently expressed its readiness to resolve outstanding issues with the federal government within the framework of the Constitution. Consequently, the KRG expresses its deep concern and strong protest regarding the statement issued on behalf of the spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Iraqi Armed Forces, which violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region. This statement is a dangerous indication of a lack of belief in the federal system and represents an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime, which contradicts the Iraqi Constitution. The KRG rejects the use of military rhetoric and threats, which appear to stem from a premeditated, long-standing plan directed against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region.”




The Council of Ministers reaffirmed that the Kurdistan Region has consistently supported measures to combat corruption and illegal activities, and has cooperated and coordinated with the federal government and will continue to do so to eliminate illicit practices. It called for the comprehensive eradication of corruption and oil smuggling across all of Iraq.




The Council of Ministers stressed that the Kurdistan Region is the product of the sacrifices of the heroic Peshmerga and thousands of martyrs; it is not a gift bestowed upon the people of Kurdistan: “The Kurdistan Region has played an active and influential role in establishing the current federal system in Iraq, regards itself as a co-owner of that system, and will never relinquish its constitutional rights, which extend far beyond salaries, budgets, and financial entitlements. They also encompass political rights and the legitimate cause of the people of Kurdistan.”




The KRG Council of Ministers stressed that issues between the Kurdistan Region and the federal government must be resolved through dialogue, negotiations, and mutual understanding within the constitutional framework, calling for the full implementation of the permanent Iraqi Constitution.




“The primary reason these issues remain unresolved is the failure to implement the Constitution, particularly Article 140, which has been neglected for years, with no steps taken to normalize the situation in the disputed Kurdish territories. In accordance with the Constitution, the Federal Council of Iraq should be established, and the Federal Supreme Court reconstituted on a constitutional basis that reflects all components of Iraq.”




The Council of Ministers expressed its gratitude to the Kurdistani people, as well as to all political parties, forces, and components, urging them to maintain their national stance, unity, and solidarity in defense of the constitutional rights of the people of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Region's constitutional framework. It also called upon the Kurdistan Region's representatives in the Iraqi Parliament and the federal government to continue their national role in defending the rights of the Kurdistani people.




The Council of Ministers reaffirmed its support for freedom of opinion and expression. However, it emphasized that anyone who acts against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region, constitutional principles, or Kurdistan’s national interests and incites people to create chaos and oppose the rights of the Kurdistani people should face appropriate legal action.

title: “Let’s Talk Manifesto”: Internationalist women in Rojava launch podcast
content:
With “Let’s Talk Manifesto,” young women from the Internationalist Commune in Rojava have launched a new podcast project. The initiative is rooted in a collective engagement with the Manifesto of Democratic Communal Society by Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan. The internationalist women aim to connect the perspectives developed in the manifesto with their own experiences of the Rojava Revolution and the realities of women’s lives in different parts of the world.




In each episode, the young women focus on a chapter of the manifesto, discuss its theoretical approaches, and explore how these can be translated into social practice. The aim is to create a shared space for learning, reflection, and political discussion across national borders.




In the tradition of the international women’s struggle




The publication date was deliberately chosen. On November 25, 1960, the Mirabal sisters were murdered in the Dominican Republic for their resistance to the dictatorship of Rafael Trujillo. In 1981, feminist movements from the Caribbean and Abya Yala declared the anniversary of their murder a day of struggle against violence against women. Today, women around the world take to the streets to protest patriarchal violence, commemorate murdered women, and carry on their struggles.




The young internationalist women also situate their project within this tradition. In their statement announcing the podcast’s launch, they draw a connection between the deepening crises of capitalist modernity, the destruction of the foundations of social life, and attacks on the organized women’s movement. “We see that women who organize, unite, and struggle for a different life are the first to become targets of attacks. This is because their organizing poses a fundamental threat to the existing patriarchal and capitalist order,” the internationalist women stated.




Collective education as a practice of self-defense




The podcast draws on the comprehensive understanding of self-defense developed by the Kurdish women’s movement, which goes beyond protection against physical attacks to encompass the acquisition of knowledge, collective education, and social organizing. “As young women in particular, we can develop perspectives, devise solutions, and contribute to building a new society. In this sense, self-defense also means developing the ability to shape one’s own living conditions autonomously,” the initiators say.




From theoretical engagement to social practice




The internationalist women view the Manifesto of Democratic Communal Society as a potential response to the current global crisis. Through their podcast, they aim to deepen discussions about alternative forms of social coexistence and make them accessible beyond Rojava. “Our podcast, ‘Let’s Talk Manifesto,’ is an invitation to read, question, and discuss together and, above all, to put the ideas developed into practice. Because a different society does not emerge on its own. It emerges wherever people come together, learn from one another, and begin to organize their lives collectively.”




A new episode of “Let’s Talk Manifesto” is released every Wednesday on 

Spotify

. Further information about the project is available on the 

Internationalist Commune’s website 

and 

Instagram account

.

title: Nearly 3 in 10 Americans Are Changing Thanksgiving Plans Due to Higher Costs
content:
The year-over-year cost of a Thanksgiving turkey has increased by 10 percent, according to the Farm Bureau.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

New polling demonstrates that millions of Americans are likely to change their Thanksgiving plans due to concerns about costs, as prices for many staple items have shot up over the past year.

An Economist/YouGov poll published earlier this week asked respondents whether they would be altering their “turkey day” plans due to price increases. According to the survey, nearly 3 in 10 Americans (28 percent) said they would be making changes to their ordinary traditions.

While 49 percent of respondents said they weren’t changing anything about Thanksgiving, a significant number said they were, yet another indicator that the economy under the Trump administration isn’t working for everybody.

Travel expenses and concerns could be one reason many are making changes to their plans. Gasoline prices have dropped somewhat since reaching over $4.50/gallon on average across the U.S. this past spring, due to restrictions on oil exports that occurred after President Donald Trump’s decision to launch a war on Iran. But even with some respite in those expenses, the average cost of gasoline for this year’s Thanksgiving is almost 20 percent higher than it was a year ago. Soaring ticket prices for air travel — in conjunction with concerns about air safety in general — could also be affecting people’s plans.

Travel isn’t the only matter on people’s minds. With those higher gas prices — and higher prices for diesel fuel — costs for food and other consumer goods have increased, too.

Indeed, the cost of the Thanksgiving meal itself has gone up. According to figures compiled by the Farm Bureau, this year’s meal will likely cost 6 percent more than last year’s — with a 10 percent increase for the turkey alone. Other staple items that are seeing increases in costs include milk, dinner rolls, potatoes, and cranberries, products that are transported across the country on vehicles that use diesel fuel.

Beyond Thanksgiving, higher consumer costs could lead families to change their holiday plans, too. One survey found, for example, that 45 percent of families are going to buy fewer gifts this year as a result of high prices.

Unfortunately, there are signs that the economy isn’t going to get better anytime soon. Indeed, on Wednesday, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index — the preferred measure for inflation that is used by the Fed — showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8 percent annual inflation rate, the highest annual rate seen in that measure since August 2025.

The Trump administration also announced this week that it is preparing to impose a new round of high tariffs on China, the European Union, and other countries. Such tariffs, many economists point out, are essentially a tax on consumers, raising prices on products they purchase from outside the U.S.

title: (KIEL, GER) Revolutionäre Frauensponti zum 25.11.
content:
Wir haben uns heute als Frauen und alle die als solche unterdrückt werden, kämpferisch die Straße und die Nacht genommen! 


Jede von uns kennt die Angst davor alleine im Dunkeln nach Hause zu laufen, die Angst davor verfolgt und belästigt zu werden. Jede von uns kennt patriarchale Gewalt. Doch wir haben von klein auf gelernt zu akzeptieren, was uns angetan wird. Gelernt darüber zu schweigen und die Schuld bei uns selbst zu suchen. Aber diese Gewalt ist Teil des patriarchalen und kapitalistischen Systems und sie ist dafür da uns einzuschüchtern und unten zu halten.




 

 

 

 

 







Wir sagen: Es reicht! 


Um diesem System den Kampf anzusagen, müssen wir uns zusammenschließen, lernen gemeinsam zu kämpfen und uns auferlegte Rollenbilder zu durchbrechen. So wird Angst in Stärke und Mut verwandelt und wir verstehen, dass wir uns diese zu nutzen machen können.




Auch müssen gerade wir als Frauen eine militante Haltung und daraus hervorgehend, eine militante Praxis entwickeln. Denn unsere Befreiung wird nicht mit Worten erkämpft werden. Dabei können wir lernen, von den Kämpferinnen der YPG, von der feministischen Bewegung Lateinamerikas und so vielen weiteren Genossinnen aus der ganzen Welt. Denn wir werden uns nur selbst schützen. Und nur wir können dem Ursprung der patriarchalen Gewalt, diesem kapitalistischen und patriarchalem System etwas entgegensetzen. Kämpfen wir also gemeinsam für den revolutionären Bruch und den Aufbau des Kommunismus!




Für die Feministische Revolution!


Heraus zum Tag gegen Gewalt an Frauen!




 

 

 

 

 







 

 

 

 

 







 

 

 

 

 







 

 

 

 

 







 

 

 

 

 







 

 

 

 

 







Anmerkung des Moderationskollektiv von barrikade.info: «Unsere Sprache spiegelt gesellschaftliche Machtverhältninsse und Unterdrückungsformen wieder. Dazu gehören Sexismus und die erzwungene Geschlechterbinarität. Dies äussert sich u.a. in der Nutzung einer binären Sprache. Dies bedeutet, dass nur in den Kategorien «Frau» und «Mann» gedacht und geschrieben wird. Als Kollektiv einer emanzipatorischen, anti-autoritären Medien-Plattform erwarten wir eine diskrimiierungsfreie Haltung. Die Geschlechtsbinarität stellt eine Unterdrückung dar und die Verwendung binärer Sprache in Momenten, in denen die Schreibenden die Geschlechtsidentität der Menschen nicht kennen und/oder Identitäten, welche nicht in dieser Binarität Platz haben, unsichtbar gemacht werden, ist diskriminierend.


Anstelle von binären Begriffen kann in solchen Momenten genderneutrale Sprache verwendet werden (z.B. Demonstrierende). Auch kann versucht werden, durch andere Begriffe die gewünschte Menschengruppe zu beschreiben (z.B. TINFA*), sowie kann auf die Nutzung von Genderzeichen, wie dem Genderstern, zurückgegriffen werden. Oder durch die Nennung, wer nicht gemeint ist, lassen sich ebenfalls inklusive Menschengruppen schaffen (z.B. alle, welche nicht Teil der hegemonialen Männlichkeit sind).


Natürlich gibt es noch weitere Möglichkeiten, welche genutzt werden können.
