author: Amy Goodman
title: National Book Award Winner Links Denial of US Visa to Palestine Advocacy
content:
Egyptian author and former political prisoner Abdelrahman ElGendy speaks about his new memoir, Huna.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an MFA in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.

“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells Democracy Now! about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”

We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet Mada Masr, whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.

“Mada carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in Mada Masr. “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

We are currently awaiting an Egyptian court decision on whether the closing of Mada Masr, the independent newspaper in Egypt, will stand. We’ll go to Cairo when we hear.

But right now we’re going to turn to what happened in the last few weeks here in this country, in New York, where we are. Novelists, essayists, poets and other writers from around the world took to the stage at the 77th annual National Book Awards ceremony in New York City last week. The winner of this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction, Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, though, was notably absent from the event, after the Trump administration denied his U.S. visa application, blocking him from entering the United States.

ElGendy’s debut book is called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, and chronicles his more than six years of imprisonment in Egypt following his arrest at the age of 17, alongside his father, during the crackdown on protests after the military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2013. He and his father were in their car, and Abdelrahman was taking a picture.

This is the moment the prize for nonfiction was presented by panel chair Robert Warrior.

ROBERT WARRIOR: It’s my distinct honor to announce that this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction goes to Abdelrahman ElGendy for Huna.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor, Helen Thomaides, then took the stage and read a statement written by ElGendy.

HELEN THOMAIDES: If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you. Years ago, in my prison cell in Egypt, I used to fantasize about writing a memoir. I would slip under a bright red duvet my mother had bribed the guards to let through, and imagine that everything happening to me would one day end up in a book, that the guard’s baton was battering not my ribs but those of the book’s protagonist, that the slap was landing on the protagonist’s face, not mine. I was the author, concerned only with how to render on the page the torture my body was enduring. The scribbles on a smuggled page became a potential essay, the essay a potential published article, the article a book. I’d imagine that book winning an award, and deliver fictional acceptance speeches under Mama’s duvet, fleetingly unincarcerated. Today, that dream should have come full circle, but like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor Helen Thomaides reading Abdelrahman’s words after his memoir Huna won the National Book Award just last week. Ahead of the ceremony, Abdelrahman wrote a piece in The New Yorker magazine. It’s headlined “I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa.”

Abdelrahman ElGendy wrote much of the book while in the United States, where he came two years after he was released from prison in Egypt. He studied at the University of Pittsburgh, where he obtained an MFA in creative nonfiction. Then, in April 2025, following the Trump administration’s widespread targeting of pro-Palestine voices, including international students and academics, Abdelrahman ElGendy decided to flee the U.S., fearing he’d be next, that he’d be detained and possibly deported back to Egypt over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations. At the time, he wrote in The Nation magazine, quote, “I was a political prisoner in Egypt. I didn’t want to become one again in America,” unquote.

For more, we’re joined now by Abdelrahman ElGendy from Europe, where he lives now.

Abdelrahman, I just want to congratulate you on this remarkable book, which I’ve just finished. And I had the joy, flying back from Turkey, the U.N. climate summit, of listening to your book, the audio book, which you read in your own words. The magnificence, the power, the pain of this book cannot be underestimated. I want to thank you so much for sharing your life with us, Abdelrahman ElGendy. Thank you for joining us.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Thank you. Thank you so much, Amy. Thanks for having me and for these kind words. Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN: So, we are awaiting word right now about whether Egypt will be forced to reopen Mada Masr, a place where you actually, I think, published your first words. You wrote throughout your six years in prison. But talk about — well, first, start with the title, and talk about what it meant to win the National Book Award in the United States, the place you wanted to stay, to be in exile, to be protected, but could not reenter for the award ceremony.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah. Thank you. I mean, of course, it was a gutting thing to not be able to, you know, attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising. You know, we all know how this U.S. administration is now trying to keep everyone who criticizes policies out, especially when it comes, you know, to our region, especially when it’s around Palestine. You know, and if you’re a citizen of another country that doesn’t, you know, need a visa, they don’t want you. They just detain you at the point of entry at the airport. But if you do, like in my case, they just deny you, you know, at the embassy.

And I just — yeah, they love repeating the idea that the visa is, you know, a privilege and not a right. This is kind of the mantra that they keep, you know, repeating to everyone. But, yeah, this, I think, is just intentional distraction from the most important point here, which is that the visa process is being weaponized, and has been now for a while, as a form of transnational repression, which we’re very familiar with in Egypt, as well, because the Egyptian state also uses this form of transnational repression, you know, denying us certain paperwork and stuff like that to punish you for political speech and to keep certain bodies that you deem undesirable outside. So, same for the U.S. So, the visa denial itself being weaponized in that way is the issue, not the fact that the, yes, consul office can deny or approve, etc. So, I think this should be, yeah, the headline, really.

But it was also, like, very sad, I think, in a way that is very specific to my personal journey, you know, as a — this is not new to me. As a kid, you know, I worked my whole life to earn a scholarship to study engineering at this great school that my family couldn’t afford at the time. And then I was arrested on the eve of my first day as a freshman. This is — I speak about this in the book — before I get to live this dream. And then, when I was released in 2020, it happened straight into COVID in 2020. And I started, like, when the lockdown was being lifted, and I started slowly rebuilding community. Because of my writing with Mada Masr, actually, because I continued writing with Mada post-prison, word kind of circulated. Relatives who were well connected told me that my name is being kind of floated again for rearrest. And eventually, I was forced to flee Egypt because of that writing with Mada Masr. And since then, you know, I’ve never been able to share a room with Egyptian readers of my work, except accidentally in exile, you know, when we’re all, like, kind of shunned away from Egypt together. So I’ve had to do it from a distance.

And now, you know, this book, which I imagined writing from prison, which I wrote, you know, throughout my time in the U.S., and then, just as I was about to graduate from my MFA in the U.S., which this book was the graduation, the thesis for — right? — you know, I was forced again to temporarily leave for safety concerns of ICE targeting, as you mentioned, because of my political writing and pro-Palestine activism on campus. And so, I had to graduate from my MFA remotely, as well, witness that moment, you know, be celebrated remotely by people in the room that I was unable to be in. And I wanted to bring my family over to the U.S. to have that graduation ceremony, that prison denied us in Egypt, and we were deprived of that again.

I couldn’t do a U.S. book tour. And now the book, you know, has made it all the way into that room of the National Book Award. And, you know, to have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love who have witnessed this journey, it is gutting. But in a way, it is also just the story of my life. This is not new.

And still, I think I need to redirect all this back, you know, to Egyptian political prisoners, because as I said in my speech, a life that I’m living right now beyond prison, in which my dreams could even be crushed in this way, that was the dream back in prison. I dreamed of a day when I have these, like, unincarcerated people problems. But there are 60,000 political prisoners, you know, who don’t even have the luxury of such precarity, that at least opens into possibility, right? So, I think, yeah, I always want to redirect it to them. I am blessed, no matter what, like, everything that happened that was very sad and gutting and everything. But I always try to put that in relation to people back home behind bars in Egypt, my friends, Ayman and everyone else still behind bars. I’m still blessed to have these problems. Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: Tell us why you named the book Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah, I mean Huna, huna is the Arabic word for “here.” And it was inspired by a popular Arab protest song, “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which means “We Will Remain Here.” And I first heard that song, you know, up close on my third night in detention. We were in this, like, military camp in the middle of the desert, very excruciating physical conditions, where 68 of us were crammed into a tiny room, piled on top of one another. There were some people that were shot and wounded, so it was very heavy. My father was with me at the time. He was dying.

And then, out of nowhere, the guards finally allowed in the homemade food our families had brought to the gate. So, our families would come every day; they’d be sent back. But that day, they just brought in the food. And then, for the first time since the arrest, we had a taste of home.

And then something very magical happened. We just began to sing. The mood got lighter, and we began to sing. And one of the songs was “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which goes, “We will remain here until the pain subsides. We will remain here. The melody will sweeten.” And, you know, we sang together, and I started feeling those chills on my arms. You could feel that everyone in the room was entering this sort of visceral moment together.

And I found myself thinking, fascinated, that I didn’t want to remain here. Like, who wants — you know, none of us wants to remain here. We couldn’t wait to escape this room fast enough. My father was dying. We were being tortured. People were shot. So, what was this huna? What was this “here” that we were so touched by, that we were all actively choosing to inhabit together? What were we entering?

And I think I would say my book — if I would kind of put it in one line, I’d say it is a six-year pursuit of this huna, like the question of what it means to inhabit a space that is designed to erase you in body, in language, in your very sense of personhood, and still find ways to be. So, I try to trace, you know, that sense of nonphysical hereness and witness, that repeatedly saves me from being wholly conquered by prison.

And you also mentioned the becoming part, which is important to me, because I was arrested — I think sometimes that gets lost, the fact that I was arrested at 17 years old. So, to me, this is not just prison and revolution. It is also becoming, because I say this is a coming-of-age story. And so many people come to this political awakening that I had, you know, in high school age. They start getting politically agitated or involved. And to me, it happened that I went into prison in those formative years. So, my whole history of activism was two months — right? — after the Rabaa massacre until October 6, and then I was arrested. So, incarceration, in a way, was this school in which I was thinking about the world and my positionality inside it.

So, I was just politically activated before I went into prison, and I went into prison with all those agitated questions that were so unsettled for me. I was so angry. I carried so much rage at the military dictatorship, the police state. And I felt like I had a moral compass. But it was mostly motivated not by, you know, theory or intellectual thought or engaging with political theory. It was just rage at seeing certain injustices and wanting to intervene and be part of removing them or restoring justice. So, to me, that was — you know, I see people massacred, a military dictatorship. I think, “These things are wrong, and I don’t want to be on this side. I want to be on the other side that is against them.”

But in prison, I get into a more, I think, sophisticated approach. In prison, I think you have — you know, you have nothing more than time, and you sit down, and you just question everything. And I think prison forces you to confront so many not only political questions, but also very existential questions, you know, about what it means to be here, to be human, to be in relation to other humans, to your own father, to your friends, your mom, and what kinds of obligations does that carry.

So, every day, I was encountering new things that agitated me even more, and that were forcing me, you know, to think. You’re beaten. You’re tortured. You’re being beaten by those batons every day. You see your father hit. Everything around you radicalizes you and makes you think, you know, “I cannot afford to look away from these things. I don’t have the luxury of looking away from these questions,” because the batons are beating me every single day. I just cannot not think about them and my relationship to them and to other people fighting them, and whether I think of them, again, as allies or even political enemies. So, momentarily in prison, I have to align with factions that, you know, I don’t align with politically. It forces me to think about these questions. Like, in my cell, I don’t agree with you politically. I’m very aggravated by you. But we step up outside the cell, and the same police officers are beating us. So, what does that mean in terms of, you know, allyship, mobilization, working together? So, yeah, all those questions at 17, you wouldn’t be thinking about, I think. But I couldn’t afford not to, because my survival depended on grappling with them in prison.

AMY GOODMAN: I mean, this is also a story of a father and son, a mother and son, a brother, a cousin. Talk about how you were first detained with your dad. And it’s a relationship that carries throughout the book. I mean, you go from being a son to being your dad’s protector, to having to separate from your father. My goodness, I mean, you were arrested at the age of 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah. One thing I always like to bring up about this is, one of my dear friends, when she read the manuscript of the book for the first time, before it was published, she told me, “Do you know what this book is?” And I told he, “What?” And she said, “This is a love letter to Baba.” And I found that very moving, because I do think this is one of — at least one of the things that this book is, because, you know, my father was apolitical. Like, he wasn’t even involved in politics. And I was a very hot-headed teenager. I really wanted to be on the streets. I was very — again, I was — I had this awakening, and I was attending protests very — you know, every single day, maybe three protests, you know, in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening. And they tolerated — my parents tolerated that for a while.

But then, on October 6, that was a particularly dangerous day. This is the Armed Forces Day. And protesters wanted to break into Tahrir Square. And because of its symbolic value, you know, revolutionary value, the police would get very brutal when people attempt to even approach Tahrir Square. Up until today, it’s a very heavily securitized area. And so, what happens, the arrangement is my mother forced my father to basically come chaperone me, you know, to this protest, to look out for me and make sure that I don’t get harmed or arrested, which, you know, doesn’t work out as planned, obviously.

So, we go there. I start shooting a video. I’m, like, speaking enthusiastically. I leave the car. He yells at me to come back, so I go back inside. I shoot from the window. And then I don’t notice there are two plainclothes officers standing right next to the window, who kind of, from my commentary, kind of deduce that I’m aligned with what’s happening. So, they, you know, pull the door open. They wrench me out. They start beating me, take my phone. And then my father comes, and he starts trying to wrench me away, you know, from their arms. And then they end up arresting him, as well. So, my father gets arrested just because, you know, I made him be in that space, which, of course, we can always argue that it’s a structural issue, it’s a state’s issue. But guilt, you know, doesn’t — it doesn’t work like that. And so, my — the whole six year begins from that kind of inciting incident and that guilt. It’s a very guilt-ridden story, you know, toward my father.

And we’ve always, my father and I, struggled, I think, to express affection to one another. There’s also commentary about Arab masculinity in the book a lot, and specifically father-son relationships. So, we struggled to do that, and I think we carried so much and so many unsaid things inside both of us. And through prison, it was very difficult to communicate, because you’re used to seeing your father as this protective figure, right? And then, in prison, you suddenly realize he is helpless, he cannot protect you. And in a way, he does his best to protect me in all those small ways in prison, of course, but in the bigger scheme of things, he cannot get me my freedom, right? And I cannot get him his freedom. And, you know, the state loves to weaponize love, the Egyptian state, any fascist state, really. So, in prison, they used that against us. They hurt my father to get to me. They hurt me to get to him, and so on. So it was a very difficult situation.

But what I also try to explore in the book is the avenues that opened up once my father and I were not only father and son in prison. I suddenly started seeing him in all those other kind of roles. He was also a prisoner in relation to the state, a prison cellmate or, you know, a prison mate to other prisoners, which was both difficult, but I think also opened up different avenues of communication between us, because sometimes, I don’t know, we’d have a fight in the cell, and we’d fight together with — like, against people and be aligned with one another, and I think, “Oh, my father and I are co-conspirators now.” There’s that first scene in the book where we do this. And through the night, my father, for the first time ever, he rests his hand, you know, on my back and leaves it there through the night. And I remember that being one of the first instances in my life where he touches me in that way.

So, when he read the book after, you know, it was published — I gave him the Arabic. I wrote it in Arabic. It’s coming out in Arabic, and he read the Arabic version. And again, he doesn’t — he was so struck, I think, by the intensity of the love, because I couldn’t express it to him verbally. So, he just said, “You know, I understand so many things much better now,” and then went on to, like, fact-check the entire book, because that’s his — you know, his language of love. So, eventually, I think this is just the sweetest, I think, closure that could have happened to this harrowing experience that we shared together. And if he was the only reader, you know, of this book, if this was the only thing to come out of it, that would have been enough for me.

AMY GOODMAN: And, of course, he gets out before you and then tries to get you out, and ultimately does, based on the fact that you were arrested at 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah, and it is — I was wrongly tried — wrongfully tried as an adult instead of a minor. And this is — again, throughout the book, you come across the absurdity and arbitrariness, you know, of the Egyptian state. I was 17 at the time of arrest, two months shy of 18, right? So I had two months to turn 18. And then, the officer that arrested me breaks my ID, or both of our IDs, delivered us to the police station. And just so randomly, because of that, I get processed as an adult, and then I just keep getting processed as an adult throughout. In the prosecution, my lawyer ends up, you know, submitting appeal after appeal. None of them gets looked into, because we’re in Egypt. We get tried as this package deal, right? All of us together in a mass trial.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman, I want to continue this conversation after the show, but I want you to stay with us, because we’re going to go to Cairo right now.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: OK, yeah, yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: This story doesn’t end, and I want you to be a part of it. We’re going to Cairo, Egypt, where an appeal was just heard in the case against Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr, for operating an unlicensed website, they’re saying, though she’s been operating it for years. Late last month, she was fined $50,000 or to shut down Mada Masr, following an expedited trial where her lawyers were denied time to prepare a defense, call witnesses or submit documentation. Lina Attalah is also facing charges for publishing so-called false news, that could lead to her imprisonment. We’re going right now outside the court to Hossam Bahgat, founder and director of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, part of Mada Masr’s legal team, just outside the courthouse. And I want Abdelrahman to respond to what you report to us. Do we have a decision from the court whether Mada Masr can be reopened, Hossam?

HOSSAM BAHGAT: Thank you, Amy, for having me.

No, I mean, the defense team finished their oral pleadings and submitted the requests. The court has adjourned the session, and we should get a decision on this final appeal by the end of today. I mean, the good thing is that at least it looked more like a courtroom and more like a normal trial today compared to the absurdity that we saw in the first instance. Unfortunately, though, we don’t have any signs that there is an intent to look fairly at the situation, the position of Mada Masr. Today, the lawyers not only challenged the decision to convict Lina and shut down Mada Masr —

AMY GOODMAN: You’re breaking up.

HOSSAM BAHGAT: — and confiscate all its —

AMY GOODMAN: Hossam, you’re breaking up, but I want to tell people you can go to see our interview with Lina Attalah that I did with Anjali Kamat just as she was facing all of this, and also you can go to democracynow.org to see our visit to Mada Masr when we were in Egypt. I want to give Abdelrahman ElGendy the last word, though. You thank Lina Attalah and our former producer Sharif Abdel Kouddous for being able to find a way to get your words out of prison. Ultimately, you would smuggle them out. Is that right?

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yes, absolutely. I began writing in that way, smuggling my words out in prison. And I think you just — you know, once you, as a political prisoner, get a taste of that magic of being able to smuggle your language out to the world, and then receive the world’s language back in response, you just cannot stop. And Mada were the first place to, you know, offer my words a home, is how I thank them. And they feature in the book, as well, because Mada, you know, they sent me wanting to publish, you know, some of the things that I smuggled out, and ever since I had this relationship with them, I published six more pieces with Mada Masr from prison. And that was important to me.

I think that the project of the current Egyptian military dictatorship is — it’s a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before. It was possible, and therefore it is possible. And they don’t want it to be a thinkable or imaginable thing anymore.

And I think Mada Masr is a huge part of that. I cannot understand or speak about the campaign against Mada Masr, you know, divorced from the idea of this more bigger project of erasure of the Egyptian state, because Mada carries so much of the archive, you know, of our revolutionary history. It is the place that people like me, in prison and after prison, can go write in. It is the place where, you know, Alaa El-Fattah, who published “Graffiti for Two People” with Ahmed Douma. It is the place that speaks about prison letters and communication. And so, to erase it is to erase an archive. And also, it is to erase the more, I think, intimate and dangerous thing, is we go to Mada Masr to feel less alone, to remember, you know, that we were many, and therefore we are many still today. We have not been — you know, as Alaa says, we have not been fully defeated. And that, to me, is important. Maybe we’re not — maybe we are defeated in a way, but not wholly, not fully.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman ElGendy, I want to thank you for being with us and for this incredible memoir. It’s called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming. It has just won the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction, and we’ll link to your New Yorker and Nation pieces. That does it for our show. I’m Amy Goodman. This is Democracy Now!

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

author: Holly Jonas
title: How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want
content:
This article 

How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







Kumi Naidoo knows a thing or two about activism. He has organized anti-apartheid school boycotts in South Africa, scaled oil rigs in frigid Arctic waters and called out world leaders for their moral failures in U.N. climate negotiations. But it was not until he eulogized a glacier that he truly realized the potent alchemy of arts, culture and activism — also known as artivism.




With decades of experience in social movements and serving in top leadership positions in international NGOs, Naidoo is better placed than most to shed light on the inner workings of activism. He is also refreshingly candid about its shortcomings. One of the biggest challenges in activism, he says, is a communications deficit. His late son, South African rapper and singer Riky Rick, lovingly pushed him to ditch the technical jargon so commonly used by climate activists and instead reach people through the heart, body and soul.




After the musician’s devastating and sudden passing in 2022, Riky’s mother Louisa, widow Bianca, and Kumi channeled their grief and resolve into the Riky Rick Foundation for the Promotion of Artivism. One of their key initiatives, 

Global Artivism

, highlights the power of arts and culture to contribute to positive change, helps cultural creatives connect and collaborate with each other, and surfaces and works to address the many challenges they face. Powered by a team of volunteers and a lean staff, in-person global convenings in South Africa and Brazil and regional virtual convenings have helped mobilize and further energize this vibrant movement. They are now in the thick of the decentralized 

Global Artivism Month

, which will culminate on International Human Rights Day on Dec. 10.




In this interview with Naidoo, who also serves as president of the 

Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative

, he discusses the power and potential of the global artivism movement, how pessimism is a luxury we cannot afford, and the continuing prescience of Martin Luther King Jr.




This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.




For those who may not be familiar with it, what is artivism, and what are the connections between artivism and nonviolent movements?




Artivism is the intersection of arts, culture and activism. Its intention is to address a major weakness in much of our activism, which is that we have aimed our messages and our narratives at the brain, and we’ve ignored the heart, the body and the soul. A song or documentary reaches many more people than a policy brief does. Politics does not drive culture; culture drives politics.




Harnessing the power of arts and culture on its own will not deliver salvation from the climate crisis and the intersecting crises that emerge from it. However, failing to harness the power of arts and culture almost guarantees that we’re going to fail because we’re never going to reach the large numbers of people that we need to.










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










We are facing a massive global mental health crisis coming from ecological and climate anxiety, war, conflict, deepening inequality, authoritarianism and fascism. Artivism has the potential to invite people into the biggest struggles of our time, in a way that creates opportunities for participation and engagement. To help us secure peace, justice and all of the good things that we want, those in power have no incentive to actually listen to what we’re saying unless we can show we have a powerful constituency.




We also need this massive mobilization and participation because participation itself will be part of the antidote to despair, despondency and depression. We can be the best versions of ourselves in this current moment if we keep a positive disposition, despite how bad things are. In this moment of history, pessimism is a luxury we simply cannot afford. The pessimism that justifiably emerges from our analysis, our lived experiences and observations can and must be responded to with the optimism of our thought, our action, our creativity, our courage and our sense of humanity.




Joyful acts of cultural expression, in which hope is embedded, offer us the best way forward. Artivism is typically nonviolent, creative and speaks to the heart. I believe artivism has a big role in the quest to create a world where we value peace and we value nonviolence.




Could you tell us about your “origin story” as an activist and how you got involved in artivism?




As a young anti-apartheid activist in South Africa, we were organizing amongst people who had low levels of literacy and education. We used all sorts of arts and culture — sport, cooking, music. Even during the state of emergency, when we could not have meetings, we held rock concerts and called them things like “groove to improve.” They were soft messages, but everybody attending was going there to resist the apartheid regime. So artivism was always part of me.







Kumi Naidoo at the Second Global Artivism Convening in Salvador, Brazil, in November 2025. (Garimpo/Global Artivism Initiative)







But when I was the head of Greenpeace and Amnesty International, those roles were so bureaucratic in some ways that that side of me got subdued. At Greenpeace, we were talking about 1.5 degrees and 350 parts per million, which means nothing to at least 90 percent of people in the world. I started engaging more and more with the arts and culture community because I knew we needed their creativity to help us communicate in a more powerful way. Then I had an epiphany moment in August 2019, when the artist Olafur Eliasson invited me to go to Iceland to join a 

funeral for a glacier

.




Early in the morning, the former President of Ireland [and U.N. Human Rights Commissioner], Mary Robinson and I offered comments and about 500 of us walked up the Okjökull glacier. When we looked at the media coverage later, I would say it was more successful than 95 percent of the actions that happened during my leadership of Greenpeace. Instead of drowning people in an acronym alphabet soup, we talked about loss. We connected with a human emotion that people could easily understand.




On the flight from Reykjavik back to London, I decided to step down as the head of Amnesty. I could have potentially stayed several more years, but I really felt I needed to address this communications deficit of activism.




In September 2021, I went to Berlin to focus on artivism as a 

fellow

 of the Robert Bosch Academy, but I was soon back in South Africa. Archbishop Desmond Tutu passed away that December. After the funeral, our son [South African rapper and singer Riky Rick] sat his mom and me down and said, “You’re not really good at what you do. You’ve been fighting for democracy, human rights, gender equity and so on since you were teenagers. When I look at the world, it’s all moving in the wrong direction.” When I asked him why we are failing, he said, “It’s very simple. You aim all the narratives at the brain, and you ignore the heart, the body and the soul. … It sounds like you’re speaking a version of English that only one percent of people in the world understand. How are you going to move people?” He was just amazing at being able to speak to working-class and middle-class people.




A month later, he called me, and he was down. I cheered him up, and he said he was going to visit me in Berlin and bring his wife and mom. But then a week later, he died by suicide.




After his passing, we set up the 

Riky Rick Foundation for the Promotion of Artivism

. We started building a global network, which has now led into the global artivism movement.




I’m so sorry again for his passing, it must still be so painful. How would you describe the role of the Foundation in relation to the global artivism movement?




We are not creating something new, but energizing and amplifying what already exists. We see our role as very modest. We see the movement per se as much broader and living in virtually every community, where culture is alive and well in its multiple, diverse manifestations. What we hope to do is to amplify its power and encourage folks to not see culture as decoration, but to see culture as power.




What do you consider as “good practices” of the artivism movement in the current context? What still needs to evolve in terms of strategy and tactics to meet the moment?




One of the roles that cultural creatives have played historically, which is the most needed role right now, is to help us imagine futures and realities yet to be born. We need the cultural community to help us imagine a world where there’s greater equality, greater peace, greater justice, greater love, less division and less conflict across the artificial boundaries that opportunistic politicians are driving today.




Artivism also gives people a sense of hope and optimism and creates spaces of joy. People are so time-poor today, sometimes working two or three jobs to get by. If they have a little time to give, you’re most likely to get them to come to an event if it not only has a purpose and a good message behind it, but it is also fun.




Cultural action is going to be an asset to help people get through this moment. We should not underestimate the need for fun right now. Don’t let the Trumps of the world rob you of your right to joy and happiness. Sing, dance, be joyful! Even when things are bad, smile at your oppressor.




I would like to hear your thoughts on the critiques and limitations of artivism. Some people say the arts are just a “nice to have.” There are also concerns about the art world being a space of privilege, with limited access for folks in working-class communities. How do you respond to those critiques?




Those are really important observations. The global artivism movement embraces cultural action for a safe and just world. Harnessing the power of arts and culture alone does not deliver salvation, so let’s not overstate it. But let’s also recognize the world of arts and culture is very broad and diverse, with everything from cuisine and fashion to music and visual art.




Some of the very high-end practices are highly problematic, such as fossil fuel companies buying off and branding museums, which already carry a lot of pain for the 88 percent of people who come from the Global South.




Artists and activists create paintings using ashes gathered from previous forest fires, during at the Second Global Artivism Convening in Salvador, Brazil, in November 2025. (Garimpo/Global Artivism Initiative)




The global artivism movement is mostly concerned about frontline artists who are rooted in communities, who are living the pain, who are not already established. While that’s our focus, we are engaging with everybody and trying to keep a broad tent approach.




We’re also saying to the artists who have made it, “You know how hard it was to get there.” We also have to be careful about it not being extractive. Global South culture has always been extracted by the North in multiple ways, and the arts world is not without contradiction and challenge. … We hope more resources flow to community arts efforts.




One of the most amazing things about Riky was that he quietly helped a lot of people as a philanthropist. He directly supported more than 100 individual artists in multiple ways, without a foundation or tax breaks. We only realized this after he died. He was a superstar in South Africa, but once he made it, he didn’t think, “Oh, it’s all about me now. How do I keep accumulating?”




What is the role of artivism in the context of closing or closed civic space and authoritarian regimes?




The shrinking of civic space has also led to thousands of artists around the world being at risk. The organization Artists at Risk is documenting the challenges that Sudanese, Palestinian, Ukrainian, Russian and other artists are facing in horrendous civic space realities. It’s also an indicator that artists have unique power in this current moment.




Artivism can open up avenues of creative public participation and pressure that can sometimes beat the restrictions of repressive authoritarian governments. It offers not only hope, but also the space to imagine realities in the future that could be much better and much different from the unjust realities of the present.




Grassroots artists may face financial precarity, and maybe even family or societal ostracization, in addition to threats they may face for being activists. How can social movements better support artivists and contribute to their individual and collective protection and well-being?




For far too long, the image of an activist was somebody who worked excessive hours and took excessive risks. We have to change the image of what an activist is. Of course, people who occupy oil rigs and lead marches are a very important part of the broader activist community. However, we have been very negligent about not sufficiently recognizing the massive trauma that human rights and environmental activists experience.




We are dealing with a global mental health crisis right now. Sometimes the pressure to just keep going means that we are not creating enough circles of support around activists who are experiencing primary and secondary trauma through the communities they’re working with and the injustice and suffering they are witnessing. We must not underestimate this.




For people who are putting their lives on the line to work for a more just future, it’s okay to take a break every now and then. Not only is it okay, it’s critically important that you build circles of support around you.




For the level of popular mobilization we need, whether it’s painting murals, running soup kitchens, building micro solar grids or protesting, all of these forms of participation are going to be necessary to pressure those with political and economic power to act with the urgency that the situation calls for.




What advice or guidance could you share with civil society and movement leaders who would like to engage more in artivism, but are unsure of how to start or sustain it?




One of the biggest challenges that activism faces historically and at the moment is that we face a massive communications deficit. We are not able to communicate to the large numbers of people that we absolutely need to reach. In fact, those who are promoting fascism and authoritarianism have found more effective ways to weaponize identity and culture to misinform and to get people to vote for the most awful racist, sexist, war-mongering regimes in the world.




There is an objective challenge: The people who own the powerful media communication channels are vested in the status quo, whether it’s the military-industrial complex or the fossil fuel-industrial complex. They are not inclined to give equitable coverage to ideas that contest that status quo, such as our dependency on fossil fuels.




For civil society organizations wanting to communicate more effectively and reach out to the artists and cultural creatives in your communities, engage them with respect, embrace the power of culture as a central part of shifting the needle and moving more people to embrace the need for urgent action. We are losing valuable time with the climate emergency getting worse and worse by the day.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













Artists are not waiting for mainstream civil society organizations to come and educate them. Many artists are already doing amazing work, based on their own understanding of the realities in their communities and in the world. Some have better ideas than formal civil society organizations on how to communicate more effectively. There needs to be a multifaceted approach, and the bottom line is embracing the power of arts and culture for a safe and just world.




You have spoken before about creative maladjustment, drawing inspiration from Martin Luther King’s popularization of this term in the 1960s. What does this mean to you in the current moment, with so many intersecting crises?




Soon after I was born, King gave a 

speech

 in which he talked about the term “maladjusted” from the field of psychology.




“[W]e all want to live the well-adjusted life in order to avoid neurotic and schizophrenic personalities. But,” he said, “there are some things in our nation and some things in the world [to] which I am proud to be maladjusted.”




He continued, “I never intend to adjust myself to segregation and discrimination. I never intend to adjust myself to religious bigotry. I never intend to become adjusted to economic conditions which will take necessities from the many to give luxuries to the few. I never intend to adjust to the madness of militarism and the self-defeating effects of physical violence.”




If this wisdom was true in 1965, it is a thousand times more relevant now in the United States as well as virtually every country around the world. Today, his logic is informing thousands of activists and multiple movements as we push back against the status quo that is broken, unjust and driving humanity to war, climate disaster and many other challenges. If there was a moment in human history in which the idea of creative maladjustment is needed more than ever, I would argue that moment is now.




This article 

How ‘artivism’ helps us create the futures we want

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: William Gillis
title: Il Vuoto della “Sinistra”
content:
Di 

William Gillis

. Originale pubblicato il 21 febbraio 2017 con il titolo 

The Emptiness of “The Left”

. Tradotto da 

Enrico Sanna

.




Non credo che la “sinistra” rappresenti qualcosa di coerente; mi sembra piuttosto una coalizione storicamente contingente di posizioni ideologiche diverse. Nell’assemblea nazionale francese, Bastiat e altri liberomercatisti sedevano a sinistra; se da un lato si trattava di una coerente tradizione di libero mercato di sinistra, dobbiamo anche ammettere però che questo non significava molto in quei particolari frangenti rivoluzionari, e ancora meno in frangenti rivoluzionari in generale. Ci sono sempre rivoluzionari che ambiscono a sistemi molto peggiori del nostro, e molti rivoluzionari riconosciuti come “di sinistra” avevano propositi che erano un veleno per la libertà.




Sinistra e destra oggi sono generalmente considerate egalitarie e gerarchiche. Si tratta non solo di una lettura imposta di una realtà storica e sociologica molto più complessa, ma anche filosoficamente priva di contenuto. Nessuno sa dire chiaramente cos’è l’egalitarismo, o anche il potere gerarchico, molte teorie non solo si escludono reciprocamente, ma evidenziano come pretese presumibilmente identiche siano in realtà profondamente antagonistiche. Egalitarismo significa la stessa esatta ricchezza (comunque la si misuri) per tutti? Significa, nell’ambito astratto delle relazioni, uguaglianza giuridica o sociale davanti al Popolo o alle leggi dello Stato? Significa la stessa opportunità di impegno economico o la stessa possibilità di accedere ai granai? L’uguaglianza sostituisce altre virtù come la libertà? È meglio che tutti siano ugualmente oppressi o che qualcuno sia più libero? Non faccio dello spirito. Noi insabbiamo queste questioni serie dicendo che vanno lasciate al “buonsenso”, o sperando che i compagni affronteranno i dettagli così come faremmo noi, valutando i pro e i contro, mentre sappiamo per esperienza che non è così. Siamo in disaccordo costante.




Si parla di “democrazia diretta collettiva” come se qualcosa che rappresenta il volere pressoché unanime di un qualche organismo costituisse una condizione egalitaria. Certo, per certi versi è così. Ma se un qualche organismo collettivo decide della mia vita, io non voglio “partecipare”, gli lancio una bomba. C’è gente di sinistra che usa slogan come “potere al popolo” o “aboliamo il potere”, e questo dovrebbe essere un forte segnale d’allarme per tutti: parliamo di sistemi concettuali e valori completamente diversi. È una grossa illusione pensare che se ci si siede a discutere alla fine ci si ritrova tutti dalla stessa parte. Il presupposto di un obiettivo comune o di una solidarietà che abbraccia tutta la sinistra è una rassicurante bugia.




La sinistra non è una serie di assiomi etici su cui accordarsi per poi dibattere sulle conseguenti pratica e strategia. La sinistra è una coalizione storica assemblata per caso. Come nelle rivoluzioni, noi tendiamo ad identificarci con i vinti, formiamo le nostre coalizioni con le classi che reputiamo perdenti in opposizione alle classi che reputiamo di governo, ma così facendo confondiamo le cose. Siamo per l’aborto perché vediamo nelle donne il lato perdente del patriarcato. Ma stiamo anche dalla parte dei vegani perché gli animali sono (a volte letteralmente) i perdenti del dominio dell’uomo. Ma attribuiamo lo stesso valore a tutte le forme di vita? E cos’è una forma di vita? Valutiamo tutte le forme di vita allo stesso modo o secondo il loro grado di coscienza? O secondo il rapporto che hanno con noi? Il nostro giudizio cambia secondo che i perdenti siano nostri famigliari o altri.




Non sto dicendo che non c’è un filo conduttore che unisce queste dinamiche diverse, o una guida etica di fondo, una pratica attenta e sfumata; anzi, credo nella sua esistenza (anche se quando dico che esiste un ampio spettro di coscienza tra zigoti o nematodi e chiunque abbia una coscienza anche lontanamente umana molti a sinistra pensano che non sono egalitario). Voglio dire che il nostro atteggiamento nei confronti dei vinti è spesso una risposta istintiva a ciò che ci appare più che il risultato di un’analisi etica. La sinistra è raramente una filosofia, più spesso è una coalizione tenuta assieme da una dottrina. Possiamo immaginare un mondo diverso in cui, in seguito a un percorso storico diverso, 

l’illegalità

 dell’aborto è una delle basi della sinistra, in linea con la lotta contro l’omofobia, il patriarcato, l’abilismo e così via. Oppure un mondo in cui una sinistra contraria all’azione giuridica sostiene e alimenta l’azione culturale e sociale contro l’aborto. (Per la cronaca, io sono a favore).




È molto pericoloso vedere il mondo in termini di vincenti e perdenti. Va bene come regola generica, ma è un approccio euristico che personalmente odio, lo considero l’opposto di un’analisi radicale. Da qui si arriva al sionismo, al leninismo, al nazionalismo postcoloniale, e ai vari 

TERF

 e SWERF e così via, con tutti i loro fallimenti. Ci sono ragioni fondate per dire che la sinistra 

non

 vede la realtà altrimenti che in termini vittimistici, nel qual caso il fascismo è quasi sempre 

di sinistra

. Con un accordo di mutuo riconoscimento non ci si accosta alla politica come un reazionario di destra che, negli Stati Generali di Francia, nel tentativo di mantenere il potere costituito, si considera una vittima. Non lo è affatto (quasi in tutti gli aspetti tranne qualche contesto estremo come il divorzio), ma sicuramente lo è 

potenzialmente

, e questo basta a riprodurre il vittimismo strutturale.




Ma, si potrebbe obiettare, il problema del vittimismo dell’alterdestra non è solo che sbagliano vittime ma è anche la sete di potere, e questo è generalmente vero (anche se ad accomunarli più che il potere forse sono le lacrime di coccodrillo). Ma lo stesso si può certamente dire anche della sinistra. Sono tanti quelli che a sinistra hanno abbracciato il vittimismo come trampolino di lancio verso il potere. Ho conosciuto autrici femministe che mi hanno confessato che se fossero state uomini sarebbero state patriarcali, o che avrebbero avuto schiavi se fossero state bianche e ricche prima della guerra civile.




Ci sono persone intelligenti che rifiutano l’oppressione evidente e allo stesso tempo convergono genericamente su certe posizioni o analisi. Varia, e di molto, il modo di conciliare o tenere assieme queste posizioni. Il fatto che la sinistra nell’attuale contesto sia una coalizione stabile non significa che per certi aspetti, che attualmente appaiono in perfetta armonia, non si frantumi al cambiare di certe condizioni.




Mi è capitato più volte di incontrare persone di sinistra che dicevano che esprimere una preferenza è indice di 

potere gerarchico

 e dunque di destra (essere di sinistra per loro è una sorta di stoicismo o di buddismo). Similmente, il pluralismo epistemico è molto comune tra gli accademici di una sinistra boriosa secondo la quale dire che certe interpretazioni della realtà sono più realistiche di altre non è “egalitario”, o è addirittura “totalitario”. Viene da riderci sopra, ma queste orribili definizioni di “egalitarismo” a volte provengono da persone intelligenti con la testa a posto ma in contesti che non gli appartengono.




Personalmente osio il principio di non aggressione, ma oggi tutti lo condannano perché “è antipragmatico”, una condanna che si estende sempre più a tutta la filosofia etica. Questa tendenza è alimentata dalle piaghe gemelle dell’estrema sinistra su internet: stalinisti e nichilisti. Ha un senso, come nel caso della giustizia sociale, per chi vuole che la sinistra crei un quadro sociale comportamentale vagamente ideologico che tenga unita una coalizione di classi perdenti. “Non è la stessa cosa!” si sente dire ogni volta che si cerca di individuare punti comuni o discordanze tra rivendicazioni, posizioni o piattaforme diverse. In questo senso non c’è una radice comune, non c’è uno spirito che unisca la sinistra, ma dobbiamo cercarlo se non vogliamo distruggere l’idea. La filosofia, l’etica, i valori fondanti, ma anche l’individualismo metodologico e l’universalismo, diventano il nemico. Non ci sono esperienze individuali né universali, solo classi relativamente semplificate con esperienze uniche. Siamo noi che le leghiamo assieme in una causa unica tramite etichette, posizioni sociali, richiami poetico affettivi e minacce di violenza.




La sinistra non è unita da niente. Il marxismo è per metà screditato dalla sua idiozia e mostruosità mentre quello che sopravvive è un ginepraio di contraddizioni più preoccupato di nascondere i propri fallimenti con l’oscurantismo, l’irrazionalità e l’antirealismo che intento a fare qualcosa, men che meno tracciare una linea. La maggior parte delle preoccupazioni della sinistra riguarda l’opposizione a sovrastrutture mitizzate, e noi ci agitiamo quando non ci sono o ogni volta che la loro composizione e il loro comportamento cambiano. Insomma, la sinistra è assolutamente allergica al radicalismo. Preferisce respingere le proprie inadeguatezze con brevi sbuffi estremistici.




Mentre le complessità ideologiche e sociali si moltiplicano nell’eco infinita dell’era informatica, le nostre tensioni interne e le ripetizioni diventano ancora più evidenti.




L’anarchismo radicale può ancora sperare di dare una base concreta e esplicita al discorso sulla libertà e l’etica. Ma per farlo dovrà allontanarsi da alleati con cui condivide qualche intuizione limitata o qualche idea momentanea. O perlomeno dovrà dissolvere la comoda illusione di un’alleanza profonda.




Se la menzogna della “sinistra” sopravvive da duecento anni è perché la sua visione manichea di due tribù più o meno uniformi, una illuminata e una incomprensibilmente corrotta, fornisce un senso comunitario che è di conforto psicologico a tanti. Per molti a sinistra, ma anche per la destra nazionalista eccetera, la fame di “comunità” è la ragione 

di fondo

. Parlando con amici, è meglio non spiegare a fondo perché anche tu sei contro i capitalisti: potresti inimicarteli.




Ma la forma di comunicazione su internet sortisce l’effetto contrario. Il contatto forzoso con Il Nemico ci spinge a imporre barriere difensive al discorso che finiscono inevitabilmente per lasciar fuori anche i nostri alleati tradizionali, spingendo sinistra e destra verso la frattura nel disperato tentativo di ritrovare purezza, fiducia o qualche altra cosa che leghi profondamente. Quei fortuiti punti comuni che ancora esistevano quando avevamo poche possibilità di sceglierci gli amici ora si stanno frantumando. Fondamentalmente è un bene, in questi ultimi vent’anni abbiamo visto orrori di ogni genere tra le nostre fila più esposte. Ma il processo che porta alla luce la divisione tra noi e gli ecologisti antiscientifici di sinistra che vorrebbero far fuori l’umanità è anche un processo di rottura della “sinistra” in frantumi irrecuperabili.




La nave sta affondando. Se gran parte dei topi scappa perché noi non dobbiamo fare altrettanto?




Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina 

Sostieni C4SS

: 

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

author: Hudson Hongo
title: 🎩 Tech Monopolies Make Outages Worse | EFFector 38.21
content:
Service outages, like the ones we've seen take down everything from airlines to email, seem to be coming faster than ever. Their specific causes might be different, but these wide-scale service disruptions share one thing in common: the over-reliance on one company or system to make our world work. In our latest EFFector newsletter, we're talking about how digital monoculture has made tech companies too big to fail.

For over 35 years, EFFector has been your guide to understanding the intersection of technology, civil liberties, and the law. This issue covers ALPR at the ballot box, surveillance wearables, and how digital monoculture makes service outages worse.

Prefer to listen in? EFFector is now available on all major podcast platforms. This time we're talking to EFF's Rory Mir about tech monopolies, service outages, and what we can do to build a more resilient internet. You can find the episode and subscribe on your podcast platform of choice:

author: C4SS
title: မုအမ္မာ ဂဒါဖီရဲ့ စာအုပ်စိမ်း – အကျိုး၊ အပြစ်နဲ့ ဇော်ကန့်လန့်ခြင်းများ
content:
By 

Jordan Jardine

. Original article: 

Muammar Gaddafi’s Green Book: The Good, The Bad, and The Weird

, published on March 9, 2022. Translated into Burmese by Hein Htet Kyaw.




မုအမ္မာ ဂဒါဖီဟာ အရင်ကရော၊ ခုရော၊ နောက်လည်း အမြဲတမ်း ငြင်းခုံဝေဖန်စရာ ပုဂ္ဂိုလ်တစ်ယောက် ဖြစ်နေမှာပါ။ ဘဒူအင် (Bedouin) မျိုးနွယ်စု လှည့်လည်သွားလာသူ ဘဝကနေ လစ်ဗျားရဲ့ ခေါင်းဆောင် ဖြစ်လာတာက အားကျစရာကောင်းပေမဲ့၊ တိုင်းပြည်ကို အုပ်ချုပ်နေစဉ်အတွင်း အာဏာရှင်ဆန်ဆန်နဲ့ ပြစ်မှုဆိုင်ရာ ကိစ္စတော်တော်များများကို ကျူးလွန်ခဲ့တာကတော့ ငြင်းလို့မရတဲ့ အချက်ပါ။




ဒါပေမဲ့ ဂဒါဖီဟာ စစချင်းမှာတော့ လွတ်မြောက်ရေးသမားတစ်ယောက်လို စခဲ့တာပါ။ ၁၉၆၀ ပြည့်လွန်နှစ်များ အစောပိုင်းမှာ လစ်ဗျားစစ်တပ်ထဲ ဝင်ခဲ့ပြီး ၁၉၆၉ ခုနှစ် ဘုရင် အိဒ်ရစ် (King Idris) ကို ဖြုတ်ချခဲ့တဲ့ အာဏာသိမ်းပွဲမှာ အဓိက ခေါင်းဆောင်တစ်ယောက် ဖြစ်လာခဲ့ပါတယ်။ ဘုရင်စနစ်ကို အောင်အောင်မြင်မြင် ဖျက်သိမ်းပြီးတဲ့နောက် ဂဒါဖီဟာ အာဏာသိမ်းပြီး လစ်ဗျားကို “လစ်ဗျား အရက်ဘ် သမ္မတနိုင်ငံ” အဖြစ် ပြောင်းလဲခဲ့ပါတယ်။ နောက်ပိုင်းမှာတော့ သူရဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေး၊ လူမှုရေးနဲ့ စီးပွားရေး အမြင်တွေကို ၁၉၇၅ မှာ ပထမဆုံး ထုတ်ဝေခဲ့တဲ့ “စာအုပ်စိမ်း” (The Green Book) ဆိုတဲ့ စာအုပ်တိုလေးထဲမှာ ရေးသားခဲ့ပြီး၊ တစ်နှစ်အကြာမှာတော့ အင်္ဂလိပ်ဘာသာပြန်နဲ့ တစ်ကမ္ဘာလုံးကို ဖြန့်ချိခဲ့ပါတယ်။




အနှစ်ချုပ်




အပိုင်း (၁) – ဒီမိုကရေစီ ပြဿနာရဲ့ အဖြေ




စာအုပ်စိမ်းရဲ့ ဒီအစပိုင်းမှာ ဂဒါဖီက တို့တွေ သိထားကြတဲ့ “ဒီမိုကရေစီ” ဆိုတာတွေဟာ တကယ်တော့ အလွန်အာဏာရှင်ဆန်ပြီး ဒီမိုကရေစီနဲ့ ဆန့်ကျင်ဘက်ဖြစ်တယ်လို့ စုဒ်တက်ထားပါတယ်။ လွှတ်တော်စနစ်တွေဟာ စေတနာကောင်းနဲ့ စခဲ့တာမှန်ပေမဲ့ နောက်ဆုံးမှာ ပြည်သူတွေရဲ့ အကျိုးစီးပွားကို မဖော်ဆောင်နိုင်တော့ဘူးလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ ပါတီနိုင်ငံရေးဟာ မဲပေးခဲ့တဲ့ ပြည်သူတွေထက် ပါတီရဲ့ အကျိုးစီးပွားကိုပဲ ကြည့်သွားကြမှာပဲလို့ သူက အခိုင်အမာ ပြောပါတယ်။ ဒါကြောင့် ကိုယ်စားလှယ်ပြု ဒီမိုကရေစီ ဒါမှမဟုတ် လွှတ်တော် ဒီမိုကရေစီအစား “တိုက်ရိုက် ဒီမိုကရေစီ” (Direct Democracy) ကသာ ဒီပြဿနာကို ဖြေရှင်းဖို့ အကောင်းဆုံး နည်းလမ်းပဲလို့ ဂဒါဖီက ဆိုပါတယ်။




ဒါ့အပြင် လူတန်းစား ပဋိပက္ခဟာ အမြဲတမ်း အင်အားကြီးတဲ့ လူတန်းစားက အောက်ခြေလူတန်းစားကို နိုင်ငံရေးနည်းနဲ့ စီးပိုးအုပ်ချုပ်ရာ ရောက်သွားစေတာမို့၊ အထက်တန်းစားတွေက အောက်ခြေလူတန်းစားကို ပုံစံခွက်တစ်ခုထဲနဲ့ ချော့မြှော့ဖို့ ကြိုးစားနေတာဟာ အလကားပဲလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ ဘာလို့လဲဆိုတော့ ချော့မြှော့ရုံနဲ့ အောက်ခြေလူတန်းစားတွေ အမြဲ မကြေနပ်နိုင်သလို၊ အုပ်စိုးသူ လူတန်းစားနဲ့ စိတ်ဝင်စားမှုချင်းလည်း ကွဲပြားနေလို့ပါ။ ဂဒါဖီက သူ စိတ်ကူးထားတဲ့ တိုက်ရိုက် ဒီမိုကရေစီ ပုံစံကို ဆက်လက် ဖော်ပြထားပါတယ်။ တိုက်ရိုက် ဒီမိုကရေစီကို “ပြည်သူ့ညီလာခံများ” (Popular Conferences) နဲ့ “ပြည်သူ့ကော်မတီများ” (People’s Committees) ဆိုတာတွေနဲ့ ဖော်ဆောင်ရမယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ အခြေခံအားဖြင့် ပြည်သူ့ညီလာခံဆိုတာ ပြည်သူတွေ တိုက်ရိုက်ရွေးချယ်ထားတဲ့ အာဏာခွဲဝေမှုအဖွဲ့အစည်းတွေဖြစ်ပြီး “အခြေခံ ပြည်သူ့ညီလာခံ” နဲ့ “အခြေခံမဟုတ်သော ပြည်သူ့ညီလာခံ” ဆိုပြီး နှစ်မျိုး ခွဲထားပါတယ်။ ဒီညီလာခံတွေကမှတစ်ဆင့် ပြည်သူ့ကော်မတီဝင်တွေကို ပြန်ရွေးချယ်တာပါ။ ဒီမိုကရေစီရဲ့ “အမှန်တကယ် အဓိပ္ပာယ်” ဆိုတာ “ပြည်သူက ပြည်သူကို ကြီးကြပ်ကွပ်ကဲခြင်း” လို့ သူက ဆိုပါတယ်။




နောက်တစ်ခုကတော့ ဥပဒေတွေနဲ့ ပတ်သက်ပြီး ဘာကို အခြေခံရမလဲဆိုတာကို ဂဒါဖီက ဆွေးနွေးထားပါတယ်။ ဥပဒေဆိုတာ ဘာသာရေး ဒါမှမဟုတ် ရိုးရာဓလေ့ မူ Post တွေကို အခြေခံရမယ်လို့ ဆိုပြီး၊ ဘာသာရေးနဲ့ မသက်ဆိုင်တဲ့ ဖွဲ့စည်းပုံအခြေခံဥပဒေတွေဟာ “တရားမဝင်သလို ယုတ္တိလည်းမရှိဘူး” လို့ ဝေဖန်ထားပါတယ်။ နောက်ပိုင်းမှာတော့ တိုက်ရိုက်ဒီမိုကရေစီဟာ စာနယ်ဇင်းလွတ်လပ်ခွင့်ကို ပိုတိုးတက်စေမယ်လို့ ဖော်ပြထားပြီး၊ ပုဂ္ဂိုလ်ရေးရော ကုမ္ပဏီအဖွဲ့အစည်းတွေပါ စာနယ်ဇင်းလွတ်လပ်ခွင့် ရှိသင့်တယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။




အပိုင်း (၂) – စီးပွားရေး ပြဿနာရဲ့ အဖြေ




ခေတ်သစ် အလုပ်သမားတွေရဲ့ အခြေအနေဟာ စက်မှုတော်လှန်ရေး စတင်ခဲ့ချိန်ကထက်စာရင် သာလွန်ကောင်းမွန်လာတာကို ဂဒါဖီက လက်ခံထားပါတယ်။ ဒါပေမဲ့ အချိန်ပိုကြေးပေးတာ၊ လူမှုဖူလုံရေး၊ သပိတ်မှောက်ခွင့်နဲ့ အလုပ်ချိန် ကန့်သတ်တာမျိုးတွေဟာ ပုံမှန် အလုပ်သမားတစ်ယောက်ရဲ့ ဘဝကို သက်သာရာရစေဖို့ မလုံလောက်သေးဘဲ၊ နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေဟာ အလုပ်သမားတွေကို နှိမ့်စက်သူတွေလက်ကနေ အမှန်တကယ် လွတ်မြောက်အောင် မလုပ်ပေးနိုင်ခဲ့ကြဘူးလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ ပြည်သူ့ဝန်ထမ်းတွေဟာလည်း ပုဂ္ဂလိက ဝန်ထမ်းတွေထက် သိပ်ပိုမကောင်းလှပါဘူး။ သူက “လုပ်ခလစာယူတဲ့သူတွေဟာ သူတို့ကို ငှားထားတဲ့ သခင်တွေရဲ့ ကျေးကျွန်တွေပဲ။ အချိန်ပိုင်း ကျေးကျွန်တွေဖြစ်ပြီး၊ သူတို့ရဲ့ ကျေးကျွန်ဘဝဟာ ပုဂ္ဂလိကဖြစ်စေ၊ ရေဒီယို/အစိုးရဖြစ်စေ အလုပ်ရှင်ဆီက လစာယူနေသမျှ ကာလပတ်လုံး တည်ရှိနေမှာပဲ” လို့ ထိထိမိမိ ရေးထားပါတယ်။




သူက လုပ်ခလစာစနစ်ကို ဖျက်သိမ်းဖို့နဲ့ ထုတ်လုပ်မှု နည်းလမ်းတွေကို ပူးပေါင်းပိုင်ဆိုင်ဖို့ စိစစ်တင်ပြထားပါတယ်။ နည်းပညာ တိုးတက်လာတာနဲ့အမျှ ကုန်စည်နဲ့ ဝန်ဆောင်မှု ပေးဖို့ လိုအပ်တဲ့ အလုပ်သမားအရေအတွက်နဲ့ အလုပ်ချိန်တွေ လျော့နည်းသွားမယ်လို့လည်း ဆိုပါတယ်။ “လူတစ်ယောက်ရဲ့ လွတ်လပ်ခွင့်ဟာ သူရဲ့ လိုအပ်ချက်တွေကို အခြားသူတွေက ထိန်းချုပ်ထားရင် ဆုံးရှုံးနေတာပဲ။ ဘာလို့လဲဆိုတော့ လိုအပ်ချက်ကနေတစ်ဆင့် တစ်ယောက်က တစ်ယောက်ကို ကျေးကျွန်ပြုတာတွေ ဖြစ်လာနိုင်လို့ပါ။ ဒါ့အပြင် ခေါင်းပုံဖြတ်တာဟာ လိုအပ်ချက်ကြောင့် ဖြစ်တာပါ” လို့ ဆက်ပြောထားပါတယ်။




ဂဒါဖီ ပေးထားတဲ့ မရှိမဖြစ် “လိုအပ်ချက်” ရဲ့ ဥပမာတစ်ခုကတော့ အိမ်ရာ ဖြစ်ပါတယ်။ လူတိုင်း အိမ်ရာရရှိရေးကို သူ အားပေးပြီး၊ အိမ်ငှားခကိုတော့ စေတနာအလျောက် လျှော်ကြေးပေးတဲ့ ပုံစံမျိုးကိုပဲ ထောက်ခံပါတယ်။ ဒါ့အပြင် လူတစ်ယောက်ဟာ အိမ်တစ်လုံးထက် ပိုမပိုင်ဆိုင်သင့်ဘူးလို့လည်း ဆိုပါတယ်။ ဝင်ငွေနဲ့ ပတ်သက်လို့ အလုပ်သမားတစ်ယောက်ဟာ သူလုပ်ထားတဲ့ လုပ်အားရဲ့ ရလဒ် အပြည့်အဝကို ရရှိသင့်ပြီး၊ လုပ်ခလစာ ဒါမှမဟုတ် လှူဒါန်းငွေ ပုံစံမျိုးနဲ့ မဟုတ်သင့်ဘူးလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ နောက်ပြီး ပုဂ္ဂလိက ပို့ဆောင်ရေးထက် အများပြည်သူ ပို့ဆောင်ရေးကို အားပေးတဲ့အကြောင်း ခဏလှည့်ပြောသွားပါတယ်။ နောက်ဆုံးမှာတော့ မြေယာဟာ မရှိမဖြစ် အရင်းအမြစ်ဖြစ်တာမို့ ပုဂ္ဂလိက မပိုင်ဆိုင်သင့်ဘဲ၊ အသိုင်းအဝိုင်းတစ်ခုလုံး ပိုင်ဆိုင်ပြီး အသုံးပြုမှုအပေါ် မူတည်၍ ခွဲဝေပေးသင့်တယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ် (ဥပမာ- တောင်သူတစ်ယောက်ဟာ စက်ရုံအလုပ်သမားထက် မြေပိုလိုမှာ သေချာပါတယ်)။




ဂဒါဖီက အမြတ်ထုတ်လိုစိတ်ကို ဆန့်ကျင်ကြောင်း၊ အလုပ်သမားသမဂ္ဂများနဲ့ သပိတ်မှောက်မှုကို ထောက်ခံကြောင်း၊ လုပ်ခလစာ အလုပ်သမားစနစ် ဖျက်သိမ်းရေးကို ထပ်လောင်း အတည်ပြုကြောင်း ဆက်ပြောထားပါတယ်။ အပိုင်း (၂) ရဲ့ နောက်ဆုံးမှာတော့ အိမ်ဖော်တွေကို ငှားရမ်းပြီး အမြတ်ထုတ်နေကြတာကို ပြင်းပြင်းထန်ထန် ဝေဖန်ထားပါတယ်။ အိမ်ဖော်တွေဟာလည်း အခြား လုပ်ခလစာယူသူတွေလိုပဲ “ကျေးကျွန်တွေ” ဖြစ်ပြီး အရမ်း မတရား ဆက်ဆံခံနေရတာပါတဲ့။ အိမ်တွင်းအလုပ် မှန်သမျှဟာ အဲဒီအိမ်ထောင်စုဝင်တွေရဲ့ တာဝန်ပဲ ဖြစ်သင့်ပြီး၊ အိမ်နဲ့ ဘာမှမဆိုင်တဲ့၊ လစာနည်းနည်းပဲရပြီး မတရားဆက်ဆံခံရတဲ့ အလုပ်သမားတွေကို ငှားရမ်းတာဟာ လက်ခံနိုင်စရာ မရှိဘူးလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။




အပိုင်း (၃) – တတိယ ကမ္ဘာ့သီအိုရီရဲ့ လူမှုရေး အခြေခံ




စာအုပ်စိမ်းရဲ့ ဒီနောက်ဆုံးအပိုင်းမှာ ဂဒါဖီက အချို့သော လူမှုရေးကိစ္စတွေအပေါ် သူရဲ့ အမြင်တွေကို ချပြထားပြီး၊ သူရဲ့ အထွေထွေ ဒဿနဖြစ်တဲ့ “တတိယ ကမ္ဘာ့သီအိုရီ” (Third Universal Theory) ဟာ အမျိုးသားရေးနဲ့ မျိုးနွယ်စု မူတွေကို အခြေခံထားတာမို့ လူ့အဖွဲ့အစည်းကို တည်ဆောက်ဖို့ အကောင်းဆုံး နည်းလမ်းပဲလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ သမိုင်းဆိုတာ လူတန်းစား တိုက်ပွဲတွေရဲ့ အစဉ်အဆက်ပဲဆိုတဲ့ မာက်စ်ဝါဒီတွေရဲ့ အယူအဆကို သမိုင်းဆိုတာ အမျိုးသားရေး တိုက်ပွဲတွေရဲ့ စိစစ်လွှမ်းမိုးမှုပဲဆိုပြီး သူက တုံ့ပြန်ထားပါတယ်။ နိုင်ငံတွေအတွင်းမှာ ဘာသာရေးနဲ့ ယဉ်ကျေးမှုလို အချက်တွေအပေါ် အခြေခံတဲ့ ပြင်းထန်တဲ့ ဂိုဏ်းဂဏ ကွဲပြားမှုတွေ ရှိနေတာကို လက်ခံပေမဲ့၊ ရှင်သန်ရပ်တည်ရေး တိုက်ပွဲက ရှေ့ဆက်ဖို့ ခြိမ်းခြောက်ခံရရင် နိုင်ငံတွေကို စည်းလုံးသွားစေမယ်လို့ သူ ယုံကြည်ပါတယ်။ အဲဒီနောက် မိသားစုဟာ လူ့အဖွဲ့အစည်းရဲ့ အဓိက အခြေခံအုတ်မြစ်ဖြစ်ပြီး၊ မျိုးနွယ်စုဆိုတာ မိသားစုထက် တစ်ဆင့် ပိုကြီးတဲ့ ယူနစ်တစ်ခုပဲလို့ ဆက်ပြောထားပါတယ်။




ဒါ့အပြင် ကမ္ဘာ့လူဦးရေ တိုးတက်လာတာနဲ့အမျှ တို့တွေဟာ တစ်ယောက်နဲ့တစ်ယောက် ပိုဝေးကွာလာကြတယ်လို့ ဆွေးနွေးထားပါတယ်။ ပဋိပက္ခဖြစ်နေတဲ့ အဖွဲ့အစည်းတွေဟာ စနစ်တစ်ခုလုံးကို ဘယ်လို ပြိုကွဲစေနိုင်လဲဆိုတာကို ပြဖို့ မျိုးနွယ်စုပုံစံကို သူက စံနမူနာအဖြစ် အသုံးပြုထားပြီး၊ ဒါဟာ တစ်ကမ္ဘာလုံး အတိုင်းအတာနဲ့ ဖြစ်ပျက်နေတယ်လို့ ယုံကြည်ပါတယ်။ ဂဒါဖီရဲ့အမြင်အရ အမျိုးသားရေးဝါဒကို ပစ်ပယ်မထားသင့်ပါဘူး။ အဲဒီအစား လူတွေကို စည်းလုံးစေပြီး ပိုမို တည်ငြိမ်တဲ့ စနစ်ထဲမှာ ကာလကြာရှည် အတူတကွ ရှိနေစေဖို့ အထိရောက်ဆုံး နည်းလမ်းဖြစ်တာကြောင့် ထိန်းသိမ်းပြီး လက်ခံကျင့်သုံးသင့်တယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။




နောက်တစ်ခုကတော့ အမျိုးသမီးတွေနဲ့ ပတ်သက်တဲ့ သူရဲ့ အမြင်တွေကို ဆွေးနွေးထားပါတယ်။ အမျိုးသမီးတွေအပေါ် ခွဲခြားဆက်ဆံတာကို ပြင်းပြင်းထန်ထန် ဝေဖန်ယင်း၊ အမျိုးသားနဲ့ အမျိုးသမီးအကြား ကွဲပြားမှုတွေ ရှိတာကို လက်ခံပေမဲ့ နှစ်ဦးလုံးကို တန်းတူ ဆက်ဆံရမယ်လို့ အခိုင်အမာ ပြောပါတယ်။ အမျိုးသားတွေဟာ ကိုယ်ဝန်ဆောင်စရာ မလို၊ ရာသီလာစရာ မလို၊ ကိုယ်ဝန်ပျက်ကျစရာ မလိုတာမို့ အမျိုးသမီးတွေထက် ပိုသက်သာတယ်လို့တောင် ထောက်ပြထားပါတယ်။ ကလေးတစ်ယောက် လိမ္မာပါးနပ်စွာ ကြီးပြင်းလာဖို့ မိခင်နဲ့ သံယောဇဉ်တွယ်ဖို့ လိုအပ်တာကြောင့် မာတာမိခင် နားခွင့်ပေးဖို့ ထောက်ခံထားပြီး၊ အုပ်ထိန်းသူတွေအနေနဲ့ မိခင်ရဲ့ တာဝန်တွေကို ဆရာမတွေ၊ ကလေးထိန်းတွေဆီ ပေးမလုပ်သင့်ဘူးလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ အမျိုးသမီးတွေကို အလုပ်အကိုင်တွေ လုပ်ဖို့ ဒါမှမဟုတ် ကျောက်ဆစ်/ကြုံရာကျပန်း အလုပ်တွေ လုပ်ဖို့ မမျှော်လင့်သင့်ဘူးလို့ ဆက်ပြောပါတယ်။ အမျိုးသမီးတွေ လုပ်ချင်ရင် အလုပ်လုပ်နိုင်ပေမဲ့ အတင်းအကျပ်တော့ မလုပ်ခိုင်းသင့်ဘူးလို့ ယုံကြည်ပါတယ်။




အဲဒီနောက် မသန်စွမ်းသူတွေနဲ့ လူနည်းစု အခွင့်အရေး ကိစ္စတွေကို ခဏတည်း ဆွေးနွေးထားပါတယ်။ အနှစ်ချုပ်အားဖြင့် နိုင်ငံတော်ဟာ လူနည်းစုတွေအပေါ် ကျူးလွန်ခဲ့တဲ့ မတရားမှုတွေကို အမှန်တကယ် ပြင်ဆင်ပေးဖို့ မသင့်တော်ဘူးလို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ လူနည်းစု အခွင့်အရေး ပေးထားပါတယ်ဆိုတဲ့ နိုင်ငံတော်တွေဟာ အဲဒီအခွင့်အရေးတွေကို လွယ်လွယ်လေး ပြန်ရုတ်သိမ်းသွားနိုင်ပါတယ်။ ဂဒါဖီအတွက်တော့ လူနည်းစု အခွင့်အရေး ပြဿနာရဲ့ တစ်ခုတည်းသော အဖြေဟာ နိုင်ငံတော်မဟုတ်တဲ့ နည်းလမ်းများ (“ပြည်သူများ”) ကနေတစ်ဆင့် လူနည်းစုတွေကို မြှင့်တင်ပေးဖို့ဖြစ်ပြီး၊ ဒါမှ နိုင်ငံတော်က သုံးလေ့ရှိတဲ့ “အာဏာရှင်ဆန်တဲ့” နည်းလမ်းကို ရှောင်ရှားနိုင်မှာ ဖြစ်ပါတယ်။




ဒါကို ဆက်လက် ရေးသားရင်း၊ ကမ္ဘာတစ်ဝှမ်းက လူမည်းတွေဟာ အလုပ်လက်မဲ့ဖြစ်မှု၊ ဆင်းရဲမွဲတေမှု၊ ကျန်းမာရေးနဲ့ သားဆက်ခြားနည်း ရရှိရခက်မှုစတဲ့ အတားအဆီးတွေ ရှိနေပေမဲ့ လူဖြူတွေကို အနိုင်ရလိမ့်မယ်လို့ ခန့်မှန်းထားပါတယ်။




အဲဒီနောက် ဂဒါဖီဟာ လွတ်လပ်ခွင့်၊ ဉာဏ်ရည်နဲ့ ဖန်တီးနိုင်စွမ်းတွေကို ဖိနှိပ်ထားပြီး “လူထုကို အတင်းအကျပ် တုံးအစေတဲ့” ဗဟိုချုပ်ကိုင်မှုရှိတဲ့ နိုင်ငံတော်ကျောင်းပညာရေးကို ပြင်းပြင်းထန်ထန် ဝေဖန်ထားပါတယ်။ ကျောင်းသားတွေဟာ နိုင်ငံတော်ရဲ့ ဖိအားကြောင့် ဘဝမှာ ဘာမှ အသုံးမကျတဲ့ ပျင်းစရာကောင်းတဲ့ ဘာသာရပ်တွေကို သင်ယူနေရမယ့်အစား မိမိတို့ စိတ်ဝင်စားတဲ့ ဘာသာရပ်တွေကို လွတ်လပ်စွာ ရွေးချယ် သင်ယူသင့်တယ်လို့ ယုံကြည်ပါတယ်။ ကျောင်းတွေမှာ ဘာသာရေးရော ဘာသာရေးမဟုတ်တဲ့ ဘာသာရပ်တွေကိုပါ သင်ကြားပေးဖို့ အားပေးပြီး တစ်ခုခုကို လုံးဝ ချန်လှပ်ထားတာဟာ အမှားတစ်ခု ဖြစ်လိမ့်မယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။




အဲဒီနောက် အနုပညာ၊ ဂီတနဲ့ ဘာသာစကားအကြောင်း ပြောင်းလဲ ဆွေးနွေးထားပါတယ်။ လူ့သမိုင်းတစ်လျှောက်မှာ တစ်ခုတည်းသော ဘာသာစကား မရှိတာဟာ ပြဿနာကြီးတစ်ခု ဖြစ်ခဲ့ပေမဲ့၊ အနုပညာကိုတော့ ဘာ ဘာသာစကားပဲပြောပြော လူတိုင်းက နားလည်ခံစားနိုင်ပါတယ်။ ကမ္ဘာသုံး ဘာသာစကားတစ်ခု မရှိတာဟာ အလိုလို ပြဿနာမဟုတ်ပေမဲ့၊ ကမ္ဘာသုံး ဘာသာစကားတစ်ခု ဖန်တီးခဲ့ရင်တောင်မှ အဲဒါဟာ မျိုးဆက်များစွာအတွက် အလိုအလျောက် သဘာဝကျကျ သုံးစရာ ဖြစ်လာဖို့ မလွယ်ကူဘူးဆိုတဲ့ အချက်ကို ရှင်းပြထားပါတယ်။




ဂဒါဖီဟာ အပိုင်း (၃) ကို အားကစားကို ဥပမာပေးပြီး နိဂုံးချုပ်ထားပါတယ်။ ချမ်းသာသူတွေက အောက်ခြေလူထုဆီကနေ ပစ္စည်းဥစ္စာတွေကို စုဆောင်းထားတာကို (ဥပမာ- ပွဲကြည့်စင်မှာ အခြားပွဲကြည့်ပရိသတ်တွေနဲ့ ယှဉ်ရင် သူတို့ ထိုင်တဲ့နေရာမျိုး) အားကစားနဲ့ နှိုင်းယှဉ်ပြထားပြီး၊ အားကစားဟာ နိုင်ငံရေးအာဏာလိုပဲ အခွင့်ရေးရ လူနည်းစုအတွက် မဟုတ်ဘဲ လူတိုင်း လက်လှမ်းမီသင့်တယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ ဂဒါဖီလို ဘဒူအင် မျိုးနွယ်စုတွေဟာ အနုပညာပြသတာထက် အားကစားကို ပိုစိတ်ဝင်စားကြကြောင်း၊ ဘာလို့လဲဆိုတော့ ဖျော်ဖြေတာကို သိပ်တန်ဖိုးမထားကြလို့ ဖြစ်ကြောင်း ပြောရင်း စာအုပ်ကို နိဂုံးချုပ်ထားပါတယ်။ ဂဒါဖီက ဒီအလားအလာ ပြောင်းလဲသွားဖို့ မျှော်လင့်ထားပါတယ်။




အကောင်းများ




ဒီစာအုပ်ကို တော်တော်များများမှာ ရိုးရှင်းပြီး တိုက်ရိုက်ကျတဲ့ ဘာသာစကားနဲ့ ရေးထားတာမို့၊ ရှုပ်ထွေးတဲ့ ပညာရပ်ဆိုင်ရာ စာအုပ်တွေထက်စာရင် ဖတ်ရတာ ပိုလွယ်ကူပါတယ်။ ဒါဟာ စာအုပ်ရဲ့ အားသာချက်တစ်ခုပါပဲ။ နောက်ထပ် အားသာချက်တစ်ခုကတော့ စာအုပ်ရဲ့ တိုတိုတုတ်တုတ် ရှိမှုပါပဲ။ စာအုပ်စိမ်းဟာ စာမျက်နှာ ၁၀၀ ကျော်ကျော်လေးပဲ ရှိပြီး၊ အချို့သော “အခန်း” တွေဆိုရင် စာမျက်နှာတစ်ခုထဲမှာ စာပိုဒ်တစ်ခု သို့မဟုတ် နှစ်ခုလောက်ပဲ ပါပါတယ်။ လူတော်တော်များများ (အထူးသဖြင့် နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေ) ဟာ အများကြီး ပြောပေမဲ့ ဘာမှ အဓိပ္ပာယ်မရှိတာမျိုး ဖြစ်တတ်ပါတယ်။ ဂဒါဖီက ဒီစာအုပ်ထဲမှာ အဲလိုမျိုး အချို့ လုပ်ထားပေမဲ့၊ လိုရင်းနဲ့ အနှစ်ချုပ် အချက်တွေကိုတော့ တိုတိုနဲ့ လိုရင်းရောက်အောင် ရေးထားပါတယ်။




အနှစ်သာရအကြောင်း ပြောရရင် ဂဒါဖီရဲ့ အချက်အတော်များများကို ကျွန်တော် သဘောတူပါတယ်။ အထက်မှာ ပြထားသလိုပဲ၊ သူဟာ နိုင်ငံတော်ဆန့်ကျင်ရေး၊ လွတ်လပ်ရေးဝါဒဘက်က အကြောင်းပြချက်အများကြီး ပေးထားပြီး အစိုးရနဲ့ လုပ်ငန်းခွင် အဆောက်အအုံတွေကို ဗဟိုချုပ်ကိုင်မှု လျှော့ချဖို့ တောင်းဆိုထားပါတယ်။ ဒါတွေဟာ ထောက်ခံချင်စရာ ကောင်းတဲ့ မူဝါဒတွေပါ၊ ဘာလို့လဲဆိုတော့ အစိုးရရော ကော်ပိုရေးရှင်းတွေရဲ့ ဖိအားပေးမှုမှ ကင်းဝေးပြီး လူတွေအနေနဲ့ အလွတ်လပ်ဆုံးနဲ့ အပျော်ရွှင်ဆုံး ဘဝကို ပိုင်ဆိုင်နိုင်စေလို့ပါ။




ဒါ့အပြင် ဂဒါဖီရဲ့ မိခင်တွေကို ကာကွယ်ပေးမှုနဲ့ မိခင်တွေအနေနဲ့ ဝမ်းစာရှာဖို့အတွက် အဓိပ္ပာယ်မရှိတဲ့ လုပ်အားတွေကို လျှော့ပြီး ကလေးတွေနဲ့ အချိန်ပိုပေးသင့်တယ်ဆိုတဲ့ အမြင်ဟာလည်း ချီးကျူးစရာပါ။ အလုပ်မှာပဲ အချိန်ကုန်နေလို့ ကလေးတွေနဲ့ အချိန်မပေးနိုင်ရင် ကလေးတွေကို ကျွေးမွေးစောင့်ရှောက်နေရတာ ဘာမှ အဓိပ္ပာယ်မရှိတော့ပါဘူး။ အဲဒါနဲ့ ဆက်စပ်ပြီး၊ ချမ်းသာတဲ့သူတွေက ဆင်းရဲတဲ့ အိမ်ဖော်တွေကို ငှားပြီး သူတို့ရဲ့ ညစ်ပတ်တဲ့ အလုပ်တွေကို ခိုင်းစေနေတာကို ဂဒါဖီက ဝေဖန်ဆဲဆိုထားတာကိုလည်း ကျွန်တော် တော်တော် သဘောကျပါတယ်။ အဲဒီ အိမ်ဖော်အများစုမှာလည်း အိမ်မှာ သူတို့ကို အလိုရှိနေတဲ့ ကလေးတွေ ရှိနေနိုင်တာပဲလေ။




ဒါ့အပြင် ဂဒါဖီရဲ့ အစဉ်တစိုက် အိမ်ရာရရှိရေး အဆိုပြုချက်ဟာ တကယ့်ကို ပြောင်မြောက်ပါတယ်။ လူတိုင်းဟာ အမိုးအကာ နဲ့ ထိုက်တန်ပြီး၊ ဂဒါဖီဟာ ဒါကို နားလည်ခဲ့ပါတယ်။ တကယ်လည်း လစ်ဗျားမှာ ဒီမူဝါဒကို ကျင့်သုံးခဲ့ပြီး အတော်လေး အောင်မြင်ခဲ့ပါတယ်။ မြေယာအားလုံးကို အသိုင်းအဝိုင်းက ပိုင်ဆိုင်ပြီး လိုအပ်ချက်အတိုင်း ခွဲဝေပေးသင့်တယ်ဆိုတဲ့ သူရဲ့ အယူအဆကိုလည်း ကျွန်တော် သဘောတူပါတယ်။




အမြတ်နဲ့ လုပ်ခလစာ ဖျက်သိမ်းရေးကို သူ ရိုးရှင်းစွာ တိုက်ရိုက် ထောက်ခံထားတာဟာ ဒီမူဝါဒတွေကို ပြည်သူတွေကို ရှင်းပြဖို့ မှန်ကန်တဲ့ နည်းဗျူဟာပါ။ ဒါဟာ ဆိုရှယ်လစ် သို့မဟုတ် အာဏာမဲ့ဝါဒ သီအိုရီတွေနဲ့ မရင်းနှီးတဲ့သူတွေနဲ့ စကားပြောရာမှာ ပိုမရှုပ်ထွေးစေပါ။ အချို့သော အယူအဆတွေကို လွန်လွန်ကဲကဲ ရှုပ်ထွေးအောင် လုပ်တာဟာ ဆိုရှယ်လစ်နဲ့ အာဏာမဲ့ဝါဒ ဆွေးနွေးပွဲတွေမှာ ပြဿနာဖြစ်နိုင်ပေမဲ့၊ စာအုပ်စိမ်းကတော့ အယူအဆအချို့ကို ရှင်းပြတဲ့အခါ စဉ်းစားစရာ အကြောင်းအရာတစ်ခုကို ပေးထားပါတယ်။




နောက်ဆုံးအနေနဲ့ ဂဒါဖီရဲ့ လူမည်းတွေနဲ့ အမျိုးသမီးဝါဒ (Feminism) အပေါ် ထောက်ခံမှုဟာ ဒီနေ့ခေတ်မှာ တို့အတွက် သိပ်မဆန်းပေမဲ့၊ ၁၉၇၀ ခေတ်လယ်ပိုင်း ကမ္ဘာ့အချို့နေရာတွေမှာတော့ ဒါတွေဟာ သစ်လွင်ပြီး “ဆန်းသစ်” တဲ့ အယူအဆတွေ ဖြစ်ခဲ့ပါတယ်။ ဒါပေမဲ့ ဂဒါဖီကတော့ ဘေးဖယ်ထားခံရတဲ့ အသိုင်းအဝိုင်းတွေကို လူသားတွေလို ဆက်ဆံဖို့ တောင်းဆိုတာကြောင့် ဘယ်သူ့ကိုမှ အားနာမနေခဲ့ပါဘူး။ အဲဒါကတော့ သူ အများကြီး လေးစားခံထိုက်တဲ့ အချက်ပါ။




အဆိုးများ




စာအုပ်စိမ်းထဲမှာ နိုင်ငံတော်ကို ဆန့်ကျင်တဲ့ အစိတ်အပိုင်းများစွာ ပါဝင်ပေမဲ့၊ ဂဒါဖီဟာ သူ သို့မဟုတ် “ပြည်သူတွေ” အနေနဲ့ နိုင်ငံတော်ရဲ့ လွှမ်းမိုးမှုကနေ ဘယ်လို ကင်းဝေးအောင် လုပ်ရမယ်ဆိုတာကို ရှင်းရှင်းလင်းလင်း ရေးမထားပါဘူး။ တော်လှန်ရေးနည်းနဲ့လား? အကြမ်းမဖက် ဆန့်ကျင်မှုနဲ့လား? အထွေထွေ သပိတ်နဲ့လား? အာဏာပိုင်စနစ်ကနေ အာဏာမဲ့ စနစ်ဆီ ပြောင်းလဲဖို့ ဘာ မူဝါဒ နည်းဗျူဟာမှ မပါတာမို့ ကျွန်တော် တကယ် မသိပါ။




ဒါ့အပြင် ဂဒါဖီဟာ စာအုပ်ထဲမှာ ဆိုရှယ်လစ်ဝါဒကို ခဏခဏ ထောက်ခံထားပေမဲ့၊ ပုဂ္ဂလိက ကော်ပိုရေးရှင်း မီဒီယာတွေကို ထောက်ခံနေပုံရပြီး၊ အခြား မီဒီယာတွေလိုပဲ စာနယ်ဇင်းလွတ်လပ်ခွင့် ရှိသင့်တယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ ဒါဟာ ဖြစ်သင့်တာမှန်ပြီး အစိုးရရဲ့ ပိတ်ပင်တားဆီးမှုဟာ ဘယ်ပြဿနာအတွက်မှ အဖြေမဟုတ်ပေမဲ့၊ ဂဒါဖီက ဘာလို့ ပုဂ္ဂလိက မီဒီယာတွေကို အဆန်းတကြယ် ရုတ်တရက် မီးမောင်းထိုးပြပြီး ကာကွယ်ပေးနေတာလဲဆိုတာ မရှင်းပါဘူး။




နောက်ဆုံးအနေနဲ့ ဂဒါဖီရဲ့ “တတိယ ကမ္ဘာ့သီအိုရီ” အပေါ် အခြေခံထားတဲ့ လူ့အဖွဲ့အစည်းနဲ့ အုပ်ချုပ်ရေး စနစ်ဟာ ကျွန်တော်တို့အတွက် အရမ်း ရှုပ်ထွေးနေပြီး စာအုပ်ရဲ့ အပိုင်းအခြားထဲမှာ လွန်လွန်ကဲကဲ ရှုပ်ထွေးကာ သေချာ မစဉ်းစားထားသလို ဖြစ်နေပါတယ်။ “ပြည်သူ့ညီလာခံ” အယူအဆက အဆင်ပြေပေမဲ့၊ ညီလာခံတွေကို အုပ်စုနှစ်ခု ခွဲထားပြီး အဲဒီအုပ်စုတွေကမှတစ်ဆင့် တစ်နှစ်ကို အကြိမ်နည်းနည်းပဲ တွေ့တဲ့ တာဝန်ယူမှုမရှိတဲ့ အဖွဲ့ (“ပြည်သူ့ကော်မတီ”) ကို ရွေးချယ်စရာ မလိုပါဘူး။ ကျွန်တော့်အတွက်တော့ ဒါဟာ နိုင်ငံတော်ရဲ့ အဆောက်အအုံနဲ့ မခြားတဲ့ လိုအပ်တာထက် ပိုမို ရုံးလုပ်ငန်းဆန်ပြီး အဆင့်အတန်းခွဲခြားထားတဲ့ စနစ်တစ်ခုလိုပါပဲ။ ဂဒါဖီဟာ ဒီရုံးလုပ်ငန်းဆန်မှုကို ဘယ်လို တားဆီးမလဲဆိုတာနဲ့ ပတ်သက်ပြီး ခိုင်မာတဲ့ အကြောင်းပြချက် မပေးထားပါဘူး။ အခြေခံအားဖြင့် သူဟာ “ဒါဟာ ပိုကောင်းတဲ့ စနစ်မို့လို့ ပိုကောင်းတာပါ” ဆိုတဲ့ ပုံသေ အကြောင်းပြချက်ပဲ ပေးထားတာပါ။ အရာရာဟာ ပိုမကောင်းပါဘူး၊ ဘာလို့လဲဆိုတော့ ရုံးလုပ်ငန်းတစ်ခုကို အခြား ရုံးလုပ်ငန်းတစ်ခုနဲ့ အစားထိုးလိုက်ရုံပဲ ရှိလို့ပါ။ ရုံးလုပ်ငန်းဆန်တဲ့ ပြဿနာအပြင်၊ လုပ်ငန်းခွင်တွေကို ဘယ်လို စနစ်တကျ တည်ဆောက်ရမလဲဆိုတာကိုလည်း သေချာ လမ်းညွှန်ချက် မပေးထားပါဘူး။ အထက်မှာ ဖော်ပြခဲ့သလိုပဲ၊ လုပ်ခလစာ အလုပ်သမားစနစ် ဖျက်သိမ်းရေး၊ အပြန်အလှန် လျှော်ကြေးပေးတဲ့ ပုံစံနဲ့ ဗဟိုချုပ်ကိုင်မှုမရှိတဲ့ လုပ်ငန်းခွင် စနစ်တွေကို ထောက်ခံထားပေမဲ့၊ လုပ်ငန်းခွင်တွေကို အလုပ်သမား ကောင်စီတွေက ကိုယ်စားပြုရမလား သို့မဟုတ် မွန်ဒရာဂွန် (Mondragon) ပုံစံမျိုးနဲ့ သွားရမလားဆိုတာကို ဘာမှ ရေးမထားပါဘူး။




ဇော်ကန့်လန့်ခြင်းများ




စာအုပ်စိမ်းမှာ သဘောကျစရာ အခိုက်အတန့်တွေ အများကြီး ရှိပါတယ်။ ကျွန်တော် မသဘောတူတဲ့ အစိတ်အပိုင်း အများစုတောင် ဖတ်ရတာ စိတ်ဝင်စားစရာကောင်းပြီး အားရစရာ ကောင်းပါတယ်။ ဒါပေမဲ့ ပါးစပ်အဟောင်းသား ဖြစ်သွားရလောက်တဲ့ အခိုက်အတန့် အချို့လည်း ရှိခဲ့ပါတယ်။ ပထမဦးစွာ၊ မစ္စတာ ဂဒါဖီဟာ စာအုပ်တစ်လျှောက်မှာ “သဘာဝဥပဒေ” နဲ့ “လူ့သဘာဝ” ဆိုတာတွေကို ခဏခဏ ရည်ညွှန်းထားပါတယ်။ ဒါဟာ ကျွန်တော့်ကို အံ့အားသင့်စေခဲ့ပါတယ်၊ ဘာလို့လဲဆိုတော့ ဒီစကားလုံးတွေကို တော်လှန်ရေးသမားတွေထက် အလွန် အစွဲအလမ်းကြီးတဲ့ ရှေးရိုးစွဲဝါဒီတွေက ပိုသုံးလေ့ရှိလို့ပါ။ လူတစ်ယောက်ဟာ စီးပွားရေးမှာ ဆိုရှယ်လစ် အမြင်ရှိပြီး လူမှုရေးမှာ ရှေးရိုးစွဲ ဖြစ်နိုင်ပေမဲ့၊ စီးပွားရေးမှာ တော်လှန်ရေး အမြင်ရှိသူတွေဟာ လူမှုရေး ကိစ္စတွေမှာလည်း တိုးတက်သော အမြင်ရှိကြတာ များပါတယ်။ သဘာဝကို အကြောင်းပြတာတွေဟာ ယုတ္တိမရှိတဲ့ အလွဲတွေဆိုတာကို ဘေးချိတ်ထားရင်တောင်၊ ဂဒါဖီဟာ လူမည်းတွေနဲ့ အမျိုးသမီးတွေကို ထောက်ခံခဲ့ပေမဲ့ ဒီစာအုပ်ထဲမှာ အဲဒီအုပ်စု နှစ်ခုလုံးအပေါ် နှိမ့်ချစော်ကားတဲ့၊ ပုံသေကားချပ်ဆန်တဲ့ မှတ်ချက်တွေကိုလည်း ပေးထားပါတယ်။ အမျိုးသမီးတွေအကြောင်း ဆွေးနွေးတဲ့အခါ ဂဒါဖီက အမျိုးသမီးတွေဟာ မွေးရာပါ “နူးညံ့” ပြီး၊ အမျိုးသားတွေဟာ မွေးရာပါ “သန်မာပြီး ကြိုးစားရုန်းကန်သူတွေ” ဖြစ်တယ်လို့ စာဖတ်သူတွေကို အာမခံထားပါတယ်။ အဲဒီနောက် လူ့အဖွဲ့အစည်းဟာ အမျိုးသားတွေကို အမျိုးသမီးတွေဖြစ်အောင်၊ အမျိုးသမီးတွေကို အမျိုးသားတွေဖြစ်အောင် လုပ်ဖို့ ကြိုးစားနေတယ်လို့ မြည်တွန်တောက်တီး ထားပါတယ်။




ဒီပြောဆိုချက်မျိုးကို ဒီနေ့ခေတ် လက်ယာစွန်း မီဒီယာမှန်သမျှမှာ လွယ်လွယ်ကဲကဲ တွေ့နိုင်ပါတယ်။ အဲဒီဆိုဒ်တွေလိုပဲ၊ ဂဒါဖီက သီးခြား ဂျန်ဒါ (Gender) အခန်းကဏ္ဍတွေနဲ့ လက္ခဏာတွေဟာ တကယ်တော့ လွတ်မြောက်မှု ဖြစ်တယ်လို့ ဆိုပါတယ်။ ဒါဟာ တကယ်ကို လမ်းလွဲနေတာပါ။ မိန်းမဆန်တဲ့ အမျိုးသားတွေ ဒါမှမဟုတ် ယောက်ျားဆန်တဲ့ အမျိုးသမီးတွေ ရှိနေတာ ဘာမှ မမှားပါဘူး။ တာန်းဂျန်ဒါ (Trans) လူမျိုးတွေ ရှိနေတာလည်း ဘာမှ မမှားပါဘူး။ ရိုးရာ ဂျန်ဒါ အခန်းကဏ္ဍတွေဆိုတာ ခေတ်ကုန်နေတဲ့ အယူအဆတစ်ခုဖြစ်ပြီး နောက်ထပ် အလေးအနက် မထားသင့်တော့ပါဘူး။




နောက်ဆုံးအနေနဲ့ ဂဒါဖီ လူမည်းတွေအကြောင်း ပြောထားတဲ့ ပုံစံက တော်တော်လေး ပြဿနာရှိပါတယ်။ သူဟာ လူမည်း လွတ်မြောက်ရေးကို ထောက်ခံတာ သေချာပြီး ဒါဟာ မွန်မြတ်တဲ့ ရပ်တည်ချက်ဖြစ်ပေမဲ့၊ လူမည်းတွေအပေါ် သူရဲ့ သဘောထားကတော့ နှိမ့်ချလိုစိတ်ပါပြီး လူမျိုးရေး ပုံသေကားချပ် အစွဲတွေ လွှမ်းမိုးနေပါတယ်။ ကမ္ဘာတစ်ဝှမ်းက လူမည်းတွေဟာ နယ်ချဲ့ဝါဒနဲ့ အမြတ်ထုတ်မှုတွေကြောင့် ဖြစ်ပေါ်လာတဲ့ စနစ်တကျ အတားအဆီးတွေ နောက်ကျကျန်ခဲ့တာကို သူ မှန်မှန်ကန်ကန် လက်ခံထားပေမဲ့၊ တစ်ဖက်မှာလည်း လူမည်းတွေဟာ အိမ်ထောင်ပြုတာ စောလွန်းတာ၊ ကလေးအများကြီး ယူတာနဲ့ ပူနွေးတဲ့ ရာသီဥတုမှာ နေထိုင်ရတာကြောင့် အခြားလူမျိုးတွေထက် “အလုပ်အပေါ် စွဲလန်းမှု နည်းပါးတာ” ဆိုပြီး ပြစ်တင်ထားပါတယ်။ အခြားစကားနဲ့ ပြောရရင် ဂဒါဖီဟာ လူမည်းတွေကို ပျင်းရိပြီး ကာမရာဂ ကြီးသူတွေအဖြစ် သွယ်ဝိုက် ဖော်ပြနေတာဖြစ်ပြီး၊ ဒါတွေဟာ သူ ဆန့်ကျင်ပါတယ်ဆိုတဲ့ နယ်ချဲ့သမားတွေ အသုံးပြုခဲ့တဲ့ အရမ်း ထိခိုက်စေပြီး အကျိုးမရှိတဲ့ ပုံသေကားချပ် အစွဲအလမ်းတွေပဲ ဖြစ်ပါတယ်။




အထွေထွေ အကဲဖြတ်ချက်




စာအုပ်စိမ်းဟာ မုအမ္မာ ဂဒါဖီ ကိုယ်တိုင်လိုပဲ အကောင်းအဆိုး ရောထွေးနေပါတယ်။ အဲဒီထဲမှာ ကောင်းမွန်တဲ့ အယူအဆတွေ၊ မကောင်းတဲ့ အယူအဆတွေ၊ ဆန့်ကျင်ဘက်တွေ၊ ယုတ္တိမရှိတဲ့ အလွဲတွေ၊ ပြောင်မြောက်တဲ့ လေ့လာတွေ့ရှိချက်တွေ၊ မရေရာတဲ့ အဖြေတွေနဲ့ ခိုင်မာတဲ့ မူဝါဒ ပန်းတိုင်တွေ ပါဝင်နေပါတယ်။ ခြုံငုံကြည့်ရင် စာအုပ်ကို ကျွန်တော် သဘောကျပြီး အာဏာမဲ့ဝါဒီတွေနဲ့ ဆိုရှယ်လစ်တွေကို ဖတ်ဖို့ ညွှန်းချင်ပါတယ်၊ ဒါပေမဲ့ ဒါဟာ Mutual Aid၊ The Conquest of Bread သို့မဟုတ် What is Property? တို့လို စာအုပ်မျိုးတော့ မဟုတ်ပါဘူး။ အဲဒီစာအုပ်တွေလည်း ပြည့်စုံတာတော့ မဟုတ်ပေမဲ့ ပိုပြီး စနစ်ကျသလို၊ နှိမ့်ချတာနဲ့ ပုံသေကားချပ် အစွဲအလမ်းတွေအပေါ် မှီခိုတာလည်း နည်းပါတယ်။ ဂဒါဖီဟာ အနောက်နိုင်ငံ အစိုးရတွေ ပုံဖော်သလို ဘီလူးသရဲ မဟုတ်ခဲ့သလို၊ အမှားမရှိတဲ့သူလည်း မဟုတ်ခဲ့ဘေ။ စာအုပ်စိမ်းက အဲဒီ အမှားတွေကို အားလုံး မြင်အောင် ပြသနေပါတယ်။ အဲဒီလိုပဲ သူရဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေး ဉာဏ်ရည်နဲ့ လူတိုင်းဟာ သူတို့ရဲ့ အခြေခံ လိုအပ်ချက်တွေကို ရရှိသင့်ပြီး သိက္ခာရှိရှိ ဆက်ဆံခံရသင့်တယ်ဆိုတဲ့ နားလည်မှုကိုလည်း မြင်တွေ့နိုင်ပြီး ဒါဟာ လေးစားစရာပါ။




နိဂုံးချုပ်အနေနဲ့ ရှင်းရှင်းလင်းလင်း ပြောပါရစေ၊ ကျွန်တော်ဟာ ဂဒါဖီအတွက် ဆင်ခြေပေးနေသူ မဟုတ်သလို၊ သူရဲ့ ပြစ်မှုဆိုင်ရာ လုပ်ရပ်တွေကိုလည်း ဘယ်လိုပုံစံနဲ့မှ ထောက်ခံမှာ မဟုတ်ပါဘူး။ သူရဲ့ မူဝါဒအချို့ဟာ ကောင်းမွန်ခဲ့ပေမဲ့၊ ဗဟိုချုပ်ကိုင်မှုရှိတဲ့ အစိုးရကနေတစ်ဆင့် အမိန့်ပေးကျင့်သုံးမယ့်အစား သူပြောခဲ့တဲ့ စကားတွေအတိုင်း သစ္စာရှိရှိ ပြည်သူတွေရဲ့ လက်ထဲကို အာဏာအပ်ခဲ့ရင် ပိုကောင်းမှာပါ။ အစတုန်းက ပြောခဲ့သလိုပဲ မုအမ္မာ ဂဒါဖီကို အာဏာရှင်တစ်ယောက်အဖြစ်သာ အမြဲ သိနေသင့်ပါတယ်။




ဒီစာအုပ်ကို ဝေဖန်သုံးသပ်ရာမှာ ကျွန်တော် ပြောချင်တဲ့ အချက်တစ်ခုကတော့ ဒီထဲက မူဝါဒအချို့ဟာ ဗဟိုချုပ်ကိုင်မှု လျှော့ချရေးနဲ့ ဒီမိုကရေစီဆီ ဦးတည်နေပုံရပေမဲ့၊ ဂဒါဖီဟာ သူကိုယ်တိုင်ရဲ့ သီအိုရီတွေနဲ့ မူဝါဒ လမ်းညွှန်ချက်တွေကို ဗြောင်ကျကျ လျစ်လျူရှုခဲ့တာပါ။ အဲဒီအတွက် ဘာဆင်ခြေမှ ပေးလို့မရပါဘူး။ ဒါကို အရင်က ရှင်းရှင်းလင်းလင်း မပြောခဲ့မိရင် တောင်းပန်ပါတယ်။
