author: Francesco Rota
title: Moyale and the Limits of Kenya’s Silence on Ethiopia
content:
At the end of October, staff from UNHCR and the Kenya Red Cross began 

issuing coded wristbands

 to Ethiopian families sheltering in schools and churches in Moyale, a town in Kenya’s Marsabit County that shares its name, and in practice its streets, with the Ethiopian town across the border. By 29 October around 

50,000 people

 had crossed in little more than a week, most of them women and children, and the Kenyan government and its humanitarian partners are now 

planning for as many as 80,000

.







These people are not fleeing the war in northern Ethiopia, where fighting resumed in Tigray in late September and federal troops 

retook Mekelle on 3 October

. That conflict has also brought Ethiopia and Eritrea to the edge of open war, as the two governments have 

broken off diplomatic relations

 and accused each other at the United Nations of 

starting a war

. They are fleeing a separate conflict more than a thousand kilometres further south, between two of Ethiopia’s own regional governments. Nevertheless, the two crises are connected, and the connection matters for Kenya, because a war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would make the present numbers at Moyale look small.




A dispute inside Ethiopia, on Kenya’s border




Ethiopian Moyale is shared between the Oromia and Somali regions, which run the town jointly and have argued for decades over the land around it. In the middle of October, Somali regional officials 

opened a new office in a district that Oromia claims and raised their regional flag over it

, and a girl of thirteen was 

killed in the violence that followed

. Within a few days the security forces of the two regions were fighting each other with heavy weapons inside the town, and the violence 

spread to the districts of Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero

.




Clashes along this same boundary in 2017 

displaced hundreds of thousands of people

, which suggests that the problem lies in the way Ethiopia’s federal system works rather than in a single provocation. The system gives territory to regions defined by ethnic identity and leaves mixed towns such as Moyale to argue over where they belong. What has changed since 2017 is that the federal army is now heavily committed in the north, and the regional forces in the south have been left to settle the question among themselves. In this sense the two crises meet, since every unit that Addis Ababa sends towards Tigray and the Eritrean border is a unit no longer available to keep rival regional forces apart elsewhere in the country.




Because the border at Moyale runs through the middle of a single town and through communities that live on both sides of it, the fighting has not stayed in Ethiopia. Kenyan police reported 

stray bullets

 landing on the Kenyan side within the first week, Kenya Defence Forces teams have since 

found and destroyed several grenades

, and a woman in Kenyan Moyale has been 

killed by what appears to have been a stray bullet

. Kenya’s acting Commissioner for Refugee Affairs, Mercy Mwasaru, now describes the situation as 

a matter of national security

.




Kenya’s selective role in the region




Kenya is sometimes described as a passive observer of conflict in the Horn of Africa, but its record suggests a country that intervenes where it judges its interests to be at stake and stays quiet elsewhere. It sent troops into Somalia in 2011 and still has soldiers there, it hosted the talks that led to the 

2005 agreement

 ending the war between northern and southern Sudan, and in November 2022 it hosted the meeting of Tigrayan and federal commanders that produced the 

Nairobi Declaration

. Under President William Ruto, Kenya went further on Sudan than any other neighbour by hosting the Rapid Support Forces as they launched a charter for a rival government, a decision that led the military authorities in Sudan to 

ban Kenyan imports

.







On Ethiopia, by contrast, Kenya has chosen to say very little, and the reasons for that choice are practical. Ethiopia is Kenya’s largest neighbour and a central economic and security partner. The two governments 

revived their 2012 Special Status Agreement

 in 2024, signed a defence cooperation agreement the following year, and in March this year 

agreed to carry out joint military operations

 along the road corridor that links Moyale, Marsabit and Turkana. Nairobi has generally treated disorder inside Ethiopia as Ethiopia’s own affair and has handled its effects on Kenyan soil as a humanitarian question, to be managed by UNHCR, the Kenya Red Cross and international donors. The events at Moyale are putting both parts of that approach under strain.




The cost of the current approach




The UN agencies have 

asked for $8.9 million

 to cover the next three months, a modest sum that must nevertheless be raised for a refugee system already short of money. Kenya hosts 

more than 836,000 refugees

, most of them in the Dadaab and Kakuma camps, both more than thirty years old. Cuts in aid last year forced the World Food Programme to 

reduce food rations by 40 per cent

. The Shirika Plan, launched in 2025 to turn the camps into settlements integrated with the surrounding towns, depends on 

donor funding that continues to fall

.




Most of the new arrivals are not in camps at all but are 

staying with local families

 in a county where many households were already short of food and water. Political leaders in Marsabit have warned that the influx could 

overwhelm the host communities

, and the Kenya Red Cross has already reported 

tensions between refugees and hosts

 at one of the sites. Humanitarian aid can ease these pressures, but it cannot resolve the territorial dispute that produced them.




A war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would place much heavier demands on Kenya than a single disputed town. Ethiopia’s south and east contain many contested regional boundaries, and a federal army fighting a neighbouring state would have even fewer troops available to control them. War also brings mass mobilisation, which tends to push young men to flee, as happened in Tigray this summer when forced recruitment 

drove many into hiding

. Kenya shares a border of more than 800 kilometres with Ethiopia, and in a wider war it would be likely to receive people from many points along it, at a time when its refugee system can barely cope with the arrivals it already has.




What Kenyan action could look like




No one is seriously suggesting that Kenyan troops should cross the border. Action in this case would mean using political influence in Addis Ababa, by pressing the federal government to separate the regional forces at Moyale, to settle a boundary dispute that it has been left open for three decades, and to accept that a conflict which sends refugees and weapons into Kenya can no longer be treated as a purely internal matter. Mwasaru says that 

extensive engagement is under way

, although the government has not said what this involves.




Kenya’s ability to play this role depends on its reputation as a fair broker, and the Sudan episode has damaged that reputation considerably. In February the International Crisis Group still named Kenya among the governments 

with access to Asmara

 that could encourage Eritrea to step back, and that access has become more valuable now that the two countries are close to open war. A government that avoids speaking frankly to Addis Ababa about violence on its own border, however, is unlikely to be taken seriously when it speaks to Asmara.




Between observer and participant




Whether Kenya becomes an actor in the region or remains an observer is a question that geography has already answered. Fifty thousand people, a town divided by the border and a frontier that is easy to cross have made Kenya a party to Ethiopia’s southern crisis, whatever its government chooses to say. What Nairobi can still decide is whether to use the relationship it has built with Addis Ababa to push for a settlement while the crisis is confined to Moyale, or to continue registering new arrivals and waiting for donors, and then to face a war between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which its long frontier will not allow it to avoid, with a refugee system that is already stretched.




The post 

Moyale and the Limits of Kenya’s Silence on Ethiopia

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: Sam Bright
title: Farage Relaunches Brexit Campaign Alongside Pro-Truss Economist
content:
Reform UK

 leader 

Nigel Farage

 has relaunched his Leave.EU pro-Brexit campaign alongside a prominent ally of former Prime Minister 

Liz Truss

.




Catherine McBride addressed the Keep Britain Out event alongside Farage and major Brexit funder Arron Banks as they ramp up their opposition to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s attempts to forge a closer relationship with the EU.




McBride, who has held positions at right-wing pro-Brexit groups for a number of years, has vocally defended Truss and her disastrous ‘mini budget’ of September 2022.




Farage has been keen to distance himself from the former prime minister’s record despite suggestions that the pair overlap on economic policy. The Reform leader 

called

 the mini budget, which announced £45 billion in unfunded tax cuts and government spending, “the best Conservative budget since 1986”.




However, with Farage attempting to prove his economic credentials, he has since changed his tune on Truss – saying that she 

wouldn’t be welcome

 in his party.




That sits uncomfortably with Farage’s alliance with McBride – who has continued to cheerlead for Truss.




McBride and Farage had a similar response to the mini budget. On 1 October 2022, a week after its release, McBride 

wrote an article

 for Briefings for Britain that enthusiastically endorsed the economic package, stating: “Three cheers for Liz Truss and her Chancellor”.




Just 19 days later, with the 

pound plummeting

 and 

borrowing costs surging

, Truss announced her resignation as prime minister.




However, unlike Farage, McBride has not backed away from Truss. In July 2023, she wrote an article for The Critic – a magazine funded by Reform donor 

Jeremy Hosking

 – entitled “

Why Truss was right

”. In the piece, McBride claimed it’s an urban myth that Truss wrecked the economy, saying “the evidence doesn’t support it.”




During the Keep Britain Out event, Farage said the campaign was “incredibly fortunate” to have McBride involved.

But McBride has also been happy to share a platform with Truss, 

interviewed on her podcast

 in February 2026 during which the pair claimed that a “socialist green lobby” is the real threat to the UK economy.




McBride is also a vocal advocate of increased fossil fuel extraction in the UK and has questioned basic climate science.




Appearing before the House of Commons International Trade Committee in March 2023, 

she said

: “I do not see carbon dioxide as this great poison” – adding that she is “very cynical” about the climate emergency.




In reality, climate impacts are already being seen in the UK and across the world, with 5,200 

heat-linked deaths

 in England this summer – almost double the previous high of 2,900 in 2022. Amid a succession of heatwaves, England also suffered its 

worst harvest on record

, with three-quarters of Brits now concerned about climate change, according 

to polling

 by Ipsos.




However, McBride supports policies that would ramp up UK fossil fuel output and contravene our climate commitments. In 

an interview

 with the Institute of Economic Affairs – a libertarian pressure group 

historically funded

 by oil majors – McBride called for the windfall tax on oil companies to be lifted, the ban on new exploration licences to be scrapped, and a reversal of the UK’s net zero commitments.




McBride has also called for the prohibition on fracking for shale gas to be lifted – a stance championed by Truss – 

saying

 that we shouldn’t ban the practice simply because it would “spoil the view” in the “north of England”.




In reality, fracking is banned in the UK due to its 

environmental and health impacts

.




McBride shares her climate opposition with Farage, who has 

claimed

 it’s “nuts” for CO2 to be considered a pollutant. Reform supports the mass expansion of fossil fuel production in the UK, including of coal, and the scrapping of clean energy schemes.




That is despite the rising price of fossil fuels 

largely being responsible

 for the increased household energy prices suffered since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the 

world’s leading climate scientists warning

 that human-caused emissions are driving extreme weather events, including droughts, flooding, and wildfires.




The Keep Britain Out campaign is a rebrand of Leave.EU – the unofficial Brexit campaign led by Farage in 2016. McBride’s exact role in the group is unclear, though she was one of just three people to address its launch.




McBride was approached for comment.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Cuba Life Expectancy Falls for First Time in 75 Years Under Illegal US Blockade
content:
Life expectancy in Cuba has fallen for the first time since 1950 as the island nation’s healthcare system buckles under a US-imposed economic and fuel blockade.




World Health Organisation (WHO) head Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus 

called for the blockade to be lifted

 on Tuesday and warned US sanctions are endangering the lives of Cuban children.




Tedros said life expectancy in Cuba had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025 – the first decline since records began in 1950.




US president Donald Trump began escalating a decades-long economic embargo on Cuba during his first term, and this year sparked an acute humanitarian crisis by imposing a fuel blockade. 




This has led to medics struggling with daily power outages amid critical shortages of food, medicines and specialised baby formula. 




Cuban officials say 

only a single tanker of oil 

has reached the island since January, crippling the country’s electrical grid. 




On a three-day visit to Havana, Tedros outlined how Cuba’s infant mortality rate more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, and maternal mortality increased from 37.4 per 1,000 live births in 2019 to 44.1 last year.




“The intensification ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of fuel restrictions and sanctions is causing direct harm to the Cuban people, especially the most vulnerable,” Tedros told reporters. 




Former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn said the blockade is “illegal, inhumane and barbaric”.




Corbyn told Novara Media: “What is Cuba’s crime? Developing public services, building universal healthcare and raising life expectancy. Somehow, this means the people of Cuba are deserving of being put under the most intense, severe and cruel sanctions imaginable. 




“Let’s be clear what this blockade is: a crime against humanity. The US’s criminal blockade is literally killing people – and our own government is standing idly by. Enough. Lift the blockade now. Viva Cuba.”




The UN has repeatedly warned of the humanitarian consequences of the blockade, calling it a violation of international law and the human rights of Cuba’s population. 




The UN General Assembly has passed a non-binding resolution calling for an end to the US embargo on Cuba every year since 1992.

author: ACG
title: National Climate Change Demo in Dublin
content:
The annual Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI) has been issued. This is a tool used to see how well 64 countries (those which produce 90% of global greenhouse gas emissions) are doing at mitigating the worst aspects of climate change.




Obviously some places are doing better than others. Ireland is one country that is performing worse than the last time conditions were evaluated. There are complexities in the details, as with any real-world situation. Nevertheless, there are some bottom-line problems that are impossible to ignore.




The report says: “Despite superficially strong frameworks, the CCPI country experts note that progress on climate action is nowhere near sufficient…” It also states clearly “The experts criticise the lack of implementation of existing legislation, frequent introduction of exclusions, and limited understanding of the severity of the situation.” (https://ccpi.org/country/irl/).#




oplus_0




One of the major culprits in preventing progress is data centres. Here “The experts stress that progress in renewables deployment is falling behind surging energy demand. Data centres are the main driver, as they accounted for 23% of total electricity supply in 2025 and now exceed the demand of all households in Ireland. To meet the rising demand, the government has continued to support and even expand fossil fuel use instead of reducing dependence on imports.” (ibid)




So you have a country where the government talks the talk but in reality fails to keep its commitments and prefers to cosy up with big businesses that harm the environment. There should be no huge surprise in that. The experts who composed the CCPI report are hardly radicals and their work on the subject doesn’t exist in isolation. It is an international phenomenon that can be replicated to varying degrees across the world. The data speaks for itself and the idea that powerful people look after their own interests above everyone elses is something a lot of folks recognise.




Evidence of this recognition came in Dublin, with a 5,000-strong National Climate Demo on November 14th, pre-dating the CCPI report by 4 days. In many ways the gathering was unremarkable. That’s certainly the case




in terms of the scheduling and route of the march. It took about an hour and went through the CBD and ended near the government buildings.




Oplus_131072




As with other recent demonstrations, the most impressive aspect of the action was the sheer range of people who participated. You could just about tick off an entire alphabetical bingo card of groups and individuals who joined. Everyone from anarchists to doctors, environmentalists to Palestinian protestors, Quakers to socialists and vegans. Those involved were aware of the seriousness of the issue, but there was a vibrancy to the march that manifested more as a colourful concern than a militant anger. That is probably to be expected in such a disparate crowd.




Its risky to assume too much, but given the overall tone of the demo, its likely many who joined would have favoured an approach similar to the writers of the CCPI report. Its an outlook characterised by recognition of a critical problem but calls on politicians to do this and that to ensure its resolution. For those of us with a more radical perspective, such demonstrations are an opportunity to initiate discussions and exchanges on why the latter view is faulty and to suggest alternatives.




It is probably fair to say environmental consciousness is currently high among the population at large, and especially so for those who actively join campaign groups and demos. The challenge is therefore not so much making people aware of the problem of climate change, as introducing them to ways of thinking or theories and methods they might not be familiar with.




Anarchists were approached during the November 14th action by fellow participants. The majority seemed curious about who we are and what we stand for. There used to be an active anarchist movement in Ireland from the 80s through to a few years ago (https://libcom.org/article/workers-solidarity-movement-closing-statement). Its not easy to maintain organisations and activity across time, and things are at a bit of a low ebb now. It has resulted in a bunch of folks (not always based on their generation or age) who aren’t familiar with anarchism or our organisations. It’s a shame, but we have to begin from how things are on the ground, not how we wish them to be.




oplus_32




On the upside, the dearth of knowledge provides fresh opportunities to put our views across. During discussions on the climate demo, there was often common agreement about the nature of the environmental crisis but pleasant surprise when people had dialogues with us about possible solutions they hadn’t be aware of. Some contacts were initiated and ideas considered.




We need reliable information. We also need to be a pole of attraction for the many people who already have information but are stuck in dead-end approaches to using it. The experience of the National Climate Demo in Ireland shows in its own way, that some progress can be made in doing so.

author: Maureen Fubara
title: Who Checks the Incumbents? Decentralization and the Cost of Electoral Violence in Nigeria
content:
On 12 November 2026, supporters of an opposition party gathered in Lagos for a political meeting. Journalists were present to cover the 

event

. Shortly after it began, attendees were attacked by a group of armed men who violently disrupted the meeting. A journalist was reportedly beaten with an axe, and his equipment was stolen. This attack in Lagos is hardly an isolated incident. Political convoys and 

campaign gatherings

 have also been attacked in Katsina, Calabar and Delta State, where one person was killed and five others injured. The 

European Union

 has already expressed concern over the growing incidents of violence and intimidation ahead of the 2027 elections.




For the ordinary Nigerian voter, the 

consequences

 of election violence can be devastating. Families 

lose

 loved ones, politically-orchestrated riots disrupts businesses, and the resulting environment of fear forces voters to choose between their safety and their right to vote. Voters should be free to choose their leaders without having to decide if voting is worth the risk. However, for political sponsors their calculations may be different and violence could be beneficial to achieve political goals. While the consequences of electoral violence are immediate for the voters, there are 

hardly any consequences

 for the political sponsors and perpetrators. This raises an important question regarding who holds the sponsors of electoral violence in Nigeria accountable? In Nigeria’s violent electoral history and for the 2027 elections and beyond, this reoccurring question is deserving of attention.




Nigeria’s federal system makes the question of accountability particularly relevant. Its 

constitutional federalism

 is based on decentralization expected to bring government closer to citizens, distribute resources and prevent excessive concentration of power. In principle, the distribution of power across levels of government should create opportunities for representation and accountability. However, distributing power does not necessarily mean 

distributing effective checks

 on that power. This problem is not limited to presidential incumbents. Incumbents in decentralized systems have access to power, resources, and networks that can give them advantages over opposition candidates. Such advantages are not inherently unlawful, they only become problematic when incumbents misuse power and divert resources to intimidate opposition parties or facilitate electoral violence, more broadly. This triggers a related question to the one raised earlier about the unintended consequences of decentralization. If power is dispersed but accountability remains weak, does decentralization simply create more opportunities for political power to be abused?




When violence pays




Electoral violence is typically discussed in terms of its consequences for voters, opposition candidates and democratic institutions. For 

incumbents sponsoring violence

, it could be beneficial for political purposes. Violence can be used to undermine opposition candidates and secure electoral victories, thereby protecting incumbents’ access to the financial benefits of holding office. Since the motivation for violence is linked to perks of power, the decentralization of that can lead to the replication of patterns of violence and intimidation at different levels. Thus, decentralization could create more opportunities for abuse of power, although these are largely unintended consequences.




Research

 on electoral violence in Nigeria has shown how fiscal decentralization in particular  can shape incumbents’ ability to recruit and maintain relationships with violence perpetrators. This suggests that electoral violence is usually not spontaneous or random, but strategically orchestrated by political actors as a means to eliminate competition and secure electoral victory. Although, Nigeria has 

laws

 against electoral offences and institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting them. Yet the existence of sanctions does not necessarily mean that politically powerful actors expect to face them. A severe punishment is ineffective if those responsible are shielded from investigations or protected from prosecution.




This is the crux of the accountability problem.




Who imposes the costs?




Consider the institutions responsible for electoral integrity. The Independent National Electoral Commission receives public funding through 

constitutionally protected arrangements

 intended to protect its independence. The 

police

 operate under federal authority, while 

prosecutorial and judicial institutions

 have their own responsibilities for enforcing electoral laws. At the state level, 

State Independent Electoral Commissions

 appointments, resources and local elections administration  are highly influenced by state governors.




While electoral institutions vary in their legal mandates and funding arrangements, incumbents  can influence the political and financial conditions under which they can enforce accountability. Take for example, 

the presidential appointment of the INEC chairman

, the independent electoral institution responsible for conducting elections. INEC is mandated to ensure credible elections, even if that means overseeing the election of a successor to the incumbent president who appointed its chairman. Given the dynamics of political appointments and the potential for bias in the selection process, such arrangements can raise questions about the institution’s independence and transparency, particularly when appointees are perceived as loyalists of the incumbent. It is therefore understandable that INEC’s institutional ties to the incumbent government remain a source of 

controversy

.




While it is easy to recommend stronger institutions, there are still pending concerns. Even where legal safeguards exist, their effectiveness depends on whether institutions can act without political interference. However, while decentralization replicates this accountability problem, centralizing power would not necessarily resolve it. Presidential incumbents may also have incentives to manipulate elections. 

Uganda’s

 centralized system exemplifies this point accurately, as weak institutions have failed to deter electoral violence and intimidation. Instead, such incidents can become concentrated at the centre, rather than eliminated altogether.




Voters gathered at polling units during Nigeria’s 2023 general elections. Photo: Ibukun Emiola




The Way Forward: Policy Recommendations




As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general elections and beyond, the debate about electoral violence needs to move beyond calls for institutional strengthening that make accountability highly challenging to evade. One starting point is to make the handling of electoral offences more transparent. Relevant election tribunals and prosecutorial authorities should provide accessible information on reported cases, investigations, prosecutions and outcomes. This would allow Nigerians to assess whether electoral offences are being investigated and whether cases involving influential politicians receive appropriate scrutiny. But transparency must be accompanied by consequences. Where credible evidence links political actors to the financing or organization of violence, investigations should extend beyond those who physically commit offences. Otherwise, accountability risks affecting only the foot soldiers rather than their political sponsors.




There is also a role for political accountability. Voters should have access to credible information about documented electoral abuses and the conduct of those seeking public office. Independent journalists, civil society organizations and election observers can help make this information available, while distinguishing allegations from established wrongdoing. This matters because prosecution is not the only way to punish political actors for their actions. Public scrutiny, reputational consequences and voters’ independent electoral judgments can also shape the incentives of political actors. However, they depend on citizens having reliable information and being able to exercise their political rights without intimidation. The longer-term challenge is to make accountability less dependent on the goodwill of those being scrutinized. This requires attention to institutional appointments, predictable funding, independent investigations and enforceable procedures for responding to political interference.




Conclusion: Making Accountability Count




Nigeria’s accountability problem cannot be simply be addressed by feasible recommendations alone. The main concern is whether the costs of sponsoring violence become high enough to change political incentives. Realistically, this is yet to happen as weak institutions enable rather than constrain the political actors. While recommendations appear feasible, their implementation depend on the willingness of political actors and institutions, the very actors benefitting from the status quo. This means the burden of accountability unfairly falls on the voters who in addition to navigating a tense electoral environment must now hold political  actors accountable, mainly through unsuccessful public backlash.




To adequately address the accountability problem, particularly regarding elections in Nigeria decentralization and democracy must work together to dismantle the status quo. While decentralization distributes political power, democracy requires something more by making the abuse of that power costly enough that even the most powerful politicians cannot afford to ignore the consequences. Until that happens, any recommendation will be an exercise in futility.




The post 

Who Checks the Incumbents? Decentralization and the Cost of Electoral Violence in Nigeria

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

author: Amy Romer, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: The word ‘kokum’ has entered the dictionary — but it’s deeper than a simple definition
content:
Cree Knowledge Keeper Elsie Paul sits surrounded by artwork and belongings in a video she shared on Youtube and TikTok. 

Screenshot courtesy Elsie Paul/

YouTube




Kôhkom (grandmother) Elsie Paul was nervous about posting her first TikTok. 




The young people Paul worked with at the Kohkum Kisewatisowin Society encouraged her to share her teachings online. Paul had established the society to pass on Cree language and teachings after being punished for speaking Cree at a day school in Saddle Lake.




“You could probably reach 500 people in one day,” her oskâpêw (helper), Kathy Hamelin, told her. 




“Oh my,” Paul, who was 77 at the time, replied. 




It was December 2021, and the COVID-19 pandemic was still keeping people apart. Hoping to reach more young people in the amiskwaciwâskahikan (Edmonton) community, Paul decided to try something new. 




From her kitchen, the Cree-Métis knowledge keeper from Treaty 6 territory could share her culture with people beyond her immediate circle. 




Ping! Her phone chimed. 




Ping! 




“I don’t know why this one keeps pinging,” said Paul.




“I bet it’s your TikTok,” Hamelin replied. 




Within an hour, Paul’s first video, a 21-second clip of her dancing the Red River jig in her kitchen, had racked up 2,000 views. By the end of the day, that number had climbed to 12,000.




Paul couldn’t believe so many people had watched it. 




“That many people around the world,” Hamelin laughed.




Paul soon became known as the 

#technokokum

, with some of her videos reaching 350,000 views. 




Her time on TikTok was relatively brief, ending when she retired in late 2022. But the response to her videos showed how far a Cree kinship term could travel, reaching people far beyond the communities where it originated — with comments like “thank you for being everyone’s kokum” and “I can smell the smudge and tea through the screen.”




In June 2026, 

kokum

 

— an anglicized spelling of the Cree word kôhkom — 

entered the Oxford English Dictionary

 (OED).




According to the OED, it’s the first kinship term from an Indigenous language in “Canada” to be added to the dictionary. 







READ MORE:

 

May we all have a kôhkom, or a kokum







For Danica Salazar, a lexicographer and the executive editor for “World Englishes” at Oxford Languages, the addition reflects a shift in how Indigenous Languages are represented in English. 




“There’s something quite anthropological about most of our early evidence for these words,” she said in an interview with IndigiNews. 




Words like 

muskimoot

 (bag or sack), 

shaganappi

 (rawhide strip, from pîsâkanâpiy) and 

pemmican

 (dried meat and berries, from pimîhkân) are all anglicized Cree words already recorded in the OED.




Those earlier entries often reflected the objects and cultural practices that outsiders encountered and documented. 




“Kokum,” on the other hand, is the first example of a word rooted in the familiar relationships and everyday lives among Indigenous communities in “Canada.” 




Salazar believes the addition reflects a growing influence of Indigenous communities on the English language, as their words circulate beyond the accounts of anthropologists and other outside observers.




“So that’s really interesting because you can really see the more direct influence of Indigenous languages on English,” she said, “without the third party involvement.” 




But for Hamelin, the word’s inclusion raised another question: what happens to a word’s meaning once it’s recorded in English?




How a word enters the dictionary




To be considered for inclusion in the OED, a word must have an established presence in the English language




Oxford Languages

, part of Oxford University Press, uses a vast digital collection of texts, known as a corpus, containing billions of words gathered from across the internet. Software helps lexicographers follow the ebb and flow of language, tracking which words are gaining momentum, how often they’re used, and by whom — whether in particular regions, communities or fields of study.

When lexicographers noticed “kokum” appearing more frequently in “Canadian” English, they flagged it for further research. They found evidence of its use dating back to 1973, when Métis writer Maria Campbell 

published her memoir 

Halfbreed

, about growing up in Saskatchewan.




Hamelin remembers the 

impact

 

Halfbreed

 had when it was first published. 




“Everybody read that book,” she said. “It’s where a lot of people were introduced to that word.”




For Salazar, this first citation was particularly meaningful: rather than someone writing about an Indigenous community and the words its members use, it was a person from the community using the word herself. 




Later examples traced “kokum” through newspapers and books, and eventually into social media and everyday vernacular. 




But the word was also circulating in Indigenous artistic and cultural spaces. In 2019, the Cree Literacy Network shared 

Kokum Rap

, a collaboration featuring “power-poets and power-kokums” including Campbell, 

Louise Bernice Halfe-Sky Dancer

, 

Rita Bouvier

, and 

Zoey Roy

.




Salazar sees the word’s increasing visibility as part of a broader shift in the public acceptance of Indigenous languages and cultures. Words that were once discouraged, if not prohibited, are now increasingly celebrated. 




“A grandmother can be on TikTok and call herself a techno kokum, and everybody thinks that’s great,” she said.







READ MORE:

 

Cree poet Louise Bernice Halfe-Sky Dancer explores her ‘life of inspiration’ in new book ‘wîhtamawik’







‘It’s so much deeper than just grandmother’




Although Hamelin is “thrilled” to see the word recognized by the OED, she takes issue with its spelling — “kokum” — and the dictionary’s definition of it as “a grandmother” or “one’s grandmother.”




“It’s kôhkom,” Hamelin — who is a kôhkom herself — asserted. 




“’Kokum’ doesn’t mean anything. All the meaning is lost.”




But the OED records how words are adopted into English, including changes to their spelling, pronunciation and meaning. Its etymology of “kokum” also acknowledges the Cree spelling, kôhkom, which it translates as “your grandmother.” 




Hamelin says even that translation doesn’t tell the whole story.




“That’s what it has come to mean,” she said. 




In Cree, Hamelin explained, kinship terms change depending on whose relative someone is speaking about. 




If she were talking about “your grandmother,” it’s kikôhkom, said Hamelin.




The language distinguishes between one’s own grandmother, another person’s grandmother, or the grandmother of someone being discussed.




Those distinctions are part of a much broader understanding of kinship.







READ MORE:

 

Beyond language learning, weekly Cree classes taught me about kinship







She recalled a teaching the 

late Henry Luboucan

 shared with her about the origins of kôhkom. He connected the word to ohkomimâw, which Hamelin understood as meaning “leader.”




In the teaching Hamelin described, kôhkoms held the authority to question and veto family decisions made by okimâwak (chiefs), particularly those affecting the community’s political or economic life.




“It’s so much deeper than just grandmother,” she said. 




You don’t have to have children of your own to become a kôhkom, either. Your siblings’ children can make you one, too. And there’s a saying. The more kôhkom’s 

you have, the richer you are. 




“So if you have 10 kôhkoms, you’re a millionaire,” chuckled Hamelin. “People don’t understand because of the disconnection from our language and culture.”




These relationships carry responsibilities for care, guidance and passing knowledge between generations. Hamelin worries that much of this understanding has been weakened by the disruption of families and languages through the residential “school” system and the 

Sixties Scoop

.




“A lot of people forgot how to say the words,” said Hamelin. “So they anglicize them without even knowing the full meaning.” 




“If I’m talking to you about my grandmother: ninôhkom. If I’m asking you about your grandmother, I say kikôhkom. And if I’m asking you about that person’s grandmother, I’d say ôhkoma,” said Hamelin.




For Hamelin, that history is part of why she believes the OED has a responsibility to represent the word’s origins accurately, given its authority and the millions of people who rely on the dictionary as an authoritative source. 




“But I’m not at all surprised,” she said of what she considers an inaccurate entry.




Salazar, however, described the OED’s role differently.




“It’s there to tell the story of the language,” she said. “We’re basically just following usage rather than dictating it. So we’re documenting it, recording it, studying it, rather than influencing it.” 




Yet the question of a dictionary’s influence is difficult to separate from its own reputation. On its website, the OED describes itself as “widely regarded as the accepted authority on the English language.” 




Whose history gets recorded?




Unlike many other English dictionaries, the OED is a “historical dictionary.” Its entries trace the development of words through documented examples of their use, sometimes spanning centuries.




But that written record is itself shaped by colonialism, which imposed written forms of documentation while suppressing Indigenous languages. 




The OED’s earliest documented use of “kokum” therefore dates only to the 1970s, despite the word’s much longer history. 




“Obviously, we cannot go back in time and listen to what people say. So it could very well be that if we could do that, we would have a much earlier date than 1973,” said Salazar. 




The distinction between a word’s earliest recorded appearance in English and its history within Cree is especially important here. The dictionary’s written citations can establish when a word appeared in sources available to its researchers, while a word’s full history is often carried through oral teachings and community knowledge.




Salazar said the OED sometimes consults local language experts when researching words from other languages, but such consultations are uncommon.




“Only when information is missing,” said Salazar. “There was enough in the text for ‘kokum.’”







READ MORE:

 

IndigiNews’ weekly Cree lessons







For “kokum,” OED etymologists drew on three online resources: the 

Online Cree Dictionary

, the 

Dictionary of Moose Cree

, and the 

East Cree Dictionary

. 




While the Online Cree Dictionary translates kôhkom as “your grandmother,” the Dictionary of Moose Cree lists ohkomimâw as “grandmother,” with ohkom as the stem and kôhkom meaning “your grandmother.” 




Salazar acknowledged that words borrowed from historically oral languages should be traced through oral histories, not solely through written records. But she also pointed to the practical constraints of this approach, arguing that information must be recorded in some form to be accessible to researchers. 




Audio recordings, she added, are relatively recent technologies in the history of languages. This reliance on recorded evidence, however, risks overlooking oral transmission itself as a knowledge system, through which language and its histories are passed down across generations. 




Salazar said the OED is also hoping to introduce “moshum” — the anglicized spelling of 

môshom

 (grandfather) — in the near future. 




That kinship word, like “kokum,” also appears in 

Halfbreed

. But it doesn’t appear in literature as often as “kokum,” and so it didn’t make it into the 2026 round. 




Hamelin believes the difference in their visibility may also reflect the impact of colonization on Indigenous men, including incarceration and premature death.




“The majority of our men die an early death or spend most of their lives incarcerated,” she said. 




Hamelin stressed that mosômak (grandfathers) are valued just as much as kôhkomak (grandmothers). 




“The mosômak deserve recognition,” she said. “I’ll look forward to seeing it in the dictionary.” 




Despite her concerns about the dictionary entry, Hamelin said she doesn’t mind kôhkom becoming a more general word for grandmothers. 




She recognizes that, for people separated from their languages, even an anglicized word can connect them to their families and cultures.  




“It’s a way of preserving the language for people who don’t know it,” she said. “That small piece of language and culture keeps them anchored.”







The post 

The word ‘kokum’ has entered the dictionary — but it’s deeper than a simple definition

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

author: Eden Fineday
title: May we all have a kôhkom — or a kokum
content:
Eden Fineday’s kokum, Irene. 

Photo by Eden Fineday




In my 20s, I used to travel regularly from California, where I was attending university, to Saskatchewan to visit my family on the rez. 




My granny, Irene Fineday, lived in a little red house on Sweetgrass Reserve, now called 

Sweetgrass First Nation

. 




Back then, in the 1990s, my cousin Etley also lived with her. Etley took care of her. Every day, she would brush her hair, cook her meals and generally do her bidding. She would drive granny into town for her appointments.




I only reconnected with my Sweetgrass family at the age of 14. Until then, I had lived with my white mother and my two white siblings in “Vancouver,” far away from my father and his side of the family. 







READ MORE:

 

Who gets to define a kôhkom?







I was told as a child that I was Native, so I understood it on an intellectual level, but I did not understand what it actually meant. Growing up, I was hungry for connection to my culture, but I had no one close to me who could teach me.




Once I was in touch with my Cree family, I began to visit at least once per year. 




Whenever I landed in Saskatoon, I would pick up a rental car and get on the road to the rez. It was about an hour and a half from the airport to my granny’s little red house. 




On the way, I always stopped in North Battleford and picked up some fried chicken. I would arrive on Sweetgrass with my offering, and my granny, my cousins, and whatever extended family was visiting would feast with me. 




Eden Fineday (right) with her kokum, Irene, around 2004. 

Photo courtesy Eden Fineday




An understated, unreactive wisdom




Sometimes, I would take my granny and my cousin Etley out for a meal. On one such occasion, at a chain restaurant in North Battleford, a waiter came to our table to take our order. 




“What can I get you, kokum?” he asked my granny Irene.




I was taken aback. 




I had never heard someone non-Indigenous use a Cree word like that. In fact, until that moment, I’m not sure I had ever heard the word. I called her granny. I felt a wave of gratitude wash over me – both for him making an effort to respect my grandmother, and for teaching me the word.




Wow!

 I thought. 

This white guy knew a Cree word.

 Not only that, but he used it to communicate something important — that my granny was indeed his kokum. 




All kokums are everybody’s kokums in public.




Granny Irene. 

Photo by Eden Fineday




My granny was an understated person. She didn’t have big, instantaneous reactions. 




Once, I accidentally lit a frying pan on fire while I was cooking her some bacon. I yelled about the fire and the smoke, grabbed a cloth to wrap around the handle, ran to the front door with the frying pan, opened the door and the screen door, and threw the entire contents of the pan out into the snow off the side of the porch — while she watched me out the corner of her eye, barely looking up from her game of solitaire on the kitchen table. 




I’ve come to learn this non-reacting is part of our culture. So my granny didn’t jump for joy when this waiter addressed her the way he did. But her eyes twinkled and I could see that she was clearly tickled pink. 




The waiter also didn’t make a big deal of it. I think they both understood Cree ways of communicating. She placed her order.




That moment has always stuck with me. I think of it often, especially when I’m learning Cree. I hadn’t heard the word kokum very often growing up.




Even my Cree cousins on Sweetgrass called my grandmother “Granny” in my presence. Others, the ones she had raised, called her “Mama.” 




There were different names for her, depending on who was speaking and their relationship to her. I wonder now how much of that was simply family habit, and how much came from the pressure to speak English.




Eden Fineday’s grandmother Irene stands outside with her grandfather Alphonse in an archival photo. 

Photo courtesy Eden Fineday




Kokum or kôhkom?




I’ve been reflecting on this because I was moved last month when I learned that the Oxford English Dictionary had added the word “kokum” in June.




It’s a version of the proper Cree word, kôhkom. Lots of people spell it without the diacritics or the letter H, both of which are actually instructions for how to pronounce the word phonetically. 




These widely accepted variety of spellings also serves a useful function — it shows us that, unlike kôhkom, which means “your grandmother” in Cree, kokum is an anglicization of the word, and the meaning has shifted a bit. Spelt in this way, it’s used to just mean “grandmother.”




In the past, my family may have felt pressured to use English words to describe their own family members. 




Now, they can use a Cree word proudly, and if anyone tells them they should be speaking English, they can tell them that they are using English, too.







READ MORE:

 

Beyond language learning, weekly Cree classes taught me about kinship







Living languages change, and that’s a beautiful thing. They grow to encompass the lived realities of the people speaking them. 




Cree people have been forced to speak English for centuries. Now, there’s a tiny piece of reciprocation, a small acknowledgement of our worldview, which feels big. 




“Canada” is a nation made of European culture on Indigenous Peoples’ lands. This country is a co-creation. 




As we continue to move toward truth, toward reconciliation, my wish is that this small act leads to more understanding. 




May more “Canadians” become aware of the many languages spoken on the sacred land under their feet. 




May understanding grow from this. 




May they learn more about the People, too and the beautiful cultures contained in our languages.




May we all have a kôhkom. Or a kokum.




The post 

May we all have a kôhkom — or a kokum

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

title: Podcast: Three Voices for Peace with Vanessa Vaglio and Alessandro Capuzzo
content:
By Marc Eliot Stein, November 25, 2026




Marc Eliot Stein, Vanessa Vaglio and Alessandro Capuzzo at the entrance to Prospect Park, Brooklyn, 2024




At the end of my freewheeling conversation with two peace activists for the November episode of the World BEYOND War podcast, Alessandro Capuzzo captured the meaning of our meeting with a succinct phrase: “A city that should be neutral, a country without a military, and the place where the United Nations exists”. The city that should be neutral is Trieste in Italy, whose government ignores protesting shipworkers and the law itself by using seaports to serve genocidal foreign militaries. The country without a military is Costa Rica, a shining and rare example of intelligent governance in a region and a planet that needs much more of the same. The place where the United Nations exists is New York City, where I first enjoyed meeting antiwar activists Vanessa Vaglio of Costa Rica and Alessandro Capuzzo of Trieste two years ago when they arrived with Juan Gomez of Chile for a global peace march, 3 Marcia Mondiale Per La Pace E La Nonviolenza.




Alessandro Capuzzo, Marc Eliot Stein, Juan Gomez and Vanessa Vaglio with a World March For Peace and Nonviolence banner in Prospect Park, Brooklyn, 2024




Vanessa and Alessandro are both part of 

World Without Wars and Nonviolence

, a global organization since 1994, and I’ll be going to the United Nations on December 1 to be part of a continuing mission in support of nuclear non-proliferation and to call attention specifically to the use of ports on the Adriatic Sea for foreign military shipments, a growing operations despite the fact that shipworkers are protesting and that these violations of neutrality are illegal on many levels.




This is only one of many topics we touched upon in this month’s podcast interview. Vanessa talked about living amidst nature, the importance of women-led governments and the need to find new ways to welcome people into antiwar movements. Alessandro talked about Italy’s rightward turn, the growing crisis in Slovenia and the corrupt encroachment of foreign militarism via initiatives like the 

India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor

 (IMEC). We chatted about the great novelist James Joyce’s years in Trieste, shared impressions of various recent global events, and managed to find a few laughs and lots of agreement. I really enjoyed this conversation with Vanessa and Alessandro, and I’ll be carrying the hopeful, joyful spirit of this interview with me when I join their organization’s delegation to the United Nations next week.

author: David Swanson
title: European Youth Strike: A Million Students Mobilise Against War and Austerity
content:
By 

Ana Vračar, 

Savage Minds

, November 25, 2026




More than 50 student organisations in 27 European countries launched an 

international strike

 against war and militarisation on Friday, 20 November, drawing a million young people onto the streets.




Students issued joint demands, including an end to rearmament and all forms of conscription, investment in education and social services, and solidarity with oppressed peoples around the world. They also declared resistance to growing authoritarian trends in the region.




“We are protesting to claim our right to a better future, and we are aware that if we stand united, no one will be able to stop us from taking it,” said 

Alessandro Di Miceli

 from the Italian organisation Rete della Conoscenza.




Actions took place in Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Romania, Turkey, Greece, Croatia, Hungary, Slovakia, Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Britain, France, Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, Malta, and Slovenia, among others.




“From the right to education to the right to housing, from the struggle against the rising costs of living and the climate crisis to the fight against militarisation and rearmament, specific demands may differ from country to country but are all deeply connected to each other,” Di Miceli said.




Attacks on education funding




One concern shared by student groups across the region is the precarious state of public education. For almost two months, high school and university students in 

France

 have led massive protests and occupations against austerity measures imposed during Emmanuel Macron’s presidency.




Similar policies took root elsewhere too. In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s administration recently announced 

cuts to student welfare

 and support while planning to invest billions in the military.




“While the government says it doesn’t have the money to invest in education or opportunities for young people without cutting welfare and potentially pushing hundreds of thousands of young people into poverty, it is right now spending an extra £15 billion a year on the military,” Stop the War’s 

Shabbir Lakha

 wrote.




Teachers and parents protested side by side with youth organisations in many cities, supporting their concerns. Still in England, the 

National Education Union

 (NEU) published a statement on planned school funding cuts on the day of the international youth strike. The union found that mainstream school funding in England will be slashed by £1.2 billion (USD 1.57 billion) in cash in 2027-28.




The cuts will affect approximately 11,000 schools in England, the NEU pointed out—many of them in the poorest parts of the country, including Hackney, Southwark and Tower Hamlets in London.




“Hackney and Tower Hamlets have the highest child poverty rates in the UK: half of their children live in poverty once housing costs are paid,” NEU general secretary Daniel Kebede warned.




Students refuse the return of conscription.




Another concern widely voiced among student groups is the return of military conscription. In 

Germany

, more than 50,000 pupils and students organised their fifth school strike in a year. The German government plans to build Europe’s “strongest conventional army” in a matter of years while slashing welfare and social security, with the youth insisting they will not be part of this scenario. Similarly, in 

Belgium

—including in Ghent, Brussels, Leuven, Liège, and Antwerp—young people tore up letters issued by the Ministry of Defence regarding military service.




In 

Slovenia

, the 

Rosa Collective

 described how thousands of students attended a recent arms fair as part of their “active citizenship” curriculum while structural needs remain unaddressed. “The military is targeting rural vocational and technical high schools,” the group wrote. “They aim to recruit young people from socially disadvantaged backgrounds, offering them money and adventure.”




Noting that Israeli arms companies Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries appeared basically next door to the location visited by students, Rosa Collective warned that “young people are being recruited in secondary and primary (!) schools while some faculties and institutes are becoming incubators for the development of technologies for military use.”




Convergence with housing and cost-of-living campaigns




In Italy, Spain, and Portugal, the student strikes echoed mass mobilisations for housing and general strikes against the cost-of-living crisis. A 

national strike

 called by the mainstream trade union confederation CGIL was ongoing as students took to the streets in Italy, with progressive student collectives calling on the public to embrace a more ambitious agenda and support new mobilisations by grassroots unions on 

12 December

.




In Spain, protesters cited the 11 November general strike as an inspiration. “We had an amazing strike last 11 November, with more than 400,000 people marching only in Barcelona,” a spokesperson for 

Sindicat d’Estudiants

 told Breakthrough

 News

. “And we said that day that this was not the ending of anything. We said that the demonstrations, that the strike had to keep going. And this is what we are doing today.”




“We are determined to continue organising and mobilising in the months ahead, until these demands become reality,” Shabbir Lakha emphasised in a statement by the Youth Strike Coalition. “The ruling classes of our countries should begin to worry, because this 20 November will only be the beginning. We will keep standing together as youth to fight for our future, not their wars.”

title: Rassemblement devant la prison des Baumettes dimanche 6 décembre
content:
Dimanche 6 décembre à 15h, rassemblons-nous devant la prison des Baumettes pour apporter notre soutien aux personnes enfermées !




Depuis la fin du mois de septembre, l'enthousiasme des lycéens à refuser l'état des choses est communicatif et nous a mis du baume au coeur. C'est cette joie et cette rage que l'État veut à tout prix empêcher de se répandre. Pour cela il réprime par tous les moyens : violences policières, interdictions de manifester, comparutions immédiates, couvre-feux et consignes explicites aux juges de distribuer des peines lourdes.




Des blocus aux manifestations, les mineur.es sont particulièrement visé.es. Iels subissent pressions et violences : mutilation et harcèlement par la police, traque et dénonciation par les proviseurs et chefs de services des foyers. Des conseils de discipline pleuvent et de nombreux·ses mineur.es passent devant le juge pour enfant.




De la rue à la prison, la justice donne à voir de manière criante son fonctionnement de classe et raciste. Comme le dit une proche d'un prisonnier des Baumettes “l'État se sert du mouvement social pour enfermer plus de pauvres et expulser plus d'arabes”. Pendant les comparutions immédiates, des peines de prison hyper dures ont été systématiquement assorties d'une ITF (Interdiction du Territoire Français) pour les personnes étrangères. Toujours la même politique raciste et sécuritaire : traquer, enfermer, expulser.




Suite aux nouvelles incarcérations, les galères des proches sont plus fortes que d'habitude : attente interminable pour obtenir un permis de visite, gros retards aux parloirs...La surpopulation des prisons atteint des records : des hamacs sont accrochés dans les cellules arrivants où s'entassent jusqu'à 4 personnes dans 9m². Les droits des prisonnier.es et de leurs proches, déjà peu respectés en temps normal, sont complètement bafoués.




Il y a de la résistance à l'intérieur, les prisonniers en promenade ont refusé massivement de rejoindre leurs cellules ces dernières semaines dans les prisons de Grenoble-Varces, de Toulouse-Seysses et de Lyon-Corbas.




Les élans de solidarité ont dépassé la rue avec des rassemblements devant les comicos et les tribunaux.


S'ils divisent pour mieux régner, notre solidarité dépasse les murs de leurs prisons. 


Pour toutes ces raisons, il est important d'aller apporter notre soutien aux personnes incarcérées aux Baumettes : 


Tous et toutes libres !




Rassemblement devant la prison des Baumettes, rendez-vous le dimanche 6 décembre à 15h à l'arrêt de bus Morgiou Beauvallon 

bus 22 22S 23

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Huna": Egyptian Author Abdelrahman ElGendy on Prison, National Book Award & Being Denied U.S. Visa
content:
This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut, 

Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming

, chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an 

MFA

 in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.




“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells 

Democracy Now!

 about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”




We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet 

Mada Masr

, whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.




“

Mada

 carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in 

Mada Masr

. “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Students serve spaghetti with help from sirens in Rankin Inlet
content:
Three Rankin Inlet elders and their households enjoyed catered spaghetti meals prepared by students at Maani Ulujuk Ilinniarvik High School on Friday.




Student chefs Theresa Ikkutaq-Kurok, left, and Jessie Twyee prepare 45 portions of garlic bread in the Maani Ulujuk Ilinniarvik kitchen on Friday. (Photo courtesy of Mark Ronald)




“It was all for the elders,” said 15-year old student chef Brandon Amarook in a phone interview about the project.




He and his classmates prepared family-sized servings — 15 portions each — of pasta with meat sauce and garlic bread as part of instructor Mark Ronald’s food studies class.




The sauce recipe came courtesy of RCMP Sgt. Darick Ramminger, who sat in on Thursday’s class as a culinary consultant.




The students agreed on a name for the officer’s signature sauce: 

“No snitchin’ in the kitchen.”




Ronald and Ramminger first cooked up the idea while collaborating on the school’s breakfast program earlier this semester.
















“It was a wonderful opportunity for students to put their awesome cooking skills to good use and share food with our elders, build relationships within our community and with RCMP,” Ronald said Monday during a phone interview.




The students gave the meals away through a radio contest, broadcast over the community’s 97.9 FM station.




Ronald said that 40 elders called in to participate, and students randomly drew three lucky names: Tommy Adams, Joan Kalaserk and Andy Aliyak.




Students delivered the meals to their front doors on Friday, chauffeured by Ramminger, Cst. Gabe Stuart and Cst. Stephen Edwards.




Ronald and school counsellor Lucy Makkigak accompanied the convoy as it drove from home to home.




“I never rode in a cop truck before,” said 15-year-old Jane Sanertanut.
















Sixteen-year-old Brooke Schweder said “it felt good” to deliver the meals.




“The elders were really grateful,” she said. “They were smiling and that made me smile.”

title: Solidarität mit den Gefangenen für den Frieden!
content:
Zum Internationalen Tag der Gefangenen für den Frieden am 1. Dezember bittet die War Resisters‘ International, zu deren Mitgliedern auch die Graswurzelrevolution als assoziierte Zeitschrift zählt, um Solidarität mit Menschen, die weltweit wegen ihrer Kriegsdienstverweigerung oder ihres Engagements für Frieden inhaftiert sind. Ihre Namen und Gefängnisadressen werden in der Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden veröffentlicht.

Die WRI ruft dazu auf, den Gefangenen Kartengrüße als Zeichen der Solidarität und der Ermutigung in die Haft zu schicken. Selbst wenn die Karten die Adressaten und Adressatinnen nicht erreichen sollten, machen sie deutlich, dass die Gefangenen nicht vergessen sind, was sich auf die Haftbedingungen günstig auswirken kann.

Die Liste enthält die Adressen von Gefangenen stellvertretend für viele andere, deren Adresse unbekannt ist oder die keine Publizität wünschen. Die Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden von 2025 ent­hielt Haft­adressen in Aser­baid­schan, Belarus, Eritrea, Sin­ga­pur, Südkorea, in der Ukraine und in den USA. Besonders katastrophal ist die Menschenrechtslage in Eritrea. Dort werden Männer und Frauen zu einem zeitlich unbegrenzten Nationaldienst gezwungen, teils Militär-, teils Arbeitsdienst unter härtesten Bedingungen. Die diesjährige Liste der Gefangenen für den Frieden soll zum 1. Dezember 2026 auf www.wri-irg.org veröffentlicht werden.

Die Karten an die Gefangenen können sowohl gemeinsam und öffentlich als auch privat geschrieben werden. Die DFG-VK Mainz-Wiesbaden lädt ein zum gemeinsamen Schreiben der Karten an die Gefangenen für den Frieden mit Live-Musik von Strohfeuer Express, mit Film, Bilder-Schau, Speis und Trank: Zornheim bei Mainz, Samstag, 5. Dezember 2026, 13 Uhr, HerrBerts Kulturscheune, Untergasse 10, 55270 Zornheim. www.dfg-vk-mainz.de

Gernot Lennert (DFG-VK Mainz-Wiesbaden)

Pat Elderfounder of Military Poisons, a project tracking how military activity impacts people and the planet.

The U.S. Army detonated nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday, potentially sending toxic lead dust and other deadly contaminants spewing across communities and farmland throughout the Mississippi River water basin. Residents, who were first informed last week, had been ordered to evacuate or else shelter in place. “The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts,” says Pat Elder, who tracks how military activity impacts people and the planet at the Military Poisons project. “There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen.”

Pat Elderfounder of Military Poisons, a project tracking how military activity impacts people and the planet.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in three counties as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa today. The detonation will cause a massive blast that could send toxic lead dust spewing across communities, farmland, and potentially into the Mississippi River. The detonation is scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time.

Officials have recommended residents of Middletown, where the plant is located, and anyone within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant to evacuate, while people living up to 20 miles away have been told to stay indoors with their windows closed. Men are being told to — in this farmland area, to bring their cows inside. A number of farmers have said that’s impossible.

Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, told a reporter he plans to go west to escape the toxic plume.

JEREMY ATWATER: But now the winds are changing directions, and it’s going to blow directly south through our town, so I guess we’re going to head west instead.

REPORTER: And what’s out west? Is it hotels? Or is it just —

JEREMY ATWATER: Anything but the bomb. … My primary concern is a lot. I mean, nobody really knows. There’s never been a documented explosion like this, as far as I could find any doing my due diligence digging in the interweb. But it’s just going to be a big problem. It’s going to be a lot of lead poisoning going on.

AMY GOODMAN: The Army published an updated map estimating the lead plume could spread all the way to northern Missouri, more than 100 miles from ground zero. There’s no safe level of lead exposure. Lead is a neurotoxin that can cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm and is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women.

The Army says the explosives, stored for decades in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, have deteriorated to the point that they could spontaneously explode. This is acting Army Secretary Adam Telle speaking at a press conference in Iowa Tuesday.

ARMY SECRETARY ADAM TELLE: There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance.

AMY GOODMAN: On Saturday, The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option, a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead.

Well, for more, we go to Lexington Park, Maryland, where we’re joined by Pat Elder, the founder of the group Military Poisons. He just wrote a piece headlined “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.”

Pat Elder, welcome back to Democracy Now! Iowans are panicked.

AMY GOODMAN: They say they have gotten very little notice about what’s about to take place. If there are hills, they’re saying people are heading to the hills. But what do they do with their cows, those who are farmers? If you could start off by saying why you see this as a warning to the world? And how on Earth did this surprise this whole community, where the governor now has declared a disaster emergency in three counties?

PAT ELDER: Well, thank you for having me, Amy. I appreciate it.

We have to go back to the words of Thomas Jefferson, who wrote in the Declaration of Independence that we must be warned of usurpations by the federal government that will strip the liberties of individual states. And so, that’s what we see today. The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts and experts with the EPA and experts with the Applied Physics Lab, Johns Hopkins here in Maryland.

There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen. And I feel sorry for the poor folks in Iowa, as I do for people around the world who suffer these same sorts of fates, because the United States Army does what it wants and has acted in a Neanderthal fashion with its detonation and supposed disposal of hazardous materials.

AMY GOODMAN: Let’s talk about the effects —

AMY GOODMAN: — of lead, Pat Elder. If you can talk about the health concerns for lead exposure, especially for children and fetuses? The New York Times says lead is a neurotoxin, and there are no safe levels for exposure. Can you take it from there?

PAT ELDER: Well, I can, Amy. Thank you so much. We know, all the way from our experiences with leaded gas and lead paint, and the fiasco in Flint, Michigan — we have the clinical data — we understand that lead is a killer. It is a killer in the embryo. It is a killer for young children. And it is a killer for all of us.

But the Army would pretend that this is not the case, because — well, because it’s very fond of lead in ammunition. And so, we look around the country, and we see where the Army has been absolutely irresponsible in the way that it handles lead. We look at Fort Ord in California, for instance, and entire sand dunes are loaded with lead, and campers are allowed to traipse. They built an entire campus at the University of California, Monterey Bay, over top of old Army buildings with lead pipes. The poor kids are drinking lead. The Army is irresponsible when it comes to lead all around the world. It has buried it, and it has — supposed to be following a process, that it does not follow, to safely dispose of lead.

PAT ELDER: And I want to add, too —

PAT ELDER: Yeah, thanks. Just, you know, we’re not just dealing with lead here. We’re dealing with lead azide. And the best way to put this into focus is that lead azide is the explosive that detonates a bomb. So, if we have a 2,000-pound bomb that is falling on Gaza, lead azide the size of a small pea is detonated, which then sends a tremendous blast into the bomb itself. So, it is the explosive agent. And this is the material the Army is getting ready to detonate. And so, we’re not just talking about lead itself. We’re also talking about contaminations like hydrogen cyanide and hydrazoic acid. These are deadly. They deprive the brain of oxygen. And this is what is getting unleashed on the people of Iowa.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to ask you about that New York Times exposé on Saturday that may have surprised many, as so much of this has just crept up on them, the people of the community. It’s not as if this is a story that broke into the whole, you know, country. But they’ve been dealing with it for a while. Many residents did not know until the last few days what was about to happen. But The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option: a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded this contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead. Pat Elder, explain.

PAT ELDER: Well, we have to go back to March of 2025 to fully understand what has transpired. The Army itself, along with experts from the EPA and experts with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab here in Maryland, sat down, and they all voted that it would be too dangerous to detonate these materials, and that the way to do it is to saturate the exterior of these barrels, and the interior of these barrels once they are opened, with a chemical compound that is made of sulfur in water. And so, we spray that over the barrels. And when the Army says, “Well, this is too dangerous,” MuniRem, the company behind this process, has said that it would use robots, as it has in decontaminating other Army ammunition sites. So, the entire process and the entire culmination in the Army deciding suddenly that they would go ahead and detonate this material is lunacy.

And the idea that way back in August of 2025, we — the Army knew that there was a problem, and MuniRem knew there was a problem, and Johns Hopkins knew, and the EPA knew. The last people to find out are the people of Iowa and the people that live in the immediate area. They didn’t find out until last week. And that’s how the Army operates.

AMY GOODMAN: Pat Elder, I want to thank you for being with us, founder of the group Military Poisons. We’ll link to your piece, “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.”

Coming up, Egyptian writer Abdelrahman ElGendy. He just won the National Book Award for Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, but he wasn’t at the award ceremony. The U.S. denied ElGendy a visa. While he was a political prisoner in Egypt, starting when he was 17 years old, he published his writings in the Egyptian independent paper Mada Masr. Right now we are awaiting a court’s decision, an appeal of the government’s just closing down Mada Masr. We’ll go to Cairo, as well. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Massive Will” by Emel Mathlouthi, performing in our Democracy Now! studio. To see all the performances and interviews in our Democracy Now! studios of musicians and artists, go to democracynow.org.
