author: Brooke Siem
title: The Episode: A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing – A Conversation With Mary Ann Kenny
content:
W

elcome to the Mad in America podcast. My name is Brooke Siem, and I am the author of the award-winning memoir on antidepressant withdrawal, 

May Cause Side Effects

.




Today I am with Mary Ann Kenny. Mary Ann is an academic, and she lives in Dublin with her children. She is the author of the book, 

The Episode: A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing

.




In her book, Mary Ann details her descent into psychosis, her hopitalization, and her journey back to health and happiness. Drawing on her detailed medical files and on her own recollections, she has created a day-by-day account of what it is like to lose touch with reality while dealing with grief and living in the dreadful knowledge that everything you care about in life is under threat.




The transcript below has been edited for length and clarity. Listen to the audio of the interview here.







Brooke Siem: Mary Ann, welcome. I read your book in about two days; I just blew through the whole thing and thought it was fantastic. I think it is one of the best accounts of the complex nature of psychosis. Please tell us a little bit about your experience and 

The Episode

.




Mary Ann Kenny:

 Thank you, Brooke, for agreeing to interview me. I’m delighted to be here. Yes, I am the author of 

The Episode

, and the subtitle is 

A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing

. 

The Episode

 was published in the UK and Ireland last year. So far it hasn’t been published in the United States, but let’s hope that this is the first step to bring it and my story to an American audience.




I absolutely do think that what I experienced was a very clear episode of psychosis. Obviously, one of the purposes of our interview today is for me to describe that and to try to explain what I think caused it.




Siem: I think what was so interesting is that it just made me so angry to read how people were treating you. I feel like maybe I’m getting a little ahead of myself here, so let’s bring it back. Please tell me, where did this all start?




Kenny:

 My story began with a bereavement. A sudden and unexpected loss: my husband and partner of 15 years went out for a jog and died from undiagnosed heart disease in 2015; that’s when it all happened. We had two small children at the time, aged eight and six. It was completely unexpected and sudden. The three of us were left as exactly as you would expect, devastated and reeling from the shock.




To begin with, what I experienced was normal grief, I would say, looking back. It was devastating, it was debilitating, and it was deeply distressing. I was particularly heartbroken for my children’s sake. Most of my focus in the early months was on them and trying to keep the show on the road. The big change in my story happened when I took an SSRI for the first time.




Siem: Sertraline (Zoloft), right?




Kenny:

 Yes, 50 milligrams of sertraline.




Siem: Another reason why your story really brought up a lot of emotion in me was because my father also dropped dead very suddenly. One day he was there; one day he wasn’t. I was the child in this situation, so I watched my mother and distinctly remember the feeling of the subtraction. You went from four to three, we went from three to two, and how odd that period can be because life still keeps going. That’s how I got medicated: I got put on psych drugs.




I think I feel a kinship with you, specifically from that standpoint of being in that situation. What stood out to me is that we meet John, he dies fairly quickly, and we immediately go to the same situation that I experienced, which was, maybe you should see someone and not much time had passed. Can we talk about that a little bit?




Kenny:

 It was approximately two months after the bereavement, when people close to me started suggesting that I needed professional help. To begin with, it was therapy that they were suggesting. I did start to see a therapist. I had never been to therapy before in my life. I’d also never experienced anything that could be categorized as depression or anxiety. I felt at the time that it was working quite well.




He was an elderly gentleman who was providing support to me, practical support, helping me to get through, I suppose, day-to-day. I was seeing him once a week, and I used to feel better while I was with him. Then I suppose the sadness would return pretty quickly afterwards.




The advice I was receiving then from other people around me was, that’s clearly not working because I wasn’t showing any signs of improvement and that I should go and find a CBT therapist. I kind of raised that with the therapist, and he laughed back and said, “Well, what do you think we’ve been doing in our sessions together?” He took a very eclectic approach, which I wouldn’t criticise at all. I think it was working fine.




But because I was very distressed and I was very sad, the next thing I was advised to do was to try some medication. I was advised by friends and family that the medication might take the edge off the pain. I didn’t need to fear the medication because I was fearful of taking medication in that situation. I was already fearful enough about everything, about the future, about my children, and to begin with, I thought, no, I don’t think I want to go there. I don’t think this is going to help me. But eventually I thought, okay, if other people think that this might help, maybe it will help. I’ve never tried any kind of psychiatric medication before.




I did take a sleeping tablet for a week or two. Didn’t notice much benefit from that. I tried Xanax for the first time with a lot of hesitation and anxiety. I just tried it very tentatively, and it did seem to help. Not surprisingly, in retrospect, it’s an anxiolytic, and I was worried and panicked.




But the big change came when I was prescribed sertraline, and I had an immediate, severe, adverse reaction within hours of taking it. That’s when my whole grief story changed. I am very clear on that in my own mind. In my book, a lot of things are left to the reader to decide, and there are various reasons for that. But in my own mind, and especially as time goes by and I talk to more and more people, even since the publication of my book, I’m very clear that without that adverse reaction to sertraline, none of the rest of the story would have happened.




Siem: That was one of the big questions I was left with at the end of the book. Before we dig a little bit more into that, can we just get a little bit of the timeline of, okay, you take the sertraline, what happens, and what does that lead to?




Kenny:

 I took the sertraline three months after the bereavement. My husband died at the end of April, and at the start of August, that’s when I first took sertraline. I took it one night before I went to bed for the first time and I woke in the night in a complete panic, sweat and nausea and prickling and burning throughout my body. I was in a state of complete terror because I didn’t know what was happening to me. I couldn’t get back to sleep.




The following day, I thought, okay, I’ll take the next two doses of the drug in the hope that it would improve. My doctor had told me, “You might feel worse before you feel better on these drugs.”




Siem: When you took that Zoloft at night and woke up, did you associate what was happening to you with the drug in that moment?




Kenny:

 Yes, straight away. I returned to my doctor’s surgery as soon as I could, but it wasn’t open the first day after I took the medication. I spent that entire day in this state of terror and agitation, and burning was the big thing for me: this prickling and burning and stinging throughout my body, throughout my limbs, throughout my torso.




I dragged myself back to my doctor, and he said, clearly, there’s some kind of reaction, and we agreed that I would stop the drug. He said it should be out of your system in a few days and you’ll feel better then. That led to a few weeks, to begin with, of intense suffering on my part when these symptoms persisted just as strongly as the very first night, even though I had stopped taking the medication.




I returned to my own doctor, I went to an emergency department, and I had a home visit from a doctor. Each of the medics I talked to in that period conveyed to me that what I was describing didn’t match any diagnostic category that they were familiar with and that it was all in my head. Now, they didn’t say that phrase in so many words, but they made me understand. My own doctor, after maybe two weeks of me returning and trying to get help from other people, said, ” Okay, well, we’ll put you on venlafaxine (Effexor) and that it will work. It works for anxiety as well.”




The burning and stinging and prickling, what it meant for me was that I couldn’t sleep. I was sleeping a couple of hours a night. I wasn’t eating, barely functioning, barely managing to mind my children over those weeks in the summer. My sense of panic was growing because nobody seemed to believe me. Not only do I have this burning and stinging and prickling; not only has my husband died, now this has happened to me, and nobody believes me.




I went back again to my doctor towards the end of August, so three weeks after all of this started. She asked me, “Do you have thoughts of harm?” For the first time I was asked that question. I answered, “No, but with this prickling and stinging throughout my body, it’s hard for me to see a future for myself.” Based on that, I was referred to the local mental health service. That’s how my journey within psychiatry began.




Siem: As you said, the crux of this whole story lies in how professionals mishandled your clear physical adverse reaction to the Zoloft. Also, just another odd parallel in our story, when I went to get off my psych drugs, I remember them asking me the thoughts of harm question. I knew that that was like, you better be careful what you say here, because there’s a whole cascade of things that happen if this question is not handled in a very specific way. What happened when you said to the doctor that you weren’t sure you could see a future?




Kenny:

 I got an urgent assessment in the local mental health service within days. I was seen there for a crisis assessment, which consisted of an interview. During that interview, I was trying to convey the seriousness of my physical suffering.


I kept saying it was physical, and she kept interrogating me about my mental health. Fair enough, she asked me about my sleep, which was severely disrupted at this stage. She asked me about thoughts of harm. She said to me, if anything you say today suggests that you or anybody else is at risk, I’ll be obliged to report it. I think that put into my mind that they’re starting to doubt my ability to parent my children.




Siem: The seed was planted.




Kenny:

 Yes. On the basis of that interview, I was asked to start attending a day hospital, and I started going there every morning while my body was burning; my body was on fire. I couldn’t sleep. I was in severe distress. When I went there first, I met my first psychiatrist; I had never met a psychiatrist before in my life. The psychiatrist adjusted my medication. I was put on a sleeping tablet, and I was put on clonazepam, a benzodiazepine. I was asked to start attending every day workshops, group sessions, art therapy, music therapy.




I was sitting through these sessions with my body on fire, not able to concentrate on anything, severely sleep-deprived, and pleading with them to give me a physical examination, and not getting anywhere with my pleas. That was when, it was in that context with my body burning, not being heard, not being able to get help, having to attend these workshops every day, having to make sure my children were minded—I’m still struggling the whole time with childminding arrangements—that I experienced a break with reality. That’s when whatever we want to call it, the madness, the psychosis, the break, happened to me.




Siem: Was it quick for you? Because my interpretation of it in the book was that it was rather gradual. It had a lot to do with the way other people kept responding, everything you said every time you questioned it.




Kenny:

 I have traced in the book where that came from, how it developed, how it developed from a situation of grieving to begin with, of being low on energy, low on resources, through the burning in my body, not being able to sleep, not eating, not drinking, not being heard. I have read up on the psychosocial causes of psychosis. It’s very plausible for me to believe that psychosis can be caused by a situation in which the person themselves believes that their situation is intolerable, and where there has been a severe, I suppose, undermining of their identity.




The situation for me then, at that time, was that nobody was hearing me. I have this excruciating burning throughout my body. I’m never going to get better. That’s what I believed, because it had been persisting now for three, four weeks. Nobody’s hearing me. Nobody’s investigating it. I’m never going to be able to mother my children again the way I want to. I’m never going to be able to go back to work. This is what I believed. So I do believe that a situation like that, where you, as the sufferer, believe that really there is no future for you, because everything that your identity consisted of up to then has been destroyed, that can tip you into psychosis.




You asked, was it gradual or sudden? I think it was both. I think the gradual decline was there over several weeks. I did start to become a bit paranoid. But you know what’s funny about paranoia, because you’re becoming suspicious about things, but there is some truth in there as well.




Siem: That’s what I felt. There is all the reason in the world to be suspicious of everything that’s coming out of these people’s mouths. She’s not being listened to at all.




Kenny:

 I became suspicious of the medication. But then I began to become a little bit more suspicious, where the suspicion flipped into something else, because they sent me for a blood test, and I kind of wondered, what are they testing? Do they think I’m on some kind of illicit drugs here or something? In my mind, that’s when it started. It all started with the medication. I started to think the medication that they’re giving me is not the medication that they’re saying it is. I started to become very suspicious about the medication. It kind of very gradually flipped into something that was not based in reality. Then the major break with reality, the actual heart of my psychosis, happened very suddenly in that context.




Siem: Was that the relationship with your children? Can you tell us what happened there?




Kenny:

 It was a specific evening; I don’t know the date off the top of my head, but it was the twenty-something of August, 2015. I went with my children to the supermarket and with a friend of ours as well. I believed for 20 minutes that I had lost my older son. I couldn’t find him. I was with the younger boy in the supermarket.




In a way, it’s a classic situation that any mother would be terrified of. I thought I’d lost him. I was looking everywhere for him. I took my younger boy by the hand and we went outside the supermarket and we were wandering around looking for him back into the supermarket. I found him there with my friend. My friend had been minding him all along, but I experienced probably half an hour of extreme terror in that supermarket. I just thought my husband had died and I’d lost my child. My body’s burning. Everything is over for me.




We returned home from the supermarket; my two children, myself and my friend, and I went to bed with my two children. I mean, we’d been sleeping in the same bed for months. I hadn’t been sleeping. They’d been sleeping. While we were in bed, while they fell asleep, I remember looking at them and thinking something had happened to them. Something had happened inside their heads. I remember looking very closely at one of my sons and, for a moment, I wasn’t sure if he was actually breathing, but he was breathing. But I thought that their brains were dissolving inside their heads. That something had happened to their brains.




Then I thought to myself, my God, they have swallowed my medication. That’s what’s happened. I’ve left that medication lying around somewhere. It’s my fault. I either carelessly left it lying somewhere, or maybe I dropped it into the food when I was cooking. But something has happened to their brains, and I was filled with horror. Nothing else happened, but what I did was I got up, and I went outside, and I walked around in the dark in a state of extreme agitation. But at least I did get myself moving, got myself out there and calmed myself down a little bit.




I know people listening will be thinking, gosh, did she do something? Was she going to do something? It was never the case that anything else happened. But I do think, looking back, that was probably the closest that I ever came in the whole episode that something might have happened. Now, when I listen to the likes of Lindsay Clancy, well, what if a voice had said something at that moment—but nothing like that happened, and it never happened.




But that was the moment when I started to believe that I had ruined my children’s lives, and I was pretty specific about it: that they had swallowed my medication and their brains were, you could say, kind of dying inside them. I can completely analyze where that belief came from because I do it in the book, but it took me three years of writing that book to understand. But that belief that I had destroyed my children’s lives through my medication, it held me in its grip for two months.




What’s also very interesting, and it’s jumping right ahead, is that when all of this was over, I was able to distinguish very clearly in my head between what had happened and what had not happened. I do not doubt what happened and what didn’t happen. The burning happened completely even though, in my records, it actually says somewhere that I was hallucinating those. It’s just so arrogant and insulting that one of the medics decided retrospectively that I had been hallucinating those bodily sensations. I hadn’t been. The burning belongs on the side of things that really happened.




There’s so little understanding out there, as you and I both know, of psychosis, of severe mental illness, and how it happens on a continuum. It was a gradual undermining of my entire person, physical and mental, that eventually led to me just losing it.




Siem: It felt like you were attempting to be heard the entire time. You said, “Other people decided and monitored what I ate, when I slept, what drugs I took, when I could see my children, and even what my words meant and what my real thoughts were.”




I thought that was particularly poignant because it kind of just summed up the whole thing to me that, at the end of the day, these professionals were making the whole story up about what they thought was happening to you. You had no power to unearth that, even though it was happening to you.




Kenny:

 There’s a lot that happens in that story and in that book. There’s a lot of layers to it. But you’re absolutely right that a thread that goes through the whole thing, pretty much from start to finish, is that nobody would listen to me. I tried to set the record straight before I was discharged from the hospital. I was met with absolutely deaf ears. I was told that I lacked insight.




I mean, it really is kind of head-wrecking, because I never had the thoughts that they said I had. But I eventually got accused of having thoughts of harm that I never had. I was found guilty by child protection services here in Ireland of having thoughts. But I’d never had the thoughts.




I tell you, trying to write that book, Brooke, it nearly broke my head, just trying to get my head around the fact that I was found guilty of thoughts of harm that I never had.




Siem: Who hasn’t had thoughts? Who, under stress, doesn’t think to themselves, well, this might be easier if I wasn’t here?




Kenny:

 No, it’s head-wrecking. The thoughts that I actually had, which was, I think I’ve done something to them, nobody would listen to me about that. But I was accused. I was found guilty of thoughts of harm that I never had, and my children’s names were put on the Child Protection Register until the age of 18. I was punished. I wasn’t just found guilty; I was punished for thoughts of harm that I never had.




Siem: It’s absolutely mind-blowing. Once you got out of the psychiatric hospital and started looking at the situation a little bit more objectively, did anyone in your life, including the professionals, question this cocktail of drugs and whether or not they were contributing to the situation?




Kenny:

 No, I’ve got my records. Obviously, they’ve been redacted, but there isn’t the slightest question in there about the drugs. There are documents in there showing that I was on unlicensed levels of antipsychotics and antidepressants that carried significant physical risks of heart problems and blood pressure. That’s in there that I needed monitoring; nobody thought to question it. Is that appropriate?




Siem: In retrospect now, what is your relationship with the amount of drugs you were on and how everything played out?




Kenny:

 Horrified. They took a sledgehammer to me, pharmaceutically. They threw everything at me. They decided that it was okay to put my physical health at risk.




Siem: What about your mental health?




Kenny:

 Those drugs turned me into a zombie. I’ve read Joanna Moncrieff and how she explains how antipsychotics and antidepressants, how those drugs can work in the sense that they turn you into a zombie and then maybe you stop worrying about your delusions. Perhaps that happened because something cleared up that delusion while I was in hospital. It was the delusional belief that I had harmed my children and destroyed their lives. That’s what plunged me into a deep depression.




I spent a total of 12 weeks in hospital, and that delusional belief did clear up. I was turned into a complete zombie. I had so many worries. I say in the book that I had so many real-world worries, from who was minding my children to the involvement of child protection services, who had been told that I had these thoughts of harm that I didn’t have.




Foster care had been mentioned to me as a possibility. I had been told that I wouldn’t have unsupervised access to my children when I was discharged from hospital. I was never given an update on that. I had so many things to be worried about while I was the zombie that somehow my delusional belief cleared up. But as I do say in the book, maybe there’s just a limit to the number of things you can worry about at the same time. Did they have to do it like that? No. I mean, could they just have given me some time, not tortured me with questions like, ” Do you have thoughts of harm?” because that was a form of torture that eventually led me to offer up incriminating details. But the fact is that I did recover while I was in hospital. But when I was discharged, I was on very heavy doses of two antipsychotics and two antidepressants, and I was gradually tapered off those.




Siem: Thank God somebody had the sense to pull you off slowly because, going through it, you went through it twice.




Kenny:

 They did start to bring me off the antipsychotics to begin with after I was discharged from the hospital, partly because I developed a metabolic problem that was increased levels of prolactin, and then eventually off the antidepressants after another year, but it took two years for the tapering process. One of the doctors I know wanted me to stay on an antidepressant long term, and I had to push to come off.




It was when I came off those drugs after two years that I started to feel the whole hurt, anger and outrage over what had happened to me at a time in my life when my husband had died. I had done nothing worse than losing my husband and suffering an adverse reaction to a drug. I was practically annihilated. I nearly lost my children. I nearly lost my physical health. None of it needed to happen.




Siem: One of the things that made me want to throw the book across the room was when you pointed out how, at the peak of this psychosis, it was the exact time when they would basically put you in front of a medical firing squad and ask you to answer questions that would determine the future of you and your children. The amount of pressure for someone who was not under the influence that you were would have been enormous, and then to do it when somebody was so compromised physically, mentally and emotionally, I just, like, I have no words for how cruel that is.




Kenny:

 I got my records, and I used those records to write the book. All those team meetings, I mean, the records are a fantastic resource. They’re horrifying, but they’re a fantastic resource to write a book with. I’d recommend it to anyone. What they used to do at those team meetings was have up to eight professionals in the room with me, interrogating me. They’d literally have a laptop with them and type in the discussion while I’m speaking. I mean, talk about counter-therapeutic.




But it’s a fantastic record of everything that was said. I used those records to reconstruct those team meetings. I’m telling my story, but at the same time, I’m holding up a mirror to the mental health service to show them their story, what their story about me was, and what my story was at the same time, and how those two stories just diverge further and further and, and how horrifying that gap is between what was happening to me and what they were writing into their records. It does capture, I think, very well, the nature of those interrogations and team meetings.




Siem: Have you spoken to any of the people on that team, since you’ve recovered and your book has been out?




Kenny:

 No, that’s the simple answer. Not a single person has contacted me, even anonymously. There were two services involved with me at the time. There was the psychiatric service, and there was the child protection service. My children’s names, as I said, were entered into an at-risk register until they turned 18 on the basis of these thoughts of harm that I’d never had. My younger son turned 18 recently. I just thought I had these extra copies of the book lying around. I picked out five people, five middle managers whose names were familiar to me for my records. I sent each of them a copy.




I said, “Given that you don’t appear to have a feedback mechanism, my children have turned 18. You haven’t asked me for my feedback about what this whole experience was like for me at the time. So please accept my book as my feedback.” Now, two of those books have been returned to me, returned to sender. Look, does it give us any satisfaction? I’m not sure.




One thing it made me think, though, was that I thought they were aware of my book, because it might not be known in the US, but it’s known in Ireland. It got a lot of traction when it came out last year; it got an awful lot of publicity in the mainstream media. Not that they necessarily dealt with all the issues I would have liked them to.




Siem: My sense of that is there’s a surprising kind of ripple effect that can happen when it finds people, and they start thinking about it. Sometimes it ends up having an impact in ways that don’t feel direct or expected. But it does make a difference.




Kenny:

 The other thing I was disappointed by really was that it would have been nice to think that there might’ve been some general response to my story. Not individual doctors or people who were involved, but just are we as a society, are we okay with this? Are we okay with somebody who’s suffered a very tragic loss and a reaction to a drug, having this happen to her, to one of our citizens? It seems we are okay with that apparently, and I just don’t think we should be. That was one of my big motivations for publishing this book.




Siem: I think it really comes down to the question you were asked over and over again, which is, do you have thoughts about, harmful thoughts about hurting yourself or somebody else? There’s an element of that that feels very altruistic but the more I think about this, that this is just a purely selfish thing out of fear, where it’s like, you are making us uncomfortable. We’re going to make it go away. I just think that there’s such a lack of common sense and deep intuition about people who may truly be committing a crime versus people who are just having a human experience.




Kenny:

 The whole area of harm is so interesting. I mean, just the harm that was done to me at a time when they were all obsessed with harm. It’s all they could think about. Does she have thoughts of harm? The harm that was done to my children and me by keeping me away from them for four weeks. That’s where the harm was done.




Siem: If you could go back and rewrite this timeline, what do you think should have been done differently?




Kenny:

 I never would have taken the medication in the first place. I didn’t have a lot of support in the early months. I’m not sure what can be done about that in the society we live in. If services are going to ramp up and get involved so much as they did later on, then how about getting involved early on? As it happens, I didn’t have a support network for various reasons to do with my family, who have all emigrated, a typical Irish diaspora and friends living far away. How about getting involved at the beginning when it matters? Treat somebody compassionately and listen to what they’re saying, I think, is absolutely key, you know, and investigate the adverse reaction.




Siem: What would you say to somebody else who is maybe in the beginning stages of a similar experience? How would you help somebody who came to you in a similar situation?




Kenny:

 Well, I do know somebody at the moment, and she’s about six months into having lost her husband, and she has children. It wasn’t a sudden loss. I met her, and she’s desperately sad. I just talked to her without trying to be clichéd, but on the basis of my experience, it’s normal to be sad; it’s normal to suffer, and she will feel better in time. It’s okay for me to say that because I know, and to keep doing what she’s doing. I meet her, we go swimming and just do stuff that makes you feel physically better and gives your mind time to catch up with this terrible blow and terrible loss that has happened.




It’s a very hard thing for the psyche to come to terms with a big loss like that with your partner and everything that that means in your life, but give it time, and don’t go near drugs. It’s not an illness; it’s a natural process, bitter and terrible as it is. I do not doubt that I would have come out the other side in time. I would have just started to feel that little bit better. I was impatient with myself. I would say to anybody, don’t be impatient, give yourself time.




Siem: Well, my goodness, I am so sorry for what you’ve been through and also so grateful that you had the experience and literary chops to write a really outstanding work about how this felt. I hope a lot of people read this.




Kenny:

 I hope it’s helpful to other people because I do think it contains a lot of insights. I worked very hard to produce this book, and I read a lot of research as well.




Siem: Do you have any last words for the audience, and where can they find you and reach out?




Kenny:

 I mean, I would love you to read my book, obviously, and I’d love you to reach out. You can Google me, and I’m on Instagram and Facebook, and my work email address will come up at TU Dublin, one of the Dublin universities. No problem at all in finding me, and I’d be delighted if anybody would like to make contact with me.

author: Acratosaurio rex
title: Un argumento a favor del voto
content:
Aquí el bueno de Graeber, pensando que soy imbécil







Hay un argumento que me ha conmovido, en esto de ir a votar: cuando la ultraderecha gobierne, los derechos de inmigrantes, mujeres, homosexuales serán cercenados… Habrá racismo antigitano, se prohibirá el aborto, se aprobarán las terapias de conversión… Volveremos a la situación que había en 1702. Y, por supuesto: yo quiero el fin del patriarcado, la desaparición de las fronteras, y la autodeterminación de los cuerpos. Así que me pongo a pensar que decididamente, tengo que votar.




Pero, un momento… ¿No es verdad que a este punto en el que estamos, hemos llegado de la mano de los partidos que habitan en el parlamento? Porque el PSOE ha gobernado en ocho legislaturas; el PP en cuatro. La ultraderecha española se refunda en 2013, y desde entonces, elección tras elección, ha incrementado su presencia parlamentaria.




¿Cómo es posible, que teniendo la izquierda más experiencia y más tiempo de funcionamiento, saque menos parlamentarios que un grupo de fascistas? ¿No son los poderes públicos los que nos han traído hasta aquí? Resulta que el PSOE ha gobernado España casi treinta años. Y el PP algo más de catorce años. ¿Y hay que votar para impedir el racismo, la xenofobia y la homofobia? ¡Ostras Reputas! ¿No es que gracias a las elecciones, cada vez hay más y más fachas? Joder, si es que el Proceso Electoral parece  una puñetera fábrica de reaccionarios recalcitrantes. Ahí va.




Bueno, me lo voy a pensar. Voy a pensar votar, por si acaso, a Podemos. Que su presidenta es muy simpática.

title: Gelawêj Ewrîn: Jin Jiyan Azadî is a philosophy beyond borders - Part Two
content:
Gelawêj Ewrîn, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), spoke to ANF about state repression against women in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat), the struggle for women's freedom, the philosophy of Jin Jiyan Azadî (Woman, Life, Freedom) and the impact of war on women.




The first part of this interview can be read 

here

. 




How have the attacks by the United States and Israel against Iran affected the lives of women and children?




The consequences of war for women are multifaceted. Losing loved ones, forced displacement, economic insecurity, deprivation of healthcare, the growing burden of childcare and having to sustain life under the constant threat of death leave deep wounds in women's lives. Since the beginning of Iran's war with the United States and Israel, we have witnessed the killing and massacre of women on an extremely horrifying scale. On the one hand, the state keeps women under constant repression through arrests, killings and severe punishments.




On the other hand, the difficulties created by wartime conditions in present-day Iran are further deepening and intensifying social problems. Domestic violence has increased significantly. When men cannot draw strength from the state and feel powerless in the face of it, they direct all their anger and hatred towards women and children. Over the past few months, more than 20 women have been murdered by men using brutal and fascistic methods.




One of the greatest dangers of war for Eastern Kurdistan is that the democratic and national demands of the Kurdish people will once again be overshadowed by security policies. During wars, states seek to place their security and existence above everything else and create a political atmosphere around this understanding. Under these conditions, the demands of different peoples for identity, freedom, equality and equal democratic representation can easily be defined as threats. This creates a dual uncertainty for Kurdish women. On the one hand, there is repression by the Iranian state; on the other, there is the instability and uncertainty of war brought about by external military interventions.




The trauma that war leaves in society's collective memory also causes immense devastation. Women are forced to live with the consequences of war not only during attacks but also long after the fighting has ended. The loss of loved ones, destruction of homes, economic poverty, trauma experienced by children and uncertainty about society's future can persist for years. Therefore, women's security in Eastern Kurdistan is not simply a matter of protecting them from military attacks. The fundamental issue is building a democratic life in which women can feel secure politically, economically, culturally and socially.




How might war affect national rights, democratic representation and the Kurdish people's demands to determine their own future?




It is wrong to assume that war will automatically produce positive results for peoples' struggles for freedom. The military weakening of a state does not mean that the peoples living within that country will automatically become free. Similarly, a change of regime does not guarantee the establishment of a democratic society. In discussions about Iran's future, the fundamental question is not merely how the current government will be replaced. The real question is what kind of political and social system will be established in its place. The future of the Kurdish people cannot be tied solely to the military and political calculations of external powers. The Kurdish people's national rights, democratic representation and demand to determine their own future cannot be defined according to the interests of any state. Nor can they be shaped according to the interests of capital.




A political system must be established in Eastern Kurdistan in which people can live freely with their own identities, languages and democratic will. For this reason, it is important to consider the solution within the perspective of a democratic republic and democratic federation. From our perspective, the issue is neither the fragmentation of Iran nor the continuation of the existing centralised structure under another name. The issue is building a political system in which different peoples and faiths can live together on the basis of equality, freedom and democracy. Women's will must be decisive in the construction of this system. A genuinely democratic system cannot be established without women's freedom.




How is the Iranian government using wartime conditions to intensify repression against opposition groups and women's rights defenders?




The Iranian government's use of wartime conditions to intensify political repression and maintain security policies is a characteristic of the state's historical nature. In an atmosphere of war, it becomes easier to silence opposition voices, unite society around a single ideology under the pretext of so-called national security and portray different political demands as acts of hostility. The portrayal of social movements as terrorist threats and the legitimisation of the state's brutal practices pave the way for fascism. The Islamic Republic is also laying the groundwork for civil war by organising various radical and extremist groups. In this way, the state seeks to portray criticism of its policies as unacceptable under wartime conditions.




Women's rights defenders, human rights activists, journalists, Kurdish political circles and other opposition groups are directly affected by this repression. The state seeks to prevent uprisings in the streets through repression. Yet social struggle in the streets can be considered one of the most effective ways of transforming authoritarian and repressive systems. The massacres last winter showed us that this regime can kill thousands of people in a single night to maintain its power and then attempt to cover it up. It is also possible to describe this massacre as the largest massacre of women in Iran's recent history.




Such massacres remind people of the Middle Ages. In those periods, thousands of women were also massacred within a few nights under pretexts legitimised by the male-dominated state to strengthen its own existence. The massacre last winter, in which more than 50,000 people were reportedly killed, including women and children, left an extremely disturbing image in the collective memory of all of us and Iranian society. Those black bags! Those who were massacred were people at the forefront of the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution and all the social and political movements in Iran. Among them were women students, teachers, intellectuals, workers and artists. The intellectual life and collective memory of Iranian society were massacred on such a dark night. An entire sea of the country's most knowledgeable, valuable and pioneering people was destroyed.




How can women's right to speak out and resist both external military intervention and the Iranian regime's repressive policies be guaranteed?




Women's struggle for freedom must not be tied to the political interests of any military power or state. Women have the right to speak out against both the repressive policies of the Iranian government and the devastation caused by external military interventions. Women must be able to express themselves through their independent political will, organise and make decisions about their own future. The current war has emerged as a result of the Iranian regime's policies. Iran is fighting to maintain its hegemony in the region. It appears that this war, the conflicts and the chaos will continue for many years. What will determine the outcome and save society from collapse is the social struggle that Iranian women can lead. This reality has been demonstrated.




For this reason, it is important for women to organise in every sphere from now on. The state regards wartime conditions as a pretext and is organising everywhere, both openly and covertly. So to speak, an entirely militaristic system that also makes extensive use of women is coming to dominate every sphere. It is forcibly accustoming young people, even young girls, to the use of weapons and dragging society down an irreversible path. Organisational, cultural, social and artistic activities can therefore lift the shadow of this fascism from Iranian society, particularly women. If society remains silent, the state will seek to organise in every sphere and impose its policies on everyone under the pretext of war and a state of emergency. The determination and spirit of the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution will once again lift this veil of death from Iranian society as a whole.




Is the nationalist and militaristic atmosphere created by war pushing women's demands for freedom into the background? How can the Jin Jiyan Azadî perspective be preserved under these conditions?




During wars, nationalism and militarism grow stronger, while social issues are pushed into the background. Women's demands for freedom are often presented as secondary matters that must be postponed. Women are told that the war must end, state security must be ensured and national unity must be established before anything else. However, history has shown us that no political system that continually postpones women's freedom to the future has brought genuine freedom. This is precisely where the importance of the Jin Jiyan Azadî philosophy becomes clear. This philosophy treats women's freedom as a demand that cannot be postponed or left for the future. Women's freedom must be regarded as the starting point of social transformation.




We now all know very well that life cannot be free without women's freedom, and that a democratic society cannot be built without a free life. Therefore, preserving the spirit of the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution under wartime conditions is the responsibility of all women. This is possible by developing women's organisations, strengthening unity among women without discrimination, taking control of their economic and social lives and developing mechanisms of self-defence. Women's struggle for freedom must not disappear within the nationalist and militaristic atmosphere created by war. On the contrary, it must become the force that builds democratic life and social peace against the devastation of war.




Can regime change or the transformation of Iran's political system alone guarantee women's freedom? Why must women play a direct role and become the decisive actors in shaping their own future?




A change of the current regime in Iran could bring about major political developments. Iranian women would be the most affected by such a change. However, would regime change alone be sufficient to meet women's demands? When a regime changes, the patriarchal mentality, statist understanding and power relations on which that structure was built may continue to exist. Simply replacing those in power does not mean that society has become free. One of the greatest dangers for Iran's future is that the current authoritarian system could be replaced by another centralised and patriarchal system. In such a situation, the problems faced by women would continue in different forms. For us as women, freedom does not merely mean bringing an administration to an end, but removing relations of power and domination from social life.




Women must not be regarded as parties who join the process only after this transformation has begun. A democratic society cannot be built without women. Women must participate equally and decisively in political decision-making mechanisms, establish their own organisations and take responsibility for every sphere of social life. Women must make decisions about their own future. This is not merely a question of representation or quotas. Politics must be freed from male-state domination and become the politics of society as a whole. Those who make laws concerning women and take important decisions are representatives of the dominant male mentality that continually excludes women from these mechanisms. Change does not mean excluding women, but ensuring that they play a fundamental role in the transformation process. Of course, this can be achieved primarily through women's own struggle. A foundation for struggle must be established in which women can speak, make their own decisions and determine their future. Genuine freedom is not a solution imposed from outside; it is a way of life built through society's organised will.




What perspective do women's demands for freedom, equality and a democratic society in Eastern Kurdistan offer for the post-war future?




The women's struggle in Eastern Kurdistan also provides an answer to the question of what kind of society should be built after the war ends. From our perspective, what needs to be done after the war is not merely rebuilding buildings, improving economic conditions or establishing a new political administration. The fundamental issue is reorganising society on a democratic basis. Within this framework, women's demands for freedom and equality must form the foundation of a new social life. Iran's anti-women laws must be changed. The rights of all peoples, beginning with women's rights, must be guaranteed by law. Women's free and equal participation in education, healthcare, the economy, politics and culture must not be limited to guaranteeing individual rights. Women must also establish their own institutions and organisations. The development of a democratic society is possible through strengthening local people's assemblies, women's assemblies, communes and democratic decision-making mechanisms.




Women have a strong historical and cultural role within the social structure of Eastern Kurdistan. It is important to combine this social standing with a perspective for a democratic future. Iran is a rich country, and the traces of the mother-woman culture run very deep within it. Through the Jin Jiyan Azadî Revolution, it has therefore returned to its roots. Today, the sociological dimensions of this return need to be properly understood. Women's freedom is also a fundamental condition for society to take responsibility for itself and govern its own life. Therefore, our perspective for the post-war period is not merely the establishment of a new state system, but the construction of a democratic society. The more democratic society becomes, the less significant the existence of laws and the state in general becomes. It is a democratic society that makes a state democratic. A democratic society, in turn, consists of free individuals.




What perspective for transformation does the struggle of the Free Women’s Society of Eastern Kurdistan (KJAR offer in the face of state repression and gender inequality?




KJAR's approach to women's freedom does not regard women as a section of society seeking to obtain more rights within the existing system. It regards women as the founding force of social life, the pioneers of democratic transformation and a force that determines its own future. In this approach, women's freedom cannot be separated from the freedom of society. Women's self-organisation, the development of their economic and social independence, their participation in political decision-making mechanisms and their struggle against the patriarchal mentality are fundamental conditions for a democratic society. One of the important dimensions of the transformation developed by KJAR is the strengthening of women's autonomous organisations. Without the organisation of society, it is impossible to ensure the continuity of demands for freedom. Women's assemblies, academies, economic solidarity networks and women's self-defence mechanisms play an important role in the development of a democratic society.




How can women's movements in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan unite their struggles?




The unification of the struggles of women's movements in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan must also be considered on this basis. Kurdish, Persian, Baloch, Azeri, Turkmen, Gilaki, Lur and women from other peoples must establish common ground for freedom while preserving their different identities and experiences. This unity does not mean eliminating differences, but bringing them together on the basis of democratic unity. The aim must be a social system in which every people can freely live according to their own language, culture and identity, and in which women become the founding force of this democratic unity. The historical impact created by Jin Jiyan Azadî in Iran demonstrates that such a common struggle is possible. The unity developing among women is not merely a collective response to state repression, but also a search for a new social life. This struggle can be strengthened when women stand together in the face of one another's suffering and resistance. However, for it to become a sustained struggle, common organisational mechanisms, intellectual discussions and social solidarity must be developed.




What is your message to women struggling against violence, repression and inequality in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan on the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November?




Violence against women is not merely an individual problem; it is a consequence of the historical and institutionalised structure of the patriarchal system of power. Therefore, the struggle against violence must not be limited to opposing its consequences, but must aim to transform the mentality and social relations that produce it. Protecting women's right to life also means protecting their right to freedom. We must not be satisfied with simply saying that women should live; we must guarantee that they can live freely, organise themselves and exercise their own will. Today, women's struggle in Iran and Eastern Kurdistan continues despite all forms of repression. This struggle goes beyond opposition to a regime; it represents a new way of life that challenges thousands of years of patriarchal mentality.




The truth that Jin Jiyan Azadî has shown us is that society cannot become free without women's freedom. A democratic future cannot be built without women's will and organised strength. Therefore, we regard 25 November not merely as a day to condemn violence, but as a day to strengthen women's struggle for freedom, organisation and a democratic society. The freedom of women and society is not something that can be postponed or left to time. Freedom is a way of life that must be built starting today. Women everywhere, under all circumstances, must refuse to accept what is imposed upon them and turn every sphere of their lives into a field of struggle.

title: Karstarlı: HABAŞ has seen repeated workplace deaths
content:
The explosion at the HABAŞ Iron and Steel Factory in the Aliağa district of Izmir, which claimed the lives of 19 workers, has once again brought occupational health and safety measures in Turkey into focus. According to data from the Workers' Health and Workplace Safety Assembly (ISIG), at least 1,930 workers lost their lives in workplace killings during the first ten months of 2026. In 2025, at least 2,105 workers were recorded as having died in workplace killings.




The decision to release the company's owner under house arrest following the explosion at HABAŞ has also sparked debate over the judicial process.




Selçuk Karstarlı, a volunteer with the ISIG Assembly and a Class A occupational safety expert, spoke to ANF about the problems affecting occupational health and safety in Turkey.




'A massacre of the working class'




Karstarlı said that the figures published in ISIG Assembly reports and the worker deaths that can be documented reflect only part of the reality. He stressed that comparisons with Social Security Institution (SGK) records reveal that the scale of workplace killings is considerably greater than reported.




Karstarlı emphasised that ISIG Assembly reports cover only the worker deaths that can be identified: "Data on occupational safety can be found to a certain extent in the ISIG Assembly's reports on workplace killings. I say 'to a certain extent' because these reports cover only the deaths we can identify. However, comparisons with SGK data show that the reality is far worse than what is visible. Because we are aware of this, we publish all our reports using the phrase 'at least'. Looking at the deaths we have been able to document, we see at least 1,930 workers killed in the first ten months of 2026 alone, and at least 2,105 in 2025.




This clearly amounts to a massacre of the working class. Moreover, deaths caused by occupational diseases are not included in these reports because occupational diseases are almost never diagnosed in our country. The system has been structured in a way that prevents their identification. Yet various academic studies indicate that between 20,000 and 30,000 deaths from diseases, particularly cancer, can be attributed to occupational risks. What we are witnessing can, in fact, be described as outright class destruction and a massacre of workers."




'The metal industry has never seen a massacre of this scale'




Karstarlı addressed the workplace killings brought back into focus by the HABAŞ explosion, noting that the metal industry had never previously experienced a disaster of this magnitude. He stressed that what happened at HABAŞ was foreseeable: "We have witnessed many such massacres in the mining industry. The massacres in Hendek, Gayrettepe, Dilovası and Davutpaşa were also major disasters. However, the metal industry had never before witnessed a massacre of this scale at such a large industrial facility. The massacre at HABAŞ was neither unforeseeable nor unexpected. We already knew that this was a workplace where workers had repeatedly been killed.




There had been explosions before, even if they did not result in deaths. A worker had died just four days before the massacre. Even the company's own sustainability reports show an increase in workplace accidents. In other words, as with all the other massacres, this was a disaster that was clearly approaching.




According to our Assembly's records, we documented 19 workplace killings between 2013 and this massacre. Press reports also reveal seven workplace killings before 2013. This means that, in addition to the 19 workers killed in the latest massacre, there had already been 26 workplace killings and dozens of injured workers whose exact number we do not know. So what sanctions did HABAŞ face despite all these deaths? Not a single day's work was suspended, and the company faced no sanctions. To use the words of Minister of Labour and Social Security Vedat Işıkhan, inspections did not cause the company any difficulties. On the contrary, the company expanded while receiving substantial financial incentives. Mehmet Rüştü Başaran received a negligible sentence for previous workplace killings, and the announcement of the verdict was deferred, effectively ensuring that he faced no punishment.




What we see here is a recurring reality in Turkey: an employer who kills workers by failing to take precautions, a state that fails to inspect the employer, and a judicial system in which those truly responsible are not punished or, even when convicted, do not go to prison. This chain can be seen in every workplace killing.




We saw the same pattern after this massacre. While Başaran was effectively rewarded with house arrest in his waterfront mansion, he issued instructions from there banning workers from entering the factory with mobile phones. Workers who opposed this decision were beaten and detained by the police. This was a clear attempt to conceal evidence. That alone should have been grounds for his detention.




So what would we expect if normal legal standards were applied? All operations at HABAŞ should have been suspended and a thorough investigation launched at the facility. Given the seriousness of the offence and the risk of flight or evidence tampering, pre-trial detention should have been imposed. But whom does the judiciary detain instead of Mehmet Rüştü Başaran? It imprisons Can Atalay and Selçuk Kozağaçlı, lawyers involved in the Soma and Hendek workplace massacre cases. In short, this massacre is a systemic problem."




'Most workplace killings occur in construction, agriculture and transport'




Karstarlı said that the highest numbers of workplace killings over the past year had occurred in the construction, agriculture and transport sectors. He drew attention to the main causes of worker deaths and the structural problems underlying them: "If you examine the ISIG Assembly's data, you will see that most deaths occur in construction, agriculture and transport. Traffic accidents, including accidents involving workers' transport vehicles, crushing incidents, collapses and falls from heights are among the leading causes of death. But these are merely the visible technical causes. Looking at the underlying reality, we can say that what has made working life so dangerous is the chain I mentioned earlier: failure to take precautions, lack of inspections and impunity.




We must also consider the organisational problems facing the working class. Today, the unionisation rate in Turkey is around 14 percent, and trade unions are unable to move beyond wage bargaining. The absence of an organised working class fighting for safe working conditions allows a system in which workers' lives are left at the mercy of employers."




'We know the Palace regime for its harsh measures against workers'




Karstarlı said that the government had failed to take a position in favour of workers in cases of workplace killings and stressed that those responsible must be prosecuted: "Perhaps the most devastating consequence of this situation is the sheer number of workplace killings. But there is another side of the picture that remains largely unseen: lost limbs, occupational diseases and deteriorating health. In this grim situation, the Palace government, which effectively protects employers, particularly the Minister of Labour and Social Security and senior officials responsible for the inspection system, bears primary responsibility for these massacres. They must be prosecuted because their failure to fulfil their duties has caused these deaths.




We also know this same Palace regime for the harsh measures it takes against workers. It bans strikes, which are workers' legal right when seeking to secure their demands. It uses police violence against workers dismissed for union membership who then organise protests. It even imposes province-wide bans on demonstrations to prevent textile workers from protesting. I would say that this regime is, in every sense, a government serving capital."




'The situation may not change even if governments change'




Karstarlı stressed that organised struggle is the most important condition for preventing workplace killings. He said that workers must organise, occupational safety measures must be strengthened and inspection mechanisms must operate effectively to prevent further deaths.




Selçuk Karstarlı outlined the measures he believes are necessary: "First and foremost, the working class and oppressed people must organise. Organised struggle is essential to refuse unsafe work and improve safety measures in workplaces. Social opposition is also necessary to force the Ministry of Labour to carry out workplace inspections.




Otherwise, the situation may remain unchanged even if governments change. Judicial practice must also change. Although the law places responsibility on employers to take every necessary precaution, it is often engineers, occupational safety experts and other salaried employees who are prosecuted instead of employers, even though they have no influence over financial decisions or investments.




Yet, as the HABAŞ case demonstrates, these employees change repeatedly over the years while conditions at the workplace remain the same. That is because the real decisions within the company are made according to the employers' wishes, and safety is often sacrificed to reduce costs or increase production speed. Judicial practice must therefore change. But as you know, the judiciary has also become politicised. Genuine accountability requires organised social opposition."




Karstarlı also criticised trade unions and civil society organisations for failing to respond adequately to workplace massacres. He said, "I think there are two reasons for this. The first is that trade unions are largely controlled by pro-employer union bureaucrats. The second, I believe, is the failure to develop a practice of unity and collective struggle around common demands. Advancing this struggle is an important responsibility facing us."
