title: Women must organize in communes against the male-dominated mentality
content:
The war unfolding in the 21st century is being waged by hegemonic powers that seek to suppress women's struggle for freedom in every possible way. Alongside the claim that the 21st century will be the century of women's liberation, women must further strengthen their systems of organization in order to respond to the attacks taking place today. Only in this way can women protect themselves and bring society around them together. Particularly in the Middle East, such organization and struggle are as essential to women as water and bread. This is because, in the Middle East, which has today become the centre of hegemonic warfare, women are subjected to violence, sexual assaults, massacres and every kind of attack. From Turkey to Iran, from Afghanistan to Sudan, Iraq, Syria and many other countries, women are becoming victims of both external and internal wars.




The war between Iran, the United States and Israel has been continuing for some time. As is well known, women are those most severely affected by this war, becoming victims of the hegemonic systems of states.




With the Taliban's rise to power in Afghanistan, women have been forced to prove their right to exist in every sphere of life. Although education and employment are their natural rights, securing these rights has itself become a major field of struggle. The Taliban, which seeks to surround women with a religiously fundamentalist mentality, is stripping them of their place in society through the laws it enacts and imposing its male-dominated system.




The situation of Sudanese women is similar. As is known, Sudan has been experiencing a civil war for approximately four years. Both the government and the armed forces known as the Rapid Support Forces are carrying out brutal acts against Sudanese women. As a result of the civil war, thousands of women have been subjected to mass sexual violence. While the two sides fight each other, both blame the people and women in pursuit of their own interests, attempting to legitimise their actions. These two forces, which provide no service or benefit to society, have forced tens of thousands of people to abandon their homes and flee.




In many different countries, women face oppression and tyranny. They are constantly forced to struggle to secure their most fundamental rights under the protection of law and to achieve further gains. State systems governed by men make no provision in their laws to protect women's interests. Laws, too, are drafted according to a male-dominated mentality. Many women are unable to access their rights because of laws designed in accordance with men's interests. They are deprived of numerous rights, from the right to divorce and children's rights to the right to work.




Today, in Tunisia, the Maghreb countries, Turkey and many other places, women are fighting to secure their legal rights. Of course, certain laws are being passed and referred to as 'family laws'. Yet even in these laws, women's rights are disregarded.




The male-dominated mentality does not consider the interests of society




Women are those most affected by the current war. Displacement, sexual assaults, unemployment and dire economic conditions are pushing women into profound distress. This is because it is women who organize society and create the conditions for life to flourish around them. However, the system of capitalist modernity, which constructs the mentality of the male-dominated state, has taken this natural role away from women and placed them at the service of its own policies. The dominant man, who gives no consideration to the interests of society, is plundering nature in order to escalate the current war, turning women into instruments of warfare and leaving society impoverished and helpless.




Of course, this picture is not limited to the countries of the Middle East. In many European countries, too, women are subjected to every form of attack and violence. Research shows that domestic violence has increased in Germany. The saying persistently repeated by reactionary men to confine women to their homes, 'The safest place is the home', has now lost its validity.




Unless there is strong organization and consciousness-raising, neither the home, the school, the workplace nor the street will be safe. This is because the mentality we are discussing is not simply the attitude of a few individuals; it is a culture. Moreover, it is a culture whose roots and foundations stretch back 30,000 years into history.




Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan]'s statement, 'The enslavement of society began with women,' makes this reality abundantly clear. When this mentality merged with state power, it became fully embedded within the system and intensified its violence against women and society.




This is also why the toll of femicides continues to grow. In many countries, the figures have reached horrific levels. In Iran, where the 

Jin, Jiyan, Azadî 

(Woman, Life, Freedom) uprising began under women's leadership, women rose up across the country; yet the existing violence has not disappeared. In Iran and Rojhilat, women continue to be killed and subjected to violence every day. Alongside social oppression, state repression is also extremely severe. Dozens of women in Iranian prisons are under the threat of execution, while dozens more have been sentenced to prison terms.




How and through which methods will women organize?




We can now say that violence has become an everyday practice throughout the world and that this violence is increasingly regarded as normal. This is precisely the most dangerous aspect. This is exactly what the system wants: to portray femicides, the destruction of nature, war, plunder, displacement and attacks against society and women as normal. Yet these practices, carried out by the hand of the male-dominated mentality, are neither normal nor ordinary. On the contrary, they run counter to the very nature of humanity and the universe.




Bakur, Shengal and Rojava are going through a process of integration. For this reason, these issues must be discussed extensively, and concrete steps must certainly be taken towards resolving them. Undoubtedly, Leader Apo has clearly outlined both the problem and its solution in his manifesto entitled 

Call for Peace and a Democratic Society

. Beginning with history, Leader Apo addresses the question of women, which is one of humanity's fundamental problems, and offers profound analyses of it. In this manifesto, he once again draws attention to the need for women and society to organize themselves.




So, how and through which methods will women organize themselves? First and foremost, women must organize in the form of communes wherever they are. Naturally, there must be a purpose behind bringing people together. What problems and needs exist? What do women want? What do they wish to offer, change and build? What should the path and method of transformation be? What kind of struggle should be waged, against whom, and in what way?




The answer to all these questions lies in the commune. Concrete steps must be taken in response to existing needs. Within these communes, economic, every day and organizational needs must all be institutionalized. In other words, these communes must develop into structures capable of meeting women's needs and supporting their work in every respect.




When we speak of communal organization, it is clear that such organisation must not be confined to its immediate surroundings. The structure we are referring to must encompass all women. Not a single woman should remain outside the commune. All women must see themselves as part of these communes, feel that they belong to them and develop an awareness that the commune is an indispensable, vital necessity for them. No matter how severe the attacks may be, it must also be recognized that women's consciousness and organization have developed much further than in the past.




Of course, the perspective for this has been put forward by Leader Apo and the Kurdistan Women's Movement. Women in all four parts of Kurdistan have now become a source of inspiration for women around the world through their struggle and organization. Kurdish women play a leading role in every field and have significantly strengthened their organizational structures. However, this organization must acquire a universal dimension, because the question of women is a universal one.




The male-dominated mentality has organized itself throughout the world and established itself as a system. For this reason, women's struggle and organization must not be confined to a single part of the world or a single country. Women must build their confederalism and wage a much stronger and more effective struggle. In this way, they can fight against darkness and make their world more beautiful and meaningful. At the same time, they can live in a free country as free individuals, with their own identities.




With the publication of the manifesto, we have once again seen that such a world is possible. What is needed to achieve it is a shared understanding and a common struggle.

author: Unknown
title: Displacement, poverty and violence: Women's endless war
content:
The war does not end for women who survive it. The real struggle begins afterwards. They lose access to housing, economic security, healthcare and food. The responsibility for keeping their children safe, finding food and water, caring for their families and earning a living often falls on their shoulders. Displacement, poverty and insecurity also expose women to new waves of violence. For decades, women across the Middle East have struggled to survive the devastating consequences of war.




Reports by the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN Women) and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) reveal how these conditions affect women in different ways across Palestine, Yemen, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon.




According to UNFPA's regional assessment published in April 2026, more than 18 million women and girls in these countries face heightened risks of gender-based violence. More than 101 safe spaces for women and girls reportedly closed over the previous 12 months, while funding for services addressing violence declined by more than 50 percent over the past two years. These figures demonstrate how war also destroys the mechanisms intended to protect women.




Palestine: Sexual violence, forced marriage and poverty




Gaza is one of the first places that comes to mind when discussing destruction, devastation, psychological and sexual violence, poverty and displacement. Conditions for women deteriorated further following the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war on 7 October 2023. The devastation experienced by women in Gaza is one of the starkest examples of how war affects every aspect of women's lives. Moreover, the situation of women and girls has not changed despite a year having passed since the announcement of the so-called ceasefire.




According to a UNFPA report published on 30 October 2026, covering the period from April to September 2026, the proportion of households headed by women rose from approximately 11 percent before the war to 25 percent. Women who have lost their husbands, been separated from their families or remain unaware of their relatives' fate are unable even to mourn. Instead, they must provide for their families and children.




Child marriage




A gender-based violence analysis covering the second quarter of 2026 recorded a 61 percent increase in cases of sexual violence. Even more alarming is the rise in forced and child marriages. According to UNFPA, reports of forced and child marriages increased by 123 percent between April and June compared with the January-March period.




Deteriorating health conditions




The severe damage to the healthcare system also exposes women to serious risks during pregnancy and childbirth. Miscarriages are increasing, access to safe abortion is unavailable, and maternal health is deteriorating. Hunger, malnutrition and the collapse of healthcare infrastructure make pregnancy particularly dangerous. The shortage of menstrual hygiene products and lack of access to clean water also represent serious violations of women's right to health.




A generation deprived of education




Disruption to education threatens the future of girls. The destruction of schools, the conversion of educational institutions into shelters and repeated displacement interrupt children's education. Girls who are forced out of school become more vulnerable to early marriage and economic exploitation.




92 percent experience psychological distress




According to a UNFPA field report published in July, 92 percent of the women surveyed experienced moderate or severe psychological distress, while the proportion displaying symptoms of post-traumatic stress rose from 55 to 62 percent. In the West Bank, war, destruction and restrictions have also severely worsened women's living conditions, leaving them with almost no freedom of movement. Access to healthcare, education, livelihoods and protection services is becoming increasingly difficult.




Yemen: Nowhere is safe




More than a decade of conflict in Yemen has once again demonstrated how economic collapse and humanitarian crisis can spread into every aspect of life. The conflict escalated in 2014 when the Iran-backed Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The intervention of the Saudi Arabia-led coalition in 2015 transformed it into a complex war involving multiple actors.




Although the 2022 ceasefire temporarily halted the fighting, the war that began between the United States and Israel on one side and Iran on the other in 2026 drew Yemen back into regional conflict. Hostilities escalated again with reciprocal attacks involving the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. Women are once again bearing the heaviest consequences, particularly through the obstruction of their right to healthcare.




Women giving birth on the roads




According to a UNFPA field report published on 5 October, pregnant women displaced by the fighting have been forced to give birth on roads because they cannot reach safe healthcare facilities. More than 145,000 people were displaced from Yemen's western coast and the Taiz front, including over 3,200 pregnant women.




Displacement has been particularly widespread in Yemen. More than 300,000 people have been displaced since August, while 82,000 were forced to leave their homes in October alone. Women and children account for more than half of those displaced, including approximately 6,400 pregnant women. Road closures, insecurity and the closure of healthcare centres make it difficult for women to access prenatal check-ups and emergency medical services.




The nightmare women face every day in Yemen is the absence of safety. This also contributes to child and forced marriages and the interruption of education. Families often marry off their children as what they see as a means of "escape". Women who have lost their economic independence are particularly vulnerable to being pushed into marriage as a means of survival.




Syria: Millions of women displaced




The war that began in Syria in 2011 devastated women's lives through forced displacement, economic collapse, sexual violence and the breakdown of family structures. Women whose relatives were forcibly disappeared or whose whereabouts remain unknown have had to provide for their families and care for their children while waiting for news of their loved ones. Those forced to leave their homes have encountered new barriers to housing, employment, healthcare and education.




Disaster following HTS takeover




The takeover of power by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) in 2024, followed by attacks against Alawites, Druze, Kurds and other communities, triggered a humanitarian crisis. Alawite, Druze and Kurdish women faced threats of abduction, enforced disappearance, sexual violence and killing.




The massacres targeting Alawites in Syria's coastal regions in March 2025 and Druze communities in Suwayda in July 2025 became some of the most severe attacks carried out under the new regime.




The fate of abducted Alawite women remains unknown




Abductions targeting Alawite women were concentrated in Latakia and Tartus. The Alevi Bektashi Federation (ABF), the Syrian Human Rights Association (AHRS), Amnesty International and the United Nations reported that more than 100 women had been abducted. According to a Reuters investigation published on 27 June 2025, at least 33 Alawite women and girls disappeared or were abducted in the Tartus, Latakia and Hama regions. Families were reportedly subjected to ransom demands ranging from $1,500 to $100,000.




At least 1,500 Alawites were also massacred at 40 separate locations across Latakia, Tartus, Homs and Hama. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) drew attention to the killing of hundreds of women.




Druze women abducted




The clashes in Suwayda in July 2025 triggered a new wave of violence against Druze women. Attacks by HTS and various armed groups resulted in hundreds of deaths.




In a statement published on 21 August 2025, UN human rights experts reported that at least 105 Druze women and girls had been abducted and that the whereabouts of 80 remained unknown. The experts also drew attention to reports that some women had been sexually assaulted and that at least three women had been killed after being raped.




A report by the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria stated that some women had been used in "prisoner exchanges", while others had been abducted from their homes by armed groups.




Lebanon: Women in the shadow of the Hezbollah-Israel war




The humanitarian devastation experienced by women in Lebanon intensified with the renewed outbreak of war between Israel and Hezbollah in March. Reciprocal attacks forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes, particularly in southern Lebanon, the Bekaa Valley and Beirut's southern suburbs.




Between 2 March and 14 June, at least 3,783 people were killed and 11,699 injured in Lebanon. Those killed included 363 women and 247 children.




620,000 women and girls displaced




According to the United Nations, approximately 620,000 women and girls were displaced by the war, including around 16,000 pregnant women. More than 1,450 women and 1,036 children were also injured. Displaced people sought refuge in collective shelters, schools and relatives' homes in and around Beirut. However, temporary accommodation facilities failed to provide safe living conditions for women and girls.




A UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) safety assessment published in May 2026, which examined 180 collective shelters, identified severe overcrowding, inadequate lighting, doors that could not be locked and poor hygiene conditions. The shortage of dedicated safe spaces for women and girls also increased the risks of sexual harassment, exploitation and other forms of gender-based violence.




Between life and death




One of the most severe consequences of war for women has been the disruption of pregnancy and childbirth services. According to a Reuters investigation, 13,500 pregnant women were displaced in Lebanon during the first weeks of the war. A UNFPA report covering the period from 26 March to 1 April 2026 also stated that approximately 1.2 million people had been displaced, including 620,000 women and girls.




Growing economic and care burdens




The conditions created by displacement have also increased women's exposure to violence. The lack of privacy and hygiene in overcrowded shelters has further heightened women's vulnerability to harassment and exploitation.




Severe psychological scars




Losing their homes, living under the constant threat of attack, worrying about their children's safety and facing uncertainty about the future are also taking a heavy toll on women's mental health. A study published by UN Women in September examined the wartime experiences of Lebanese women from different generations.




Women's accounts highlighted separation from their families and social networks, anxiety about their children's future, constant fear of attacks and uncertainty about whether they would ever be able to rebuild their homes. Women who bear sole responsibility for caring for their children, in particular, are trying to keep their families together while putting their own fears and trauma aside.

title: Tarım ve Orman Bakanlığı 2027 Bütçesi: Bütçede ormanları korumaya pay yok
content:
Özlem Songül Abayoğlu [email protected]

Tarım ve Orman Bakanlığı’nın 2027 Yılı Bütçe Teklifi bugün TBMM Plan ve Bütçe Komisyonunda görülecek. Bakanlığın 760 milyar 597 milyon TL’yi aşan devasa bütçe teklifi incelendiğinde; "Ormanların ve Doğanın Korunması ile Sürdürülebilir Yönetimi" programının tamamen sıfırlandığı, doğa koruma yatırımlarının merkezi bütçeden silindiği, arazi kullanım planlamalarında hedeflerin çöktüğü ve mera koruma faaliyetlerinin kilitlendiği görülüyor.

Bakanlık bütçe cetvellerinde yer alan "Programlar İtibarıyla Ödenek Teklifleri İcmali" tablosunda, ilk göze çarpan doğrudan ormanları ve biyoçeşitliliği korumayı amaçlayan ana program kaleminin silinmiş olması. 2025 yılı başlangıç ödeneği olarak 2 milyar 824 milyon 84 bin TL (2.824.084.000 TL) ayrılan ve yıl içinde 1 milyar 653 milyon 908 bin TL harcama yapılan "Ormanların ve Doğanın Korunması ile Sürdürülebilir Yönetimi Programı" kalemine; 2026 başlangıç ödeneği, 2026 Haziran harcaması ve 2027 yılı bütçe teklifinde tam 0 TL yani hiç bütçe ayırmamış. Bakanlık, 2028 yılı için 0 TL ve 2029 yılı için de 0 TL ödenek tahmininde bulunarak, orman ve doğa koruma programını merkezi bütçe yapısından en az 2029 sonuna kadar gözden çıkardı.

Ayrıca bütçe ayrıntılarında bu program altında yer alan "Doğa Koruma ve Milli Parklar Genel Müdürlüğü" kalemine de 2026, 2027, 2028 ve 2029 yılları için tek bir kuruş dahi bütçe ayrılmadı.

Türkiye'nin her yaz ağır orman yangınlarıyla sarsıldığı ve yüz binlerce hektar orman dokusunu kaybettiği bir dönemde, merkezi bütçeden orman korumaya ayrılan pay sıfırlandı. “Devleti, şirket gibi yöneten” iktidar eliyle Orman Genel Müdürlüğü'nün döner sermaye ve özel bütçeli yapısına devredilen finansman modeli, Genel Bütçe kapsamındaki bakanlık bütçesinden doğrudan orman koruma desteğinin çekildiğini gösteriyor. Yangınların önlenmesi, yangın emniyet yollarının tesisi, gözetleme kulelerinin idamesi, biyoçeşitlilik kaybının engellenmesi ve hava-kara araçlarının alımına yönelik merkezi bütçe garantisi yok.

2027 yılı bütçe teklifinde edinilecek taşıtlar listesinde Bakanlık bünyesine 10 adet arazi binek (4x4), 5 adet pick-up, 10 adet arazi hizmet pick-up'ı (4x4) ve 1 adet kamyon alınması öngörülürken, bu taşıtların tamamının "Döner Sermaye" ve "Hibe" kaynaklarından karşılanacağı, doğrudan genel bütçe sermaye alımının olmadığı görülüyor.

Doğa ve orman alanlarının kaçak yapılaşma, madencilik ve sanayi baskısından korunmasını sağlayacak olan “Arazi Kullanım Planlaması" performans göstergelerine göre, 2026 yılı için 2.000.000 hektar alanda arazi kullanım planlaması yapılması hedeflenmişken, 2026 Yıl Sonu Gerçekleşme Tahmini 0 Hektar olarak revize edilmiş.

Erozyon ve çölleşmeyle mücadelenin en temel ayağı olan meraların korunması ve ıslahı çalışmalarında da bütçe teklifi ilerleme değil duraklama vaat ediyor. Maden ve enerji yatırımlarıyla talan edilen meralar için 2026 yılında koruma altına alınan mera sayısı 502 adetken; 2027, 2028 ve 2029 için de 502 olacak.

Kuraklık, orman yangınları ve sellerle sık sık karşılaştığımız; tarımının ve ormanlarını tehdit edildiği bir süreçte, Bakanlık iklim değişikliği ile mücadeleye sembolik bir kaynak ayırdı. title: Meghan Markle'ın babası çocuk istismarından yargılanıyor
content:
Fotoğraf: Mark Jones/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Sussex Düşesi Meghan Markle'ın babası Thomas Markle hakkında resmi suçlama yöneltildi. Halihazırda tutuklu bulunan 82 yaşındaki Markle'a ilişkin açıklama yapan yetkililer, kendisine çocuklara yönelik istismar materyalleri bulundurma suçunun isnat edildiğini duyurdu.

Yetkililerin paylaştığı bilgilere göre, yöneltilen suçlamadan hüküm giymesi halinde Thomas Markle 40 yıla kadar hapis cezasıyla yargılanacak.

Markle hakkındaki adli süreç, Meghan Markle'ın üvey kardeşinin yaptığı ihbar üzerine ABD'de başlatılan soruşturmayla gündeme gelmişti. Üvey kardeş, babası Thomas Markle'ın Filipinler'deki ikametinde çocuk istismarı materyalleri tespit ettiğini bildirmişti.

İngiltere Kralı 3. Charles'ın küçük oğlu Prens Harry ile ABD'li oyuncu Meghan Markle 2018 yılında evlenmiş, 2020'de ise Kraliyet görevlerini bırakarak ABD'ye taşınmıştı. Çiftin, Kraliyet Ailesi'ne yönelik ırkçılık ve dışlanma eleştirilerinin ardından Kral 3. Charles ve Galler Prensi William ile olan bağları kopma noktasına gelmişti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Proton Apartmanı davasında 13 yıl 4 ay hapis cezası alan müteahhit, 3 haftadır yakalanamadı
content:
Kahramanmaraş'ta 6 Şubat depremlerinde 64 kişinin hayatını kaybettiği Proton Apartmanı davasında 13 yıl 4 ay hapis cezasına çarptırılan müteahhit Rafet Küsmüş'ün, hakkında verilen tutuklama kararına rağmen üç haftadır yakalanamaması üzerine müşteki avukatı Nilay Yıldırım Yaşar, yetkililere sanığın yakalanması çağrısında bulundu.

Maraş’ın Onikişubat ilçesi Abdullah Çavuş Mahallesi'ndeki Proton Apartmanı'nın 6 Şubat depremlerinde yıkılması sonucu, 5 aylık bebek dahil 64 kişi hayatını kaybetti.

Kahramanmaraş 4. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi'ndeki 5 Kasım'da görülen karar duruşmasında, müteahhit ve fenni mesul Rafet Küsmüş ile statik proje müellifi Sıtkı Okumuş'a "bilinçli taksirle ölüme ve yaralanmaya neden olma" suçundan iyi hal indirimi uygulanarak 13 yıl 4 ay hapis cezası verildi. İki sanığın hükümle birlikte tutuklanmasına ve 2 yıl meslekten men edilmelerine karar verilirken, Rafet Küsmüş hakkında yakalama kararı çıkarıldı.

Sanıklar Küsmüş ve Okumuş'un avukatlarının tutukluluğa itiraz ederek tahliye talebinde bulunmasını reddeden Kahramanmaraş 4. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi, dosyayı Kahramanmaraş 5. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi'ne gönderdi. Mahkemenin dosya üzerinden yaptığı incelemede, sanık avukatlarının itirazlarını reddettiği öğrenildi.

Müşteki avukatlarından Nilay Yıldırım Yaşar, süreci şöyle değerlendirdi:

"Müteahhit sanık Rafet Küsmüş, 13 yıl 4 ay hapis cezasına mahkum edildi. Hakkında hükmen tutuklama kararı verildi. Peki, Rafet Küsmüş nerede? Aradan üç hafta geçti ancak hala yakalanmış değil. Üstelik bu sanık, Haziran 2025'te tutuklu bulunduğu dosyadan tahliye edilmişti. Biz bu tehlikeyi görmüştük. Karar verilmeden önce defalarca uyardık. Yargılamanın geldiği aşamayı, sanıkların karşı karşıya olduğu cezaların ağırlığını ve kaçma ihtimalini dile getirerek tutuklama veya en azından kaçma riskini önleyecek sıkı adli kontrol tedbirlerinin uygulanmasını talep ettik. Bugün maalesef haklı çıktık. Şimdi buradan soruyorum: 13 yıl 4 ay hapis cezası verilen ve hakkında tutuklama kararı bulunan bir sanık neden hala yakalanamadı?

Depremde yakınlarını kaybeden aileler yıllardır adalet mücadelesi verirken, hakkında mahkumiyet kararı verilen bir sanığın hala yakalanamamış olması nasıl açıklanacak? Yetkili makamlara açıkça sesleniyoruz: Rafet Küsmüş hakkında verilen tutuklama kararının infazı için bütün yasal imkanlar gecikmeksizin kullanılmalıdır. Deprem davalarında aynı durumların tekrar yaşanmaması için kaçma riski bulunan sanıklar hakkında gerekli tutuklama ve adli kontrol tedbirleri zamanında uygulanmalıdır. Rafet Küsmüş yakalanmadığı sürece biz de her gün aynı soruyu sormaya devam edeceğiz: 64 insanın hayatını kaybettiği bir davada 13 yıl 4 ay hapis cezası alan ve hakkında tutuklama kararı verilen Rafet Küsmüş nerede? Bu sorunun cevabını alana kadar susmayacağız."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: ROAPE
title: When ‘the people’ become a problem
content:
The return of political economy to the centre of debates on minerals, sovereignty, and wealth also politicises a more concealed but fundamental category of politics: the people. The people as the foundational logic of politics is obscured either by reducing agency to voting and institutionally mediated participation or through the introduction of ‘meta’ categories for understanding people and their behaviour, such as those found in modern economics. While both tendencies draw legitimacy from the people, neither represents the ultimate contour of popular participation.




In fact, the liberal framework itself often produces a greater degree of depoliticisation of popular will, contradicting its claims to popular legitimacy. Within the neoliberal ‘free trade’ world, this depoliticisation is further amplified by reducing state capacity in favour of private enterprise and ownership.




As I argued in my 

earlier piece

, the recent political trajectory of Burkina Faso is significant precisely because questions of ownership, extraction, production, and economic sovereignty have returned to the sphere of popular political contestation. Reduced state capacity does not simply diminish sovereign power; it transforms the role of the state into an arbitrator of bourgeois interests over popular representation, privileging profit over people while representing the category of the people through differentiated and graded notions of ‘development’.




The question of state agency in Africa against neoliberal and neo-imperial interventions has long been a subject of scholarly and theoretical debate. Reduced state capacity facilitates neoliberal extraction of resources, the INGO raj, environmental destruction, and the undermining of mechanisms of popular representation. When popular will is asserted, a subtler yet visible distinction between the liberal and the illiberal is often mobilised to critique the economics and politics of such movements.




In popular discourse, this binary is largely treated as a neutral descriptive category, almost self-evident in its meaning. Yet an inquiry into its history reveals it as a political technology: a method of political discourse through which popular movements – particularly in the Third World – have been classified, disciplined, and, when necessary, delegitimised by pitching one side against the other.




The liberal/illiberal binary has, of course, acquired considerable complexity, and recent scholarly interventions have captured its variability, particularly in Africa and Latin America. But its political uses remain consequential.




From the hypocrisy of the West to the selective deployment of human rights, justice, and other ‘moral’ equivalents – while ongoing crises in Gaza, Sudan, and elsewhere in the Global South are largely ignored by the mainstream – to the concealment of economic dependency and the relationship of the ‘First’ World to the ‘Third’, depoliticisation has become a norm rather than an exception.




As Eyob Balcha Gebremariam has 

recently argued

 writing for roape.net, Eurocentrism and the selective application of the so-called ‘rules-based world order’ continue to shape international narratives in ways that privilege Western interests while presenting them as universal norms. Liberal-democratic states, whether the United States, France, or India, have themselves mobilised brutal armed power to crush popular agitations by farmers, students, and workers.




The fissures in the liberal/illiberal binary, therefore, reveal not only its poverty as an account of political life, but also the hollowness of ‘by the people, for the people’ sloganeering when confronted with people acting beyond the institutional boundaries prescribed for them. The question, then, is what can some of the political-economic changes in today’s Africa teach us about the people and their political agency?




One of the first and most important lessons from Burkina Faso and the political transitions there comes from de-concealing the concealed: the people. The Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDPs) have been 

a particular focus of discussion

 on Burkina Faso. Established in 2020, the VDPs are 

locally and voluntarily recruited civilian auxiliaries

, provided with arms and military training, who support the national armed forces in defending communities against jihadist insurgent groups. Their 

mobilisation was substantially expanded

 under Ibrahim Traoré after 2022.




A significant strand of contemporary scholarship and policy discussion has approached the VDPs through the language of 

coercion, militarisation

, and the 

risks of vigilante violence and abuses against civilian populations

. The problem arises, however, when such categories become exhaustive explanations of the mobilisation. What is 

depoliticised

 in this process is not simply the history of mobilisation but the political question of who has the authority to organise, represent, and act in the name of the people.




In this sense, depoliticisation also entails the displacement of popular political agency by institutionalised and ostensibly neutral categories through which political participation is recognised and evaluated. The VDPs then appear only as instruments of coercion, rather than as a political phenomenon that also needs to be situated within Burkina Faso’s longer histories of popular mobilisation, revolutionary organisation, and state formation and, more broadly, within Africa’s histories of popular political mobilisation and revolutionary transformation.




In 

my recently published article

, I demonstrate how today’s VDPs in Burkina Faso follow a similar historical and ideological trajectory to the Committees for the Defence of the Revolution (CDRs) and the Union of Women of Burkina Faso (UFBs) during the time of Thomas Sankara. Moreover, simply using the framework of coercion without inquiring into its political contours risks “…overlooking their role in actively producing political subjectivity and collective participation.”




This historical continuity between the CDRs and UFBs of the Sankara period and the VDPs of today should not, however, be mistaken for political equivalence. As Bettina Engels has 

recently argued

 writing for roape.net, the comparison between Sankara and Traoré requires attention not only to their shared anti-imperialist rhetoric and certain similarities in policy, but also to the significant differences between Sankara’s ‘pragmatic socialism’ and Traoré’s more pragmatic politics.




The popular mobilisation in Traoré’s Burkina Faso and the Alliance of Sahel States is also not without global precedent. From the revolutionary politics of China, Cuba, and Vietnam from the 1940s to 1970s in their historical resistance to brutal occupations by imperialists, to Africa’s 

own history

 of national liberation and state formation, popular mobilisation has been intricately linked with nation-building and state-capacity expansion. To undermine the political agency of the people, therefore, is to undermine not merely popularity but the precise trajectory of state formation in the Third World altogether.




Moreover, the ‘people’ of the CDRs, UFBs, and VDPs are not structural equivalents of the antagonistic and contained mobilisation of the ‘people’ in liberal-democratic states. Nor does liberal democracy offer a normative standard against which ‘illiberal’ forms of popular mobilisation can simply be measured. The liberal/illiberal binary of politics – especially when centred on the people – reveals both its poverty in understanding the constituent conditions of state formation and the necessity of 

rethinking popular participation beyond electoral politics

.




A nation-state is not merely an imaginative or territorial claim; it also requires popular acceptance of that claim insofar as popular legitimacy sustains statist claims to sovereignty. The people, in this way, are and have always been central to politics, even when participation is masked, regulated, and constrained through constitutionalism, parliamentary democracy, and the limited ability of liberal-democratic systems to represent popular interests.




In this way, 

contemporary critiques

 of the VDPs – particularly those centred on coercion, militarisation, and abuses against civilian populations – bear an eerie similitude to critiques of the CDRs and UFBs in Sankara’s Burkina Faso. It is similarly 

not

 surprising that critiques of popular mobilisation can implicitly reproduce a Cold War logic of liberal/illiberal classification that could neither counter nor respond in praxis to Chinese, North Korean, and Vietnamese mobilisations in defence of national integrity and sovereignty.




These critiques also reveal something more concealed: the people and their (de)mobilisation have always presented a normative horizon for liberal-democratic politics, which finds itself pushed against a wall when confronted with student-led and agrarian agitations – two of the most disenfranchised sections of any liberal-democratic society. And when the ‘wretched’ of the earth begin to threaten the political arrangements that claim to represent them, perhaps we should ask a more uncomfortable question: can a system that trembles at the slightest agitation of its own disempowered citizens fundamentally and sincerely condemn a military seizure of power simply because that seizure is military?




The question becomes even more uncomfortable when the military takeover presents itself not as an abandonment of popular politics, but as an attempt – however, with its own contradictions – to mobilise the people, expand state capacity, and reclaim national sovereignty. This is precisely the problem posed by what Adam Mayer has called 

Military Marxism

: the possibility that military intervention can become entangled with, rather than simply opposed to, traditions of popular mobilisation and revolutionary state formation in Africa.




The question posed by Burkina Faso, therefore, is not simply whether its political trajectory is liberal or illiberal. It is whether the liberal/illiberal binary is capable of recognising forms of popular sovereignty that emerge from different histories of colonialism, national liberation, state formation, and economic dependency. When the people cease to be merely voters, consumers, or objects of development and begin to act as political subjects, they can become a problem for the categories through which liberal politics has learned to recognise them.




In this sense, “the people” become a problem precisely when they become politically mobilised beyond the normative threshold of liberal democracy and its advocates. Burkina Faso today pushes that conundrum forward.





The post 

When ‘the people’ become a problem

 appeared first on 

ROAPE

.

author: Brian Hioe
title: The Referendum Nobody is Talking About
content:
THE ONLY REFERENDUM question that will be asked of the general public during the vote that takes place on Saturday will be on nuclear energy. Specifically, the public will be asked about phasing out current government policy on enacting a nuclear-free homeland.

The referendum question proves ironic. For one, this will be the fourth time that the Taiwanese public has been asked about nuclear energy in a referendum in eight years. All of these referendums on nuclear energy were proposed by pro-nuclear advocates.

Likewise, one wonders if the referendum is even necessary at this juncture. The Lai administration has long since reversed course on nuclear energy to allow for restarts. Plans to restart the No. 2 and No. 3 nuclear reactors were submitted by state-run power utility Taipower to the Atomic Energy Commission earlier this year.

The Lai administration reversing course on the DPP’s opposition to nuclear energy, a plank of the party that dates back to democratization, is primarily due to two reasons. One is concern about how Taiwan would maintain a stable power supply in the event of a Chinese invasion or blockade, seeing as Taiwan is highly reliant on shipments of liquefied natural gas for its energy supply.

Taiwan has a limited supply of liquefied natural gas that it can rely on if supplies are cut off, which has led the Lai administration to contemplate the possibility of emergency restarts in the event of a crisis. The Lai administration has been willing to risk controversy in the past, coming into conflict with environmentalist groups, by building LNG receiving terminals even when they threaten coral reefs and maritime diversity.

The second reason as to why the Lai administration would reverse course on nuclear energy, however, is because of concern from the international community about how Taiwan intends to maintain semiconductor manufacturing to continue to fuel the AI boom without nuclear energy. Indeed, nuclear energy was never a silver bullet for Taiwan’s energy needs, constituting 1.2% to 4% by the time it was phased out in May 2025. But international business concerns came to discuss nuclear energy as though nuclear energy would solve all of Taiwan’s energy needs.

The KMT has hit out at what it claims to be the Lai administration’s hypocrisy in reversing course on nuclear energy, while still calling for the referendum. The Lai administration took a political risk in reversing course on what historically has been a pan-Green platform and it was, surprisingly, able to get the pan-Green camp to accept the decision, not necessarily because it did so from a position of power, but because of rising concerns about invasion scenarios and how to maintain social operations in the event of no LNG shipments.

Yet one notes the KMT could have taken action using its current control of the legislature, which dates from 2024, to try to prevent the Lai administration from phasing out nuclear energy. The recommissioning process for nuclear reactors will probably take several years, when the KMT was in a position to have taken more decisive action against it. The KMT does not necessarily need to hold a referendum either when it has the majority in the legislature when it votes alongside the TPP and could simply press certain legal measures into law through this majority. The KMT itself probably strategically decided to allow for the nuclear phase-out to occur because it realized it could later leverage on the campaign promise to restore nuclear energy for electoral ends.

Moreover, if the Lai administration has already reversed course on nuclear energy, it proves a question as to why the referendum is still necessary–except for that the KMT hopes to benefit electorally from it. More generally, the KMT hopes to repeat its successes in the 2018 local elections, in which it was able to successfully leverage on a series of nine referendum questions asked of the Taiwanese public to win district elections across Taiwan.

Indeed, one notes that the KMT and its pan-Blue ally, the TPP, had previously pushed for other referendum questions to be on the ballot beyond simply nuclear energy. Apart from the issue of nuclear energy, the KMT and TPP had also pushed for a referendum that would institute caning for serious crimes, and a referendum to call for allocation of fines from traffic violations to local governments in order to improve traffic safety.

There was no previous social demand for caning, which the KMT claimed would be used for crimes such as sexual assault, large-scale fraud, and child abuse, and would serve as a deterrent to such crimes by setting a social example. This would be in line with the KMT’s historic support for the use of capital punishment in Taiwan, which the KMT claims deters violent crimes by setting an example.

The KMT previously claimed that violent crimes were on the rise in Taiwan because of the Lai administration’s refusal to implement capital punishment, depicting a 2024 Constitutional Court ruling that narrowed the scope of its application as having abolished capital punishment, and calling for a referendum in favor of capital punishment last year. This would be a claim perhaps not unlike how the KMT has continued to push for its current pro-nuclear referendum despite that the Lai administration is in fact in favor of nuclear reactors. But the Central Election Commission refused to allow the referendum to occur, seeing as capital punishment is still on the books.

Indeed, one notes that most countries in the world that implement caning are former British colonies or countries with Sharia law. Instituting caning would result in a wave of international mockery of Taiwan on human rights grounds. To this extent, allocating funds from traffic violations to traffic safety does not require a national referendum, but could simply be passed as a measure by the KMT-controlled legislature.

In this sense, both referendums were blocked by the Central Election Commission, even if the nuclear referendum was still allowed. For its part, the KMT remains committed at least to the notion of a caning referendum, and claims that it will attempt to pass laws to this effect in the legislature–even as a caning referendum might fall afoul of international human rights conventions that Taiwan voluntarily ratified under the Ma Ying-jeou administration.

And yet with the DPP itself having reversed course on nuclear energy in a manner that runs contrary to how the KMT has attempted to depict it, it is possible that the DPP has taken the wind out of the KMT’s sails when it comes to its pro-nuclear referendum. Moreover, one notes that compared to 2018, there is relatively little social discussion of the referendum in an election cycle dominated by Puma Shen’s “Ocean Current.”

This perhaps returns to the fact that the KMT did not actually collect signatures with the public and campaign for the referendum to take place, building momentum around the issue and raising publicity for it, but simply did so by passing the referendum using its current majority in the legislature. If this results in little publicity for the referendum and fails to benefit in district elections, perhaps the KMT will be seen as frivolous for yet again attempting to make the public vote on nuclear energy in the belief that this will help its election chances.

Indeed, indications are that the KMT has started to realize its failure to emphasize the referendum in campaigning. Reportedly, this could be one of the reasons why the KMT has switched to attacks on solar energy in the final stage of campaigning, rather than championing nuclear energy. This is to be seen. Either way, one notes that the KMT’s advocacy of nuclear energy is not based on scientific rationale but primarily based on appeals to past history, during which nuclear energy constituted more than 50% of the energy mix, the KMT held sole power, and Taiwan’s economy saw high growth. The claim, then, is that returning to a traditional form of power would lead to the return of such economic prosperity.

author: CNT Granada
title: 25N 2026: «Yo por ellas, madre, y ellas por mí»
content:
Nos sentamos a escribir este comunicado todavía afónicas, recuperándonos de la intensidad de la huelga de hace dos semanas. Pero felices, celebrando este nuevo despertar de la clase trabajadora y el poder darle cobijo y estructura, gracias al trabajo cotidiano de todas nuestras compañeras de CNT y, sin olvidar, nunca, a las que nos precedieron. 




Aunque muchos echaban de menos una huelga general y databan la última hace catorce años, nosotras recordamos con orgullo la 

huelga general feminista del 8M de 2018

, convocada por la CNT durante todo el día, a diferencia de los paros parciales de los sindicatos de concertación. Fue una huelga laboral, de cuidados, de consumo y educativa, una huelga histórica cuya invisibilización solo habla, de nuevo, de que siguen queriendo silenciar la lucha por la defensa de nuestra integridad. Como entonces, nos sobran los motivos para levantarnos, aunque se intenten banalizar las cifras de asesinatos machistas ante millones de espectadores. Desde que se contabilizan los casos de violencia de género en 2003, pocos años después de que la granaína Ana Orantes alzara la voz en Canal Sur, han sido registrados 1385 asesinatos machistas, y podrían ascender casi al doble fuera de la pareja. Desde 2013, se han matado a 78 menores, mientras que 545 han quedado huérfanos. No son solo números, son vidas arrebatadas por el patriarcado. Son asesinatos evitables. Es la punta del iceberg de todas las violencias que sufrimos a diario y que se extienden a nuestras hijas e hijos, ya que seguimos siendo las principales cuidadoras en nuestros entornos.




Se calcula que cada media hora hombres atentan contra la libertad sexual de las mujeres en España, llegando a unas 14 violaciones diarias. Denunciamos con especial dolor la 

violencia que sufren las mujeres y niñas migrantes en Ceuta

: entre el 30 de julio y el 14 de septiembre, se han registrado agresiones sexuales contra 39 víctimas. 14 eran niñas. No nos cansaremos de señalar a los responsables: gobiernos que aplican políticas migratorias vejatorias, controlan con violencia las fronteras y desprotejen a mujeres y niñas. Migrar, con dignidad e integridad, es también un derecho.




Ya no solo nos da miedo volver solas a casa, ahora además tenemos miedo de perder nuestra casa y no tener dónde volver. Solo en Granada, durante el primer semestre de 2026, se ha producido más de un desahucio diario. No existe un registro estadístico segregado por género, pero según un estudio de la Universidad de Málaga, 

más del 70% de las personas que acuden a las plataformas antidesahucios son mujeres

. Nuestro riesgo de pobreza sigue siendo el mayor. Nuestras condiciones precarias, las jornadas parciales, el trabajo doméstico no pagado, la sobrecarga de cuidados, la violencia machista… nos imposibilita acceder a una vivienda digna de forma estable, y eso también es violencia contra las mujeres. No nos conformamos con alternativas vacías, queremos un hogar en el que sentirnos seguras. Esta huelga fue también una huelga feminista. 




Desde CNT Granada, clamamos que es el momento de organizarse para defender nuestros derechos independientemente de quien gobierne. En nuestra ciudad, el 11N volvimos a ser conscientes como clase de que tenemos la capacidad de parar la ciudad. Demostramos que las trabajadoras, las estudiantes, las madres, las migrantes, las trans, podemos organizarnos bajo nuestros propios intereses, sin marchar detrás de los sindicatos cómplices de los gobiernos que forman parte de la estructura que nos mata. A pesar de la represión del Estado, los palos de la policía golpeándonos, el gas en los ojos… no daremos ni un paso atrás.




Mari Carmen luchó hasta el final para poder quedarse en la casa donde había vivido siempre. Ella no puede volver, pero nosotras continuaremos la lucha, por todas. Por las asesinadas, por las mujeres despojadas de su libertad y de su hogar. 




Hoy, como todos los días, 

demostraremos lo que la sororidad puede: yo por ellas, madre, y ellas por mí.







Manifestación:




Nos vemos en las calles de Granada este 25N, a las 17:45h en la escultura de Elena Martín Vivaldi junto a Triunfo.




La entrada 

25N 2026: «Yo por ellas, madre, y ellas por mí»

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: infolibre
title: Προβολή ταινίας και συζήτηση – «Regenerating Life (Αναγεννώντας τη Ζωή)», Πέμπτη 26/11/2026 στις 18.00, στο EKX Σχολείο
content:
Το «Regenerating Life» («Αναγεννώντας τη Ζωή») είναι ένα ντοκυμαντέρ μεγάλου μήκους που προσεγγίζει την κλιματική κρίση μέσα από μια οικολογική οπτική

. Αμφισβητεί την κυρίαρχη ιδέα ότι οι εκπομπές άνθρακα από την καύση ορυκτών καυσίμων είναι η αιτία της. Ανταυτού η ταινία προτείνει ότι είναι η αδυσώπητη καταστροφή του φυσικού κόσμου από την ανθρωπότητα που έχει προκαλέσει την κλιματική κρίση. Αυτό συμβαίνει επειδή η φύση – η τεράστια βιοποικιλότητα που υπάρχει στον πλανήτη μας – ρυθμίζει και εξισορροπεί το κλίμα της Γης. Μπορούμε να αντιστρέψουμε αυτή την καταστροφική διαδικασία – Αναγεννώντας τη ζωή.




Ο σκηνοθέτης John Feldman εξερευνά τους τρόπους με τους οποίους η ζωή ρυθμίζει το κλίμα: μέσα από τη φωτοσύνθεση και τον κύκλο του άνθρακα, τον κύκλο του νερού και των ζωικών λιπασμάτων, καθώς και το τεράστιο, αλληλοσυνδεόμενο υπόγειο δίκτυο μυκήτων, μικροοργανισμών και ριζών των φυτών.




Παράλληλα, εξετάζει τα οικονομικά και πολιτικά συστήματα που έχουν ενθαρρύνει την καταστροφή της Γης, μέσα από την αδιάκοπη επιδίωξη του πλούτου και της κυριαρχίας.




Επισκέπτεται ανθρώπους που αναζητούν μεθόδους να αντιστρέψουν την καταστροφή, που επεξεργάζονται λύσεις δουλεύοντας μαζί με τη φύση, αποκαθιστώντας δάση, αγρούς, υγροτόπους και ωκεανούς. Αποκαθιστώντας το έδαφος παράγουν υγιή τροφή και οικοδομούν υγιείς κοινότητες.




Η προβολή θα έχει ελληνικούς υπότιτλους.




Μετά την προβολή θα ακολουθήσει συζήτηση με θέμα: “Η καταστροφή του φυσικού κόσμου από την ανθρωπότητα και ο ρόλος της οικολογικής γεωργίας.”




Η προβολή είναι κοινή εκδήλωση των παρακάτω τριών πρωτοβουλιών/ομάδων:




1) 

Ομάδα χωραφιού ΕΚΧΣ “Η Τσουκνίδα”

: Εμπνευσμένοι από τις αρχές της κοινωνικής οικολογίας, της αυτάρκειας και της αποανάπτυξης, η ομάδα λειτουργεί ως χώρος διαλόγου και δράσης γύρω από ζητήματα γης, φύσης, γεωργίας και εναλλακτικών μορφών ζωής. Βλέπουμε αυτό ως ένα απαραίτητο σημείο εκκίνησης για τη δημιουργία πρακτικών μορφών αυτονομίας έξω από την καπιταλιστική μηχανή. Πιστεύουμε ότι μια ρήξη με τον καπιταλισμό ξεκινά από την αμφισβήτηση της κυριαρχίας πάνω στη φύση, περνά μέσα από την προστασία της γης, του νερού, του αέρα και της φύσης γενικότερα και την επαναδιεκδίκηση τους ως τα «κοινά» μας, και μέσα από τη δημιουργία μορφών κοινοτικής ζωής, μέσω της συγκρότησης δομών άμεσης δημοκρατίας και εναλλακτικών οικονομιών αυτάρκειας.




2)

Πρωτοβουλία Θεσσαλονίκης για το Περιβάλλον και την Ενέργεια

: Μέσα στον ενεργειακό παροξυσμό της αποκαλούμενης Πράσινης Ανάπτυξης, με την επέλαση βιομηχανικών εγκαταστάσεων να απειλεί τη Φύση και την παραγωγική γη της χώρας και του πλανήτη συνολικά, συγκροτήσαμε πριν δύο χρόνια στη Θεσσαλονίκη μια πρωτοβουλία πολιτών, για να αντισταθούμε.


Βασικοί στόχοι μας είναι: 1) Η στήριξη τοπικών αγώνων και η ενίσχυσή τους, για την αποτροπή των βιομηχανικών εγκαταστάσεων ΑΠΕ, Κέντρων Δεδομένων και του Ενεργειακού παραλογισμού. 2) Η απομυθοποίηση του κυρίαρχου αφηγήματος της «Πράσινης Συμφωνίας» (Green Deal) με ενημέρωση της κοινωνίας και ανάπτυξη δημόσιου διαλόγου.




3) 

Ομάδα Βουνού ΕΚΧΣ “Ανάβασις”

: Είμαστε μια ανοιχτή, αυτοοργανωμένη συλλογικότητα ανθρώπων που επιλέγουν να ξαναβρούν τη σχέση τους με τη φύση, μακριά από την αποξένωση της πόλης και το άγχος της σύγχρονης ζωής. Χωρίς ιεραρχίες, χωρίς αρχηγούς, με βάση την εμπιστοσύνη, τη συντροφικότητα και την αλληλεγγύη. Η ομάδα μας δεν είναι απλώς μια παρέα για εκδρομές. Είναι ένας ζωντανός πυρήνας εμπειρίας, γνώσης και δράσης.
