Teamleiter*in Agrarreferat (w/d/m)

Vollzeit (35 Wochenstunden) · unbefristet · Berlin




Zum nächstmöglichen Zeitpunkt suchen wir eine Teamleitung für das Agrarreferat in Vollzeit (35 Wochenstunden), unbefristet in Berlin.




Deine Aufgabenbereiche

Du leitest das Agrarreferat (aktuell 3 Mitarbeitende inkl. dir) inhaltlich und organisatorisch

Du koordinierst unsere Projekte in deinem Schwerpunktbereich fachlich

Du erarbeitest zusammen mit deinem Team die inhaltlichen Themen

Du bildest die Schnittstelle zwischen deinem Team und unseren anderen Teams

Du wertest das uns zur Verfügung gestellte Bildmaterial mit Blick auf Verstöße gegen das Tierschutzgesetz aus und erstellst daraus Roh- und Presseschnitte

Du schreibst Anzeigen für aufgedeckte Gesetzesverstöße und verfolgst diese nach

Du organisierst die externe Erstellung von Gutachten und gibst diese frei

Du bist mit unserem Anwaltsteam zu allen rechtlichen Fragen im Agrarbereich im Kontakt

Du bearbeitest Tierschutzmeldungen, die uns per E-Mail erreichen, und prüfst, inwieweit wir aktiv werden können

Du pflegst eine Datenbank, in der Gesetzesverstöße dokumentiert werden

Du sorgst für eine gute Meetingkultur (Vorbereitung, Durchführung, Nachbereitung) innerhalb deines Teams

Du betreust unsere externe Cloud für Veröffentlichungsmaterial

Du tauschst dich mit anderen Menschen in unserem Arbeitsbereich aus und bringst dein Fachwissen in übergeordnete Fragestellungen des Vereins ein

Das bringst du mit

Du identifizierst dich mit unserem Selbstverständnis, unseren Werten und unserem Verein (

ariwa.org/selbstverstaendnis

)

Du hast eine strukturierte und präzise Arbeitsweise und kannst vertraulich arbeiten

Du bist kreativ und teamfähig, hast ein Gespür für Details und bringst eigene Ideen ein

Du bist sicher im Umgang mit gängigen Office-Tools zur Erstellung von Dokumenten und hast idealerweise grundlegende Kenntnisse im Videoschnitt

Du hast nachweisbare Erfahrung in der Tierrechtsarbeit, der Landwirtschaft oder einem tierärztlichen Bereich und bereits erste Erfolge vorzuweisen

Du kannst bei der Sichtung von Videomaterial die harte Realität der Tierindustrie mit professioneller Distanz langfristig aushalten

Du hast bestenfalls schon erste Führungserfahrung in einem diversen Team gesammelt

Du bist flexibel und kurzfristige Änderungen bringen dich nicht aus dem Konzept

Du hast idealerweise einen agrarwissenschaftlichen oder tierärztlichen Hintergrund

Sehr gute Deutsch- und Englischkenntnisse in Wort und Schrift sind Grundvoraussetzung

Arbeiten in einem gemeinnützigen Verein und tatkräftiger Einsatz für Tierrechte in einem intrinsisch motivierten Team

author: Unknown
title: ISIS attacks military bus in Deir ez-Zor
content:
The Islamic State (ISIS) militant group has attacked a bus carrying personnel from the Syrian Ministry of Defense in the eastern Syrian province of Deir ez-Zor. The attack took place in al-Baghouz, once ISIS’s last territorial stronghold in Syria.




According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the attack triggered armed clashes between ISIS militants and government forces. Both sides reportedly suffered casualties, with people killed and injured. No precise casualty figures were initially provided.

author: Kodao Productions
title: NPA-Mindoro reports failed AFP attack, 4 gov’t casualties
content:
The New People’s Army (NPA) reported the death of four government troopers in a clash at Bulalacao, Oriental Mindoro on Monday, thwarting a 1

st

 Infantry Battalion-Philippine Army strike operation.




The NPA said a unit of its Lucio de Guzman Command successfully defended itself against the raid at its temporary encampment in Sitio Gatol, Barangay San Roque, withdrawing safely after the firefight.




An ABS-CBN report of the incident quoted 203rd Infantry Brigade-Philippine Army commander Brig. Gen. Melencio Ragudo claiming only two soldiers were wounded and are at a stable condition at a hospital. The report also stated that said the clash started at around 8:35 AM.




The NPA, however, said civilians who were at the scene after the encounter reported that four soldiers were killed. The Red army likewise refuted 1st IB’s claim that firearms and equipment were seized from the guerillas.




The NPA added that its fighters spotted the approaching soldiers and opened fire on them before they could reach the camp.NPA-Mindoro spokesperson Madaay Gasic said their latest victory against the Armed Forces of the Philippines demonstrate the Red army’s will to fight and the people’s “unwavering support.” Gasic also belied Ragudo’s claim civilians tipped off the miitary about the NPA’s presence in the area.




“The people of Bulalacao and all the people of Mindoro celebrate the heroic resistance of their army against the enemy,” Gasic said. # 

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: ‘I did fear for my life,’ RCMP officer testifies at inquest into shooting death of Rankin Inlet man
content:
In a tense second day at the coroner’s inquest into the death of a 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man, an officer who fired at the victim said that he feared for his safety.




Const. Clark Plaetinck was part of the RCMP’s emergency response team that flew in from Winnipeg on Nov. 6, 2021, while Trey Angootealuk was in a standoff with police. Plaetinck testified that after chemical irritants were deployed through the back window of the truck Angootealuk was in, the man exited with his rifle appearing to be turned toward them.




“I feared for my safety at that point, so I used my firearm to stop him,” Plaetinck told the inquest jury Tuesday in Rankin Inlet.




On Nov. 6, 2021, Angootealuk hijacked a truck, drove it to the outskirts of town, shot at police officers, then began a standoff with police that lasted several hours. Police fatally shot him early the following morning.




The inquest by Nunavut Chief Coroner Marianna Cervantes will determine the circumstances surrounding Angootealuk’s death. It began Monday at the Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet and is scheduled to last until Friday. The coroner’s office gave Nunatsiaq News a video link to cover the inquest remotely.




Nikolai Sittman, the Angootealuk family’s lawyer, asked why officers didn’t shoot him somewhere non-fatal.




Plaetnick said they didn’t want to risk missing him because they were shooting from afar.
















At one point, during a pause in Plaetnick’s testimony, an audience member could be heard yelling a profanity at him.




Sgt. Russ Hulme, another member of the RCMP’s emergency response team, also testified Tuesday.




He said he flew to Rankin Inlet from Winnipeg the night the standoff began.




Hulme and one other team member launched a gas canister into the stolen truck from its rear window, right before Angootealuk’s death.




Drone footage of that moment was played at the inquest.




It showed Angootealuk exiting the vehicle. Soon after police had shot at him, he laid on the ground outside the driver’s door.
















After the footage played, some inquest attendees could be heard crying. Some left the room.




Jury members asked Hulme why his team, which consisted of four members, didn’t consider shooting at the man’s vehicle to immobilize it.




Doing so would not have separated Angootealuk from his gun, and any escalation on their end may have risked a violent reaction from him, Hulme said.




“It sounds like it’s an easy task, but it carries risks,” he said.




Earlier on Tuesday, Sgt. Benjamin Comely, the detachment commander at the time, also testified.

 
















Comely said Angootealuk had a tactical advantage at one point during the standoff because of where he was positioned.




“I did fear for my life,” Comely said.

 




Coroner’s inquests are mandatory under Nunavut law for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved.




It will resume Tuesday at 9:30 a.m. CT, with more RCMP personnel expected to testify.

author: By Dan Feidt, Unicorn Riot
title: Blockbuster BAAJA Bill a ‘Hail Mary’ for Billionaires on Data Centers, Oil & Gas
content:
Washington, D.C. – The nearly 500-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) would cut a huge swath in the environmental laws passed since the Nixon Administration – including diminishing protections in the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, National Environmental Policy Act and National Historic Preservation Act. This bill would slash the consultative process and legal paths to prevent harms, including deadly pollution exposure, faced by Native tribes.




Under immense lobbying pressure from right-wing groups like the Heritage Foundation and 

the oil and gas industry

, the BAAJA bill 

passed through the U.S. Senate 62-33 on November 19

.




Though BAAJA is marketed as an “affordability” bill, it is an enormous shortcut for mining, oil and gas interests, and 

data centers

. It would sweep aside decades-old roadblocks and speed bumps energy and tech companies face under U.S. law, enabling companies to accelerate projects that create pollution and health damage for humans and the environment. The Revelator warned this would 

dismantle the bedrock of U.S. environmental law

.




Tribal governments and Native organizers are warning that the bill will severely damage the fates of their people, and obviously benefits gold and silver mining corporations. Unicorn Riot heard from one organizer that BAAJA would systematically remove a decade of activist tactics to block harmful industrial projects.




BAAJA could quickly lead to a 

“bonanza”

 of new pipelines and natural gas-fueled data centers on formerly pristine public land. Trillions of dollars are at stake. Hyperscaler companies like Oracle that are trying to build data centers that would include colocated natural gas turbines which need new pipelines — such as 

a pipeline blocked by New Mexico’s land commissioner

 in July for Oracle’s Jupiter project — stand to benefit from this legislation’s passage.




According to Politico, on November 19, U.S. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) 

tried to force a vote on an amendment

 that would ban data centers on public land, but was stifled.







Native Consultation Would be Slashed




One critical issue for the tribal nations is called Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), elected to become Minnesota’s next governor, voted for BAAJA. Retiring U.S. Sen. Tina Smith (D-MN) voted against it.




Robert Deschampe, Chairman of the Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa 

warned the November 7 version of the bill

 would “strip the Band of the authorities we rely on to protect our cultural and treaty-reserved resources throughout the 1854 ceded territory … by eliminating the Band’s existing authorities under Section 106, this bill would open the door to that pollution.” They warned “Section 106 enables the Band to seek judicial relief before irreparable damage occurs. BAAJA would eliminate each of these protections.”




Deschampe said additionally that “federal agencies, not tribal nations, would determine what is protected … agencies could disregard tribal concerns at their discretion” and that “Tribes would lose meaningful judicial remedies.”




One of the most critical elements involves Tribal Historic Preservation Offices. The earlier version of the bill let the Secretary of the Interior take over those powers directly. The latter version introduces a different yoke: those programs “could still be found deficient, and its funding suspended for failing to ‘regularly’ meet federal timelines or undefined ‘required metrics,'” cautioned Deschampe.




By dropping regulations around industrial projects, the controversial Twin Metals proposal could become unstoppable even if the corporation breaks laws around environmental reviews, and the Minnesota State Legislature would have far less leverage to curtail the project, 

Boundary Waters advocates warned

.




Several tribes around Minnesota have called to stop BAAJA and warn of irreparable harm, amid Klobuchar’s support for this legislation, 

Sahan Journal found

. The Coalition for Tribal Sovereignty lists 

dozens of similar letters from tribal governments to politicians in Washington,

 along with guides to Section 106 and the other laws.







Data Centers and Decarbonization




As a piece of pro-corporate legislation, BAAJA would make industrial projects nearly impossible to appeal, and it would prevent 

third-party organizations like Earthjustice from filing lawsuits

 to stop construction. Cleverly, local residents would be forbidden from suing over harms from projects unless that specific harm was addressed in the comment period, 

according

 to Indigenous organizer Dallas Goldtooth. The Bipartisan Policy Center, which supports the bill, 

agreed in their analysis

 that “BAAJA would limit standing to parties that raised their concerns during the comment period and can show direct harm.”




Across the country, dozens of data center projects, and new electrical transmission lines, have gotten stopped or slowed in permitting. Bill supporters believe it will support decarbonization and enable bringing cleaner energy projects into the power grid. 




Citizens Climate Lobby, a 501(c)(4) advocacy group, 

endorsed BAAJA

 in early October, saying the bill included “measures that will speed the buildout of transmission lines and get new clean energy projects connected to the grid faster.”




Decarbonization of the U.S. economy has been a frustrating goal for the environmental advocacy world. Energy projects with lower emissions than fossil fuel-powered facilities, like solar and wind farms, as well as nuclear projects, require an enormous new supply of copper and placing new transmission lines and substations all over the country. According to Scientific American, 

BAAJA also would streamline nuclear development

, an industry that historically has especially harmed Native communities.




Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) 

supports parts of the bill but acknowledges that dirtier industry interests are the main winners

:







“Even as amended, however, it could still benefit fossil fuel, mining, data center, and other industrial projects more than clean energy. It also threatens to limit agencies’ ability to address newly discovered harms, constrain future pollution regulation, and create large taxpayer-funded corporate handouts.”




Natural Resources Defense Council




NRDC concedes “these rollbacks would represent the most significant weakening of federal environmental laws since they were established more than a half a century ago.”







Path in U.S. House is Narrow




The congressional elections this year swung towards the Democrats in part due to large-scale organizing against data centers. Across swaths of the public, from the usual environmental crowd to disengaged people, libertarians and the right wing, voters gave the next Congress, after the “lame duck” period, a strong anti-data center mandate.




The U.S. Senate passed the legislation through cloture to limit debate, with a large part of the Democratic caucus in support. 




However, in the U.S. House, outgoing Republican speaker Mike Johnson is currently working to pass a major defense bill, and it’s unclear if they can get a vote on BAAJA before the next term starts on January 3, 2027. 




Dozens of now-defeated Republicans are swiftly losing interest in staying in Washington before the next session. 

Johnson told Politico

 he would first “try to pass the bill under suspension, a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority and bars floor amendments” and then try to bring it up under the standard rules of procedure which require a simple majority.




Democrat Hakeem Jeffries has already been tapped to become Speaker of the House. He could rally the House Dems to cover for missing Republicans and drag BAAJA over the finish line, even though many of his colleagues were elected on promises to curtail precisely these kinds of noxious and aggressive industrial projects. 

Jeffries told Politico

 BAAJA “‘falls short’ and needs changes” to NEPA and tribal provisions. If it isn’t passed by the time Jeffries takes over, the bill is dead and the process would start over.




Friends of the Boundary Waters

 is strongly opposed to BAAJA and warn about devastating provisions “buried” in the bill including:







“Locking in mining leases 

— if the Trump administration hands mineral leases over to Twin Metals, future administrations could be barred from revoking or even amending them.




Limiting your day in court

 — people would have just 150 days to challenge a project. Even when a court finds an environmental review broke the law, the project could keep going.




Weakening the Clean Water Act

 — states and tribes would have a harder time stopping projects that threaten their water.”




Friends of the Boundary Waters

























Video: 

Honor the Earth BAAJA Power Hour

 with Dallas Goldtooth.







Think Tanks and ‘Abundance Movement’ Line Up for BAAJA




The broad sweep of this bill helps illustrate that the climate movement could get caught between opposing forces, a 

piece by Grist detailed

 in October. It shows the hand of centrist and center-right think tanks, as well as their allies in the newly fashioned “abundance movement.” Here’s a quick snapshot to understand the players involved.




“Abundance” became a messaging vehicle for refocusing on neoliberal market deregulation, named after a 

book promoting this agenda released by Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson

 last year. Silicon Valley billionaires have 

lined up a whopping nine-figure commitment

 to move their “abundance” points of view forward in public discourse. 




Not surprisingly, leaders in this crowd are brimming with enthusiasm for BAAJA, which would greatly simplify industrial projects for the ultrawealthy figures funding their scene. The director of the Breakthrough Institute 

boasted that

 BAAJA is “culminating years of energy abundance advocacy.”




A non-profit called Inclusive Abundance did 

message testing

 and 

backs the bill

. Amid the dozens of organizations that signed onto 

an Abundance Institute letter

, many are affiliated with key conservative umbrella groups, like the Council for National Policy and State Policy Network.




Centrist 

Blue Dog Coalition Democrats

 and 

New Democrat Coalition

 are on board. Third Way, the principal centrist think tank, 

supports the bill

, as does 

the Searchlight Institute

, another centrist think tank founded last year 

aimed at “curbing the influence of liberal groups,”

 according to the New York Times. The Heritage Foundation, a cornerstone of D.C.’s right-wing think tank scene, 

supports the bill

. The Bipartisan Policy Center supports the bill and 

published a long analysis of its details

.




The 

National Association of Counties

 strongly supports the bill for a variety of subtle reasons. The center-right 

American Action Forum

 and libertarian 

Cato Institute

 support the bill. 




The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions 

supports the bill

 and provided a 

long analysis

, as does the 

Center for Public Enterprise

. The National Taxpayers Union 

supports the bill

. 




Liskow, a law firm involved with fossil fuels, 

touted the bill’s Senate passage as important

, and a similar law firm called Hunton is 

monitoring it closely

. The Environmental Defense Fund released an 

ambiguous statement

 saying it was “worth the hard work to fix.”




NAACP

 and Defenders of Wildlife are 

strongly opposed

, along with 

hundreds

 of environmental groups. The political non-profit 5 Calls Civic Action pushed members to 

oppose the bill

 and the beltway insider website Punchbowl News 

leaked an internal Zoom chat transcript

 between BAAJA opponents.




It looks like BAAJA faces steep odds in the U.S. House before the end of the year. However, the situation is still worth looking at carefully. A huge bill like this brings countless interested players in Washington out into the open. 




It clearly shows that even after an election that is going to move Congress to the left, cuts to the Clean Water Act and other bedrock legislation are considered acceptable sacrifices when carrots like transmission line construction got put on the table. 




Alliances of convenience between conservatives, oil and gas lobbyists, abundance evangelists, and the cleaner end of the energy industry could keep turning up.

photo by Jean Beaufort

.

author: Dennis Ward
title: Métis country singer Catie St. Germain and her journey from insecurity to the top of the charts
content:
It has only been about three years since Catie St. Germain released his first single but she has been racking up the accolades, ever since.

Growing up, St. Germain says she had a front-row seat to a legendary musician and television host, crushing it on stage every night.

Her grandfather, Ray St. Germain, is a Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame inductee, who also created and hosted a nationally syndicated variety show, Big Sky Country.

However, having a famous grandfather and a very musical family did not ensure she would follow in their footsteps.

St. Germain’s mother even tried to push her in another direction.

“She didn’t have the best experience, I think doing music. The pressure of it all was a lot for her, so, she kind of steered us away. She didn’t want her kids to have to go through the hardships of the music industry and everything,” says St. Germain on the latest episode of Face to Face.

“For a long time I just didn’t think this was something in the cards for me. But I did perform, I did sing. I joined a rock tribute band and was kind of touring with them for a while but I ended up quitting and just having kids myself and thinking it was easier and better to do the 9 to 5 thing and obviously the scheduling worked better for having kids. And then I got back to it though.

“I really wasn’t fulfilled and so I decided to write my original song, The Taxman in 2023 and release that and see what would come of it and it just sparked a whole new passion for me,” adds St. Germain.

The time on the road had St. Germain feeling like she was away from her family all of the time.

Breaking out on her own was also a way to challenge herself and show some bravery.

“I’ve always been somebody who is a little bit more insecure and never would try, I didn’t want to put myself out there. Even in the family too, I would do the family shows with them but I was always the shy one, like I wasn’t the one that was out there, at all. Very shy, very timid. I had my kids and I just really wanted to show them that they could do anything they put their mind to and they can be brave and if I was going to tell them to do that, then I probably should do it too,” says St. Germain.

The reaction to that first song and following EP, Cleaning House (Or Trying) was even more incredible that St. Germain had imagined.

In the three years since then, St. Germain has sang the national anthem at the 2025 CFL Grey Cup in Winnipeg, been named one of Amazon Music’s breakthrough artists, and racked up three number one hits on the Indigenous Music Countdown.

In November at the 2026 Manitoba Country Music Awards, St. Germain was named Female Artist of the Year and took home Interactive Artist, Duo or Group of the Year, for the third straight year.

St. Germain says social media has allowed her to reach a bigger audience.

“I think too, a lot of people get to relate to me as a human, as a person and not just the music, which is really fun. Again, I just create better relationships that way and I think it entices them more to go listen to the music after that,” says St. Germain.

St. Germain’s latest single, a duet with Don Amero called Home hit the Indigenous Music Countdown on November 21.

Her next single, I Ain’t Free will be released on Nov. 27.

Dennis is Métis from southern Manitoba. After spending a decade working in TV in Alberta and Ontario, Dennis returned to Manitoba to join APTN. In 2016, he won a Canadian Association of Journalists award for his story A Soldier Scorned for APTN Investigates. In 2017, he became a host/producer for APTN National News and Face to Face.

author: Fraser Needham
title: AFN calls for strengthening of First Nations Clean Water Act
content:
The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the Carney government’s proposed Bill C-37 falls short when it comes to the necessary health, legal and environmental protections to ensure access to clean drinking water.

“Clean drinking water is a human right that has been denied for generations of First Nations families across Canada,” Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said in a press release.

“Sadly, with Bill C-37, the federal government is still refusing to recognize the human right to water for First Nations in Canada.”

Woodhouse Nepinak was a witness before the Indigenous and Northern Affairs Committee on Tuesday, which is studying the proposed legislation.

The AFN says Bill C-37, also known as the First Nations Clean Water Act, is significantly weaker than legislation drafted by the previous Trudeau government.

Bill C-61, which did not pass because Parliament was prorogued under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, recognized First Nations access to clean drinking water as a human right, but has been weakened under the current legislation to the “progressive realization.”

It took Carney more than a year to reintroduce the new legislation.

According to the United Nations, progressive realization means that states “have a duty to respect, protect and fulfil economic, social and cultural rights,” and are “required to progressively achieve the full realization of these rights over a period of time. Regardless of resource availability, States have an immediate obligation to take appropriate steps to ensure continuous and sustained improvement in the enjoyment of these rights over time.”

The AFN also says the proposed legislation gives provinces a veto, lacks adequate protections for source water and doesn’t live up to Canada’s United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples commitments.

“We are calling on Parliament to take the time needed to work with First Nations on required improvements, clarifications and amendments to Bill C-37 that respect our rights and jurisdiction,” Woodhouse Nepinak said.

Bill C-37 has passed second reading in the House of Commons and is currently in committee.

The previous water legislation was drafted in response to a lawsuit that was settled in 2021.

That bill also included an option for source water protection but failed to pass before Parliament was dissolved for the 2025 election.

The new bill is backed by $4.6 billion in funding over five years, which the federal government describes as the single largest commitment ever made to First Nations water protection.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has said the new legislation was written to “stand the test of time” and insists it does not weaken the protections in the previous bill.

Fraser spent the last 20 years working in both print and radio in Saskatchewan – mostly in the northern part of the province. Before joining APTN’s Ottawa bureau, he was news director for the Missinipi Broadcasting Corporation working out of their Prince Albert office. He holds a bachelor of arts degree in political science from Carleton University and a diploma of journalism from Algonquin College.

author: Sonny Melencio
title: Pax Silica: Who benefits, whose industrial strategy? A rejoinder to supporters of Pax Silica
content:
Proponents of Pax Silica promise factories, exports, and skilled jobs. We’ve heard those promises before.

After decades of building export zones and selling electronics abroad, Philippine semiconductor production remains concentrated in assembly, testing and packaging.

Under the terms being offered, Pax Silica will deepen this pattern and further stunt Philippine industrialisation. The government is committing public land, infrastructure and worker training to a foreign-led supply chain without securing the commitments needed to build our own industrial capacity.

The US State Department launched Pax Silica in December 2025 to secure supply chains critical to Washington’s rivalry with China. The founding group included the United States, Israel, Australia, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Britain. They came to the table with industrial, financial, or technological advantages of their own.

By November 16, the declaration reportedly had 26 signatories, with Singapore and the Philippines reported as the only ASEAN members among them.

The Philippines joined after Washington had set the initiative’s priorities. In an April 9 letter to US Under Secretary of State Jacob Helberg, Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) President Joshua Bingcang proposed a Pax Silica coordination hub in a 4000-acre [1619 hectare] economic security zone in New Clark City, Tarlac.

To sweeten the offer, the BCDA proposed a two-year rent-free period as the Philippine government’s contribution.

Washington has clear economic, geopolitical and military interests in the initiative. It wants reliable access to critical minerals, advanced chips, computing power and data infrastructure. It wants to organise those supply chains around the United States and its partners in its rivalry with China.

Advanced computing serves both civilian and military purposes, and Washington is pursuing Pax Silica alongside its broader military alliance strategy in the Indo-Pacific.

That broader strategy was on display on November 4 in Cebu. On the sidelines of the ASEAN defense ministers’ meeting, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and his counterparts from the Philippines, Japan and Australia met under the informal grouping known as the “Squad”.

They agreed on a Manila-based coordination centre to align defense investments, intelligence sharing and military deterrence against China.

The Philippines enters this arrangement without a geostrategy of its own. The Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 gives the state an active role in building infrastructure, training workers and supporting selected industries.

Yet it relies on the neoliberal framework of private investment, public-private partnerships and integration into global supply chains. That leaves investors with considerable power over what gets built and who captures the gains.

This is how dependent capitalism works. Decisions about financing, technology and production are often made abroad.

At home, Philippine oligarchs earn substantial returns from land, property and concessions. For them, building factories, engineering teams and supplier networks takes years of investment with less certain returns.

The semiconductor industry shows where the leverage lies. US-based NVIDIA dominates the market for AI accelerators. Taiwan’s TSMC leads in advanced chip fabrication. The Netherlands’ ASML is the sole commercial supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography systems. Each controls a capability that takes years and enormous investment to build.

Their governments use these points of leverage to restrict China’s access to advanced technology.

The 2023 agreement among the United States, the Netherlands and Japan covered certain chip-making equipment. Dutch licensing rules restrict exports of advanced ASML machines, while US export controls separately affect certain NVIDIA chip sales and TSMC shipments to China.

The Philippines is offering to host a semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing hub in Tarlac that would serve this supply chain.

The question is what capabilities the country would gain. Building the engineering teams, research institutions, and supplier networks that would give us greater control over what we produce requires an industrial strategy of our own.

Successive Philippine governments have treated access to foreign markets and capital as a substitute for building domestic productive capacity.

Years back before Philippine independence, the 1946 Bell Trade Act shaped postwar economic relations, including through an arrangement that gave Americans parity rights in exploiting Philippine natural resources and operating public utilities. The Laurel–Langley Agreement later revised those trade terms. A separate military bases agreement entrenched US military access.

Under Fidel V Ramos, entry into the World Trade Organization was sold as a route to greater competitiveness. Import competition intensified while many Filipino farmers and producers still lacked affordable credit, irrigation, storage and processing facilities.

Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo’s promise of food on every table carried forward the same faith in liberalisation. Opening markets did little to fill the gaps successive governments had left in agriculture and industry.

Our export zones offer the clearest test of what Pax Silica promises.

Since the creation of the Bataan Export Processing Zone in Mariveles, these zones have brought few factories, jobs, exports, and technical skills. Yet semiconductor production still centers on assembly, testing and packaging, with limited chip design and no major commercial wafer fabrication.

The head of the Semiconductor and Electronics Industries in the Philippines (SEIPI) has argued that wafer fabrication is important to the industry’s long-term competitiveness and has identified shortages of specialised workers, local suppliers, and a proven production base as barriers to attracting a major plant.

The World Bank estimates that foreign value added accounts for roughly half the gross export value of Philippine computer and electronics manufacturing. That helps explain how billions in electronics exports can coexist with a thin local supplier base.

Meanwhile, manufacturing’s share of GDP fell from roughly a quarter in 2001 to around a sixth in 2024. Several forces drove that decline, and decades of expanding economic zones failed to reverse it.

Under the proposal, the government supplies land, infrastructure, and incentives. Foreign firms can locate the operations that suit their supply chains here while keeping control of the technology and the most profitable stages of production elsewhere.

Domestic conglomerates can earn from property and concessions even if Philippine industry gains little productive capacity.

Every public peso and hectare committed on those terms is a resource we could use to develop local producers and meet domestic needs. That is how a project can add factories and still stunt industrialisation.

The costs also fall unevenly. If the conversion of thousands of acres displaces farmers or encroaches on Indigenous ancestral lands, who bears the loss? The people whose land and livelihoods are at stake must have the right to decide what happens in their communities. Their rights must carry more weight than the government’s bid to attract investors.

A large AI data center is a plausible component, given the country’s limited computing infrastructure at that scale. If it goes ahead, the government must show who will control the computing capacity, which Philippine industries will be able to use it, and who will bear the cost of the electricity and water it requires considering that all these were privatized to firms out to earn more profits and pass on the costs to consumers.

Supporters who dismiss socialist and progressive critics as ideological should defend their own premise.

After decades of liberalisation and investor incentives, what grounds do they have for claiming that another foreign-led economic zone will build the industries the country needs?

The burden is on the Marcos Jr. administration to show who will own the technology, which Filipino industries will grow, and what the country will retain after the incentives expire.

The Philippines needs an industrial strategy anchored in public investment, domestic production and the needs of workers, farmers and communities.

That means building local supplier networks, funding public research and engineering, and tying public support for investors to enforceable commitments to develop Philippine capabilities.

Washington is using Pax Silica to consolidate its lead in AI and shape the supply chains that sustain it. The Marcos Jnr administration is offering our land, minerals and labour to carry out that strategy.

Our task is to build an industrial strategy of our own. Not through the dynasties, oligarchs and their neoliberal cohorts.

[Sonny Melencio is the chairperson of the Partido Lakas Ng Masa (Party of the Labouring Masses).]

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Poll: Most Dems Want Congress to Defund War Next Month, Even at Risk of Shutdown
content:
Top Republicans have signaled an openness to defunding the war, as Democrats like Hakeem Jeffries have demurred.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

New polling finds that the majority of Democrats want members of Congress to use next month’s government funding bill to withhold funds for the Iran war, a strategy embraced by progressives and figures like Senate majority leader candidate Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) to end the war as soon as possible.

According to University of Maryland polling conducted this past weekend, 51 percent of Democrats say that they support the use of the upcoming funding bill, with a deadline of December 11, to defund the war even if it risks a government shutdown or a presidential veto. By contrast, only 16 percent of Democrats said they oppose the idea — a -35 point margin — while 32 percent said they don’t know.

The idea is also narrowly favored when responses from all ideologies are considered, 31 percent support to 28 percent opposition, despite 48 percent of Republicans opposing the idea.

Earlier this month, a group of four senators — Van Hollen, Michael Bennet (D-Colorado), Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), and Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) — vowed in a joint statement to oppose any funding bill that would fund the war. Lawmakers in favor of the effort have made clear that their intention is to effectively dare President Donald Trump to shut down the government in order to fund his war.

“Congress cannot allow Trump to continue his conflict — we must force him to end it,” the lawmakers said. “When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war.”

The proposal is imminently achievable. The Washington Post reported this week that top Republicans have said that they are open to allowing the bill to be used to cut off funding for the war in exchange for keeping the government funded. The Post cited Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) as two Republicans who said they are open to the effort.

Thune said that he is “open to anything that keeps the government funded and makes sure that we’ve got our military and national security requirements and needs met.”

In other words, the Democratic base wants Congress to defund the war at the soonest possible opportunity; several Democrats in Congress are pushing for the proposal; and even Republican leaders may be on board.

Part of the reason for this broad-based support may be the vast unpopularity of the war, in which U.S.-Israeli strikes have killed roughly 3,500 people in Iran.

University of Maryland’s polling found that a staggering 80 percent of Democrats say that they want the war to end now “regardless of the terms,” meaning that they would be fine with accepting any of Iran’s and U.S.’s terms in exchange for the war’s end. A majority of all respondents felt the same, at 55 percent, compared to 21 percent who said they prefer the current course, and 18 percent saying they favor a military escalation.

Experts have said that defunding the war is one of the most effective ways to force President Donald Trump to end the military portion of the war, with options like war powers resolutions unable to force his hand.

Some of the people not in support of the proposal, however, are top Democrats. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) said last week that he opposes even the idea of barring funds from being used for the war, in favor of a war powers resolution that the Trump administration is likely to ignore. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York), facing a challenge to his leadership from one of the top Senate champions of the proposal to defund the war, has been mum on the issue.

The top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, Rosa DeLauro (Connecticut), has suggested that she does not want to use the continuing resolution to shut down the war.

“I think that the American people would like to see us end the war. I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war,” she said last week, her comments undercut by polling finding otherwise.

author: Rindala Alajaji
title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year
content:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

At the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, New York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org.

Take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Huang’s Return to Nvidia Shows the Unsustainable Power of AI Over the Economy
content:
The scandal over Jensen Huang reflects efforts from establishment hawks to ramp up hostilities between the US and China.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Nvidia stock prices surged over 30% on Monday as the chip maker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang had stepped down earlier in November amid reports he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI boom, and the leadership turmoil had erased trillions in value from the U.S. stock market. President Donald Trump acknowledged he had encouraged the company’s board to bring Huang back.

“The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the [S&P 500] this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable,” says Aya Ibrahim, senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute.

We also speak with organizer and researcher Tobita Chow, who says Huang’s “spy scandal” that led to his ouster is part of a larger effort by anti-China figures in the U.S. national security establishment to escalate tensions between the countries.

“The national security leadership in both parties in D.C. has been greatly frustrated with President Trump, who has over the past year pursued policies to maintain very warm relations with Xi Jinping,” says Chow, who notes that Secretary of State Marco Rubio is one of the “chief” frustrated China hawks in the administration.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: Jensen Huang is back as CEO of the chip giant Nvidia, after President Trump personally called into a company board meeting Sunday to push for Huang’s reinstatement. Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago, after news reports revealed he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly in communication with China’s top spy agency. The woman worked with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of buying advanced Nvidia chips, then diverting them to China in violation of U.S. export rules. On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist.

During an interview on CNBC, Trump was questioned about his role reinstating Huang.

EAMON JAVERS: Mr. President, did you give the board of directors an assurance that Jensen Huang would not be prosecuted at all for any of these —

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I didn’t use the word “prosecuted.”

EAMON JAVERS: — questions around export controls?

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: But I said — I said that we believe — and I put out a statement. I think you probably saw that.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: That we believe he’s fine, he’s absolutely fine. I gave them enough —

CARL QUINTANILLA: There was a —

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: — assurance.

AMY GOODMAN: President Trump also admitted that falling stock prices played a role in his decision to push for Huang to be reinstated. After Huang resigned, Nvidia’s stock fell sharply, along with those of several other AI and technology companies with ties to Nvidia.

One major holder of Nvidia stock has been Cantor Fitzgerald. The Wall Street investment firm is run by the sons of Howard Lutnick, Cantor’s former CEO, who serves as President Trump’s commerce secretary. Cantor Fitzgerald held shares in Nvidia worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The New York Times reports Lutnick pushed to weaken chip export rules that overlapped with his family’s business.

The Financial Times reports President Trump personally made up to $15 million on Monday alone, after Nvidia’s stock soared 30% following Huang’s return.

On Monday, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani responded to the Nvidia news and its impact on working people.

MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI: I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage. And yet, for many days, that had a massive impact. And what we’re also talking about here, speaking about Mr. Huang, we’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumored to be around $81 billion. That would be the cost of providing universal childcare for every 3- and 4-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year.

And a lot of this just brings to mind what Justice Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is that we can have democracy, we can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few, we cannot have both. And when you look at our stock market and you look at how disproportionately dependent it is on artificial intelligence-related stocks, it cannot help but give you a sense of concern about just how — how much this technology is now dominant, not just in terms of the discourse that we are having around it on a day-to-day basis, but also the strength of the United States economy.

AMY GOODMAN: To talk more about Nvidia and the reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang, we’re joined by two guests. In Chicago, we’re joined by Tobita Chow, an organizer there. His most recent article for The Nation is headlined “Why Jensen Huang’s Downfall Is No Victory for Progressives.” Aya Ibrahim is with us here in New York. She’s a senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute. She previously served as a senior adviser on the secretary of state’s policy planning staff, the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy and on the National Economic Council. She also served as senior economic adviser to Massachusetts Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley.

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! I want to get your response to the resignation, and then the reinstatement at the behest of President Trump, of Jensen Huang, and also the comments of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Aya.

AYA IBRAHIM: Thank you for having me, Amy.

You know, I think that the mayor’s comments really get at the heart of this issue, which is who is in control of our economy, who is critical to our national security, and who gets to decide the trajectory of both. For so long, we have had discussions that centered on the value of the free hand of the market, and now we have an economy where it seems to be the singular hand of President Trump. The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the S&P this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable. And that the president would feel the need to step in, and do so in a way that undermines serious concerns around national security, is a problem.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Aya, what about these concerns around national security? The Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Sunday that there’s an investigation into Alice Huang, one of the women with which Jensen Huang had a relationship with, and her firm Megaspeed, that that’s ongoing. But it’s still unclear that Alice Huang is an alleged spy for the Chinese government. Your thoughts about this?

AYA IBRAHIM: Well, whatever the conclusion or finding as to the exact nature of the relationship, I think, is ultimately irrelevant, to the extent that regardless of the nature of the relationship, the result was that Jensen Huang was sidestepping and circumventing export controls. Right? These are violations of the law. So, the relationship itself is beside the point.

The bigger issue here is that we have one man, one firm, that many people, including those in our government, now believe are indispensable both to our economic growth and financial stability and to national security. And there’s an emerging discourse of “separate the artist from the art,” but usually the artist doesn’t have an impact on my retirement. So, this is a very unique set of circumstances, but it’s also the result of decades of technology and national security exceptionalism that allows the rise for firms to have such singular power and influence.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, I’d like to bring Tobita Chow into the conversation. Your initial thoughts on the breaking news that Jensen was reinstated? And I also — I’m wondering if you could talk some, because most of Nvidia’s chips — I mean, sorry, all of Nvidia’s advanced chips are manufactured in Taiwan by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, TSMC, and the the irony here of most of these most advanced chips being manufactured just 80 miles away from the Chinese mainland.

TOBITA CHOW: Yeah. Thanks for having me.

I would also lift up Mayor Mamdani’s comments on this issue as a real model. The fundamental issue here is that a handful of these AI oligarchs have seized total control of the future of the U.S. economy, enormous power over the jobs and welfare and pensions, and so on, of all of us without our consent. And the real solution is that we need to build a new economy that is not dependent on this AI industry as its sole source of growth.

Another thing that I admire about Mayor Mamdani’s comments is that he steered the conversation away from the whole issue of the U.S.-China relationship and national security. My read of this scandal and news cycle is that it has been a strategy led by China hawks in the national security establishment to accomplish two goals. One is to build greater political support for chip restrictions against China, and to build greater political support particularly within the Trump administration, because Trump has been inclined to ease these chip restrictions against China, which hurts the Chinese AI industry — the restrictions hurt the Chinese AI industry. The other goal that the China hawks had was to get rid of Jensen Huang, who has been the chief proponent within Silicon Valley of continued engagement between the U.S. and Chinese tech industries and very successfully lobbied the Trump administration around this issue of chip restrictions against China. So, I think there — we need to understand the role that these China hawks within the national security establishment have played in driving this whole news cycle.

As far as the role of TSMC within the global chip industry goes, yeah, it is located in Taiwan. It is critical to the global chip industry. But I think, like, you know, there are recurring concerns about China’s claims to — claims to have sovereignty over Taiwan and their talk of reunification between Taiwan and the Chinese mainland. This creates fears of some sort of Chinese military action against Taiwan that would disrupt the global chip industry. There are real concerns there, but I think that fears of imminent military action around Taiwan tend to be overblown in a lot of discourse.

AMY GOODMAN: Toby Chow, you talked about the rift in the national security establishment. Give it names — for example, Marco Rubio, a true China hawk, who is secretary of state. I think The Wall Street Journal has a piece today calling on him to step down so he doesn’t become this face of a failed foreign policy. And then you have Vice President Vance, and these two, Vance and Rubio, perhaps vying for the presidency in 2028. Explain the positions they’re taking here.

TOBITA CHOW: Marco Rubio is maybe chief among the frustrated China hawks within the Trump administration. So, the national security leadership in both parties in D.C. has been greatly frustrated with President Trump, who has over the past year pursued policies to maintain very warm relations with Xi Jinping, who he seems to admire as a fellow strongman leader. And so, his approach has been seen as way too, you know, soft on China by basically the entire national security establishment, and this includes a number of frustrated national security leaders within Trump’s own administration, Marco Rubio being chief among them. And yes, there are reports that Marco Rubio played a key role in leaking a report that drove this whole scandal around Jensen Huang.

JD Vance has taken a very different position. According to reports, he was instrumental in working with venture capitalists and other of Jensen Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley to pressure Trump to support the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia, and which led to a very successful meeting where Donald Trump met with the board of Nvidia and got them to reinstate Jensen Huang.

There are splits within Silicon Valley on this key question of chip controls vis-à-vis China that are at play here. On the one hand, you have companies like Nvidia, which can profit off of the Chinese tech industry. You also have venture capitalists in Silicon Valley — and JD Vance was one of these venture capitalists — who are investing in companies that can make profitable use of cheaper Chinese AI models. So, this is a faction of Silicon Valley that supports Jensen Huang and his efforts to ease chip restrictions against China. This is opposed to a different faction of Silicon Valley, which includes the frontier AI labs of Anthropic and OpenAI. These companies do not have any opportunity to profit off of the Chinese tech industry. For them, the Chinese tech industry is only a severe competitive threat, and even an existential threat to their business models, and so they have consistently lobbied for stronger chip restrictions against China, which puts them in a natural alliance with the China Hawks. So, that’s the division that we’re seeing at play here, both within Silicon Valley and within D.C., and even within Trump’s own administration.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, I’m wondering also if you could talk, Tobita, about the — we hear a lot about the relationship between Chinese companies, especially these advanced companies, and the Chinese government. But what about the relationship of the major companies here in the United States to the U.S. government and the U.S. military?

TOBITA CHOW: Yeah, there is — among national security leaders and China watchers, sometimes you’ll see them talk in very concerned tones about this thing that is called military-civil fusion in China, which is this growing — this effort to increase the level of integration between civilian industries, particularly in the tech industry, and the Chinese military. I agree that’s a very dangerous trend.

But that trend is, I feel like, if anything, more advanced in the United States. We are seeing within Silicon Valley movement of greater convergence and integration into the national security state, moving into, you know, arms manufacturing, into Pentagon contracts. Many of these companies also see — increasingly see the national security establishment as allies in protecting them from rising populist anger at Silicon Valley, and also getting them favorable policies.

I mean, part of what we have seen in this Jensen Huang scandal is that it was good for Anthropic and OpenAI. It very coincidentally overlapped with Anthropic’s debut on the stock market. But Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia suggested that the U.S. government might indeed move to strengthen these chip restrictions against China, thereby undermining the Chinese AI industry, which is a boon for both Anthropic and OpenAI. So, this is a demonstration of what national security leaders can provide to actors in Silicon Valley.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to go back to Aya Ibrahim. Apple still manufactures most of its iPhones in China. Tesla designs and sells electric vehicles plus energy storage systems in China. Google’s Android operating system runs on nearly 80% of smartphones in China. Can you talk about the significance of the focus on Nvidia shipping AI chips to China? Who benefits from Jensen’s ousting from the company? And ultimately, do you simply think he was too big to fail?

AYA IBRAHIM: So, no, nobody is too big to fail or too big to fire, and no one should be, again, this indispensable, whether to our economy or national security.

The question of companies that are operating in China, I mean, they’re — not all technologies are created the same. So, this is fundamentally a question about cutting-edge technology, advanced chips, that are necessary for defense and intelligence and national security purposes, and many view them as critical to our ability to maintain those systems. That is different than, you know, legacy chips that go into other products, like EVs.

I think that the focus on export controls misses a bigger issue. By all means, if there are loopholes, close the loopholes. But closing the loopholes is not an exhaustive solution, and it also does not get at the structural and systemic issues that allowed for the situation to come together in the first place. Right? Closing the loopholes in export control are not going to address the opaque financing that’s underpinning this ecosystem and its buildout. It’s not going to address the deep imbalances in our economy and financial markets, where one company’s IPO means that 5,000 people have more wealth than the bottom third of Americans. It is not going to address the lack of competition, such that we only have one company and we’re sitting here for weeks trying to figure out, well, how do we make sure that this company operates in a way that is consistent with national interest, ignoring the fact that at the end of the day, a company has commercial interests, and those are not always one and the same as national interest.

AMY GOODMAN: So, there is a huge change, the blue wave, with the incoming Congress. Both will be controlled by the Democrats. President Trump has made very clear that he doesn’t want AI regulated. What do you think should be the approach of this new wave?

AYA IBRAHIM: I think that AI and data centers specifically were an 80-20 issue for voters, and it really has scrambled our politics. So, it’s a cross-cutting and, frankly, a bipartisan issue. And we saw many Republicans shift, including Governor Abbott in Texas, who imposed a temporary moratorium. That is the level of frustration and anger, and to the degree that, again, even folks who are nominally very hands-off regulation-wise felt the need to respond.

I think that voters have made very clear the two big issues in this election were cost of living and corruption, and both of those issues are embodied fairly well in this larger debate about the AI buildout and who bears the cost and pays the price, and then who benefits. And it’s very clear that a handful of folks are benefiting at the expense of many people. The American people want us to regulate these companies. They want to see accountability for leaders that have made it very clear that they’re indifferent to what is in the interest of anyone but themselves or their share price.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re going to leave it there, but, of course, we’re going to continue to cover this issue. Aya Ibrahim is senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute. And Tobita Chow, Toby Chow, organizer in Chicago, we’ll link to your recent piece in The Nation, “Why Jensen Huang’s Downfall Is No Victory for Progressives.”

Coming up, masked, unidentified, plainclothes ICE agents detain a father and daughter on the jetway at Sea-Tac Airport in Seattle as they’re trying to board a plane to attend a family baptism. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Really Real” by Allison Russell and Ganessa James of Rainbow Coalition, performing in our Democracy Now! studio.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Truthout produces reporting you won’t see in the mainstream: journalism from the frontlines of global conflict, interviews with grassroots movement leaders, high-quality legal analysis and more.

title: Bağdat, Kürdistan'ın tüm sınır kapıları ve Erbil kontrolündeki bazı petrol sahalarının devrini emretti stedi
content:
Irak'ta federal hükümet ile Kürdistan Bölgesel Yönetimi (KBY) arasında petrol kaynaklarının işletilmesi, gelirlerin paylaşılması ve tartışmalı bölgelerin statüsü konusunda yıllardır süregelen anlaşmazlık büyüdü: Irak Başbakanı'nın federal güvenlik güçlerine ve kamu kurumlarına verdiği bir dizi talimatla Erbil'in sınır kapıları ve petrol sahalarındaki yetkileri kaldırıldı.




Bağdat'ın kararları




Başbakanın askeri sözcüsü Sabah en-Numan, devlete ait Kuzey Petrol Şirketi sahalarından petrol kaçırıldığı iddialarını araştıran soruşturma komisyonunun raporunun değerlendirilmesinin ardından alınan kararları açıkladı.




Irak Başbakanı'nın talimatları uyarınca:



















Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin bütün sınır kapıları Federal Sınır Kapıları İdaresi'nin denetimine geçirilecek.










Kerkük, Diyala, Selahaddin ve Ninova vilayetlerinde Kürt güvenlik güçlerinin denetimindeki ve Bağdat'ın federal Petrol Bakanlığına ait olduğunu belirttiği petrol sahalarının yönetimi Bakanlığa, güvenliği ise federal enerji polisine devredilecek.










KBY, federal Petrol Bakanlığı'nın bilgisi dışında ham petrol ve petrol ürünleri ihracatına izin veremeyecek.










Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin komşu ülkelerle arasındaki gayriresmî sınır geçişleri kapatılacak.










Kürdistan Bölgesi ile söz konusu dört Irak vilayeti arasındaki gayriresmî geçiş yollarının kapatılması için iki ortak güvenlik tugayı görevlendirilecek.










Erbil, Süleymaniye ve Duhok girişlerinde petrol ürünlerinin denetlenmesi için kontrol noktaları kurulacak.



















Bağdat yönetimi, kararların ülkenin egemenliğini ve ulusal servetini korumayı amaçladığını savunuyor. Kararların uygulanmasına ilişkin henüz bir takvim açıklanmadı.




Mesrur Barzani: “Hiçbir şekilde kabul edilemez”




KBY Başbakanı Mesrur Barzani, Erbil'de düzenlenen Dünya Gençlik Zirvesi'nde gazetecilerin sorularını yanıtlarken Bağdat'ın kararlarının kısa süre önce gerçekleştirilen görüşmelerde varılan mutabakatla çeliştiğini söyledi:







“Bugün Bağdat'tan çıkan kararlar bizi şaşırttı. Çünkü içerikleri federal makamlarla önceki görüşmelerimizde ulaştığımız sonuçlarla örtüşmüyor.”







Kararları “hiçbir şekilde kabul edilemez” olarak nitelendiren Barzani, anlaşmazlıkların anayasa temelinde çözülmesi için müzakereleri sürdürmeye hazır olduklarını belirtti.




Barzani, 9 Kasım'da Bağdat'ta Irak Başbakanı Zeydi ile bir araya gelmişti. Görüşmede petrol kaynaklarının anayasa uyarınca yönetilmesi ve federal petrol ve doğal gaz yasasının çıkarılması ele alınmıştı.




Irak Halk Seferberlik Güçleri (Haşdi Şabi) Başkanı Falih Feyyad da 21 Kasım'da Erbil'de Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin yöneticileriyle görüşmüştü. KBY, görüşmelerin ardından anlaşmazlıkların anayasa çerçevesinde ve diyalog yoluyla çözülmesi konusunda mutabakata varıldığını açıklamıştı.




KDP ve KYB: “Kürdistan'ın hakları kırmızı çizgimiz”




Bağdat'ın kararları, Ekim 2024'teki Kürdistan Parlamentosu seçimlerinden bu yana yeni bölgesel hükümetin oluşturulması konusunda anlaşamayan iki büyük Kürt partisini ortak tutum almaya yöneltti.




Mesud Barzani liderliğindeki Kürdistan Demokrat Partisi (KDP) ile Bafıl Talabani liderliğindeki Kürdistan Yurtseverler Birliği (KYB), 24 Kasım'da yayımladıkları ortak bildiride Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin, anayasal hakları dışında herhangi bir talepte bulunmadığını, buna karşılık bölgenin anayasal haklarının yıllardır ihlal edildiğini belirttiler.




İki parti, federal hükümet ve Kürdistan Bölgesi arasındaki anlaşmazlıklarda anayasanın nihai başvuru mercii olması gerektiğini vurguladı:







“Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin haklarına ve kazanımlarına yönelik her türlü ihlal kırmızı çizgidir.”







Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin Kürdistan halkının onlarca yıllık mücadelesinin ürünü olduğunu hatırlatan KDP ve KYB, "anayasal çerçeve dışında alınan kararları reddettiklerini, diyalog, şeffaflık ve karşılıklı anlayış yoluyla çözümü desteklediklerini" açıkladılar.




Mesud Barzani: “Boyun eğmeyeceğiz”




KDP Başkanı Mesud Barzani de akşam saatlerinde yayımladığı açıklamada Irak'taki karar merkezlerinde federalizmin ilkelerini ve Kürt halkının haklarını ihlal etmeye yönelik bir hareket geliştiğini söyledi.




Barzani, Saddam Hüseyin rejiminin devrilmesinin ardından kabul edilen anayasanın Irak'ın bütün halklarının haklarını güvence altına alacağına ilişkin beklentilerin karşılanmadığını, Kürt halkının haklarının giderek daha fazla ihlal edildiğini belirtti.




Irak Başbakanı'nın yolsuzluk ve kaçakçılıkla mücadelesini desteklediklerini, ancak bu mücadelenin hukuki ve anayasal yollarla yürütülmesi gerektiğini vurgulayan Barzani şöyle dedi:







“Kürdistan Bölgesi anayasaya aykırı kararlara ve herhangi birinin iradesinin dayatılmasına boyun eğmeyecek.”







Şii partileri Zeydi'nin arkasında




Irak hükümetinin başlıca siyasi dayanağı olan Şii partilerinin Koordinasyon Çerçevesi de akşam saatlerinde yaptığı açıklamada Başbakan Zeydi'nin kararlarını kamu kaynaklarının korunmasına yönelik adımlar olarak destekledi. İttifak, bununla birlikte Bağdat ve Erbil arasındaki anlaşmazlıkların diyalog yoluyla çözülmesi çağrısında bulundu.




KDP ile KYB'nin ortak tutumu ve Şii partilerinin Zeydi'ye verdiği destekle Bağdat-Erbil  anlaşmazlığı, merkezi ve yerel hükümetler arasındaki idari yetki tartışmasının ötesine geçerek Irak'ın başlıca siyasi ittifaklarını da içine alan bir kamplaşmaya dönüştü. 




Kaçakçılık iddiaları




Bağdat'ın yürüttüğü soruşturmada Kuzey Petrol Şirketine ait sahalardan alınan petrolün Kerkük ve Süleymaniye üzerinden İran ve Afganistan'a ulaştırılan kaçakçılık ağlarına aktarıldığı ileri sürülüyor.




Reuters, soruşturmada ulaşıldığı söylenen bu bulguları bağımsız kaynaklardan doğrulatamadığını bildirdi.




Zeydi hükümeti, Kürdistan Bölgesi'ne ilişkin kararlarını açıklamadan önce, İran'la ilişkili silahlı örgütlerden Ketaib Hizbullah'ın denetiminde bulunan, Bağdat'ın güneyindeki, Curf es-Sahr bölgesinde de petrol kaçakçılığı iddialarına yönelik soruşturma başlatmış, 20 Kasım'da bölgenin güvenlik denetiminin federal güçlere devredilmesi talimatını vermişti.




Kürdistan'a ilişkin kararlar soruşturma kapsamının ötesine geçerek anayasal statüye sahip bir bölgesel yönetimin yetkilerini de tartışmaya açması bakımından olağanüstü nitelikte. 




Anlaşmazlığın temeli: Federal yetkilerin paylaşımı




Irak'ın 2005 Anayasası Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin federe statüsünü tanıyor. Anayasanın 112. Maddesi mevcut sahalardan çıkarılan petrol ve doğal gazın federal hükümet ile üretici bölgelerin ve vilayetlerin yönetimleri tarafından ortaklaşa yönetilmesini öngörüyor.




Ancak petrol üretimi, yabancı şirketlerle sözleşmeler, ihracat yetkisi ve gelirlerin paylaşılması konularındaki anlaşmazlıkları giderecek federal petrol ve doğal gaz yasası bugüne kadar çıkarılmadı.




Irak Federal Yüksek Mahkemesi, 2022'de Kürdistan Bölgesi'nin petrol ve doğal gaz yasasını anayasaya aykırı bulmuş; Kürdistan yönetimi ise bu kararı reddetmişti.




2025'te taraflar arasında sağlanan geçici anlaşmayla Kürdistan Bölgesi'nden Türkiye yoluyla  petrol ihracatına yeniden başlanmış ve ihracat, federal petrol pazarlama şirketi SOMO aracılığıyla gerçekleştirilmeye başlanmıştı.




Bağdat'ın son kararları, petrol kaynaklarının yönetiminin yanı sıra, sınır kapılarının denetimini ve federal güvenlik güçlerinin yetkilerini de anlaşmazlık konusu haline getiriyor.




2017'deki Kürdistan bağımsızlık referandumunun ardından federal güçlerin Kerkük'ün kontrolünü yeniden ele geçirmesiyle yaşanan gerilimin üzerinden 9 yıl geçmesine karşın, Bağdat ve Kürt partileri arasındaki yetki anlaşmazlığını çözecek mekanizmaların yokluğunda Bağdat ve Erbil yeni bir krize doğru yol alıyor. 




(AEK)

author: CMI Argentina
title: Milton Tolomeo suspendió su huelga de hambre
content:
El preso político Milton Tolomeo, encarcelado por haber participado del rechazo popular contra la regresiva reforma laboral, suspendió la medida tras lograr una serie de conquistas en favor de todo su pabellón.







Compartimos el comunicado de la Coordinadora por la libertad de lxs presxs políticxs:




Milton suspende su huelga de hambre




Luego de haber sostenido dos semanas de huelga de hambre, Milton Tolomeo, preso por haber participado de la movilización popular contra la reforma laboral, decidió suspender la medida porque logró una serie de conquistas en favor de todo su pabellón.




Los detenidos del módulo 4 sector A3B derecho interpusieron un Habeas Corpus Colectivo Correctivo para exigir mejoras en las condiciones de alojamiento del Complejo Penitenciario Federal nº VIII al que fueron trasladados.




A través de este recurso y de otras gestiones judiciales, y tras una audiencia con el Juzgado Federal de Morón, representantes de distintos sectores del personal del complejo se entrevistaron con Milton y se comprometieron a garantizar la puesta en marcha de sus reclamos: acceso a la salud, derecho de estudiar y trabajar, restitución de pertenencias, provisión de agua potable, etcétera.




Es por ello que Milton aceptó suspender por el momento la medida de fuerza, supeditado a que todo lo informado por las autoridades judiciales y penitenciarias se cumpla. Caso contrario, retomará la huelga.




Nuestro compañero está entero, se siente bien de salud y a la espera de que el Servicio Penitenciario cumpla lo que se comprometió a hacer.




Una vez más, decimos todos juntos que luchar sirve.
