author: anred
title: Gordon: el eslabón perdido del genocidio
content:
Aníbal Gordon fue un delincuente común que se vinculó a la Concentración Nacional Universitaria (CNU), un grupo de ultraderecha que se acercó al peronismo a principios de los 70′. Posteriormente, se vinculó a la Triple A, organización parapolicial creada por el ministro José López Rega en 1973 y terminó trabajando para la dictadura militar iniciada por Videla el 24 de marzo de 1976. La miniserie “Gordon”, basada en la novela de Marcelo Larraquy, y filmada con la mirada insobornable de Pablo Trapero y Pablo Fendrik, hace un muy buen aporte a las nuevas generaciones para advertir las continuidades de estructuras represivas y la apelación de los grupos concentrados del capital a las peores escorias humanas, para conseguir objetivos políticos y económicos que después son presentados como propios de “los argentinos de bien”. Hoy en nuestro país, en la política, la economía, el poder judicial y las fuerzas de “seguridad”, no faltan mercenarios como Aníbal Gordon, que son vulgares ladrones capaces de cometer los actos más crueles e inhumanos, con el solo objetivo de acumular dinero y conseguir protección de los que supuestamente pueden hacerlo. Solo hace falta desenmascararlos.

 

Por Guillermo Cieza, para Huella del Sur.







Aníbal Gordon fue un delincuente común que se vinculó a la Concentración Nacional Universitaria (CNU), un grupo de ultraderecha que se acercó al peronismo a principios de los 70. Posteriormente se vinculó a la Triple A, organización parapolicial creada por el ministro José López Rega en 1973 y terminó trabajando para la dictadura militar iniciada por Videla el 24 de marzo de 1976.




Nadie ilustra mejor que Gordon la participación de delincuentes comunes asociados a la derecha en distintos momentos de la política de exterminio que culminó con el genocidio en la Argentina. Pablo Trapero, un cineasta excepcional, que se informa y muestra como nadie los temas que aborda, desnuda a Gordon y sus múltiples vinculaciones en una miniserie imprescindible que está en la Plataforma Netflix.




El verdadero Gordon, cuando fue detenido en 1984. Foto: C5N




Aníbal Gordon fue un criminal que se inició como ladrón de autos y de bancos. Sin más ideología que enriquecerse, no solo robaba y asesinaba, sino que disfrutaba de la crueldad con que realizaba sus delitos. Era un perfecto amoral, capaz de asesinar por dinero al que se le ponía por delante y traicionar a sus cómplices, pero también de esforzarse por buscar protección en el poder político de turno para garantizarse impunidad. Podría asegurarse que Gordon, anticipa a las peores lacras del capitalismo que hoy se exponen impúdicamente en el terreno de la política y los negocios empresariales.




Gordon consiguió vincularse a la Concentración Nacional Universitaria, un grupo neofascista cuya principal referencia ideológica fue el profesor de Lenguas Vivas de la UNLP, Carlos Alberto Di Sandro, un nacionalista de derecha que se acercó al peronismo a principios de la década del 70. Durante la dictadura de la autodenominada Revolución Argentina (gobiernos de Ongania, Levingston y Lanusse), la CNU enfrentó con sus patotas de universitarios y lúmpenes, a todas las expresiones de la izquierda, en particular a la tendencia revolucionaria del peronismo. Tenía grupos organizados en La Plata y Mar del Plata, y fue responsable del asesinato de la estudiante de 18 años, Silvia Filler. Este crimen se concretó el 6 de setiembre de 1971, cuando irrumpieron violentamente en la Facultad de Arquitectura de Mar del Plata, para romper una asamblea universitaria. En la miniserie no se menciona con el nombre verdadero a la estudiante asesinada, pero se muestra a Gordon participando del bando agresor.




Cuando el peronismo llegó al gobierno en las elecciones del 11 de marzo de 1973, Gordon se vinculó al sector de la burocracia sindical y grupos derechistas que inmediatamente se referenciaron en el Ministro de Bienestar Social, José López Rega.




Desplazado Héctor Cámpora del gobierno, se creó la banda parapolicial la Triple A, quien como los “somatén” creados en la época franquista tenía como objetivo principal “cazar rojos”. En la Argentina tuvieron especial predilección por militantes de la izquierda peronista y activistas obreros. Gordon fue parte fundacional de esa banda criminal paraestatal, que aportó al terrorismo de Estado. La triple A, nació con el aval de Perón y fue responsable de alrededor de 3000 asesinatos. Algunos de sus víctimas son muy conocidas: el sacerdote Carlos Mujica, el diputado del peronismo de base, Rodolfo Ortega Peña, el brillante intelectual Silvio Frondizi, el símbolo de la Resistencia Peronista, Julio Troxler, del dirigente sindical y ex vicegobernador de Córdoba, Atilio López, etc.




Hay un hecho muy ilustrativo de cómo actuaba Gordon. Entre el 6 y 7 de agosto de 1974, su grupo se dirige a la ciudad de La Plata con una lista de militantes a secuestrar: Carlos “Gringo” Pierini, dirigente peronista petrolero; Luis Macor, estudiante universitario ligado a la JUP; y Gonzalo Chávez, referente de la Juventud Trabajadora Peronista y vinculado a Montoneros. Pero ocurre que al llegar al domicilio de la familia Chávez no lo encuentran a Gonzalo. Entonces se lo llevan a su padre Horacio Irineo Chávez, un símbolo de la resistencia peronista y ex Presidente del Partido Justicialista Platense y a su hermano Horacio Rolando. Los cadáveres de los 4 asesinados aparecieron al día siguiente en un descampado. Habían sido torturados y acribillados a balazos.




La serie muestra que Gordon en tiempos de la Triple A se había relacionado con miembros de la SIDE, que sobreviven a la caída del gobierno de Isabel Perón y que siguió actuando con la dictadura que se instaló en marzo de 1976.




Tuvo un rol destacado en el genocidio perpetrado por los militares, estando a cargo de “Automotores Orletti”, un campo de concentración donde transitaron más de 300 secuestrados, la mayoría de los cuales hoy continúan desaparecidos.




La miniserie “Gordon”, basada en la novela de Marcelo Larraquy, y filmada con la mirada insobornable de Pablo Trapero y Pablo Fendrik, hace un muy buen aporte a las nuevas generaciones para advertir las continuidades de estructuras represivas y la apelación de los grupos concentrados del capital a las peores escorias humanas, para conseguir objetivos políticos y económicos que después son presentados como propios de “los argentinos de bien”. La actuación de Rodrigo de la Serna que muestra, sin sobreactuar, las múltiples facetas de un personaje tan siniestro, es excelente.




Gordon no fue más que un psicópata con poder. Hoy en nuestro país: en la política, la economía, el poder judicial y las fuerzas de “seguridad”, no faltan mercenarios como Aníbal Gordon, que son vulgares ladrones capaces de cometer los actos más crueles e inhumanos, con el solo objetivo de acumular dinero y conseguir protección de los que supuestamente pueden hacerlo. Solo hace falta desenmascararlos.




Fuente: 

https://huelladelsur.ar/2026/11/21/gordon-el-eslabon-perdido-del-genocidio/

author: Acratosaurio rex
title: Que vote un robot
content:
Estamos en época de cuentas y matemáticas electorales. Me ha hecho mucha gracia el tema del cálculo de probabilidades en torno al “voto útil”. Ya no necesitas leer los programas electorales, ni conocer al candidato/a (cosa que nadie hace en realidad), ni votar según tu pensamiento político. No.  




Ya hay aplicaciones que te dicen lo que hay que votar por provincia, para que tu voto sea “útil” y no nos las veamos con un gobierno de coalición ultraderechista. Hemos llegado al punto que una simple dirección de internet, que ningún humano va a mirar quién la ha hecho o a qué intereses responde, y que se basa en los datos electorales de la pasadas elecciones para hacer una elucubración… Te dice a quién tienes que votar, y a quién no. Por ejemplo, los pobrecitos de Podemos, dice la calculadora que no hay que votarles en ninguna provincia…




¿Para cuando unas elecciones que se resuelvan con una Inteligencia Artificial y un algoritmo? Al menos votaría a la derecha, como siempre, sin ningún tipo de coacción.

author: anred
title: No les molesta la “violencia”, les molesta el derecho a rebelarse
content:
Cuando ya está desatado el debate sobre «Gordon», aparece una reacción brutal ante un homenaje a Mario Roberto Santucho, a 50 años de su secuestro y desaparición por parte de la dictadura genocida. No creo que ambos hechos estén tan desconectados. Yofre muestra los papelitos que se llevó de la SIDE y otros se olvidan de que prestaron funcionarios a la dictadura y ponen el énfasis en que hay que “condenar toda violencia”. El genocidio del 76′ tuvo su antesala en la Triple A, en el Operativo Independencia y la Escuelita de Famaillá, en el Operativo Serpiente Roja y en tantas otras acciones contra la vanguardia obrera y popular, en un contexto marcado por grandes levantamientos como el Cordobazo, pero también por 18 años de proscripción del peronismo. No estamos discutiendo la estrategia guerrillera ni la política del ERP. Estamos asistiendo a una sobreactuación que tiene como objetivo impedir que se cuele cualquier referencia, discusión o aspiración que remita a esa ambición de transformación social radical de los años 60′ y 70′, de la que fue parte toda una generación en la Argentina y en el mundo para liberarnos de las cadenas del imperialismo, terminar con la explotación y la opresión. 

Por Myriam Bregman.







Recién puedo empezar a ver la serie Gordon y ya me impresionaron las imágenes del subsuelo del ex Ministerio de Bienestar Social porque como empleada del Banco Hipotecario trabajé algunos años en ese mismo subsuelo, donde circulaban muchas leyendas. Luego, como querellante en causas de lesa humanidad, sobrevivientes me contaron lo que efectivamente había pasado allí.




También, más allá de la lectura política que pueda hacerse del relato de la serie, me impactó que Pablo Trapero, con la interpretación de Rodrigo de la Serna, se anime a reconstruir el rol brutal de la burocracia sindical, la CNU y las bandas paraestatales que actuaron bajo un gobierno constitucional y dejaron miles de víctimas.




Cuando ya está desatado el debate sobre «Gordon», aparece una reacción brutal ante un homenaje a Mario Roberto Santucho, a 50 años de su secuestro y desaparición por parte de la dictadura genocida.




No creo que ambos hechos estén tan desconectados. Algunos aprovechan para intentar reinstalar la teoría de la propia dictadura, expresada por uno de sus voceros, el Tata Yofre, que se resume en “Fuimos todos”; otros buscan restablecer la nefasta “teoría de los dos demonios”, según la cual se enfrentaron “violencias de distinto signo” ante una sociedad que “no tenía nada que ver”.




Yofre muestra los papelitos que se llevó de la SIDE y otros se olvidan de que prestaron funcionarios a la dictadura y ponen el énfasis en que hay que “condenar toda violencia”. Pero, por ejemplo, hace unos días, un importante funcionario de la dictadura como Domingo Felipe Cavallo, estuvo dando una charla en la Facultad de Ciencias Económicas de la UBA, en el marco del seminario “La historia económica y sus protagonistas”, y a los demócratas no se les movió un pelo, a pesar de que fue responsable de estatizar la deuda de las empresas privadas y cargarla sobre las espaldas de todo un pueblo. Tampoco se les mueve un rulero cuando empresarios que integran grupos económicos estrechamente vinculados con la dictadura, que tuvieron centros de exterminio en sus propias fábricas, son recibidos como señores en las universidades.




Demás está aclarar que no comparto la estrategia política de Santucho. Sí es necesario señalar que está desaparecido, que su cuerpo permanece oculto hasta el día de hoy, como una forma macabra de perpetuar el mensaje y el dolor. Los Santucho son una familia diezmada.




Por ende, es legítimo homenajear a un desaparecido que vivió toda su vida como un revolucionario, a alguien que se la jugó por transformar la sociedad. A genocidas como el general Roca les levantan monumentos; a las víctimas de los genocidios se las intenta borrar. Porque un genocidio no es un acto, es un proceso, y sus consecuencias se perpetúan hasta el día de hoy, como la atadura al FMI mediante la deuda externa que Cavallo alimentó.




El genocidio del 76 tuvo su antesala en la Triple A -algunas de sus acciones nos tocan más de cerca, como el asesinato de César Robles o las masacres de Pacheco y de La Plata contra militantes del PST-, en el Operativo Independencia y la Escuelita de Famaillá, en el Operativo Serpiente Roja y en tantas otras acciones contra la vanguardia obrera y popular, en un contexto marcado por grandes levantamientos como el Cordobazo, pero también por 18 años de proscripción del peronismo.




La dictadura cívico-militar vino a imponer una reconfiguración de las relaciones económicas, sociales, políticas y hasta culturales. Y también vino a aplastar cualquier aspiración de transformación radical de la sociedad. Como declaró en la causa ESMA el sobreviviente e integrante de la Asociación de Ex Detenidos Desaparecidos Osvaldo Barros, acerca de un comentario entre interrogatorios que le hizo el represor Juan Carlos del Cerro, alias “Colores”: “Me dijo ESTAMOS TRABAJANDO PARA 20 AÑOS DE TRANQUILIDAD SOCIAL”.




Algo similar a lo que afirmó en su momento Thiers, el arquitecto de la masacre de 30.000 obreras y obreros de la Comuna de París en 1871, cuando se vanagloriaba de haberse sacado de encima la perspectiva de la revolución por una generación.




Por eso, no estamos discutiendo la estrategia guerrillera ni la política del ERP. Estamos asistiendo a una sobreactuación que tiene como objetivo impedir que se cuele cualquier referencia, discusión o aspiración que remita a esa ambición de transformación social radical de los años 60 y 70, de la que fue parte toda una generación en la Argentina y en el mundo para liberarnos de las cadenas del imperialismo, terminar con la explotación y la opresión.




Santucho, como los 30.000, fue víctima de un genocidio. Y, como dice Rodolfo Walsh en su Carta abierta de un escritor a la Junta Militar: “Las 3 A son hoy las 3 Armas, y la Junta que ustedes presiden no es el fiel de la balanza entre ‘violencias de distintos signos’ ni el árbitro justo entre ‘dos terrorismos’, sino la fuente misma del terror que ha perdido el rumbo y sólo puede balbucear el discurso de la muerte”.




Además, aprovechan para desprestigiar a la UBA. Es un acto de censura inadmisible. No se suban.

author: Jordyn Tovey
title: What Would Marsha Linehan Do?
content:
Over the past few weeks, the world has shown up to mourn and honor the impact of Marsha Linehan. And I among them.

I had the formative experience of interning at a DBT clinic in Michigan on my way to becoming a licensed clinical social worker and psychotherapist. I spent over a year learning, teaching, and practicing the “gold standard” treatment.

Now, years later, I find that the tenets, theoretical formulation, skills, and dare I say, spirit of DBT have remained with me. As have the questions which ultimately led me away from practicing in a full-fidelity setting.

I struggled at the time to put words to my Catholic upbringing (and subsequent rebellion) rearing its head. Now, in her death, I am reminded of the peculiarities of what it was like to hear Marsha Linehan’s name invoked in clinical spaces.

For example, in required consultation, there would be callbacks to things Marsha had said and done in demonstrations to guide the therapist, rather than grounding in the individual, totally separate relationship of therapist and client. Dialectical behavior therapists practicing true to the texts are encouraged to borrow directly from Marsha’s style. Her cadence. Her turns of phrase. Her irreverence. Her intensity. Ask themselves the question: what would Marsha do?

The idea being that cutting through bullshit and speaking directly to a client’s pain with confidence and care was an active ingredient in the therapy. What I observed frequently, but far from always, however, was clients (and therapists) experiencing these words as arrogance or flagrant invalidation. The skills and behaviorism could read as instructional or cold despite what I would consider a near-identical delivery to the videos and writing of Marsha.

I’m reminded of her style in a popular and circulating audio clip of her guaranteeing to a client that they will get out of hell, they will not always hurt so bad…but on the condition that they don’t kill themselves.

I find the clip moving. Nearly hypnotic. Maybe it’s in my head that I feel it in my heart. She’s speaking with something adjacent to but not quite the same as authority. It’s a knowing.

Marsha Linehan empowered the field with a novel approach to outpatient care, fierce and disruptive calls for accountability where treatment can cause harm, and unrelenting empathy for an otherwise dismissed population. She related to and championed those deemed prognostically poor. Clinician-scholar and pioneer, certainly.

All things considered, as I, alongside many right now, reflect on her life, death, and legacy, I continue to go back to the open secret that Marsha relied on more than a mythical ideal of pure theory and empirical evidence.

Linehan’s obituary discusses her reluctance to speak to her own story, waiting until the scientific legitimacy of her work was sufficiently established (to whose standards, I still wonder) before discussing her own psychiatric history and how it intersected with dialectical behavior therapy.

As I’ve continued to grow and develop as a therapist, patient, critic, and maybe even hypocrite working proudly in a department of psychiatry despite misgivings about historical and current practices… I find myself experiencing never-ending conflict with the concept of evidence-based therapies. DBT as my ground zero.

I question, dialectically, how the evidence base is holding up an undeniably personal therapeutic approach. And where the lines become blurry about what is working and why.

I wonder what we lose in efforts toward replicability. Individual style, genuine moments, real connection.

Marsha Linehan’s famous irreverence was hard-earned. The passion she had was personal. The path she pointed to was forged through her now famously known story of choosing life despite being labeled a hopeless case. There are limits to repeating her words, her story, her approach.

I believe those limits are felt.

Rest in Peace, Marsha. Pray for Us.

Mad in America hosts blogs by a diverse group of writers. These posts are designed to serve as a public forum for a discussion—broadly speaking—of psychiatry and its treatments. The opinions expressed are the writers’ own.

author: Otiato Guguyu
title: The Decline of The Nation: From Taifa to Taarifa
content:
When I worked at the Nation Media Group (NMG), there was a running joke about the immortality of 

Taifa Leo

, the Swahili newspaper printed by the media group that 20-year-old Prince Karim had bought in 1959 when he became the Fourth Aga Khan.




From this £10,000 purchase from British officer and former District Commissioner Charles Hayes, the group would grow to control the largest circulation of newspapers, and television stations and websites across East Africa.




Over time, the Swahili paper did face dwindling audiences as demographic changes produced a more cosmopolitan youth who found reading news in grammatical Swahili a hard sell and was more inclined to consume short video content online. 




Despite this handicap, 

Taifa Leo

 owes its longevity to the sentimental connection to its founder, His Highness the Aga Khan. For its survival, it also relied on punchy yet witty headlines, humorous angles, and 

Bi Taifa

, a cover model featured on one of its pages that was primarily produced by Taifa Leo photographers. If you hung around these photographers long enough, you would get to see how the allure of appearing on the tabloid would create new customers looking out for their photos. 




Then the Fourth Aga Khan died, and 

Taifa Leo

’s business model was finally facing the test of succession, a shift in the media landscape, and an uncertain future under Tanzanian billionaire Rostam Aziz who may share the paper’s Swahili heritage but not the paper’s founding ideals that had inspired its punchy headlines. 




Succession




The Fourth Aga Khan’s strategy with 

Taifa Leo

 was to create a sustainable, independent, and influential media platform that would inform the public and strengthen the fabric of the newly independent nation.




A younger Aga Khan had borne the cost of the loss-making venture in its first decade and had 

fought off attempts

 by the family of Kenya’s first president, Jomo Kenyatta, to gain control of the media house and turn it into an organ of state propaganda. 




But as the Aga Khan grew older and gradually relinquished his stake to other shareholders and to a professional board, this legacy of defending the sanctity of media freedom began to wane. 




Under the younger Kenyatta, the old Aga Khan’s legacy project 

gave in to state interference

 in what could be linked to privileges and immunities granted to the Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN) and its affiliated agencies, which were classified as philanthropic, charitable and non-profit-making.




But even tax exemptions and the economies of scale of running Aga Khan’s conglomerates across East Africa could not save the businesses’ fortunes and their decline in profitability would lead to divestments under his son, Prince Rahim Al-Hussaini, the Fifth Aga Khan, shortly after the patriarch’s death.




Shifting landscapes




I owe a huge part of my journalism career to the late Prince Karim Aga Khan, having worked at Nation Media Group where I learned the trade until I transitioned into private practice a couple of years ago.




But even as I transitioned out, I was still a beneficiary of his benevolence when I enlisted for a course titled “Beyond the Newsroom” that aimed to help journalists move on following the job cuts that had become the norm in the industry.




This programme demonstrated that the Aga Khan understood the dynamics of our evolving media industry and had chosen to help incubate future media start-ups through the Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications.




I found myself sitting in a lecture hall where two of the trainers now teaching journalists how to cope beyond the newsroom had been the managers who had hired me into the profession.




David Aduda had hired me at the Nation Media Group in 2013, then three years later, Joseph Odindo poached me to join Standard Media Group. But they were now both with the Aga Khan University School of Media, providing sponsored training to the scores of journalists made redundant by the decline of traditional media.




Golden age




I muscled my way into journalism as a fresh graduate from Maseno University, moving to the capital and into a profession that was brimming with opportunity.




In 2013, Kenya was undergoing a rather calm political transition and the world had forgotten about the financial crisis. Anything seemed possible, including printing money.




I first interned at the NMG when it was making KSh13.3 billion in revenues and netting KSh2.5 billion in profits. You can imagine my surprise when, after undergoing intense interviews, psychometric tests, and questions about quantitative easing (the new name of printing money), I was handed a KSh7,000 contract.




But I believed in the calling. I remember visiting the Kenya Television Network as a member of the Debate and Journalism club while in high school, and the Nation Centre when I was a university student, and telling myself that one day I would work where once Whispers had worked; he fascinated me when I was young. I lived in a derelict building somewhere in Kariobangi where the rent was KSh5,000, but I still signed on the dotted line and then convinced my father and my sister to underwrite the risk.




It paid off; I walked into a vibrant newsroom and got to meet and work with Ken Walibora. I sat in that part of the newsroom known as “Migingo”, the desks nearest those of Ugandans Onyango Obbo and Daniel Kalinaki. Back then the newsroom was so vibrant it scouted universities for the best talent to bring into its media lab programme – writers like Jacqueline Kubania, Cornell Ngare, and Waga Odongo.




Decline




I tell anyone who cares to listen that I have witnessed the industry transform. At the time, we interns were not assigned computers, so we would hang around, sitting on the chairs meant for the group’s drivers, waiting for “Mayor of Migingo” John Ngirachu to leave for parliament, or for some other senior journalist to go for an assignment, and pounce on their desks to write those little briefs whose authorship no one knew.




But by the time I left the newsroom, I was surrounded by four empty desks; I could have written an introduction at one and concluded my story at another of those unused workstations where once such and such a colleague used to sit. Where are they now? 




I met some of them while attending the Beyond the Newsroom training; right in front of me on the very first day were Aduda and Odindo. They had transitioned themselves and were now passing on their wealth of experience to us.




I had attended Odindo’s leaving party and had felt at the time that this was what media success looked like; the charming speeches celebrated him, and he seemed almost agreeable to what was an inevitable goodbye.




Business convergence, digital reorganizations




Since then journalists have not been given such lavish send-offs. Their departures have instead been announced by internal memo or through the regular cycles of redundancies, business convergence, and all manner of digital reorganizations. Exits have become a source of industry anxiety; the despair, the uncertainty and the anger at having loved a dog’s life and being rejected via a cursory letter, a phone call, a disabled email address, or a cancelled entry pass.




It turns out Odindo took it just as hard as the rest of us when we left the newsroom. He made a short return to the industry at the 

Standard

 before joining the Aga Khan Media School as a trainer. Through it all, the lesson for the veteran had been to remember who he really was – a good editor who did his work diligently, managing other editors and overseeing a newsroom over the years – and therein lay his strength.




And as he sought himself in the shock therapy that is retirement, digging through piles of old documents, the words of a distant headmaster on his report card saying, “Joseph is capable of much more” lent him the courage to try new things.




But tell that to a pack of depressed former journalists thrown into the tailspin of sudden joblessness – the struggle to pay rent and school fees, learning to take rejection from job applications, being worried sick about lacking insurance and, above all, losing the power and privileges that come with working for a huge news organization. Journalism is a strange profession, built around the façade of the glamorous television anchors, powerful owners, backed by human rights defenders and international patronage. But once you step off, the entire network freezes you out.




But even in the midst of this despair, a group of journalists attending the training found solace in each other’s company, sharing their experiences, their unvoiced emotions. As we shared our stories and learned the limitations of our mindsets to our present careers, the opportunities available to our skill sets and, really thinking about our industry, it became apparent why the Aga Khan’s initiative to help transition the industry was so important.




Structured monopoly




Prince Karim Aga Khan, who grew up in Nairobi and founded the 

Daily Nation

 in the 1960s, has for decades underwritten media freedom and its success in Kenya, using his financial muscle to shoulder the capital-intensive business and leveraging its power to support his massive business ventures in hospitality, energy, agriculture, insurance, and finance. 




The newspaper model had, over the years, become archaic, relying on central printing and physical distribution through an expensive logistical network. This costly structure acted as an entry barrier, making the industry a near monopoly for those who could afford to own it.




The internet completely disrupted this distribution model, replacing the newspaper with a mobile telephone and a computer screen that virtually made anyone with an internet connection a potential journalist. This happened at a time when America was printing money through quantitative easing, which was funnelled to tech companies to finance experiments on customer targeting. The social media model that allowed companies to study the individual and influence their behaviour changed how advertising was done and the role of the media as gatekeeper of audiences. Social media ate legacy media’s lunch, and as advertising revenues dropped, the cost of maintaining media operations became increasingly high. Media houses reacted by cutting costs and trimming staff numbers.




The Nation Group’s profits have been in sharp decline, falling from KSh2.5 billion when I joined the company in 2013 to a loss of KSh308.6 million in 2025. In the same period, the group’s staff nearly halved – from 1,980 to 

1,100

 – due to the annual ritual of rationalization that has only served to heighten anxiety in the newsroom.




“We were too busy doing the traditional thing. We knew about the disruptions from technology but were engrossed in the product to make money for the employer that we ignored digital. We were so engrossed in competition for the little space doing what we had done for so long,” Odindo told us during the training.




Now digital is viewed as the magic bullet even though newsrooms know that the same technology is spelling their end. 




“Notwithstanding the operating performance for the period, the gains recorded in digital and broadcasting underscore the Group’s sustained pivot toward a scalable digital business and optimization of the growth headroom in broadcasting. Therefore, the Group continues to invest in unified technology to enhance customer experience across our platforms, diversify audience demographics and accelerate monetization of our expansive digital assets,” the 

Nation

’s board of directors said in its 2025 results outlook.




Business interests 




It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. As the media business shrank, so did the interest of its benevolent founder. 




Even as the newspaper model began to collapse, the Aga Khan’s interests shifted elsewhere – to his multiple businesses that include the Aga Khan Hospital, the TPS Serena hotel chain, Jubilee Insurers and Diamond Trust Bank, IPSK and Farmers Choice, and power stations. He sought to secure tax concessions for them at the expense of media independence. 




Inevitably, politicians took advantage of the dire straits in which the media found itself, using advertising revenues to leverage friendly coverage. The government weaponized media revenues, using its power as the largest advertiser to accumulate invoices that crippled the newsrooms and then withholding advertising altogether before negotiating the cost of advertising downwards by having the leading newspapers carry the government’s 

MyGov

 pamphlet as an insert.




As the handshake extended beyond the elbow, so did the pressure to push out dissenting journalists like Dennis Galava and Godfrey Mwampembwa (Gaddo), which gave the Aga Khan a bad press for what was seen as giving in to the demands of a government averse to criticism. 




Like the Children of Gebelawi, we wondered what the Aga Khan thought as he watched the empire that he had built over decades go into decline.




Last man standing




After President Daniel Moi left office, fortunes at the 

Standard

 were not good either. Between 2024 and 2015, the firm only made profits twice in a decade as the losses widened to over a billion in the last years (KSh1.1 billion in 2024). In newsrooms, the Standard Group’s losses were glossed over while the company struggled to pay correspondents – contract writers who are paid by the length of each published article. The silence continued even as the late payment of salaries finally hit permanent staff and the industry slid slowly into the practice of not paying journalists on time and sometimes not at all.




The 

Standard

 newspaper blamed its troubles on the state’s non-payment of outstanding bills despite the fact that its owner, Gideon Moi, was part of President Uhuru Kenyatta’s inner circle in Azimio.




Despite the dip in fortunes, the paper has maintained its relevance through bold headlines critical of President William Ruto’s regime to recover falling circulation. The newspaper gives Gideon Moi leverage in shaping public opinion. He is reported to have 

turned down

 an offer from Ruto’s allies who had been seeking to acquire a stake in the struggling Standard Group.




According to Africa Intelligence, President Ruto then turned his 

sights on NMG

, having bagged 

The Star

 to start building a media empire through which to control the narrative ahead of the 2027 presidential election.




With the Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development agreeing to sell its entire 

shareholding in NPRT Holdings Africa Limited

 to Taarifa Limited, which is owned by Tanzanian Business Magnate Rostam Aziz, many see this as the takeover of East Africa’s most powerful media house by politically linked patronage. It is expected that Aziz’s business and political interests will either rapidly reshape the editorial line or cull the paper’s ranks much in the manner that Jeff Bezos did at the 

Washington Post.




Nation Media Group has already reorganized its board of directors and shaken the editorial team, pushing out senior editors to subsidiaries across the region and replacing them with acting managers. With rumours of incoming fresh blood to replace some of the senior team members, those in acting roles will be under pressure to be more pliable in fronting the state’s narratives.




Owning the public square




Traditionally, Kenyan newsrooms have suffered rifts among editors as elections draw closer. But when the newsrooms were full, you could mediate interests because no one could capture all the editors, and both sides of the story got to be told. But as the job cuts did away with the fat flesh and came close to the bone, the newsroom grew smaller and became easier and cheaper to capture. 




The editors who should have seen this coming were busy fighting each other in a battle for survival. Editors conspired to push each other out in a game of musical chairs that made it a slippery climb to the top deck. 




With fewer and fewer journalists to deal with, the political class was better able to manage the media. Politicians also saw an opportunity to turn prominent media voices that used to keep them in check into tools for propaganda. They are now hiring scores of former journalists to sing their praises as they further weaken the fourth estate.




I believe that journalists still have a chance to save the profession if we can see our demise and organize quickly to build alternatives. The industry needs a large enough shared space that can safeguard media independence, underwrite the security of journalists, and leverage having several journalists offering a range of public opinion that is not controlled by large corporates or politicians.  




In the end, storytelling is immortal notwithstanding the channels and models through which it is delivered through time.




The post 

The Decline of The Nation: From Taifa to Taarifa 

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Shen Reaches Across Political Aisle, Chiang Hits Out at Solar Panels in Second Mayoral Policy Presentation
content:
THE SECOND and last Taipei mayoral policy presentation was held on Saturday, November 21st. The major candidates are Puma Shen of the DPP and Chiang Wan-an of the KMT. Though a number of fringe candidates also presented, this article will focus on Shen and Chiang. The policy presentation was not a formal debate, in that there were no opportunities provided for candidates to question each other. Though the Shen campaign had pressed for further debates beyond the one formal debate that has taken place to date, the Chiang campaign is thought to be more reluctant.

Shen was the first to go. Shen first began by stressing bipartisanship, mentioning how Huang Shan-shan of the TPP had gifted him two signed copies of her book. To this extent, Shen raised how he hoped to learn from the experiences of past Taipei mayors, regardless of political affiliation. Indeed, non-partisanship has been something that Shen has been at odds to emphasize in past days, as a DPP candidate running in traditionally blue Taipei.

Shen proved more combative than in other debates or policy presentations, however. Shen criticized the Taipei city government for being insufficiently responsive to the public, as observed in its slow response to child abuse cases, a building collapse in Dazhi, and a food poisoning incident that killed six people in 2024. Shen also criticized the Chiang campaign for its unrealistic campaign pledges, such as relocating the Songshan Airport. At the same time, Shen continued to emphasize that his campaign had doubled down on positive campaigning, rather than a negative one that sought to take down political enemies, in framing them as hyperbolically bad.

Perhaps it was the fact that his campaign had emphasized negative campaigning to date that shaped Chiang’s response. Chiang’s policy presentation, then, primarily consisted of policy proposals and pledges. Chiang pledged a twenty-year plan for Taipei’s future development, including stimulating growth of the AI industry through the Shilin-Beitou Technology Park. In line with the KMT’s efforts to frame solar energy as dangerous, Chiang also reiterated a campaign pledge to remove solar panels at the Feitsui Reservoir.

To this extent, Chiang pledged to strengthen and further integrate transportation networks in Taipei, as well as to set up a new institute to research issues facing civil servants. Chiang also pledged to plant more trees in Taipei and expand the amount of greenery in the city. It proves of note that Chiang has made such a pledge, seeing as Puma Shen has doubled down on criticisms of the Taipei city government for reductions in the amount of greenery. In his policy presentation, Chiang mostly recited a long list of campaign pledges, taking advantage of his status as the incumbent

Chiang has increasingly leaned into framing Shen as a radical on cross-strait issues, while raising the possibility of a DPP victory provoking China in his campaign rallies. This occurs despite the fact that local elections are primarily about local issues, rather than cross-strait issues, and may occur because of desperation. It is of note, then, that he avoided such attacks in the debate, perhaps having gone too far in the direction of negative attacks on Shen.

It is probable that the policy presentation debate will not have much of an impact on voting, with little new that was exchanged between the two candidates, and relatively few differences from the first policy presentation. Shen leaned more into criticisms of Chiang that he had previously avoided, with Chiang having refused to engage in further debates because of the probable view that he would come off worse in a debate–indeed, Shen is known for his debating and public speaking skills, while Chiang has acquired a reputation as a relatively stiff and wooden speaker.

Still, one notes that Shen began both the first and second Taipei mayoral policy presentations with efforts to reach across the political aisle. This is telling about how his campaign hopes to win in historically blue-leaning Taipei.

author: Stan Miller, Victor Osprey
title: France: ‘The leadership of the movement belongs to the students themselves’
content:
Stan Miller is a member of the French revolutionary socialist organisation Nouveau parti anticapitaliste — Révolutionnaires (New Anticapitalist Party — Revolutionary, NPA–R) in Montpellier. He spoke to Victor Osprey on November 9 about the youth uprising in France and the role being played by trade unions and the revolutionary left.

What were the immediate political results of the November 5 general strike called by French trade unions in response to cost-of-living pressures and public service cuts, which mobilised an estimated 1 million people or more?

Today [November 9], the prime minister [Sébastien Lecornu] met with union leaders for the first time in a while. This was a direct consequence of the mobilisation by high school students who strong-armed the unions to do anything. The prime minister said was willing to raise the minimum wage by 1.6 % (about €1502 a month), which is way below inflation.

There are eight national trade union confederations in France. Almost all local unions are affiliated to one of them. The politics of these eight confederations is shaped by history: for example, the CGT [Confédération Générale du Travail, General Confederation of Labour] used to be controlled by the Communist Party and was very strong in blue collar industries; the CFDT [Confédération française démocratique du travail, French Democratic Confederation of Labour] is more social democratic; the FSU [Fédération Syndicale Unitaire, United Trade Union Federation] almost exclusively covers teachers.

Some people divide them between “reformists” and “radicals”, but all defend the interests of their own bureaucracy rather than the interests of the movement. Some unions, such as the CFDT, say the wage hike is not high enough but believe the government is an honest partner and want to negotiate wages across different industries.

The CGT believes in negotiating but wants to convince the government that they cannot be ignored; that is why they have called a day of strikes and actions on November 17 to show off a bit of muscle. The CFDT has decided not to join the strike on November 17. The CGT called the November 5 strike just one month before, showing that they had no genuine desire to help the youth movement [which started in September], otherwise they would have called it sooner.

The spark for the general strike was the powerful movement of youth and students against the under-funding of the education system. Has it led to offers of further concessions from the French government, on top of previous offers given to youth and students? Is the government attempting to sideline the demands of organised workers and separate them from the students by appealing for “dialogue” with trade union leaders?

The prime minister invited youth organisations to discuss the future of education. Also present at the meeting was the far-right youth organisation UNI [Union Nationale Inter-universitaire, Inter-University Union] and several far-right MPs, so the left representatives walked out. We will not discuss anything in the presence of the far right.

There are several youth organisations and student unions, but participation in student elections is very low, generally only a few percent of students vote. They do not act as unions defending the immediate interests of students — though there are some exceptions at a very local level. Instead, they mainly act as political organisations defending a particular vision.

A few weeks ago, the education minister [Édouard Geffray] tried to calm the youth movement with scraps such as creating 15,000 additional higher education places. But youth organisations are asking for 260,000 new university spots.

The government is trying to divide workers and students, but many are not falling for it. Tomorrow [November 10] is a day of action and strike for both teachers and students.

How has the far-right Rassemblement national (National Rally, RN) reacted to the general strike and the movement overall?

This movement is polarising people. There are many instances of people reacting to police brutality against the youth. We have had almost as many police arrests of youth protesters in one month as we did in one year of Yellow Vest protests. But some workers are also saying the police should shoot the protesters.

Overall, it is a hard time for the far right because [President Emmanuel] Macron is kind of stealing their talking points: more police, more brutality, etc.

Can the movement effectively translate its anti-government activity against the Macron administration into anti-fascist action to confront the RN and far-right groups in the streets?

I feel we may not be there yet. In Montpellier, some fascists tried to organise their own “militia” to protect local stores against looting. They boasted that cops were working with them. The fascists have a lot of sympathisers in the police force, but the state is not really using them as its main tool at the moment.

But even without arming thugs to beat up workers, racism still kills: on October 23, a 26-year-old Black man was shot and killed by a far-right terrorist who wanted to target “Blacks and Arabs”. The far right clearly carries responsibility for this murder, and many others.

What is the role and status in these protests of the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed, LFI), which is led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon? Does LFI tend to initiate protests and attempt to assert a leadership role in them, or do they simply seek to influence them?

LFI controls one student union, L'Union Étudiante [Student Union], and they are part of the movement, but it is an exaggeration to say that they or any other organisation controls it. The ruling class pushes this narrative to paint youth as incapable of leading their own struggle and claim someone must be “behind” all of this.

In reality, youth organisations in general are quite small. The leadership of the movement really belongs to the students themselves through their general assemblies and national coordinations. All the universities and high schools on strike send delegates to a national coordination, which sets the agenda and decides what to do to ensure that students control the movement, rather than any specific organisation.

[Abridged from LINKS — International Journal of Socialist Renewal.]

author: Unknown
title: ÎHD: Li herêmê di salekê de herî kêm 57 zarok mirin
content:
Komîsyona Zarokan a Şaxa Komeleya Mafên Mirovan a Amedê, rapora binpêkirinên mafên zarokan a bajarên Kurdan ya di navbera 20ê Mijdara 2025an û 20ê Mijdara 2026an de li avahiya komeleyê bi daxuyaniyekî eşkere kir.




Li gorî nûçeya Ajansa Welat daxuyanî ji aliyê Rêvebera Şaxa ÎHDê ya Amedê Eylem Kaya ve hat xwendin.




Bîlançoya salekê ya binpêkirinan




Eylem Kayayê daneyên di raporê de wiha parve kir:







* Herî kêm 57 zarokan jiyana xwe ji dest da û 34 zarok birîndar bûn.




* 22 mirinên biguman ên zarokan û 5 xwekuştin hatin tomarkirin.




* 9 zarok di dema karkirinê de li qadên çandiniyê, înşeatan û kargehan mirin.




* 3 zarok di encama tundiya nav malbatê de û 5 zarok jî di encama tundiya civakî de mirin.




* 36 zarok hatin binçavkirin, 26 zarok hatin girtin û 8 zarok jî bi îşkence û miameleya xirab re rû bi rû man.







"Divê mafê perwerdeya bi zimanê dayikê were naskirin"




Eylem Kayayê bal kişand polîtîkayên bişaftinê yên ku bandoreke giran li ser zarokan dike û wiha got:







“Divê mirinên biguman werin ronîkirin, dawî li karkeriya di bin navê perwerdeya pîşeyî de were anîn û zarok ji tundiyê werin parastin. Her wiha divê Tirkiye şerhên li ser Peymana Mafên Zarokan a Neteweyên Yekbûyî rake, astengiyên li pêşiya perwerdeya bi zimanê dayikê rabe û di avakirina aştiyê de mafên zarokan esas werin girtin.”







(AY)

title: Mersin'de bir haftadır kayıp olarak aranan kadın bulundu
content:
Mersin – Erdemli ilçesine bağlı Sinap Mahallesi sınırlarında bulunan Küçükfındık Yaylası’nda yaşayan 76 yaşındaki Mümine Kılıç isimli kadından haber alamayan yakınları, 18 Kasım akşamı yetkililere kayıp ihbarında bulundu.

İhbar üzerine bölgeye jandarma, AFAD, UMKE ve Erdemli Belediyesi ekipleri sevk edildi. Arama çalışmalarına gönüllüler, mahalleli ve Kılıç’ın yakınları da katıldı. Mümine Kılıç, yapılan geniş çaplı çalışmaların ardından evinden yaklaşık 7 kilometre uzakta dere çevresinde sağ olarak bulundu.

Sağlık durumunun iyi olduğu öğrenilen Kılıç, ekiplerin ilk müdahalesinin ardından hastaneye sevk edildi.

Olayla ilgili soruşturma devam ediyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Women can achieve freedom through organization and self-defense
content:
Free Women’s Troops (YJA Star) guerrillas Edessa Roj and Aryen Zînar Botan spoke to ANF on the occasion of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. The YJA Star guerrillas discussed the struggle against the male-dominated system and the role of women in society, saying that women must rise up through strong organization against all forms of violence, enslavement and oppression.







 







Guerrilla Edessa Roj said that capitalist modernity particularly targets women's lives and seeks to enslave them in every respect. She said that a relentless struggle must be waged against this mentality in every sphere of life. Edessa Roj stated that organization and the establishment of self-defense mechanisms are essential for women to survive and resist violence. She pointed out that violence against women is not confined to any particular region and that millions of women around the world face violence. Edessa Roj said, "The women's struggle against this violence must also be global," and emphasized the importance of building a democratic and free life.




Edessa Roj said that building a free society is impossible unless women embrace the values of freedom while defending their identities, cultures and ideas. Edessa Roj concluded: "Women must struggle not only with their physical strength but also with their consciousness, knowledge and willpower. Women across the world must join hands, resist shoulder to shoulder against genocide, violence and imperialism, and defend their freedom. Women's struggle for freedom is a sacred legacy, and every woman must act with this awareness."




Violence against women is increasing every day







 







Guerrilla Aryen Zînar Botan began by saluting all women engaged in struggle on the occasion of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. Aryen Zînar Botan said: "I call on all women who are active in the fields of freedom, resistance and struggle. The more women develop and strengthen themselves politically, organizationally and through action, the stronger they can stand against the male-dominated system. The more women distance themselves from the male-dominated system and assert their existence, the freer society becomes.




Violence against women is increasing every day, and the main reason for this is the inadequacy of the struggle being waged. If we strengthen our struggle and resistance in every sphere and every society, we can succeed against the male-dominated system and special warfare strategies. Special warfare strategies are extremely widespread today. Rojîn Kabaiş and Özgecan Arslan are among the clearest examples of this.




This war is being waged particularly against women because the dominant system knows very well that any change in society will come through women's strength and resistance. Leader Apo's (Abdullah Öcalan) philosophy is based on enabling women to reveal their own identities. We must therefore act in accordance with this philosophy and raise the level of our resistance even further. Violence against women is not merely physical.




The dominant system wants to confine women to the home and portray them as incapable of doing anything else. Yet we are not objects. We have identities of our own. By establishing communes, we can build our self-defense system in homes, neighborhoods and every sphere of life. Through organization and self-defense, our path to freedom can withstand all attacks by the dominant system. As the 50-year history of the Freedom Movement has demonstrated, successful results can be achieved when women stand together in solidarity and organize in every sphere of life."

author: Unknown
title: Sabahat Sever: Precarious work and unpaid care deepen women's poverty
content:
Women face inequality in working life not only because of poverty and precarious employment conditions but also because of the burden of unpaid care work at home. The responsibility for caring for children, older people and sick family members falls largely on women, making it more difficult for them to participate in employment and increasing their economic dependence. Women's economic independence is considered essential in combating violence, while attention is also being drawn to the need to make economic violence visible. There are growing calls for public policies to protect women's labour and ensure equal working conditions.




According to September 2026 data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK), the unemployment rate stood at 11.3 percent for women, compared with 6.9 percent for men. The employment rate among women was just 31.2 percent, while it reached 65.8 percent among men. The figures reveal the persistent gender gap in employment.




Sabahat Sever, co-chair of Branch No. 2 of the Genel-Iş Union, affiliated with the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DISK), in Amed (Diyarbakır), spoke to ANF about women's poverty and the problems they face in working life.




'Women's poverty is a result of male-dominated production relations'




Sabahat Sever said that women's poverty cannot be explained solely by the economic crisis or low wages, stressing that the problem is directly linked to gender inequality and male-dominated relations of production.




Sabahat Sever said that women perform much of the work necessary to sustain social life, including caring for children, older people and sick family members, cooking and cleaning, without receiving payment.




Sever said: "Women are predominantly employed in precarious, low-paid, temporary and informal jobs. At the same time, they undertake essential unpaid work within the home, including caring for children, older people and sick family members, as well as cooking and cleaning. We are facing a twofold system of exploitation. Women are regarded as cheap and insecure labour in production, while also being made responsible for invisible care work at home. Making this labour invisible restricts women's economic independence, their participation in social life and their opportunities to organise.




Therefore, combating women's poverty cannot be limited to finding jobs for women. Women's labour must be recognised, secure working conditions must be established, and care services must become a public responsibility. If we want to eliminate women's poverty, we must first make women's labour visible and ensure that women enjoy equal conditions both in production and in social life."




'Economic dependence creates conditions for violence to continue'




Sabahat Sever stressed that economic independence is one of the fundamental conditions for women's liberation. She said: "Economic dependence creates a serious obstacle to women's ability to make free decisions about their own lives. When a woman experiencing violence has no income of her own, no access to housing and no social security, it becomes much harder for her to escape an abusive environment.




For this reason, economic dependence is one of the structural problems that allow violence to continue. Economic violence also often remains invisible. Preventing a woman from working, confiscating her earnings, controlling her money and excluding her from economic decision-making are different forms of violence. We see women's economic freedom not merely as the right to work, but also as their ability to make decisions about their own bodies, lives and futures.




However, we also know that economic independence alone will not eliminate violence. This requires transforming male-dominated social relations, ensuring that legal protection mechanisms function effectively and strengthening solidarity among women. Women's liberation is possible not only through access to economic resources but also through their ability to exist as equal and free individuals in every area of life."




'Care services must become a public responsibility'




Sabahat Sever said that economic and social policies must be reorganised on the basis of equality to protect women's labour. She identified secure employment, equal pay for equal work and the removal of obstacles to trade union organisation as priority measures.




Sabahat Sever outlined the steps needed to protect women's labour: "First, economic and social policies must be reorganised on the basis of equality to protect women's labour. Women must have access to secure employment, the principle of equal pay for equal work must be implemented, informal employment must be prevented, and obstacles to women's organisation must be removed.




Second, care services must be treated as a public responsibility. Free nurseries, childcare centres and care services for older people and people with disabilities must be established in every neighbourhood. The burden of care placed on women's shoulders must become a shared social responsibility. Care work is not solely women's responsibility. These services, which are essential for the continuation of social life, must be provided through public policies.




Third, cooperatives and collective production models that increase women's participation in production must be supported. Women's role as producers must be strengthened, particularly in agriculture, ecological production and local economies. However, cooperatives must not become a model in which women are employed as cheap and precarious labour. Women's cooperatives should be structures in which women gain economic strength, receive fair compensation for their labour and have a say in decision-making.




Fourth, local governments must move beyond an approach to women's policies based solely on social assistance. Spaces where women can participate in production, vocational training centres, women's solidarity centres, nurseries and cooperatives must become more widespread. Fifth, women experiencing violence must receive not only legal assistance but also economic support. Safe housing, a regular income, employment and social security must be considered together.




In addition, equal representation of women must be ensured in trade unions, local governments and economic decision-making bodies. For us, the issue is not simply women's employment, but ensuring that women have an equal voice and equal decision-making power in every area of production and social life."




'The labour struggle cannot be complete without women's freedom'




Sabahat Sever said that the struggle for women's labour rights cannot be separated from the broader labour struggle, but warned that it would also be wrong to reduce the inequalities women experience solely to class issues.




Sever continued: "We cannot consider the struggle for women's labour rights separately from the broader labour struggle. However, it would also be wrong to subsume the inequalities women experience entirely under class issues. Women must struggle against both labour exploitation and male-dominated social relations.




Trade unions need to assume greater responsibility in this regard. It is important that women are not merely members of trade unions but become active participants in leadership, decision-making processes and areas of struggle. Particularly in local governments, policies must be developed that prioritise women's labour, regard care services as a public responsibility, support women's cooperatives and strengthen women's economic independence.




Ultimately, we cannot achieve social equality without making women's invisible labour visible, sharing economic resources equally and transforming male-dominated relations. The labour struggle remains incomplete wherever women's labour is not liberated. And genuine social freedom is impossible in a society where women are not free."

author: Unknown
title: Şükran Demir: We have a voice against violence and war!
content:
This year's International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November comes amid increasing attacks by the government on women's hard-won rights. In Turkey, where at least six women are killed by male violence every day and impunity has become systematic, women are preparing to take to the streets across the country to break the cycle of "submission or death" imposed on them. Şükran Demir, Chair of the Board of Directors of the Women's Time Association (Kadın Zamanı Derneği), spoke to ANF about the cycle of violence against women that permeates every aspect of life through the interconnected structures of family, state, capital and judiciary, as well as ways to overcome this violence. Demir said, "We will stand together more often and organise more strongly."




'Mother tongue services, gender equality and combating violence against women'




Şükran Demir said that the Women's Time Association has been actively working on gender equality and combating violence against women since its establishment. Explaining that the association was founded in 2020 in response to the needs of Kurdish women who faced barriers to accessing services in their mother tongue, Demir said: "There are very few institutions in Istanbul that provide services in Kurdish, so the mechanisms available to Kurdish women are extremely limited. The Women's Time Association was established to address this need and gradually began working actively on gender equality and combating violence against women. Our association primarily provides psychological and legal support to women. For other matters, we refer women to institutions with which we cooperate."




'Women are subjected to multiple forms of violence'




Şükran Demir said that women are once again approaching 25 November amid an atmosphere of violence in multiple forms. Demir pointed out that women are now forced to struggle not only to access their economic, social and political rights but also simply to survive. Demir said: "The problems women face do not change significantly from one period to another. Women are already treated as second-class citizens in political, social and economic life and are therefore forced to make additional efforts to access their rights. Today, women face serious difficulties in entering the workforce, experiencing workplace bullying once employed, or being confined to insecure jobs. We are talking about women who already face enormous obstacles in accessing their social and economic rights because every sphere of life has been further restricted and closed off to them. Alongside all these difficulties, women are also subjected to widespread physical and psychological violence. Femicides increase every year, yet preventive policies capable of stopping this growing violence are not implemented. As we approach 25 November this year, one of the main priorities of women's struggle will be to stop femicide and develop effective preventive policies instead of the policies of impunity that pave the way for women's killings."




'Women's lives are being restricted through family-centred policies'




Şükran Demir said that the government's attacks on women's achievements have intensified over time, adding that the "Decade of the Family" initiative seeks to restrict women's lives through family-centred policies. Demir explained that this approach was not new but represented a continuation of historically patriarchal state policies, which have been implemented more intensively and openly under the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government. Demir said that family policies aim to confine women to childbirth, childcare and unpaid domestic labour: "They want women confined to the family, reduced to bearing children, caring for them and remaining inside the home. There is a persistent policy of ensuring that unpaid and insecure labour within the family is provided entirely by women. Yet the family is itself a mechanism through which women are directly exploited and silenced. Even women's objections within the family are met with intense hostility. Statistical data clearly show that women are most frequently subjected to violence or killed by men within their own families. Despite this reality, the government is attempting to legitimise women's exclusion from public life and confinement to the home through policies such as the 'Decade of the Family'. If the government attaches so much importance to its 'My Family Is Safe' policy, it must first implement measures that protect women from violence and end the policies of impunity that enable it. But its priorities lie elsewhere. The government attacks women's achievements, including the Istanbul Convention, while closing women's institutions, imprisoning women involved in the women's struggle and censoring women's news outlets such as Jinnews. It is attempting to eliminate every platform through which women can communicate directly and make their voices heard."




'Technology has become another means of violence'




Şükran Demir said that the growing role of technology in everyday life has transformed and intensified the forms of violence women experience: "Technology has created the conditions for new forms of violence against women, including stalking, harassment and threats through social media accounts. Technology-facilitated violence is among the issues frequently reported to our association. However, this violence continues alongside other forms of abuse. As I mentioned earlier, most women who contact us are subjected to violence within their families. It is not easy for these women to approach our association. Because they are constantly threatened with death or threats against their children, they often seek help only when the cycle of violence has reached its final stage. These threats and acts of violence are most frequently perpetrated by their husbands. However, we also receive applications from women subjected to violence by fathers, brothers and people in their immediate surroundings, including neighbours."




'Women now know they are not alone'




Şükran Demir said that women have become more aware of their rights and the violence they experience compared with previous years. Demir highlighted the growing connections between women and the expansion of solidarity networks: "Women were aware of the violence they experienced at home in the past, too. But perhaps they could not find the strength to resist it. Today, that has changed. Thanks to communication and solidarity across the world, women have begun establishing stronger connections with one another and becoming more involved in collective solidarity and struggle. Women now know they are not alone. This awareness allows the struggle to develop in a more concrete direction. The consciousness that emerges from this awareness gives women the strength to object and resist. Of course, there are gender norms that have been imposed on us as women and that we have also internalised. But today, these norms are increasingly being challenged through the women's struggle. We feel this particularly strongly on 25 November and 8 March, when more women come together in public squares. But the women's struggle has also developed in everyday life to the point where even a woman alone in her home can find the strength to resist. I think this is extremely valuable."




'Women have a voice as active participants in building peace'




Şükran Demir said that women have established a common front against war, where the patriarchal state manifests itself most intensely. Demir recalled that women's organisations recently came together to establish the Women's Peace Monitoring and Follow-up Commission. Demir said that the commission's founding declaration was announced at the Women's Time Association and emphasised that violence against women cannot be separated from policies of war. Discussing the devastating impact of war policies on women's lives, Demir pointed out that women forcibly displaced from Kurdistan, particularly during the 1990s and the 2015-2016 period, faced exclusion and poverty after arriving in Istanbul. Demir explained that displaced women struggled both to participate in urban life and to access adequate institutional support: "This was one of the greatest difficulties we encountered in our work. The absence of institutional mechanisms that could help forcibly displaced women overcome their trauma and the problems they faced in Istanbul made our work extremely difficult. We have witnessed how war as a whole affects the lives of women living in these lands and restricts their living spaces. As seen in the cases of Gülistan Doku, Rojin Kabaiş, Ipek Er and Ayşe Tokyaz, women are constantly being eliminated through special warfare policies, and attempts are frequently made to cover up these killings by describing them as 'suspicious deaths'. Today, women are trying to take concrete steps against war as a whole and against the special warfare policies that take women away from life. The Peace and Democratic Society Process is currently underway. We are discussing extensively what direction this process will take because uncertainty prevails. But there is one thing women are absolutely clear about: the struggle for peace. We want steps to be taken towards ending the destruction caused by war, guaranteeing human rights and building a dignified life through the establishment of peace. The Women's Peace Monitoring and Follow-up Commission, which brings together women from different cities and different identities across the country, represents an important step in this regard. The reason we established this monitoring commission as women is that we have not been sufficiently included in the process. Women are often pushed into the background in political and social processes, and sometimes excluded entirely. Women reject this approach. The Women's Peace Monitoring and Follow-up Commission was established so that women could express their own views and assert their role as active participants. Today, society is experiencing serious divisions, fragmentation and an inability to understand or listen to one another. This is actually a broader problem rooted in the imposition of a monolithic mentality since the foundation of the Republic and the hostility cultivated towards those who are different. But I believe this situation has now reached its most extreme levels. That is why I believe society can overcome these divisions by creating spaces where people come together and listen to one another. The establishment of this commission by women is extremely important for making peace a shared social commitment in the face of war. We have something to say against both violence and war. We will stand together more often, organise more strongly and put our demands into practice with greater determination. I have absolute faith in this."

author: Unknown
title: Fighting for peace for 22 years at her daughter's request
content:
In the 1990s, escalating violence by Hezbollah and state forces in Kurdistan targeted the Özbey family, who lived in Silvan (Farqîn), a district of Amed (Diyarbakır), along with many other families. Their home was repeatedly attacked with gunfire, their doors and windows were smashed, and their daughters were subjected to repression. The family was forced to flee twice for their safety. However, the violence and repression they experienced did not put an end to their struggle.




Raife Özbey, who resisted the repression during those years, continues her struggle for peace today as a member of the Amed Peace Mothers' Assembly. Raife Özbey spoke to ANF about her husband being placed on Hezbollah's "death list", the torture her daughters experienced in prison and the reasons she joined the peace struggle.







 







Raife Özbey recalled that Hezbollah had targeted and killed many people in Amed, Kızıltepe (Qoser), Batman (Êlih) and Silvan, adding that her family had also been subjected to this violence. Raife Özbey said that her husband was on a list of 80 people marked for death and described the fear and repression they experienced: "My husband had to leave home, and I was left alone with my young children. In the evenings, we did not even dare go out onto the balcony to collect firewood for the stove. They would open fire as soon as they saw someone outside. They attacked our home, saying, 'This is the home of a Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) member.' My children could not go to school. I hid them beneath the concrete kitchen counter and under the bed frame."




Displaced three times to protect her children




One of Raife Özbey's daughters was attacked on her way to school and suffered a head injury requiring 20 stitches. The family was forced to leave Silvan and settled in Adana. Raife Özbey said that the repression continued there: "The state did not leave us alone in Adana either. People were constantly being detained and released. The raids and imprisonments never ended. One night, they came and took my husband away, and on 15 August, they took my daughter Xangul. My other daughter, Semra, was also under arrest. I went and waited outside the courthouse. They tried to make me leave, but I insisted, sat down and refused to move. Eventually, they said, 'All right, we will let you see them, but you must not tell anyone.' I had gone there with a friend. They asked whether we could read and write. I could, but my friend was illiterate. They took my friend away and tried to make her sign a document stating that nothing had been done to the children. I did not allow it and went myself. They did not let me see my children. They transferred them to Konya."




A mother's resistance at the prison gates




After the arrest of her two daughters, life in Adana became unbearable for the family, forcing them to move to Antalya. Raife Özbey described how she continued struggling to protect her children amid ongoing repression: "We did not register our address or send the children to school because we wanted to avoid being tracked down. One night, they raided our home again. They said, 'You think you are hiding, but we have all your files. Wherever you go in the world, we know what you are doing.' We were so frightened that we could no longer go outside, and the raids continued. Once, when police officers came to our door, I told them, 'If you come to my door again, I will set myself and my children on fire.'"




Her daughter's final request




The family decided to return to Amed after the release of Raife Özbey's daughters, but the repression continued. Semra, who had repeatedly been detained and arrested and had been denied her right to education, eventually decided to go to the mountains of Kurdistan. Before leaving, Semra asked her mother to join the Peace Mothers and continue the struggle. Raife Özbey recalled their conversation: "Semra said, 'Mother, if you listen to me, join the Peace Mothers and struggle.' I said, 'All right.' It has been 22 years, and I have been among the Peace Mothers ever since."

title: Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya ev hapsi ile tahliye edildi
content:
Gazeteci Ceylan Sever'in aktardığına göre, Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya'nın ev hapsi şeklinde adli kontrol şartıyla serbest bırakılmasına karar verildi.




Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya, fon soruşturması kapsamında 18 gün önce tutuklanmıştı. 




Fon soruşturması kapsamında tutuklu olarak Silivri Cezaevi'nde bulunan Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya'nın, 18 Kasım'da koğuşunda baygınlık geçirmesi üzerine hastaneye sevk edildiği öğrenildi. Hastanede yapılan ilk müdahale ve kontrollerin ardından Kaya'nın yeniden cezaevine nakledildiği bildirildi.




Soruşturmanın Geçmişi ve Suçlamalar




Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya, yürütülen fon soruşturması çerçevesinde gözaltına alınmış ve 6 Kasım tarihinde çıkarıldığı mahkemece tutuklanmıştı. Kaya'ya yöneltilen suçlamalar arasında "Sermaye Piyasası Kanunu'na muhalefet" ile "suç işlemek amacıyla kurulan örgüte üye olma" yer alıyor.




Savcılığın nöbetçi sulh ceza hakimliğine sunduğu sevk yazısında, Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu'nun (SPK) hazırladığı rapora dikkat çekildi. Raporda, Özata Denizcilik San. ve Tic. AŞ hisselerindeki işlem hareketleri incelendiğinde, Kaya'nın hisse fiyatını ve yatırımcı kararlarını doğrudan etkileyebilecek nitelikteki kamuya açıklanmamış içsel bilgilere erişimi olduğunun değerlendirildiği aktarıldı.




2,2 Milyar Liralık Kazanç İddiası




SPK'nın suç duyurusu üzerine derinleştirilen soruşturmanın sevk yazısında, Kamu Aydınlatma Platformu (KAP) verileri ve hisse işlem kayıtlarına dair şu tespitlere yer verildi:










Tera Grubu'nun şirket ve fon bazında "OZATD" kodlu hissede yoğun alımlar gerçekleştirdiği belirlendi.










Soruşturmanın merkezinde, söz konusu hisse işlemleri ile fonların tasfiye süreciyle bağlantılı olduğu öne sürülen finansal hareketler yer alıyor.










Yapılan incelemelerde Kaya'nın, Özata Denizcilik hisselerine yatırdığı 160 milyon TL karşılığında, 5 ay gibi kısa bir sürede yaklaşık 2,2 milyar TL kazanç sağladığı tespit edildi.










(EMK)
