author: Rafael Oliveira
title: “Apenas acusações”: como o Deutsche Bank tratou as gigantes brasileiras da carne
content:
Vazamento mostra escândalos de um dos maiores bancos do mundo. A

 Pública

 é o único parceiro no Brasil. Leia o especial 

Inside Deutsche Bank

 

aqui.


































Vazamento mostra escândalos de um dos maiores bancos do mundo. A

 Pública

 é o único parceiro no Brasil. Leia o especial 

Inside Deutsche Bank

 

aqui.
















Quando a Polícia Federal deflagrou a Operação Carne Fraca, até então a maior da história da corporação, com mais de 1.100 agentes mobilizados e 309 mandados judiciais cumpridos, o impacto foi imediato. O que a PF revelava naquele março de 2017 – um extenso esquema de adulteração de carne vencida, que envolvia grandes frigoríficos e a corrupção de fiscais do governo – colocava em dúvida a qualidade e mesmo a segurança sanitária de um dos carros-chefe da economia nacional.




Duas das principais empresas envolvidas, a BRF (hoje MBRF, após fusão com a Marfrig) e a JBS, dos irmãos Joesley e Wesley Batista, viram suas ações na bolsa despencarem. A União Europeia pediu uma reunião de emergência sobre o assunto e os principais jornais do mundo questionaram o futuro do agronegócio brasileiro.




As acusações geraram condenações e acordos de leniência. Mas houve também erros na divulgação de algumas informações pela PF, como a afirmação de que empresas adicionavam papelão à carne, quando na verdade os fiscais que foram gravados pela polícia se referiam à embalagem do produto.




Como resultado, países suspenderam a compra de carne brasileira e as exportações do produto 

desabaram

. A BRF, concorrente da JBS e dona das marcas Sadia e Perdigão, teve 

um executivo

 preso. 




Mas, para alguns executivos do Deutsche Bank, as acusações mereciam outro enquadramento. Duas versões de um relatório da Unidade de Inteligência de Negócios (BIU, na sigla em inglês) do banco, datadas de junho de 2017, mostram que, 

apesar de ter classificado a BRF como “alto risco” após o escândalo vir à tona, o banco alemão resolveu continuar fazendo negócios normalmente com a empresa brasileira, que era sua cliente.




O relatório, que serve de subsídio para preservar o banco de riscos, acatou as medidas de mitigação adotadas pela BRF e relativizou a relevância do problema. O material afirma, por exemplo, que 

a maior parte das acusações “não parecem se aplicar à BRF” e que “o mau gerenciamento do caso pela polícia” diminuiu “a gravidade da acusação contra a empresa”. 




O material é parte do 

Inside Deutsche Bank

, investigação transnacional da qual a 

Agência Pública

 faz parte, baseada no vazamento de mais de 15 milhões de documentos do banco, obtido pelo jornalista indiano Josy Joseph e por Khadija Sharife, jornalista investigativa da África do Sul. O projeto tem coordenação global da Barracuda Media e do Centro Latinoamericano de Periodismo de Investigación (CLIP) na região.




Os documentos vazados para o projeto mostram, 

segundo detalhado em diversas reportagens

, como o banco alemão repetidamente ignorou sinais de alerta de possível lavagem de dinheiro e violações de sanções e como descumpriu suas próprias regras para clientes poderosos.




O comportamento da instituição alemã – presente no Brasil há mais de um século – frente ao envolvimento de um cliente importante em um escândalo não é um episódio isolado. Emails, relatórios e planilhas internas mostram o mesmo padrão de atuação com outros clientes brasileiros de peso implicados em investigações ou até mesmo acusados de crimes. Como mostraram reportagens da 

Pública

 que foram ao ar nos últimos dias, a lista inclui multinacionais como 

Vale, Banco Safra, Andrade Gutierrez, Braskem

 e 

Cutrale

.




A 

primeira reportagem

 da série detalhou uma grande controvérsia em torno do BTG Pactual de André Esteves, com quem o chefe de Commodities do Deutsche Bank se recusou a fazer negócios, chamando-o de “pilantra”. Outros executivos defenderam a relação com o banco, dizendo ser um dos principais clientes do DB no Brasil.




A carne é fraca




Os relatórios da Unidade de Inteligência de Negócios e o trabalho de outros setores, como o de Combate aos Crimes Financeiros (AFC, na sigla em inglês) e Gestão de Risco de Crédito (CRM, na sigla em inglês), são normalmente utilizados para frear negócios que podem oferecer risco à instituição. Ao fazer valer regras de 

compliance

 e eventualmente desligar clientes lucrativos, eles podem frustrar as áreas do banco mais focadas em lucros e resultados.




Mas, no caso da BRF e da Operação Carne Fraca, o relatório de BIU do Deutsche Bank amenizou as denúncias. 




“A rápida resposta da BRF à crise, a pressão das relações públicas e as informações subsequentes sobre a suposta negligência da polícia na Operação Carne Fraca contribuíram para a contenção da crise por parte da empresa”, diz um dos trechos do relatório. No vazamento, há duas versões do documento, uma com 16 e outra com 19 páginas; não é possível saber qual delas foi a definitiva.




Ambas as versões, produzidas quatro meses após a operação, são ancoradas em matérias da imprensa brasileira. Chama a atenção que parte delas fosse de veículos locais e com ligação direta com o setor rural, como a Revista Safra, autointitulada “revista do agronegócio”, que cita críticas à “espetacularização da divulgação da operação pela PF”. O veículo, registrado em nome de um ex-presidente de sindicato rural goiano, não está mais no ar. 




Também há referência a uma reportagem do ExpressoMT, veículo do polo agropecuário Lucas do Rio Verde (MT), município que tem uma sede da BRF.




Em março de 2018, a gigante do setor alimentício foi o alvo central de uma nova fase da Carne Fraca que prendeu uma dezena de seus executivos, incluindo o ex-presidente global da companhia. Apesar de a maior parte dos executivos e funcionários terem sido inocentados, a empresa não escapou incólume: em 2022, a então BRF concordou em 

pagar

 mais de R$ 583 milhões aos cofres públicos em um acordo de leniência em que admitia responsabilidade por atos de improbidade administrativa e corrupção de agentes públicos e se comprometia a aprimorar seus programas de 

compliance

.
















JBS: planilha interna do DB relativizou acusações contra os irmãos Batista




São “apenas acusações”




A MBRF, no entanto, não é a única campeã do setor de proteína animal tratada dessa forma pelo banco alemão. Em uma planilha de janeiro de 2017, em que o banco lista potenciais clientes na América Latina para o setor de 

Wealth Management

 (que cuida de grandes fortunas), 

os irmãos Joesley e Wesley Batista, donos da holding J&F e da empresa JBS, são citados com destaque. 




A planilha ressalta o enorme crescimento da JBS ao longo daquela década, destacando o apoio do governo brasileiro à empresa por meio do BNDES, e aponta que a companhia mantinha “relação ativa com o Deutsche Bank no Brasil”. 




A “relação ativa” é reforçada por uma troca de emails que trata da aprovação de um financiamento de 42 milhões de dólares para a JBS, aprovado em 2012, e com prazo de pagamento de 10 anos. A negociação prosperou mesmo com funcionários apontando que o empréstimo era desfavorável economicamente para o banco, já que não atingia a taxa mínima de retorno. Os emails indicam que o negócio foi aprovado como estratégia de se aproximar da empresa, destacada como uma das maiores do país.





































 Emails mostram conflito interno sobre negociação com a JBS apontada como desvantajosa por funcionários do DB




Ainda sobre a planilha do setor responsável por grandes fortunas, o material lista uma série de acusações contra a empresa e seus donos, mas relativiza sua relevância.




Quanto a supostos subornos ligados à Eldorado, empresa de papel e celulose do grupo, a justificativa na planilha afirma serem “apenas acusações” e diz que não havia “provas de irregularidade”. 




Nas semanas seguintes, porém, o próprio Joesley 

afirmou

 em delação que o grupo econômico que ele comanda com seu irmão teria pagado propina em mais de uma ocasião no processo de 

formação

 da Eldorado: para obter financiamento bilionário do BNDES; para conseguir recursos junto ao Fundo de Investimento do Fundo de Garantia do Tempo de Serviço (FI-FGTS); e para criar a Florestal (também do grupo J&F, depois fundida com a Eldorado), nesse caso junto a fundos de pensão da Caixa e da Petrobras.




Em relação ao envolvimento na Lava Jato, na Operação Greenfield (ligada ao caso Eldorado) e em outras investigações por corrupção, o texto da planilha diz que “os irmãos não foram diretamente implicados em nenhuma irregularidade” – só que, mesmo no mês em que a planilha é datada, antes dos piores escândalos da JBS virem a público, os irmãos já eram 

suspeitos

 de envolvimento direto em irregularidades.




É bem verdade que a Unidade de Inteligência de Negócios recomendou que os irmãos fossem colocados no “Tier 1”, a classificação de mais alto risco, por conta do histórico de investigações contra a JBS. Por outro lado, tanto Joesley quanto Wesley são citados como “prospective clients”, isto é, pessoas nas quais o banco estava interessado em trazer para sua carteira de clientes. A planilha também menciona “uma oportunidade concreta de oferecer um financiamento imobiliário em Nova York”.




Os meses imediatamente seguintes à data da planilha, entretanto, não foram exatamente os mais abonadores para os irmãos Batista. Em março, com a deflagração da Operação Carne Fraca, a JBS surgiu como uma das empresas envolvidas na fraude, o que causou estragos – ainda que temporários – na reputação da companhia.




Em maio, algo ainda mais grave: veio a público a gravação que Joesley fez do então presidente Michel Temer, em que um dos donos da JBS admitia pagamento de propina para o à época presidente da Câmara, Eduardo Cunha, e para outros políticos, incluindo Guido Mantega, ministro da Fazenda de governos petistas.




Ao longo dos anos seguintes, os irmãos foram presos e depois soltos; acusados de usar informações privilegiadas da própria 

delação

 premiada para lucrar com a venda de ações e depois absolvidos; assinaram o maior acordo de leniência da história (R$ 10,3 bilhões) e depois viram o pagamento ser 

suspenso

 pelo ministro Dias Toffoli, do Supremo Tribunal Federal, que colocou em dúvida se o acordo teria sido firmado por vontade própria ou por pressão do Ministério Público Federal (MPF).




Nos últimos anos, depois de um período longe dos holofotes, eles 

voltaram a ficar em evidência

 quando a JBS se tornou a maior empresa de proteína animal do mundo – contando com o apoio de bancos e da classe política.




Outro lado




A 

Pública

 enviou uma série de perguntas relacionadas ao comportamento do banco e de seus funcionários em casos relativos às empresas citadas nesta e nas demais reportagens do especial 

Inside Deutsche Bank

, tanto para a sede global do banco alemão quanto para a filial brasileira, que respondeu em nota.




“Não comentamos sobre relacionamentos potenciais, anteriores ou atuais com clientes. Temos políticas e controles estabelecidos para garantir o cumprimento dos requisitos legais, regulatórios e internos aplicáveis. O modelo de Três Linhas de Defesa do banco foi concebido para garantir que as avaliações de risco sejam submetidas à revisão e contestação independentes pelas áreas de controle, independentemente da relevância comercial das relações com os clientes.”




A J&F não respondeu ao pedido de posicionamento e a MBRF disse que não vai se manifestar.

author: Malik Chiconela Santana
title: Mozambique: A Judicial Solution to a Political Problem
content:
Venâncio Bila Mondlane, the leader of the Mozambican opposition, finds himself awaiting trial (scheduled for November 17) for his alleged role as the progenitor of the seismic protests that followed the 2024 elections and threatened to topple the state. Mondlane is president of the recently formed National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (ANAMOLA) party. He is accused of five crimes by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, namely 

public justification of crime, incitement of collective disobedience, public instigation of crime, instigation of terrorism, and incitement of terrorism

. A conviction could mean up to 20 years in prison for the presidential runner-up, the crippling of the opposition, and a transition in the state’s handling of political opponents.




Mondlane’s road to the 2024 ballot was lined with legal and procedural obstacles. 

Blocked

 from contesting the leadership of his party at the time, the Mozambican National Resistance (RENAMO), he left it and allied his campaign with the Democratic Alliance Coalition (CAD), whose electoral eligibility was confirmed on May 9, but was excluded by the National Election Commission (CNE) on July 18. The Constitutional Council (CC) upheld the decision on appeal, arguing that the parties who had formed CAD failed to notify the 

Ministry of Justice and Constitutional and Religious Matters

 of their intention to form a coalition. The court framed the decision as a purely technical issue; however, its consequences were undeniably political. Mondlane found himself politically isolated only two months before the elections. Forced to reorganize his campaign, Mondlane forged a last-minute partnership with the Optimistic People for the Development of Mozambique (PODEMOS), running as an independent with the party’s political and parliamentary support.




This chronology illustrates how the political agency of Mondlane and his supporters was repeatedly at odds with applications of the electoral law. It may not establish that each application of electoral law was politically motivated, but, at the very least, it raises a broader question of how ostensibly procedural outcomes can reshape the field of political competition, and suggests that legal procedure is not necessarily neutral.




After the October 9, 2024, vote, the CNE declared Daniel Chapo, candidate of the ruling Mozambique Liberation Front (Frelimo), the winner with about 70%, to Mondlane’s 20%. In December, after more than 300 complaints of electoral crimes and irregularities had been lodged with local and district courts, the Constitutional Council revised those figures to roughly 65% and 24% respectively. The revision was, in effect, an admission that the election commission’s results were dubious at best and fictional at worst. The CC altered the results when, as a body of electoral oversight, it could only order the CNE to recount the votes or annul the elections. Unsurprisingly, 

the Mozambican Bar Association

 (OAM), opposition parties, and civil society groups expressed concerns over the CC’s vague legal reasoning and the lack of an evidentiary basis for its alteration of the results.




What ensued in the wake of these opaque elections was a six-month period of unprecedented violence. In Mozambique, several elections have been followed by periods of armed conflict. What made this period unprecedented, however, was that the antagonism was not between the state and an organized army, but rather between the state and a mobilized mass of unarmed civilians. According to a 

report

 by the Mozambican NGO Plataforma Decide, 411 civilians were killed, some 3,700 were injured, and around 7,200 were illegally detained between October 2024 and January 2025. These figures were disputed by the then commander-general of the police, Bernardino Rafael, who stated that 96 civilians were killed. Even so, charges have only been brought 

against two officers

, and, with no updates, it is unclear whether the prosecution is pursuing these cases at all.




The protests began on October 21, when Mondlane called for a peaceful march in tribute to Elvino Dias, his lawyer, who was assassinated by assailants of no particular origin as he prepared an appeal challenging the preliminary election results. This march, like many that followed, was dispersed violently, including through the use of tear gas and live ammunition. In an environment where constitutionally protected political activities are met with violence, the credibility of official mechanisms is decimated. Inevitably, direct, “extralegal” forms of political action are increasingly regarded as the only legitimate mechanisms of contestation.




The result is a call-and-response cycle of escalation, in which protesters become increasingly militant as they respond to outrages perpetrated by security forces. Mondlane and others have alleged that state security agents infiltrated the protests with the mandate of spreading terror and destruction and discrediting the protests in the eyes of more moderate observers. While these allegations require independent substantiation, what is undeniable is that the protests were accompanied by widespread destruction of private and public property. The Confederation of Economic Associations of Mozambique (CTA) 

estimated

 that some 17,000 jobs were lost.




Almost two years to the day since the months of rage, Mondlane finds himself awaiting trial for inciting, stoking and justifying the chaos. The trial and his potential conviction carry implications which extend far beyond Mondlane’s personal criminal liability. According to article 118 (a–b) of Law no. 7/2004 and article 147 of the Constitution, candidates who have been convicted of an intentional criminal offense lose their active electoral capacity and are rendered ineligible for public office. The question of electoral eligibility is determined by the National Election Commission and the Constitutional Council as the court of appeal. Once Mondlane exhausts his appeals and a conviction is final, the opposition leader would be unable ever again to run for public office. Through this trial, the judicial process would succeed, bloodlessly, where electoral fraud and political violence failed. In one fell swoop, the political opposition would be castrated, and the current administration would have found a judicial solution to a political problem.




So much for the trial’s political stakes. What of the case itself? In determining whether the prosecution is politically motivated or represents a legitimate application of the law, its legal merits, or lack thereof, must be considered. It is important to note at the outset that, at the time of writing, neither the then commander-general of the national police nor, for that matter, any government official has been charged in connection with the protests. Additionally, no high-ranking member of PODEMOS has been charged. This disparity does not on its own establish political motivation, but, read in the wider context, it raises questions as to what motivates the law to be applied so rigorously in some instances and not at all in others.




To the tens of thousands of viewers who watched Mondlane’s Facebook livestreams or the millions who engaged with the politician’s social media accounts, it is obvious that Mondlane did in fact incite the people to protest, block public roads and refuse to pay utility taxes and toll fees. One question before the courts, then, is whether these acts can be considered criminal conduct under the law.




Mondlane has a strong argument that his exhortations fall within the protections afforded by articles 48 (1), 51, and 80 of the Constitution. These enshrine, respectively, the freedom of expression, assembly, and resistance. The latter protects the right of citizens “not to comply with orders that are unlawful, or that infringe on their rights, freedoms and guarantees.” The rights in the Constitution are not absolute and are subject to restriction. However, their limitation is regulated by article 56 (2–4), which states that rights can only be limited through legislation in order to “safeguard other rights and interests of the constitution” and “in cases expressly provided for by the constitution.” 

Law No. 1/2020

 was promulgated on March 31, 2020, to limit citizens’ rights, such as the right of movement, during the COVID-19 pandemic. During the protests, however, there was no such legislation nor any declaration of emergency in effect. These constitutional protections do not on their own settle the question of criminal liability. Another question to be determined by the courts is whether the restrictions on Mondlane’s political speech and mobilization are proportionate to Mondlane’s political actions.




In determining the proportionality of the limitation, it must be recognized that at no point did Mondlane incite or encourage the destruction or theft of public and private property. On the contrary, he 

condemned

 these acts on several occasions, going as far as threatening 

to refuse to take up any position

 in the government should the destruction continue. It is at this point that it becomes unclear who exactly is on trial here: Mondlane or the protesters? It is obvious that Mondlane encouraged civil disobedience; it is, apparently, less obvious that those who engaged in direct action did so not because “Venâncio said” but because of their daily run-ins with death, both corporeal and social. If it is the case that those who attacked police stations, state institutions and private businesses were instructed to do so, then this instruction came from within, inspired by a collective consciousness and informed by a material reality. Put plainly, those who revolted did so simply because, for many reasons, they could no longer breathe.




As the protests evolved from a focus on electoral justice toward broader issues such as the cost of living, youth unemployment and a desire to be recognized as living, thinking beings by the state, the already thin case for Mondlane’s criminal liability grew thinner still. Candidly, it is not Mondlane who stands accused in the dock but a conception of politics, one that contests beyond the comfortability of the state. The destruction that Mondlane is being tried for did take place, but it would be far too convenient to believe it happened on his orders.




To broadcast or not to broadcast




The Supreme Court has 

dismissed an appeal

 lodged by Mondlane’s legal team challenging the court’s decision to ban the live audiovisual transmission and recording of court proceedings. The Court substantiated this decision by invoking Article 452 (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provides for the non-appealability of any decisions that fall under the discretionary power of the Court. The position rests on the view that the audiovisual transmission of court proceedings is not a constitutional right. However, in addition to being enshrined in article 48 of the Constitution, the freedom of information is supported by the Right to Information Law (Law n.º 34/2014). The Court will allow journalists to sit in on the proceedings and record the events in writing. Nevertheless, the interpretation of criminal procedure law which the court has utilized to restrict constitutional rights is inconsistent with constitutional principles to the extent that it violates the spirit thereof.




The spokesperson of the Supreme Court has defended the ban, 

arguing

 that livestreamed proceedings could be taken out of context, circulated as short clips on social media, and instrumentalized for propaganda. He also raised concerns that broadcasting could expose judges and witnesses to political pressure. It is true that live transmission of witness testimony could influence future testimonies, while the circulation of decontextualized footage can distort public understanding of proceedings. Nevertheless, if the courts regard public opinion as detrimental to the administration of justice, then what safeguards protect these same judges from pressure exerted by the legislative and executive branches of government?




Furthermore, there is strong historical precedent for the live broadcasting of politically sensitive trials in Mozambique. The 2002 murder trial of Mozambican journalist Carlos Cardoso is one example. Cardoso was assassinated in 2000 while investigating the 

theft of $14 million

 from the state-owned Banco Comercial de Moçambique (BCM) on the eve of its privatization, as Mozambique transitioned to a free-market economy. The murder of Cardoso, the nation’s foremost journalist, created a particularly delicate issue for the state. At the time, Mozambican democracy was only eight years old, and the government needed to present itself as a genuine democracy, transparent enough to attract foreign investment and distance itself from its authoritarian past. The trial was broadcast live on state television and radio. The then minister of justice 

explained

 the rationale, stating, “this is to show the country that there is transparency here, and that we are serious. . . .  people don’t trust the government, but this trial and the way it is being held publicly will help to end that.”




For similar reasons, the trial in the 

“Hidden Debts”

 case (

dívidas ocultas

) was broadcast live in 2021 and 2022. The case involved 19 defendants and $2 billion in loans granted in 2013 and 2014 by European and Russian banks. These loans were granted in secrecy without parliamentary approval. Both of these cases involved highly sensitive political information; nevertheless, they were broadcast. These precedents demonstrate that broadcasting a politically sensitive trial is not inherently incompatible with the administration of justice. Additionally, they illustrate that the decision to deny transmission requires more substantiation than an abstract appeal to judicial discretion.




The use of social media as a tool of political participation and mobilization is central to this discussion. During the protests, Mondlane developed a strategy that leveraged the generativity of the digital public. His livestreams were conducted on Facebook to tens of thousands of users, peaking on October 25, when he reached 115,000 concurrent viewers. The final report of the European Union Election Observation Mission documents that the very next day there was a 

national internet shutdown

.




Understood within the context of Mondlane’s political strategy, the court’s decision strips him of his principal vehicle of messaging. This may serve as yet another warning for political movements that have leveraged the digital public. Though the internet and social media may promise a safer, more democratic public within which people may strategize, organize, and mobilize, access to the internet is very much dispensed at the discretion of the state and corporations and can be suspended at their whims. The 

Zimbabwean

 and 

Kenyan

 protests of 2019 and 2024, respectively, provide examples of how easily states are able to react to social movements and collapse communications infrastructure. The point is not to foreclose the generative potential of social media but rather to illustrate how the control of digital infrastructure and platforms is central to guaranteeing this potential.




To be or not to be




The fact that this trial is taking place at all demonstrates the “stealth authoritarianism” of the Mozambican state. The legal scholar Melissa Crouch, building on Ozan Varol, 

uses the phrase

 to describe the manner in which an ostensibly democratic system can be wielded by the dominant political formation as a means of maintaining its power. Such a stealthily authoritarian state is furnished with a plethora of ideological and repressive apparatuses with which to quash opposition. The law is one such mechanism, available, at all times, to further authoritarian ends. It can palatably achieve results which could otherwise only be achieved through murders and kidnappings.




Apartheid-era South Africa was not a “stealth authoritarian” state, but a comparison is worth making. In 1968, the Department of Foreign Affairs proclaimed that “[t]he South African legal system is soundly based on the rule of law”; seven years later, the minister of justice, Jimmy Kruger, boasted in parliament that the country’s legal system was “held in high esteem in all Western countries,” as Alfred 

Cockrell records

. The point is not that the contemporary Mozambican state is equivalent to apartheid South Africa. Rather, the comparison illustrates how legal procedures and discourse can be deployed to legitimize a state that is obviously illegitimate. When the sheen of democracy and the rule of law is draped over a state, it becomes easy for those who are so inclined to pretend that what’s gilded is solid gold.




The 

2026 Bertelsmann Transformation Index (BTI) Country Report

 classifies Mozambique as a “clientelist state” presenting “the facade of electoral democracy.” This facade is an integral part of the resilience of authoritarian states. As a state constructed around and catered toward the interests of international, multinational, and multilateral clients, it is crucial that the state present itself as a palatable business partner. The concern is not with the actual operation of the state but rather with how it appears to operate. One is reminded of the famous joke told by Soviet workers: “We pretend to work, and they pretend to pay us.”




The seismic shock of the protests has shifted the landscape and disrupted the status quo of Mozambican politics. The government now finds itself in a double bind. On the one hand, the state cannot simply allow the opposition to organize itself and disseminate information as it very well pleases; this would spell the death of the liberation party’s 50-year rule. On the other hand, the government cannot resort to its tried and tested methods again in 2029, not only because the international client community is watching but, more importantly, because the chaos and destruction that may ensue could create an even more volatile situation.




The Mozambican state stands in the wake of a mass protest movement that presented the most politically legible threat to the liberation party since independence. Thus, it must be pragmatic in considering how best to secure its power. At this juncture, it appears that the safest choice is to rely on the judicial process to eliminate its most formidable threat from the political stage. While Mondlane will most likely not be jailed, he may be convicted, and in any case, the mere fact of this trial spells a transition in the state’s handling of political opposition. Moreover, the decision not to broadcast the trial seems to form part of this strategy, raising questions about the role of the digital public in the future of Mozambican political participation. 




The truth of the matter is that the merits of the state’s case are not of great importance; it would be naive to imagine that they are. Rather, the importance lies in the state’s quest for new methods of guaranteeing its resilience. If you will indulge the hyperbole, it is an existential quest: to be or not to be.




–




This post is from a partnership between 

Africa Is a Country

 and The Elephant. We will be publishing 

a series of posts

 from their site every week

.

The post 

Mozambique: A Judicial Solution to a Political Problem

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

title: Ecological destruction driven by profit in west, security in Kurdistan
content:
The environmental destruction caused by the climate crisis is deepening across Turkey. According to data from the Agriculture and Forestry Workers' Union (Tarım Orman-Iş), 257,000 hectares of forestland have been destroyed in Turkey over the past decade.




The drying up of numerous natural lakes and the transformation of Turkey into a dumping ground for waste are further disrupting the ecological balance. Seasonal differences are becoming less pronounced, temperatures are rising and drought is becoming increasingly widespread.




Academic Metin V. Bayrak, a member of the Climate Justice Coalition and a volunteer with the Peoples' Climate Summit, spoke to ANF about environmental destruction in Turkey and the consequences of the climate crisis.




Bayrak described the climate crisis as the visible manifestation of a crisis of civilisation in nature. He said that humanity's relationship with nature has historically been shaped by domination.




Bayrak said: "What we call the 'climate crisis' is actually the crisis of civilisation becoming visible in nature. Since the Industrial Revolution, we have understood humanity's relationship with nature in terms of domination. Since Francis Bacon, we have regarded knowledge as a tool for controlling nature and nature itself as a resource. This perspective emerged because humanity positioned itself outside nature. Yet we coexist with all living and non-living beings. We are fellow inhabitants of this planet.




We are now reaping the consequences of this way of thinking. We encounter these consequences in every aspect of our lives, from the air we breathe and the water we drink to our food and shelter. However, just as our contributions to creating this crisis are unequal, so too are the ways in which we experience its consequences. The climate crisis is therefore also a question of justice."




'We opened agricultural land to construction'




Bayrak said that Turkey faces environmental problems exacerbated by public policies, in addition to the effects of the global climate crisis: "The global causes of climate change and the problems Turkey has created through its own actions are different. Turkey is located in the Mediterranean basin, a region highly vulnerable to climate change. So what have public authorities done with this knowledge? For decades, we have reduced development to growth, and growth largely to construction, extraction, consumption and, so to speak, plunder. We opened agricultural land to construction, altered riverbeds, drained wetlands and opened forests to mining activities.




How rational is it to measure a country's wealth by the income it generates from consuming its own assets? We claim to create economic value by destroying forests. But is the value of the destroyed forest included in this 'accounting'? What we leave out of these calculations returns to us as ecological debt."




'Destruction in Kurdish regions is justified on security grounds'




Bayrak said that ecological destruction justified on economic grounds in western Turkey is carried out through security policies in Kurdish regions, drawing attention to forest clearing in Şırnak (Şirnex). He said that tree felling in Cudi, Gabar and Besta demonstrates the relationship between security policies and ecological destruction, adding that documents emerging during judicial proceedings also revealed requests for tree felling on security grounds.




Bayrak asked, "We need to question the very concept of 'security' here. Whose security are we talking about, and what are we trying to protect? Whose security are we ensuring by destroying the geography and living spaces of a people?" and added: "We are talking about a region where dams are being built on 'security' grounds, even though dams are known to cause permanent ecological destruction. Security cannot be used as a justification for removing public decisions from public scrutiny. Peace also has an ecological dimension. Can we establish social peace without repairing a people's relationship with the land they inhabit, for example, without reopening pastures?"




'People's relationship with the land has changed'




Bayrak said that the industrialisation of agriculture in Turkey has transformed people's relationship with the land: "With the industrialisation of agriculture, it is not only the mode of production that has changed, but also humanity's relationship with the soil. Farmers were once the bearers of knowledge about life passed down through generations, but they have increasingly become replaceable or expendable links in the industrial production chain.




We confuse soil fertility with soil productivity. In pursuit of higher yields per unit of land, we are exhausting the soil's capacity to regenerate itself. Excessive use of fertilisers and pesticides, monoculture and production that disregards available water resources have become instruments of this process.




The issue is not abandoning technology, but determining what knowledge and values guide its use. The existing model of production and consumption, which disregards the conditions that make production possible, namely nature, is unsustainable. We must consider food sovereignty, biodiversity and farmers' autonomy together."




'

The ecological struggle is a long-term struggle'




Bayrak described the ecological struggle as a long-term endeavour and said that local movements form one of its most important foundations. He stressed the importance of bringing together the experiences of local struggles: "Social struggle is a long-term process. Local struggles are its most important driving force. However, we can achieve the results we seek only to the extent that we create forms of organisation that enable these struggles to learn from one another and share their experiences.




An environmentalist perspective and an ecological perspective are different. When we speak of the environment, we place humanity at the centre and other beings around it. Ecological thinking calls on us to recognise and understand the interdependence of all beings, the concept of coexistence.




The ecological struggle is a struggle to save trees and rivers, but it goes beyond that. It is also a struggle to transform the ways we work, produce, consume, govern and live together. It means discovering what different struggles have in common."




'Climate policies are too important to leave to governments and corporations'




Metin V. Bayrak said that the ecological struggle cannot be separated from society's political and cultural environment, noting that the ecological movement in Turkey is also influenced by nationalism, discrimination and habits of state-centred thinking.




Bayrak said that thousands of activists from different countries had gathered in Antalya for the Peoples' Climate Summit, organised as an alternative to the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31). He emphasised the importance of consistency in the principles guiding the ecological struggle: "The ecological movement in Turkey is not free from the political and cultural baggage of the society in which we live. We cannot claim that nationalism, discrimination and habits of state-centred thinking have not permeated the ecological struggle.




Look, thousands of activists from dozens of countries around the world are now in Antalya for the Peoples' Climate Summit, which we organised as an alternative to COP31, to internationalise the struggle. If we object to the cutting down of a tree in Akbelen but can excuse the felling of a tree in Cudi on security grounds, or if we ignore the genocide in Gaza and the relentless bombing of Yemen in one way or another, we must reconsider the values on which our objections are based. One of the things that distinguishes an ethical position from an opinion is that its underlying principles do not change according to individuals, identities or geographical locations. The ecological struggle can be liberating only to the extent that it challenges all relations of domination established between human beings, nature and peoples."




Bayrak also addressed the possible consequences of the climate crisis, warning that if current policies continue, difficulties in accessing water and food, agricultural production losses, forest fires, internal migration and the resulting social inequalities could increase. He stressed that the future is not defined solely by the negative developments that may occur: "This is also why I attach importance to the Peoples' Climate Summit, which we organised as an alternative to COP31. The formulation of climate policies is far too vital to be left to negotiations between governments and corporations. Lasting solutions cannot be developed unless those whose lives are affected by these decisions become active participants in the decision-making process. After all, we are the ones who will implement these decisions. What we need cannot be reduced to 'renewable energy'. We must develop a renewed political, economic and ethical understanding and create an awareness of our shared existence.




At what cost are we living this life, which is a gift? I do not believe we can build an ecological future without asking this question and confronting our answers. But I believe that our optimism in the will to live is, and will remain, our guide. Because the will to live is real."

title: Ji Weşanxaneya Pallê pirtûkek nû: “Kurtebehsek li ser Sosyalîzmê”
content:
Berhema Ebdurrehman Qasimlo bi navê “Kurtebehsek li ser Sosyalîzmê” bi kurmancî ji aliyê Pall Weşanê ve hat çapkirin. Di vê pirtûkê de gotar û şîroveyên Dr. Ebdurrehman Qasimlo yên li ser sosyalîzmê cih digirin.




Pirtûk ji aliyê Mustafa Zengîn ve ji Soranî li Kurmanciyê hat wergerandin û wî bi xwe jî pêşgotineke berfireh ji bo pirtûkê nivîsiye.




Nivîsa paşbergê




Mijarên wekî rexnekirina sosyalîzma reel, redkirina dîktatoriya proletaryayê, radîkalîzekirina demokrasiyê û parastina mafê çarenivîsê bi salan e di nav kurdan de bi awayekî tên nîqaşkirin. Lê di vî warî de metn û bernameyên ku ev mijar bi şêweyekî metodolojîk teorîze kirine, pir zêde li ber destê me tunene. Ev metna 

Kurtebehsek li ser Sosyalîzmê

 ya ku ji aliyê Ebdurrehman Qasimlo ve hatiye nivisîn, dikare cihekî mezin ê vê valahiyê dagire di vê qadê de.

 

Ev berhem li gor serdema xwe ya salên 80yan, bi taybetî jî di nav kurdan de metn û fikreke nû ye ku di wan salan de hîn bayê sosyalîzma reel û ortodoks xurt bû, rexnekirina vî şêweyê sosyalîzmê û li şûna wê pêşniyazkirina sosyalîzmeke demokratîk ji aliyê fikrî û îdeolojîk ve helwesteke wêrekî bû. Di vê çarçoveyê de determînîzma îqtisadî, çînparêzî û dîktatoriya proletaryayê tê redkirin û armanceke wisa tê girtin ku çareseriya pirsgirêkên neteweyî û mafê çarenivîsa neteweyî ji bin nîrê nêrîn û hegemonyaya sosyalîst bê xelaskirin.

 

Di 

Kurtebehs

ê de herçiqas dest ji sosyalîzmê nehatibe kêşan jî, hewlek xwe dide der ku di navbera pirsgirêka neteweyî û civakî-aborî de hevsengiyekê deyne. Bidestxistina otonomiyê ji bo avakirina sosyalîzmê wekî pêşmerc tê dîtin û pirsgirêka neteweyî ji pirsgirêka îdeolojîk a sosyalîst pêşdetir tê qebûlkirin. 

Kurtebehsek li ser Sosyalîzmê

, bi pêşgotina berfireh û wergera Mustafa Zengin me vedixwîne danûstandineke fikrî.







Derbarê Ebdurrehman Qasimloyî de




Di 1930yê de li Ûrmiyeyê dayik bû. Di sala 1945ê de li Ûrmiyeyê bi tevlêbûna Yekîtiya Ciwanên Demokrat ên Kurdistana Îranê dest bi xebatên xwe yên siyasî kir.




Dibistana seretayî û navîn li Ûrmiyeyê, dibistana amadeyiyê jî li Tehranê xwend. Ji bo xwendina zanîngehê çû Parîsê û ji wir jî derbasî Praga paytexta Çekoslovakyayê bû. Gava li Pragê bû, bi çend hevalên xwe yên kurd re Komeleya Xwendekarên Kurd ya li Ewropayê dadimezirand.




Di sala 1962yê de li Dibistana Aborî ya Pragê di warê aborînasiyê de doktoraya xwe temam kir û heta sala 1970yê li heman dibistanê li ser teoriyên aboriyê û aborînasiya marksîst û li Zanîngeha Sorbonneê li ser xebatên kurdî ders dan. Di wê heyamê de pirtûka wî ya navdar a bi navê 

Kurd û Kurdistan

 (1965) çap bû. Piştî Peymana 11ê Adarê ya di navbera Başûrê Kurdistanê û rejîma Beesê de vegeriya Kurdistanê û beşdarî xebatên siyasî yên PDK-Îyê bû.




Sala 1973yê di Kongreya 3yem a PDK-Îyê de wekî endamê rêveberiyê û sekreterê giştî hat hilbijartin û ev peywira xwe heta dawiya jiyana xwe berdewam kir. Dr. Qasimlo, di 13ê Tîrmeha 1989an de li Viyanaya paytexta Awistiryayê bi du hevalên xwe re di dema hevdîtineke li gel şandeyeke Îranê de, ji aliyê wan ve hat kuştin.










Derbarê Mustafa Zenginî de




Sala 1986ê li navçeya Siwêregê ya bi ser Rihayê ve ji dayik bû. Piştî guhertina çend zanîngeh û beşan derbasî Zanîngeha Acıbademê bû, li wir beşa Teknîkeriya Radyoterapiyê xwend û piştre beşa sosyolojiyê ya ji-dûr-ve xwend.

Kürd Araştırmaları 

ava kir û di lijneya kovarê de cih girt.




Niha li Zanîngeha Mardîn Artukluyê li ser Xebatên Çandî master dike. Nivîsên wî bi tirkî û kurdî di malper û kovarên wekî

author: CNT Guadalajara
title: ¿Cambian algo realmente las elecciones?
content:
El próximo 29 de noviembre estamos llamados a acudir en masa a votar para elegir quien nos gobernará los próximos 4 años apuntalando este sistema corrupto, criminal, ecocida y sin sentido que es el capitalismo, disfrazado o no, bajo unas siglas u otras, ¿pero realmente necesitamos que nos gobiernen o podríamos organizarnos de manera colectiva y asamblearia como ya se ha hecho y se sigue haciendo hoy día en otras partes?




Nuestros problemas: la sanidad, la educación, la vivienda, las pésimas condiciones laborales, el cambio climático y la explotación de los recursos y seres vivos del planeta, así como una verdadera transición energética de carácter social y no empresarial (entre otras muchas cosas) no se resolverán simplemente cambiando a unos políticos por otros. Quienes ocupan las instituciones gestionan un sistema cuyas reglas económicas y sociales vienen determinadas por el capitalismo, las grandes empresas, los bancos y los lobbies que son quienes realmente imponen sus decisiones que a la postre se traducen en unas políticas u otras llevadas a la realidad en el teatrillo que escenifican los partidos, la patronal y los sindicatos mayoritarios (la santísima trinidad) a través de su paz social.




Nuestros problemas, los de la clase trabajadora, no son hechos aislados ni inevitables; tienen su origen en el sistema capitalista y en una democracia representativa que sitúa la propiedad privada, el beneficio económico y la rentabilidad en el centro de la vida social. De ese modelo se desprenden valores como el egoísmo, la competencia y el individualismo, mientras la búsqueda permanente del beneficio termina imponiéndose sobre las necesidades de la mayoría, abocándola a una vida de miseria. Es por esto que nosotros creemos que hay que actuar de manera radical (esto quiere decir ir a la raíz del problema) contra este sistema que sostiene estas injusticias y luchar de manera organizada para destruirlo y construir uno más justo, libre y equitativo donde todas las personas puedan participar en la toma de decisiones.




Ante la amenaza a lo que pueda venir —ante un fascismo que nunca desapareció de las instituciones—, algunos partidos apelan al llamado «voto útil». Pero el voto, no va a sacar a la clase trabajadora de su situación de precariedad, ni garantiza que nuestras demandas y reivindicaciones sean atendidas. No hay que votar sino organizarse, participar, y unir todas las luchas en una, bajo el paraguas del apoyo mutuo, la autogestión y la solidaridad para defender los intereses de la clase trabajadora -vivienda, sanidad, defensa de la tierra, educación y servicios públicos-.




El sistema electoral concentra la capacidad de decisión en manos de una minoría de representantes y gestores, mientras que quienes realmente gobiernan son: Multinacionales, fondos de inversión y bancos tomando las decisiones que afectan directamente a nuestras vidas.




Frente a los problemas sociales, las instituciones responden con parches legislativos (en el mejor de los casos) para mantener la paz social entre clases, mientras la clase trabajadora permanece alejada de las decisiones fundamentales sobre la organización de los medios de producción, los recursos naturales y culturales, la sanidad, la educación y los servicios esenciales; en definitiva, en cómo quiere gestionar su vida y todo aquello que nos rodea entre iguales.

Por eso, votar cada cuatro años, o cuando a ellos les venga en gana a uno u otro partido político no cambiará nada, a lo sumo pequeñas reformas que nos mantendrán en la ilusión de que hemos logrado alguna mejora sustancial gracias a nuestro voto; cuando la realidad es que cuando se han logrado cambios sustanciales que afecten de manera colectiva a la clase trabajadora ha sido a través de la lucha organizada mediante movilizaciones y huelgas.




Votar, aunque sea en blanco o nulo, solo legitima el sistema. Por eso, los políticos siempre piden una gran participación. Hay que dejar de sostener este sistema corrupto, depredador y criminal con el voto y acabar con la clase política para terminar con él, que es el culpable de todo lo que determina nuestras condiciones de vida; y por eso hacemos un llamamiento a la abstención activa, para que de manera consciente y responsable escojamos no contribuir a ello y nos organicemos para construir un mundo nuevo.




Dejemos de mantener a toda esa panda de vividores (políticos, banqueros, empresarios, militares, policías, liberados sindicales, clero, monarquía, etc.) que nos roban diariamente lo conseguido con el esfuerzo de nuestro trabajo y empecemos a colaborar para cambiar nuestro futuro y el de nuestra tierra de manera consensuada y no a través del voto.




¡No hay que elegir al títere que gestione la paz social entre clases, sino abolir el sistema capitalista para construir una sociedad realmente libre y sin clases basada en el asamblearismo y la autogestión, los valores de la solidaridad y el apoyo mutuo, y el rechazo al Estado y sus instituciones!

¿Cambian algo realmente las elecciones?

author: Freedom Editor
title: Silicon Valley’s blueprint for autocracy
content:
For years, tech oligarchs have been converting their corporate absolutism into political leverage

Examine the current global transition from liberal-democratic societies toward autocratic, state-capitalist models, and a clear pattern emerges. Alongside a renewed greed for scarce natural resources sits a concerted drive to secure control over emerging technologies. Among key figures in the tech industry—including Elon Musk, Alexander Karp, and Peter Thiel—a conviction has taken root that CEOs would make far more suitable ruling elites than elected officials. While they currently rely on autocratic political frameworks as a foundation, their ultimate ambition is to govern states just as they run corporations.

Nobody illustrates this convergence of monopoly power and political ambition better than Peter Thiel. Having played a pivotal role in steering J. D. Vance toward the American Vice Presidency, Thiel exerts profound influence on both sides of the Atlantic through his company, Palantir Technologies, and his private networks.

The intellectual blueprint for both Thiel and Vance comes from the “neo-reactionary” theorist Curtis Yarvin, who operates the platform Urbit with Thiel’s financial backing. Yarvin openly advocates for the abolition of democracy, dismissing it as inefficient, corrupt, and incapable of solving long-term problems. In its place, he envisions a modern monarchy led by CEO-sovereigns. To justify this centralised, unilateral authority, Yarvin frequently cites historical precedents: Julius Caesar and Augustus, Napoleon as a “start-up monarch,” Franklin D. Roosevelt overseeing the Manhattan Project, and Abraham Lincoln raising troops and censoring the press without congressional consent.

Thiel’s corporate philosophy mirrors this political theory. Born in Frankfurt in 1967 and raised in California and apartheid-era South Africa, Thiel studied philosophy and law at Stanford before co-founding PayPal with Elon Musk, launching Palantir in 2003, and establishing the venture firm Founders Fund. In his book Zero to One, co-authored with Blake Masters, Thiel argues that competition and capitalism are fundamentally incompatible. True success requires building a monopoly through radical technological innovation, allowing a company to dictate pricing and plan in decades. Like Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, Thiel insulates Palantir from shareholder accountability through super-voting shares, ensuring the founder remains a kind of monopolistic monarch even when institutional giants like BlackRock hold vast stock blocks.

After mentoring J. D. Vance at Yale Law School, hiring him at Mithril Capital, and funding his firm Narya Capital, Thiel invested $10 million into Vance’s successful 2022 Ohio Senate bid—alongside fellow “PayPal Mafia” alum David O. Sacks—and backed Blake Masters in Arizona. Although Democratic candidates ultimately won both Senate seats in the 2026 midterm elections, Thiel’s deepest influence lies within the executive branch.

Following Donald Trump’s election victory, Thiel’s network embedded itself directly into the federal apparatus. His former Palantir chief of staff, Michael Kratsios, became head of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. Longtime Palantir veterans Gregory Barbaccia and Clark Minor assumed top federal Chief Information Officer roles, while Michael Obadal moved from Anduril Industries—an AI defence contractor chaired by Thiel’s close associate Trae Stephens and backed by Founders Fund—to become Assistant Secretary of the Army.

This revolving door blurs the boundary between private tech monopolies and state security. Palantir’s software platforms, such as Gotham, aggregate massive datasets to guide decision-making across defence, intelligence, finance, and pharmaceuticals—often reinforcing pre-existing forms of discrimination embedded in historical data. Meanwhile, Anduril supplies the military with autonomous drones, underwater systems, and border surveillance via its AI-driven “Lattice” platform. As Palantir increasingly explores military applications—from voice-recognition monitoring and drone reconnaissance to AI partnerships with firms like Anthropic to assess operational probabilities—the tools of warfare and surveillance are consolidating under a handful of unaccountable executives.

Beyond public politics, Thiel operates a secretive economic policy circle founded in 2006 with entrepreneur Auren Hoffman. Exposed in June 2026 by the Swiss hacker “maia arson crimew,” this invitation-only “dialogue network” brings together elite figures from politics, business, and the military across European retreats. At its August 2026 gathering in Dublin, 222 members convened to discuss “dealing with a Third World War,” “technologies for the battlefield,” “establishing one’s own cults,” and “reactivating nuclear power.”

Dismissing these gatherings as mere “prepper” fantasies ignores the calibre of the attendees. Alongside Hoffman—whose companies SafeGraph and LiveRamp amass trillions of monthly consumer location and behavioural data points—the network includes U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Senator Ted Cruz, and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale, whose software is utilised by ICE and the US Department of Defense.

When the same closed circle of billionaires controls mass data surveillance, autonomous weaponry, venture capital, and key government appointments, the State is no longer even a nominal democracy, but an institution shaped completely for the benefit of a self-appointed elite.

author: CNT Bilbao
title: Desconvocada la huelga de los días 26 y 27 de noviembre en EAE
content:
Desde los sindicatos miembros de la mesa negociadora de espectáculos y eventos de la CAV nos alegra comunicar que queda desconvocada la huelga prevista para los días 26 y 27 de noviembre, tras la reunión mantenida hoy mismo con la patronal.







Desde los sindicatos miembros de la mesa negociadora de espectáculos y eventos de la CAV nos alegra comunicar que 

queda desconvocada la huelga prevista para los días 26 y 27 de noviembre

, tras la reunión mantenida hoy mismo con la patronal. Este es el resultado directo de la lucha de las trabajadoras y los trabajadores  que se han organizado, que se han plantado y han demostrado que con unión y organización se consiguen objetivos.




Más de año y medio ha costado que nos volvamos a reunir con la patronal de Euskadi. Fue en abril de 2025 cuando todos los sindicatos que formamos parte de la mesa decidimos levantarnos de la negociación con un objetivo claro: transmitir a la parte empresarial que las reuniones debían hacerse con propuestas concretas y que aunque entendemos que la flexibilidad es necesaria, el Convenio no se iba a convertir en un instrumento que legitimara las prácticas habituales.




Las negociaciones hasta esa fecha fueron muy largas y complejas. Al tratar el tema de los preavisos y calendarios nos dimos cuenta de que no tenía sentido seguir negociando en esos términos, su reafirmación de que con más de 5 días no podían organizar a sus plantillas fue el punto de inflexión.




Han hecho falta varias denuncias ante la Inspección de Trabajo y seis jornadas de huelga convocadas para que la patronal saliera por fin de su inmovilismo y se sentará a negociar con una actitud distinta.




Por fin, y eso celebramos, hemos recibido propuestas concretas y plazos y en esa reunión hemos conseguido avances en los puntos que más nos afectan y que detallamos a continuación:




Entrega del calendario: compromiso firme para recoger en el futuro convenio una entrega de calendarios cierto con:







  Días de libranzas y trabajo con 6 semanas de antelación




  Horarios con 2 semanas de antelación




 Fines de semana semestrales, saber cuales son nuestros fines de semana  libre del mes con seis meses de antelación.







Estas jornadas de huelga se convocaron con el objetivo de avanzar y desatascar, por eso entendemos que por responsabilidad nos tocaba valorar las propuestas y los posibles avances. Siempre hemos demostrado nuestra disposición a negociar y este es el ejemplo, cuando hemos visto una oportunidad la hemos aprovechado.  




Pero queremos aclarar que desconvocar no es desmovilizarse. Si los compromisos no se cumplen, si la patronal vuelve a intentar dilatar o incumplir lo acordado, volveremos a salir a las calles, y esta vez con más fuerza, y más razones que nunca.




Por otro lado, tenemos también propuestas inmediatas –que son ejemplo de las formas de trabajo del sector, que van a comenzar a aplicarse a partir del 1 de enero de 2027 y que no se cumplían hasta la fecha:







Se comunicará con un preaviso mínimo de 5 días los turnos y horarios.




Se comunicarán los días de libranza en fin de semana (sábado y domingo) trimestralmente (1 de enero, 1 de abril, 1 de julio y 1 de octubre)







Seguiremos peleando por unas condiciones laborales dignas en este sector de espectáculos y eventos, para que en cada bolo las plantillas estén protegidos y con sus derechos laborales más básicos cubiertos.




Aprovechamos para 

agradecer a toda la gente que ha secundado las huelgas y también a todas las bandas, salas, compañías y organizaciones

 en general que han mostrado su apoyo a nuestra convocatoria de huelga cancelando sus eventos.




Milesker!

 Pedimos disculpas por las molestias que haya podido ocasionar esta lucha.




Confiamos en que se entienda el porqué de nuestra movilización, se han convocado estas huelgas al no ver otra salida, ojalá no nos veamos obligadas a volver a convocarlas.




Este resultado demuestra que la unión y la fuerza de la clase trabajadora son el único camino para conseguir los derechos laborales básicos que tanto necesitamos.




¡BORROKAK DARRAI!

Desconvocada la huelga de los días 26 y 27 de noviembre en EAE

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: Unknown
title: Zilan Oktay: Impunity has serious social consequences
content:
In the first ten months of 2026, at least 247 women were killed by men in cities across Kurdistan and Turkey, while 286 women died under suspicious circumstances. Investigations and trials concerning femicides are ongoing, but perpetrators in four femicide cases heard during the year received reductions in their sentences for good conduct. There are no official figures on how many cases in previous years resulted in decisions not to prosecute or were closed without punishment. Despite requests from women's organisations and MPs, up-to-date data has not been made public.




Six women killed and four died suspiciously in Amed




Six women were killed by men in Amed (Diyarbakır) in 2026, while four others died under suspicious circumstances. Most recently, Rojda Odabaşı was shot by her downstairs neighbour, Mazlum Çelebi. Çelebi was arrested following the attack but released two months later.




Women in the city began a justice vigil in response to the rise in femicides and judicial decisions concerning perpetrators. Lawyer Zilan Oktay, a board member of the Women's Rights Centre of the Amed Bar Association, said that decisions reflecting a policy of impunity have consequences that extend beyond courtrooms and affect society as a whole.




Zilan Oktay stressed that such decisions should not be considered solely in relation to individual cases or perpetrators. She said: "These decisions have a profound impact on women's lives and on society."




1,500 applications received in ten months




Zilan Oktay said that the centre had received a total of 1,500 applications since January 2026, with psychological violence accounting for the largest proportion. She explained that while applications concerning physical violence had previously been more common, psychological violence had become increasingly visible in recent years. She attributed this change partly to awareness-raising activities.




Zilan Oktay discussed the distribution of applications and the different forms of violence reported to the centre. Oktay said: "In previous years, applications concerning physical violence were more common, but today we see that psychological violence has become more visible. We believe that the training programmes organised by our centre, local administrations and civil society organisations have contributed to this change.




Women are now better able to identify the forms of violence they experience. The low number of applications concerning sexual violence is related to the fact that this form of violence is not always recognised. Sexual coercion within marriage, in particular, can be normalised. We therefore believe that the number of applications does not fully reflect the actual situation."




'Policies are encouraging perpetrators'




Zilan Oktay said that the perception of impunity is a major problem in combating violence against women. She explained that ineffective investigations, shortcomings in the assessment of evidence, lengthy judicial proceedings and sentence reductions granted in certain cases reinforce this perception. She noted that women seeking justice are repeatedly forced to recount and prove what they have experienced, undermining their confidence in the judiciary.




Oktay emphasised that impunity is not merely a problem confined to judicial proceedings but also influences how perpetrators commit acts of violence. She said that perpetrators calculate the sentences they might receive and the legal reductions they could benefit from before committing their crimes.




Zilan Oktay explained how the perception of impunity develops and how it affects perpetrators. She said: "Even before committing an act, the perpetrator investigates how to receive a lighter sentence and which legal avenues might reduce the punishment. This is because judicial practice sends perpetrators the message that such opportunities exist. Acting with this confidence, perpetrators carry out more planned, coordinated and extensive acts of violence. They make calculations such as, 'I will receive this much punishment, serve some time and then be released, or benefit from supervised release.' In this way, they can anticipate the consequences of their actions and believe that they may somehow escape punishment.




In fact, the state's pursuit of policies that pave the way for perpetrators and encourage them means that they do not fear the consequences of their actions and can commit violence with considerable ease. Even after the act, there is often no fundamental change in the perpetrator's life, and they can simply continue living as before."




'Judicial decisions do not remain within courtrooms'




Zilan Oktay also drew attention to the social consequences of impunity, stressing that a decision in one case does not affect only that particular trial but also the lives and safety of other women. She said that impunity can become an encouraging example for other perpetrators.




Oktay said: "Impunity in one case can become an encouraging example for other perpetrators and pave the way for further acts of violence. Consequently, we cannot assess the impact of decisions resulting in impunity solely in relation to the relevant case or perpetrator. These decisions have social consequences that affect the lives and safety of all women.




Just as we cannot regard violence as an isolated incident, we must not approach policies of impunity solely through individual cases. Every instance of impunity has consequences that can also determine the course of other women's lives."




'Law No. 6284 must be implemented'




Zilan Oktay said that women also encounter problems with the operation of legal mechanisms intended to protect them. She pointed to shortcomings in the implementation and monitoring of protective and preventive orders issued under Law No. 6284.




Oktay stressed that delays in intervention when protective orders are violated, inadequate coordination between institutions and the failure to take the risk of violence sufficiently seriously endanger women's lives. She said that issuing protection orders alone is not enough to guarantee women's safety and emphasised the vital importance of enforcing these orders and responding rapidly to violations.




'Women cannot speak out about violence because of pressure'




Zilan Oktay identified three main obstacles preventing women from reporting violence: social pressure, economic dependence and institutional problems. Oktay said: "Pressure from family members and the wider community, fear of stigmatisation and concerns about children can make it difficult for women to disclose the violence they experience. The lack of economic independence is also a major obstacle preventing women from leaving violent environments. From an institutional perspective, applications not being taken sufficiently seriously, bureaucratic obstacles and approaches that cause secondary victimisation make it more difficult for women to access justice. We must not forget that women's silence does not mean that violence is absent."




Zilan Oktay emphasised that combating violence against women must not be limited to judicial proceedings and that social support policies must be strengthened alongside legal protection mechanisms. She stressed the importance of regular training for judges, prosecutors and law enforcement personnel on gender equality and violence against women. She also called for effective investigations, monitoring of the implementation of protection orders and the completion of judicial proceedings within a reasonable time.




Zilan Oktay said that the capacity of women's shelters must be increased, free legal and psychological support must be provided, and conditions must be created to enable women to achieve economic independence. She also issued an appeal to judicial institutions and decision-makers ahead of 25 November.




Oktay stressed that combating violence against women must go beyond statements of intent and be supported by concrete policies. She said that protecting women's right to life is a fundamental obligation of the state.




'Effective policies against violence must be implemented'




Zilan Oktay delivered a message to judicial institutions and decision-makers on the occasion of 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. Oktay said: "Our message to judicial institutions and decision-makers on 25 November is that the struggle against violence against women must not remain merely rhetorical but must be supported by concrete policies. Protecting women's right to life is a fundamental obligation of the state. To achieve this, effective investigations must be conducted, practices that lead to impunity must be prevented, and women's acquired rights must be protected. The experience of women's organisations and bar associations in this struggle must also be utilised, and their active participation in decision-making processes must be ensured. Women's right to live free and equal lives without violence is not a privilege but a fundamental human right."




Zilan Oktay reiterated that guaranteeing women's right to life is their foremost demand. She called for the effective implementation of Law No. 6284 and the elimination of the perception of impunity, outlining their demands as follows: "Our foremost demand is that women's right to life be guaranteed and that violence be combated through effective policies. We demand the effective implementation of Law No. 6284, penalties proportionate to the crimes committed by perpetrators of violence, and the elimination of the perception of impunity.




In addition, conditions must be created to enable women to achieve economic independence, the number of shelters must be increased, and access to free legal and psychological support must be guaranteed. Women's ability to live safely is not merely an aspiration but a legal and social responsibility that the state must fulfil."

author: Unknown
title: Vigil outside the Ministry of Justice for ill prisoners enters its seventh day
content:
The sit-in, organised by the Federation of Associations for Legal Solidarity with Prisoners and Convicts’ Families (TUHAD-FED), the DEM Party and the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), continued outside the Ministry of Justice for a sixth day, calling for the right of ill prisoners to receive medical treatment and be released.




Families of ill prisoners, representatives of political parties and civil society organisations took part in the protest, calling for the release of sick prisoners.




Kamuran Tanhan, a DEM Party MP for Mêrdîn (Mardin), stated that the lives of prisoners who are not receiving medical treatment in prison are at risk, and called on the Ministry of Justice to fulfil its responsibilities.




Recalling that some prisoners had died shortly after their release because they had not received treatment while in prison, Tanhan said: “If you want peace, then prisons must be emptied as soon as possible.”




Zehra Camcı, a member of the Socialist Party of the Oppressed (ESP), meanwhile, drew attention to the fact that some political prisoners were still being held despite having completed their sentences.




Stating that ill prisoners whose health conditions make it impossible for them to remain in prison are unable to access adequate medical care, Camcı said that solidarity and collective struggle must be strengthened.




The protest reiterated the demand that ill prisoners be granted their rights to medical treatment and release.

author: Unknown
title: Narges Mohammadi calls for the protection of women against cyber threats
content:
Women in Iran face legal and societal threats. While women's rights organisations continue to call for the strengthening and enforcement of existing laws and institutions that safeguard women's dignity and security, Nobel Peace Prize-winning activist Narges Mohammadi has released a video message.




In her message, shared on a digital platform, Narges Mohammadi called for solidarity with and support for women who are subjected to organised cyber threats and interference because of their activities in social, political, media and human rights fields.




Narges Mohammadi said that, in recent years, she herself has faced harassment, insults, death threats and widespread gender-based cyber violence, adding that these attacks continued even while she was imprisoned.




Addressing the methods of cyber harassment targeting women, Narges Mohammadi explained that these attacks include organised smear campaigns, the exposure of personal information, insults, misogyny, the spread of misinformation and the circulation of fabricated images generated using artificial intelligence (AI). She emphasised that the aim of these attacks is to isolate, intimidate and silence women.




Drawing attention to statistics, Narges Mohammadi said that more than 70 percent of women journalists, activists and those in leadership positions experience cyber harassment. She warned that such attacks must not silence women or force them to withdraw from public life.




At the end of her statement, Narges Mohammadi reiterated the need for solidarity and collective support to protect women facing smear campaigns and cyber threats.

title: İzmir'de şifa vaadiyle dolandırıcılık ve cinsel saldırı iddiası: 4 kişi yakalandı
content:
Temsili | Fotoğraf: Kindel Media/Pexels

İzmir’de, kendisini “Mehdi” olarak tanıtan bir kişi, iddiaya göre bir aileyi 3 milyon TL değerinde dolandırdı. Ayrıca ailedeki kadına cinsel saldırıda bulundu.

İzmir Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığından yapılan açıklamaya göre, bir televizyon kanalında yayımlanan haberdeki iddialar üzerine soruşturma başlatıldı. Haberde, kendisini "Mehdi" olarak tanıtan bir kişinin şifa vaadiyle bir aileyi yaklaşık 3 milyon lira dolandırdığı, ailedeki kadına yönelik cinsel saldırıda bulunduğu ve 3,5 yaşındaki çocuğa fiziksel müdahalede bulunduğu öne sürüldü.

İl Emniyet Müdürlüğü Mali Suçlarla Mücadele ve İstihbarat şube müdürlüklerinin çalışması sonucu habere konu kişinin Mehdi D. olduğu belirlendi.

Polis ekipleri, şüpheli Mehdi D'yi Şanlıurfa'nın Ceylanpınar ilçesinde yakaladı.

Olayla bağlantılı oldukları değerlendirilen şüphelinin babası A.D, annesi M.D. ve kız kardeşi M.D. gözaltına alındı.

Adreste yapılan aramalarda ele geçirilen dijital materyallere el konuldu.

Gözaltındaki şüphelilerin işlemleri sürüyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: CNT Madrid
title: La nueva subcontrata del Circo Price también incumple
content:
La sección sindical de CNT de la acomodación del 

Teatro Circo Price

 sigue luchando por lo que 

ya quedó reflejado en una resolución de Inspección de Trabajo

: sus puestos son estructurales y deben ser contrataciones directas de la empresa pública de cultura y turismo del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, Madrid Destino SA. La nueva empresa subcontratada, Unium Servicios Auxiliares, paga 

por debajo de lo establecido en los pliegos de contratación y del convenio colectivo

 de espacios escénicos e incumple los marcos de contratación con falsos contratos por obra y servicio.




CNT logró este verano una resolución favorable de Inspección de Trabajo que demostraba la cesión ilegal de las trabajadoras de la subcontrata anterior, 

Centralia Global SL

, a Madrid Destino SA. La empresa pública reaccionó resolviendo el contrato y cubriendo la programación en el Circo Price con personal propio, razón por la que la sección sindical organizó varios piquetes tanto en Conde Duque (el espacio en el que están las oficinas de la empresa municipal) como en el mismo teatro.




Fruto de esa resolución, CNT interpuso una denuncia en los juzgados (pendiente de fecha) tanto a la empresa pública como a la anterior subcontrata, acusándolas de esa cesión ilegal ya contrastada así como de despido nulo. Indistintamente, las compañeras de acomodación del Circo Price vuelven a trabajar en el teatro porque forman parte de la lista de subrogados (gracias también al trabajo sindical de CNT) y están ahora dadas de alta por 

Unium Servicios Auxiliares SL

, otra de esas empresas cuyo modelo consiste en obtener contratos de la Administración.




Con esa cuestión todavía judicializada y por resolver, las trabajadoras de Acomodación del Circo Price organizadas en CNT tenemos que volver a alzar la voz para denunciar que 

la plantilla está cobrando por debajo de lo que dicta el convenio de espacios escénicos

 de la Comunidad de Madrid y de lo que indica 

el propio pliego de Madrid Destino SA.

 Tampoco se están aplicando otros aspectos del pliego, como categorías profesionales designadas arbitrariamente o la aplicación efectiva de la subrogación.




Por esta misma razón la sección de CNT en la acomodación del Teatro Circo Price ha dado una semana de plazo a Unium Servicios Auxiliares SL para que den respuesta e ingresen lo adeudado a toda la plantilla afectada. Así mismo, la sección de CNT en el Circo Price vuelve a reiterar la oferta de reunirse con esta parte social para buscar soluciones a un modelo, el de la subcontratación, que ha quedado claro que no funciona: estos puestos son estructurales y exigen gestión directa a través de la empresa pública Madrid Destino. 

No pararemos hasta conseguirlo.







La entrada 

La nueva subcontrata del Circo Price también incumple

 se publicó primero en 

Sindicato CNT de Madrid

.




La entrada 

La nueva subcontrata del Circo Price también incumple

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: Unknown
title: Kolombiya hükümeti, eski Cumhurbaşkanı Petro'nun X hesabının askıya alınmasını istedi
content:
Kolombiya'da Bilgi ve İletişim Teknolojileri Bakanlığı, ABD merkezli X şirketinden, paylaşımında sokaklarda eylem çağrısı yapan eski Cumhurbaşkanı Gustavo Petro'nun sosyal medya platformundaki hesabının askıya alınmasını talep etti.

Bakanlıktan, Petro'nun 21 Kasım'da Kolombiya halkına seslenerek, "Halkı, (Cumhurbaşkanı) Abelardo'nun derhal istifasını talep etmeye çağırıyorum." ifadelerini kullandığı paylaşımına ilişkin açıklama yapıldı.

Açıklamada, bu ifadelerin Cumhurbaşkanı Abelardo de la Espriella'nın haziranda demokratik yollarla seçildiği gerçeğini göz ardı ettiği öne sürüldü.

Söz konusu paylaşım nedeniyle X'e başvuruda bulunulduğu aktarılan açıklamada, şirketten Petro'nun hesabının askıya alınmasının istendiği ifade edildi.

Açıklamada, platformun "Kolombiya devletinin kurumlarını tehdit eden ve hedef alan demokrasi karşıtı ve istikrarsızlaştırıcı bir gündemin yayılmasında başlıca araç haline gelemeyeceği" savunuldu.

Şirketin şiddeti teşvik eden içeriklere ilişkin açık politikaları bulunduğun öne süren açıklamada, Petro'nun paylaşımının toplumsal baskıyı artırmayı hedeflediği ve insanları "derhal sokaklarda harekete geçmeye" teşvik ettiği iddia edildi.

Petro ise yaptığı açıklamada, hükümetin hesabının askıya alınması yönündeki talebini kamuoyuyla iletişimini sansürleme girişimi olarak nitelendirdi.

Eski Cumhurbaşkanı Petro'nun 21 Kasım'daki paylaşımında, yaptığı bir konuşmadan kesitlerin yer aldığı 1 dakika 48 saniyelik video da bulunuyor. Petro videoda halka "hemen sokaklarda harekete geçme" çağrısı yaparak milyonlarca kişinin seferber olması halinde "gerçek demokrasiyi" yeniden tesis etme sorumluluğunun halka düşeceğini söylemişti.
