Landrat Martin Bayerstorfer hielt trotz ständiger Kritik an der Karte fest. Sie fand erst 2020 ein unfreiwilliges Ende: Der Finanzdienstleister Wirecard ging in einem spektakulären Betrugsfall insolvent. (…) Zunächst wollte man eine Nachfolge für Wirecard suchen, doch daraus wurde nichts. Stattdessen begann der Landkreis im Mai 2021 mit einer Methode, die sowohl die Verwaltung entlastete als auch Geflüchteten einen selbstbestimmten Umgang mit dem knappen Geld ermöglichte: Erding überwies das Geld standardmäßig auf die Konten der Asylsuchenden. Es gibt nur eine Menschenwürde! 200 Verbände für sozialrechtliche Gleichbehandlung Geflüchteter  




„… Vor 30 Jahren – am 26. Mai 1993 – hat der damalige Bundestag im sogenannten »Asylkompromiss« beschlossen, das in der Verfassung garantierte Grundrecht auf Asyl stark zu beschneiden, um Flüchtlinge möglichst fernzuhalten. Gleichzeitig wurde mit dem »Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz« (AsylbLG) ein neues Gesetz geschaffen, das die Lebensverhältnisse von Asylsuchenden in Deutschland gezielt verschlechtern und die soziale Versorgung auf ein Niveau deutlich unterhalb der normalen Sozialleistungen absenken sollte. Das AsylbLG trat am 1. November 1993 in Kraft. Im 30. Jahr seines Bestehens fordert nun ein breites zivilgesellschaftliches Bündnis die Abschaffung des Asylbewerberleistungsgesetzes. Motiviert war das AsylbLG durch einen zentralen Gedanken: den der Abschreckung. Ziel war es, geflüchtete Menschen durch eine möglichst schäbige Behandlung und verordnete Geldnot, verbunden mit dem verpflichtenden Wohnen in Sammelunterkünften und einem Arbeitsverbot, von der Flucht nach Deutschland abzuhalten  oder zur Ausreise zu bewegen. Damit kam man den aggressiven und menschenfeindlichen Stimmen in Politik und Gesellschaft Anfang der 1990er Jahre weit entgegen. Im gerade erst »wiedervereinigten« Deutschland dienten deutlich gestiegene Asylantragszahlen als Anlass für eine explosive flüchtlingsfeindliche Stimmungsmache von Politik und Medien. Der Mob der Straße gab seinerseits das Echo mit rassistischen Attacken auf Unterkünfte und Mordanschlägen auf Migrant*innen, von denen die brutalen Exzesse von Rostock-Lichtenhagen und Hoyerswerda oder die Morde von Mölln oder Solingen nur einige der bekanntesten sind. (…) Die Beschlüsse, die die Ministerpräsident*innen und der Bund beim Flüchtlingsgipfel am 10. Mai 2023 gefasst haben, brechen mit dem menschlichen Anstand wie auch mit dem Völkerrecht: An den (EU‑) Grenzen sollen Asylsuchende künftig inhaftiert und in Drittstaaten zurückgewiesen werden, und auch im Innern sollen staatliche Gewaltmaßnahmen den Ausreisedruck erhöhen. Bestärkt durch den politischen Alarmismus auch aus den Reihen der roten, grünen oder gelben Koalitionsparteien droht 30 Jahre nach dem Asylkompromiss die Solidarität in der breiten Gesellschaft bedrohlich zu wackeln. Erneut werden Sammellager für Geflüchtete niedergebrannt, erneut fürchten Menschen in rassistischen Angriffen um ihr Leben. Die Bundesregierung muss in dieser Situation eine klare Haltung zu Diskriminierung und Rassismus entwickeln, alte Fehler korrigieren und nicht – auch nicht symbolisch – dem Mob hinterherlaufen. (…) Eine weitere Entgleisung droht auch sozialpolitisch. Klar ist: Die Leistungen des AsylbLG unterschreiten bereits das gesetzlich festgelegte Existenzminimum für ein menschenwürdiges Leben. Eine zweite, abgesenkte Menschenwürde kann es nicht geben. Statt dies endlich zu korrigieren, lassen die aktuellen Vorstellungen der Ministerpräsident*innen befürchten, dass künftig sogar erneut ein größerer Teil der Geflüchteten – vielleicht gar bereits anerkannte Geflüchtete – gekürzte Leistungen erhalten soll (…) Eine Änderung im Sozialgesetzbuch (SGB) statt im AsylbLG würde eine Angleichung nach unten für diejenigen bedeuten, die gerade nicht mehr die gekürzten Leistungen nach AsylbLG erhalten. Mit einer Herabsetzung der menschenrechtlich gebotenen Leistungen etwa für anerkannte Geflüchtete würde der heute schon verfassungswidrigen Praxis die Krone aufgesetzt. Es verstieße auch gegen Artikel 23 der Genfer Flüchtlingskonvention: Danach gewähren die Staaten den Flüchtlingen, die sich rechtmäßig in ihrem Staatsgebiet aufhalten, auf dem Gebiet der öffentlichen Fürsorge und sonstigen Hilfeleistungen die gleiche Behandlung wie ihren eigenen Staatsangehörigen. Kaum zu glauben, dass eine solche Regelung in Deutschland verfassungsrechtlich Bestand hätte, aber der Weg zu einer Korrektur dauert Jahre – ein Schelm, wer Kalkül unterstellt. (…) Zum unrühmlichen 30-jährigen Bestehen des AsylbLG hat sich 2023 ein breites Bündnis zivilgesellschaftlicher Organisationen unter dem Motto »Es gibt nur eine Menschenwürde – Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz abschaffen« zusammengefunden: Menschenrechtsorganisationen, Wohlfahrtsverbände, Organisationen von Migrant*innen, Vereinigungen von Anwält*innen, Jurist*innen, Ärzt*innen, Psychotherapeut*innen, Frauenverbände und Kinderrechtsorganisationen und andere fordern gleiche menschenrechtliche Standards: Geflüchtete müssen in das reguläre Sozialleistungssystem eingegliedert werden. Inzwischen haben 200 Organisationen die Forderung unterzeichnet: 45 bundesweite, 46 landesweite und 110 regionale und lokale Initiativen…“

Es gibt nur eine Menschenwürde – Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz abschaffen! Gemeinsames Statement von 62 Organisationen 




„Viele Geflüchtete erhalten zum Leben lediglich Leistungen nach dem Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz – und damit weniger als das neue Bürgergeld, das laut Gesetz das menschenwürdige Existenzminimum sicherstellen soll. Aber die Menschenwürde kennt nicht zweierlei Maß. Menschenrechtsorganisationen, Wohlfahrtsverbände und Anwält*innenverbände fordern gleiche Standards für alle: Das Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz muss abgeschafft werden. Die Betroffenen müssen in das reguläre Sozialleistungssystem eingegliedert werden. (…)  Es kann nicht zweierlei Maß für die Menschenwürde geben. Wir fordern das gleiche Recht auf Sozialleistungen für alle in Deutschland lebenden Menschen, ohne diskriminierende Unterschiede. Das Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz muss abgeschafft werden. Die Betroffenen müssen in das reguläre Sozialleistungssystem einbezogen werden. Dies erfordert insbesondere folgende Änderungen: 1. Abschaffung des Asylbewerberleistungsgesetzes und Einbeziehung Geflüchteter ins Bürgergeld bzw. die Sozialhilfe (SGB II/XII). Auf migrationspolitisch motivierte Kürzungen und Sanktionen ist gemäß dem Urteil des BVerfG aus 2012 ausnahmslos zu verzichten. 2. Einbeziehung aller Geflüchteten in die Sprach‑, Qualifizierungs- und Arbeitsförderungsinstrumente des SGB II. 3. Einbeziehung geflüchteter Menschen in die gesetzliche Kranken- und Pflegeversicherung (SGB V/XI). Dabei muss sichergestellt sein, dass auch Menschen ohne Papiere jederzeit ohne Angst vor Abschiebung Zugang zum Gesundheitssystem haben. Insbesondere muss ein Anspruch auf Sprachmittlung bei Inanspruchnahme von Leistungen im Gesundheitswesen verankert werden. 4. Von Krankheit, Traumatisierung, Behinderung, Pflegebedürftigkeit Betroffene sowie schwangere, alleinerziehende und ältere Menschen und geflüchtete Kinder müssen – entsprechend ihrem Recht aus der EU-Aufnahmerichtlinie – einen Anspruch auf alle aufgrund ihrer besonderen Situation erforderlichen zusätzlichen Leistungen erhalten (insbesondere nach SGB IX, SGB VIII u.a.). 5. Leistungen zur Sicherung des Lebensunterhaltes sind als Geldleistungen auszugestalten…“

Das Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz und das Existenzminimum. Eine Analyse der Regelsätze 




„Eine umfassende Analyse von PRO ASYL und dem Flüchtlingsrat Berlin zeigt im Detail die Defizite bei der Berechnung und Begründung der Regelsätze nach dem AsylbLG und anderer Sozialleistungen sowie die Leistungskürzungen durch das AsylbLG in der Praxis. Klar wird: Das Sondergesetz für Asylsuchende ist diskriminierend und gehört abgeschafft. (…) Die diskriminierenden Ausschlüsse für Asylsuchende und Geduldete aus Hartz IV werden unverändert in das Bürgergeldgesetz übernommen (§ 7 Abs. 1 SGB II) – sie werden weiterhin auf das sogenannte Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz (AsylbLG) verwiesen. Damit vertut die Bundesregierung die große Chance, alle Geflüchteten endlich in das normale Sozialsystem zu integrieren. Anlässlich der Verabschiedung des Bürgergeldgesetzes legt PRO ASYL gemeinsam mit dem Flüchtlingsrat Berlin eine umfassende Analyse vor: »Das Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz – Einschränkungen des Grundrechts auf ein menschenwürdiges Existenzminimum für Geflüchtete. Bedarfsdeckung und Regelsätze nach Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz, Hartz IV und Bürgergeldgesetz.« (…) Das AsylbLG sieht Sachleistungen für Essen, Kleidung und Unterkunft, eine menschenrechtswidrige Minimalmedizin, gekürzte Geldleistungen für Erwachsene und Kinder, eine nochmalige 10%ige Kürzung für Alleinstehende und Alleinerziehende in Sammelunterkünften sowie Sanktionen mit Kürzungen der Regelleistungen um weit mehr als die Hälfte vor. Damit wurde mit dem AsylbLG ein Leistungsniveau deutlich unterhalb der normalen Sozialleistungen geschaffen. Die sollen aber laut Gesetz den Leistungsberechtigten ermöglichen, ein Leben zu führen, »dass der Würde des Menschen entspricht« – so steht es unter anderem in § 1 Abs.1 SGB II. Das Bundesverfassungsgericht hat 2012 ausdrücklich festgestellt, dass das Grundrecht auf Gewährleistung eines menschenwürdigen Existenzminimums für alle in Deutschland lebenden Menschen gleichermaßen gilt, und dass dieses Grundrecht nicht aus migrationspolitischen Gründen relativiert werden darf. Derzeit – Ende 2022 – steht das AsylbLG erneut beim Bundesverfassungsgericht in Karlsruhe auf dem Prüfstand (Aktenzeichen 1 BvL 3/21 und 1 BvL 5/21). In diversen juristischen Stellungnahmen haben angefragte Organisationen ihre Zweifel an der Verfassungsmäßigkeit des AsylbLG ausgeführt. Auch die vorliegende Analyse von PRO ASYL und Berliner Flüchtlingsrat ist in ihrer ursprünglichen Fassung als Stellungnahme für das Bundesverfassungsgericht geschrieben worden. (…) PRO ASYL und Flüchtlingsräte fordern die Abschaffung des diskriminierenden Sondergesetzes und die Einbeziehung aller Geflüchteten in das Bürgergeldgesetz.“

Konzertierte Aktion von Seehofer und Heil: Flüchtlinge sollen ausgehungert werden 




„

Ein 

Gesetzentwurf aus dem BMI

 

 

 sieht erhebliche Verschärfungen im AsylbLG vor. Insbesondere sollen maßlose und radikale Leistungskürzungen bis auf null eingeführt und schon vorhandene Kürzungen ausgeweitet werden. Mit dem Gesetz würde dann in erster Linie der Zweck eines „Aushungerns“ nicht erwünschter ausländischer Personen erfüllt werden. Daneben soll die Vorbezugszeit für Analogleistungen nach § 2 AsylbLG auf 18 Monate hochgesetzt werden. Ein weiterer Gesetzentwurf aus dem BMAS sieht zusätzliche Leistungskürzungen für sehr viele Leistungsberechtigte vor, wenn sie die „normalen“ Grund- oder Analogleistungen erhalten. BMAS und BMI planen somit, in einer konzertierten Aktion das Menschenrecht auf ein verfassungsmäßig garantiertes menschenwürdiges Existenzminimum für Flüchtlinge zu schleifen. Beide Gesetzentwürfe sollen schon am kommenden Mittwoch vom Bundeskabinett verabschiedet werden. Um zu wissen, welche gravierenden Änderungen geplant sind, haben die GGUA Kollegen die Änderungsvorschläge in den bestehenden Fließtext des AsylbLG eingebaut und farblich markiert. Wie ihr seht, wird von dem bestehenden – jetzt schon miserablen! – Gesetz nicht mehr viel übrig bleiben.Nur, um es noch einmal zu wiederholen: Das Bundesverfassungsgericht hatte 2012 in einem Urteil zum damaligen AsylbLG festgeschrieben: „Die Menschenwürde ist migrationspolitisch nicht zu relativieren.“ In der Bundesregierung scheint dies weder Union noch SPD auch nur einen Hauch zu interessieren

.“ Aus dem 

Thomé Newsletter 15/2019 vom 14.04.2019 










Gesetzgebungswut ohne Ende – keine Zeit für verfassungsrechtliche Maßstäbe?


„

Die gestern bekannt gewordenen Gesetzesänderungen zielen auf Entrechtung, mehr Haft, soziale Isolierung und Verdrängen aus Deutschland durch Entzug von Sozialleistungen. Menschen, die bereits in einem anderen EU-Staat einen Schutzstatus haben, sollen für maximal zwei Wochen eine »Überbrückungsleistung« erhalten. Leistungen sollen für Schutzsuchende nach dem Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz unter bestimmten Bedingungen auf null gesetzt werden. Der Gesetzentwurf aus dem Bundesinnenministerium sieht vor, dass Personen, die bereits in einem anderen Mitgliedstaat anerkannt wurden und ausreisepflichtig sind, keine Leistungen nach dem Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz (AsylbLG) mehr erhalten. Maximal für zwei Wochen soll es für Hilfebedürftige eine »Überbrückungsleistung« geben – aber nur einmal innerhalb von zwei Jahren. In dem Wissen also, dass diese Menschen durchaus länger als zwei Wochen hier bleiben, will das  Bundesinnenministerium Leistungen verwehren. Die Gefahr von anerkannten Flüchtlingen, die aufgrund der menschenunwürdigen Zustände in Griechenland, Italien oder Bulgarien hier leben und dann auf der Straße landen, ist groß. Eine eingefügte Härtefallregelung wird dem wohl kaum grundsätzlich entgegenwirken. Auch Personen, deren Asylantrag nach der Dublin-Verordnung in einem anderen Mitgliedstaat zu prüfen wäre, sollen nur noch eingeschränkte Leistungen erhalten. Zudem soll das schon dann gelten, wenn die Dublin-Entscheidung noch gar nicht unanfechtbar ist. Das heißt: Selbst wenn die Entscheidung von einem Gericht geprüft wird, gibt es in diesem Zeitraum keinen Anspruch auf volle Leistung. (…) Ein solch weitreichendes Gesetz, welches weitere Verschärfungen wie im Bereich der Rechtsstellung Geduldeter und dem verfassungsrechtlich höchst sensiblen Bereich der Abschiebungshaft vorsieht, nun noch vor der Osterpause durchzupeitschen, ist höchst verantwortungslos. Nicht einmal zweieinhalb Arbeitstage haben die Expertinnen und Experten im Rahmen der Verbändebeteiligung Zeit, den Entwurf zu analysieren und zu bewerten. Keine zwei Tage später wiederum soll – eigentlich unter Berücksichtigung der eingereichten Bewertungen und Stellungnahmen – der Kabinettsbeschluss erfolgen. Schon auf den ersten Blick fällt auf: Die Verbändebeteiligung verkümmert damit zur reinen Farce. PRO ASYL fordert die Bundesregierung auf, die vom BMI geplante Vertreibungsstrategie nicht wie geplant am kommenden Mittwoch im Bundeskabinett zu verabschieden

…“

Entwurf des Dritten Gesetzes zur Änderung des Asylbewerberleistungsgesetzes – und Stellungnahme  




„… Zum AsylbLG 3.ÄndG: Das Leistungsniveau soll an die Preisentwicklung angepasst, die zum 1.1.2017, 1.1.2018 und 1.1.2019 ausgebliebene Anpassung der Leistungssätze nachgeholt werden. Die Erhöhung soll „kostenneutral“ erfolgen, indem die Leistungssätze nach §§ 2 und 3 AsylbLG für Alleinstehende in Sammelunterkünften um 10 % gekürzt werden. Begründet wird dies mit der Fiktion, dass Alleinstehende in Sammelunterkünften als „Schicksalsgemeinschaft“ die „Obliegenheit“ hätten, wie Ehepartner gemeinsam aus einem Topf zu wirtschaften…“

Weniger Geld ab 2020: Sozialministerium will Leistungen für Asylbewerber kürzen


„

Die große Koalition nimmt einen neuen Anlauf für eine Reform der Asylbewerberleistungen. Unter dem Strich ihrer Pläne steht eine Senkung der aktuellen Bezüge. Grüne und Linke sind empört. (…) Wie am Mittwoch aus dem Ressort von Bundesarbeitsminister Hubertus Heil (SPD) verlautete, sollen die monatlichen Zuwendungen für alleinstehende Asylbewerber künftig 344 Euro betragen, zehn Euro weniger als aktuell. Für Kinder im Schulalter sollen die Leistungen im Zuge der geplanten Reform des Asylbewerberleistungsgesetzes dagegen steigen. Zudem soll ein Ehrenamts-Freibetrag eingeführt werden. (…) Die Reform sieht vor, dass die Leistungen für den „notwendigen Bedarf“ an Lebensmitteln und Kleidung sinken und die für den „notwendigen persönlichen Bedarf“ etwa an Hygieneartikeln etwas steigen. In der Summe bleibt für meisten Gruppen eine Kürzung: Paare oder in Sammelunterkünften untergebrachte Asylbewerber sollen künftig pro Person 310 Euro bekommen. Derzeit sind es 318 Euro. Begründet werden die Kürzungen damit, dass in Sammelunterkünften für die Asylbewerber geringere Kosten beim „notwendigen Bedarf“ anfallen. Für jüngere Kinder und Jugendliche ab 13 Jahren bleibt der Leistungssatz den Plänen zufolge auf dem aktuellen Niveau. Für Kinder zwischen sechs und 13 Jahren sollen die monatlichen Leistungen von aktuell 242 auf 268 Euro steigen. (…)Die Leistungen liegen unter dem Niveau der Grundsicherung in Deutschland und werden für Asylbewerber für die ersten 15 Monate in Deutschland gezahlt. Letztmalig wurden die Sätze 2015 angehoben, nachdem das Bundesverfassungsgericht geurteilt hatte, dass alle in Deutschland lebenden Menschen ein menschenwürdiges Existenzminimum bekommen müssen. 2016 wollte die Bundesregierung die Leistungen schon einmal kürzen. Das vom Bundestag beschlossene Gesetz, das eine Senkung auf 332 Euro für erwachsene Alleinstehende vorsah, scheiterte aber im Bundesrat. Die jetzt geplante Reform ist damit der zweite Versuch für eine Änderung des Asylbewerberleistungsgesetzes

…“

Auch wenn die Marionetten des Kapitalismus ihre Kriegslust und Unterdrückung im Moment auf die Spitze treiben, um unseren ewigen Mut zu brechen, machen wir das, was wir schon immer gemacht haben und immer machen werden:




Wir Frauen und genderqueere Menschen organisieren uns, vernetzen uns und bündeln unsere Wut, gemeinsam mit allen Unterdrückten auf der ganzen Welt, um mit vereinter Kraft weiter gegen die Ordnung der Herrschenden zu kämpfen.

title: Trump Order Aims to Restrict What Federal Contractors Can Tell Congress
content:
The move was widely seen as part of a broader effort by the president to obstruct Democrats’ planned probes.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

With Democratic leaders promising “accountability” when the party takes over the US Senate and House of Representatives in January, Republican President Donald Trump late Friday signed an executive order directing federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House before sharing information with Congress and withhold anything his administration deems confidential.

Any contractor or subcontractor that fails to comply could face “potential termination or cancellation of contracts,” the order says.

The White House claimed that “Trump is ensuring that Americans’ confidential information and national and homeland security work is protected, and that the executive branch is able to serve the American people efficiently and economically.”

Major news: President Trump has signed an executive order requiring federal contractors to notify and coordinate with the executive branch on congressional oversight asks. Democrats have vowed to make defense contractors a major target next year. https://t.co/MMeFhNJWDy

However, his move was widely seen as part of a broader effort by the president to limit Democrats’ planned probes into not only the federal government and its contractors but also Trump and businesses that may have benefited from his return to power.

Acknowledging the anticipated Democrat-led investigations, the White House fact sheet says that “certain congressional leaders have threatened to intrude on these executive prerogatives by seeking confidential executive branch information from executive agencies and harassing private companies that contract with the federal government.”

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of of the watchdog group Public Citizen, stressed in a Saturday statement that “contractors are paid with Americans’ tax money and must be the best for the job, full stop.”

“However, throughout the Trump administration we’ve seen widespread abuse of the contracting process, with lucrative contracts doled out to political allies, inexperienced startups, and flatly unqualified bidders, for everything from major ICE operations to Trump’s vanity projects,” she noted, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “No-bid and emergency awards have become the norm, circumventing rules designed to prevent corrupt contracting.”

“The new Congress rightfully has its sites set on this obvious cronyism for investigation and oversight,” she continued. “The American people have a right to know how their money is being spent, that it is going to capable contractors, and that is not be used to reward allies and punish perceived enemies.”

Gilbert added that the new order, “dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies, is nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption. It will not succeed. Sunlight is coming and corrupt administration insiders and contractors, both, will have to face the American people.”

Friday’s order follows a directive issued this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Scharf said certain Democratic investigations could amount to criminal conduct, a claim that has raised questions about the administration’s attempts to limit congressional oversight.“

The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas. Executive privilege allows presidents to protect certain confidential communications, but courts can ⁠intervene in disputes over Congress’ authority to obtain information.

Earlier this week Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee, sent document preservation letters to a dozen current and former Trump administration officials, and Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), likely the next House Judiciary Committee chair, sent similar notices to federal law enforcement agencies.

“Voters gave congressional Democrats a sweeping mandate to root out corruption and ensure that the government is accountable to the people,” Garcia wrote in his letters, referring to the blue tsunami in the midterm elections earlier this month. “We intend to act on that mandate in the 120th Congress by conducting the critically important oversight essential for legislative reform.”

Raskin — who managed Trump’s historic second impeachment after his supporters stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021 — said on social media Friday: “We will confront White House corruption and lawlessness with the full powers of Congress, the ‘predominant’ branch of government (Madison), the representatives of the people. Preserve all your records, Mr. President.”

Trump has been widely condemned as “the most openly corrupt president in American history” and, during just his first year back in the White House, pocketed at least $2.2 billion — over half of it from his family’s cryptocurrency grift. Companies affiliated with the president’s two eldest sons are have also scored key federal contracts during his second term.

In addition to Trump’s sons, Elon Musk — a former member of the administration, leading Republican donor, and the world’s richest person — could also be a key target of Democratic probes, as he leads multiple tech companies. Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, sent a Friday letter to Musk about SpaceX’s role in the Starshield service disruptions in Ukraine last month.

Noting that inquiry on Musk’s social media platform X on Saturday, Jonathan Cohn, political director of the group Progressive Mass, said that “contracts with Musk are a national security risk and should be treated as such.”

title: Graham Purchase - Kropotkin and the Rise of Revolutionary Anarchism
content:
Author

: Graham Purchase

Title

: Kropotkin and the Rise of Revolutionary Anarchism

Subtitle

: Review

Date

: 2001, April

Source

: Scanned from Anarcho-Syndicalist Review 31 (April 2001)




 a review of 







 Kropotkin and the Rise of Revolutionary Anarchism 1872-1886, by Caroline Cahm, Cambridge University Press, 1989. 







 This excellent work of modern scholarship focuses upon a specific period of Kropotkin's life, 1872-1886, during which he was intensely involved in the development and propagation of European anarchism, through his actions, speeches and articles. This period of intense activism lies between Kropotkin's earlier involvement with Russian populism and his long exile in England, where he wrote the many longer books for which he remains famous today. 




 During these years he travelled widely throughout Western Europe, living for long periods in Switzerland (expelled 1881) and France, where he was imprisoned for three years (1883-6). Kropotkin's travels to countries with strong anarchist movements such as Belgium and Spain influenced his thinking. He also participated in anarchist conferences in Switzerland, Germany and London. 




 His achievements during this period were many and varied. Shortly after arriving in Switzerland he enthusiastically took part in a demonstration involving illegally carrying the red flag in honor of the Paris Commune. The success of the Berne demonstration rejuvenated, for a short time, the Jura federation which had fallen into decline since the death of Bakunin and his own internment in a Russian prison. This point in time also saw the beginning of Kropotkin's journalistic career. He contributed quite a number of articles to the Bulletin of the Jura Federation of the IWA during 1876-7. These articles were never published in English, nor since republished in French. 




 The value of Cahm's study is that it thoroughly examines important themes within this early journalism. Eminent scholars of Kropotkin, such as Martin Miller, regard Kropotkin's writings for the Bulletin and Rebel as some of his "best" and most "neglected." This neglect is a pity, for although about half of his contributions to the Bulletin were reports upon Russian affairs, primarily the trial of 1893, the other half include interesting and important contributions upon the ills of imperialism, parliamentary socialism and Marxism, a three-part analysis of the ills of British unionism, and articles upon U.S. labor issues. 




 In 1879, following the collapse of the Bulletin and L'Avant Garde (to which he contributed one article on the Pittsburgh strikes), Kropotkin founded, edited and contributed to a new newspaper, Rebel (Le Revolte), published at Geneva until 1885. Although Kropotkin's first political book Words of a Rebel (Paris 1885, edited and compiled by Reclus), contains a very readable selection of the leading articles from the Rebel, there are a few, particularly concerning unionism which might also have been reasonably included. There are also other minor articles, such as those dealing with the value and desirability of direct-action strike tactics as a method of reversing reformist parliamentary unionism in Britain and France, which are also of interest in this respect. Again Cahm, in focusing attention upon his neglected works upon the subject of reformist and revolutionary unionism, provides a valuable resource upon which to better assess Kropotkin's thinking upon these issues. This scholarship is very valuable as his complex and interesting viewpoints concerning syndicalism, unionism and anarchism have been obscured by anarchist-communist scholars with anti-syndicalist prejudices. 




 Towards the end of the period under review (1872-1886) Kropotkin took a central role in the defence at the Lyon Trial of 1883, which led to the imprisonment for several years of most of France's leading anarchists, including Kropotkin himself, in a farcical display of state-justice, which, for a short time at least, led to widespread public sympathy for the prisoners and what they stood for. The imprisonment of the most active anarchists and the subsequent intense state repression of the movement meant that little remained upon his release in 1886 when he began his long exile from continental Europe in England, where he could no longer take an active part in its affairs (though he helped found and finance two subsequent French-language newspapers to which he contributed scores of articles over the next 30 years). 




 In addition to Kropotkin's journalism Cahm also draws heavily upon Kropotkin's correspondence with other comrades, much of which remains unpublished. The book also contains many useful general summaries of the views and activities of various groupings, newspapers and personalities of the period. 




 Having provided a general overview of the book, I will briefly summarize its central themes and conclusions. 




Collectivism, Communism and Communalism




 The study first explores the development of the anarchist communist idea by Reclus, Kropotkin and others. The discussion is largely concerned with debates concerning the broad vision of the anarchist society at which they were aiming: whether the anarchist ideal was to be conceived in terms of collectivism or communism. In anarchist communism, as advocated by Reclus and Kropotkin, consumption was to be dictated by needs rather than according to one's contribution as was the case under earlier collectivist or mutualist conceptions associated with Proudhon and Bakunin. Anarchist-communism conceived collectivism as being at best a stage along the road to anarchist-communism.

title: KULTUR DER UNREGIERBARKEIT
content:
Neue Bucherscheinung bei Unrast Verlag: Dieses Buch benennt die Leerstellen anarchistischer Praxis: Organisation als Selbstzweck, fehlende Kontinuität, soziale Isolation. Eine Intervention in die Bewegung, die benennt, warum wir uns selbst blockieren und was sich ändern muss.




In den letzten zwanzig Jahren haben Anarchist*innen entscheidend dazu beigetragen, Widerstand über Kipppunkte hinaus in offene Aufstände zu treiben – in Ägypten, Hongkong, Katalonien, Griechenland, Frankreich, den USA, Mexiko, Chile oder Brasilien. Zugleich sind sie immer wieder hinter ihren gesellschaftlichen Möglichkeiten zurückgeblieben, haben vorhersehbare Gefahren nicht erkannt oder waren nicht in der Lage, die nächsten Schritte zu gehen.




Dieses Buch benennt die dabei in den Blick geratenen Leerstellen anarchistischer Praxis: Viele dieser Niederlagen lassen sich auf ungelöste Fragen von Organisation, Kontinuität und Gemeinschaft zurückführen. Die anarchistische Bewegung fetischisiert Organisation, anstatt sie als begrenztes Werkzeug zu begreifen; sie versteht nicht, warum sie sich von Generation zu Generation immer wieder neu erfindet und dabei ähnliche Fehler wiederholt; und sie unterschätzt ihre Isolation – eine Isolation, die ihre Handlungsfähigkeit einschränkt und sie anfällig für Repression macht.




Falsche Bescheidenheit hat die Bewegung daran gehindert, zu erkennen, wie wirksam sie tatsächlich war, während ihr Ego die Bewegten blind für die systematischen Fehler gemacht hat, mit denen sie revolutionäre Situationen immer wieder verspielen. Peter Gelderloos fordert dazu auf: Es ist Zeit, die Dinge klar zu sehen!

author: Thomas Kennedy
title: Immigrants in US and Palestinians Face Mirroring Systems of Oppression
content:
In Florida, the movements for Palestine liberation and immigrant justice can create strength in solidarity.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The treatment of immigrants in the United States has long been brutal and cruel.

Since the 1980s, propelled by false narratives of migrant criminality associated with the Mariel boatlift, migration management has shifted sharply towards confinement and control, while portraying people crossing borders as uniquely dangerous. Immigration detention has expanded dramatically since the Mariel boatlift episode. By the early 2020s, most individuals held in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) were detained in privately operated facilities with a for-profit motive. At that time, corporate revenues from immigration detention center contracts had reached historic highs and kept climbing.

Florida’s inhumane concentration camp, dubbed “Alligator Alcatraz,” in which over 6,700 immigrants were detained, is a perfect example of this carceral approach to migration. The conditions at this detention center were deplorable. The Department of Homeland Security itself reported that 32 detainees were packed into cages that were literally situated under flimsy tents, which had a maximum capacity of just 11 people. Detained individuals had to deal with overflowing toilets, which led to raw sewage and fecal matter seeping across the floor and sleeping areas. Showers were infrequent and limited by authorities to three days a week in bug-infested bathrooms. Detainees were offered food contaminated with insects.

In Alligator Alcatraz, which has since shut down, and other detention centers throughout South Florida, detainees were and are denied proper medical care in addition to living in poor, inhuman conditions. Sendra, a Cuban American immigrant, is a diabetic and was sent to Krome detention center. According to his wife, news reports, and court filings, Sendra suffered pancreatitis while in detention because he was not given the medical treatment he needed and required hospitalization.

Ending up in one of these dystopian detention centers is not a distant possibility; because of increased ICE raids, an immigrant who has been residing in Florida for decades can be arrested and sucked into this awful incarceration system simply by stepping outside. Additionally, a multitude of Florida localities and state entities have signed on to 287(g) agreements. These agreements allow local and state police officers to perform federal immigration enforcement functions, essentially transforming those police departments into appendages of ICE. Florida is among the leaders in the nation in immigration enforcement, with more than 25,000 arrests in the last year. Most arrests arise from racial profiling and routine traffic stops, such as having a vehicle with a broken taillight. Once individuals are arrested, there is a severe lack of due process. Detention facilities have blocked detained immigrants from accessing legal documents, having confidential phone calls, and receiving visits from their attorneys.

Meanwhile, those who advocate for immigrant rights in this bleak moment have faced immense backlash. We have seen in Minnesota how U.S. citizens demanding justice for immigrants have been surveilled, attacked by ICE agents, and in some cases, even killed. This suppression against immigration advocates exists in Florida too. At Florida International University, seven students who silently and peacefully protested the university’s police collaboration with ICE were disciplined by the university and ordered to submit a two-minute video reflecting on their behavior. The students sued the university on the basis of free speech and won.

The incarceration of immigrants and repression of immigrant advocates in Florida in some ways mirrors what Palestinian Americans, advocates for Palestine in the United States, and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are experiencing.

In the West Bank, Palestinian American Sama Safi, who has ties to Tampa, Florida, is currently detained in Damon Prison in Israel, a prison that solely holds female prisoners and is notorious for human rights abuses. For example, Israeli occupation authorities at Damon prison have confiscated detainees’ hijabs and forced them to wear only gray sports suits without head coverings. Women who refused to remove their hijabs were reportedly beaten, with these beatings often filmed. During winter, Israel occupation authorities at Damon prison regularly raid detainees’ rooms, handcuff and blindfold them, and force them to kneel with their heads lowered outside in the cold for several hours while police dogs and stun grenades are used against them.

Just like Alligator Alcatraz and Krome Detention Center, Damon prison has documented cases of overcrowding and unsanitary conditions. In some cases, more than a dozen women are made to share rooms with only four beds, with many women sleeping on the floor. Toilets are inside the cells, creating constant health problems. Dozens of detainees share one bar of soap, and there is an insufficient amount of sanitary pads for people on their periods. And just like Sendra, the Cuban American who was detained at Alligator Alcatraz, Sama suffers from medical conditions that are not being treated while she is detained. Safi suffers from a debilitating auto-inflammatory disease that requires regular medication and monitoring that her family reports she is not receiving.

Surveillance systems utilized along the U.S.-Mexico border are first tested in Palestine, and deportation infrastructure is weaponized against immigrants and Palestine advocates in the U.S.

We noted the increasing number of ICE raids in Florida, and the lack of due process that exists for immigrants once they are detained. In Palestine, there are increased raids occurring in the West Bank. The United Nations noted that settler-violence in Palestine hit an all-time high in 2026, and has increased every year since 2023. Just as in the United States, where even the smallest traffic violations can be used as a pretext to stop and detain an immigrant, Palestinians in the West Bank are often stopped by Israeli security forces who find ridiculous reasons to stop and detain them. For example, holding a Palestinian flag is enough grounds to detain a Palestinian, an injustice that is even more insulting when grounded in the context that Palestinians are indigenous to the land on which they currently live under a settler-colonial military occupation — land that they are fighting to stay on.

In total, an estimated 7,000 Palestinians are in prison. Once detained, they don’t have access to due process, just like the majority of detained immigrants in the United States. Detained Palestinians are often denied access to lawyers. Israeli courts can use secret evidence to detain a Palestinian accused of a crime, and the detained individual and their lawyer cannot see the evidence. Approximately 99 percent of detained Palestinians processed through Israeli military courts are convicted of a crime. Several Palestinian Americans have suffered from this system of unjust incarceration as well, including 17-year-old Floridian Mohammed Ibrahim, who was held for nine months in two different prisons (Ofer prison and Megiddo prison) from February-November 2025. During those nine months, Mohammed was given minimal regular nutrition, lost over 25 pounds, and developed scabies. A family representative who has acted as a spokesperson for Mohammed personally told us that a fellow prisoner, who was 17 years old and a close friend of Mohammed’s, died in his cell from scabies, in Mohammed’s arms.

Like the silencing and persecution of immigration justice advocates in the United States, U.S. advocates who stand up for Palestine face harsh repression. Hundreds of students have been disciplined or have even had their degrees revoked for advocating for Palestine and against genocide on campus. Immigrants in the United States who stand up for Palestine have suffered extreme consequences for their advocacy, and this repression shows how related these two fights can be.

Take Rümeysa Öztürk, a doctoral student at Tufts University, who wrote an op-ed criticizing her school’s response to the Gaza genocide. Shortly after the op-ed was published, ICE officials arrested her, her visa was revoked by the State Department, and she was detained in Louisiana for six weeks. Or take Salah Sarsour, the president of the largest mosque in Wisconsin, and a lawful permanent resident of the United States. Salah was arrested by ICE agents due to his advocacy for Palestine, and the federal government is now seeking to unfairly deport him to intimidate others.

These injustices don’t just happen in a vacuum. They happen because people in power make them — or at the very least, let them — happen. And it is often the same exact people in power who fuel both immigration-related and Palestine-related injustices. Take Florida’s Palm Beach County, for example. The county has signed a 287(g) agreement, and has invested a whopping $1 billion in Israel Bonds, which directly finance the genocide in Gaza and the occupation of Palestine. The injustices perpetrated by Israeli forces would not happen without the United States providing billions of dollars of funding and weapons to assist the occupation of Palestine, and Palm Beach County itself is culpable in this as the largest municipal investor in Israel Bonds in the world. Likewise, Palm Beach County has the highest rate of ICE arrests in Florida (and remember that Florida has among the highest rate of ICE arrests in the country). The logic of both cruelties is the same: profit and political clout for a few, at the expense of Black, Arab, and Brown communities’ lives, homes, and dignity.

Our struggles are interconnected. We can, and must, work toward our freedom together.

While these problems are interconnected, their solutions are often as well; we suffer indignities caused by the same offices and same politicians, and we have the same types of policies to dismantle. The movements for justice in Palestine and justice for immigrants will only benefit by seeing our struggles as interconnected, and as advocates we must move to bridge this gap. Our opposition sees no difference between the two movements: There are training exchanges between ICE and Israeli military forces, surveillance systems utilized along the U.S.-Mexico border are first tested in Palestine, and deportation infrastructure is weaponized against immigrants and Palestine advocates in the U.S.

Immigration advocates in the U.S. must explicitly adopt anti-Zionist principles in their work and be bold in centering Palestine and working with Palestinian organizations. Advocates for Palestine must mobilize their base to assist the immigrant rights movement in tangible ways, such as working to pass the DIGNITY Act or participating in court accompaniment programs for immigration court.

Our struggles are interconnected. We can, and must, work toward our freedom together.

author: Marianne Dhenin
title: Trump Administration Is Hiking Immigration Bond Costs to Keep Migrants Locked Up
content:
Bond prices in many jurisdictions have doubled under the Trump administration, and bond funds are struggling to keep up.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

When Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 after campaigning on mass deportation, his administration got to work expanding immigration detention and reshaping the nation’s immigration courts to make it more difficult for jailed migrants to seek release. Almost two years later, data show just how successful those policies have been.

The number of people jailed in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention nationwide is up roughly 80 percent since President Joe Biden left office. The Trump administration has foreclosed most avenues through which jailed migrants have historically sought release. For the shrinking share of the jailed population that does access an immigration bond hearing, the average bond denial rate has jumped. It rose to about 60 percent in the first year of Trump 2.0, up from about 53 percent in the last year of Biden’s tenure. The denial rate has continued to rise this year.

Even when a bond is granted, freedom remains out of reach for many caught in the Trump administration’s deportation machine because median bond amounts have also increased. Those amounts have even doubled from 2024 to the first months of 2026 in some of the federal circuit court jurisdictions with the most immigration bond cases, according to data compiled and analyzed by Bklg.org.

“This is a linchpin in the administration’s deportation strategy,” Michael Tan, deputy director of the Immigrants’ Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), told Truthout. “The primary reason they’re subjecting people to detention with no avenue for release is to coerce them into giving up their immigration cases, their claims to legal status, to remaining in the country, and to acquiesce to a deportation because they can’t stand being locked up for so long.”

The number of people jailed in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention nationwide is up roughly 80 percent since President Joe Biden left office.

Even for those who do not agree to so-called self-deportation, outcomes tend to be worse for those who fight their immigration cases while detained. Those who are released are more likely to have their immigration cases resolved with permission to remain in the U.S. than with deportation orders. Once freed, a person tends to have more resources and more time to participate in their case, gather evidence, and access other needed support. “It’s a lot harder to fight your immigration case when you’re in a jail cell,” Tan told Truthout. Especially, he added, “when ICE moves people all over the place, and so it’s not the case that you’ll be detained often in your community or near your family [and] your lawyer. Instead, ICE is routinely shipping people to far-flung locations.”

Fisayo Okare, digital communications manager at Envision Freedom Fund, told Truthout that migrant community members with whom her organization works regularly face these pressures. “Families are thinking of whether it’s worth it or not to even remain in the country or just choosing to voluntarily deport,” she said. The nonprofit Envision Freedom Fund is the largest immigration bond fund in the nation; it helps cover bonds for individuals jailed in New York or New Jersey and those who will return home to the area on release. Since the fund launched in 2018, it has provided over $15 million in bond support to help secure the release of over 1,600 people from immigration jails.

An October report from Envision Freedom Fund shows how the increase in the number of migrants jailed and struggling to access release is affecting communities in New York and New Jersey. The volume of requests for support that the bond fund receives has risen so much that it projects it will cover nine times as many bonds in 2026 as in 2024, if it can raise the funds needed to meet demand through the end of the calendar year.

“The primary reason they’re subjecting people to detention with no avenue for release is to coerce them into giving up their immigration cases.”

The average bond amounts submitted to the fund for support have also risen from $6,200 in 2024 to $14,200 in 2026. Half of the requests the fund has received this year have involved bonds exceeding $10,000, and it has seen bonds set as high as $85,000 since Trump returned to the White House. The fund has also tracked tens of thousands of individuals who have been booked in to detention facilities in New York and New Jersey and then transferred to more than 100 other detention facilities across 25 states.

“The fact is that we’re forced to bond so many more people out now because the sheer volume of the system — everything is increasing,” Ben McCoubrey, Envision Freedom Fund’s data and advocacy manager, told Truthout.

It has never been easy for those in ICE jails to access bond, a process that entails securing a bond hearing in immigration court, finding a lawyer to present the case, then convincing the immigration judge to grant a bond, and ultimately finding someone outside with U.S. citizenship or a green card and the funds needed to post the bond. But the obstacles to accessing bond are now greater than ever before thanks to what Tan characterized to Truthout as the Trump administration’s “takeover of the immigration courts.”

Since Trump returned to office, he has signed executive orders to expand detention and restrict release. Based on those directives, ICE’s lawyers have made legal arguments and issued guidance meant to subject as many immigrants as possible to mandatory detention and limit their access to bond. Those directives have become standard practice following administration-friendly decisions from the Board of Immigration Appeals, which governs the immigration courts and judges from within the Department of Justice.

The Trump administration has also purged dozens of immigration judges and recruited replacements that it now calls “deportation judges,” rather than immigration judges. Many of these new judges come from the ranks of former military lawyers, ICE lawyers, and prosecutors with little or no experience or training in immigration law.

“They’ve fired immigration judges that they think, in their view, are too friendly to immigrants and replaced them with so-called deportation judges [and] for the judges who remain, who didn’t get fired, we know that the administration is exerting pressure on them to deny relief, and to really crack down, and serve as foot soldiers in a mass deportation campaign,” Tan told Truthout. “They’ve taken an immigration court system that is supposed to be neutral and fair and made it into an arm of the immigration enforcement system.”

The ACLU has litigated the Trump administration’s mandatory detention scheme in every circuit court where it could be heard, a total of 11 of the nation’s 13. Only two circuits have concurred with the administration’s interpretation of the law. Nine have rejected it, opening the door for more individuals to access bond hearings in the 40 states covered by those circuits. The Supreme Court will hear the issue in a case arising from the Second Circuit, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, next year; Tan told Truthout a decision is expected by the end of June. The outcome will affect access to bond hearings for those in ICE jails nationwide.

While the legal fight continues, the humanitarian crisis created by the Trump administration’s policy changes is deepening. Envision Freedom Fund’s recent report helps put a human face on the issue. “We paint a picture of what’s happening in the context of detention and deportation, how things are growing, and go beyond what we see when it’s just [the number of] people getting released on bonds,” McCoubrey told Truthout about the report’s aims.

The report includes stories of immigrants who have suffered medical neglect and other traumas in ICE jails and are navigating the lasting effects after being bonded out with Envision Freedom Fund’s support.

One man for whom the fund helped cover a $50,000 bond to secure his release in July 2026 shared that he “felt unmeasurably happy when [he] got released from the jail.” He had been jailed for over two months, and after release, said, “I believed that now everything will be okay. Because when I was in there, I was stressing a lot. I didn’t know what would happen because nowadays it’s really tough.” Just two weeks after the man’s release, his asylum case was granted — ending a more than four-year wait that began in 2022.

For each of the tens of thousands of people jailed in the country’s ICE detention facilities, there are families missing a parent or a sibling and communities missing a neighbor.

More recently, Okare told Truthout that Envision Freedom Fund secured release for a man in his mid-thirties who had been transferred from Delaney Hall in New Jersey to an ICE jail in Georgia. The fund then coordinated with partners to arrange transportation to bring him home in time to be with his wife and witness the birth of his child. “His wife was actually in the hospital when we got the bond request, and he got out right in time,” she said.

Okare told Truthout that stories like these are common in the work of Envision Freedom Fund and other immigration bond funds operating nationwide. For each of the tens of thousands of people jailed in the country’s ICE detention facilities, there are families missing a parent or a sibling and communities missing a neighbor.

As the Trump administration continues pulling these communities apart, Okare told Truthout that organizations like hers will keep fighting to make them whole again: “[We’re] not just paying their bond but ensuring that they get out and make it back to their community.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

title: La GenZ sera le genre humain / une émission de Minuit Décousu
content:
Cette semaine dans Minuit Décousu, alors que la jeunesse européenne se mobilise contre l'austérité et la guerre le vendredi 20 novemnbre, on revietn aux origines de la GenZ-212 au Maroc et comment elle donne à voir des jeunesses inégales à l'international dans ses répliques au Népal, Pérou, en Indonésie... On regarde aussi comment ici, la GenZ à la française fait entendre les populations non-blanches depuis le mouvement lycéen et comment elle participe à construire un mouvement européen de la jeunesse. Dans cette émission, tu pourras entendre :




 «

 

Des jeunes qui ne savent pas se battre

 

» : Badinter face à la GenZ

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Anarchism, The Star of the Antipodes
content:
by Christian Ferrer




Revista Ají

, 24/05/2020




Nothing is more mysterious than the fate of anarchism, an ideal that might seem far-fetched were it not for the fact that it is extremely sensible. Although the passage of time has dimmed its lustre, and it was even declared extinct, the “libertarian cause” has continued to demonstrate its tenacity, as anarchists seem to possess the qualities of the phoenix – the ability to be reborn from their own ashes – like avatars that are reincarnated in various neighbouring spheres and offshoots. The anarchist ideal, while once politically and culturally prominent, remains incomprehensible in our times unless one first turns the world upside down. In truth, anarchy has always had a bad press—right from the start—: a “utopia”; a messianic call, then, something wild, at times otherworldly, always piercing.







Do as you please, live as you would like people to live in the future, do not join the military, do not eat animal carcasses, you are the king’s enemy, abhor prisons, glorify sex, stand your ground, do not obey or give orders, do not humiliate and do not let yourself be humiliated, do not leave a comrade in the lurch, better an outcast than a leader, you may take sides and be part of the action but do not form a party, borders are false and the law a fiction exploited by the powerful, love is free and long live loss. Such are the slogans, or counterbalances, the decalogue of antagonism and wonder. As for the anarchists, they were said to be scarecrows, and at times the label was deserved.




It is pointless to weigh up their actions, ups and downs, and achievements solely by the yardstick that measures success or failure, because the very fact that “the Idea” – as they called the sum of their principles – has appeared in the world remains a mystery of history. It does not seem a natural occurrence. Generally speaking, even if reluctantly, people come to terms with the world as it is, soothing their inevitable unease with benefits, subsidies and a few public holidays throughout the gruelling working year. Few are those who seek to turn it on its head in the blink of an eye. Pyramids, too, are built to be climbed, not to be torn down, stone by stone. Anarchism can be seen as an unusual, forceful and unyielding response to the existence of powers separate from the community, no less than to the obstacles and prohibitions placed in the way of the will to personal self-creation—in short, to everything that discourages or derails the mad desire to live, and that is precisely why the anarchist creed advocated a multifaceted revolution: cultural, psychological and political all at once. It was to ask a great deal; it was to be overly rational; it was to live without fear, with or without organisation; it was to enjoy the feast, in unity, at least while the affinity lasted. No more than that, no less than that.




From the very beginnings of anarchism, when Proudhon, Bakunin and Kropotkin laid the foundations, various branches and offshoots very quickly emerged, each emphasising, in its own way, different aspects: mutualism, collectivism, free love, concern for the fate of nature, vegetarianism, trade unionism, individualism, religiosity without established churches, spontaneism, women’s emancipation, morality without dogma, experimental communes and a number of other challenges that, in their day, seemed risky, if not “flowers of evil”: a scent at times sharp, at others sensual, always diverse and inventive. It is also worth highlighting anarchism’s ability to influence people, ideas and groups—and sometimes crowds—who did not necessarily identify as anarchists but who felt ‘”called” to sympathise with these principles or to reconsider their own convictions. In every case, hierarchical power was regarded as a human catastrophe, an enemy of lives that might otherwise have been less oppressed.




The opponents of anarchism are well known: the clergy, the powerful, the military, the employers, the “patriots”, those in power – not to mention the communists, their old enemies from before the now-forgotten Soviet Union even existed. These opponents knew that libertarian thought emphasised issues and problems that could not be resolved within the system of domination as it stood, including, amongst others, its very early critique of technology and industrialism, its warnings about ecological excesses, its exhortations to break away from failed emotional relationships, its advocacy of sexual emancipation, as well as its rejection of imperialists – an aspect not always emphasised. Anarchist practices—that is, their ways of life—sought to dissociate themselves from hierarchical power, whose image, inherited by all generations, is vertical, concentric, ascending, indestructible and time-honoured. But anarchists were not so much concerned with what came before or after the State, but rather with what eluded its control. Not enough thought is given to the fact that the majority of human activities take place “outside” the principle of hierarchy, be it networks of friendly social interaction, peer groups or the countless conversations in so many intimate settings.




It is not easy for us to imagine a world of “disinterested” relationships—that is to say, free from any desire for domination. The overcoming of a society based on the domination of some over others, in the uncompromising terms of anarchism, continues to provoke disbelief, even fear, or, at best, a sense of political enigma, all the more so because the victims have grown accustomed to collaborating in their own misfortune and reproduce the self-perpetuating cycle of misfortune, barely mitigated by promises, consumption and adjustments to a level of coercion that is still bearable. But these are mere crumbs, for any social organisation that differentiates and separates the rulers from the ruled, the rich from the poor, the powerful from the dispossessed, is a declaration of hostility towards existence. The truth is that no more radical idea of freedom has yet been devised than that proclaimed in its day by the anarchists. The entire pyramid would have tumbled into that abyss. It is a pity that they ran out of time, that they left too soon, and that they have not yet returned. They had sharp chisels and had come to write the epitaph of our society.

title: Пикет солидарности с Алексеем Макаровым в Варшаве
content:
29 ноября 14:00 Варшава, Bogatela, 3

Беларусские анархисты Варшавы призывают присоединиться к пикету солидарности с анархистом Алексеем Макаровым, который организуют товарищи из Czarnego Sztandaru

Алексей проживает в Швеции с 2011 года как беженец, бежавший от политических репрессий в России. В июне 2022 года он отправился в Украину, чтобы присоединиться к вооруженной борьбе против российского империалистического вторжения. Во время службы Алексей дважды получил тяжелые ранения. Второе ранение задело голову и руку, и он так и не смог полностью восстановить подвижность пальцев правой руки.

Сейчас товарищ столкнулся с репрессиями со стороны шведского государства за свои анархические убеждения и участие в интернациональной борьбе.

Редакция «Автономного действия» напоминает, что в поддержку анархиста Алексея Макарова создан канал Solidarity with Alexey Makarov / Солидарность с Алексеем Макаровым, где можно узнать подробнее о том, какие репрессии в отношении него в Швеции, и ознакомиться со всеми последними новостями.

author: Reddebrek
title: Carl Steuermann (Otto Rühle) - La Crise Mondial (1931)
content:
Pour la quatrième fois, le capitalisme allemand annonce sa banqueroute. La première fois, celle-ci se montra sous l’uniforme des soldats vaincus, à leur retour du front. La guerre mondiale était perdue, le rêve de domination mondiale était cruellement brisé. Le peuple souffrait, en proie à la famine, à la misère, à l’épuisement, au désespoir, mais il ne voulut pas admettre la banqueroute de l’économie. Il renvoya le messager de Job et chanta : « L’Allemagne, l’Alle­ magne au-dessus de tout ! » La seconde annonce suivit de près la première. Celui qui la fit parla avec la voix de la révolution. En effet, l’armée effondrée, ce fut la révolution. « Socialisme ou chute dans la barbarie ! » tel fut le mot d’ordre. « Il n’est d’autre salut que l’orientation à l’Est, le sys­ tème des soviets, la dictature du prolétariat, la socia­ lisation ! » La terreur s’empara de la bourgeoisie et la paralysa. Sans y croire elle-même, secouée de tremble­ ments, elle put à peine articuler : « Reconstruction ! Nous nous relèverons ! » Vibrant d’enthousiasme et d’espoirs, l’écho des masses lui répondit : « Oui, recons­ truction !» Et la révolution fut réprimée dans le sang. La troisième fois, la banqueroute fut annoncée sur

les ruines de l’inflation. Il sembla que c’était réelle­ ment la fin. Des millions d’hommes devenus des men­ diants sombrèrent dans le néant d’une existence sans ressources. Mais avec le courage du désespoir ils se cramponnèrent au fétu de paille d’une dernière ten­ tative : « L’Allemagne ne peut pas, ne doit pas périr !... » Et voici que, pour la quatrième fois, on nous annonce la banqueroute, et c’cst le cri de détresse de l’économie mondiale qui nous en avertit. Les Bourses s’écroulent, les fondements de l’industrie branlent ; c’est une suite d’effondrements. La panique gagne de proche en proche. Plus de vingt millions d’hommes sont jetés à la rue, sans pain, et demandent du travail. La moitié du genre humain presque vit de secours publics. Partout dominent les dettes, la corruption, la fail­ lite... Une atmosphère de fin du monde. Qu’allons- nous devenir ? se demandent les uns aux autres les hommes perplexes et impuissants. « Cela ne peut pas continuer ainsi ! » assure la sagesse des rues. Nul ne sait quel conseil donner. Chacun sait seulement ou a le sentiment infaillible que, cette fois-ci, c’est sérieux ; c’est vraiment la faillite. Il n’y a plus ni aide, ni espoir à attendre. Le capitalisme a fait son temps. C’est la fin, en effet. Mais y a-t-il une fin sans recom­ mencement ? Un déclin sans renaissance ? L’histoire mondiale continue. Et tant qu’il y aura des hommes animés du désir de vivre, ces hommes travailleront, créeront, produiront pour se maintenir en vie. Ce n’est pas l’économie qui meurt, c’est le capitalisme ; c’est la forme économique dominante aujourd’hui en Amérique, en Europe, et dans les régions du monde les plus évoluées, qui est condamnée à mort. C’est la fin d’un système, non la fin de l’économie tout court.

La crise constitue un tournant. L’effondrement est suivi de renaissance ; du chaos s’élabore un ordre nouveau. Nous ignorons encore tout du rythme, du genre et de l’envergure des événements qui nous attendent. Nous ignorons la durée et les phases du processus par lequel nous devrons passer. Nous ne nous représentons pas encore les luttes que nous devrons soutenir, ni les sacrifices qu’une évolution implacable exigera de nous. Nous allons à tâtons dans l’inconnu. Une seule chose nous semble certaine : c’est que le grand système économique qui succédera nécessaire­ ment au capitalisme sera le socialisme. Il est vrai que la route est longue qui mène vers lui. C’est vraisem­ blablement une route pénible, ardue, semée d’obstacles et comportant beaucoup d’arrêts et de paliers, beau­ coup d’étapes et de haltes intermédiaires. Si les signes ne sont pas trompeurs, l’étape pro­ chaine de cette transformation de l’humanité est une variété du capitalisme d’État. L’histoire qui nous emporte dans son tourbillon met le cap dans cette direction. Suivons-la !

author: Reddebrek
title: Weltkrise – Weltwende. Kurs auf den Staatskapitalismus, Carl Steuermann (Otto Rühle)
content:
Weltkrise - Weltwende. Kurs auf Staatskapitalismus.

Zum vierten Male meldet der deutsche Kapitalismus seinen Bankrott an. Das erstemal erschien er in der Montur des geschlagenen Frontsoldaten. Der Weltkrieg war verloren, der Traum von einer Weltherrschaft grau- sam zerstört. Das Volk wurde geschüttelt von Hunger, Elend, Erschöpfung, Verzweiflung. Aber von einemBan- krott der Wirtschaft wollte es nichts wissen. Es wies den Hiobsboten ab und sang: Deutschland, Deutschland über alles ! Da folgte der ersten Meldung aufdem Fuße die zweite . Der sie überbrachte, sprach mit der Stimme des Revolu- tionärs . Denn dem militärischen Zusammenbruch war die Revolution gefolgt. „Sozialismus oder Untergang in Barbarei !" lautete die Losung. „Es gibt keine andere Ret- tung als östliche Orientierung, Rätesystem, Diktatur des Proletariats, Sozialisierung !" Lähmendes Entsetzen packte dieBourgeoisie. Kaumdaß sie es selber glaubte, stammelte sie unter Zittern und Beben: „Wiederaufbau ! Wir kom- men wieder hoch!" Begeistert und hoffnungsgläubig ant- wortete ihrdasEchoderMassen: ,,Jawohl,Wiederaufbau ! " Und der Revolutionär wurde blutig niedergeschlagen. Das drittemal erfolgte die Bankrotterklärung auf den

Trümmern der Inflation. Das Ende schien wirklich ge- kommen. Millionen waren zu Bettlern geworden und ver- sanken in das Nichts der Existenzlosigkeit. Aber sie klam- merten sich mit dem Mute der Verzweiflung an den Stroh- halm eines letzten Versuchs. „Deutschland kann nicht, darf nicht untergehen ! ... " Nun ist die vierte Bankrottansage da. Der Angstschrei der Weltwirtschaftskrise hat sie verkündet. Die Börsen krachen. Fundamente der Industrie wanken. Zusammen- brüche folgen. Panik greift um sich. Mehr als zwanzig Millionen Menschen stehen brotlos auf der Straße und fordern Arbeit. Fast die Hälfte aller Menschen fristet das Leben von öffentlicher Fürsorge. Überall Verschuldung, Korruption, Bankrott, Weltuntergangsstimmung. Was soll werden ? fragt verstört und kopflos einer den andern. So kann es nicht weitergehen ! versichert triviale Gassen- weisheit von Mund zu Mund. Keiner weiß Rat. Jeder weiß nur oder hat das untrügliche Gefühl: diesmal ist es ernst mit der Konkursmeldung. Es gibt keine Hoffnung und Hilfe mehr. Der Kapitalismus ist am Ende. In der Tat : das ist das Ende. Aber wo wäre ein Ende ohne neuen Anfang? Ein Untergang ohne Auferstehen ? Die Weltgeschichte geht weiter. Und so lange es Menschen gibt, die leben wollen, werden diese Menschen arbeiten, schaffen, wirtschaften, um ihr Leben zu fristen. Nicht die Wirtschaft geht zugrunde, sondern nur die Wirtschaft des Kapitalismus. Es ist die heute herrschende, in Europa und Amerika, in den fortgeschrittenen Regionen des Erdballs führende Wirtschaftsform, die zum Untergang verurteilt ist. Das Ende eines Systems. Nicht das Ende der Wirt- schaft überhaupt. Die Weltkrise wird zur Weltwende. Dem Niederbruch folgt Aufstieg. Das Chaos gebiert eine neue Ordnung. II Wirwissen noch nichts über Tempo, Art und Ausmaße der Ereignisse, die uns bevorstehen. Kennen nicht Dauer und Phasen des Prozesses, den wir durchlaufen müssen. Ahnen noch nicht die Kämpfe, die wir werden auszu- fechten haben. Nicht die Opfer, die eine erbarmungslose Entwicklung von uns verlangt. Wir tappen ins Ungewisse. Eins nur scheint uns gewiß zu sein: daß das nächste große System der Wirtschaft, das dem Kapitalismus not- wendig folgt, der Sozialismus sein wird. Zu ihm führt freilich ein langer Weg. Wahrscheinlich ein mühseliger, schwerer, opferreicherWeg mit vielen Stationen undÜber- gängen, Etappen und Zwischenräumen. Wenn nicht alle Zeichen trügen, ist die nächste Etappe dieser Menschheitswanderung eine Art Staatskapitalismus. Der Kurs der Geschichte, in deren Wirbeln wir stehen, ist auf ihn gerichtet. Folgen wir diesem Kurs!

title: Füsun Demirel calls on artists to march for women
content:
Actress and translator Füsun Demirel, who delivered a message against violence against women and femicides through ANF, stressed that artists must take responsibility for social issues.




Füsun Demirel drew attention to the fact that violence against women and femicides have become a deep social wound and a political issue. She said: "In this period, speaking out has become not merely a choice for artists, especially women artists, but a moral and humanitarian responsibility."




'We should not simply wait for money or awards'




Füsun Demirel said that actors do more than simply bring characters to life. She said: "Those who create art are not people who should simply produce their works, step aside and wait for awards or money. They should not be."




Füsun Demirel emphasised that artists are also witnesses to their times and the conscience of society. Demirel continued: "When a woman is killed, it is not only one life that ends. A future, a hope and a story also come to an end. We must become the voice of those unfinished stories. Our real responsibility is not to speak when and where everyone else is speaking, but to raise our voices when and where everyone else remains silent. Isn't it those silences that give birth to art?"




'Women artists were forced to behave like men'




Füsun Demirel also drew attention to male dominance in the arts, saying that it determines not only women's visibility but also how they are represented, which stories they can tell and whether they can become the subjects of their own stories.




Demirel said: "Women have been involved in art for centuries, but because they were not given the opportunity to express themselves as creators, they existed as the male artist's muse, the painter's model, the beautiful woman in a film or the self-sacrificing mother in a story. Women's stories were told, but because they were told from a male-dominated perspective, women were either wives, mistresses, mothers or victims. In other words, women were figures who merely complemented men's stories. Their rebellion, anger, objections and dreams were always treated as though they did not exist.




Even Bilge Olgaç, who established herself in the male-dominated world of Yeşilçam cinema and made films that brought women's stories to the forefront from a woman's perspective, was described as 'a director like a man'. In other words, we were forced to behave like men in order to survive in that world.




Of course, there are also things I have personally witnessed. For example, in one television series, the storyline had begun to focus more on the female lead, and the male lead immediately objected. The dispute escalated considerably, and the series eventually came to an end."




'

Sıdıka' memory: 'Whenever the father hit me, I hit back'




Füsun Demirel said that scripts which normalise violence deeply disturb her and that she tries to avoid such projects from the outset. However, she explained that problematic situations can sometimes emerge as a story develops and that she intervenes whenever possible.




Füsun Demirel described an incident from the television series Sıdıka. She said: "As much as possible, I avoid accepting such projects from the beginning. But sometimes situations develop later in the story. I intervene as much as I can. For example, in the series Sıdıka, there was constant violence by the father at home. It was a comedy series, filmed from a critical perspective. Nevertheless, to avoid legitimising violence against women, I eventually intervened one day. Whenever the father hit me, I hit back and defended myself. Our director was also a woman. She did not impose any limits on me. She said, 'Do whatever you want.' As a result, the male actor objected. He said, 'There is feminist solidarity on this set.' Filming stopped that day."




Füsun Demirel said that she takes inspiration from Iranian cinema. She said: "In the face of all forms of social and political oppression against women, directors in Iranian cinema have always found a way to speak out for women's freedom. Some were imprisoned, others were forced into exile. But they never refrained from speaking their minds."




'Those posing on red carpets should march for women for once'




Füsun Demirel also stressed that art should become a space of struggle and solidarity against violence against women. She made the following appeal: "Institutions representing the industry, such as the Actors' Union and the Writers' Union, as well as directors, should organise protests against femicides. Would it really be so bad if female actors, stars, those earning millions, those talented beauties who pose on red carpets every night at an opening, a premiere or a party, marched for murdered women for once?"

title: "Existence and Freedom" celebration in Grosseto
content:
An event entitled "Şahiya Hebûn û Azadî" ("Existence and Freedom" celebration) was held in the town of Castel del Piano, in the municipality of Grosseto, in Italy’s Tuscany region. Attended by dozens of Kurds from Kurdistan and their friends, the event highlighted the Kurdish people's historical struggle, their determination to exist and their will to achieve freedom.




The event began with a minute's silence in memory of the Martyrs of Kurdistan's Freedom Struggle, followed by a speech from FCDK Co-Chair Zübeyde Zümrüt. She spoke about the Kurdish people's struggle against policies of denial and assimilation, the historical significance of 27 November, and the Peace and Democratic Society Process.







 







27 November is the birthday of the Kurdish people and women




Describing 27 November as a significant date for the Kurdish people, Zübeyde Zümrüt characterised it as a symbol of the rebirth of the Kurdish people and women.




Zümrüt said that a major struggle had been waged against systems that had historically denied Kurdish identity, language, culture and existence. She stated that this struggle had been initiated by Leader Apo and his comrades.




Noting that the Kurdish people had been subjected to severe oppression and policies of denial and annihilation for many years, Zümrüt emphasised that the struggle being waged was important not only for the Kurdish people but also for all peoples seeking freedom and democracy.




Zümrüt said that different peoples and sections of society were now rallying around this struggle, adding that the Kurdish people's freedom struggle had also found significant international support.




Negotiations and struggle must go hand in hand




Stating that the Kurdish people had paid a heavy price throughout their struggle for freedom and lost thousands of lives, Zümrüt said that the state's willingness to sit at the negotiating table with Abdullah Öcalan today was a result of the struggle waged and the sacrifices made.




Emphasising, as Öcalan has also stated, that negotiations and struggle cannot be considered separately, Zümrüt said the struggle must continue through democratic and peaceful means if the Peace and Democratic Society Process is to move forward.




Drawing attention to the important responsibilities of Kurds living in Europe, Zümrüt called on Kurdish organisations, democratic circles and friends across Europe to give stronger support to the struggle for peace and a democratic society.




The state must take concrete steps




Stating that the state must take concrete steps without delay for the process to progress in a healthy manner, Zümrüt highlighted the importance of removing obstacles that prevent Öcalan from conducting the process through direct communication with all peoples.




Emphasising that peace cannot be achieved through words alone, Zümrüt underlined the need for democratisation, mutual dialogue and concrete action. She also stressed that Kurds living in Europe must strengthen their efforts to ensure the success of the process.




Following the speech by KCDK-E Co-Chair Zübeyde Zümrüt, the event continued with a musical programme. Accompanied by Kurdish songs performed by Hozan Comerd, people joined hands to dance the halay and sang along together.




The celebration, which placed Kurdish culture, music and community solidarity at its heart, continued late into the night in a lively and enthusiastic atmosphere.
