author: Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Guardians of the Buffalo: New bison-care guide supports efforts to bring iconic species home
content:
The three authors behind a new bison-care manual, 

Guardians of the Buffalo

, speak about their book at ‘Fort Qu’Appelle, Sask.’ in September during this year’s Treaty 4 Gathering. From left: the book’s photographer Johane Janelle, and co-writers Wes Olson and Cody Spencer.

 Photo by Brittany Boschman




Under the bright September sun, school buses arrived and departed from the valley as an announcer’s voice carried across the powwow grounds. 




Youth chatted, learned and moved between tipis for hands-on demonstrations during the 40th Annual Treaty 4 Gathering in Fort Qu’Appelle, Saskatchewan.




Inside one of the canvas tipis, a Buffalo hide lay near the entrance, where co-authors Wes Olson and Cody Spencer sat with photographer Johane Janelle to introduce a new book on bison care. 




The presentation was part of a September book tour for 

Guardians of the Buffalo: The Essential Guide to Bison Care

, which offers practical guidance for Indigenous communities, farmers and others interested in restoring and caring for bison herds




Spencer himself was first introduced to bison — and inspired to work as a rancher and herd manager — thanks to Olson’s first book, 

Portraits of the Bison

, which was co-written with Janelle, his spouse.




“I just caught the bug,” Spencer recalled, “and I just had to figure out ways to get involved with the species.”




He said the book grew out of the questions he and Olson have received from people interested in starting their own bison herds.




“One of the most frequent questions I’ve had during that time was from people who want to get into the industry: How do I start?” Olson said. “Where do I even begin?” 




The Fort Qu’Appelle event took place on Sept. 17, during the 

annual gathering

 to honour the 1874 treaty’s spirit and intent, bringing communities together to celebrate culture and share teachings with the next generations. Youth from surrounding communities attended the week-long gathering for its education days.




Decades of bison stewardship




Olson spent 32 years working in national parks, much of that time focused on bison management and establishing new wild populations. Spencer is a bison rancher from southwest Alberta who has managed several herds in Alberta and Texas.




“We’ve also been in the bison industry, raising bison in captivity for a long time,” Olson said. “Between us, I think we calculated 87 years of bison stewardship.”




Spencer grew up on a farm where his family raised grain and cattle. He said his lack of experience with bison initially allowed him to approach the animals without bringing assumptions about cattle management into his work.




“I didn’t have direct experience with bison, which can be a benefit for a lot of people,” Spencer said. “You’re not coming into management with preconceptions about how you need to be managing cattle and applying that to buffalo.”




He said his work has focused on finding management practices that benefit both the animals and the land.







READ MORE:

 

In Manitoba, a growing herd of bagwaji-bizhikiwag offers lessons in community







“We’re just always committed to finding out what are the best ways that we can manage these animals and caretake them for their own health,” Spencer said, “but also the health of the land.”




The book is intended to help readers understand the responsibilities involved in establishing and managing a herd. Its opening chapter includes a questionnaire to help readers consider the responsibilities involved in establishing and managing a herd.




“This is a manual,” Spencer said. “This is 

the

 manual.”




The remaining chapters combine technical information about bison management with cultural, ecological and conservation perspectives. Topics include animal care, fencing, water systems, handling facilities, herd management and land restoration. 




“There’s a lot that you need to know, and so it’s all in the book,” Spencer said.




One section of the book compares the physical characteristics of wood and plains buffalo, helping readers understand how to tell the two types apart. It also explains why maintaining genetic integrity is important when establishing and managing herds.




Guardians of the Buffalo

 explains differences between wood and plains bison, including why preserving their genetic integrity is important. 

Image courtesy International Buffalo Relations Institute




‘How to care for life’




The book is intended for a broad audience, including ranchers, conservationists, Indigenous caretakers seeking to return bison to their lands and people who simply want to learn more about the animals.




“It’s for everybody,” Spencer said.




“It’s a deep dive into how to care for life,” Olson said.




Technically, there are no ‘buffalo’ in North America. 




“We use the word ‘Buffalo’ as a cultural word, and ‘bison’ as a scientific word,” Janelle explains.




The book was published by the 

International Buffalo Relations Institute

 (IBRI), which supports the implementation of the 

Buffalo Treaty

.




First signed in 2014 by eight Indigenous Nations, the Buffalo Treaty is an agreement to support the return of Buffalo to their traditional territories and renew cultural, ecological and spiritual relationships with the animals.







READ MORE:

 

Travelling the Buffalo road: Indigenous nations are rematriating bison to the prairies




IN CREE:

 

e-pimohtâtamihk paskwâw mostos meskanaw







“The Buffalo Treaty is a treaty that was signed by 

60-some nations

 across North America,” Spencer said. 




“It was developed by individuals in Blackfoot Country to essentially promote the restoration of bison across North America.”




Janelle’s photographs illustrate the book’s technical information, including different fencing and water systems. They also show bison in conservation settings and provide visual examples of the relationship between the animals and the land.




“Sometimes photographs speak 1,000 words,” Janelle said.




She said photographs can help readers understand subjects such as fencing and water systems in ways that written explanations alone cannot.




An open page from 

Guardians of the Buffalo

 shows photographs of gates, water crossings and other infrastructure.




The book is designed to be visually engaging, rather than solely technical. 




“This is much more vibrant and more interesting to look at,” Olson said.







“I just caught the bug, and I just had to figure out ways to get involved with the species.”




—Cody Spencer







Inspiring the next generation




Olson said opportunities to establish conservation herds are limited, but Indigenous lands may provide important opportunities for bison restoration.




The authors also emphasized the importance of Youth education and cultural reconnection.




“If we plant the seed that they need to reconnect with their culture and learn more about them,” he said, “that’s my goal.”




Spencer said the book contains information he wished had been available when he first became interested in bison.




“This book is what I wish I had when I was starting out,” he said.




He also hopes the project will lead to more opportunities for people to learn directly from bison.




“There’s no replacement for that,” Spencer said. “You have to actually be with the animals and learn how they are, and what they require.”







READ MORE:

 

Cree filmmaker’s documentary explores ‘buffalo justice’ and a vision for herds returning







Spencer said the book is also intended to help create more opportunities for hands-on-learning.




Spencer is developing an on-site facility in southern Alberta where people could learn practical skills related to bison care and management.




“I would like to now develop more opportunities for people to come and actually learn hands-on,” he said.




An online 

Guardians of the Buffalo

 curriculum is being developed through the International Buffalo Relations Institute. The curriculum will adapt material from the book and include additional resources.




The authors hope to have the curriculum available online sometime this winter.




Olson, Spencer and Janelle will also take part in a 

free online conversation

 about the book on Dec. 3 at 7 p.m. MST, followed by a live question-and-answer period.




The post 

Guardians of the Buffalo: New bison-care guide supports efforts to bring iconic species home

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: Rose Nneoma Abba
title: Labors of liberation
content:
Ricci Shryock’s 

The Moon Will Not Burn Us

 is marketed as an account of the women who helped win the 11-year guerrilla war for independence from Portuguese colonial rule in Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Shryock’s book delivers on that promise with hyperrealistic scenes that drop you into mangrove forests where female teenagers and young adults shoot and dodge bullets, manage makeshift clinics, become mothers, devise new cooking technology, teach, gossip, and boil water for breakfast. 

It also exposes prejudice that women in the struggle faced at the hands of their fellow African men. A funny scene in the book exemplifies both the prejudice and the women’s handling of it. Shortly after Joana Gomes, a nurse and the book’s protagonist, joins a new base, the commander, who is also her distant cousin, threatens her that if she gets hurt, he will have to kill her. She replies that “as a nurse. . . .  even you, if you are injured and no-one can carry you I can give this medicine to you [to kill you].” As Carmen Pereira, a prominent guerrilla fighter with the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), nurse, and later acting head of state, famously observed: “In Guinea-Bissau, we say that women must fight against two colonialisms. One against the Portuguese, the other against men.”

But beyond illustrating women’s agency in the struggle, the book also offers timely provocations on our relationship with nature, the labor that sustains revolutions, elite-led movements, and the individual costs of collective struggle.

One of the book’s greatest strengths is its exploration of how the PAIGC’s vision of a future state manifested in practice long before victory was formally declared. The PAIGC was founded in 1956 to achieve independence for Guinea and Cape Verde from Portuguese colonial rule. For the party, building for the future state was just as vital as tearing down Portuguese colonial rule. 

This state-building effort is most visible in the book’s heartwarming scenes of education. We witness it when Joana’s father goes out of his way to secure teachers for his daughters. And again when 11-year-old Joana and her friends are instructed by Amílcar Cabral to teach the other teenagers on a boat trip from Guinea-Bissau to Guinea-Conakry. We learn that the PAIGC built 156 primary schools during the war across liberated territories compared to 11 created under Portuguese neglect. We also see the PAIGC send young Guineans to the Soviet Union and Cuba to master guerrilla combat tactics as well as medicine, engineering, agronomy, and teaching for the nation they were bringing into existence.

The book takes a firm stand: The success of a liberation struggle depends on the viable, egalitarian alternative structure you build to ground your sovereignty while you fight the oppressive power. As Shryock writes in the introduction, it is “a story worth knowing as a universal lesson in the undeniable courage it takes to imagine a new world, the way creation rather than destruction is integral to that new world.” Through Joana’s story, Shryock holds a steady lens on women’s central role in designing and executing that vital labor of building Guinean sovereignty from the ground up.

Shryock opens the book with a scene that haunts the entire reading experience: 22-year-old Joana inside a dry-season mangrove forest, where she had gone to retrieve a commander who was recovering from a lung infection. “Gnarly, bare mangrove branches protruding from the muddy riverbed stare back at [Joana],” setting the tone for the book from the very first page. 

The land, its trees, and its waters are alive. At times angry, at times hungry, mostly gracious, and systematically exploited by the Portuguese regime. And it was precisely this ecological exploitation that precipitated the revolution. Cabral, the founder of the PAIGC, was an agronomist by training, and his radicalization took root while he was conducting an agricultural census commissioned by the United Nations and the colonial Portuguese government. There, he saw firsthand how Portuguese land policies and price controls were squeezing the life out of both the land and the people tilling it.

As the Guineans fought for the land, the land protected them. Whether it is Joana tripping over an exposed root and narrowly dodging a bullet or people abandoning their towns to seek shelter in the forest, “besides the Soviets and the Cubans, the land [proved] to be the liberation fighters’ best ally,” Shryock writes.

Shryock’s writing of the gritty realities of the fighters’ encounter with nature serves as a necessary reminder that human survival ultimately rests on a nurturing and reciprocal relationship with the land. And by foregrounding and animating the landscape, the book invites an ecofeminist reading that exposes how colonial extraction of the land and gendered oppression draw from the same logic of subjugation that treats both the earth and women’s labor as infinite, free resources to be exploited without consequence.

It is understandable to witness a guerrilla war and assume the war began as a grassroots uprising. Shryock’s narration contributes to this illusion when she writes that “so, too, did the armed struggle not start in the capital. . . .  but deep in the countryside. . . .  in a rural and relatively isolated area,” referring to the first battle of the war in January 1963. Meanwhile, the party that led and coordinated the war’s efforts, including this battle, was founded in 1956 by urban Cape Verdeans.

History teaches us that even when elites carry the flag of revolution, popular discontent has usually fermented long before elite leadership articulates it. So it was with the PAIGC: They did not invent anticolonial anger, but they used their privileges to initiate and organize the revolution. The book shows the immense labor it took for urban, landowning, or comparatively privileged 

assimilado

 figures like Cabral and Joana to spread their vision of freedom, convincing rural people why their anticolonial rebellion mattered, why it could succeed, and why they should risk their lives for it. And as the war unfolds, readers experience the claustrophobia of the central command. We see Joana suddenly run into her cousins, siblings, or childhood neighbors leading command bases or brought to her care as wounded soldiers.

The story is marked by internal rivalries and tensions over regional and class privilege, frictions that the Portuguese constantly tried to exploit. In its realism, the book offers a historical case study for a vital question in contemporary political discourse: When privilege exists, what is the moral responsibility of those who hold it?

The Moon Will Not Burn Us

 makes clear how staggering the individual cost of collective struggle can be. By and large, the revolution was fought by kids and teenagers who never had the chance to discover who they were before the historic weight of a national movement for independence decided for them. Once, when he heard that Carmen Pereira was reluctant to leave her children for a mission to the Soviet Union, Cabral asked her, “Who do you love more: your country or your children?” Pereira eventually answered, “My homeland.”

Postcolonial African societies today may no longer face formal imperial rule, but the fight for justice, dignity, and self-determination is far from over. Oppressive systems persist through deeply entrenched forms of economic, social, political, and psychological control and exploitation. Beyond its account of women’s participation in the independence struggle, Shryock’s book reminds us that true liberation is never achieved only by tearing down an old order. It also requires the rigorous, daily work of creating a more just world in its place.

title: BM Genel Kurulu, Filistin halkının bağımsızlık hakkına ilişkin tasarıyı 162 oyla kabul etti
content:
Fotoğraf: Basil D Soufi/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 3.0

BM Genel Kurulu’nda ilistin halkının kendi kaderini tayin etme ve bağımsızlık hakkını teyit eden karar taslağı kabul edildi.

İnsan hakları ve insani işlerle ilgilenen Genel Kurulun 3. Komitesi tarafından sunulan tasarı oylandı.

Oylamada 162 ülke, Filistin halkının kendi kaderini tayin etme ve bağımsızlık hakkını teyit eden tasarıya "evet" oyu verirken, 8 ülke "hayır" oyu kullandı, 8 ülke ise çekimser kaldı.

Lehte oy kullanan ülkeler arasında Türkiye başta olmak üzere tüm Avrupa Birliği üye devletleri, Kanada, Avustralya ile Güney Amerika, Asya ve Afrika'daki ülkelerin çoğunluğu yer alırken, ABD, İsrail, Arjantin, Paraguay, Mikronezya, Nauru, Papua Yeni Gine ve Palau aleyhte oy kullandı.

Karar, Filistin halkının İsrail işgalinden uzak, kendi topraklarında özgürce yaşama ve bağımsız olma hakkının devredilemez olduğunu teyit ediyor. Ayrıca bu hakkın koşulsuz, vazgeçilemez, müzakere edilemez veya uzlaşmaya konu edilemez olduğunu vurguluyor.

author: Unknown
title: 25 ülkede gençler "gelecekleri için ve savaşlara karşı" sokaktaydı
content:
20 Kasım Cuma günü, Avrupa'da öğrenciler ve genç emekçiler,“Geleceğimiz için mücadele, onların savaşları için değil” çağrısıyla sokaklara çıktı. 50'yi aşkın gençlik ve öğrenci örgütünün oluşturduğu Uluslararası Gençlik Grevi Koalisyonu'nun çağrısıyla 25'ten fazla ülkede düzenlenen gösterilerde eğitim ve sosyal hizmetlere daha fazla kaynak ayrılması, barınma hakkı, insanca ücretler, iklim adaleti ve silahlanma harcamalarının azaltılması istendi.



















"GELECEĞİMİZ İÇİN ONLARIN SAVAŞLARINA KARŞI"




Avrupa, 20 Kasım'a en az 25 ülkede gençlik grevleriyle uyanıyor




Bugün  03:59










Roma'dan Lizbon'a, Paris'ten Londra'ya uzanan eylemlerde ortak talepler öne çıksa da katılımın ölçeği ve protestoların gündemi yerel önceliklere de bağlı olarak ülkeden ülkeye değişti. En kitlesel gösteriler İtalya'da gerçekleşirken diğer ülkelerde de yürüyüşlerde binlerce kişi bir araya geldi. 




Koalisyon yaklaşık 400 kentte eylem planlandığını açıklamıştı. Gerçekleşme düzeyi henüz net olarak belirlenmedi. .




İtalya: Gençlik eylemleri genel grevle birleşti




Günün en geniş katılımlı gösterileri İtalya'daydı. Ülkenin en büyük sendika konfederasyonu CGIL'in ücret artışı ve kamu hizmetlerine daha fazla yatırım talebiyle düzenlediği genel greve öğrenciler de katıldı.




Roma, Milano, Bologna ve diğer kentlerde on binlerce işçi ve öğrenci yürüdü. CGIL Genel Sekreteri Maurizio Landini, 100'den fazla kentteki gösterilere toplam bir milyondan fazla kişinin katıldığını ileri sürdü. İçişleri Bakanlığı ise kendi bulgularını açıklamadı. 




Landini, Roma'daki gösteride Avrupa çapındaki hareketle dayanışmasını şu sözlerle dile getirdi:







“Bugün çok önemli bir gün. Çünkü yalnızca İtalya'da değil, Avrupa'nın dört bir yanında gençler sokaklara çıkıyor.




“Avrupa genelinde ve sıradan insanlar arasında değişim talebi büyüyor.”







 Başbakan Giorgia Meloni hükümetinin 2027 bütçesine yönelik tepkiler grevin odağındaydı. Sendikalar, ücretlerin ve sosyal hizmetlerin desteklenmesi, eğitim ve sağlığa daha fazla kaynak ayrılması talebini yükseltti. 




24 yaşındaki üniversite öğrencisi Laura Peritore, hükümetin tercihlerini şöyle eleştirdi:







“Sağlık ve eğitim harcamalarını parça parça kesen, bugünümüzü elimizden alan ve geleceğimizi çalmaya çalışan bir hükümetin yönetimi altında yaşıyoruz.”







Peritore, geri çekilmeyeceklerini ve geleceklerini geri alacaklarını söyledi.




Roma'da Eğitim Bakanlığı önünde gösteriler düzenlendi. Bologna'da bazı protestocularla polis arasında çatışmalar yaşandı. Milano'da ise göstericiler kartondan yapılmış bir tankeri ve Donald Trump ile Binyamin Netanyahu'yu temsil eden maketleri yaktı.




Fransa: Süren öğrenci hareketinden Avrupa dayanışmasına




Avrupa çapındaki eylem çağrısının arka planında, Fransa'da haftalardır devam eden lise ve üniversite protestoları da bulunuyor.




Eğitim koşullarının kötüleşmesine, kamu hizmetlerindeki kesintilere ve toplumsal eşitsizliklere karşı gelişen hareket, 20 Kasım'da Avrupa'nın diğer ülkelerindeki gençlik örgütleriyle ortak talepler etrafında buluştu.




Paris'teki gösteride konuşan 25 yaşındaki öğrenci Evelyn, hayat pahalılığı ile iklim krizinin gençlerin gelecek kaygısını birlikte derinleştirdiğini söyledi:







“Kararları bugün veren insanlara bırakırsak bizi, ölümle dolu bir gelecek bekliyor.”







Fransa'dan Union Étudiante temsilcisi Alice Cohen ise uluslararası eylemin tek günlük bir protestoyla sınırlı kalmaması gerektiğini vurguladı:







“Ne kadar büyük olursa olsun, tek günlük bir grevin ihtiyacımız olan değişiklikleri sağlamaya yetmeyeceğini biliyoruz.”







Cohen, öğrencileri ve emekçileri ortak talepler etrafında birleştirecek kalıcı bir uluslararası hareket oluşturmayı hedeflediklerini belirtti.




Portekiz ve İspanya: Barınma hakkı ve sosyal adalet




Lizbon'da öğrenciler ortak grev çağrısına katılırken Portekizli gençlik örgütleri barınma krizini, eğitim hakkını ve Avrupa'nın silahlanma politikalarını gündeme taşıdı.




Estudantes pelo Fim ao Fóssil örgütünden Leonor Chicó, gençlerin kendi geleceklerini savunmak için örgütlenmeleri gerektiğini söyledi:







“Gençler olarak geleceğimiz için örgütlenmemiz ve mücadele etmemiz gerektiğini biliyoruz. Çünkü bunu bizim yerimize kimse yapmayacak.”







Chicó, Avrupa Birliği'nin 

Readiness 2030

 adıyla yürüttüğü, 800 milyar avroya kadar savunma yatırımı seferber etmeyi hedefleyen planını eleştirerek kaynakların eğitim, barınma ve sosyal refaha yönlendirilmesini istedi.




İspanya da uluslararası grev çağrısına katılan ülkeler arasındaydı. Buradaki eylemlerde sosyal haklar ve silahlanma karşıtlığı ortak gündemin parçalarını oluşturdu. Ancak ülke çapında doğrulanmış bir katılım toplamı henüz bulunmuyor.




Britanya: “Dersi kırmıyordum, hayatta kalmak için çalışıyordum”




Londra'da Parlamento Meydanı ve Whitehall çevresindeki gösterilere yüzlerce kişi katıldı. Öğrenciler eğitim maliyetlerini, geçim sıkıntısını, savaş politikalarını ve iklim krizini protesto etti.




Bir göstericinin taşıdığı pankart, gençlerin ekonomik koşullarını özetliyordu:







“Ders kırmıyordum, hayatta kalmak için çalışıyordum.”







Yürüyüşte savaş, ırkçılık, iklim krizi ve kapitalizm karşıtı sloganlar taşındı.




Britanya'dan Stop the War Coalition temsilcisi Shabbir Lakha, eylemleri gençleri, öğrencileri ve işçileri ortak talepler etrafında buluşturabilecek kalıcı bir uluslararası hareketin kurulması açısından önemli bir adım olarak değerlendirdi.




Almanya: Eğitim kesintilerine ve zorunlu askerliğe karşı




Almanya'da 

Gen Z regelt

 hareketi 73 kentte gösteri çağrısı yaptı. Köln'de binlerce öğrenci eğitim bütçesindeki kesintilere karşı yürürken Berlin'de yaklaşık 4 bin kişi toplandı.




Köln'deki gösteriye katılan üniversite öğrencisi Jasmin Hamadi, eğitim alanındaki kesintilere tepki gösterdi:







“Her yerde kesinti yapılmasından hiç memnun değilim. Ne üniversitemde ne genel olarak eğitim sisteminde ne de okullarda. Bu yüzden buradayım; bir değişim için ses çıkarmak istiyorum.”







Almanya'daki eylemlerde, hükümetin askerlik politikaları ve zorunlu askerliğin geri getirilmesi ihtimali de öne çıkan konular arasındaydı.




Avrupa çapında ortak talepler, farklı katılım düzeyleri




Avusturya, Belçika, Yunanistan, Hırvatistan ve İsveç de uluslararası eylem dalgasında adı geçen ülkeler arasındaydı. Bununla birlikte bu ülkelerdeki gösterilere ilişkin kent ve katılımcı sayıları henüz aynı düzeyde doğrulanabilmiş değil.




Eylemlerin ortak bildirgesinde beş talep öne çıktı: Silahlanmanın ve zorunlu askerliğin sona erdirilmesi; eğitim ve sosyal hizmetlere yapısal yatırım; Filistin halkıyla dayanışma; iklim ve sosyal adalet; mevcut ekonomik ve siyasal düzende köklü dönüşüm.




İtalya'dan Rete della Conoscenza temsilcisi Alessandro Di Miceli, ulusal hareketlerin farklı sorunlarla karşı karşıya olsalar da ortak bir gelecek talebinde buluştuklarını söyledi:







“Mücadelelerimiz farklı ülkelerde farklı biçimler alabilir, ama hepimiz aynı talep etrafında birleşiyoruz: Eğitim, barınma ve sosyal haklara erişebildiğimiz, uğruna mücadele etmeye değer bir gelecek.”







Koalisyon, 20 Kasım eylemlerini bir başlangıç olarak görüyor. Bazı ülkelerde 21 ve 22 Kasım'da da gösterilerin sürmesi planlanıyor.

title: Iraqi army takes control of Jurf al-Sakhar, stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah
content:
The Iraqi central government has taken control of security in the Jurf al-Sakhar region, which has been dominated by the pro-Iranian militia Kataib Hezbollah for more than a decade. On Friday, army units and other security forces entered the town, located approximately 60 kilometers southwest of Baghdad. The deployment followed an agreement that temporarily averted an armed confrontation between government forces and the influential militia.




Jurf al-Sakhar, renamed Jurf al-Nasr by Shiite militias after its recapture from the Islamic State (ISIS) in 2014, is considered one of Kataib Hezbollah’s most important strongholds. The Iran-aligned militia has spent years establishing military structures there largely independently of the Iraqi central government. Baghdad’s attempt to regain control is therefore seen as a major test for Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.




Joint security command assumes responsibilities




According to Iraqi security officials, a joint command comprising units of the army, federal police, Popular Mobilization Forces (Hashd al-Shaabi), and police responsible for energy infrastructure began operating on Friday morning. The new command structure is expected to gradually assume responsibility for security and coordinate the withdrawal of the militia units previously stationed in the area. According to Iraqi government spokesperson Saad Maan, security forces have already begun monitoring the oil pipelines running through the region.




A major road link toward Karbala is also scheduled to reopen on Saturday. Units of the Iraqi army and federal police are expected to secure the route. The agreement stipulates that Kataib Hezbollah groups will leave the area and make way for state security forces. However, it remains unclear whether the militia will actually lose its longstanding influence over the region. The handover is expected to take place over an extended period.




Press conference by Iraqi officials




Iraqi officials held a press conference on the security situation in the Jurf al-Sakhar region on Friday.




Speaking here, Ahmed Hatim Hamid, commander of the Main Control Base, announced that a base had been established for the Iraqi army and police forces. He also reported that the Chief of Staff of the Iraqi Army had visited the region to monitor the deployment of military forces and inspect the measures taken.




The spokesperson for the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces stated that all administrative and management responsibilities in the Jurf al-Sakhar region had been transferred to the control base.




Meanwhile, the head of the Security Media Cell announced that a commando battalion had been deployed to the region to protect its oil pipelines. Stating that handover procedures were underway between the forces in the area, the head of the Security Media Cell said that security in the Jurf al-Sakhar region would now be under the control of federal forces.







Oil smuggling triggered power struggle




The latest confrontation was sparked by investigations into an alleged network involved in the illegal trade of Iraqi oil. According to an investigation by the Reuters news agency, members of Kataib Hezbollah, together with individuals from state security agencies and oil authorities, are suspected of having diverted crude oil from pipelines and smuggled it for years. Investigators reportedly discovered tampered pipelines, concealed pumping facilities, and a small refinery. The financial losses could amount to several hundred million dollars. Kataib Hezbollah denies the allegations and views the government’s actions as an attempt to force the militia to surrender its weapons.




In connection with the investigations, Prime Minister al-Zaidi ordered the dismissal of nine senior officials from security agencies and the oil sector. At the same time, government troops were placed on alert and prepared for a possible operation against the militia. The escalating tensions eventually led to negotiations involving influential Shiite politicians. Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Quds Force, also reportedly traveled to Baghdad to mediate between the parties. The handover now underway is seen as the outcome of these talks.




Closed off to the local population since 2014




The developments also affect the former residents of Jurf al-Sakhar. Before the town was captured by ISIS in 2014, it and the surrounding area were predominantly inhabited by Sunni families. Following its recapture by Shiite militias, residents were displaced or prevented from returning. Kataib Hezbollah subsequently transformed the area into a largely sealed-off military zone. Secret detention facilities are also believed to have been established there alongside military installations. The displaced population was barred from returning for years. With the deployment of state security forces, the question has once again arisen as to whether restrictions on access to the area will be lifted and displaced residents allowed to return. So far, no concrete commitments or timetable have been announced.

title: Solidarity reception for Rojava at New South Wales parliament
content:
The Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia (FDKS-A), the Sydney Democratic Kurdish Community Centre, and the Sydney Kurdish Youth Association organized a solidarity reception for Rojava at the Parliament of New South Wales (NSW), Australia.




Speaking at the event, members of parliament expressed their support for the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom, peace, and democracy. Representatives of political parties, civil society organizations, and members of the Kurdish community attended the reception.




Greens MP Abigail Boyd described the resistance in Kobanê as a symbol of international solidarity and the right of peoples to self-defense, affirming her party’s solidarity with the Kurdish people.




Labor Party MP Charishma Kaliyanda emphasized that Kobanê had become a symbol of courage, resistance, and, in particular, women’s struggle for freedom.




Liberal Party MP Justin Clancy also highlighted the significance of the Kurds’ struggle against ISIS for Australia and the wider world.




FDKS-A (Federation of Democratic Kurdish Societies in Australia) Co-Chair Gülfer Olan stated that the resistance in Kobanê was a struggle that concerned not only the Kurdish people but all of humanity, stressing that protecting the achievements of Rojava was a shared responsibility.




Baran Söğüt, spokesperson for the Federation’s Diplomacy Commission, commemorated Australian YPG volunteers 

Reece Harding

, 

Ashley Johnson

, and Jamie Bright, who lost their lives in the fight against ISIS in Rojava.




Michelle Harding, the mother of YPG internationalist Reece Harding (Bagok Serhed) who fell in Rojava in 2015, praised the Kurdish fighters for putting up remarkable resistance despite their limited resources. “I have enormous respect for them. Despite everything they went through, they managed to find solutions with the limited resources available to them,” she said.




The event also addressed the significance of the traditional floral-patterned headscarf symbolizing the resistance of Kurdish women, the Yazidi community’s solidarity with the resistance in Kobanê, and the Kurdish people’s struggle.




Speaking on behalf of the Reverend Bill Crews Foundation, Dr. Anjalika Wijesurendra reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining solidarity with the Kurdish people and their struggle for freedom.




The reception concluded with chants of “Bijî Kobanê” and “Bijî Berxwedana Rojava” and a musical performance.

title: COP31: Women’s organizations criticize inequitable distribution of climate finance
content:
Criticism of international climate finance is mounting at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya. Women’s rights and environmental organizations accuse industrialized countries of failing to adequately meet their financial commitments and disadvantaging the populations most affected by the climate crisis in the allocation of funds. They say the focus is not only on the amount of funding pledged, but also on who decides how it is used and which initiatives actually gain access to international climate funds.




On Thursday, the Women and Gender Constituency (WGC), a coalition of women’s rights and gender organizations involved in the UN climate negotiations, highlighted significant shortcomings in funding for climate adaptation measures, the participation of local communities, and a socially just energy transition. Together with other civil society organizations, it is calling for public climate finance to be directed specifically toward the people and communities most severely affected by the consequences of global warming.




Little funding reaches women-led initiatives




Figures from the Dutch environmental and development organization Both ENDS illustrate how unequally international climate finance is distributed. According to the organization, only around 0.1 percent of global climate finance goes to initiatives supporting women and the environment. Women’s organizations and local communities developing their own solutions to the impacts of the climate crisis thus receive only a tiny fraction of the available funding.




The Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action (GAGGA) points to another figure: Just 0.22 percent of climate-related official development finance reaches women’s rights organizations. Although the two figures are based on different definitions and scopes, the organizations argue that both highlight the structural barriers faced particularly by smaller initiatives.




International climate funds are largely administered through governments, development banks, and major institutions. For local women’s organizations, complicated application procedures, demanding administrative requirements, and short funding periods often pose significant obstacles. Daan Robben, who is responsible for locally led climate finance at Both ENDS, criticizes the notion that merely promising public participation is sufficient. Instead, women’s organizations and local communities need direct access to flexible, long-term funding.




Adaptation Fund falls far short of funding target




The funding gap is also evident in the international Adaptation Fund, which supports developing countries in addressing the impacts of climate change that have already occurred or are anticipated. Among other things, the fund supports projects aimed at protecting communities from droughts and floods, securing water supplies, and strengthening local livelihoods. At a high-level funding meeting on November 17, only Spain, Germany, and Ireland announced new contributions. Together with earlier pledges from Estonia, Portugal, and the Belgian region of Brussels, the announced contributions totaled US$50 million by the following day.




This means that only one-sixth of the annual minimum target of $300 million has been met. In a joint statement issued on November 18, the WGC and other civil society coalitions described the contributions as wholly inadequate. They called on industrialized countries to provide additional funding before the climate conference concludes.




The scale of the funding gap becomes clear when compared with actual needs. According to calculations by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), developing countries will require approximately $305 billion annually by 2035 to adapt to climate change. Taking inflation into account, this figure could rise to around $420 billion. The organizations emphasize that additional funding must not lead to further indebtedness among the affected countries. Instead of loans, they are calling for grants that do not have to be repaid and can be used as directly as possible for local adaptation measures.




Public responsibility instead of dependence on investors




Underlying the dispute over funding is a fundamental question of international climate policy. Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement obliges industrialized countries to provide financial support to developing countries for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and adapting to the impacts of climate change. Women’s organizations warn against increasingly shifting this responsibility onto private investors. While private-sector investment can help finance the energy transition, many essential adaptation measures offer no immediate financial returns.




These include, for example, protecting small farms from droughts, improving water supplies in remote regions, and implementing local measures to prevent damage from flooding and extreme heat. Such projects are vital for the communities affected but are often of little interest to profit-driven investors. The WGC is therefore calling for a climate finance system guided by human rights and social needs. Public funding must be provided reliably rather than leaving its allocation largely to market mechanisms.




Energy transition must address social inequalities




Another key focus of the debates in Antalya is the social conditions under which the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy takes place. Ecofeminist Melania Chiponda of the international network Shine Collab warns against reducing the energy transition to technological modernization and the replacement of energy sources. She stressed that a just transition must also take into account people who currently lack adequate access to energy or live and work under precarious conditions.




Women’s organizations point out that new solar installations, electric vehicles, and investments in renewable energy do not, in themselves, guarantee socially equitable energy access. What matters, they argue, is whether previously disadvantaged communities gain access to affordable electricity, schools and hospitals receive a reliable energy supply, and new employment opportunities are created. Accordingly, the distribution of economic benefits must also be taken into account. Women and informal workers must not be excluded from new jobs and decision-making structures.




GAGGA also warns of the risk that the energy transition could perpetuate existing forms of exploitation, stating that the extraction of raw materials for new energy technologies could involve land dispossession and violations of the rights of Indigenous communities. The alliance therefore advocates community-led energy projects, the protection of natural resources, and greater recognition of unpaid care work.




Participation also means decision-making power




The demands of women’s organizations extend beyond increased financial support. They are also calling for a fundamental transformation of decision-making structures within international climate policy. Pabrya Lobos, who works on climate adaptation policy within the framework of the climate negotiations, emphasized that women and local communities must be involved in developing and implementing the programs that directly affect their living conditions.




According to the organizations, inviting women representatives to conferences or listening to their experiences during consultation processes is not enough. They must also have a say in deciding which projects receive funding, which priorities are set, and how the available resources are allocated. The experiences of women, girls, Indigenous communities, and other particularly affected population groups should therefore not merely be taken into account as an additional consideration but should form a foundation of climate policy.




More than 2,600 local initiatives supported




GAGGA points to its own funding practices as evidence that more locally focused financing is possible. According to the alliance, more than €50 million has so far been channeled to over 2,600 initiatives led by women and local communities across 60 countries. The funded projects address issues including forest protection, biodiversity conservation, the restoration of degraded soils, and strengthening the resilience of local communities to climate-related disasters.




GAGGA emphasizes that such initiatives need more than short-term project funding. According to the alliance, flexible, multi-year funding commitments are essential to enable them to operate effectively over the long term. The organizations and networks that connect local groups and facilitate their access to funding must also be strengthened.




As COP31 draws to a close, women’s and environmental organizations are calling on governments to move beyond general statements of intent. They are demanding additional public funding for climate change adaptation, binding financing mechanisms that do not create debt, and policies to ensure a socially just energy transition. The WGC emphasizes that the success of the climate negotiations must not be measured solely by the decisions adopted. What matters, it argues, is whether these decisions lead to tangible improvements for women, workers, Indigenous peoples, and communities particularly affected by the climate crisis.

title: “Tree of Remembrance” created for murdered women in Amed
content:
Since Friday, a “Tree of Remembrance” in Sümer Park in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) has commemorated women who were murdered in the city over the past two years. The Women’s Council of the Metropolitan Municipality attached the names of the murdered women to the branches of a tree to preserve their life stories in collective memory. The initiative was organized as part of events marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.




At the unveiling of the memorial tree, Rojda Çeçen from the Women’s Council Secretariat stated that violence against women was not limited to acts of violence themselves. “Looking the other way is also part of the violence. Confronting violence is therefore a shared responsibility of society as a whole," she emphasized.




Çeçen particularly commemorated two women who have been murdered in Sümer Park only recently. She said the pain of their deaths was still deeply felt. "The names attached to the tree represent not only individual victims of femicide but also lives cut short, voices silenced, and women whose memory must not be erased," she stated.













“Remembrance also means responsibility”




Özden Gürbüz Sümer, head of the Metropolitan Municipality’s Department of Women’s Policies, explained that the project had been jointly developed and implemented by the Women’s Council. She said the tree was intended not only to create a place of remembrance but also to encourage people to reflect on their own responsibilities.




“Sometimes we find it difficult to remember what we cannot see. With this Tree of Remembrance, we want not only to make these women visible but also to encourage people to take responsibility for what they see,” Sümer explained.













“May its roots strengthen collective memory”




Sümer continued: "In this way, the life stories of the murdered women are intended to become a lasting part of collective memory and the history of the women’s struggle. Remembrance must give rise to a sense of responsibility that strengthens solidarity and advances the struggle for a life of equality, freedom, and freedom from violence."




In closing, Sümer drew on the symbolism of the tree: “May its roots strengthen collective memory, while its branches reach toward a future free from violence.” She also pledged to continue the struggle against violence against women so that no more names would have to be added to the tree.

title: Kurdish women discuss shared political perspectives in Sulaymaniyah
content:
Representatives of women’s organizations from all four parts of Kurdistan gathered in Sulaymaniyah on Friday to discuss political developments in the region, national unity, and the future of the Kurdish women’s movement. Organized by the Platform for the National Unity of Kurdish Women, the meeting also serves as preparation for the third Conference on the National Unity of Kurdish Women. The central question is how women’s organizations can develop common positions amid political upheavals and strengthen their participation in decision-making processes.




In addition to representatives of women’s organizations, the gathering is attended by women politicians, activists, and other prominent figures from Kurdistan. In her opening speech, Şîrîn Tahir described the meeting as an important and decisive step in shaping the platform’s future work.




Tahir outlined three main priorities: assessing political developments in Kurdistan and the Middle East and their impact on women’s rights, critically reviewing the work carried out so far, and making organizational preparations for the third women’s conference. The aim, she said, was to bring Kurdish women’s collective strength and capacity for action into closer alignment across the borders of all four parts of Kurdistan.










https://rojnews.video/upload/videos/2026/11/w9XHyjDvqAHxEhNecCQM_20_5c6c0282c82d8f10f993c5ab1d3a7e1e_video_1080p_converted.mp4










Prioritizing national unity over party-political interests




During the first session, participants discussed the political challenges facing the Kurdish people and the impact of regional shifts in power on women’s rights and political status. It was emphasized that Kurdish women are internationally recognized as members of a single people, regardless of which part of Kurdistan they come from. “This shared identity must be matched by stronger political cooperation.”




The participants stressed that the national unity of Kurdish women must not be subordinated to party-political interests. Instead, they underlined, autonomous women’s organizing must take a leading role in developing shared political perspectives.




At the same time, participants warned against leaving the current transformations solely in the hands of existing, predominantly male-dominated power structures. They pointed put that, without women taking an active leadership role, there was a risk that political decisions would continue to be shaped by patriarchal attitudes. “The Kurds are not powerless in the face of the changes taking place in the Middle East. Through democratic struggle and collective political action, they can strengthen their rights and political status,” participants emphasized during the discussions.













Southern Kurdistan: Warning against political division




The political situation in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) featured prominently in the discussions. The participants strongly opposed any division of the region or weakening of its political status. In their assessment, such developments would primarily serve the interests of Turkey, Iran, and the Syrian transitional government, leaving the people of Southern Kurdistan more vulnerable to external interference.




The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) were therefore urged not to pursue their political differences at the expense of existing achievements. “Preserving the region’s political status must take precedence over party-political disputes,” the participants demanded.




The participants identified democracy, social unity, and political freedom as fundamental prerequisites for safeguarding these achievements. In this context, they also discussed a message from Abdullah Öcalan to the political forces of Southern Kurdistan, in which he had emphasized the formation of a democratic government and women’s participation in leadership as important steps toward overcoming the current situation.




The participants criticized the widespread exclusion of women from political decision-making processes. As a concrete initiative, they proposed forming a women’s delegation to hold talks with political parties and other political actors. The delegation, they said, would advocate for the protection of the political status of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq and the effective participation of women.













Rojava: Recognition of Kurdish rights in the integration process




Another key focus was developments in Rojava and the political restructuring of Syria. The participants discussed the ongoing integration process, the future of the autonomous administration structures, and how the rights of the Kurdish population could be safeguarded within a new political order. The integration process was described as difficult and sensitive. According to participants, further efforts will be needed to ensure that the Kurds are recognized as a distinct social and political component of Syria.




The participants emphasized the importance of a social contract that would define Syria’s future political order and ensure meaningful Kurdish participation in political decision-making. “This must not be merely about the formal recognition of Kurdish existence. What matters is that Kurds are able to participate in shaping political and social structures.”




The efforts made so far to defend Kurdish rights and organize society were acknowledged, but were also considered insufficient. The participants called for continued support for democratic integration efforts, stronger grassroots organization, and greater political capacity for action among the Kurdish population.










https://rojnews.video/upload/videos/2026/11/gvTa4EsLd1tSAhdsmTRJ_20_9a769dfebbe9e7c32b7cdc113fa76622_video_1080p_converted.mp4










Eastern Kurdistan: Repression and death sentences against women




The situation in Eastern Kurdistan was also discussed in detail. The discussions focused on the economic and political crises in Iran, the ongoing repression of the Kurdish population, and the impact of regional conflicts. The participants pointed to the execution of at least 691 people of various national backgrounds since the beginning of the year, as well as death sentences imposed on several Kurdish women. They interpreted the state repression as a reflection of the Iranian regime’s fear of social resistance and independent political organizing.




At the same time, the participants warned of the consequences of regional power struggles, stating that the current external pressure would not necessarily lead to the end of the Iranian regime. Conversely, they said, a strengthening of the existing regime could further jeopardize the rights and security of the Kurdish population. Against this backdrop, the participants emphasized the need for an independent political strategy for Eastern Kurdistan. “The Kurds must have a clear strategy for protecting their population and securing recognition of their national identity.”




Particular importance was attached to raising the international visibility of women in Eastern Kurdistan. It was stressed that their experiences of repression, political demands, and resistance must receive greater attention worldwide.




Third women’s conference aims to deepen cooperation




Alongside current political developments, the organizational future of the platform is also on the agenda. Şîrîn Tahir explained in her opening remarks that previous activities and experiences are to be critically evaluated in order to draw lessons for future cooperation. The planned third Conference on the National Unity of Kurdish Women is intended to help renew organizational structures and bring the forces of the women’s movement closer together. To this end, the meeting in Sulaymaniyah is expected to develop concrete preparatory steps, working mechanisms, and shared political perspectives.

title: Bakırhan: The goal of the peace process is democracy and equal citizenship
content:
Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), criticized the Turkish government’s budget policies and outlined the objectives of the ongoing peace process at a meeting with civil society organizations in Mersin. The event was held as part of the DEM Party’s campaign, "Budget for Bread, Peace and Justice.” Bakırhan began by highlighting the social diversity of Mersin, where people of different backgrounds and faiths live together. He said the city, with its strong tradition of social and trade union struggles, could serve as an example for the whole of Turkey.




Budget not being used to meet the people’s needs




Referring to the budget deliberations, Bakırhan accused the government of spending tax revenues primarily on armaments, conflict-driven policies, interest payments, and companies with close ties to the government, rather than on the needs of the people. By contrast, he said, the DEM Party sought to prioritize the interests of workers, pensioners, women, young people, and low-income groups.




The DEM Party Co-Chair was particularly critical of rising child poverty, stating that many students could no longer afford their education expenses or were having to contribute to their families’ income. He described the rejection of proposals for free school meals in parliament as shameful: “One of the most shameful things in this world is being unable to provide even a single meal to children who go to school hungry.”




Bakırhan also addressed the current fund crisis. He demanded a full investigation into the irregularities, disclosure of who had received the funds, and reimbursement of the losses suffered by the affected workers, including interest.




“Peace is not a gift, but the result of social struggles”




Regarding the ongoing peace and democratic society process, Bakırhan stated: “Peace is not a gift, but the result of social struggles. The process must not be reduced solely to ending the armed conflict. What matters is establishing a democratic order in which Kurds, Alevis, and other ethnic and religious communities can freely express their identities and enjoy equal rights."




He appealed to political forces that have remained distant from the process, calling in particular on Yeni Party Chair Özgür Özel to reconsider his position. “A genuine and strong opposition is not one that runs away from peace, but one that moves toward it.”




Bakırhan also rejected the notion that the process would be complete once the armed conflict ended: “We will continue this struggle until democracy and equal citizenship are achieved. No one should therefore imagine any other outcome. Anyone who believes that the Kurds can be deceived at the negotiating table or turned into an instrument of another political agenda, or who thinks this is merely about a peace process, is mistaken. The goal is democracy and equal citizenship.”




Call for an end to government-appointed trusteeships




Bakırhan identified ending the state-imposed trusteeships of elected municipalities and safeguarding the rights of political prisoners as necessary steps. He called for the reinstatement of the dismissed co-mayors of Akdeniz district, the release of imprisoned politicians pending trial, and adequate medical care for prisoners suffering from illness. According to the DEM Party’s assessment, a peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question could save up to US$50 billion annually. The party states that these funds should benefit workers, pensioners, students, low-income families, and small business owners.




In closing, Bakırhan praised the public support for peace and democratization: “Repression and undemocratic practices come and go. But this hall, the will of the people gathered here, and their diversity will remain.”

title: Resistance against solar power project in Arzoxlî on day 30
content:
The resistance against the construction of a solar power plant in Arzoxlî (Turkish: Kervanpınar), in the Sur district of Amed (Diyarbakır), has entered its second month. For 30 days, residents have been protesting against the energy project, which threatens their agricultural land and, consequently, their livelihoods. On Friday, numerous people once again gathered at the protest tent to continue the mobilization, which has been led primarily by women.




In addition to villagers, representatives of political parties, activists from the Peace Mothers Council, and members of civil society and environmental organizations took part in the protest. Chanting slogans including “We will prevail through resistance” and “Em axa xwe nadin” (“We will not give up our land”), the demonstrators marched from the village square to the protest tent.




“We will not bow to these companies”




Peace Mother Nezahat Teke, who also joined the protest, was particularly critical of the support the company was receiving from uniformed state personnel. “We will not bow to these companies. The women and men here must not be left alone in the rain,” Teke declared. She said the company could rely on military support in carrying out its activities. “This is not a matter for the soldiers, but for the company owner. Yet soldiers and police are supporting him. We mothers will resist until the end.”




Villager Güler Çiftçi also reaffirmed that the residents would not give up despite increasingly difficult weather conditions. “We wish the whole world had come out to support us today. We are fighting for our own land and our own water, through rain and drought, enduring hardship and difficult conditions. We will not surrender our land to anyone.”




Çiftçi accused the state security forces of siding with the company, saying: “The company has the state behind it. We do not want to see soldiers and the gendarmerie as our adversaries. We wish they would stand behind us. But unfortunately, today they are standing behind the company rather than us.” Çiftçi stressed that residents would continue to defend their living environment and the future of their children.




“Women are defending their livelihoods”




Halide Türkoğlu, spokesperson for the Women’s Council of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), praised the leading role of women in the resistance in Arzoxlî. Their struggle, she said, was directed not merely against a single construction project, but against the loss of the economic and ecological foundations of village life.




“The villagers’ resistance began under the leadership of women. Because when women defend their land, they are also defending their livelihoods and the future of their children,” Türkoğlu stated.




She stated that the government has deployed gendarmerie forces to surround the protest site rather than taking the concerns of the people seriously.




Türkoğlu criticized the fact that solar and geothermal energy projects, as well as mining operations, were threatening the livelihoods of rural communities in numerous regions of Kurdistan.




“While the alliance between capital and the government brings poverty into our lives, our natural environment is being destroyed day by day. Defending natural habitats is also a matter of fundamental rights: Our right to exist encompasses our identity, our language, and our natural environment. If anyone tries to take these away from us, we will never surrender them,” the DEM Party politician said.




Criticism of environmental policy amid the ongoing peace process




“The villagers’ resistance began under the leadership of women. Because when women defend their land, they are also defending their livelihoods and the future of their children,” Türkoğlu stated. Rather than taking the concerns of the population seriously, the government had deployed gendarmerie forces to surround the protest site, she said. Türkoğlu criticized the fact that solar and geothermal energy projects, as well as mining operations, were threatening the livelihoods of rural communities in numerous regions of Kurdistan.




Türkoğlu continued: “While the alliance between the capital and the government brings poverty into our lives, our natural environment is being destroyed day by day. Defending natural habitats is also a matter of fundamental rights. Our right to exist encompasses our identity, our language, and our natural environment. If anyone tries to take these away from us, we will never surrender them.”




Criticism of environmental policy amid the ongoing peace process




Türkoğlu also linked the conflict in Arzoxlî to the ongoing Peace and Democratic Society Process. She stressed that policies that threaten the livelihoods of the Kurdish population are continuing while peace is being discussed at the political level.  “We describe the process we are currently going through as a peace process. But at the same time, another war seems to have been launched against the Kurds and other peoples. A war has been declared on nature,” she said.




Türkoğlu pointed out that the pursuit of profit by companies, in cooperation with state authorities, had developed into a policy that displaced people from their land and drove women in particular into poverty. “If our natural environment is taken away from us, what are we supposed to eat, how are we supposed to live, how are we supposed to exist at all?” Türkoğlu asked, expressing her solidarity with the protesting women.




For the residents of Arzoxlî, protecting their land remains the central motivation behind their resistance, even after a month of protests. Güler Çiftçi said: “We will continue to defend our land, the future of our children, and the places where we live.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Lack of security guard rules could expose GN, professor says
content:
The Government of Nunavut could be sued if unregulated private security guards in the territory break the law, says a criminologist, who studies surveillance and security regulation.




That’s because Nunavut has no legislation that governs the training and certification of security guards.




“What are they waiting for? I don’t understand the rationale for not pursuing it and passing it into law,” University of Windsor professor Randy Lippert said in a phone interview.




The government does not appear to share that sense of urgency.




It has received calls to enact regulation during sessions of the legislative assembly in 2018, 2023 and 2025.




The latest call for regulation came from current Justice Minister George Hickes during the winter 2025 sitting of the legislative assembly, about 10 months before he joined cabinet.




He also highlighted the need for Nunavummiut to be hired in security roles.
















“I want to encourage all entities of the government to consider working together on setting the stage of bringing forward legislation in the next government,” Hickes said as a regular MLA on Feb. 26, 2025, about nine months before he became a cabinet minister.




Last week, however, he declined to comment on the issue.




Justice Department spokesperson Stephen Shaddock said in an email earlier this month that the department 

“is monitoring regulatory approaches in other Canadian jurisdictions.”




“However, there is no specific timeline for considering similar legislation in Nunavut.”




The Northwest Territories is the only other jurisdiction in Canada that does not regulate the private security industry.




But in Ontario, for example, the Private Security and Investigative Services Act requires companies to ensure guards have and maintain a valid agency licence. If security guards employed by the agency are charged for working without a valid licence, their employer may also face charges.
















The licencing process includes a criminal records check and completion of mandatory basic training, which is at least 40 hours.




Ontario’s law allows people to submit complaints in instances where they believe a guard violated the act. The solicitor general’s office reviews those complaints.




Iqaluit’s Northern store recently 

ramped up

 its security to include guards in tactical uniforms equipped with body cameras and what appear to be retractable batons.




The North West Co., the Winnipeg-based parent company of Northern, contracts the guards through Iqaluit-based Canadian Arctic Protective Services.




In an email earlier this month, the security company’s regional director, Paul Hunter,

 

declined to say whether the device that the guards carry is a baton.
















A supervisor with Canadian Arctic Protective Services stands at the exit of Iqaluit’s Northern store with a body-worn camera in October. A University of Windsor professor warns the Government of Nunavut could be civilly liable if a security guard breaks the law because the territory is one of two Canadian jurisdictions without a law regulating the private security industry. (File phot Daron Letts)




Retractable batons and other instruments that may be used as weapons are regulated under the Criminal Code, said Shaddock.




“Organizations should ensure that equipment carried by employees complies with the law, as non-compliance may result in criminal charges and potential civil liability,” he said.




Lippert said that liability could extend to the government itself.




“If something bad happens, it seems like a lot of people are going to get sued, and it may well include the government,” he said.




When asked about Lippert’s warning, the Justice Department’s spokesperson said the department would not comment on “a hypothetical scenario.”




“In all instances where the Government of Nunavut is served with a lawsuit, the government will review the matter on its merits and respond accordingly,” Shaddock said in an email.

title: Amazon Workers Say: We Won’t Build It. A Better Future is Possible (No Tech for Apartheid)
content:
WE WON’T BUILD IT—A BETTER FUTURE IS POSSIBLE: Amazon workers with #NoTechForApartheid are outraged by the news that Amazon executives enabled the Israeli military to use the company’s proprietary AI facial recognition program to surveil and target Palestinians during Israel’s genocidal onslaught of Gaza, as confirmed by The Guardian this week.

We stand in unwavering solidarity with the people of Palestine who have endured over three years of Israel’s atrocity crimes made possible by Amazon’s weaponized dual-use technology. And we believe Amazon workers have a responsibility to speak out, to organize, and to act.

Are you an Amazon worker ready to build a better world with your coworkers? Attend a worker forum on December 1st to process this news, connect with your coworkers, and chart out our next steps together: nota.sbs/s/amzworkermasscall

We’ve long warned that Project Nimbus – Amazon and Google’s joint $1B cloud computing contract with the Israeli military and government – has been a military program from the start. Now, we know that our bosses have knowingly played an active role to aid and abet Israel’s crimes since day 1 of this genocide.

There is a staggering amount of public evidence detailing the harms Amazon technology has helped inflict on the Palestinian people. The revelation that Amazon executives knew about the illegal and violent uses of the technology means that these executives must be held personally accountable for their knowing and intentional violations of international law.

We understand that, under Project Nimbus’ contract terms, Amazon signed away all authority and ability to restrict how Israel uses its facial recognition technology or any of the other technology Amazon provides them.

The path forward is clear: Amazon workers must continue organizing to ensure Amazon commits to not renewing Project Nimbus when it expires in 2028.

And if our bosses won’t take action, workers will.
