author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Israel Uploaded 3.5M Photos of Palestinians to Amazon Facial Recognition Tech
content:
For years, Israel has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and restrict Palestinian movement.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A new report reveals that Israel uploaded 3.5 million photos of Palestinians to Amazon’s facial recognition platform shortly after it launched its genocide in Gaza — shining yet more light on the tech industry’s complicity in repression and human rights abuses around the world.

The report, written by Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham and published in The Guardian this week, documents how the Israeli military uploaded the images to Amazon’s cloud soon after the start of Israel’s invasion and bombardment of Gaza in 2023. The military told Amazon that they uploaded the images specifically for the purpose of using Amazon’s Rekognition platform for facial recognition, according to documents leaked to the Guardian.

For years, the Israeli military has used facial recognition technology to enforce its occupation and enact harsh restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement. Soldiers use a smartphone app called Blue Wolf, for example, to scan and catalog the faces of Palestinians passing through Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank.

In Gaza, Israel has increased its use of facial recognition technology since the start of its 2023 assault. In early 2024, The New York Times called Israel’s facial recognition program in Gaza an “experimental effort” — acknowledging that the mass surveillance at times “wrongly flagged civilians as wanted Hamas militants.”

Davies and Abraham’s latest report builds on Abraham’s prior reporting for The Guardian and +972 Magazine, as well as the findings discussed in NAZA, a 2026 documentary co-directed by Abraham. The film highlights how Israel has used AI-based surveillance systems to facilitate Israel’s remote killings of thousands of civilians in Gaza since 2023.

The report also demonstrates how Israel has deepened its relationship with Amazon over the course of its genocide in Gaza. As noted by Who Profits, Israel awarded Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS) a large-scale tender in 2021, known as Project Nimbus, allowing Israel to transfer large quantities of data onto its services. Israel’s use of AWS has only expanded since then.

Last December, Mohammed Mhawish, a Palestinian journalist from Gaza, wrote about how Israel has intensified its use of surveillance since the start of the genocide.

The Israeli military has used “artificial intelligence to generate kill lists, monitoring our social-media accounts, and storing in bulk the audio of our phone calls,” he wrote.

Israel used these technologies to target journalists specifically — both within their own homes and while they were reporting, Mhawish said. Microsoft, Google, and Amazon, as well as other companies like Palantir Technologies, provide the infrastructure for the Israeli military to store Palestinians’ phone calls, analyze their communication, and decide who to target with a drone strike and when.

Last year, an investigative report by Abraham revealed the extensive use of Microsoft’s Azure platform by the Israeli military in order to surveil Palestinians’ phone calls before identifying targets for aerial bombardment. The revelations prompted tech workers to organize to force Microsoft to end Azure cloud storage and AI services in a partial withdrawal of contracts with Israel, though activists say that the company still retains contracts with the country.

Activists, including tech workers in No Tech for Apartheid, continue to organize against Google and Amazon’s Project Nimbus, and campaigns have grown internationally against Palantir.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Rizomatica
title: En línea y gratis: Película inspirada en la vida de Matías Catrileo está disponible en OndaMedia
content:
Con dos años de recorrido nacional e internacional, premios a Mejor Película en festivales de Barcelona, Arica, Tierra del Fuego y Aysén y cerca de 70 muestras gratuitas en distintas regiones de Chile, el largometraje de ficción “Algún día las raíces” se incorporó este 18 de noviembre a la plataforma de cine chileno

 

OndaMedia

. Inspirada en la vida de Matías Catrileo, joven mapuche de 23 años asesinado por Carabineros de Chile el 2008.

 




Por Morín Ortiz. 










Cada comienzo de año gregoriano, el pueblo mapuche recuerda a Matías Catrileo, joven mapuche que el 3 de enero del 2008 fue asesinado en una acción de control territorial de la que fue parte junto a la Coordinadora Arauco Malleco. Se probó que Matías estaba desarmado y que recibió un disparo por la espalda, perpetrado por el cabo segundo Walter Ramírez de Carabineros de Chile. 




El 2011, la Corte Suprema ratificó la sentencia de la Justicia Militar que lo declaró culpable de violencia innecesaria con resultado de muerte. La condena: tres años y un día en libertad. El 2012 la familia Catrileo Quezada presentó el caso en la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos y siguen a la espera. Un año después, Ramírez fue desvinculado de su cargo “por ser un desprestigio para la institución”, pero la familia de Matías sostiene que esto se logró a causa de la presión social. 




Fue en Temuco en enero del 2024, en la 16º conmemoración por la vida y muerte de Matías Catrileo, que se exhibió por primera vez el largometraje “Algún día las raíces” (65 min.), tras ocho años de que comenzara a gestarse por un joven equipo de estudiantes de Cine de la Universidad Mayor: Alejandro Valdeavellano Ramaciotti en dirección, guion y montaje; Catalina Saavedra Reyes en producción ejecutiva y Cristóbal Díaz en dirección de foto y montaje. 




Cuando propusieron la idea de hacer esta película a la familia Catrileo Quezada, aceptaron su condición: realizarla desde la autogesión, dadas las responsabilidades del Estado chileno en el asesinato de Matías. Fue gracias a una campaña de recolección de fondos y las voluntades de diversas personas que se logró. 




El rodaje fue el 2018 y duró tres semanas. Una de sus principales locaciones fue en la comunidad de Rucañanko, en el Lago Lleu Lleu, territorio mapuche en cuyo proceso de recuperación participó Matías. Angélica Ñancupil y Tania Antileo, fueron grandes apoyos en áreas de la investigación, producción y actuación. 







En palabras de Catalina Catrileo, la única hermana de Matías, Algún día las raíces 

“logra denunciar a las forestales y deja en claro que hay una pérdida territorial, la necesidad de las comunidades por recuperar nuestro territorio y cómo eso es criminalizado y reprimido”. 

Por esto recibe como una buena noticia que la obra pueda ser vista de manera gratuita en la plataforma de OndaMedia:

 “es bueno para ir transmitiendo la historia entre nosotros mismos y para dársela a conocer a gente que no la conoce”. 







Los procesos de realización de cine son largos, más aún si no se cuenta con el financiamiento necesario. Por lo que su director, Alejandro Valdeavellano recibe con goce la incorporación al catálogo de OndaMedia: 







“significa seguir llegando a más imaginarios mapuche y no mapuche a través de la memoria de Matías Catrileo. Estoy muy contento de que la película pueda seguir apreciándose y muy agradecido de que la familia Catrileo Quezada estuvieran de acuerdo con exhibirla en esta plataforma”. 







Su productora general, Catalina Saavedra, destacó que la película:







 “llegue a otros públicos sin que el acceso económico sea una barrera. El cine también tiene que ver con generar encuentros, abrir conversaciones y permitir que las historias circulen”. Después de tantos años de trabajo colectivo “la película puede expandirse, ser mirada, interpretada y de alguna manera, aportar su granito de arena en la preservación de la memoria”. 







Entre otros logros de “Algún día las raíces”, están el ser la película más vista del Festival Internacional de Cine por los Derechos Humanos de Colombia el 2024 y la nominación a Mejor Actor en los Premios Caleuche para su protagonista, Felipe Arce, quien comparte elenco junto a Rallen Montenegro, Manuel Díaz y Nicolás Aliaga.

Desde el 18 de noviembre del 2026, “Algún día las raíces” está disponible para ser vista en Chile de manera online y sin costo en OndaMedia, plataforma de streaming de cine chileno. Quienes quieran verla desde el extranjero, pueden hacerlo en la plataforma Mirada Nativa, que permite acceder al catálogo de manera gratuita con aporte voluntario tras cada visionado.

title: Acá, en la montaña. (Información importante para transportistas y familias buscadoras)
content:
Acá, en la montaña. (Información importante para transportistas y familias buscadoras)

La luna cae como guadaña sobre el horizonte de occidente, segando sueños y pesadillas.

La montaña se va descobijando por un sol impertinente. Desperezándose está. En su avance, el día la va descubriendo: primero el extenso bies de la alargada y verde nagua. Luego la arbolada de las rodillas, la cintura de la bulla de pájaros y animales, los breves senos asomándose, tímidos, entre la neblina. Y, al fin, la cabellera que, en lo más alto, le peina un viento frío a esa hora de la ya no tan madrugada.

Una mujer ya de edad baja por un sendero. En una mano lleva un manojo de hierbas. En la otra una niña de pocos años y cuartas sobre el suelo.

“Esta planta alivia el cólico. La montaña, que es como mujeres que somos, nos da esta hierba como regalo para que podamos caminar y trabajar, y no estar todo el día botadas como costal de pergamino vacío, haraganeando con el dolor de pretexto. Ahorita no lo sabes todavía, pero vas a saber. De por sí lo vas a saber ya que críes más”.

“Y esto que te cuento, me lo contó mi abuela, y a mi abuela su abuela. Y así por muchos años, tantos que las matemáticas no alcanzan a contar. Porque nosotras pasamos, pero la tierra queda. Igual nosotras quedamos en ustedes, las hijas y las nietas. Por eso nos preocupa si comen, si enferman, si faltan. Por eso las buscamos, para enseñarles, orientarlas, decirles que tengan bueno su pie y bueno su paso”

“A las abuelas nos toca enseñar, es nuestro trabajo. Ustedes, las niñas, su trabajo es vivir”

La niña asiente y mira el paso. Sabe que la mano de su abuela no es para que no se pierda, sino para apoyarse en ella, bastón vivo para la anciana que camina lento.

La abuela cree que ayuda y protege a la niña. La niña cree que protege y ayuda a la abuela.

Abajo, al pie de la montaña, en la champa, la madre espera las hierbas que le aliviarán el cólico que le muerde las entrañas. Un olor a maíz cocido, tortilla recién hecha y leña palpitando, rodea la champa. El padre y el hijo mayor salieron más temprano, pozol en las morraletas, a la milpa.

Un bebé llora, porque sí, porque no encuentra todavía las palabras, por decir “aquí estoy”.

Porque el llanto, amigas y enemigas, es también una señal de vida.

En el cuartel insurgente siguen los trabajos para crear los regalos para las madres buscadoras. Como las muñecas van con retraso, el SubMoy ha ordenado que algunos varones dejen la carpintería y se pasen al bordado.

Pero antes, cuando sólo estaban como mujeres que somos, las compañeras insurgentas intercambian informaciones. Comentan el último baile en la comunidad de jóvenes en común. Murmuran y ríen mientras miran de reojo a los hombres que, en la carpintería hacen las casitas-cajitas que servirán para que las muñecas no se abollen en el largo camino a la capital del país.

“Ese compa”, dice una, “sabe de bailar de sonidero, que es una nueva música que inventaron los ciudadanos”. Sin dejar de bordar la blusa, completa: “Urr, ahí andaba de un lado a otro, hasta parece que va a volar que de una vez que no se puede creer. Y los critica a los otros que no saben bailar sin pareja. Que sea sueltos. Nada de que la manita y esas cosas. Y los otros lo critican a él porque dicen que baila sonidero porque no encuentra pareja”.

“¿Y cómo sabes?” “Por una información que me compartieron” Todas ríen cómplices. “Yo”, dice otra, “acaso sé bailar. Nunca me bailé en mi pueblo, no sé, como que no me llama la atención. Pero entonces dijo el SubMoy que vayan al baile. Y, ni modos, es orden que hay que bailar. Y ahí estamos con mi prima dando nomás patadas como yegua brava. Creo nadie se dio cuenta o creyeron que es un nuevo baile”. Siguen platicando sin dejar de bordar los regalos que recuerdo y memoria serán para las familias buscadoras. Sin varones cerca, son libres para hablar de cosas de “como mujeres que somos”.

Pero ahora que hay varones compartiendo el trabajo, todo cambió. Ahora hasta se peinan. Y están como muy serias, como que son muy bien portadas. Y las risas son suplidas por los rubores que se pierden tras el cubrebocas, “porque hay mucha influenza” dijo la insurgenta de sanidad. Se arreglan la blusa, se ponen el pantalón bien trincado, que de una vez no se puede creer. Y se ponen violáceas de pena, porque como son de piel oscura, cuando se sonrojan quedan moradas sus mejillas.

Mirando la torpeza de los varones, una insurgenta, hábil en crear colores y figuras, dice: “yo creo que las mamaces dan vida y oficio a las niñas. A los niños no, por eso salen haraganes y maloras”.

Y cuenta de su mamá. Se embarazó de su hermanita y fue a la clínica para ver si todo bien. Le hicieron estudios de laboratorio y una cosa que se llama “ultrasonido”.

“En el ultrasonido sale la foto de la niña en la panza con sus manos así”, la compañera simula con sus manos las del bordado.

Un compa insurgente protesta. Él también está bordando y no lo toman en cuenta. Las insurgentas le replican: “Mira, es como ser insurgente. Primero entras de recluta, te enseñan, te regañan, te corrigen. Ya luego que lo miran que ya aprendiste, pasas a otro un nivel, que quiere decir que ya puedes aprender otras cosas y así. Bueno, pues resulta que las niñas se entran antes de “reclutas” de mujeres, porque en la panza de sus mamaces van aprendiendo lo que les enseñan sus mamás. Cuando nacen, ya tienen como quien dice la parte básica”.

“¿Y los niños pues?”, protesta el varón. “Ah, pues no. ¿Cuándo lo has visto a un hombre embarazado? No hay cómo. Entonces los niños apenas empiezan a aprender cuando nacen. Por eso son más tarugos que hacen muchas tonterías y no aprenden luego, sino que tardan. En cambio, las niñas, cuando criamos ya llevamos un buen tanto de conocimiento.”

Yo, como todo caballero andante que se precie de serlo, siempre buscando conciliar y evitando la polémica, solté: “El capitán dice que las mujeres no saben cocinar bien, que son los hombres los que cocinan mejor”

Hubo un silencio como el que se da antes de la tormenta. Entonces las insurgentas, casi al mismo tiempo, resoplaron con furia. Ahí lo supe que el mundo se va a acabar. Y todo por su culpa del capitán.

Cuando me fui, seguía la bulla de la discusión. Me crucé con el SubMoy cuando iba a poner orden. Me acerqué con prudencia y escuché: “No lo crean, el capitán no dijo eso. Dijo que ni hombres ni mujeres saben cocinar. Que cuando sepan hacer pastel de moka, entonces ahí lo va a ver si se autocritica”.

Creo que al capitán le zumbaron los oídos toda la noche. Y no por los zancudos.

Entonces solté la frase que me llevará a la posteridad:

“El chisme es la continuación de la política por otros medios”.

Oh, no problema, sí, pueden citarme.

Desde las montañas del Sureste Mexicano.

Don Durito de La Lacandona. Copyleft citando la fuente y un kilo de arroz o frijol en Casa Samir. Noviembre del 2026.

P.D. QUE COMPARTE INFORMACIÓN PARA CHOFERÓLOGOS, TRANSPORTISTAS Y CONDUCTORES EN GENERAL. – Por recomendación de los choferólogos, saldremos del CIDECI el día sábado 28 de noviembre a las 1700 aproximadamente. De modo de viajar un tramo de noche, para así no afectar mucho a los transportistas en carretera. Será una caravana de hasta 35 autobuses. Tomen sus precauciones. Recomendamos no hacer acompañamiento en vehículos porque es un tramo pesado de día, y peor de noche.

Calculamos llegar a la Ciudad de México el domingo 29 noviembre (si no hay bloqueos, plantones y etcétera), de modo de no afectar mucho a los conductores citadinos que de por sí ya la tienen pesada. Nos instalaremos en la Casa de los Pueblos “Samir Flores Soberanes”, y nuestras salidas serán las menos posibles.

P.D.- PARA FAMILIAS BUSCADORAS. – Todos los registros han sido revisados y aprobados. Si su registro no ha obtenido respuesta todavía, no preocupar. Llegue usted el día que tenía pensado e insista en registrarse con el Frayba. Igual le recibiremos y abrazaremos. También les informamos que ya le avisamos al Frayba que proceda con la compra de boletos (principalmente de avión), iniciando con los estados del norte del país, Yucatán y Quintana Roo. Los más retirados pues.

title: 21 Νοέμβρη: Παγκόσμια Ημέρα Δράσης ενάντια στον Πόλεμο, Σάββατο 21/11, στις 14.00, στα Προπύλαια, Αθήνα
content:
Κάλεσμα/Αφίσα από την

 ΟΚΔΕ

:







ΕΞΩ Η ΕΛΛΑΔΑ ΑΠΟ ΤΑ ΠΟΛΕΜΙΚΑ ΣΦΑΓΕΙΑ!




ΛΕΦΤΑ ΓΙΑ ΤΙΣ ΑΝΑΓΚΕΣ ΜΑΣ – ΟΧΙ ΓΙΑ ΕΞΟΠΛΙΣΜΟΥΣ!




Η ανθρωπότητα βρίσκεται μπροστά σε μια επικίνδυνη κλιμάκωση των πολεμικών συγκρούσεων. 

Από την Ουκρανία μέχρι τη Μέση Ανατολή, οι λαοί πληρώνουν με αίμα την κρίση και τους ανταγωνισμούς του παγκόσμιου καπιταλιστικού συστήματος. Οι ΗΠΑ, το ΝΑΤΟ και η ΕΕ, στην προσπάθειά τους να διατηρήσουν την κυριαρχία τους απέναντι στην Κίνα και τη Ρωσία, πολλαπλασιάζουν εξοπλισμούς, επεμβάσεις και απειλές.

 Η ΗΠΑ δεν μπορούν να αποδεχτούν την ήττα τους και γι’ αυτό συνεχίζουν να χτυπούν το Ιράν. Πίσω από τις υποσχέσεις για «ειρήνη» και «ασφάλεια» βρίσκονται τα συμφέροντα των πολυεθνικών, ο έλεγχος των αγορών, των ενεργειακών πόρων και των δρόμων μεταφοράς. 

Ο κίνδυνος γενικευμένου πολέμου μεγαλώνει.

 Η κούρσα των εξοπλισμών δεν προστατεύει τους λαούς, προετοιμάζει νέες σφαγές και απειλεί να μετατρέψει περιοχές σε πεδία αντιπαράθεσης.




Παράλληλα, εδώ και τρία χρόνια ο παλαιστινιακός λαός αντιμετωπίζει τη βία, τον εκτοπισμό και την γενοκτονία από το κράτος του Ισραήλ, με τη στήριξη των δυτικών ιμπεριαλιστών.

 Η αλληλεγγύη στην Παλαιστίνη δεν είναι ζήτημα φιλανθρωπίας, αλλά κοινός αγώνας ενάντια στην καταπίεση και τον ιμπεριαλισμό. Απαιτούμε να σταματήσουν οι επιθέσεις και η κατοχή, να αναγνωριστεί το δικαίωμα του παλαιστινιακού λαού σε ανεξάρτητο κράτος και αυτοδιάθεση.




Η κυβέρνηση Μητσοτάκη μάς βυθίζει βαθύτερα σε αυτούς τους σχεδιασμούς.

 Παραχωρεί στρατιωτικές βάσεις και υποδομές, μετατρέπει τα λιμάνια της Αλεξανδρούπολης, του Πειραιά και της Ελευσίνας σε κρίκους της πολεμικής αλυσίδας και εμφανίζει την πλήρη πρόσδεση σε ΗΠΑ και ΝΑΤΟ ως «γεωπολιτική αναβάθμιση». Αγοράζει διαρκώς εξοπλισμούς ύψους πολλών δις ευρώ, με πρόσφατη την αγορά στρατιωτικού υλικού ύψους 4 δισ. από τις ΗΠΑ και συμφωνία-μαμούθ 3 δισ. με το Ισραήλ για την κατασκευή της λεγόμενης «Ασπίδας του Αχιλλέα». Μετατρέπουν εργαζόμενους και νεολαία σε όμηρους επικίνδυνων ανταγωνισμών. Δε θα γίνουμε κρέας για τα κανόνια τους! Να κλείσουν οι στρατιωτικές βάσεις, να σταματήσει η αγορά οποιουδήποτε στρατιωτικού υλικού και να μην αξιοποιείται κανένα λιμάνι για επιθετικές επιχειρήσεις. Να σταματήσουμε τους επικίνδυνους, πολεμοκάπηλους τυχοδιωκτισμούς των αστικών τάξεων σε Ελλάδα-Τουρκία, που απειλούν και τους δύο λαούς με στρατιωτική σύγκρουση.




Την ίδια στιγμή, για εργαζόμενους, νέους, φτωχά λαϊκά στρώματα περισσεύουν μόνο θυσίες. 

Δισεκατομμύρια κατευθύνονται σε εξοπλισμούς, ενώ οι μισθοί εξανεμίζονται από την ακρίβεια, τα νοίκια, τους λογαριασμούς. Υγεία, Παιδεία, υπηρεσίες υποβαθμίζονται, οι ιδιωτικοποιήσεις απλώνονται παντού, τα εργασιακά δικαιώματα τσακίζονται.

 Η πολεμική οικονομία συμβαδίζει με τη φοροληστεία και την καταστολή: θέλουν τους εργαζόμενους να πληρώνουν, να σιωπούν και να πολεμούν για ξένα συμφέροντα και για να επιβάλουν αυτή την πορεία, χτυπούν τις κινητοποιήσεις και τους αγωνιστές, περιορίζουν τις ελευθερίες και ενισχύουν τους μηχανισμούς καταστολής.




ΩΣ ΕΔΩ!

 Η απάντηση δεν βρίσκεται σε ευχολόγια ούτε στην αναμονή κάποιας «ειρηνικής» συμφωνίας των ισχυρών. Βρίσκεται στην ανεξάρτητη δράση των εργαζόμενων, της νεολαίας και των φτωχών λαϊκών στρωμάτων: στα σωματεία, στους χώρους δουλειάς, στις σχολές και στις γειτονιές. 

Με οδηγό τους αγώνες και την κοινωνική έκρηξη στη Γαλλία και στην υπόλοιπη Ευρώπη να οικοδομήσουμε ένα μαζικό, μαχητικό, διεθνιστικό αντιπολεμικό και αντιιμπεριαλιστικό κίνημα, με απεργίες, διαδηλώσεις και κοινή δράση των λαών. Να ανατρέψουμε την κυβέρνηση και τις νεοφιλελεύθερες πολιτικές της φτώχειας, του πολέμου και της καταστολής.

 Αγώνας ενάντια στον πόλεμο σημαίνει αγώνας για ψωμί, αξιοπρέπεια και δημοκρατικά δικαιώματα. Διεκδικούμε αυξήσεις σε μισθούς και συντάξεις, δημόσια δωρεάν Υγεία και Παιδεία, κοινωνικό έλεγχο στους τομείς της οικονομίας. Παλεύουμε για μια Κυβέρνηση των Εργαζομένων, για μια σοσιαλιστική κοινωνία χωρίς εκμετάλλευση και πολέμους.







ΕΞΩ ΟΙ ΒΑΣΕΙΣ – ΕΞΩ ΑΠΟ ΤΟ ΝΑΤΟ!




ΚΑΜΙΑ ΣΥΜΜΕΤΟΧΗ ΣΤΟΝ ΠΟΛΕΜΟ




ΕΛΛΑΔΑ – ΤΟΥΡΚΙΑ, ΚΟΙΝΟΣ ΑΓΩΝΑΣ ΤΩΝ ΛΑΩΝ




ΚΑΤΩ Η ΚΥΒΕΡΝΗΣΗ ΜΗΤΣΟΤΑΚΗ




ΛΕΥΤΕΡΙΑ ΣΤΗΝ ΠΑΛΑΙΣΤΙΝΗ!

title: The anarchy of power
content:
Pier Paolo Pasolini, 

Salò

, 

or the 120 Days of Sodom

 (1976)







Nothing is more anarchic than power. Power does what it wants and what it wants is totally arbitrary or dictated by its economic reasons which escape common logic.




…




Power is always a codifier and ritual. But [that] which ritualizes [,that] which codifies, is always nothingness, pure will, that is, its own anarchy.




Pier Paolo Pasolini, [Pasolini Next to us (intervista di Gideon Bachmann 1975) – 

Letteratura Italia







SHENZHEN, Nov. 19 [2026] – The following is the full text of the China-Russia-U.S. Heads of State Declaration toward Peace, released on Thursday.




China-Russia-U.S. Heads of State Declaration toward Peace




Xi Jinping, President of the People’s Republic of China, Vladimir Putin, President of the Russian Federation, and Donald J. Trump, President of the United States of America, met in Shenzhen on November 19, 2026. The Russian and U.S. heads of state expressed appreciation to China for hosting this historic trilateral Summit. The three heads of state had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security.




1. As permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, China, Russia, and the United States committed to reform the U.N. so that the U.N. can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security.




2. The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows.

4. The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: The Flatbush Building Collapse Is a Window Into Gentrification in Brooklyn
content:
Activists say the collapse was due to “a series of decisions that placed the profit model over the lives of the people.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On the afternoon of November 11, a three-story building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, collapsed into an adjacent construction site. 1321 Flatbush Avenue — which hosted four apartment units and a store on its ground floor — collapsed within seconds, as did the wall of the neighboring building, exposing its interior.

The collapse killed eight people, all of them immigrants under the age of 32, two of them young children. Among those killed were people born in Guinea, Ecuador, Guatemala, and Colombia. Dozens more were injured and displaced.

The site of the collapse is one of negligence and oversight — the developer of the construction site is known for violating orders and failing to put in place safety precautions, and the adjacent building accumulated at least 98 housing code violations before its collapse. While the construction site had been approved for a three-story building, developers were seeking to build a nine-story building with 64 residential units.

But these violations are part of a larger story, local organizers say. The collapse comes as Flatbush, which is largely Black, with significant Haitian, Afro-Caribbean, and Latino communities, faces a gentrification and displacement crisis that has intensified over the past 15 years. And it’s not just Flatbush: Since 2010, nearly 70,000 Black people have been displaced from Brooklyn, historically a center for Black New Yorkers.

Gentrification — and the city’s decades of neglect of Black and immigrant neighborhoods — is at the heart of this tragedy, one organizer told Truthout.

“We, as Black and brown people, have been feeling the brunt of gentrification in our communities — it is permanent, involuntary displacement,” said Imani Henry of Equality for Flatbush, which has been organizing around issues like gentrification, police violence, and tenants’ rights in Brooklyn since 2013.

“We are constantly dealing with new luxury developments being built in our neighborhoods, and the complete and utter neglect” of buildings where Black and brown people live, with “the infrastructure crumbling and landlords doing nothing,” Henry said. “That’s our norm.”

He pointed to the collapse of a building in the Bronx in December 2023, which displaced 140 New Yorkers, most of them working class, Latino, Caribbean, and Black.

This latest building collapse reveals “the conditions that people in Flatbush have been living under for the last 15 years. We are dealing with slumlords,” as well as “landlords calling ICE” on their tenants, Henry said.

Yasmine Tiana, an activist from the Palaver Collective, which has been organizing in response to the collapse, told Truthout that the tragedy raises the question: “What is more important — the lives of people and families who live within these buildings and apartments, or developers, whose main goal is profit?”

“We can’t pretend this happened in a vacuum,” Tiana said. “It was a series of decisions that placed the profit model over the lives of the people, and now there’s eight people gone. The landlord knew about [the violations], but continued to neglect them.”

Angelina Landress, an organizer with the 75 Lenox Road Tenant Association, told Truthout that her building in Flatbush has hundreds of violations. Her union has been on rent strike for four months due to dangerous conditions and management’s neglect of the property.

Landress disputed the narrative that buildings are falling apart because they’re old, instead citing neglect and deregulation, often of previously rent-stabilized buildings.

Landlords buy up buildings in Flatbush and “don’t put any money into it, collect all the rent, make the conditions sub-par, and drive people out,” Landress said.

Among other problems, landlords are falsely stating they have fixed the problems in their buildings, she added. The tenants of 75 Lenox Road are organizing because they realize they “cannot let the system tell us that we have to follow the current process, because the current process will kill us, just like it killed our neighbors.”

When Truthout reached out to the management of 75 Lenox Road for comment, an office manager who went by Esther and declined to give her last name stated that the tenants association is “just 10 people looking to make trouble.”

“The allegations are totally untrue and false and have absolutely no merit,” she told Truthout over the phone. “Out of 80 apartments, if 10 of them decide to make trouble, because they’re thousands of dollars behind rent, they shouldn’t besmirch our name.”

Like Henry, Landress spoke about landlords’ use of ICE as an intimidation tactic against tenants. Just as some of the victims of the collapsed building stayed inside in the weeks before their deaths due to their fear of ICE, the residents of 75 Lenox, who are predominantly Caribbean immigrants, have also been affected by ICE raids in recent months.

“In October, our neighbor Roberto Lamour was taken by ICE around 6:30 in the morning,” Landress said. The three armed men said they were New York City Police Department (NYPD), and then “just grabbed him and took him,” bringing him to Delaney Hall in New Jersey before transferring him to an ICE jail in Mississippi. Later that month, the tenants union held a press conference demanding that their neighbor be brought home — and calling for the firing of NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch due to the NYPD’s collusion with ICE, Landress said.

Local activists have expressed frustration at inaction by the local government, both since the building collapse and as the issues of gentrification and neglect piled up over the years.

Henry said that “a lot of campaign promises” have been broken regarding protecting Black and brown people’s right to housing — in previous administrations, and now under the Mamdani administration. Despite repeatedly promising to expand public housing, for example, the current administration is carrying out demolitions of public housing in Manhattan.

“There’s a whole struggle around the Elliott-Chelsea Houses,” Henry told Truthout, referring to the fight against a redevelopment plan in Manhattan that involves demolishing over 2,000 public housing apartments and shifting to private management. The project has been backed and overseen by the Mamdani administration, and has sparked debate and pushback from residents and activists.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani “ran on a campaign of going after these landlords to the fullest extent, and that’s new, because typically, New York tends to support the money, the landlords, and the developers,” Landress told Truthout. “Since he’s been in office, we have seen a lot of promise of things, and all these task forces being created, but they don’t materialize as anything.” Landress gave the example of deed thefts and heat complaint investigations.

Landress put a measure of responsibility on New York City’s Department of Buildings (DOB) for the Flatbush building collapse, saying that it has a history of taking bribes from landlords and developers. “We knew that the response to this from the city, even from the Mamdani administration, would be to clean their hands of their own agency, and not hold the other parties accountable,” she said.

So the 75 Lenox Road Tenants Association created a coalition, joining with United Parkside Tenants, the Palaver Collective, Affordable For You, Tenant Union Flatbush, Flatbush Neighbors, and other community groups to organize a response.

“It was not acceptable for us that this would just be seen as another tragedy, and that’s it,” Landress said. “So we organized a three-day emergency mutual aid distribution table, right across the street from the site.”

Landress said that the coalition is in direct contact with families affected by the collapse, who say that the aid they have been given so far is insufficient.

“There’s been no transparency from the city as of yet in terms of the funds that have been collected by the Red Cross and when it’s going to be distributed,” said Tiana. “We [the coalition] have raised over $100,000, and in just a few days we’ve made a concrete plan to try to distribute this money as quickly as possible. And we don’t have a tenth of the mayor’s resources to be able to distribute these funds. But there’s been no concrete plan from the city about how the victims will be assisted.”

The coalition has also compiled a list of demands for the city, calling for the firing of the DOB commissioner; permanent housing for tenants within their local communities and for their rent to be covered for two years; the prosecution of the landlord responsible; all developers and construction companies involved to be held accountable; and a complete investigation into what occurred.

“There are empty, rent-stabilized apartments. There are empty, luxury high-rises,” Landress said. “You have the power to house these people, and pay their rent for two years while they rebuild their lives from a tragedy that was orchestrated out of greed and capitalism and the desire for gentrification.”

Tiana noted that among the donations the coalition received for the displaced families was “20 or 30 dollars” from Palestine.

“Somebody who is going through a genocide right now saw what was happening in Brooklyn, and felt they had to donate,” she said. “In moments like that, we realize that the struggle is not just isolated to New York. This is part of a global struggle against displacement, and a pattern of placing profit over the lives of people.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Jake Johnson
title: 15 Democrats Join GOP to Pass Big Oil-Backed Permitting Bill in the Senate
content:
The bill would weaken environmental protections to fast-track approvals for data centers and fossil fuel projects.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The Republican-controlled US Senate, with the support of more than a dozen Democrats, passed a hotly contested bill that would weaken the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and other key environmental laws to accelerate approval and development of energy projects, including climate-wrecking gas pipelines and data centers.

The final vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) was 62-33, with nearly every Republican and 15 Democrats supporting passage. The 15 members of the Senate Democratic caucus who voted for the bill were Chris Coons (Del.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Martin Heinrich (NM), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), Angus King (Maine), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Jack Reed (RI), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chuck Schumer (NY), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.), Mark Warner (Va.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI).

The legislation passed without ever facing a hearing in the Senate, a fact that Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) — an outspoken opponent of the bill — called “pretty damn outrageous and offensive.”

If passed by the House and signed into law by President Donald Trump — whose White House has backed the measure — BAAJA would limit the authority of federal courts to block energy projects due to violations of environmental protection laws. The measure would also exempt pipeline expansions from National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review, potentially bar future administrations from rolling back previously approved projects, and restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to block projects under the Clean Water Act.

The legislation was endorsed by the American Petroleum Institute, the largest fossil fuel industry lobbying organization in the US. The group applauded Thursday’s vote as “a major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms” and praised the legislation’s lead sponsors, including Whitehouse and Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah).

Environmental organizations expressed support for some elements of the legislation, such as provisions that would speed up transmission and grid modernization. But the good provisions don’t outweigh the destructive ones, green groups said, arguing the bill’s benefits are heavily tilted toward fossil fuel projects — and would likely be further tilted in that direction by the Big Oil-friendly Trump administration.

“Senators who voted for this bill should be ashamed,” said Erich Pica, president of Friends of the Earth US. “Just weeks after Americans made clear they are tired of politicians putting corporate profits ahead of people, the Senate approved a giant giveaway to Big Tech and polluters. Calling this a bipartisan compromise doesn’t change what it is: a reckless attack on our clean air, clean water, wildlife, public lands, oceans, and communities.”

“It’s bad enough that Republicans wanted to gut our environmental laws,” Pica added. “It’s unconscionable that Democrats helped them do it.”

Some Democrats who supported advancing the bill in previous procedural votes switched their votes to no on final passage, including Sen. Andy Kim (NJ). In a statement posted to social media, Kim said he “voted earlier in the process to allow a debate and amendment process that could improve the bill before final passage.”

“Unfortunately those improvements, which would rein in the worst impulses of the Trump administration, were not made, and the potential consequences for New Jersey are unacceptable,” said Kim.

BAAJA’s opponents called on the House, which will be narrowly controlled by Republicans until January, to reject the legislation.

“This bill identified the wrong problems and has therefore arrived at the wrong solutions,” said David Watkins, director of federal government relations for the Climate and Energy Programs at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “The Clean Water Act isn’t the problem — the fossil fuel industry and their enablers in the Trump administration are responsible for throttling renewable energy deployment across the United States.”

“The Senate’s bill is totally out of step with the message of the midterm elections. Policymakers must move on from the status quo driving high energy bills and record fossil fuel profits,” Watkins added. “The House should reject BAAJA and negotiate a better bill in the new Congress in January, one that protects our environment, includes meaningful input from communities burdened by fossil fuel pollution, and makes cheaper and cleaner renewable energy more accessible to everyone.”

author: Cami Koons
title: Army Postpones Detonation of Toxic Lead Azide in Iowa After Public Outcry
content:
Lead particles could spread 100 miles from the detonation site. The army says the detonation is now planned for Monday.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Environmental groups filed a lawsuit Thursday afternoon in an attempt to halt the planned detonation of degraded, lead-based explosive material at a munitions plant in southeast Iowa.

The lawsuit was filed hours before acting Secretary of the Army, Hon. Adam Telle announced the detonation would be postponed to Monday, Nov. 23, noting that “public safety is the Army’s top priority.” U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley said on social media the delay was to “further educate the public.”

Telle said in a post on social media that Monday was the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

Earthjustice, on behalf of Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, is suing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over its decision to grant an emergency permit to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to intentionally detonate 68 drums of deteriorated lead azide, an explosive that is unstable in its deteriorated state.

The detonation, which will occur inside concrete bunkers that are surrounded by sand barriers approximately two stories high according to news releases from the Army, will cause a plume of air “with some lead-containing particles.” Nearby areas have been warned to stay inside while the lead particles are expected to be airborne and to spray down outdoor materials after lead-containing dust has settled on the surfaces.

In the lawsuit, filed in the U.S. Appellate Court for the Eighth District, environmental groups ask the court to either rule on the motion before Friday at 10 a.m. or issue an administrative stay until the motion can be fully heard in court.

Iowa Environmental Council Executive Director Sarah Green said in a statement Thursday that it “could be the case that the U.S. Army has no other safe alternative to disposing of the toxic lead azide.”

“But our federal government needs to do better at communicating the potential health risks of lead contamination in our communities and providing more time to keep our communities and vulnerable groups safe, like children and pregnant women,” Green said.

Petitioners allege the emergency permit from EPA failed to: incorporate applicable environmental performance standards, require all permit conditions necessary to protect human health and the environment, consider less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead, and adequately notify the public of the plan.

“The Army’s planned detonation of 9,700 pounds of explosive lead material poses a significant risk of irreparable harm that cannot later be remedied,” the lawsuit said.

The Army and EPA have said the intentional detonation allows them to mitigate the “explosion risk” of the degraded lead azide which presented an “imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”

Essentially, they said the intentional detonation of the material allows for precautions and public awareness that would not be possible if the material exploded on its own.

Environmental groups said they “do not dispute the EPA and Army’s assertion that there is risk involved in leaving the lead azide at the IAAP untreated” but said the Army left the explosive “to degrade for roughly two decades until it decided that the only safe option became detonating them near populated areas.”

According to the proposed action report from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, the lead azide was submerged in a water/ethanol storage solution. Temperature fluctuations caused the material to “dissolve and recrystallize” into a form that is “acutely sensitive to shock, friction, static electricity, and heat.” The Army determined in March the material had degraded, and in April had a briefing with EPA, according to the emergency permit.

“That turned the Army’s storage management failure into a public health event for people in at least two states,” the lawsuit said. “This rushed final week is a symptom of that; the Army has been aware of the risk since at least March, yet it gave public notice of its plans a mere five days before intended detonation.”

The Army held an open house in Middletown in mid-October informing residents about the planned detonation, though the Friday schedule was not announced until Nov. 15, when the Army also provided air dispersion models that showed lead particles could be spread up to 100 miles from the detonation site, and dust deposition models that showed a potential spread of around 40 miles.

More recent maps, released by the Army Thursday showed the plume was expected to move more directly north, as opposed to northeast of the detonation site, and not stretch as far as the earlier model showed. The Army has said it will continue to release updated maps up until the detonation with information accurate to the latest atmospheric conditions.

The initial plume map showed air dispersion was intended to stretch across the Mississippi River and into New Boston, Illinois. The lawsuit alleges Illinois officials had not been notified of the detonation and potential risks.

On Thursday, the Illinois Department of Public Health issued public health guidance about the detonation. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services also posted safety tips and information Thursday about the detonation which it said it was “only very recently made aware of.”

Safety precautions include staying indoors, running air purifiers and turning off heating and cooling units while there is a potential for air dispersion, which the Army estimates will last about an hour. The Army, and state health departments have also said people in the affected areas should consider washing outdoor surfaces, like playground equipment, doors and cars to minimize the risk of consuming lead dust.

The lawsuit pushed back on this advice, noting that there is no safe level of lead exposure for children.

“The idea that widespread lead dust can simply be rinsed away with no harmful effect is absurd, counterfactual, and extremely harmful misinformation to share with the public,” the lawsuit said.

EPA and Army media contacts did not respond to a request for comment Thursday regarding the lawsuit.

Environmental groups allege EPA’s permit “largely ignored” the potential for the lead to spread to groundwater, surface water, soil and the atmosphere.

For example, the environmental groups point out, the EPA permit shows no conditions addressing the detonation’s potential for damage to domestic animals, wildlife, crops, vegetation and physical structures.

On Wednesday, the Iowa Department of Agriculture posted guidance for livestock producers near the detonation site, urging them to move livestock elsewhere or into a barn if possible and to move or cover feed and water supplies to “prevent possible contamination.”

While the EPA permit requires the Army to collect samples before, during and after the detonation at “all parks, public facilities, and private properties” they were given the right of entry, the lawsuit holds the testing requirements are not robust.

Researchers at the University of Iowa met with reporters Thursday afternoon and said they are conducting their own research. David Cwiertny, director of the Environmental Policy Research Program at UI, said researchers will be deploying air sensors, particle filters and collecting soil samples and surface wipes across the affected area.

“We’re doing all of this to add to the public record, not because we have any real doubt in the official monitoring that’s planned by the EPA or the Army,” Cwiertny said. “In an unprecedented event with so many unpredictable factors, we believe that having more independent data is always better for public transparency and for public health.”

The lawsuit urges the court to issue a stay and prevent the detonation because, it says, “once lead dust is dispersed, there is no undoing the harm.”

“What the Court must balance is the risks associated with the possibility of unplanned detonation while crucial additional time is given to take actions necessary to protect human health and the environment, against the very significant known harm of a massive lead dust plume,” the lawsuit read.

author: Zane McNeill
title: The “Blue Tsunami” Can’t Leave Trans People Behind
content:
On this Trans Day of Remembrance, Democrats must recommit to rolling back the anti-trans assault of the past two years.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Many are interpreting the “blue tsunami” that swept the nation earlier this month as a resounding rebuke of the MAGA movement’s fearmongering around transgender rights. But this Trans Day of Remembrance (TDOR), we owe it to ourselves and those we have lost to anti-trans violence to sit with the complicated, nuanced truth and not just comfort ourselves with a convenient, feel-good narrative.

It is true that many candidates who campaigned on explicitly anti-trans messaging and policies lost their elections, in spite of the hundreds of millions of dollars they spent on anti-trans ads. In fact, despite the deluge of anti-transgender messaging, many Democrats who refused to throw trans people under the bus, no matter what anti-trans rhetoric was thrown at them from their opponents, won their races across the country. Ten transgender people were elected into office — in Alabama, Georgia, Delaware, Montana, Florida, Washington, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan. Vermont voters approved a constitutional amendment adding explicit equal protection guarantees for sexual orientation, gender identity, and gender expression.

Polling suggests that voters have grown weary of the weaponization of trans issues by the far right, which they view as an attempt to distract them from the issues that matter most in their lives: inflation and the cost of living; jobs and the economy; and skyrocketing health care bills. Voters who were disenchanted with Donald Trump and the Republicans’ failure to deliver a better life for them mostly ignored the anti-trans messaging and voted blue.

But voting blue doesn’t automatically equate to being pro-trans. Some Democrats who did run on anti-trans policies still won their elections. Further, anti-trans ballot initiatives targeting transgender youth in schools passed in Washington, Arizona, Colorado, and Nebraska, and NBC exit polling showed that 52 percent of people in the U.S. feel that support for transgender rights has “gone too far.”

This sentiment persists despite the fact that at least 25 transgender people have died as a result of violence in the United States over the past year. The actual number of transgender people who have been murdered is certainly higher because the rampant misgendering and deadnaming in news reports and the lack of formal data collection makes accurate tracking and reporting difficult.

The United States has become increasingly untenable for trans people, who now must struggle greatly to survive, let alone thrive. More than half the country has banned medically necessary medication and surgical care for transgender youth and restricted their ability to participate in sports consistent with their gender identity. Across the country, 10 states prohibit people from correcting the gender marker on their birth certificates, eight states ban updates to gender markers on driver’s licenses, and nine states prohibit transgender people from using bathrooms and facilities that align with their gender identity in government-owned buildings and spaces, including K–12 schools and colleges.

Such policies have prompted 9 percent of trans people polled to relocate since 2024, fleeing states with anti-trans laws for supposedly safer havens like Washington and Colorado. But those states, too, have now passed similar anti-trans measures through ballot initiatives (though trans rights advocates have said they will fight to repeal them via legislation and litigation).

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has made attacks on transgender rights a central policy priority, making it increasingly difficult for trans youth to feel safe anywhere in the country. The Trump administration is especially fixated on undermining medical research and standards of care for transgender youth and has challenged states’ sovereign authority to regulate the practice of medicine within their borders. The Trump administration has also issued civil and grand jury subpoenas to hospitals in attempts to obtain transgender youths’ private medical records, targeted the medical associations responsible for researching and developing standards of care for transgender youth through civil investigative subpoenas and litigation, and stopped reimbursing states for Medicaid/CHIP coverage for trans medical care received by youth.

The administration has doubled down on false statements saying transgender people are violent, even in official memos, despite research finding that transgender people are more than four times more likely than cisgender people to be victims (not perpetrators) of violent crime. The Trump administration has also increasingly funded or commissioned misleading reports falsely framing being transgender or supporting transgender communities as indicators of political violence to justify using the nation’s national security apparatus to target and disenfranchise Democratic voters.

The administration has also weakened employment protections for transgender workers, restricted transgender people’s ability to obtain federal identification documents that reflect their gender identity, and disrupted hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding for research and services supporting transgender communities. These anti-trans policies restrict transgender people’s access to employment, health care, housing, and public services, thus increasing trans people’s risk of facing harassment, discrimination, and violence, and causing significant psychological harm.

Trans youth are especially vulnerable to internalizing anti-trans rhetoric. According to research by The Trevor Project, 94 percent of transgender and nonbinary youth reported that anti-LGBTQ+ policies, laws, and public debates caused them stress or anxiety. Additionally, research has found that transgender and nonbinary youth living in states that enacted anti-transgender laws reported up to a 72 percent increase in suicide attempts.

In light of this research, we cannot ignore the role and responsibility of anti-trans policies and state violence in the deaths of transgender people. Anti-trans policies appear to play an active part in normalizing violence against transgender people and contributing to death by suicide. As transgender journalist Erin Reed has written, “every trans suicide is a murder by those in power.” At least 20 transgender people have died from suicide over the past year.

Democratic attorneys general have challenged some of the Trump administration’s most egregious anti-trans policies in court and defended civil rights in their states. Bolstered by the “blue tsunami,” it is time for Democrats across the country to shift from defense to offense on trans rights.

Democrats now have the power to act, and they must use it to honor those who are no longer with us on this Trans Day of Remembrance. That means using state civil rights laws to hold accountable all the hospitals that preemptively discontinued care for transgender youth. It means transforming states like Texas, which has been among the most anti-trans states in the country, into places that protect trans youth by repealing anti-trans executive orders and withdrawing from anti-trans lawsuits. It means using the Democratic Party’s congressional power to hold the Trump administration and its political appointees across federal agencies accountable for their unlawful actions over the past two years.

It is up to us to hold the Democrats accountable for defending trans lives and undoing some of the tremendous violence wrought over the past few years, and ensuring that by the next Trans Day of Remembrance, the world is a safer place for trans people.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Z Waite
title: AI Is Monitoring and Scoring Fast-Food Workers’ Every Move
content:
One app measures how quickly workers walk to and from their cars. Another judges how warmly workers greet customers.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see.

The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. Each trip is scored from 0 to 100 based on factors including acceleration, braking, cornering and speed. According to Kearney, drivers at their store are expected to keep their scores above 85. Anyone below that score is written up by managers and eventually locked out of the Domino’s system. “Drivosity can effectively fire people,” Kearney said. As a driver captain, Kearney has to write up other drivers, even though they have found the app doesn’t recognize the nuance of many real-world situations. Drivers can be penalized for sudden braking to avoid a collision or rapid acceleration to merge on a highway, forcing them to choose between risking an accident or getting points docked, according to Kearney. “It’s infuriating,” Kearney said. “The AI can tell you you haven’t driven well enough and you get fired.”

Drivosity also sells coaching and analytics features, including HustleTime®, which measures how fast employees walk from the store to their car, how long they take handing the pizza to a customer and how long they take walking back. In Drivosity’s promotional videos, franchise owners and managers at Domino’s and Papa John’s praise HustleTime®’s ability to track workers in real time down to the second. Stores can “gamify” this, according to the company website, by having workers compete for better scores.

Domino’s and Drivosity did not respond to requests for comment.

Fast-food companies are increasingly using AI-powered technology to turn worker behavior — how fast you drive, how warmly you greet a customer, how long you spend in the bathroom — into data that can score, rank, discipline and manage employees. To understand how these AI-driven tools are impacting fast-food workers, Capital & Main interviewed over a dozen workers, researchers and labor advocates, who described error-prone technologies being deployed at a rapid pace, without the consent or awareness of staff, even as their pay and promotions are increasingly shaped by AI-enabled monitoring.

“They basically use their population of workers as guinea pigs,” Alexandra Mateescu, a researcher at the nonprofit Data & Society, said of the way that fast-food companies are deploying these new tools.

In February, Burger King announced that an OpenAI-powered assistant named Patty was being rolled out at about 500 U.S. restaurants, with plans to reach all U.S. stores by the end of 2026. A few weeks later, the tool arrived at the Burger King in Niagara Falls, New York, where Dante Vasquez took drive-thru orders.

“It started with a little AI voice in our headset,” said Vasquez.

Then the monitoring features started. Each drive-thru conversation was scored on friendliness and upselling, with the numbers displayed on a screen in front of Vasquez as he worked. Anyone could click on a transaction to hear a recording and review the AI-generated transcripts. Green boxes marked what he’d done well — a “Good morning!” or “You rule!” Red boxes marked what Patty counted against him: points off for saying “please hold,” or “um,” or not speaking clearly.

Managers watched the scores closely, constantly reminding the crew to stay above the 70% friendliness target, Vasquez said. Workers who scored low were cut from the schedule, he added.

Vasquez learned to speak the way that Patty wanted. He got so good at it, that customers started asking if he was a bot. His co-workers nicknamed him “Gemini.” “The system wants me to talk like a robot, so I’m talking like a robot,” Vasquez said. “It just gets so mentally degrading.”

Burger King has said publicly that the system was not designed to evaluate individual employees. But Capital & Main reviewed screenshots from a Burger King training module, and images of the dashboard in use, showing individual drive-thru conversations timestamped and marked for tone and upselling. Vasquez, and other Burger King employees, some of whom spoke to Capital & Main on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said it was easy to identify and discipline individual employees for low scores.

Later, Patty started scoring workers on “warmth,” a metric Vasquez couldn’t make sense of. When he asked his district manager how it was calculated, he recalled, she told him to just talk “like a warm blanket.”

According to Vasquez, Patty seemed to penalize his Black co-workers more than others for what the system flagged as “improper tone.” Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said that scoring workers on warmth or friendliness is “sort of pseudoscience” and that those tools risk penalizing workers for their accents or disabilities.

Asked to respond to these concerns, Kristen Viersen, Burger King’s director of communications, emailed Capital & Main a company statement that said, “We have never before heard any example similar to the questions you raised about team members being penalized based on race, gender, ethnicity or accent.” Burger King declined to answer when asked if the company had tested these features for bias.

The new monitoring features were intended “to celebrate great examples of friendly service” and allow managers to coach their team, according to the statement, which also said that Burger King has since disabled both features “for further improvements.” Burger King would not say when the features were disabled, and workers said the monitoring was active through August of this year.

Co-workers at Vasquez’s restaurant joked that Vasquez would soon be gone, replaced by Patty entirely, a looming threat that was amplified by a sign in the store that reminded workers that Patty was being trained on every headset conversation. Eventually, the stress just wasn’t worth it.

“If Patty wasn’t introduced,” Vasquez said, “I would still be working at Burger King.”

While large chains have struck high-profile deals with major AI companies — Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill, announced last year that it was deploying Nvidia-powered computer vision for “back-of-house labor management through real-time analytics and alerts” — a crowd of smaller vendors sells the same kind of AI monitoring to individual franchisees, with far less visibility.

Among the more established vendors is Solink, an Ottawa-based company backed by Goldman Sachs that describes itself as “the leader in AI-driven video intelligence.” It works with franchisees of Domino’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, Jack in the Box, Five Guys and other chains.

Solink’s product documentation describes a video-surveillance system capable of flagging workers who arrive late or leave early, take too long on their breaks, fail to wear a hairnet or the correct uniform, use their phones while on the clock or simply stand idle. The software can layer onto a restaurant’s existing security cameras, and it lets managers type in prompts to find footage of specific behaviors or set up automatic alerts.

In a statement, a Solink spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company’s platform helps businesses “improve operations, sales, safety, and customer experience.” It also stressed that Solink “does not offer identification tools such as biometrics or facial recognition,” and that its terms require customers to comply with the law.

Data & Society’s Mateescu said these tools are rarely marketed as worker surveillance. Instead they are sold as “loss prevention” or “workflow management” tools. This language, she said, obscures what the technology actually does “both to employees and to consumers.”

While some companies use corporate euphemisms to obscure worker monitoring, others are more direct. MashMore, a new potato-themed fast-food restaurant in Albany, New York, is explicit about its AI use. Using commercially available AI models, its co-founders built an HR chatbot, named Mashy after the store’s mascot, that schedules, scores and ranks all employees.

Mashy runs on a stream of data employees generate as they work. Workers clock into routines, complete assigned “quests” and upload photos proving that tasks are completed. In exchange they earn “Mashy points,” which set their level in the restaurant’s ranking system and can determine bonuses and promotions. When co-founder and CEO Andy Gor let Capital & Main interact with the chatbot, it didn’t hesitate about who the employee of the month should be. “Shontia Thomas, and it genuinely isn’t a contest,” the chatbot wrote on a screen that Gor shared with a reporter. Gor said the system would never be used to fire an employee, but the chatbot had created rankings for all workers, including those with the lowest scores.

Gor wants to make every routine, cleaning task and customer-service expectation tracked, scored and eventually copied from one location to another, so he can check anything from anywhere. “I’m in China right now,” he said. “I can see that during rush hour they cleaned the table nicely. Today, they pass.”

MashMore currently has just one location, but Gor wants to franchise fast. His pitch to investors is that the AI tool can manage employees across dozens of locations. Mashy, Gor said, is “our boss. Basically I’m working for him, too.”

Efforts to rein in algorithmic management have mostly stalled at the federal level. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of first-in-the-nation workplace-AI laws on Sept. 30. SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act, bars employers from relying solely on AI to fire or discipline workers. AB 1883 prohibits tools that use AI to infer an employee’s emotional state or collect “neural data.” SB 951 requires employers to notify workers when AI is behind a mass layoff.

Tobin-Miyaji said in an email that the emotion-scoring ban would likely cover a tool like Patty — but that No Robo Bosses could be satisfied by “cursory” human oversight, leaving workers “constantly surveilled and quantified.”

Unions could in theory negotiate stricter protections than legislation might afford. In 2023, workers in California won the creation of a Fast Food Council, a state body empowered by law to set wages and weigh in on working conditions across the industry. But despite worker efforts to apply pressure to Gov. Newsom, the council currently lacks a chairperson and has not met for over a year. A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.” Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off.

When Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he said they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t plan to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing.

Ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.”

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

author: Software Architektur im Stream
title: Produktivität mit KI: Das Harvard-Paper
content:
Wie viel schneller werden Entwickler:innen durch den Einsatz von KI? Viele Studien untersuchen vor allem, wie stark KI das Coding beschleunigt. Doch schnellerer Code bedeutet nicht automatisch mehr Produktivität. Entscheidend ist letztlich, ob tatsächlich mehr sinnvolle Features entstehen und bei den Kunden ankommen.




Die 

Harvard-Studie

 hat Daten von 720.542 Entwicklern aus 655 Firmen ausgewertet und dabei mehr als nur die Coding-Leistung bewertet. In dieser Folge erläutert Eberhard die Ergebnisse der Studie an und diskutieren sie. Was lässt sich aus den Zahlen tatsächlich ableiten? Und was sagen sie über den Produktivitätsgewinn durch KI in der Software-Entwicklung aus?




Links







Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production, Fiona Chen, James Stratton, Harvard University
