infolibre

.

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31 week one: A summit without discussion of fossil fuels
content:
If you followed the first week of COP31 from Australia, you probably heard about the $32,000 coffee cart at the Australian pavilion and the hot mic that caught Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and energy minister Chris Bowen joking about where to keep their phones.

Much less was said about what happened in Türkiye on the opening day.

On November 9, while the summit opened with a lavish ceremony in Antalya, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan came out of a cabinet meeting in Ankara with good news: 135 million barrels of new oil potential had been found at Gabar, in Türkiye’s south-east.

The same day, at the HABAŞ steel plant in Aliağa, near İzmir, an overhead crane fell and ruptured a gas line. The explosion that followed killed 19 workers.

This workplace disaster did not make the agenda of the climate summit. HABAŞ runs its arc furnace on electricity from coal and gas, and supplies steel to the construction and car industries.

But COP31 does not talk about fossil fuels as a material order made of steel, cement and workers. It talks about an abstract “emission” to be managed from a distance. A worker killed in a fossil plant falls, by definition, is outside the frame.

Three days later, union confederations met inside the COP31 venue to discuss “just transition”. Nineteen workers were killed and Türkiye is speeding up its transition to fossil fuels but neither was on their agenda.

Türkiye, which holds the COP31 presidency, prepared well for a climate-changing summit. Since it was named host, it has signed 19 fossil fuel supply and exploration agreements, plus six nuclear and mining deals. It kept signing during the summit.

Australia, which presides over the negotiations, is no different. Labor had already approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects. Weeks before the summit it made it 38, clearing the Boggabri coal mine to dig another 30 million tonnes.

In Antalya, Albanese put the Pacific Island nations at the centre of his speech and then spent more time on home batteries than on coal and gas.

Bowen told the ABC that coal and gas exports have not damaged Australia's standing in the talks, and that his job is to land “the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow”.

Tuvalu’s Prime Minister Feleti Teo described new fossil fuel projects “a death sentence for us”.

The Pacific Resilience Facility, Australia’s showpiece, reached US$200 million in Antalya. By Albanese’s own account, 46% of the money, so far, has come from Pacific countries themselves.

Meanwhile, according to Climate Action Network, Australia has joined the European Union, Japan and Norway in opposing a commitment to triple adaptation finance, in the very text it is supposed to be steering.

This is what I call climate-changing policy. Once you know it, you can see the climate-changing summit behind the “climate summit” and the transition to fossil fuels behind the “just transition” slogan.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s environment minister, did not say the word “fossil” once in his opening speech. Bowen said it twice. At the leaders’ summit, Erdoğan and Albanese barely touched it.

In the first week, 56 negotiating documents were published; draft texts, informal notes, draft conclusions and decisions. They run to 268 pages. Coal and oil do not appear in them. “Fossil” turns up, at most, in a heading.

The only text that plainly mentions transitioning away from fossil fuels is a non-binding summary of views from the presidency. It repeats the 2023 Dubai sentence, limited to “energy systems”, so asphalt, cement and plastics are out from the start.

Brazil’s road map is voluntary. Even so, the Arab Group reportedly objected from day one to any reference to the road map in decision texts.

The words are missing because of how COP31 works. Decisions are taken by consensus, so a single bloc can strike it. The hosts are sitting on their own fossil expansion and have no wish to force it. The silence suits everyone.

Instead, Türkiye and Australia are selling another target: Lifting electricity’s share of final energy use to 35% by 2035. Whether that electricity comes from renewables or from fossil fuels is not the question. Bowen says tying it to renewables would be too hard for many countries.

Türkiye generates much of its own electricity by burning coal and gas, and Australia is among its top five coal suppliers.

The other big topic is finance: Extra money for climate projects, while the public keeps paying for the fossil order. Free public transport would cut urban fuel use sharply, and it is not on the table for discussion.

Next door, at the trade fair, you can buy green cement.

The hot topic among delegates for the first three days was traffic.

Antalya is the capital of Türkiye’s car republic: A city of 2.7 million with 366 municipal buses and three tram lines, carrying about 300,000 passengers a day. The summit registered 92,000 people. With one direction of the access road closed for official convoys, people spent three and a half hours covering 30 kilometres.

The fix? The governor sent schools online in seven districts for two days and put public servants on leave.

A city built for cars is a city that has guaranteed its fossil demand. Every jam is answered with more asphalt and more vehicles, and public transport is always postponed. The negotiating table works the same way and so do Australia’s car-built cities.

Kick Big Polluters Out counts 103 polluting companies and industry bodies with delegations at COP31. Sixty are from the fossil fuel sector. Forty-five came as guests of Türkiye.

The climate question is a coal, oil and gas question, and it is three wars at once.

There is a war over meaning, in which fossil fuels are renamed “electrification” and destruction “just transition”.

There is a war of capital over who sets the table.

And there is physical war: The attacks on Venezuela and Iran belong to the same fight over energy.

Australia and Türkiye fought on opposite sides in World War I. Today, they trade coal and gas, share a summit and wage war on the climate together.

If they will not talk about fossil fuels, we have to.

In Antalya, that means talking about free public transport and how we change the fossil order. In Australia, it means talking about 38 approvals and the coal ships, not the coffee cart.

Otherwise COP31 will be remembered as an exercise in populism and inaction.

[Önder Algedik is a climate researcher and activist with 350Ankara. His new book, Ya Fosil Düzen Ya Devrim (Fossil Order or Revolution), is published by İletişim.]

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #306 w James Hogg on inter-war fascism and radical Melbourne history : November 19, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to James Hogg. James is an historian and one of the organisers of ‘Radical Melbourne! A People’s History Festival’, which takes place this Saturday at balam balam place in Brunswick:

Radical Melbourne! is a full-day festival celebrating Melbourne’s incredible history of ordinary people fighting collectively for a better life and a better world – from migrant strikes, to fighting the far-right, to Aboriginal resistance to colonisation.

For tickets, see here and see/hear also : People’s History of Australia.

We last spoke to James in September 2024 about Greek & Yugoslavian Anti-Fascism in Melbourne’s “Long 1960s”. On this occasion, we talked to James a little about the conference (where he’ll be presenting on ‘Fighting Imperial Fascism in Melbourne: the British Fascisti and the Australian Labour Movement, 1921-26′), and his research into inter-war anti-fascism in (‘so-called!’) Australia.

See/hear also : Yeah Nah Pasaran! #074 w Julie Gottlieb on ‘Feminine Fascism: Women in Britain’s Fascist Movement’ : June 24, 2021.

4.30pm, November 19, 2026 /// 855AM, digital, streaming, Community Radio Plus, podcats.

author: Max Hampel Altheide
title: Wenn jede Kamera zum Auge des Verfassungsschutzes wird
content:
Bild: Jon Tyson, micheile henderson und P R, Unsplash-Lizenzen; Bearbeitung: Melanie Lübbert

Seit April 2026 hat der nordrhein-westfälische Verfassungsschutz neue Überwachungsbefugnisse. Besonders weitreichend ist der Zugriff auf öffentliche und private Überwachungskameras. Zusammen mit automatisierter Datensammlung und künstlicher Intelligenz entsteht ein Überwachungspotenzial, das wir für unvereinbar mit unseren Grundrechten halten. Deshalb bereiten wir eine Verfassungsbeschwerde gegen das neue Verfassungsschutzgesetz NRW vor.

Eine junge Frau fährt in Köln mit der Straßenbahn zu einer Demonstration gegen Rechtsextremismus. In der Innenstadt trifft sie zuerst eine Freundin. Gemeinsam gehen sie einkaufen und anschließend zur Demo. Sie laufen durch die Straßen, hören Redebeiträge und unterhalten sich mit anderen Teilnehmenden. Nach der Demonstration sitzen sie noch mit einigen Bekannten in einer Kneipe, bevor sie nach Hause fahren.

Auf ihrem Weg werden sie immer wieder von Kameras erfasst: in der Straßenbahn, am Bahnhof, vor Geschäften, an Geldautomaten oder in der Fußgängerzone. Aufnahmen, die ganz unterschiedlichen Zwecken dienen. Mal sollen sie Diebstähle verhindern, mal Vandalismus aufklären oder der Sicherheit im Nahverkehr dienen.

Was die beiden nicht wissen: Der Verfassungsschutz darf nun bei den Kameras mitsehen.

Die Demonstration und die junge Frau sind erfunden. Die Überwachungsmöglichkeiten, um die es geht, sind es leider nicht. Das neue Verfassungsschutzgesetz in NRW räumt dem Inlandsgeheimdienst weitgehende Überwachungsbefugnisse ein. Die einzelnen Maßnahmen sind bereits jede für sich genommen weitreichend. In ihrem Zusammenspiel ermöglichen sie eine potenziell nahezu lückenlose Überwachung des analogen öffentlichen Raums. Hinzu kommt die Möglichkeit, den digitalen öffentlichen Raum automatisiert nach personenbezogenen Informationen zu durchsuchen und gewonnene Erkenntnisse mit künstlicher Intelligenz auszuwerten.

Der Verfassungsschutz erhält damit Überwachungsmöglichkeiten, deren Ausmaß wir bisher vor allem mit autoritären Staaten verbunden haben.

Besonders problematisch ist § 20 des neuen Verfassungsschutzgesetzes. Die Regelung erlaubt es dem Geheimdienst, vorhandene private und öffentliche Überwachungskameras im öffentlich zugänglichen Raum mitzunutzen. Er darf sich in Echtzeit auf Kameras aufschalten und Betreiber.innen dazu verpflichten, Bild- und Tonaufzeichnungen live auszuleiten oder vorhandene Aufnahmen herauszugeben. Das kann sogar Aufzeichnungen betreffen, die bis zu einem Jahr vor der Anordnung entstanden sind.

Damit wird aus den dezentral betriebenen Kamerasystemen von Verkehrsberieben, Geschäften, öffentlichen Einrichtungen und weiteren Stellen ein zentralisiertes Netz potenzieller nachrichtendiesntlicher Videoüberwachung geschaffen, das grade in Städten flächendeckende Ausmaße annehmen kann. Und die Betreiber.innen können verpflichtet werden, dabei mitzuwirken. Hiervon sind zwangläufig viele Menschen betroffen. Das ist in besonderem Maße problematisch, weil das Gesetz keinen hinreichenden Schutz für besonders sensible und grundrechtlich geschützte Lebensbereiche vorsieht: Demonstrationen sowie berufliche Kontakte von Journalist.innen, Rechtsanwält.innen oder Seelsorger.innen können grundsätzlich erfasst werden.

Der Inlandsgeheimdienst bekommt damit Möglichkeiten zur Überwachung des öffentlichen Raums, die in ihrer Reichweite einem Überwachungsstaat gleicht. Diese Wertung ist keineswegs übertrieben. Schon im Gesetzgebungsverfahren bezeichnete ein Rechtswissenschaftler die Regelung als „inakzeptabel“ und warnte vor der Gefahr eines Überwachungsstaats. Auch die Landesdatenschutzbeauftragte äußerte erhebliche verfassungsrechtliche Bedenken.

Besonders schwer wiegt, dass die Kameras nicht nur diejenigen erfassen, für die sich der Verfassungsschutz interessiert. Auf den Bildern sind zwangsläufig auch alle anderen Menschen zu sehen, die sich zufällig dort aufhalten.

Unsere Demonstrantin könnte deshalb schon dann auf einer Aufzeichnung landen, wenn der Verfassungsschutz eine andere Person auf derselben Demonstration beobachten will. Die junge Frau selbst muss dafür überhaupt keinen Anlass gegeben haben.

Die Möglichkeit einer derart weitreichenden Überwachung greift nicht nur in das Recht auf informationelle Selbstbestimmung ein. Sie bedroht auch andere Grundrechte, allen voran die Versammlungsfreiheit.

Wer demonstriert, äußert öffentlich eine politische Haltung. Die Entscheidung, an welcher Demonstration man teilnimmt, geht einen Geheimdienst aber grundsätzlich nichts an. Menschen müssen ihre Meinung auf der Straße vertreten können, ohne befürchten zu müssen, dass ihre Teilnahme heimlich dokumentiert und später ausgewertet wird.

Dass die Überwachung möglicherweise nie stattfindet, macht die Sache nicht harmlos. Denn niemand kann wissen, ob der Verfassungsschutz gerade auf eine Kamera zugreift oder später die Aufnahmen anfordert. In NRW gibt es seit April de facto keinen geschützen öffentlichen Raum mehr.

Das kann ausreichen, damit Menschen ihr Verhalten ändern. Vielleicht geht die junge Frau beim nächsten Mal lieber nicht mehr auf eine Demonstration. Vielleicht verzichtet sie darauf, mit bestimmten Menschen gesehen zu werden. Vielleicht bleibt sie ganz zu Hause.

Das ist der Chilling Effect, ein Abschreckungseffekt. Menschen nehmen ihre Grundrechte aus Angst vor möglichen Konsequenzen nicht mehr oder nur noch eingeschränkt wahr. Ein Staat muss nicht jeden Menschen tatsächlich überwachen, um dessen Freiheit einzuschränken. Es kann schon reichen, wenn alle jederzeit mit einer Überwachung rechnen müssen. Das ist kein neues Problem. Schon im Volkszählungsurteil von 1983 warnte das Bundesverfassungsgericht davor. Die freie Entfaltung der Persönlichkeit leidet, wenn Menschen aus Sorge vor staatlicher Datensammlung darauf verzichten, ihre Grundrechte auszuüben.

Und das betrifft nicht nur Demonstrationen. Was ist mit Journalist.innen, die vertrauliche Quellen treffen? Mit Rechtsanwält.innen und ihren Mandant.innen? Mit Menschen, die Seelsorge suchen? All diese Berufsgruppen brauchen Vertrauliche Gespräche und diese sind unzulässig geschützt in dem neuen Gesetz. Schon die Information, wer eine bestimmte Person besucht oder sich mit ihr trifft, kann hochsensibel sein. Wer jederzeit damit rechnen muss überwacht zu werden, wird vorsichtiger.

Die neuen Befugnisse zur Videoüberwachung sind nur ein Teil des Problems. Das Gesetz erlaubt dem Verfassungsschutz große Mengen personenbezogener Daten automatisiert zu sammeln und auszuwerten.

Nach § 6 Absatz 4 VSG NRW kann er beispielsweise öffentlich zugängliche Internetseiten und soziale Netzwerke automatisiert durchsuchen. Beim sogenannten Webcrawling können in kurzer Zeit Informationen über zahlreiche Menschen erfasst werden. Dabei macht es einen erheblichen Unterschied, ob jemand einen einzelnen öffentlichen Beitrag liest oder ob ein Geheimdienst große Datenmengen systematisch sammelt und für weitere Auswertungen erschließt.

§ 26 VSG NRW erlaubt anschließend die automatisierte Analyse dieser nun vorhandener Datenbestände, auch mithilfe künstlicher Intelligenz (KI). Dabei können Informationen aus unterschiedlichen Quellen zusammengeführt und Beziehungen zwischen Personen, Gruppen und Organisationen sichtbar gemacht werden.

Zurück zu unserer Demonstrantin: Sie könnte auf einer Kameraaufnahme neben einer Person auftauchen, die vom Verfassungsschutz beobachtet wird. Vielleicht ist sie auf einem öffentlich zugänglichen Demonstrationsfoto zu sehen. Vielleicht hat sie einen Beitrag zu der Veranstaltung geteilt. Dazu kommen Bilder und Videos von Pressefotograf.innen, welche die Bilder der Demonstration im Internet veröffentlichen oder auch rechte Streamer.innen, die immer öfter antifaschistische Demonstrationen bewusst aufsuchen, um sie abzufilmen und zu provozieren. Fotos und Videos landen schließlich auf TikTok, Instagram und Youtube. Nichts Ungewöhnliches, aber der Abend hinterlässt Spuren darüber, wer sich wo aufgehalten hat und mit wem jemand unterwegs war.

Jede dieser Informationen mag für sich genommen belanglos sein. Werden sie automatisiert zusammengeführt, können daraus vermeintliche Zusammenhänge entstehen. Dabei ist längst nicht jede Begegnung ein relevanter Kontakt und nicht jede Verbindung ein Hinweis auf gemeinsame politische Ziele. Trotzdem können solche Verknüpfungen mithilfe von KI zum Gegenstand geheimdienstlicher Auswertungen werden.

Das betrifft auch Menschen, gegen die keinerlei Verdacht besteht. Denn unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen ist auch die Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten Unbeteiligter erlaubt. Besonders fragwürdig finden wir schließlich, dass der Verfassungsschutz solche Daten nach § 26 Absatz 6 sogar zum Training seiner IT-Systeme verwenden darf. § 36 erlaubt sogar die Weitergabe personenbezogener Daten an externe Stellen, darunter private Unternehmen, zu Entwicklungs- und Trainingszwecken.

So können Informationen über Menschen, die selbst überhaupt nicht im Fokus des Geheimdienstes stehen, in immer neue Auswertungs- und Verarbeitungsvorgänge geraten. Und weil Nachrichtendienste weitgehend im Geheimen arbeiten, erfahren Betroffene davon möglicherweise nie. Bis man sich eines Tages für einen Job bewirbt, bei dem eine Sicherheitsüberpüfung nötig ist und durchfällt, oder Mitarbeiter.innen des Verfassungsschutz an der Wohnungstür klingeln, um Auskünfte über vermeintlich bekannte Personen zu bekommen.

Insgesamt ist dieses Gesetz ein Skandal: Es gibt einem weitgehend im Verborgenen arbeitenden Geheimdienst Überwachungsbefugnisse an die Hand, die eine nahezu lückenlose Beobachtung des öffentlichen Raums ermöglichen und damit grundlegende Freiheitsrechte gefährden, und in Richtung Überwachungstaat weisen.

Digitalcourage bereitet gemeinsam mit Betroffenen eine Verfassungsbeschwerde gegen zentrale Neuerungen des nordrhein-westfälischen Verfassungsschutzgesetzes vor. Wir wenden uns dabei insbesondere gegen den automatisierten Zugriff auf Internetdaten, die Nutzung öffentlicher und privater Überwachungskameras, die Verarbeitung von Daten Unbeteiligter, die KI-gestützte Datenanalyse und die Weitergabe personenbezogener Daten zu Trainingszwecken.

An unserer Beschwerde beteiligen sich Menschen aus unterschiedlichen gesellschaftlichen Bereichen, darunter ein Journalist, ein Seelsorger, ein Anwalt und politisch engagierte Menschen. Sie stehen stellvertetend für unterschiedliche Schutzbereiche, die durch die neuen Überwachungsbefugnisse gefährdet werden.

Journalist.innen müssen mit Quellen sprechen können, ohne befürchten zu müssen, dass ihre Kontakte nachvollzogen werden. Menschen müssen sich mit persönlichen Problemen an Seelsorger.innen wenden können. Und politische Aktivist.innen müssen sich organisieren und austauschen können, ohne dass ihre Kontakte zum Gegenstand umfassender staatlicher Auswertung werden.

Aus unserer Sicht sind darüber hinaus auch die Eingriffsmöglichkeiten zu weitreichend und die gesetzlichen Voraussetzungen dafür zu niedrig und zu unbestimmt. Besonders schwer wiegt, dass die Befugnisse auch Menschen treffen können, die selbst keinen Anlass für eine Überwachung gegeben haben.

Wir halten diese Befugnisse insgesamt für verfassungswidrig. Dabei geht es nicht nur um die Frage, wie der heutige Verfassungsschutz mit seinen Möglichkeiten umgeht. Wir müssen auch darüber sprechen, was wir einem Geheimdienst grundsätzlich erlauben wollen. Es geht schließlich um einem Geheimdienst, dessen Geschichte von Skandalen und mangelnder Transparenz geprägt ist. Nicht zuletzt der NSU-Komplex hat gezeigt, wie schwer Verfassungsschutzbehörden parlamentarisch zu kontrollieren sind und welches Eigenleben sie entwickeln können. Ausgerechnet solchen Behörden sollen nun weitreichende intransparente Überwachungsmöglichkeiten an die Hand gegeben werden, mit denen sich die Bewegungen und Kontakte unzähliger Menschen nachvollziehen lassen? Gerade in Zeiten, in denen rechtsextreme und autoritäre Kräfte erstarken, müssen wir uns fragen, ob wir staatlichen Behörden wirklich derart mächtige Überwachungsinstrumente überlassen wollen. Denn Überwachungsbefugnisse bleiben bestehen, auch wenn Regierungen wechseln. Wer garantiert uns, dass sie nicht irgendwann von denjenigen genutzt werden, vor denen sie unsere Demokratie eigentlich schützen sollen? Gerade heute müssen wir auch daran denken, wer künftig über solche Befugnisse verfügen könnte.

Unsere Demonstrantin vom Anfang hat nichts anderes getan, als von ihren Grundrechten Gebrauch zu machen. Sie sollte dafür nicht befürchten müssen, später in einer Datenanalyse eines Geheimdiensts aufzutauchen.

Grundrechte sind kein Hindernis beim Schutz unserer Demokratie. Sie sind ihre Grundlage. Eine demokratische Gesellschaft braucht Menschen, die diese Grundrechte nutzen um sich einmischen, zu demonstrieren, zu recherchieren und auch unbequeme Positionen zu vertreten, aber keine Überwachungsinfrastruktur, die diese Menschen vorsichtiger und stiller macht.

Deshalb bereiten wir seit Monaten eine Verfassungsbeschwerde gegen das neue Verfassungsschutzgesetz NRW vor. Über die Einreichung beim Bundesverfassungsgericht und das weitere Verfahren werden wir noch in diesem Jahr berichten.

author: infolibre
title: Συγκέντρωση διαμαρτυρίας για τις νέες κλήσεις εκπαιδευτικών για αξιολόγηση, την Τετάρτη 18/11, 13.30, στη Δ/νση Π.Ε. Δυτ. Θεσσαλονίκης
content:
Αφίσα/Κάλεσμα από Ζ΄ Σ.Ε.Π.Ε. Θεσ/νίκης:







Συγκέντρωση διαμαρτυρίας για τις νέες κλήσεις εκπαιδευτικών για




αξιολόγηση, την Τετάρτη 18 Νοέμβρη, 1.30μ.μ., στη Δ/νση Π.Ε. Δυτ.




Θεσσαλονίκης –Στάση εργασίας




Συνάδελφοι/ισσες,




Πολύ μαζική αλλά και πλούσια σε συζήτηση και αποφασιστικότητα ήταν η συνάντηση με τους




εκπαιδευτικούς που κλήθηκαν πρόσφατα σε αξιολόγηση, που οργανώθηκε από το Δ.Σ. του




Ζ΄Σ.Ε.Π.Ε.-Θ. και πραγματοποιήθηκε την Τετάρτη 11 Νοεμβρίου 2026. Στη συνάντηση




επιβεβαιώθηκαν και επαληθεύτηκαν με συγκεκριμένα παραδείγματα από τους παρόντες




εκπαιδευτικούς όλα αυτά που καταγράφαμε στις 4/11/2026:




«Μπορεί η Διεύθυνση Π.Ε. Δυτικής Θεσσαλονίκης να δηλώνει αδυναμία εύρεσης λύσης και για




το πιο μικρό πρόβλημα στη λειτουργία των σχολείων της περιοχής μας (από την ανακοίνωση




π.χ. όλων των κενών για τις τοποθετήσεις και την κάλυψη των εκατοντάδων κενών




εκπαιδευτικών που μέχρι σήμερα υπάρχουν μέχρι τα ταβάνια που καθημερινά πέφτουν στα




σχολεία) αλλά για την προώθηση της αξιολόγησης των εκπαιδευτικών πάντα υπάρχει χρόνος.




Έτσι νωρίς νωρίς, στα μέσα του Οκτώβρη πρόλαβε και έκανε τις αντιστοιχίσεις αξιολογητή-




αξιολογούμενου, αναθέτοντας 25 εκπαιδευτικούς στον κάθε αξιολογητή-Συμβουλο.




Από τη διαδικασία δεν έλειψαν και φέτος οι γνωστές παραβιάσεις του νόμου, όταν «από




λάθος» καλούνται ξανά σε αξιολόγηση εκπαιδευτικοί που κλήθηκαν πέρυσι ή πρόπερσι και




δήλωσαν απεργία-αποχή και ενώ ο νόμος 4823/2021 προβλέπει για τους μονιμοποιημένους




εκπαιδευτικούς κλήση σε αξιολόγηση μία φορά στην 4ετία για τα Α1 και Α2 πεδία και μία φορά




στη 2ετία για το πεδίο Β. Η παρέμβαση των Σωματείων μας απέτρεψε γρήγορα την παρατυπία




που ξεκάθαρα στόχευε στον εκφοβισμό και οι συγκεκριμένες κλήσεις σε αξιολόγηση




ανακλήθηκαν.




Αλλά και οι κλήσεις σε αξιολόγηση των παλαιότερων εκπαιδευτικών (π.χ. των ΠΕ70 με




διορισμό το 2002, αλλά και ορισμένους/ες που φτάνουν το 1998) δεν είχαν καλύτερη τύχη.




Οπλισμένοι με δύναμη από τις νίκες του καλοκαιριού (απαλλαγή των εκπαιδευτικών από τα




πειθαρχικά για συμμετοχή στην απεργία-αποχή ενάντια στην αξιολόγηση κ.ά.) οι




περισσότεροι από τους εκπαιδευτικούς που κλήθηκαν μέχρι τώρα από τους




αξιολογητές-Συμβούλους της περιοχής μας, δήλωσαν ήδη συμμετοχή στην




απεργία-αποχή.




Όπως και τα 5 προηγούμενα χρόνια, συνεχίζουμε και φέτος τη μάχη ενάντια στην αξιολόγηση




(εκπαιδευτικού και σχολικής μονάδας). Οι πολλές δεκάδες εκπαιδευτικών του Συλλόγου μας




που είναι ήδη από τα προηγούμενα χρόνια στην απεργία-αποχή και οι δεκάδες αυτών που




μπαίνουν τώρα, δείχνει ότι οι εκπαιδευτικοί του Συλλόγου μας αντιλαμβάννται πολύ καλά ότι




στη μάχη ενάντια στην αξιολόγηση-εμπορευματοποίηση και ιδιωτικοποίηση του




δημόσιου σχολείου μπορούμε να νικήσουμε με όπλο την αλληλεγγύη»!

author: Freedom Editor
title: Why anarchists hate James Bond
content:
Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007 at a time of global unrest and distaste for government

It’s been announced that Robert Pattinson has been chosen to play the next James Bond. This has come after years of speculation as to who would follow Daniel Craig. The Bond franchise in particular pins itself to a very specific time and era of Cold War espionage and patriotic spy games. Whilst we’re certainly not rid of nuclear tensions and geopolitical posturing, the general public’s attitude towards the government has changed enough to leave me wondering – what sort of person are Bond films made for?

Plenty of pragmatic anarchists are able to maintain their values whilst leisurely enjoying a pop culture franchise with morals that run counter to it. If we weren’t able to do this, we’d never get through a basic board game like chess. Star Wars, for instance, fits rather easily with our values – we can see a cautionary tale of a neoliberal society slipping into fascism in the prequels. We can then root for the revolutionaries that combat it in the original trilogy. Star Trek has a similar shared territory, with themes of communistic living (albeit still hierarchical). But the James Bond franchise presents a character that is so antithetical to anarchist values, that it becomes impossible to take seriously.

Firstly, there’s the propaganda aspect. Ian Fleming wrote ‘Casino Royale’ (the first James Bond book) back in 1953; four years after the establishment of NATO. Since then, much of the franchise features the usual tropes of damsels in distress, orientalism and an external nation that threatens (so-called) freedom and democracy. Each film was released throughout the Cold War, up until Pierce Brosnan became the first post-Soviet Bond. How entertaining the films are is neither here nor there; but the themes and stakes in which it requires the viewer to be invested act quite purposely to normalise militarism and neoliberal assumptions.

Full disclosure: I can’t honestly say I’ve seen more than one James Bond film. My friend sat me down when I was a teenager and showed me ‘Die Another Day’. At the time, I found it rather cringe to see Bond rescue a damsel in distress only to travel to a beach and make-out. Perhaps I generalise too much, but I can’t imagine being in the mood right after narrowly escaping death. My friend insisted otherwise and swore it was realistic. I can’t remember much else of the film, apart from being accused of being needlessly critical.

But certain media deserves the pushback; particularly one as backwards as James Bond. Not only from an anarchist viewpoint, but even from a Feminist one: I’ve hardly come across a woman who enthusiastically recommends I watch the likes of Sean Connery (who in an interview with Barbara Walters advocated hitting women if they “can’t leave it alone”). Nor have I known any that have been excited to see yet another actress play an objectified Bond girl.

Randolph Bourne famously stated that “war is the health of the state”; that they are one in the same. The Bond franchise mirrors the exact trajectory of people’s view towards government: problematic, and constantly requiring updates and rebrands. Without the latent external threat of some enemy government, I’m unsure what there would truly be to root for with regards to Bond. His story very much depends on the assumption that the government, bureaucracy and the military have our best interests at heart. Anarchists have long known for centuries that this isn’t the case for neither radicals nor everyday working people.

One of the nearest USA examples that comes to mind (there are many) would be the fictional agent Jack Bauer (played by Kiefer Sutherland) in the post-9/11 series 24. The series took place largely during the War on Terror and depicted torture and surveillance as a necessary evils in order to stop terrorists – very much aligning with Bush’s Patriot Act. Later, towards the end of the franchise, in 2014, 24: Live Another Day was released. In this series, Bauer was an enemy of the state and federal fugitive. By this point the show felt like it was attempting to reconcile the character’s image with the changing attitudes towards the war crimes of the early 2000s. Whilst 24 remains a relic of that era, the Bond films still continue to regenerate well past the fall of the Soviet Union.

As Pattinson is announced to be the next Bond, protests by workers and students are occurring around the world, from Albania and France to Brazil and the Canada. Giant tech oligarchs are closely working with the government. Data centres continue to be built, and militarism continues to expand. Anarchists hate James Bond, not because we want a foreign government to win, but because we wish for a franchise that disingenuously pretends to value freedom (the concept we champion so dearly) to finally lose.

author: Alicia Houser
title: Tanzania’s Peace Was Never Peaceful
content:
One year ago, on October 29, 2025, the sound of bombs and bullets rang out around Dar es Salaam and several other cities across Tanzania. Before last year’s election, Tanzania had enjoyed an international reputation as a peaceful haven in an often tumultuous region. Foreign governments and tour companies certainly helped craft this image, but so did Tanzania’s government and population. Since I started visiting the country in 2017, people have often cited 

amani

 (peace) as one of Tanzania’s best attributes. People attributed this purported peace not to satisfaction with the government or living conditions, but to fear. 

Watanzania ni woga

 (Tanzanians are cowards), my friends tell me self-deprecatingly. This fear belies the peaceful image Tanzania has cultivated overseas. 




Histories, or perhaps more accurately colonial histories, place Tanzania in the category of African countries that peacefully acquired independence. To consider Tanzania’s transition to independence as peaceful is to take a short view of history. This narrative ignores the Hehe killed during seven years of fighting against the Germans, which ended in 1898 with 

Chief Mkwawa

 killing himself rather than surrendering and his skull being taken to Germany. It ignores the organized resistance that involved the entire southern half of Tanzania, the 

Maji Maji

 war of 1905–1908, which some consider the first Pan-African anticolonial resistance movement. The Tanzanian historian Gilbert Gwassa estimated that 300,000 Africans died in this movement, most of them from starvation. The narrative of peaceful transition also ignores the roughly 600,000 Africans who died as a result of 

World War I

 military incursions on Tanzanian soil. In these three events alone, almost one million would-be Tanzanians lost their lives to colonization. 




I was in Dar es Salaam last year during the election. The internet cut out at about noon, and the sounds of bombs and bullets started around 1 pm and continued off and on for another four days. Without internet, radio, or television, I got my news the old-fashioned way: through other people. My friends in Arusha and Moshi sent frequent messages, and I went out to my courtyard and sat with my neighbors who were connected to other cities across the country. We exchanged what we had heard: someone’s niece had stepped outside her apartment in Dar and encountered a body, Muhimbili Hospital was overflowing; bodies were being stacked outside mortuaries; ballot boxes had been burned. There would be no votes to count. By day three of the lockdown, rumors were circulating that the government was preparing for a prolonged battle, and that Dar’s drinking water might be poisoned. By day five, the store next door to me had sold out of airtime, water, sodas, and milk. Amid the fear, though, was excitement.




Watanzania wameamka, one of my neighbors said proudly. Tanzanians have woken up. A neighbor who stopped by noted that 

hakuna mafanikio bila

 sacrifice. No success without sacrifice. Another neighbor said she was going to give 10,000 shillings to any 

bodaboda

 and 

bajaji

 drivers (the motorcycle and three-wheeler taxi drivers who ferry much of urban Tanzania) she saw; they were the ones leading the protests.




On day six, Mama Samia—as President Samia Suluhu Hassan is popularly known—was sworn in as president at a ceremony closed to the public. The sounds of bombs and bullets had fizzled out over the days, and the morning marking one week since the election radiated with the usual city sounds of buses, 

bajajis

, and 

bodabodas

 that had gone quiet for so long. The halt in violence did not result from any recognition by Samia of the illegitimacy of the election, which did not include any candidates from the country’s main opposition parties. The electoral commission barred CHADEMA, the largest of them, and disqualified the candidate of ACT-Wazalendo. After days of police shooting 

live rounds

 into crowds and indiscriminately killing 

civilians

 caught in the wrong place at the wrong time, the protests stopped. Tanzanians decided they did not want to die. After the election, there was a general feeling of “Where do we go from here?”




Months before the election, in March of last year, I attended a memorial event on the slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in Old Moshi, remembering the 19 area chiefs whom the Germans hanged on March 2, 1900, on accusations of subversion. One of the elders recalled a phrase he heard often growing up, anytime a bad event happened: 

Hatujazika babu zetu

 (We have not yet buried our grandfathers). 




What if we apply that thinking to the 2025 election? What if we consider the violence of 2025 not only as a result of the intimidation, 

abductions

, and 

political violence

 President Samia’s regime has enacted, but also as a product of decades of unaddressed generational trauma still lingering from the violence Tanzanians experienced under colonization? This kind of recognition would require formerly colonizing powers to share in the responsibility for election violence and do more than issue statements of condemnation. Addressing generational trauma requires addressing the continued damage caused by colonization. How can a country peacefully move forward when its people haven’t yet buried their grandfathers?




–




This post is from a partnership between 

Africa Is a Country

 and The Elephant. We will be publishing 

a series of posts

 from their site every week

.

Tanzania’s Peace Was Never Peaceful

author: Unknown
title: Karayılan: The PKK created a national spirit and consciousness
content:
Murat Karayılan, Commander of the People's Defence Centre (HSM), talked to Egîd Sîrwan on Stêrk TV about the ongoing political process.




In the second part of the interview, he spoke about the importance of the PKK in bringing the Kurdish people "back from the brink of extinction." Talking about the upcoming 25 November, he said that "talking about creating a free society without liberating women is an empty claim with no foundation."




The first part of the interview can be read 

here

. 




The PKK fought for Kurdish freedom for half a century. What impact did it have on the struggle for freedom, not only in Kurdistan but throughout the region? In short, what has the PKK achieved over these 48 years?




The Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) brought the Kurdish people back from the brink of extinction, helped them rise to their feet and brought them to the negotiating table. That is what it achieved, to put it very briefly. But if we elaborate, we can assess this from several perspectives.




At the national level, 48 years of resistance put an end to the genocide carried out in Kurdistan under the Eastern Reform Plan (Şark Islahat Planı), the Turkish state's historical policy of assimilation and repression. In doing so, it guaranteed the existence of the Kurdish people and brought their existence onto the agenda in a way that nobody could deny.




At the social level, this resistance developed like a renaissance in Kurdistan. It overcame centuries of backwardness. At the intellectual level, there was almost a revolution in thought. A complete transformation took place, bringing about a profound renewal of society. It developed a social revolution. It transformed a people who had given up on themselves and lost hope into a people who had risen to their feet, regained hope and begun to struggle, carrying forward the struggle for freedom and democracy of our age. It reached that level.




At the same time, it developed the Women's Revolution in Kurdistan. Through the struggle against the male-dominated mentality and efforts to transform that mentality, it enabled women to develop their own will and agency. It laid the foundations for such profound social transformations.




'The PKK guaranteed the existence of the Kurdish people'




At the political level, it brought the Kurdish question to the negotiating table. Through struggle, resistance and different methods, it created Kurdish politics. Previously, Kurds fought only in the mountains. The political sphere had effectively been left to the colonial powers. The movement developed a tradition of conducting politics on the political ground established by the state itself. This struggle also has its martyrs and prisoners. Important developments have been achieved in this field as well.




'The PKK created a national spirit and consciousness'




This struggle influenced all four parts of Kurdistan. It created a national spirit and consciousness. Previously, the different parts of Kurdistan were distant from one another, separated by borders. The struggle rendered those borders meaningless. A young person from Lorestan turned their attention towards another part of Kurdistan, towards Dersim. Young people from Kermanshah and Ardalan turned their attention towards all of Kurdistan. The same happened in Qamishlo, Kobanê, Amed (Diyarbakır), Erbil (Hewlêr) and Sulaymaniyah (Silêmanî). In short, people from every part participated. This attracted the attention of many people. It was, in particular, a movement of intellectuals. It always had an influence among university students. Through its cadres, it created a national spirit and consciousness at that level.




It also achieved very important developments at the internationalist level. As is known, internationalism has been part of this movement from its very foundation. Comrades Haki and Kemal were among its founders. These ideas became known throughout the world. Today, there are many Arab and Turkish cadres, as well as cadres from numerous other peoples. In other words, it became a universal idea. A foundation for internationalist work has now emerged. This, too, represents an achievement.




During the period when the PKK was carrying out its struggle, actually existing socialism collapsed. It appeared as though humanity had become condemned to capitalism. However, the struggle that was carried out, together with the theoretical depth developed by Leader Apo (Abdullah Öcalan), both before and after his imprisonment on Imrali Island, sent a message to the world: "No, we are not condemned to capitalist modernity. We have an alternative. It is true that nation-state socialism collapsed, but there is democratic society socialism. It can bring victory and show the way forward." He developed Democratic Modernity, a democratic and ecological paradigm based on women's freedom, as an alternative to capitalist modernity. As these ideas spread around the world, they generated influence and hope.




This movement also achieved major developments through resistance. The emergence of ISIS (Islamic State of Iraq and Syria) created a grave danger. However, the interventions in Shengal and Kobanê, and the resistance extending from Kirkuk to Afrin (Efrîn), effectively formed a barrier against the ISIS threat. The Rojava Revolution developed as a result of this historic resistance. Most importantly, never before in Kurdish history had there been a struggle in which fighters held the same positions for five years, resisted and remained undefeated. With NATO's support, the Turkish state attempted to destroy us not once but dozens of times. The International Conspiracy was carried out. An unprecedented resistance developed. At the point we have reached today, revolution is on the agenda not only in one country but throughout the region, together with change and transformation. In particular, the new initiative developed by Leader Apo, the initiative for peace, democratic society and democratic integration, has opened the way for major developments throughout the region.




'

People rallied around the Apoist movement because its words matched its actions'




None of this was easy, of course. These achievements were the result of the efforts of many heroes. Beginning with Leader Apo, all members of this movement remained faithful to their words. Whatever promises they made to their society, they put them into practice. They worked towards fulfilling those promises. They did not betray their dreams. That is how they proceeded. People rallied around the movement because they saw that its words and actions were consistent. There were many other organisations before us. Why did they fall behind and become marginalised? Some explain this in various ways, but the truth is that the Apoist members of this movement, formerly known as PKK members, put whatever they said into practice. They did so even at the cost of their lives. The courage of women and men became evident. That is why the people rallied around this movement, and they will continue to do so. Because the struggle continues. In the new period, with a new strategy, the Apoist Movement will grow and develop even further.




'Everyone, from the founders to the commanders, fought with self-sacrifice'




Comrades Haki Karer, Mazlum Doğan, Mehmet Hayri Durmuş, Kemal Pir, Ferhat Kurtay and Mehmet Karasungur, as well as Heval Fuat (Ali Haydar Kaytan), Rıza Altun, Sara (Sakine Cansız) and Seyfi Zoğurlu, who carried out a long period of practical struggle, and many other comrades were founders of this movement, yet they gave their lives in the course of the struggle. At the level of the general guerrilla command, from comrade Egîd to the Erdals, Bedrans, Azimes, Zelals and Zîlans; following the 1 June Initiative, the Adıls, Nudas, Reşits and Rojîns; and, more recently, comrades Nurettîn Sofî, Atakan Mahir, Delal Amed, Leyla Amed and Gulçiya Gabar, who served in the general command and were among those leading this movement; as well as comrades Sabri Tendürek, Egîd Civyan, Şivan Gever, Azad Sîser, Doğan Didêrî, Berçem Cîlo, Yılmaz Dersîm, Çetin Siverek, Zinê Cizre, Şêxmus Malazgirt, Berwar Dersîm and Axîn Mûş, all led this movement and were at the forefront when they fell as martyrs. In the recent tunnel resistance, comrades Nurî Yekta, Azê Şirnex, Alan Malazgirt, Siyabend, Mizgîn Ronahî, Cumali and Çavrê, Delil Zagros, Mordem Çewlig and Sarya Qamışlo, along with many other comrades serving in regional and provincial commands, all stood at the forefront, gave their lives and attained martyrdom.




'We lost 50,000 martyrs in 48 years of struggle'




Taken as a whole, the Apoist Movement has lost approximately 50,000 martyrs across all four parts of Kurdistan, including leaders, guerrillas, fighters, militia members, supporters, workers and civilians, because, as is known, resistance along this political line was also carried out in the other parts of Kurdistan. So many martyrs were lost over these 48 years, and these developments were achieved through their sacrifices. Today, as a result of these developments, our people can look towards the future with their heads held high and have reached a level where they can achieve their goals.




25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, is approaching. Violence against women remains extremely widespread in society. How effective is the struggle against violence against women worldwide? How do you assess it?




A struggle against violence against women is being carried out today. Firstly, I salute everyone involved in this struggle. This is also our struggle as a movement. What is the source of violence against women? It is male domination. The male-dominated mentality is the source of violence against women. We want to eliminate male domination. As a movement, we are carrying out a profound struggle to transform this mentality. Because women must be liberated for society to become free.




'We want to achieve a free society by creating free women and men'




Talking about creating a free society without liberating women is an empty claim with no foundation. If you genuinely want to create a free society, the sexes must first be liberated. Women must be liberated. For women, and therefore society, to become free, the male-dominated mentality must be eliminated. This is necessary not only for women's freedom but also for the freedom of society. That is why we pursue a much more fundamental struggle. If this struggle advances and achieves results, the source of violence against women will also be eliminated, and the foundations of a free society will be established. If women become free in a society, and men can free themselves from the hollow mentality of domination, men will also become free. That is our aim. We want to achieve a free society by creating free women and free men. This is extremely important, historic and sacred. That is why everyone struggling against violence against women is valuable, and we fully support this struggle. We also want to integrate this struggle much more fundamentally into our revolutionary struggle and genuinely turn a free society into a reality. Of course, on this basis, we also say, "Jin, Jiyan, Azadî" (Woman, Life, Freedom).




Recently the Press Liaison Centre of the People's Defense Forces (HPG) announced commemorations of martyrs from Eastern Kurdistan (Rojhilat). We see this as an expression of the spirit of national unity among the different parts of Kurdistan. You had issued a message to the families of the martyrs. What can you say about the participation of young people from Eastern Kurdistan? Everyone is also wondering where the situation in Eastern Kurdistan is heading and what will happen.




Firstly, I would like to take this opportunity to greet our valued people of Eastern Kurdistan with respect and affection. We have recently announced the names of some of our martyrs. We will announce the remaining names within the next ten days. I commemorate all these martyrs with respect and gratitude. I bow respectfully before their memory. They are the heroes of this era. All our valued families should know that the daughters and sons they raised played an important role for the Kurdish people and attained martyrdom. So far, we have announced the martyrs from certain regions. The martyrs from Urmia will be announced today or tomorrow. Then approximately 40 comrades from Salmas, Khoy (Xoy), Kotol, Marivan (Merîwan) and the Kalhor region will remain. We will announce those comrades within the next ten days as well.




'The martyrs have paved the way for national unity'




They are national heroes. They set out from places as far away as Kalhor or Ardalan, travelled to Northern Kurdistan (Bakur) and Southern Kurdistan (Başûr), and joined the national struggle. What could be more valuable and honourable than that? The young women and men of the Kurdish people regard this as their responsibility. They leave their own regions and travel to another part of Kurdistan to struggle for a united and free Kurdistan. They fight wholeheartedly for years and attain martyrdom. This is a sign of the Kurdish people's victory. This is the path towards Kurdish national unity. Someone from Lorestan, Kalhor or Ilam turns towards Northern Kurdistan. This is no ordinary matter. Moreover, these are not children. Many of them attended university. They studied, came to believe in Leader Apo's ideas and, on that basis, decided to become militants, fighters and commanders of this people. Indeed, many of them reached that level.




'They did everything they could to destroy us'




There is another matter that all our people in Eastern Kurdistan should know. I believe many of them are already following these developments and are aware of them. Particularly over the past ten years, we have faced extremely severe attacks. As you know, our Yazidi (Êzidî) people use the word "ferman" to describe campaigns of genocide and extermination. It refers to a ruler issuing a decree of extermination, bringing catastrophe upon a people. Over the past ten years, the Turkish state has effectively declared such a campaign of destruction against us. To destroy us as a movement, it obtained support from NATO, acquired modern weapons, reorganised the state internally and concentrated all power in a single authority. It sought to destroy us through attacks using the most advanced weapons of our time. Twice, they set deadlines for our destruction. First, they said the PKK would be finished by April 2017. April 2017 came and went, but the PKK was not defeated. Then, in 2021, they developed another plan and launched an attack on Garê. At that time, they formed alliances with various forces, including Iraq, and gave themselves three months to finish us. To destroy us, they used prohibited chemical weapons, tactical nuclear weapons and every kind of modern weapon against us. But an historic resistance developed against them.




'I respectfully salute the families of the martyrs'




Never in the history of our people's struggle has there been such prolonged resistance in the same position. For example, there was the resistance of Kela Dimdimê, which is said to have lasted more than a year. But the resistance in Zap lasted five years. For five years, resistance was maintained in the same positions against these powerful and prohibited weapons. There is intelligence, willpower and determination behind this resistance. This is not something ordinary people could accomplish. The heroes whose names we have announced were participants in this resistance. That is why I bow before their heroism with the deepest respect. They are extremely valuable people, the heroes of this people and this era. They are truly the pioneers of our revolution. If we are here today, if we can speak in this way, if the Turkish state was forced to approach Leader Apo, and if this process has begun in Northern Kurdistan, it is thanks to these heroes. Our people in Eastern Kurdistan should understand this very well. These comrades, their own daughters and sons, created epic resistance along a historic path and attained martyrdom. For us, they are immortal. Their memory will illuminate our path, and their cause will achieve victory. Our families should approach them in this spirit and uphold the political line and cause of the martyrs. Once again, I commemorate those heroes with respect. I respectfully salute all the families of the martyrs, particularly the mothers, and offer my condolences. Our hearts have also been deeply wounded. They were our comrades. I offer my condolences to you and to all the people of Eastern Kurdistan.




'My condolences to the PJAK comrades and the people of Eastern Kurdistan'




The entire region is going through a period of great uncertainty. I believe the same is true of Eastern Kurdistan. Before addressing this issue, I would like to mention something. A statement was released to the press yesterday. Comrade Dersîm Bihar, a member of the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), has been martyred. I commemorate this valued martyr with respect and offer my condolences to the family of comrade Dersîm Bihar, all PJAK comrades and the people of Eastern Kurdistan. According to the statement, comrade Dersîm resisted and used their own weapon against themselves rather than surrender. This represents an extremely valuable, self-sacrificing and sacred spirit.




'Developments in the region will affect Eastern Kurdistan'




Our people in Eastern Kurdistan have maintained a particular position until now. This is a very meaningful position. They have not become anyone's instrument. That is extremely important. Our people should pursue a third way, avoid aligning themselves with either side and remain independent. This has been their position so far. All the organisations, including PJAK, have followed this line. We consider it appropriate. The region is going through an extremely important and uncertain period. Developments in the region will undoubtedly affect Eastern Kurdistan as well. Our people must be prepared for every possibility during this period, because anything could happen. That is why they must be ready for every eventuality. They must rely on their own strength and their own organisations. They must organise themselves, help one another as a society and strengthen solidarity. Nobody should feel alone. Society as a whole must remain united, protect one another everywhere and remain vigilant during this important period.




'The Iranian state must not regard Kurds as enemies'




What matters is doing the right thing at the right time. Doing the right thing at the wrong time can lead to mistakes. The right actions must be taken at the right time. That is why our people and their political representatives must be extremely attentive to this issue. We are optimistic about the future of Eastern Kurdistan. We believe that the developments ahead will be positive for our people. But everyone must remain calm and approach the situation with restraint. Politics, rather than war, must be the priority. The Iranian state must not attack the Kurds during this critical period or regard them as enemies. For example, when the Iranian state was at its weakest, the Kurds did nothing to harm it. This should be taken into consideration. The Kurds must also remain calm, follow developments and act accordingly. They should prioritise dialogue rather than methods based on violence. They must create a spirit of unity among themselves and with all the peoples of Iran. That would be the best approach. I believe that the future of our people in Eastern Kurdistan will be positive and successful. On this basis, I once again respectfully greet our people in Eastern Kurdistan and wish everyone success.
