author: Unknown
title: The AKP is expected to take steps
content:
In recent days, several statements have been made by both the state and the Kurdish side concerning the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Although the AKP government has taken no concrete steps, optimistic interpretations and expectations have nevertheless been expressed.




At a time when people are speaking of a deadlock and stagnation in the process, and the AKP government is being seriously criticised for this, it is unclear where these optimistic interpretations are coming from. We hope that the Free Movement of the Kurdish People's Leader, as demanded by the Kurdish people and public opinion, will be ensured. This leadership should be able to hold regular meetings with journalists, intellectuals, politicians and civil society organisations. After all, all the peoples of Turkey, as well as domestic and international political circles, are curious about the views of Imrali.




A few days ago, the Movement's Leadership issued a statement. Although it was not explicitly stated, the statement was criticising remarks made by Ibrahim Kalın, the head of the National Intelligence Organisation (MİT), during a meeting. Ibrahim Kalın had identified the leadership of the Kurdish Freedom Movement as the reason why the process was not progressing. He had claimed that no progress was being made because the organisation's leaders were concerned about their own positions. However, just a few sentences later, he contradicted himself by acknowledging that the Movement's Leadership remained committed to the process. Ibrahim Kalın's remarks had created confusion. In its statement, the Movement Leadership emphasised that, despite the AKP government taking no steps, Ibrahim Kalın was attempting to conceal this reality.




Both international and Turkish public opinion believe that the PKK has taken radical steps that nobody expected, while the AKP government has failed to take any significant steps of its own. The Kurdish people and all democratic institutions are already expressing their frustration with the AKP's inaction. The Kurdish People's Leader is still unable to work freely, nor are those imprisoned being released. Even prisoners who have completed their sentences are not being freed.




The Movement's Leadership announced that it had withdrawn all military units from within Turkey and abandoned military positions near the border, including fighting positions in caves (known as 

şikeft

). It also emphasised that no factors remained that could pose a risk of confrontation for the Turkish state or military. For this reason, it stated that the AKP government must now take action. In short, the Movement's Leadership demonstrated that Ibrahim Kalın's accusations against it did not reflect reality; on the contrary, it had acted with considerable responsibility.




Indeed, the steps taken by the Kurdish side have been surprising, and it was expected that the AKP would respond accordingly. It appears that the Kurdish side has done everything required of it. The statement also indicated that the guerrillas could return to Turkey if the Turkish state enacted laws guaranteeing the freedom to engage in democratic politics. It is difficult to understand why the AKP government is not taking the steps necessary to facilitate and accelerate their return to Turkey.




The Turkish state is demanding that the fighters return without first enacting laws protecting democratic political activity. It is even excluding all leaders, commanders and organisational cadres from this process of return. Everyone knows that the fighters will not return if no legislation is introduced covering the leaders and commanders as well. It is also well known that the entire leadership and organisational structure of the PKK is committed to the Kurdish People's Leader. Unless the Kurdish People's Leader is able to work freely and the path towards his freedom is opened, no organisational cadre or fighter will return to Turkey. Yet the Kurdish People's Leader has still not been granted a status that would allow him to freely direct and manage the process.




At a time when the AKP has failed to take the necessary steps and public opinion is expecting action from the government, Ibrahim Kalın's claim that the leaders are worried about their own positions is a distortion of reality. The Movement's Leadership has not expressed any concerns about its own interests so far. It has called for steps to establish a democratic political environment. Indeed, in its statements, it has made clear that its only concern is democratisation and the resolution of the Kurdish question.




Ibrahim Kalın acknowledges that the factors which gave rise to the Kurdish question still exist. For this reason, he says that disarmament alone will not resolve the problem. If so, the necessary steps should be taken in accordance with these statements, and measures towards democratisation should be implemented. Yet, rather than taking democratic steps, the AKP government continues to insist on anti-democratic practices. Ibrahim Kalın should be calling on the AKP government to take steps towards democratisation. Otherwise, statements claiming that the process is progressing well are meaningless. When AKP officials say that the process is going well, their words amount to nothing more than an attempt to buy time.




Most recently, Devlet Bahçeli has also spoken of taking certain democratic steps without explicitly mentioning the fundamental democratic rights of the Kurds. Devlet Bahçeli, who played a role in initiating the process, now needs to speak more openly and clearly.




The Kurdish side has fulfilled its responsibilities to an unexpected extent. Therefore, the AKP government no longer has any justification for failing to take action.




Source: Yeni Yaşam Newspaper

author: Unknown
title: Clara Mattei: Capitalism deliberately produces poverty
content:
Historically, how have governments used austerity policies as an economic instrument to protect capitalism, suppress wages, dismantle social protections and prevent democratic oversight? Economist Clara Mattei, who examines these issues in her book 

The Capital Order: How Economists Invented Austerity and Paved the Way to Fascism

, answered our questions.




With Mattei, one of the most prominent researchers working on the history and critique of austerity policies, we discussed the rise of right-wing governments around the world, wars in the Middle East and the rapidly accelerating militarisation of Europe from a political economy perspective. We also explored how an effective strategy of resistance against these developments could be built.




According to Oxfam, the twelve richest people in the world — all men — now own more money than the poorest half of the world's population, which is more than four billion people. How is this exploitative “capital order” created? 




Inequality is not an accidental or corruptive element of our economy. Inequality is deeply rooted in the very formation of economic growth and what can be called “accumulation of wealth”.  




There wouldn't be any wealth without the creation of market dependence and the precarity to compel workers to work for a wage — for someone else. This is a crucial point about the capital order — capital money is really based on this political relation of exploitation that is never mentioned by economists but is fundamental to understanding any dynamic of capitalism, including impoverishment, inequality, and structural violence. 




Many people find economics incomprehensible — yet politicians make far-reaching decisions. Is "complexity" a real problem or also a political tool to depoliticize decisions? Who wins when the public merely watches instead of participating in decision-making? 




This is crucial, and it is the reason why we founded the Forum for Real Economic  Emancipation (freefreeforum.org): to create a space where economic ideas can actually  become empowering to people, a space to explain the problems people feel in their own skin. 




The fact is, economics is a discipline meant to be kept in the hands of very few, who protect that knowledge as something absolutely inaccessible to the undereducated majority. Yes, complexification, mathematization, and technical language are wonderful ways to maintain explanatory power, and thus retain political power. 




And so, the reason people have not fully rebelled against the system is that they are told they don’t understand how it works, and have to listen to the experts. But these experts are merely hiding all of their extremely classist assumptions beneath formulas, mathematics. These assumptions oblige people to accept a system based on structural exploitation and violence. One important example of this that I give in my book is the harsh rejection of the labor theory of value – that explains profit as the product of unpaid labor – in favor of a theory of abstinence by which value is not coming from exploitation of one class over the other, but rather it is the outcome of the virtuous capacity to save of the rational savers-investors. 




You criticize the Western-dominated academic world: to what extent is modern economics/economic science historically and politically influenced by the West? What does this obscure, and what models of thinking and politics are exported globally as a result? 




I show in my first book how mainstream economics — the economics that is still taught in schools and still informs public debate — was championed at a moment of extreme and widespread criticism and challenges to capitalism as a way of organizing our society. This is because economics was meant to protect society from any upheaval and from any challenge.




And so, what you find is that a lot of its theories, for example, the idea that exploitation does not exist, that everything is just and fair because people get exactly what they deserve from their market transactions, and the idea that the entrepreneur counts much more than the worker, or that harmony is the consequence of self-interested behavior — are ideas that really help propel a sense of the impossibility of escaping capitalism. They deeply naturalize capitalism and the hierarchy that it produces. 




So economic ideas emerged especially to tell workers that they could not participate in  changing the world. And this is still the case today. Clearly, these ideas are exported to the Global South, where people suffer even more from plunder and exploitation. They also help create a sense of impotence among the experts who lead economic organizations in the Global South, because they feel that they are epistemically inferior to Western scholars and thus cannot emancipate themselves intellectually. And this means no emancipation in policy. 




Part of the world structurally thrives on the exploitation of other regions — through resources, trade conditions, supply chains, wages, debt and unequal power. How would you explain this structure without resorting to pure moralizing: what rules and institutions make it possible? 




This is a crucial point. My new book, 

Escape from Capitalism

, really tries to explain the functioning of the system, its tendencies, and the deeply rooted historical features of capitalism, without resorting to the typical left-wing moralizing that says it is all because we have bad people in power or greedy heads of corporations. 




What we see is that, of course, so-called development in the rich parts of the world presupposes a lot of inequality within rich nations, too. In the United States, over 70% of workers can't afford an emergency expense of around $400, and so they are structurally indebted and are working poor. 




But apart from this, the point is that the wealth hoarded largely in the Global North  depends on the underdevelopment of the Global South. So I revive a very longstanding  tradition of dependency theory, which shows, again, that it's not as if so-called developing countries can just catch up, improve their market efficiency, and thus become just as developed and modernized as Western countries. Rather, they have been made poor and kept underdeveloped in order to provide cheaper raw materials, cheap labor, and especially markets — open markets — for capitalists in the West. 




Oxfam reports that in 2024, the super rich in the Global North extracted $30 million per hour from the Global South — an amount far exceeding any money coming in through official development aid. It’s actually through interest rates, debt payments, and capital outflows where you really see how developed countries are completely subsidized by the Global South.




The Middle East is being transformed by wars, interventions and restructuring, often with reference to stability, security or development. Who benefits economically from this restructuring (raw materials, reconstruction, armaments, infrastructure, control of trade routes)? Why do democracy and freedom regularly fall by the wayside in the process? 




Yes, I just did a really great interview with Francesca Albanese on our FREE podcast (@freefreeforum). She looked at one specific but very, very telling example of how all sectors of the economy are complicit in the Palestinian genocide. 




The Palestinian genocide is a very profitable deal for the capitalist economy, in terms of the markets and means for destruction. Investing in bombs, surveillance, and very advanced military technologies, for example, are among the most profitable sectors of the economy right now. But also, all the reconstruction efforts and huge investments in real estate and related apparatus — including asset managers, Airbnb, universities, and so many different sectors of our economy, benefit from this.  




So we also know that, of course, Israel is the outpost through which the West controls the Middle East and, in general, the Global South. So it is a very strategic point, also in terms of raw materials and oil. 




It is impossible to understand the genocide and the constant destruction in the Middle East without understanding them from an economic perspective, which is, of course, the perspective that is least discussed in the public media. 




Actors such as Trump, Modi, Milei and Meloni exploit crises to push the boundaries of what is permissible, for example, through emergency rhetoric, deregulation or shifts to the right. What exactly is happening economically: which interests are being protected and which rights are being weakened? 




Yeah, I think what's interesting about the extreme austerity hawks of today is that they have completely eliminated the farce — proper to liberal capitalism — of the idea that the state represents the so-called general interest. The idea that the state is neutral and genuinely wants to foster economic growth for its own sake, as if that were something that benefits everyone. 




I think what we see here is that they are overtly and explicitly benefiting certain sectors of the economy, especially those that are currently the most profitable, such as extractive industries, technology, surveillance, and war. 




In this way, they are really showing how you couldn't have capitalist relations without  constant government intervention. And I explain how austerity is not about less state and more market. It's actually about the state shifting resources from the many to the few, and how this is done even more aggressively by these right-wing governments. So what we see here is nothing new. It's just much more explicit and more violent. But this is the real face of capitalism. 




Europe is doing relatively well in global comparison, yet military spending is rising sharply, militarization is increasing, and debates about conscription are returning. How does this relate to economic policy, and what are people afraid of, who are they arming themselves against? What role do industrial interests, energy and raw material issues, and geopolitical competition play? 




Yeah, I think militarization really shows the real point about austerity: the state is spending a lot of money. It is very expensive not to tax the rich and instead to use this money to permanently subsidize the war machine. 




And this is important because crises of overproduction are endemic to capitalism. One of the roles of the state is to protect against overproduction by making sure that taxpayer money, especially money from workers, goes to subsidize the sphere of destruction. 




I think this helps us understand how irrational capitalism is as a way of organizing society, even though it is not irrational according to its own logic. The logic of capitalism, the logic of profit, is very much fulfilled by austerity. But austerity is irrational, and capitalism is irrational according to the logic of need. 




So, of course, people are made to be afraid, or made to think that somehow government officials are investing to protect them. The reality is that the interest is in constantly  creating a need to purchase more weapons. And, as we know, this means permanent destruction and reconstruction. 




Why does extreme inequality not automatically lead to uprisings, and why does austerity often strengthen right-wing/authoritarian forces? What would an effective counter-strategy (left-wing, civil society, collective) need to achieve? 




This is the interesting point: a lot of Marxist analysis is based on an accelerationist theory, according to which the more people are starving, the more they will rise up. I think what you see is that it is far more complex, and it also speaks to the fact that there is no deterministic answer to how we change our economic system. It really requires a good dose of organizing and effort to bring people together. 




Because what we see is that the more precarious you have been made by austerity policies, the more divided and suspicious you become, and the more you come to hate  those who are weaker than you. And this is, in fact, the success of austerity that I speak  about in my book: austerity works very well to disempower workers by increasing their precarity.




This is what industrial austerity does by killing labor laws that protect workers and making work more flexible. This is what cutting social expenditures does. This is what increasing taxes on workers and taking taxes away from capitalists does. This is what increasing unemployment through monetary austerity does. It just creates a very vulnerable working class that then, of course, ends up buying into the scapegoating narratives of the extreme right. 




So what we know is that it is not going to be enough for people to be in a very uncomfortable economic situation to rise up. What we need is active organizing efforts. This is what the Forum for Real Economic Emancipation is attempting to do, like many other groups around the world. And we want to be in solidarity with these groups, to open up the experiments that already exist. 




I think it is also very interesting to think more realistically about what China is doing right now and how China differs from our economic system, even if it maintains certain aspects of capitalism. It certainly provides some aspects that are really visionary for the future. There are a lot of democratic assemblies. Of course, Rojava is a very good example of how, when people get together, they can challenge the structure of exploitation that is the foundation of economic growth under capitalism. 




So I believe that this is what we need to do: not just wait for people to fare worse, because when people fare worse, they turn towards the right. We need to be able to provide our own resources, push government officials, and learn from existing alternatives around the world. We need to learn from them and grow stronger through collaboration.




Clara Mattei




Born in the United States in 1988, while her parents were studying law, Clara Mattei grew up in Italy. The granddaughter of partisans who took part in the resistance movement against fascism during the Second World War, Mattei completed her undergraduate degree in philosophy at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom. She subsequently earned a master's degree in Pavia, Italy.




She completed her PhD on the history of austerity policies, and the book that emerged from this research has since been translated into ten languages.




Mattei is a Professor of Economics at the University of Tulsa in the United States, where she also serves as the director of the Center for Heterodox Economics, established in February 2025. In addition, she is the founder of the Forum for Real Economic Emancipation (FREE), an initiative established to challenge economic myths.




She is the author of 

The Capital Order

.




Source: Yeni Özgür Politika

author: CNT Villaverde Alto - Comarcal Sur de Madrid
title: Crónica: la Huelga General del 11N desde CNT Comarcal Sur
content:
Con algo menos de un mes de trabajo a las espaldas, la noche del pasado 10 de noviembre, CNT Comarcal Sur desplegó toda su preparación en la jornada de Huelga General con una premisa clara: 

subir los salarios, bajar los alquileres

. Fueron algo más de tres semanas de presencia en la mesa sindical, en asambleas de barrios y municipios, en los centros de trabajo y en el seno del propio Sindicato, traducidas en 

24 horas que bien pudieron durar décadas

.




Arrancamos la jornada acompañando a 

nuestra Sección Sindical en EMT

 durante los piquetes desarrollados en las cocheras de Carabanchel. Como con cada día de Huelga General, el despliegue de la acción sindical sobre el transporte —sea de la condición que sea— es indispensable para asegurar el éxito de la jornada; así como para garantizar el cumplimiento de los servicios mínimos e informar a las y los compañeros no obligados a trabajar este día de su derecho a secundar la jornada de paro.




Dada la importancia del sector del transporte rodado, no solo respaldamos el trabajo de las compañeras de la Sección de EMT, sino que, también, acompañando a los Comités Unitarios tanto de Getafe como de Leganés, acudimos a las cocheras de autobuses de ambas ciudades.




En esta misma línea y, siguiendo el trabajo desarrollado en las semanas previas, marcado por la militancia de base, desde el territorio y en sentido unitario, 

la presencia del Sindicato junto a los Comités Unitarios fue fundamental en la jornada

. Si bien de por sí la aparición de estos comités territoriales marcaba un rasgo diferencial con respecto a anteriores convocatorias de Huelga General; 

la apuesta de este Sindicato por la organización unitaria de la Huelga

, así como su naturaleza de Comarcal Sur, facultó que tanto las afiliadas a título individual pudiesen participar en sus comités más cercanos, así como que la organización apoyase con fuerza logística y militante las acciones de distintos comités.




A las acciones en cocheras, tanto en Getafe como en Leganés, se sumó la presencia de 

piquetes tanto en zonas industriales como comerciales

, así como durante las reclamas nocturnas que, en algunos casos, se convirtieron en marchas que iniciaron la actividad informativa por los establecimientos que, ya de madrugada, se encontraban abiertos y fueron notificados del arranque de la Huelga General. Así, se consiguió 

con éxito tanto la distribución de información entre trabajadoras como el cierre de negocios secundando la convocatoria

; con especial hincapié en el piquete comercial desplegado por Villaverde junto a su comité de huelga, dada la vinculación de este Sindicato con el barrio por su raigambre a través del Ateneo Libertario de Villaverde.







Comida popular en el Ateneo Libertario







Este espacio, nuestro local, fue epicentro para la actividad del Sindicato desde la misma madrugada, sirviendo como punto de encuentro para huelguistas, afiliadas o no; espacio de descanso y reposo, así como de avituallamiento para reponer fuerzas comiendo y bebiendo lo necesario o secando la ropa en una jornada pasada por agua. Porque nuestro objetivo siempre ha sido prefigurar el mundo nuevo que queremos en cada uno de los pasos que damos, un día de Huelga General es el espacio para llevar hasta su extremo este principio. Así, al apoyo mutuo en los piquetes, a los cuidados entre compañeras y a nuestro local como lugar de refugio y descanso, se sumó 

una gran comida popular preparada por las militantes y para las militantes

, con las puertas abiertas a todo el barrio en huelga; porque las que comen juntas conspiran juntas.




Simultáneamente, como en el caso de la EMT, mientras se desplegaban piquetes por los municipios del sur, 

las compañeras organizadas en Secciones Sindicales extendieron a sus centros de trabajo la convocatoria de Huelga General

, compartiendo la labor con compañeras de otros sindicatos y con el apoyo de la propia afiliación de este Sindicato que, solidariamente, pudo reforzar cada convocatoria.







Piquete del Sector Social en Madrid







Así, tras un descanso fraternal, pusimos rumbo hacia el centro de Madrid, donde nos esperaba una convocatoria que desbordó cualquier expectativa. Allí, 

junto a las compañeras de las CNT de la Comunidad y de los anarcosindicatos Solidaridad Obrera y CGT

, conformamos un bloque sindicalista, anarquista y de base, que diese cuerpo y voz a los principios y objetivos que nos venían guiando, no desde el arranque de la jornada, sino desde su preparación semanas atrás.







Bloque CNT al arranque de la manifestación







Junto a las compañeras, formamos parte de una manifestación que 

bloqueó por completo el centro de la ciudad

, pese a una lluvia torrencial que no amainó en ningún momento y, si el final de esta convocatoria se vio marcado por algo, fue por la tónica que acompañó a toda la jornada de Huelga General: la represión y persecución policial.




Desde el arranque de la Huelga hasta su conclusión, 

las agresiones

, ya fuesen físicas o mediante el uso de gas pimienta y gases lacrimógenos; 

las identificaciones

 arbitrarias con fines intimidatorios e incluso 

las detenciones

 fueron la constante con la que los piquetes informativos y las manifestantes se toparon. Si bien la coerción del derecho a ejercer huelga no supone una novedad para la historia del movimiento obrero, este último caso encarna la enésima confirmación de la naturaleza del “gobierno progresista” que, aunque jalea con ánimo electoral la convocatoria de huelga, deja rienda suelta a sus perros de presa y fuerzas de choque para cargar indiscriminadamente contra las huelguistas.




Así, esta huelga, pese a quien pese, 

emprendida contra todos los gobiernos y fuerzas parlamentarias

; culminó con el convencimiento a partes iguales de haber encontrado nuevas fórmulas, recuperado estrategias clásicas, afianzado lazos necesarios y reafirmado el objetivo último. Para CNT Comarcal Sur lo hizo, además, con el convencimiento de que 

esto acaba de empezar

.




Seguimos organizadas, seguimos luchando, seguimos haciendo sindicalismo para un mundo nuevo

.




La entrada 

Crónica: la Huelga General del 11N desde CNT Comarcal Sur

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: dialogocomospovos
title: Recuperação Espiritual
content:
Em sua formação no Assentamento Terra Vista, Moira Millán aprofundou a luta do povo Mapuche para além da terra: “A luta do Povo Mapuche é uma luta por um modo de vida na terra. Não é uma luta pela terra, mas por um modo de vida na terra.” Para ela, não basta tomar a terra; é preciso perguntar: “O que vamos fazer nessa terra?” A resposta mapuche passa por compreender o espaço na terra como espaço de descolonização. Por isso, a educação própria não pode ser igual à educação do Estado, que impõe formas de organização que não são originárias e silencia o pensamento e o mapudungun.




Moira explicou que, para os Mapuche, a recuperação territorial precisa ser, primeiro, uma recuperação espiritual. É um território onde o povo se repara, volta e recomponha um vínculo sagrado com a terra por meio das cerimônias e da filosofia própria. Nesse sentido, ela tocou num tema sensível também no Brasil: a religião colonial. Segundo Moira, quando as religiões cristãs chegam às comunidades indígenas, muitas vezes se esquecem das cerimônias e dos cantos, o povo vai tomando distância da identidade e da terra.




Na comunidade onde vive, há consenso de não permitir a entrada de igrejas cristãs: “só há espiritualidade Mapuche”. Também não há postos sanitários do Estado; a única forma de cura é com as autoridades da medicina Mapuche. A fala de Moira reforça que a luta mapuche é territorial, espiritual e política, e dialoga com as resistências indígenas e camponesas presentes no Terra Vista.

author: hsa_oryx
title: A Licence to Hunt: “Cruel, Inhumane and Selfish” Lauderdale Huntswoman Sentenced: 300 Hours’ Unpaid Work and Ten-Year Dog Ban
content:
Scotland’s first conviction under the Hunting with Dogs (Scotland) Act 2023 has resulted in a substantial community sentence for ex-huntswoman Claire Bellamy, following evidence gathered by Glasgow Hunt Saboteurs.




Claire Bellamy after breaching the licence. 

Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs.




Former Lauderdale Hunt master and huntswoman Claire Bellamy has been sentenced to 300 hours of unpaid work and banned from owning or keeping most dogs for ten years after being convicted of deliberately hunting a fox with hounds. 




Bellamy appeared at Paisley Sheriff Court on Monday 9th November, where Sheriff Gill imposed the maximum 300 hours of unpaid work permitted under a Community Payback Order, to be completed within 12 months. 




The sentence follows 

Bellamy’s conviction in October

, the first secured under Scotland’s Hunting with Dogs (Scotland) Act 2023.




The prosecution was made possible thanks to footage captured by Glasgow Hunt Saboteurs, who have been documenting the ongoing illegal hunting in Scotland that has continued since the new licensing system became law. 




On the 4th January 2025 – almost 2 years after the new law came into force – Bellamy was hunting with approximately 17 hounds near Kirkton Woods, between Houston in Renfrewshire and Kilmacolm in Inverclyde.




The hunt had obtained a licence from NatureScot, the public body responsible for administering Scotland’s licensing scheme.




However, the licence did not give the hunt unrestricted permission to hunt foxes. It was also strictly restricted to a certain geographical area.




“The recording of the fox being chased by multiple hounds was particularly harrowing to watch.” Sheriff Gill

 

Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs.




Footage captured by sabs, showed hounds hunting a fox into an open field beyond the boundaries specified in the licence. The dogs were not under control – also a requirement of the licence.




During the trial Sheriff Gill described the footage as harrowing and rejected Bellamy’s claim that she had not deliberately hunted the fox. 




A member of the Glasgow Hunt Sabs filming the hunt as they breach the NatureScot issued license. 

Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs. 




At sentencing the sheriff praised the evidence of the witnesses, singling out the hunt sab who recorded the pursuit.




In contrast, Sheriff Gill addressing Bellamy directly described her actions as “

cruel, inhumane and selfish

”.




“Cruel, inhumane and selfish” – words used by Sheriff Gill to describe Bellamy during her sentencing hearing.  Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs.




The court heard that Bellamy had taken part in approximately 1,500 hunts during her ‘career’ as a fox-killer. Despite this, she had shown no responsibility for what occurred that day.




A background report prepared by probation services for sentencing recorded that Bellamy believed she had done nothing wrong, showed no empathy towards the hunted fox, and considered herself to be the victim of an example being made.




The hounds chasing the fox.

 

“What you don’t understand is that the law is the law, and you are bound by the law.” Sheriff Gill. 

Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs.




She also complained that Scotland’s legislation made hunting foxes more difficult, to which Sheriff Gill’s response was an astonished 

“Ms Bellamy, that is the purpose of the legislation

”.




The court also made it clear that Bellamy was bound by the law regardless of whether she personally agreed with it.




The belief among the hunting community that their traditional animal cruelty should take precedence over legislation designed to protect wildlife was shattered in Paisley Sheriff courts.




Bellamy escaped a custodial sentence, although Sheriff Gill made it clear that prison was a genuine possibility.




Claire Bellamy hunting the fox in breach of the licence. 

Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs.




The Community Payback Order requiring 300 hours of unpaid work was imposed as a direct alternative to imprisonment. Bellamy was further warned that failing to comply with the order could result in her returning to court and potentially receiving a custodial sentence. 




Bellamy was also disqualified from keeping dogs for 10 years, though there is an exemption which allowed her to retain her pet terrier (it would be a terrier wouldn’t it), and the collies she uses in her shepherding work.




Whilst Bellamy is no longer master of the Lauderdale Hunt, this didn’t stop the Lauderdale recently advertising a 

‘Newcomers to Trail Hunting Week’

, which was quickly removed after sabs pointed out that trail hunting is banned in Scotland.




Even after the guilty verdict the Lauderdale advertising trail hunting in a place where trail hunting is banned. .




The Hunting with Dogs (Scotland) Act 2023 was introduced to strengthen protection for wildlife and close loopholes in the previous legislation; the Protection of Wild Mammals (Scotland) Act 2002, which had been in force since 1 August 2002. At the time this was Scotland’s first major fox-hunting ban, and it was introduced more than two years before the Hunting Act 2004 took effect in England and Wales.




All to kill a tiny wild animal. 

Image: Glasgow Hunt Sabs.




The 2002 Act banned the deliberate hunting of wild mammals with dogs, but, like the legislation in England and Wales, retained exemptions. These include provisions for what hunts and their supporters euphemistically call ‘pest control’, allowing foxes to be flushed from cover and shot.




The 2023 Act sought to close those loopholes by limiting the numbers of dogs used to flush foxes to two. However, it also introduced a licensing system allowing larger packs to be used under similar guises, leaving another loophole for hunts to continue to operate to hunt foxes.




Recently a legal challenge was launched over these licences, following Freedom of Information requests made by the League Against Cruel Sports (LACS). 




The information provided show NatureScot is granting licences without fulfilling the requirement of ‘exceptional circumstances’ and is wrongly allowing foxhounds to be used by licence holders, meaning that fox hunts which should be banned are still taking place. 




According to its own figures, NatureScot issued 52 licences during the 2025-26 hunting season, of which 43 were used.




NatureScot attended just ONE licenced hunt to check compliance in person.




Meanwhile, it was hunt saboteurs, not NatureScot, who gathered the footage that helped secure Scotland’s first conviction under the new legislation.




You can follow the 

legal challenge here

.




A Hunt Saboteur Spokesperson said:




“Let this serve as a warning to legislators currently strengthening the law in England and Wales, wherever there is even the slightest sniff of a loophole, determined, ruthless, cruel, inhumane and selfish fox hunters will be queuing up to exploit it.




“We have had the consultation, the government has all the evidence it needs. Now it’s time to deliver on its promise and ban every last morsel of this despicable pastime.




“And it’s time for NatureScot to do the same. The Lauderdale case has demonstrated exactly what happens when hunts are handed licences to take packs of hounds into the countryside. End the loopholes, and finally consign fox hunting to history”

.

Glasgow Hunt Sabs here

A Licence to Hunt: “Cruel, Inhumane and Selfish” Lauderdale Huntswoman Sentenced: 300 Hours’ Unpaid Work and Ten-Year Dog Ban

Hunt Saboteurs Association

author: ROAPE
title: Africa’s green stewardship
content:
“First we were dispossessed in the name of kings and emperors, later in the name of state development, and now in the name of conservation” –Indigenous delegation, Fifth World Parks Congress (2003)




I remember that familiar anecdote beneath email signatures during my brief time within the United Nations (UN) system. It read, “please consider the environment before printing this email.” Similar reminders far beyond the UN invoke a familiar ethic of environmental responsibility, particularly around the use of paper and the depletion of natural carbon sinks, namely trees.




Such institutional gestures are largely unobjectionable and even function as legitimising paraphernalia for highly corporatised entities, including NGOs. Much like ethical sourcing labels attached to coffee, clothing and other consumer goods, they can furnish institutions and businesses with the symbolic credentials of environmental stewardship, leaving the structures of production and accumulation seemingly untouched and, by implication, legitimate.




This also speaks to a broader ‘bandwagonism’ within international development, and to the insularity of development professionals when it comes to interrogating the political questions embedded within such global framings. In hindsight, the email footnotes reveal not only symbolic expression of environmental responsibility within development practice, but also the moralising and legitimising weight attached to green stewardship and, more broadly, sustainable development.




Yet this moral vocabulary leaves largely unexamined how sustainability is defined, whose interests environmental policies serve, who bears their disproportionate costs, who captures their benefits, and whose lands and livelihoods become subject to environmental governance. These political-economic questions are also bound up with the knowledge systems through which nature and sustainable development are understood and governed.




Don’t take this the wrong way. I am not suggesting that climate change is a hoax, nor am I opposed to greening development. Rather, I am concerned with how proponents of market-led development, including the UN, IMF and World Bank, predominantly sidestep the profit motives embedded within contemporary environmentalism. In doing so, my UN email footnote risks becoming little more than a LinkedIn hashtag, a symbolic display of environmental virtue within a corporatised world.




Yet the market, understood here in its neoliberal capitalist form, is neither benign nor guided by an invisible hand capable of resolving ecological crises. Its constellation around profiteering and accumulation has historically subordinated human and ecological wellbeing to the imperatives of capital. Situating climate change within the history of global capitalism makes legible how the extraordinary wealth enjoyed by many countries in the Global North was built through centuries of fossil-fuelled expansion, resource extraction and colonial dispossession.




What is particularly troubling today is the transformation of this historical contradiction into a new environmental frontier, where the mechanisms of accumulation that have contributed to ecological crisis are increasingly mobilised and legitimised as means of resolving it.




This logic takes shape in multiple guises, including banking nature, green capital, carbon trading, biodiversity credits, ecosystem payment services, 

REDD+

, conservation finance and nature tourism. Put simply, forests become carbon sinks, biodiversity becomes natural capital, ecological processes become ecosystem services, and landscapes become financial and tourism assets capable of generating economic value.




Nature is thus increasingly rendered legible through the language of capital, where its ecological functions can be measured, priced and incorporated into circuits of global investment and accumulation. Environmental protection is consequently framed not as a challenge to capitalism, but as a new frontier for investment, accumulation and market expansion.




Once these concepts enter the vocabulary of global development, and more specifically the language of institutions such as the UN, they acquire considerable moral and institutional authority. They travel from donor conditionalities into national policy frameworks, where market-based approaches to environmental protection become normalised as legitimate and even necessary pathways to sustainability. In this process, the language of conservation obscures the underlying political economy, particularly questions of who owns, controls and benefits from the economic value generated through the protection and commodification of nature.




To foreground this case, Africa’s abundance of natural resources, forests and biodiversity, coupled with its heavy dependence on external development financing, has made the continent fertile ground for what is often conceived as ‘

green grabbing’

 and, in some cases, ‘

green colonialism

’. Beyond the policy rhetoric of making Africa’s natural forest profitable, these processes can be understood through the appropriation of land, the restriction of access to natural resources and the dispossession of communities from their livelihoods, often justified through the moral imperative of environmental stewardship.




The irony is difficult to overlook. Africa has contributed comparatively very little to the climate crisis, yet its forests, lands and communities have become increasingly central to global efforts to address it. The growth of REDD+, or Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation, illustrates this dynamic. Framed as part of international efforts to combat climate change, REDD+ seeks to create financial incentives for forest conservation by attaching economic value to the carbon stored in forests. In doing so, forests are not only protected as ecological spaces but also rendered legible as carbon assets within emerging markets for environmental value.




Often touted as a win-win proposition for people and nature, REDD+ is frequently underpinned by the assumption that local communities are the primary drivers of forest degradation. Also, in practice, it predominantly operates through donor-led, top-down interventions channelled through African governments, with profound consequences for the livelihoods, land rights and autonomy of forest dwellers.




The experience of the 

Sengwer indigenous community

 in Kenya’s Embobut Forest offers a telling illustration of these dynamics. A critical reading of the acclaimed documentary 

Honey at the Top

 paints a grim picture of restrictions on forest access, displacement and persistent contestation over land rights. Working alongside donor-supported REDD+ initiatives, the Kenyan government has continued to justify the forced eviction of this indigenous community from its ancestral lands on the grounds that they are squatters whose activities threaten the forest ecosystem. This has engendered what might be called ‘

conservation refugees’

, people forcefully evicted from their lands and livelihoods in the name of environmental conservation.




Such interventions not only carry the moral ethos of green development but also reproduce colonial and racialised logics of ‘

fortress conservation

’, whereby environmental protection was historically intertwined with the creation of protected areas and land controls, legitimised through the language of civilisation, scientific management and environmental stewardship. Beyond their material implications, such practices arguably helped institutionalise the ‘

coloniality of knowledge

’ in African environmental stewardship, privileging Western scientific understandings of nature, expertise and stewardship while relegating or silencing indigenous knowledge systems.




Maasai community member in the Serengeti-Ngorongoro area of Tanzania (Copyright Abdoulie Kurang, 2026)




The Sengwer case is not unique. Comparable forms of dispossession have beset 

Maasai communities

 in Tanzania’s Serengeti-Ngorongoro region, where the pursuit of conservation and tourism has often come at the expense of indigenous land rights and livelihoods. This points to the tensions embedded in the often-touted conservation-tourism nexus. The tourism industry routinely commodifies Maasai culture, showcasing red attire, jumping dances, bomas (homesteads) and warrior-like traditions as symbols of authentic African heritage, even as conservation policies restrict access to the ancestral lands upon which these identities and ways of life depend.




These indigenous experiences, alongside similar cases across the continent, illustrate how the economic and market imperatives underpinning conservation and environmentalism do not merely dispossess communities; they can also commodify dispossession and deprivation themselves. Poverty, landlessness and displacement are then transformed into elements of the ‘wild Africa’ experience, consumed by Western tourists seeking authentic encounters with nature and culture.




This journey from the email footnote to ancestral lands reveals that Africa’s green stewardship is about more than questions of morality. It is inseparable from the political economy of global capitalism, which shapes who bears the costs of conservation, who controls nature, and who ultimately benefits from its protection. These competing interests are not only material but also epistemic. Marked-oriented dispossession and the knowledge systems attendant to conservation are mutually constitutive. From high technical framings and market-based valuations to donor priorities and nature-based investments, conservation is organised around ‘expert’ (often Western) ways of knowing and governing nature, frequently at the expense of local understanding of land, ecology, stewardship and livelihoods.




Thus, the question is not only who possesses the material power to control nature, but whose knowledge informs environmental stewardship. This invites further interrogation of the intersecting workings of knowledge and power within the political economy of conservation, a broader debate that, while beyond the scope of this piece, warrants closer examination.





The post 

Africa’s green stewardship

 appeared first on 

ROAPE

title: Hürmüz Boğazı'nda BAE petrol şirketinin gemisine saldırı
content:
Temsili görsel | Fotoğraf: Eric Seddon/Pexels

BAE resmi haber ajansı WAM'ın ADNOC açıklamasına dayandırdığı habere göre saldırı, 17 Kasım akşamı meydana geldi. Yaralanan 11 mürettebatın tedavisi sürerken kayıp kişi için arama kurtarma çalışmaları devam ediyor.

Şirket, saldırının nasıl gerçekleştirildiği ve gemide meydana gelen hasar hakkında ayrıntı paylaşmadı.

ABD ile İran arasındaki tırmanan gerilim, küresel enerji taşımacılığının en önemli geçiş noktalarından Hürmüz Boğazı'nda güvenlik kaygılarını artırıyor. Boğazdaki sevkiyat aksamaları petrol ve doğalgaz piyasalarını da etkiliyor. ADNOC gemisine yönelik saldırının ardından bölgedeki deniz trafiğine ilişkin endişeler yeniden gündeme geldi.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: AKP'de fon vurgunu krizi: "Cami cemaatinin tepkisi bizi korkuttu"
content:
Fon vurgununun ardından AKP içinde tepkilerin büyüdüğü, partinin kendi tabanından gelen eleştiriler karşısında zorlandığı öne sürüldü. Nefes yazarı Nuray Babacan, bugünkü köşesinde fon krizinin AKP içinde yarattığı rahatsızlığı ve iktidar partisinin tabanından gelen tepkileri ele aldı. Babacan, iktidar partisinde özellikle “cami cemaatinin tepkisi”nden çekinildiğine ilişkin kulis bilgilerini aktardı. Babacan'ın aktardığına göre, AKP'li bir kurmay, partinin kendi tabanından gelen eleştirilerin önceki sorunlardan farklı olduğunu belirterek şunları söyledi;

“Vatandaş cebinden parasının çalındığı ve zenginlere verildiği hissinde. Hiçbir sorun, tabanda bu kadar yankı bulmamıştı. Kemik taban sorunu yaşanıyor. Beraber siyaset yaptığımız, bize oy verdiğini bildiğimiz isimlerin eleştirisi çok sert. Haklı olduklarını, sonuna kadar hesap soracağımızı söylüyoruz. Aynı düşünceleri paylaştığımızı söylemek bile onları yatıştırmıyor.”

Babacan, fon vurgununun kamuoyuna yansımasından üç hafta sonra yapılan nabız yoklamalarında tepkilerin arttığının görüldüğünü yazdı. İlk anket sonuçlarının ardından “Vatandaş hâlâ bunu konuşuyor mu ya…” diye şaşıranlar olduğunu aktaran Babacan, anketlerin her seferinde daha kötü sonuç vermesi üzerine parti içinde harekete geçme kararı alındığını belirtti.

Babacan'ın aktardığı kulis bilgilerine göre, seçimlere kadar krizin yarattığı tepki giderilemezse AKP'nin oy oranının yüzde 25'lerde kalabileceği değerlendiriliyor. Fon vurgunuyla ilgili kamuoyuna yansıyan “Listede 60 milletvekili var” iddiasının da tepki gördüğünü belirten Babacan, Ankara Ulus Hali'nde bir pazarcının bir siyasetçiye “O vekillerin koluna kelepçeyi takmadan buraya gelmeyin” diye bağırdığı olayın da konuşulduğunu yazdı.

Babacan, yazısına şöyle devam etti; “Yurt dışına kaçan 40-50 ismin iktidardaki operasyon hareketliliğini fark eder etmez, 1-15 Eylül tarihleri arasında çıkış yaptığı saptanıyor. Yani, konunun kapatılamayacak kadar büyük olduğuna karar verilmesinden hemen sonra, 17 Eylül’de başlayan gözaltı dalgasından hemen önce… Zamanlama manidar!

Bir yandan TMSF, bu fonlara 10 milyon liranın üzerinde para yatıran herkesi tek tek görüşmeye çağırıp, kazandıkları parayı geri yatırmalarını istiyor. Aylar öncesinden fonla vedalaşmış olan kişiler durumu şaşkınlıkla karşılarken, ‘Yatırmazsak ne olur?’ sorusuna görevlilerin, ‘Bilmiyoruz, biz sadece takip ve uyarı ile sorumluyuz’ dediği anlatılıyor. Soruşturma ve tutuklanma korkusu hızla yayılıyor.

Diğer yandan Borsa İstanbul Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı ve Türkiye Varlık Fonu Yönetim Kurulu Başkan Vekili Erişah Arıcan’ın görevden alınacağı, hatta geç kalındığı konuşuluyor. Beştepe’de düzenlenen her ekonomi toplantısına katılan ve ekonomi yönetiminin tezlerinin tam tersini savunan Arıcan’la ilgili partide aylar öncesinden oluşmuş bir tepki zaten var. Toplantılarda, yurt dışına kaçan paralar konusunda uluslararası alanda devreye girildiği, kaçan isimlerle ilgili de kırmızı bülten hazırlandığı bilgisi paylaşılıyor."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.
