[1] This went alongside an argument about what forms of class struggle were most effective, the revolutionary potential of different kinds of worker, and how the word ‘proletariat’ should be defined (which is a different question from how worker should be defined). For Bakunin’s views on the peasantry and the so-called destitute proletariat see Bakunin 1973, 253-54; Bakunin 1990, 6-8, 177-78, 198-217; Bakunin 2002, 189-209. For the various meanings of the proletariat in 19th century socialism see Baker 2024.

[2] A recurring accusation that anarchists and Marxists made against each other was plagiarism. In 1851 Engels told Marx that the mutualist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, who was the first known person to politically self-identify as an anarchist, had “indubitably lifted” his analysis of the state as an instrument of class rule that will disappear with the resolution of class contradictions from the Communist Manifesto and perhaps Marx’s articles in the press (MECW 38, 435). In an amusing twist of fate, Proudhon himself believed that parts of Marx’s The Poverty of Philosophy plagiarised ideas without credit from the very book it was critiquing, namely Proudhon’s System of Economic Contradictions. He wrote in the margins of Marx’s book, “Does Marx have the pretentiousness to claim all of this as his own, in opposition to something contrary which I am supposed to have said?”, “But all that it is me!”, “Plagiarism of my first chapter”, “What! Come on now! But the preceding pages are copies of my own” (Quoted in McKay, 2017). Decades later in the early 1900s the Georgian anarchist Varlam Cherkezishvili accused Marx and Engels of having plagiarised the Communist Manifesto from an earlier book by the French socialist Victor Considerant (Cherkezishvili 1902, 55-66). This claim was then repeated by other anarchists like Malatesta (Malatesta 2023, 213) and Rocker (Rocker 1925).

[3] Both Marx and Bakunin believed that biological races with different characteristics existed. This was a widespread false belief among biologists at the time. Importantly, Bakunin did not think that what he called moral characteristics, such as cowardice or a commitment to freedom, were biologically heritable and instead credited their transmission to socialisation and life experience. How this process of social development occurs is influenced by prenatal factors, but these generally have a smaller impact than the environment at an individual level. He wrote that, “natural and innate difference, small as it may be, is nevertheless positive and real: difference in temperament, in vital energy, in the predominance of one sense or one group of organic functions over others, difference in vivacity and natural capacities. We have tried to prove that vices as well as moral qualities—facts of individual and social consciousness—cannot be physically inherited, and that man cannot be physiologically predetermined toward evil, nor irrevocably rendered incapable of good. But we have never meant to deny that individual natures differ widely among themselves, that some of them are endowed to a greater extent than others with a capacity for a full human development. True, we believe that these natural differences are now quite exaggerated and that most of them should be attributed not to Nature but to the different education which has been allotted to each individual . . . We have even recognized that in some exceptional cases, in men of genius or of great talent for example, as well as idiots or highly perverse natures, this influence of natural determination upon the development of the individual—a determination as inevitable as the influence of education and society—may be great.” (Bakunin 1964, 153-54). To learn more about Marx’s views on race see Paul 1981. For Bakunin see Bakunin 1964, 147-54; Bakunin 1970, 65-7; Bakunin 1989, 178-79.

[4] In the appendix to Statism and Anarchy Bakunin made the more plausible argument that the positive aspects of Russia’s peasant communes, which were called the mir, could provide the basis for the emergence of anarchist socialist consciousness in the country. Importantly, he did not think this would occur automatically. He instead emphasised that an organisation of committed revolutionaries had to help forge links between both different peasant communes and between the peasantry and urban workers. He believed that a core goal of this organising should be revolutionaries persuading the peasantry to abandon what he regarded as the three main barriers to them developing anarchist socialist consciousness: patriarchy and faith in the Tsar, alongside the authoritarian tendency of the mir to override individual liberties, be a tool of the state, and a servant of rich peasants (Bakunin 1990, 198-217).

[5] The following interpretation is indebted to conversations with Paul Raekstad and unpublished drafts he has shown me, alongside my study of Mészáros 2011 and Marx himself.

[6] Another attendee of the 1865 London conference, the mutualist and later collectivist César De Paepe, used Marx’s critique of Proudhon in polemics with anti-collectivist mutualists. In 1868 he wrote, “thanks to a dialectics put in the service of a method more often metaphysical than scientific (which it is necessary to avoid confusing with the historical and objective method of Karl Marx), Proudhon has discovered in the social world some laws that observation confirms more from day to day; it is, however, incontestable that hypothesis still plays an infinitely more considerable role in the works of that thinker and that often he has concluded a priori or from insufficient observations: witness the conclusions of his last works relative to the social role of strikes and trades-unions, and those relative to the tendencies of modern production towards association and thus towards the collective appropriation of land and the large instruments of labor, two phenomena of which Proudhon has misunderstood the immense scope from the point of view of the organization of the future, and that he condemned even in the name of reason and logic, while Marx, already well before 1848, in the name of observation and history, considers them the two principal elements of the solution of the social problem. The majority of the writers of Liberté have made the defects of Proudhon their own by sacrificing, so to speak absolutely, his scientific side” (De Paepe 2014). It is unclear how De Paepe, who was six when The Poverty of Philosophy was published, acquired knowledge of Marx’s critique of Proudhon. He may have found an old copy of the book. Or perhaps he learnt this information from conversations with Marx and Eccarius at the conference and Marx’s critical obituary of Proudhon, which was published in February 1865 within Der Social-Demokrat (MECW 20, 26-33).

[7] It is not known how Cafiero first read the Communist Manifesto. One obvious source is Bakunin, who owned a German copy and his own Russian translation of it. Cafiero arrived at Bakunin’s on 20 May 1872 and then read aloud to Bakunin the first part of his letter to Engels on 31 May and the rest on 3 June. It was then sent to Engels on 19 June from Milan, one day after he had left Switzerland (Eckhardt 2016, 223-25). This was enough time in which to read the Manifesto, but I do not know if Cafiero had the required language skills. He definitely read Italian, English, and French to a high level. I have been unable to find evidence that he read German or Russian. This is indirectly supported by the fact that he first read Marx’s Capital in its French translation and not the German original. Bakunin could have read out the Manifesto to Cafiero by translating it in real time as he spoke, but there is no direct evidence that this happened. It has been suggested that the edition of the Manifesto that Cafiero read was the December 1871 English edition published by the American paper Woodhull & Claflin’s Weekly under the title German Communism – Manifesto of the German Communist Party. This is because it would explain why Cafiero referred to the originally titled Manifesto of the Communist Party as the “Manifesto of the German Communist Party” in the letter (Eckhardt 2016, 224, 518n167). Engels had mentioned the publication of this translation in a 15 February 1872 letter to Wilhelm Liebknecht (MECW 44, 319). On 17 March Engels complained to Friedrich Sorge, who lived in the United States, about the quality of the recent translations and asked him to send over “50 copies of the issue of Woodhull & Claflin’s which contains the translation of the Communist Manifesto, and 50-100 of the issues of the Socialiste with the French translation” (ibid, 343, 643n440). Engels could have forwarded one of these new copies, or the previous one he owned, to Cafiero. Previously when Engels had sent documents to Cafiero he wrote a letter informing him that they were on their way (ibid, 171). No such letter for the Manifesto has been found. If Engels sent Cafiero a copy it was probably attached to the lost letter that was written between 29 February and 9 March (Eckhardt 2016, 225). It should also be kept in mind that Bakunin referred to the Manifesto as “the famous manifesto of the German Communists” in the unsent October 1872 letter to the editors of La Liberté and his 1873 book Statism and Anarchy (Bakunin 1973, 252; Bakunin 1990, 146). As a result, Bakunin could potentially have also been the reason why Cafiero used this phrase.

[8] Engels privately complained about this distortion of his and Marx’s ideas in a few letters. See MECW 49, 34-6, 59-63, 197; MECW 50, 163-65, 264-67.

[9] It is unclear why this is the case. In the preface they claim that “the present memoir, ‘God and the State,’ is really a fragment of a letter or report. Composed in the same manner as most of Bakunin’s other writings, it has the same literary fault, lack of proportion; moreover it breaks off abruptly: we have searched in vain to discover the end of the manuscript” (Bakunin 1970, 6). But this account was later contradicted by Guillaume, who had originally provided Reclus with the relevant manuscripts. He complained in 1908, “that last assertion is incomprehensible to me, for the end of the manuscript (pages 248-340) was found, along with the part published by Reclus and Cafiero, in the case passed by me to Élisée Reclus; that case also contained pages 139-148, which Reclus and Cafiero have not included, a proof of pages 139-148, and a proof of pages 149-210; the second of these proofs bore corrections of style and some deletions in the hand of Reclus and in one other hand; I find it still more difficult to explain, in view of that circumstance, that the editors of 1882 could have called this piece “a fragment from a letter or report.” This little literary artifice — for that is probably what it is — was not necessary to make the reader appreciate the high value of those pages” (Guillaume, 2016).

author: John David Parol
title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

Sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na kilos-protesta, iginiit ng mga progresibong grupo na hindi natatapos sa pagtatapos ng ASEAN Summit at sa pag-alis ni Trump ang laban sa lansangan.

Anila, hangga’t may nakakulong na mamamayang naninindigan at nakatali ang bansa sa dikta ng dayuhan, nanindigan ang hanay ng sambayanan na magpapatuloy ang pagkilos.

author: Clare Carlile and Hazel Healy
title: Fertiliser, Big Meat and Biofuels Industry Among 260 Food Sector Lobbyists at COP31
content:
Polluting food and agriculture companies are present in large numbers at this year’s UN COP31 climate talks, with a total of 260 lobbyists on the ground in Turkey’s southern city of Antalya, new analysis shows.




The meat and dairy sector, which 

produces

 over 14 percent of global emissions, brought 71 delegates, the highest number of all food and agriculture sectors. Its representatives outnumber delegates from Honduras, where millions of people currently 

face

 severe drought. 




Fertiliser lobbyists showed the biggest jump in delegates year on year, with a 45 percent increase. The CEOs of several powerful trade groups representing the meat, fertiliser, pesticides and biofuels sectors are also present in Antalya. 




Some of the world’s largest agribusiness firms, including meat company 

JBS

 and dairy multinationals 

Nestlé

 and Danone, as well as pesticides firm 

Bayer

 and food giant Unilever, also travelled to Turkey for the talks, which run from 9-20 November.




The analysis shows the power and influence enjoyed by the sector, with more than a hundred lobbyists participating as part of their country governments, lending them privileged access to negotiations. More than 44 percent of food and agriculture delegates travelled on country badges, up from 5 percent at COP27 five years ago.




For fertiliser firms, the share of delegates on party badges rises to 90 percent. Russia’s party included 12 delegates from two fertiliser companies linked to sanctioned individuals, DeSmog found. 







A 

version

 of this article was published by franceinfo.







DeSmog’s revelations come as disappointment sets in for advocates hoping for action to reform food systems, which account for a third of global emissions. Agriculture 

negotiations

 have 

broken down

 after four years of discussion, with some observers pointing to the contributing “role of vested interests” in their collapse.

 

At the time of going to press, all references to food and farming are 

missing

 from the draft cover text, which informs the basis of a final deal at the talks. And a high-level 

initiative

 to spur government action on methane is languishing on seven signatories.  




Both meat and fertiliser groups are keen to make their voices heard at a summit where the Turkish presidency has made curbing the short-lived “superpollutant gases” emitted by agricultural sectors – such as nitrous oxide and methane – a 

top priority

.

DeSmog has witnessed meat industry groups lobbying to 

weaken

 the accounting metrics for methane at side events while observers describe the high fertiliser sector turnout as “a big PR campaign” to be recognised as vital to food security.




The UN’s leading science body, the IPCC, says the world must make urgent and deep cuts to greenhouse gas emissions to avoid catastrophic climate change. Global heating is already set to 

breach

 1.5C, with each additional degree of warming increasing deadly impacts from droughts, floods, and cyclones. 




“This is a direct affront to billions of people who are suffering from the climate emergency,” said Million Belay, co-founder and general coordinator of the Alliance for Food Sovereignty in Africa (AFSA). “They have created the crisis that we all live in. And they are here to influence the whole process through lobbying, thwarting a real discussion and action against emissions, and flooding pavilions with empty talk.”




Farmers are facing unprecedented 

losses

 from droughts, floods, and tropical cyclones – 49 million more people 

could face

 acute hunger in 2026-27 due to the El Niño weather system that has been turbo-charged by climate breakdown.

“We need to talk about the impact that lobbying is having on our democracy,” Nusa Urbancic from advocacy group 

Changing Markets Foundation

 told DeSmog. “The number of agribusiness lobbyists is shocking and shows why agriculture has not yet made it into any official documents.” 




A spokesperson from Bayer said: “Global challenges need places where the world still comes together”. They added: “Combating climate change requires governments, civil society, local communities and the private sector to work together on effective solutions. This is particularly important for agriculture, which is severely affected by climate change”.

Nestlé told DeSmog: “COP31 is a major global gathering and an important opportunity to engage with governments, civil society, farmers and other stakeholders to accelerate climate action. Our engagement is focused on advancing practical solutions.”




Fertiliser “PR campaign” 




DeSmog analysed the provisional 

list

 of 68,374 in-person 

delegates

 published by the 

United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

 (UNFCCC) for representatives from the largest corporations and trade groups in major food sectors. (More information on the methodology can be found at the article’s end.)

The number of food lobbyists has dropped by 18 percent year-on-year compared to COP30, but they stand 40 percent higher than COP27 five years ago, showing an enduring industry interest in influencing the climate conversation.

Climate summits offer delegates many routes to influence – from sponsoring pavilions to promoting 

unproven solutions

 or greenwashing at side events – putting lobby groups in prime position to sideline meaningful climate action.




This year’s summit includes 45 lobbyists from fertiliser companies, a three-fold increase since the COP27 summit in Sharm el-Sheikh five years ago.

Fertilisers are a leading driver of nitrous oxide emissions, which cause around 270 times more warming than CO2. These chemical outputs 

emit more

 greenhouse gases than commercial aviation.




DeSmog’s analysis shows the 

$230-billion

 industry wields significant influence. Nearly all fertiliser representatives (40 of 45) travelled inside their country delegations, and the International Fertiliser Association (IFA), the leading lobby group for the world’s biggest fertiliser producers, brought four delegates to the summit.




A ‘Make Polluters Pay’ sign at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

Credit: DeSmog




In the run-up to COP31 the IFA has 

promoted

 chemical inputs as indispensable to food security – an argument frequently 

used

 by industry to oppose any moves to reduce fertiliser use. It has also 

called

 for the sector to be given a “stronger voice” in multilateral negotiations and for it to be recognised as a “national security asset”. 




Food systems experts at the IPES food thinktank 

take

 the opposite view. They have argued that farming must break its dependency on nitrogen fertilisers, 99 percent of which 

are made

 from fossil fuels, and encourage governments to fund climate-friendly alternatives, as extreme weather and conflict disrupt global supply chains, 

causing

 widespread hunger and food price spikes.




But long-running civil society attempts to insert references to greener farming practises into the agriculture negotiations at COP31 ran aground on Friday (13 November). Sources close to the talks told DeSmog that anger from the Arab negotiating group at the impact of EU climate legislation on its fertiliser firms was a key factor in negotiations ending with no agreement. 




Arab group members Oman and Morocco brought in 10 delegates between them from the Oman India Fertiliser Company and OCP Group. The latter, which had a turnover of more than $12 billion last year, also sponsored Morocco’s pavilion.




In an emailed statement OCP Group told DeSmog it “plays an important role in global food security as a global leader in plant nutrition and phosphate-based solutions”. It added that its “participation provides an opportunity to bring an industry perspective and share our expertise in how customised fertilisers and better agricultural practices can help farmers improve productivity, protect soil health and reduce environmental impacts.”




Indonesia and Russia’s guestlists likewise included dozens of representatives from fertiliser firms, with Russia bringing 11 representatives from PhosAgro and one from Uralchem. 




Both companies are part-owned by their respective founders 

Andrey Gurvey

 and 

Dmitry Mazepin

 or their families, billionaire Russians who have been sanctioned by the European Union and the UK. Their delegation outsized the climate vulnerable states of Trinidad and Tobago, Eritrea, and Nicaragua combined.




Countries at the summit used the event to cut deals for fertiliser expansion. 

Oman

 and 

Nepal

 both seek investment for plants that will produce fertiliser from renewable power – products that groups like the International Fertiliser Association argue can decarbonise the sector, and enable it to grow. 




Independent climate expert Lili Fuhr accused the sector of “selling the world a greenwashed fantasy”. Campaigners 

say

 the ‘clean’ production techniques touted by the sector are often unfeasible, too 

costly

 at scale, and fail to cancel out nitrous oxide, a superpollutant 270 times more potent than CO2, which is 

emitted

 in large quantities once fertilisers are used on the field. 




“The fertiliser presence is clearly linked to the Strait of Hormuz crisis. It’s part of this big PR exercise, where they say we are the solution to the climate crisis and food security,” says Marie Cosquer from Action Against Hunger, who is following the talks on the ground.

“They are afraid that countries would agree to more agroecology, phase out chemical outputs, and help farmers break dependency on polluting outputs,” she said.







A 

version

 of this article was published by Consenso.







Meat Targets Methane




Brazil brought seven representatives of the world’s largest meat company JBS, including its CEO, Gilberto Tomazoni. In July, the highest-emitting livestock firm 

abandoned

 its target to be net-zero by 2040 and dropped commitments to tackle deforestation. 




Elodie Guillon of advocacy group World Animal Protection told DeSmog that JBS, a regular at COPs, often attends as part of country delegations to ensure climate action does not “get in the way” of its expansion. 




“In the last couple of years, JBS expanded rapidly in Africa and Asia, risking displacing communities and driving deforestation, threatening the livelihoods of pastoralists and small producers,” she said.

At past climate summits, the meat sector – and industry-aligned states – have repeatedly pushed to delay or block climate actions targeting its sector. At COP26, US beef lobbyists 

celebrated

 weak voluntary commitments for agriculture in the Global Methane Pledge. The lobby watered 

down

 targets in the reports of the UN’s leading climate science body the IPCC, and it has also 

run

 pro-meat PR campaigns to present agriculture as the “solution” to climate change.

This year, trade groups lobbying on behalf of the meat industry at the talks include Australia’s National Farmers Federation (NFF), Beef+Lamb New Zealand, and the Global Roundtable for Sustainable Beef.




All three groups are 

pushing

 for changes to the way that international agreements calculate methane emissions, which critics say could leave pollution unchecked for a sector that accounts for around 32 percent of the global total. 







Subscribe to Desmog




Get the weekly intelligence you need to hold polluters accountable
















Email Address







Sign Up










Send me intelligence from:







All




US/Global team




UK/Europe team

























Methane reduction offers one of the fastest opportunities to slow global warming, as a short-lived superpollutant that causes over 80 times more warming than carbon dioxide over a 20-year timeframe. 




During an event at the UN climate summit on Monday (16 November), Macaulay Jones from the Beef+Lamb NZ trade group 

called

 for governments “to look at the use of alternative warming-based metrics” – an apparent reference to the metric GWP*, which has been 

dubbed

 a methane “accounting trick”.




Jones went on to mention an upcoming “review of metrics” at the UNFCCC. He said his group would be asking countries to support their bid to have “alternative warming-based metrics” accepted for calculating nationally determined contributions, every signatory state’s action plan to meet its commitments under the Paris Agreement.

When New Zealand became the first country to 

adopt

 the GWP* metric into its domestic climate goals in 2025, it cut its methane reduction targets down to 14-24 percent by 2050 from 24-47 percent.

The drop in ambition lends credence to researchers’ 

warnings

 that adopting GWP* will allow big polluters to claim “climate neutrality” without cutting herd sizes, or methane output.

A 2024 study that surveyed more than 200 climate experts 

said

 that livestock emissions must be reduced by 61 percent globally by 2036 in order to meet the targets set by the 2015 Paris Agreement.




“We know we are going to overshoot 1.5C warming. The question is how long and at what level,” Urbancic of Changing Markets said. “If you suddenly magically wish methane away, it changes the accounting but not the impact on the atmosphere. Super pollutants like methane have to be part of the discussion.”




Voluntary Pledges




Agribusiness trade groups at COP31 have also lobbied countries hard to keep action on methane voluntary – and even to undermine already-voluntary pledges.

In the wake of 

pressure

 from the country’s National Farmers’ Federation, COP co-host Australia announced last week that it would not sign the new Global Methane Pledge Ministerial Declaration – a 

commitment

 by countries including Germany and the UK to strengthen a pledge agreed in Glasgow at COP26.

The NFF, which 

thanked

 the government “for responding quickly” to its concerns, received 

funding

 from Australia to travel to the summit, as did trade group Dairy Australia – both of which are attending as part of the country’s delegation. 




U.S. meat trade groups were notably absent from Turkey, following the lead of the Trump administration, which boycotted talks for the second year in a row. 




The dairy sector, however, maintained its presence year-on-year, using the event to promote its efforts to cut methane. Dairy giants Yili and Mengniu brought seven delegates between them, as part of China’s delegation, while the Netherlands brought one representative from FrieslandCampina, and France brought four representatives from Danone. 




Members of civil society demonstrate in the corridors of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

Credit: 

UN Climate Change – Kubilay Ciftci 

 

(CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)




Along with the largest meat companies, the dairy industry is 

responsible

 for as much methane as the UK and EU combined. The sector is projected to grow at a steady 2 percent per year over the next decade.




Danone is one of few companies at the summit that has significantly 

cut

 its methane footprint, reducing it by almost 30 percent since 2020. The company told DeSmog that it had “contributed to discussions on methane reduction, climate resilience and mobilizing private investment in nature” during the summit. 




In an emailed statement, dairy giant Nestlé said: “Our advocacy is guided by a clear objective: supporting the implementation of the Paris Agreement and accelerating the transition to a more sustainable and resilient food system.” It added that it was “proud to be 

recognised

 by InfluenceMap as a leader in responsible and transparent climate lobbying.”




Dutch dairy company FrieslandCampina stated that it had “attended COP31 to contribute constructively to climate action and to help accelerate practical implementation”. It added: “Our aim was to listen, learn, share practical experience and explore partnerships that can deliver impact on farms and throughout supply chains. We engaged with stakeholders on methane reduction, regenerative and climate-smart agriculture, climate adaptation and biodiversity.”




Bioeconomy




Building on its success at COP30 – where host Brazil called for major expansion of the use of food crops for fuel – the 

$155 billion

 bioenergy industry also sent a substantial delegation with 30 representatives on the ground.




These outnumbered delegates from Sri Lanka, which is 

bracing

 for the impacts of a climate-charged El Niño this year and has set aside millions to fight severe drought and deliver water to families. 




Critics say the term ‘

bioeconomy

’ has been 

hijacked

 to put a green spin on the expansion of highly destructive monoculture grain crops. It now operates as a byword for controversial “biofuels” – liquid fuels produced from organic materials, such as corn-based ethanol or biodiesel made from soybean oil – which studies have 

labelled

 a “false solution” to climate change.




Companies and trade groups from the U.S. and Brazil, the world’s top two biofuels producers, brought over a third of the bioenergy representatives to COP31. 




They include the Corn Refiners Association (CRA), whose members include two of the world’s biggest grain companies: Cargill, the largest privately held agribusiness in the world, and Archer Daniels Midland. The CRA is a co-sponsor of a summit event titled: “Scaling the circular bioeconomy: agricultural solutions to climate change”. 




Cian Delaney, biofuels campaigner at Transport & Environment 

has described

 biofuels as “a terrible climate solution, and a staggering waste of land, food and millions in subsidies” in a 2025 report.

Criticisms levelled at the biofuels sector include: the 

clearance

 of huge tracts of land; 

harm

 to Amazonian communities; water 

pollution

 and 

poisoned

 ecosystems, and 

jeopardising

 endangered wildlife.




Countries at the frontline of these impacts are clear that the time has come for action on agriculture and food, as the UN 

warns

 that climate change will cause at least 250,000 additional deaths per year between 2030 and 2050. 




“The message is still going out that agriculture is not a worthy consideration because of politics,” prime minister of Barbados Mia Mottley 

told

 world leaders on Thursday (12 November), the day before agriculture talks broke down.




“We can’t leave it as a topic we cannot touch.”




All companies and countries named in this article were contacted for comment. 




Additional research by Brigitte Wear and Rachel Sherrington







Methodology note




DeSmog analysed the provisional list of UNFCCC COP31 delegates, with assistance from a large language model. The list was checked for the largest corporations in major food sectors which wield significant control in a highly concentrated food chain, and account for the majority of trade, of the following type: meat and dairy, pesticide and fertiliser firms, food processors, commodity and seed traders, (agricultural) bioenergy, grocery retail, commodity trader and shipping, and food packaging. Large national companies were included only when they are known to be high-emitting firms and/or have a track record of lobbying against environmental and climate policy.




DeSmog also included global and regional industry trade groups, some of which brought their own delegations to Antalya, along with national farmer unions and institutes that have corporate affiliations and/or a history of lobbying aligned with industry demands.




The post 

Fertiliser, Big Meat and Biofuels Industry Among 260 Food Sector Lobbyists at COP31

 appeared first on 

DeSmog

.

author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Labor and One Nation compete to arrest their way out of a mental health crisis
content:
Labor and One Nation agree on almost nothing, with the exception being on crime, where they read from the same script.

Premier Ben Carroll wants 1500 more police. One Nation wants more police, harsher treatment of repeat offenders and a 24/7 bail court. Its campaign launch promised to make Victoria the toughest state on crime. The Coalition has simply raised the bid to 3000. Labor's Attorney-General insists “tough bail is working”.

Victoria has run this experiment before. Labor funded 3135 more police between 2016 and 2021. Over 2024-25, the number of criminal incidents hit its highest level since records began.

Ask Victoria Police what drives crime and the answer reads like a social policy brief.

In June, it named the cost of living, recidivism, organised crime and drugs. In September, it listed organised crime, recidivism, mental health and illicit drugs.

Who ends up on the inside? In the latest national survey of people entering prison, from last year, 51% had been diagnosed with a mental health condition and 73% had used illicit drugs in the past year. In the month before prison, 43% were homeless and 46% were unemployed.

These statistics show that rather than being hardened criminals, prisoners are people who have been failed by a squeezed economy, a broken health system and by communities with nowhere to turn.

When people do reach out, the door is often shut.

About 4550 Victorians were waiting for drug and alcohol treatment on any given day last year. In June 2025, 14 men sat in custody waiting for a bed at Thomas Embling, the state’s secure psychiatric hospital. Victoria’s own royal commission found the mental health system had “catastrophically failed”.

On November 6, HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming was stabbed to death near the Queen Victoria Market. He was 47, a father of two, and had spent nine years working here to support his family. A second rider was seriously injured.

Roberto Urbano, 51, has been charged with the murder. He is presumed innocent, but the court has already seen something every politician promising more police should think about. Urbano’s lawyer told the court that he experiences schizophrenia.

Appearing by video link from a police cell, in front of a magistrate, Urbano stood on a stool and exposed himself to the courtroom. Police custody, a camera and a magistrate; there is no more heavily-policed place. If the law cannot reach a person in that state, another 1500 police officers on the street certainly will not.

People in a mental health crisis need care; they need treatment before things fall apart. Was Urbano seeing a doctor? Did he have somewhere safe to live? Those are the questions this case should prompt every party running in the election to answer.

None of this means people with mental illness are dangerous; they are several times more likely than others to be assaulted.

The lesson is simple: A society where vulnerable people can ask for help and get it is a safer society.

Instead, the money flows to prison cells. Since Labor’s “toughest bail laws in Australia” began in March last year, the prison population has grown by about 19%.

This year’s state budget found $229 million for new prison beds and $43 million for programs that keep people out of them.

Each prisoner costs the public purse almost $600 a day and more than a third of those released are back inside within two years.

One Nation’s other big idea — tougher sentences — is weaker still.

The Coalition offers more of the same. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson’s 3000 extra police would include recruits from Britain, Ireland and New Zealand.

The Coalition also promises a “one-strike” bail rule for serious offences and has promised to expand Adult Time for Violent Crime from eight offences to 20. Youth diversion gets a mention after the police, bail and sentencing pledges.

The Victorian Sentencing Advisory Council found that longer prison terms do not produce a matching increase in deterrence. A longer stretch inside does not treat what it was that put the person there.

You cannot handcuff the cost of living. You cannot arrest a mental illness.

This is not a call on parties to be “soft” on crime. It is about being more serious about crime prevention. That means funding mental health and drug treatment until the queues disappear. It means building the forensic beds, called for by the royal commission. People leaving prison need secure homes to go to. Nationally, a third expect to be homeless on release.

There needs to be investment in the struggling suburbs and towns, where disadvantage and prison admissions pile up.

Before buying another 1500 uniforms, find out why people end up in a cell.

Victoria should fund an independent, ongoing study that asks thousands of people in its prisons what went wrong in their lives, and tie prevention budgets to the answers.

Communities have shown another way. In Bourke, in north-west NSW, the Aboriginal-led Maranguka project, guided by the Bourke Tribal Council, has spent more than a decade shifting the focus from punishment to community-led solutions.

Labor and One Nation are selling the same police band-aid, but in different colours. Until we ask why are people ending up in a cell, the public will keep paying for more cells and more cops, and there will be more grieving families.

Before November 28, ask your candidates one question: What will you do before the crime, not after it?

author: Unknown
title: Prisoner Newroz Bozkurt brought to hospital
content:
Newroz Bozkurt, who suffers from Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL), was transferred to Etlik City Hospital on Saturday, 14 November, after becoming unwell.




Newroz Bozkurt has been in detention since January 1999 and was diagnosed with leukaemia in June.




It was reported that Newroz Bozkurt had previously been taken to Etlik City Hospital in December 2025. Despite medical examinations revealing that her blood levels were low, no medical intervention was carried out. It was subsequently reported that her lawyers filed a criminal complaint against the doctor concerned.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Community picket shuts down Bisalloy Steel for 36-hours over ties to Israel’s genocide
content:
A community picket has shut down operations the Bisalloy Steel factor in Unanderra, in Tharawal/Wollongong, for the 11th time, over November 15–17, for its role in arming Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Bisalloy Steel supplies armoured steel to Israel that is used for armoured vehicles, tanks and other military technology used in its genocide of Palestinian’s in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank.

The picket was organised by Wollongong Friends of Palestine (WFoP) and supported by many Palestine solidarity and anti-militarism groups.

“We had amazing community support,” Safaa Rayan, social worker and WFoP spokesperson, told Green Left. “It was cold and rainy but we still managed to have hundreds of people not just turn up, but camp out. The street was lined with tents, each full with people.

“Parents turned up with their children, we had three DJ performances each day … we even had people join in who have never been to a protest or picket before.”

At the previous picket in June, NSW Police attempted to break up the picket, arresting at least one person and pushing others to the ground. One woman was concussed after police allegedly pushed her head into the pavement.

“The police violence at the last picket really shows how Bisalloy and the cops are working together to protect the genocide supply chain,” Rayan said. “It's clear the NSW government values business as usual for genocide suppliers far more than the rights of citizens, let alone the lives of Palestinians.”

Rayan said the police presence was minimal this time. “They sent out a car every three hours, would drive past and leave.

“Our pickets are extraordinarily peaceful, and people are very respectful of the area and the environment.”

Local campaigner and Jewish woman Kim Sattler said the deepening militarisation of Wollongong and the appointment of Bisalloy into the AUKUS supply chain was concerning. “This endangers our local community and leads us into war.”

Rayan said “AUKUS is a threat to not only Australia's sovereignty, but also to our environment bringing nuclear submarines at our shores, particularly as they want to build a base here at Port Kembla”.

Climate organiser and youth worker Jayne Hoschke said Bisalloy should make things that the community needs to address the climate crisis. “Instead, they’re determined to help make things that make the world worse … our community won’t let that happen.”

“It's all interconnected,” Rayyan told GL. “We will continue to picket at Bisalloy until they divest from the military industrial complex.”

She also called on the federal and state government to take action. “It is their obligation under the United Nations statue to not supply weapons or weapons parts to a country committing a genocide.

“Because of their inaction, we as the citizens are having to do the work.”

Wollongong Friends of Palestine

author: Cas Smith
title: Hazelmere locals reject plans for mega AI data centre
content:
About 200 people rallied outside Midland Town Hall on November 11 to oppose plans for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data centre in Hazelmere, in Perth’s eastern suburbs.

Gwenaël (Gwen) Velge, a Research Associate at Murdoch University’s Mineral Policy Institute; Kate Herron from Trillion Trees; and former Labor MLA Matthew Hughes addressed the rally and highlighted the disruptive nature of CDC Data Centres’ planned project, which is expected to cause significant noise pollution and energy usage.

At a consultation meeting last month, a CDC technician said the data centre would have an energy allotment of 192 megawatts (MW) with 96 generators.

This would make it significantly larger than the 120 MW, 88 generator data centre previously proposed by Greensquare, which was rejected earlier this year by the City of Swan, following community backlash and concerns about noise pollution.

Velge noted the significance of this decision in the Mining Monitor on October 29. “Earlier this year, the City recommended refusing the GreenSquare proposal over the potential noise of its 88 generators.

“CDC proposes 96 generators, [which] come within 1dB (decibels) of the limit modelled at 75% load, and approach ‘the limits of compliance’; whereas Greensquare was asked to model at 100% load.”

He said the “sheer scale” of the energy demand of hyperscale data centres makes it harder to achieve a renewable energy transition.

“Renewable energy capacity meant to replace coal and gas is directly absorbed by this new demand. In the best-case scenario, this added demand slows down the transition, in the worst-case scenario the narrative and promises of ‘transition’ justifies and legitimates actual energy addition.

“Of course, some grid growth is to be expected as we electrify. But data centres are a clear case of addition: that demand did not exist before and it competes directly with the electrification part of the transition.”

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) expects consumption on the region’s electrical grid to increase by 57% in the next decade, from 20.4 to 32.1 terrawatt-hours (TWh).

However, this excludes the energy demands from data centre projects already in the pipeline, which are expected to be excessive, based on the ‘cooling’ requirement for servers.

Two planned projects in WA, the Hazelmere data centre and a project in Maddington — both proposed by CDC — are expected to consume 4.3TWh a year in total (or on a single hot day, up to 550–590MW).

Velge said this would be “more than five times AEMO’s forecast for the entire sector, and nearly 40% of the total projected growth for the next decade”.

“With huge amounts of heat comes huge amounts of emissions, and heat which must be displaced with either water or with fans.

“So, the choice is between huge water usage or noise. Adding this much extra demand on the grid is bound to push the price of electricity much higher than it already is.”

Another concern is the lack of transparency around the Hazelmere project, with many questions remaining about how it might develop. CDC’s application, for example, refers to the planned building as “HA1”, which raises the question: should people be expecting a HA2?

Local residents have discovered that CDC has acquired the adjoining lots at 170 Bushmead Road and 40 and 50 Hazelmere Crescent, making a larger project down the track a real possibility, even if the acquisitions had not been included in the current application.

This meant that CDC could be using a “salami-slicing” approach, splitting the project into smaller units, so that its cumulative impacts can’t be assessed as a whole.

In any case, Gwen argued that data centre projects should be approached like mining ones.

“Treating data centres like mining projects means applying our Mining Policy Principles: the right of affected communities to veto, assessment of cumulative impacts not just project by project assessments and a meaningful test of whether the project serves communities and the transition or if it serves private profits....

“We shouldn’t let ourselves be priced out of our own public utilities to release more carbon emissions and more heat into our globally warming atmosphere.

“As we know from the US, data centres are also an opportunity to rally people from all walks of life and all political stripes around something everyone opposes — a genuinely positive sight in the polarising times we live in.

“The numbers don’t add up. People and ecosystems will be left paying the price. We can still say no.”

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: No red carpet for empire: State repression and the fight against Pax Silica
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates hold an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

At the center of this escalation is Pax Silica, Washington’s emerging high-tech, resource-intensive war infrastructure. If NATO is the military apparatus built to fight U.S.-led wars, Pax Silica is the pre-war supply chain alliance designed to sustain them.

6,000-strong at Liwasang Bonifacio alone—and the numbers continue to surge as protesters march toward the PICC as U.S. President Donald Trump sets foot on Philippine soil. For over a century, U.S. imperialism has plundered this territory and oppressed its people, dating back to how it usurped the Katipunan’s hard-won 1896 triumph over Spanish colonialism. This is not the first time the Filipino people have fiercely rejected a Trump visit; they rose in protest during the ASEAN Summit in November 2017, and they are rising again.

The Filipino public’s refusal to welcome Trump—standing in sharp contrast to the Marcos Jr. administration’s eagerness to accommodate Washington—cannot justify the sweeping crackdown on activists exercising their fundamental rights to assembly, expression, and association. International observers have been alarmed by the scale and intensity of police brutality under Marcos Jr., which echoes the state terror unleashed over half a century ago under the U.S.-backed Martial Law dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.—a regime only toppled in 1986 after a protracted, heroic struggle against U.S. imperialism and its client-dictator.

Yet this violence is not merely a nostalgic return to his father’s Martial Law era; it is the continuation of an unbroken war against the poor. In the Philippine countryside, landless peasants live in a state of perpetual siege, battered by recurring tiempo muerto (dead seasons), massacres, and state-backed counterinsurgency campaigns that target cooperative leaders and their families. In the cities, whenever public anger boils over—such as during last year’s mass anti-corruption demonstrations—state repression falls hardest on patriotic youth—students and urban poor—the very demographics with the greatest stake in systemic change.

At the center of this escalation is Pax Silica, Washington’s emerging high-tech, resource-intensive war infrastructure. If NATO is the military apparatus built to fight U.S.-led wars, Pax Silica is the pre-war supply chain alliance designed to sustain them. Before a single bomb is dropped, it secures the physical pillars of modern warfare and artificial intelligence—water, energy grids, land, and semiconductor supply chains—within allied borders. Designated as the United States’ key strategic ally in Asia, the Philippines is being positioned as a primary resource frontline.

The lethal purpose of Pax Silica’s weaponry and intelligence apparatus is already on full display in Palestine—one of its primary targets, and the sharpest expression of a settler colonialism that never stops settling. As this colonial project expands, so too does the global infrastructure required to endlessly reproduce the war machine. That relentless reproduction of war stands in stark, irreconcilable opposition to the social reproduction of human life and labor. This is precisely why the Filipino working poor and youth are determined to junk Pax Silica and reject the presence of a war criminal like Trump. For us Filipinos, defiance against this weaponized interdependence is an imperative of national self-defense.

In oppressed nations like the Philippines, where the people are actively working to resolve their primary contradiction against U.S. imperialism, defending the social reproduction of life and labor inevitably requires taking to the streets. When protesters march despite knowing they will face state violence and police brutality, it is not because they invite harm or court repression; rather, it is how the peoples of oppressed nations shed the illusions of safety and docility under U.S. imperialist diktat. Only by confronting that violence do we reclaim our dignity—a dignity rooted in land, national patrimony, solidarity, and the camaraderie in struggle that Filipinos have always been proud of and known for.

This collective resolve has deep historical roots. From the basic masses and Indigenous Peoples to professionals, students, cultural workers, and progressive lawmakers, nationwide opposition remains firm. That same power found historic, legal expression on September 12, 1991, when the Philippine Senate voted to reject the renewal of the U.S. basing treaty—a victory won through a relentless mass campaign against the occupation of ancestral lands, the plunder of our resources, the systemic abuse of Filipino women and children, and the stripping of our national sovereignty.

Recent global events underscore the urgency of this struggle. The year opened with a devastating U.S. assault on Venezuela that claimed over a hundred lives and saw the abduction and unlawful detention of President Nicolás Maduro and First Combatant Cilia Flores. Weeks later, U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iran killed over 150 schoolchildren in Minab along with Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei. While the world was initially stunned, grief has hardened into sustained anti-imperialist resistance across West Asia. Simultaneously, mass protests in cities like Paris reveal that even in the imperial core, capitalism’s “peacetime” delivers only austerity, state abuse, and economic precarity.

An imperialist world order offers no viable future for humanity or the biosphere. Persisting down the path championed by leaders like Trump and Marcos Jr. stands in direct opposition to historical progress, ecological survival, and the basic material conditions needed for human life to thrive. Time and again, we show—and are reminded—that our identity as a free and dignified people can only be forged through class struggle against U.S. imperialism. Today’s mobilization is nothing short of historic: it transforms the memory of an anti-colonial revolution usurped by foreign powers into the undeniable thunder of resolute footsteps, marching forward and defending the nation.

title: ‘No red carpet’ for Trump’s arrival in the Philippines
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates hold an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

By Aaron Ernest Cruz and Anne Marxze Umil

“The Filipino people will never welcome a warmonger, racist, fascist, misogynist, sexual offender, and corrupt leader like Trump.”

Despite attempts to derail their protest, progressive groups continued with their action as US President Donald Trump arrived in the country on November 17.

“The Filipino people will never welcome a warmonger, racist, fascist, misogynist, sexual offender, and corrupt leader like Trump,” Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) said in a statement.

“His war on Iran, support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, military interventions in Venezuela, Cuba, and the Carribean, tariff wars and brutal trade sanctions, and racist immigration policies have hurt people all over the world, destroyed the global economy, and undermined world peace,” Bayan added.

An estimated 6,000 individuals trooped at Liwasang Bonifacio to express their condemnation of the government’s red carpet welcome for Trump and the Pax Silica deal.

According to Bayan, the police blocked the truck to be used in their program and attempted to get their sound system. But the group managed to bring the sound system to Liwasang Bonifacio. During the early morning, the group reported that there were many police deployed in the area.

“Manila is just like a garrison as police were scattered around the city’s entry point,” Bayan Secretary-General Mong Palatino said in an interview.

Bayan President Renato Reyes Jr. also condemned the police for attempting to tow their vehicle, stressing that police violated the Batas Pambansa Blg. 880 which protects the right to hold protests in designated freedom parks without permits. “We don’t need your [police] here and we won’t allow you to tow our vehicle just like what happened last Sunday [November 15].”

Funa-ay Claver, secretary-general of Indigenous group Katribu described the Marcos Jr. administration as a lapdog of the US government, giving up the country’s land for Pax Silica.

“They say it is for development, but we should always ask: Who will benefit from it? It is clear that Pax Silica serves foreign interests rather than the interests of its own people,” Claver said.

Karapatan said that it is not surprising that Marcos Jr. had an extravagant welcome for Trump. “Trump is a fascist, a warmonger and enabler of brutal, genocidal regimes, making the extravagant welcome prepared for him by his fellow fascist and tyrant Ferdinand Marcos Jr. come as no surprise,” the group said in a statement.

Karapata said that it was under Trump that the Marcos Jr. regime began to transform the Philippines into a manufacturing hub for US armaments.

They said that the country became a cog in the US global supply chain, making parts for weapons now being used in US wars of aggression against countries that have stood up against US hegemony. “Only a fellow fascist and tyrant like Ferdinand Marcos Jr. could be motivated to welcome the likes of Donald Trump to our shores.”

The groups tried to march to the ASEAN Summit venue but were blocked by the police. There are also Special Weapon and Tactics (SWAT) personnel holding rifles at the flyover. Under Batas Pambasa Bldg. 880, law enforcers are prohibited to bring guns in a peaceful protest.

“These guards of Trump are arrogant because they have shields and weapons. But the weapons of the Filipino people are truth, democracy, and militant struggle,” Bayan Chairperson Teddy Casiño said in front of the police. He added that even though they were not able to march through PICC where Trump is, he said, their protest is resonating around the world. (DAA)

author: Pip Hinman
title: NSW Labor goes full tilt to support coal
content:
As Yasmin Catley, police minister and NSW Labor MP for Swansea, in the Hunter, continues to rail about a climate protest she had wanted to ban, NSW Labor is rushing through a pro-coal bill which critics say undermines a recent federal High Court ruling.

The Paddle for the Planet, organised by Rising Tide, drew around 1000 people to Horseshoe Beach in Muloobinba/Newcastle on November 14. The protest was designed to highlight Australia’s lack of leadership at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye.

Its attendance was boosted by NSW Labor’s last-ditch undemocratic attempts to prevent it from going ahead. This included Premier Chris Minns’ direct intervention into Newcastle City Council, demanding it ban Rising Tide and, shockingly, “associates, subsidiaries, other groups and individuals” from holding events or protests on council land.

The motion only passed with the casting vote of independent Mayor Gavin Morris, after Labor councillor Declan Clausen crossed the floor to support the ban.

But the NSW Supreme Court’s decision to favour individuals’ right to peacefully express themselves knocked NSW Police’s efforts to ban the protest on its head.

At least 800 people took to the water in canoes and kayaks on a calm and sunny day. There was not one NSW Police officer in sight — nor any coal ships.

Climate activists occupied the channel for an hour to make their views known about Labor’s pretense over its commitment to the climate while approving new coal and gas projects.

Even after the peaceful event, Catley continued to rail against the climate activists for being “reckless” and “dangerous for everybody”.

Meanwhile, Cately and Minns are pushing a new pro-coal bill, favouring MACH Energy, which aims to circumvent a High Court decision on that company’s mine in the Hunter Valley.

The Environmental Defenders’ Office (EDO) described the Mount Pleasant Mine Bill 2026 bill, which went to parliament on November 10, as “eroding the rule of law, the separation of powers and public trust in independent decision-making”.

The bill, which Labor wants to push through this week, authorises MACH Energy to continue mining thermal coal at Mount Pleasant until 2032 (up to 16.5 million tonnes).

The EDO said not only does it override the pending process and decision of the Land and Environment Court of NSW, following the High Court decision, it contains a dangerously broad clause which allows the Planning Minister to be the consent authority for the approval, not the Independent Planning Commission. It would circumvent parliamentary scrutiny.

Jacqui Mumford, Nature Conservation Council NSW (NCC) CEO, said this “would give the Resources Minister unfettered power to override all other laws in relation to the Mount Pleasant coal mine” adding, “this kind of power is a major corruption risk”. She said such a law “would take NSW back to the days of [disgraced Labor MP] Eddie Obeid by bypassing independent assessments and public consultation”.

Labor’s talking points about “protecting jobs” at the Mount Pleasant mine are also being challenged.

While the bill contains a “jobs guarantee”, to which mining corporations must agree, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) pointed out that Labor has not shown a commitment to coal workers at Mount Pleasant, as most are on insecure labour hire contracts.

Labor signed off on a transition authority and investment fund which are supposed to support workers wanting to leave the fossil fuel industry. But with no dedicated funding figure in the Future Jobs and Investment Fund, it remains abstract.

Retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy and barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson have publicly criticised NSW Labor over its new coal bill. “I think it’s disgraceful,” Watson, a director at the Centre for Public Integrity and former senior counsel assisting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, told The Guardian on October 21.

“This is, in effect, to overturn a decision of the high court of Australia after a fair hearing. In my book it’s contrary to the separation of powers which acknowledges that each branch of government has its own area or domain.”

Whealy told the ABC on October 20 that the government’s bill is “reprehensible” because it “obliterates” the legal process.

“With an election early in 2027, such matters do not seem to phase NSW Labor, which seems more singularly concerned about winning votes back from One Nation in coal mining regions,” Steve O’Brien, the Socialist Alliance candidate for Newcastle, told Green Left. “Of course, that could also be done by accelerating a just transition for fossil fuel workers to sustainable industries, plans for which have already been made over several decades.”

author: Shirley Killen
title: Building the socialist movement in regional Victoria
content:
Victorians from Mildura to Mallacoota will have the chance to vote socialist for the first time in generations at this month’s state election. In a campaign that’s been full of milestones for the Victorian Socialists, one of the biggest is that the party is standing candidates in all 88 lower house seats for the first time. 

Networks of socialist activists have sprung up across the state with the goal of getting these candidates elected, putting on meetings, organising local rallies, door knocking and letterboxing. In some places, like Bendigo and Ballarat, local branches already existed, while in others, coordinators are starting from scratch.

David Suter is one of the local coordinators starting from scratch. He describes turning up to a polling booth after moving to Garfield, in eastern Victoria and part of the electorate of Narracan, looking at his options and thinking “this is bullshit”. The dearth of organised radical politics in regional areas could easily make a person feel disheartened. But David was encouraged by the result the Victorian Socialists achieved in last year’s federal election, so he signed up to attend the party’s state conference later that year. He left with a list of phone numbers and a plan to activate socialists in his region, and established a crew of seven who began sketching out a state election campaign. Now, the party has candidates contesting all eleven lower house seats, and the beginnings of local branches in Narracan, Shepparton, Bairnsdale and the Mornington Peninsula—to name just a few. 

These are “baby steps”, according to David. It’s a big task to rebuild (or just build, sometimes) a socialist tradition in regional Victoria. But the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign so far has proved it is not impossible, and that with a common goal and some organisational infrastructure, socialists who previously felt isolated in the regions can make a difference.

Renee Nayef, the Victorian Socialists candidate for Mildura in Victoria’s north-west, described a “meet the candidate” event she put on recently. Two men drove into Mildura separately from a nearby town of 97 people, both assuming they were the only socialists for kilometres. They met for the first time at Renee’s event. Without the scaffolding of a statewide socialist campaign, they might have gone on for years not knowing there was another radical a couple of streets over. 

Sometimes these connections are made in unorthodox ways. For socialist campaigners in metropolitan Melbourne, the movement is built by knocking on other people’s doors and starting up conversations about socialism. Socialists in the regions report the opposite experience—locals are instead knocking on 

their 

doors because they’ve seen a yard sign and are thrilled to know there’s another socialist in town. 

In some parts of the state, the campaign is reviving largely forgotten radical traditions. Bass candidate for Victorian Socialists Chris Jobe had to correct the record when the local paper announced his candidacy with the headline “Red flag planted in Bass for the first time”. In fact, the seat of Bass takes in the old mining town Wonthaggi, known for much of the twentieth century as “Red Wonthaggi” because of the militancy of the local communist-led miners’ union. A more accurate headline would have been “Red flag planted in Bass 

again

”. 

The picture in regional Victoria today is clearly very different from the days when the Wonthaggi miners fought bitter industrial battles with coal bosses and the state. With few exceptions, these seats are the preserve of the Liberals and Nationals, with One Nation now poised to make serious gains. Socialists campaigning outside Melbourne don’t sugarcoat the challenges they are facing.

But socialist politics haven’t been seriously tested outside the state’s biggest cities in decades. It’s not surprising that conservative politics dominate when there’s nothing much else on offer. 

And working-class people in rural Victoria face the same stresses as their counterparts in Melbourne. The rising cost of living, the health system stretched to breaking point, the failure of successive governments to invest in transport and education—these issues are coming up all across the state. 

For Hera Sheppard, Victorian Socialists candidate for the South-West Coast, it was growing up in Warrnambool’s public housing that made her a socialist. She witnessed the way Labor neglected its housing stock and failed to address ballooning waiting lists for housing. Later, she got a job at McDonald's, only to experience all the injustices of being a young worker, from copping junior pay rates to dodging live electrical wires at work. She’s proud of her efforts to unionise McDonald's and enter bargaining for the first time in a decade. But perhaps the greatest compliment came from the 

Portland Observer

, which ran an article about her candidacy with the headline “Sheppard vows to stand up for workers”.

Renee’s grandparents migrated to Mildura from Greece and worked picking and packing grapes in tin sheds in 40-degree heat. She says growing up in the region exposed her to the racism of Australian capitalism, the brutal dispossession and segregation endured by Aboriginal communities and the injustice of a society where those who work the hardest have to scrimp and save just to get by. She’s running to “give hope to people across Victoria that the world can be different if we fight for it”.

In Bendigo, coordinator (and local councillor) Owen Cosgriff jokes that if the outer northern and western suburbs of Melbourne are the front lines of the state election campaign, then he and his comrades are several hundred kilometres “deep in enemy territory”. But even so, he expects they’ll be staffing all four pre-poll booths in Bendigo and Castlemaine, and a sizeable number of the election day voting centres. This is a major achievement for a socialist party any day of the week—and they’ve got big plans to keep building after the election, with a new Castlemaine branch on the horizon.

“Baby steps”. That’s how David describes the work he’s helping to coordinate across eastern Victoria. But only from baby steps can bigger things ever come.

title: Μαζικές διαδηλώσεις για την επέτειο του Πολυτεχνείου σε Αθήνα και Θεσσαλονίκη (φωτορεπορτάζ & video)
content:
Μαζικές διαδηλώσεις για την επέτειο του Πολυτεχνείου σε Αθήνα και Θεσσαλονίκη (φωτορεπορτάζ & video).




Αθήνα




Δεκάδες χιλιάδες άνθρωποι έδωσαν και φέτος το παρόν στους δρόμους της πρωτεύουσας τιμώντας τη μνήμη της εξέγερσης του Πολυτεχνείου. 53 χρόνια μετά από εκείνον τον Νοέμβρη του 1973, η εξέγερση συνεχίζει να εμπνέει και να αποτελεί σημείο αναφοράς στους σημερινούς αγώνες. Ο λαός της Αθήνας κατέκλυσε το κέντρο της Αθήνας στην καθιερωμένη πορεία προς την αμερικάνικη πρεσβεία. Τις προηγούμενες μέρες είχε σπάσει ντε φάκτο η απαγόρευση του πρύτανη του ΕΜΠ με την 

κατάληψη του κτηρίου Γκίνη και το άνοιγμα της πύλης στη Στουρνάρη

.




Πιστή στο ραντεβού της κι η ΕΛ.ΑΣ. Για ακόμη μια φορά έδωσε ρεσιτάλ αποκτήνωσης και χυδαιότητας. Στο τέλος της πορείας τα κορδόνια των ΜΑΤ απαγόρευσαν στον κόσμο που συμμετείχε στα αναρχικά/αντιεξουσιαστικά μπλοκ να διαλυθεί προς την πλατεία Μαβίλη και τον ωθούσαν προς τη λεωφόρο Αλεξάνδρας. Εκεί τα ΜΑΤ επιτέθηκαν αναίτια, τραυματίζοντας σοβαρά 4 γυναίκες στο κεφάλι. Τουλάχιστον μια κοπέλα χτυπήθηκε με γκλοπ στο πίσω μέρος του κεφαλιού της.










https://www.alerta.gr/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/v-e-l-o-c-i-t-y-antireport-17-11-2026-Tonight：-the-moment-a-riot-cop—from-the-larges.mp4




Τα ΜΑΤ επιτέθηκαν επίσης μέσα στον σταθμό μετρό Αμπελοκήπων και έκαναν προσαγωγές στον σωρό μαζεύοντας κυρίως ανήλικους που φορούσαν μαύρα ρούχα.







Συνολικά έγιναν 15 προσαγωγές εκ των οποίων 2 μετατράπηκαν σε συλλήψεις. Αργά το βράδυ εκδόθηκε 

κάλεσμα αλληλεγγύης στη ΓΑΔΑ

 για τους προσαχθέντες και συλληφθέντες της πορείας.




Θεσσαλονίκη




Πάνω από 10 χιλιάδες άτομα ανταποκρίθηκαν στα 

καλέσματα

 φοιτητικών συλλόγων και σχημάτων, εργατικών σωματείων, κομμάτων και οργανώσεων της Αριστεράς και οργανώσεων και συλλογικοτήτων του αναρχικού/αντιεξουσιαστικού χώρου. Η πορεία, ξεκινώντας από την Πολυτεχνική Σχολή ΑΠΘ, διέσχισε όλο το κέντρο της Θεσσαλονίκης μέσω των οδών Εθνικής Αμύνης, Τσιμισκή, Βενιζέλου και Εγνατία ενώ κατέληξε στο άγαλμα Βενιζέλου. Καθ’ όλη τη διάρκεια τα αναρχικά/αντιεξουσιαστικά μπλοκ ήταν περικυκλωμένα από ισχυρές δυνάμεις των ΜΑΤ αλλά και από δεκάδες μαυροφορεμένους και κουκουλοφόρους ασφαλίτες που έφεραν σακίδια. Ένα φαινόμενο που επαναλαμβάνεται σε κάθε μεγάλη πορεία. Μετά το τέλος της πορείας μικροεπεισόδια ξέσπασαν στη Ρωμαϊκή Αγορά με δυνάμεις της ΕΛ.ΑΣ. να περικυκλώνουν και να αποκλείουν την περιοχή για παραπάνω από μια ώρα.
