author: Sarah Garnham
title: One Nation is waging war on progress. Why won't progressives fight back?
content:
In 2018, One Nation struggled to get registered as a political party in Victoria, and progressives across the state took pride in it. Labor won the state election that year with a whopping 43 percent primary vote. Twenty years earlier, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson had been prevented from organising in Melbourne by protests, blockades and community events.

Today, the snarling menace and enemy of workers and the left that is One Nation is a major force in Victoria; it enjoys mass support, is vying for lower house seats, and setting the agenda in the state election campaign. The party and its policies have been legitimised by the capitalist press, the Liberal Party and, to a lesser extent, Labor. One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, has been invited to appear at the leaders’ debate.  

Progressive Victoria should be in uproar. This is the state of Trades Hall, Treaty and Pride. But aside from a few important exceptions—most notably high school students—the response to One Nation’s rise has been decidedly muted. Progressive NGOs and organisations have mostly stayed silent or offered tepid statements focusing on the fears of their constituents rather than forthright denunciation of One Nation and all it represents. The mood is closer to stunned awe than anger, almost as if the capacity to generate the ever-more-elusive commodity of popularity makes a party worthy of respect, however the popularity might be gained. 

Worse still, a layer of trade union organisers, Greens members and other progressives is arguing that the left must sympathise with the concerns of One Nation voters, or at least avoid antagonising them through political argument. In practice, this means sidestepping the signature issues that One Nation is pushing and building a base around. 

GetUp and Victorian Trades Hall Council (VTHC) are 

directing

 campaigners not to “play the racism card” or explicitly attack Pauline Hanson. After its costly and high-profile intervention in the Farrer by-election, GetUp concluded that criticising Hanson, her wealthy backer Gina Rinehart, celebrity defector Barnaby Joyce or the party’s links to Trump is not electorally expedient. Campaigners should instead seek to establish common ground with potential One Nation voters based on economic grievances. 

Senior VTHC researcher Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett 

argues

 to ignore the politics: “Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying”. The beat, he says, is dissatisfaction with the status quo, so supporters should be helped to “tease out” what that looks like and how it makes them feel. 

Federal Greens leader David Shoebridge 

says

 he has “understood the anger” driving One Nation support. Former Queensland Greens MP Max Chandler-Mathers 

goes further

, arguing that One Nation voters, especially the workers among them, are expressing legitimate protest against the system. He says they are driven by an “almost political nihilism”, and a desire to “blow it up” that makes them open to left-wing arguments and solutions. 

The same basic approach is being taken by more establishment political forces. Teal consultant Sue Barret gives the 

same advice

in four steps: validate the feeling, not the target; ask a genuine question and then be quiet; acknowledge the ground you share; offer a different path, not a different diagnosis.

Labor’s federal treasurer likewise 

warns

 progressives not to “scold” One Nation supporters, and to approach them “from a place of genuine respect and understanding”. The same advice is given by the media, from the establishment right through to liberal outlets. And all of this helps to reinforce One Nation’s 

spin

 about itself: that it is the party of “everyday Australians” who are “sick and tired of being ignored”. 

This appeasement goes further than merely tempering criticisms of One Nation for fear of alienating the party’s voters; it leads to actively opposing efforts to build resistance. 

The Labor-controlled National Union of Students, for example, pulled out of supporting the second student walkout against One Nation, and attacked office bearers for promoting it. Some Greens MPs have endorsed and spoken at the rallies, but others refused to speak on the grounds that it is not strategic and would alienate bigots. When a socialist promoted an anti-One Nation rally in a union activist online forum, the Victorian secretary of the CPSU and long-time leftist Jiselle Hanna replied that it is “more powerful to understand why so many of the working class are being persuaded by One Nation, than dismissing them all as a bunch of racists”. She then removed unionists who backed the protest from the forum.

What is going on?

For some, the lack of interest in denouncing or confronting far-right supporters today comes from a sense of defeatism: One Nation is connecting with the moment better than our side of politics, so we have no credibility to challenge it. Unfortunately, this only leads to further normalisation of the right and the further weakening of our side. 

For others, it may be that they see protest and other forms of resistance aimed at polarising sentiment as an outdated method. Yet history is full of successful movements against the far right. In the 1990s, mass and sustained demonstrations helped push One Nation back to the margins. Last month in Serbia, a two-year, student-led protest movement ended the rule of a right-wing nationalist government. Even if the far right can’t be defeated immediately, efforts towards building mass resistance have more to recommend them than cowering passivity.

But by far the most pervasive argument made by progressives is that One Nation voters are confused victims of the system and therefore potentially open to influence. The stereotype of the everyday person fed up with official politics, the major parties and motivated primarily by their bread-and-butter concerns, is the common-sense explanation of the rise of the “populist” right in Australia as well as many other places. 

Commentators across the political spectrum have their own version of it, with flourishes based on their particular political outlook. Right-wing journalist Phil Coorey

 

says

 

people are pining for an Australia before multiculturalism and “elite progressivism”. Labor-aligned Kos Samaras 

says

 they are the victims of disintegrating local community, health and public services. Chandler-Mathers

 

says

 

the hollowing-out of collective organisation has “left a febrile and unstable political democracy because now the vast majority of people are completely disconnected from either major party”, with housing and financial stress as the spark.

But as French anti-fascist writer Andrew Hussey has 

noted

, “populism” is a dubious label. It is applied to parties of the right in a way that reflects “the elitist prejudice that the people are ignorant and irrational, impulsive and incoherent, easily manipulated and prone to authoritarian excess and frenzies of xenophobia”. Political disengagement is high, and incoherence is its corollary, but the idea that One Nation voters cannot meaningfully be associated with the party’s actual politics is misorienting.

It is these politics that matter the most. The reasons why people might vote for One Nation do not determine what it stands for. And there is little ambiguity on this score: a new White Australia, mass deportations, attacks on workers’ rights, more freedom for business, fewer environmental protections and more power for the state to lock people up and repress dissent.

Like its counterparts worldwide, its program is a reaction to every progressive advance since the last major wave of struggle in the 1960s and ’70s, dressed up as no-nonsense common sense. It defines itself against pro-Palestine sentiment, migrant and refugee rights, strong unions, women’s rights, trans inclusion, net zero and public health measures. It opposes these not because they are aspects of a neoliberal status quo, but because they represent the agenda of the left and the working-class movement. 

One Nation sees the major parties as having bowed to these “woke” demands and is open about its intention to reverse them. Whatever individual voters feel, this is the goal of the party and the corporate donors that bankroll it. This is what distinguishes it from all the other parties. And it’s why One Nation has made the greatest gains when political developments have favoured this reactionary agenda. Indeed, the party’s key breakthrough from the margins to the mainstream came following the Bondi massacre, when anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, ultra-nationalist sentiment was at a righteous high.

A preoccupation with sugar-coating the support base of One Nation, and the assumption underlying it that One Nation supporters are uniquely disconnected from the formal politics of the party for some unexplained reason, has the effect of downplaying the importance of One Nation’s formal politics and the threat they pose. The beneficiaries of this emphasis are those, like the Labor Party, wanting to adopt elements of One Nation’s policies, whether because they have no alternative agenda to argue convincingly for, they want to chase the right-wing vote or because they recognise that many in the capitalist class approve of those policies, and that’s what matters to them. 

These forces will do anything to avoid admitting that a significant section of the population has been won over to supporting a fascist-adjacent political machine. To do so means facing up to the inherent responsibility to resist.     

So what should we do?

First, we need to acknowledge that One Nation is a reactionary blight on society. To confront it, we need to have two approaches simultaneously. The first is to build opposition to One Nation in the here and now, by being clear and firm about how reactionary the party is and by mobilising and giving confidence to those already hostile to it. The second is the longer-term project of rebuilding a strong left, tied to a powerful workers’ movement, on the scale needed to decisively set the far right back. Those arguing for pandering to One Nation supporters are working towards neither. 

Chandler-Mathers 

argues

 for a Greens program of “progressive populism”, to be presented via one-on-one conversations that don’t challenge voters’ diagnosis of the problems with the system but offer alternative policies, such as better services, welfare and wealth redistribution. He regularly cites anecdotes to endorse this approach, for instance winning a One Nation voter to the Greens by explaining their free lunches program. For him and others on the Greens’ left, this strategy is the bedrock of an ambition to electorally replace Labor. 

The unions offer a similar approach: one-on-one conversations with workers flirting with the right, focused on Hanson’s anti-worker record, with a vote for Labor as the hopeful outcome. They refuse to hold Labor responsible for attacks on the working class—even unions that have scaled back their campaigning efforts in the Victorian election still orient to it and lobby it. The VTHC 

pamphlet

 by Kaspi-Crutchett, 

Antidote: trade unionism as a vaccine against far-right politics

, argues that unions offer workers a better cultural home and identity, and that union membership correlates with voting Labor. It says a lot about the movement’s low horizons that the pamphlet makes no case for industrial struggle and power, either to win working-class demands or to build support for working-class politics.

For socialists, politics isn’t about offering a program to a passive public. It isn’t about convincing individuals to vote for what we decide is good for them. It is about winning arguments at a deeper level, to actually change people’s worldview to one of recognising working-class interests and power. And it is about building a movement that can impose that worldview on society, that can chalk up wins for workers and the oppressed, and demonstrate in practice that the left has the answers. Elections are part of that, but left electoral programs will only be truly effective as an extension of existing class power and organisation. 

If we did have a strong fighting left and union movement right now, it would be possible to make a meaningful dent in the momentum of the far right. We could have mass protests against racism, in support of migrant rights and demonstrations of solidarity between workers across racial lines. Unions could arrest the cost-of-living crisis, win higher wages for particular groups of workers and force broader social gains like price controls, interest payment freezes and more funding for services. We could extend the Palestine movement to force the government to break ties with Israel and build a powerful anti-war movement against AUKUS and the US alliance. We could stop the construction of AI data centres, force the government to build public housing and put the environment before the profits of fossil fuel companies. We could put black bans on projects connected to Rinehart, Musk or any far-right figures here or globally, and organise hospitality staff and others to ensure Hanson and her cronies can’t meet in peace anywhere, as happened in the movement against the apartheid South African Springbok tour.

This is the kind of power and momentum the left needs to strive to build. Such a movement would then open the way to arguing with reactionary layers and with workers who hold backward ideas, both by having a bigger platform from which to attack their politics and through our ability to impose ours. A serious working-class force could also pose real solutions to most grievances—not as a defensive offering in exchange for a vote, but as an alternative to dog-eat-dog capitalism. In this context, sections of the middle class, such as small business owners, can be won to a program that disciplines the big capitalists and provides welfare for all.

This also raises the question of power. If the collective organisation of workers, in bodies like workplace and strike committees, can win gains, why not maintain them as day-to-day governing bodies rather than just defensive organisations? This starts to become a challenge to the power of the capitalist class in its entirety and raises the possibility of a different type of society based on direct democratic control of society’s wealth: socialism.

We are a long way from such a movement. The long-term degeneration of the unions and the left means we lack the forces, influence and capacity to initiate the struggle that is needed, and the right far outnumbers us. It has international and domestic conditions in its favour and will remain a serious force for the medium term, whatever One Nation’s exact electoral results. History offers no blueprint for stopping the far right’s momentum, though successful anti-fascist movements contain many lessons. But we have to keep in our sights the scale of the movement and organised force needed to push it back.

We have to start somewhere. That means building among people who are horrified by One Nation and can recognise it for what it is, and drawing them together to act, organising protests and resistance, and by putting our political opposition to the far right front and centre. Our dealings with the far right should be about confronting and denouncing its politics, not excusing it through sympathy with its supporters, or nodding along when they scapegoat their migrant neighbours. 

The far right have in part been successful because they know their enemy and fight it ruthlessly. They do not focus on how misunderstood and decent left-wing people are. They detest us and everything we stand for, and use that hatred to build. We need to do the same.

Beyond organising opposition to the far right, we need to build the power and institutions of our side generally. The organised socialist movement is the force that can draw together the immediate and long-term tasks we face: that can offer staunch and principled opposition to the far right today, and that can work towards the kind of power and struggle necessary to defeat it and the entire system that breeds it.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: As Congress Debates Ending Iran War, Trump Sends a Third Aircraft Carrier
content:
CENTCOM announced on Tuesday that it had carried out more strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A third U.S. aircraft carrier with thousands of U.S. troops has arrived in the Middle East to support the Iran war, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Monday, adding to the U.S.’s arsenal in the area as President Donald Trump keeps his options open for escalating the war.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the area on Sunday, joining two other aircraft carriers, each with roughly 5,000 soldiers and dozens of fighter jets aboard, and about 20 other warships.

The carrier’s arrival comes as the U.S. continues its war on Iran with a naval blockade of Iranian ports, a sanctions campaign, and strikes. Reuters reported that the U.S. carried out a new round of airstrikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Tuesday. Iran began firing back on U.S. assets in the region in recent days after reports found earlier this month that the U.S. has been secretly attacking Qeshm for weeks, despite President Donald Trump saying at the time that “we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.”

Since then, Trump has said that the war is “militarily effectively over” and that he’s aiming to maintain “the status quo.” The status quo does still include U.S. military activity, and analysts have warned that inaction by Congress to force a withdrawal is stretching the conflict into a forever war.

Further, the arrival of the new aircraft carrier, which left its base in San Diego in September, gives Trump access to a massive amount of military might in the region that he could use at any time.

Reuters reported on Sunday that Trump has been telling allies that he may hold off on attacks if the U.S. doesn’t face new attacks from Iran or Houthi, or Ansar Allah, militants in Yemen. In public comments, he has indeed preferred to say that the war is winding down or is over.

However, Reuters, citing current and former U.S. officials, also noted that “Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear ‌to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict.”

Trump has reportedly been calling around to regional allies, like Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip ​Erdogan, apparently telling bin Salman in October that he was planning to resume intense attacks after the midterm elections. Both allies apparently asked him not to intensify strikes again.

Though the temperamental commander-in-chief may conduct a devastating campaign in Iran any time, Democrats in Congress who have pledged to end the war are dragging their feet on actually doing so. Though some progressives and Democrats have said that they plan to try to force a defunding of the war through the next government spending package, which is due December 11, others have said that they don’t want to risk a shutdown in order to end the war that killed roughly 3,500 Iranians as of July.

At the same time, lengthy deployments for U.S. soldiers on the aircraft carriers in the Middle East are overstretching the Navy, as reports have found that sailors have faced extreme hardship while on board, including a lack of food and a spike in suicidal ideation and attempts.

However, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao downplayed these concerns during his Senate confirmation hearing on Tuesday. Cao said that sailors who reported losing weight while deployed were just picky, “like my kids.” He said that the reported eight suicide attempts from the USS Abraham Lincoln earlier this year were not suicide attempts, but “eight suicide mitigations.”

Cao also displayed a complete disregard for basic facts about the costs of the war. Cao said he doesn’t know what the U.S.’s naval blockade on Iranian ports is costing daily in another line of questioning, and that Pentagon inspectors have still yet to fully assess damage to naval bases in the Middle East that were struck by Iran earlier in the war.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

title: Peoples’ Climate Summit addresses energy trade and war in Gaza
content:
At the Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya, international environmental and solidarity organizations focused their discussions on the economic links between the fossil fuel industry and military violence. On the third day of the gathering, organized as an alternative to the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), discussions centered on the destruction of livelihoods in Gaza, the role of international energy supplies and demands for a comprehensive embargo against Israel. Participants examined the extent to which climate justice also required overcoming war, occupation and military expansion.




Representatives of Energy Embargo for Palestine, the Global Sumud Flotilla, the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and various international solidarity networks were among those taking part in the event.




Destruction in Gaza as an ecological crisis




Asad Rehman of Friends of the Earth highlighted the long-term environmental consequences of the war in Gaza. He stated that the destruction of water supply and sewage systems, damage to essential infrastructure and soil contamination caused by munitions, debris and untreated wastewater had devastated livelihoods that could take decades to restore.




Rehman argued that this destruction should also be examined from the perspective of ecocide. He also raised the question of political and economic control over natural resources: “Who extracts which resources, from whom, for whose benefit and under whose authority? That is the fundamental question.”




Ana Sanchez drew a connection between Israeli military policy, international arms trade relationships and the rise of far-right movements. In her assessment, Israel benefited from diplomatic support while supplying military and security technologies to right-wing governments. She argued that an effective arms embargo must go beyond halting individual arms deals and encompass entire supply chains, including the disruption of fuel shipments.




“Solidarity means disrupting supply chains. That means a two-way embargo: neither buying nor selling. It means stopping fuel deliveries,” Sanchez explained.




She emphasized that the liberation of Palestine was not an issue separate from the climate movement. Rather, she said, the fossil fuel-based economic system, patriarchal power structures and military violence were closely interconnected. “There can be no climate justice without freedom for Palestine,” she stressed.




Criticism of oil shipments through Turkey




Celine Isimbi of Energy Embargo for Palestine addressed specific economic ties, highlighting the importance of international oil trade to Israel’s energy supply, particularly shipments from Azerbaijan. According to Isimbi, Israel obtains more than 40 percent of its crude oil requirements from Azerbaijan. The oil is transported through the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline to Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, from where it is shipped to Israel by tanker.




Isimbi stated that her organization had documented a total of 77 oil shipments along this route to Israeli ports between May 2024 and June 2026. She alleged that vessels had temporarily switched off their automatic tracking signals to conceal their actual destination ports.




Isimbi also said that Turkey’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure had confirmed that ships had provided false information to port authorities and that legal proceedings had been initiated in connection with these incidents.




The activist called for fossil fuel supplies to no longer be considered separately from their military and political uses. She argued that an energy embargo must also cover transportation routes and the companies involved.




Calls for reparations rather than development aid




Abeer Al Butmeh of the Palestinian environmental network PENGON called for reparations and the restoration of destroyed livelihoods. She argued that international development aid alone could not adequately address the political and material consequences of the destruction. She pointed out that the Palestinian population must be able to make its own decisions regarding energy supplies, water resources, land and reconstruction. “Palestinians must determine their own future and have the right to remain on their land, return to it and rebuild it,” Al Butmeh stated.




Şenol Karakaş of the Freedom for Palestine Platform also placed the war in Gaza within the context of global economic and political power structures. He criticized the support Israel receives from international capitalist and imperialist structures and emphasized that solidarity with Palestine must not be limited to individual protest campaigns. Rather, he said, the struggle for Palestinian freedom must become an integral part of movements for social emancipation worldwide. “The struggle for Palestine must not be interrupted,” Karakaş said.




Şeyma Altundal of the Thousand Youth for Palestine initiative called on the Turkish government to sever all trade relations as well as diplomatic and military ties with Israel. She criticized the continuation of economic relations despite public declarations of solidarity with Palestine. “For us, the freedom of Palestine is not a secondary issue in the climate struggle, but its political compass,” Altundal stated.




Militarism and authoritarian politics on the agenda




Later in the day, the Peoples’ Climate Summit continued its discussions under the slogan “No to Fascism – Siamo Tutti Antifascisti.” The program includes presentations on political repression in Turkey, the situation of dismissed public sector employees, the peace movement and the struggles of LGBTIQ+ organizations.




Other topics include the appointment of government trustees to opposition-run municipalities in Turkey and North Kurdistan, as well as the rise of far-right and authoritarian movements in Europe and Latin America. A commemorative event honoring women’s rights activist Margaret Papandreou is also planned.

title: Six lawyers detained in raids in Izmir
content:
Six lawyers were detained during a police operation in the western Turkish city of Izmir on Tuesday morning. Five of them are members of the Contemporary Lawyers’ Association (ÇHD). According to the organization, the lawyers were taken into custody during searches of their homes in the early morning hours.




Those detained include Veysi Çetin, secretary of the ÇHD’s Izmir branch, as well as association members Yemen Cankan, Emrah Kanbay, Göksel Akbaba and Erdoğan Akdoğdu. Lawyer Bahattin Özdemir was also detained.




According to the ÇHD, police seized electronic devices and data storage media during the house searches. Access to the investigation file has also been restricted. The detained lawyers have reportedly been unable to exercise their right to consult with legal counsel.




The ÇHD views the detentions as part of a systematic policy of repression against social opposition movements. The authorities are attempting to criminalize the practice of law and intimidate independent defense lawyers, the association’s Izmir branch stated. “This attack on the right to legal defense is nothing more than an attempt by the government to cover up the violations of the law, arbitrary practices and human rights abuses it perpetrates through the judiciary,” the statement said.




The ÇHD announced that it would provide legal support throughout the proceedings against the six detainees and continue to resist restrictions on the right to legal defense.

author: Gladys Stagno
title: Donde hay un trabajador precarizado, nace un moroso
content:
Un relevamiento provincia por provincia muestra la superposición entre precariedad laboral y endeudamiento familiar. Seis millones de personas acumulan atrasos en sus pagos y casi cuatro de cada diez jóvenes menores de 25 años están en situación de mora.




Ilustración: Marcelo Spotti




Por Gladys Stagno




En un escenario de alto endeudamiento familiar y morosidad récord, un estudio aporta un dato nuevo que surge de analizar las condiciones laborales de los endeudados.




En su último informe, el Mirador de la Actualidad del Trabajo y la Economía (MATE) realizó un mapeo de la caída del empleo formal y del aumento de la precariedad, provincia por provincia, en base a datos de la Secretaría de Trabajo, Empleo y Seguridad Social.




De igual manera, y sobre cifras del Banco Central (BCRA), el centro de investigación construyó un “mapa de la mora”, donde se evidencia en qué provincias el fenómeno se ha vuelto más grave.




Tucumán y San Juan son las dos que se encuentran al tope de ambas categorías: más del 50% de trabajadores en la informalidad, y más del 34% de personas en situación de mora. En situaciones similares se encuentran Catamarca, Corrientes, Chaco, Formosa, La Rioja, Mendoza, Misiones, Salta, San Luis y Santiago del Estero.




Una situación atípica ocurre en Santa Cruz, provincia con la menor tasa de informalidad (-30%) –junto con Neuquén– pero alta tasa de morosidad (entre el 30 y el 34%). La Pampa es la provincia con menos mora del país, con menos del 22%.




Fuente: MATE




Jóvenes y precarizados




En toda la Argentina, la deuda en mora de las familias en el sistema bancario ronda el 18%. El número crece si tenemos en cuenta a los proveedores no financieros y billeteras virtuales, donde la cifra supera el 30%, según informes recientes del Centro de Economía Política Argentina (CEPA). Se trata de los niveles más altos desde la crisis de 2001.




En cantidad de personas, se trata de cerca 6 millones de argentinos con deudas atrasadas, de un total de 20 millones de endeudados, lo que representa 1 de cada 4 en situación de mora.




Fuente: MATE




Según el Mapa de la Deuda publicado por el del Centro de Estudios para la Ciudad junto a la fundación alemana Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, la situación se agrava en los más jóvenes, donde casi 4 de cada 10 menores de 25 años registran atrasos en el pago de su deuda. Se trata también del sector poblacional más alcanzado por la informalidad laboral. De acuerdo con MATE, en el sector de 15 a 24 años la informalidad ya alcanza al 39,2%.




“La demografía de la mora y la del empleo se vinculan íntimamente: la precariedad laboral avanza sobre los jóvenes y sobre las provincias olvidadas por este modelo económico y la distribución de la mora refleja esta situación”, analiza el instituto liderado por los economistas Diego Kofman, Lavih Abraham, Marco Kofman, Natalia Pérez Barreda y Sergio Arelovich.




La informalidad crece en línea con la pérdida de empleos formales. Según el relevamiento del MATE, la economía argentina pierde más de 370 empleos formales por día.




“El sector privado ya expulsó a 265.765 trabajadores registrados: la industria y la construcción son los sectores que más puestos de trabajo destruyeron”, detallan. Por su parte, el sector público perdió 89.620 puestos, contabilizados desde diciembre de 2023. Se trata, en total, de 375.016 empleos formales menos desde la asunción de Javier Milei.




Ilustración: Marcelo Spotti

author: Chris Walker
title: Trump Says Nationwide Outages Are “Fine” as More Systems Go Down
content:
Two additional outages occurred after Trump’s comments, affecting the NSA and Apple products.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

President Donald Trump appeared to downplay the nationwide outages that have affected millions of Americans over the past week, suggesting they aren’t anything to worry about.

In remarks to reporters in the Philippines on Tuesday, Trump indicated that he had spoken to Chase executives about one of the latest outages, which affected banking services for Chase, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo. When reporters asked Trump whether he was concerned about the outages, the president said he wasn’t worried.

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful, and you have all of the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” he said.

Q: Have you spoken tothe banks regarding the outage at Chase?TRUMP: I haveQ: What are they saying?T: It's going to be very much under controlQ: Are you concerned about these outages?T: No. It's life. When you're big & powerful & have all the money, things like this happen. It's fine

Trump’s response is unlikely to calm the fears of millions of Americans, some of whom may be wondering if the outages are connected in some way. So far, there is nothing to indicate that, or that any of the outages are the result of cyberattacks.

Shortly after Trump’s comments, another outage was reported, this time affecting the National Security Agency (NSA). According to sources speaking to CNN, the agency’s internal communications system used to transmit classified information, called NSA Net, had gone down. The sources added that there was no reason to believe the outage had been caused by a cyberattack, and that it did not affect the NSA’s ability to continue informing Trump about national security matters.

Another source told The New York Times that NSA Net has been unstable for weeks.

Beyond the banks and the NSA, other outages have included problems with Microsoft products reported by users worldwide, which occurred on Thursday. Perhaps most notably, on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all domestic flights for several hours, citing communications and radar errors that were later revealed to have been caused by the replacement of a copper-wired router connection at a facility in Arkansas. Flights have yet to resume at normal operating speeds at airports across the country, with some delays and cancellations still occurring.

Later on Tuesday, thousands of users worldwide reported problems accessing Apple services, including iCloud, Apple Pay, the App Store, and Apple Support. The issue with those products was ongoing as of 2 pm Eastern Time, according to reporting from DownDetector.

title: Sebahat Tuncel: Silencing the guns is not enough; rights must be guaranteed
content:
The relationship between militarism, the climate crisis and ecological destruction was discussed during a session titled “Combating Militarism from a Climate Justice Perspective” at the Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya. The session addressed the environmental impact of military spending and armed conflicts, as well as opportunities for cooperation between the climate justice movement and antimilitarist movements.




Speaking at the session, Free Women’s Movement (TJA) activist Sebahat Tuncel highlighted the links between the climate crisis and the capitalist system, policies of exploitation, wars and repressive practices.




Tuncel stated that while government representatives at COP31 were discussing ways to maintain capitalism and the system of exploitation, the Peoples’ Climate Summit was exploring how to build an alternative way of life in opposition to these policies.




Sebahat Tuncel stated that the situation in Palestine could not be considered separately from the policies of repression and violence faced by peoples in other parts of the world. “The injustice, climate crisis, policies of war and policies of genocide we are witnessing in Palestine actually affect all peoples. Replace Palestine with Kurdistan. Similar policies are being pursued in Kurdistan as well. Think of the Alawites in Syria, or all the peoples in the Middle East who face repression because of their identity, faith or culture. Therefore, the struggle for climate justice is a struggle that concerns us all,” she said.




Emphasizing that wars cause not only loss of life but also ecological destruction, Tuncel stated that the situation in Palestine, Kurdistan and Lebanon concerned all of humanity. She said that policies of war and conflict devastated living environments and that the effects of the ecological crisis were not limited to those living in conflict zones.




‘Solidarity alone is not enough’




Sebahat Tuncel stated that policies of war erected barriers between societies and alienated peoples from one another, calling for a united struggle against these policies.




“The policy imposed on us by states is one of divide and rule. What we must do in response is unite and struggle together. Solidarity alone is not enough. We need to go beyond solidarity and build a common internationalist struggle to change and transform the male-dominated capitalist system. Only an organized society can achieve this,” Tuncel said.




Referring to the LGBTI+ movement’s slogan, “We exist, and we will continue to exist,” Tuncel stated that Kurds, women and people of different identities would also continue their struggle for existence. Describing the denial of peoples, identities and beliefs as fascism, she said that it brought with it repression, oppression, exploitation and marginalization.




‘Turkey has been turned into a giant prison’




Addressing prison policies in Turkey, Sebahat Tuncel stated that there were 16 prisons of various types in Antalya. She criticized the government for presenting the construction of new prisons as good news, describing it as a continuation of policies of repression and punishment.




Recalling the arrest of Kurdish politicians in 2009 as part of the KCK investigations, Tuncel said that those demanding rights, freedom, democracy and peace faced the threat of prosecution. Arguing that the law had been turned into a political instrument, Tuncel said, “They have turned Turkey into a giant prison.”




Tuncel argued that the isolation imposed on Abdullah Öcalan in İmralı had spread throughout Turkey and its prisons. “In fact, it has spread across the whole of Turkey and into every prison. There are not only prisons being built physically, but also prisons being constructed in our minds. We cannot achieve freedom without dismantling all these policies of isolation,” she said.




Tuncel emphasized that freedom could not be achieved without overcoming the policies of isolation, stating that freedom required a social order in which people could express their thoughts, organize and live with dignity.




Time to build positive peace




Addressing the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Sebahat Tuncel said that a struggle had been waged for many years to resolve the Kurdish question through democratic means rather than war and conflict.




Emphasizing that silencing the guns alone did not constitute peace, Tuncel stated the following:




“The state wants negative peace. It wants the guns to fall silent without granting rights to Kurds, without granting rights to women, without granting any rights to socialists, and with everyone submitting to its authority. We, on the other hand, say that we will build peace based on our rights and freedoms. Can there be peace without addressing the Kurdish question? Even if the guns fall silent today, much deeper conflicts could erupt in the future if the issue remains unresolved.




What do we want? We want equality, freedom, democracy, justice and a free future. We want to be equal and free citizens who do not have to worry about whether something will happen to us when we go out into the streets or whether we will be imprisoned for speaking our minds.




Society must have confidence in its own strength. The power lies within us; it lies within women. We must not underestimate our own strength. Whatever needs to be achieved, we can achieve it ourselves. This struggle cannot succeed through solidarity alone, but only through a common struggle.




From Palestine to Kurdistan, from Latin America to Lebanon, we will succeed if we stand together and unite our struggles in an internationalist movement for equality, freedom, justice and democracy. We will succeed. We have no other choice.”




The session also featured presentations by Karen Hallows on behalf of Peace Boat, Hala Kilani on behalf of the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom, Ellie Kinney on behalf of the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS), Deborah Burton on behalf of Tipping Point, Andrew Metheven on behalf of War Resisters’ International, Stephan Brües on behalf of the Federation for Social Defence, and Merve Arkun on behalf of Conscientious Objection Watch.




The presentations addressed the environmental impact of wars and militarist policies, ecological destruction, anti-war activism and conscientious objection, while participants from different countries shared their experiences of struggle.

title: Oil exports begin through Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline
content:
Iraq’s Ministry of Oil issued a statement announcing the resumption of oil exports through the Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline.




The statement confirmed that crude oil would be exported through the old pipeline between Iraq and Turkey, with an initial export volume of 120,000 barrels per day.




Export capacity is expected to increase gradually in the coming period, with plans to reach 500,000 barrels per day.




The ministry described the reactivation of the pipeline and the resumption of exports as a “strategic step,” stating that it would strengthen Iraq’s oil export capacity and help diversify the country’s oil export routes.




The statement emphasized that reopening this export route would provide an important source of additional revenue and support the Iraqi economy.

title: Women’s Justice and Memory Vigil in Amed: Stories of seven women shared
content:
At the “Women’s Justice and Memory Vigil” organized by the Network Against Violence outside the courthouse in Amed (tr: Diyarbakır), participants carried photographs of women who had been killed. Representatives of numerous political parties and civil society organizations attended the demonstration, chanting slogans including “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom), “Femicide is political” and “Stop protecting and exonerating perpetrators, prosecute them.”




Reading the statement on behalf of the organizers, Nermin Unat, a member of the Rosa Women’s Association, said that the stories of seven women who lost their lives in different cities between November 9 and 15 had been added to the collective memory. Unat emphasized that women who had been killed despite filing complaints and requesting protection, as well as those whose families were still seeking justice, would not be forgotten.




The women whose stories were shared this week included Pelin Pınar and Nuran Tay, who died after falling from balconies in Istanbul, Rukiye Demirel, who lost her life in Niğde, and Sema Gündüz, who died in Uşak. The stories of Aysel Sakaldaş, who was stabbed to death by her former husband in the Bayramiç district of Çanakkale; Ayşen Güneş, who was found dead in her home in the Elbistan district of Maraş; and Hanife K., who was shot dead by her husband in the Suluova district of Amasya, were also read aloud.




Speaking at the vigil, Amed Metropolitan Municipality Co-Mayor Serra Bucak said that activities organized as part of the November 25 International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women aimed to prevent further femicides.




Calling on the government to review its policies and take into account the efforts of local administrations to prevent violence against women, Bucak stated that 16 femicides had been officially recorded in Amed in 2026. She also drew attention to suspicious deaths of women, emphasizing the need to investigate these cases and hold those responsible accountable. “We will never give up demanding accountability,” Bucak said.




The vigil concluded with chants following a silent protest.

title: IRGC bans civilian access to Shaho Mountains
content:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has banned civilian access to the Shaho Mountains in Ravansar County until 21 November, citing military exercises.




Residents of several nearby villages told the Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) that the IRGC announced the ban through village councils and village heads on 15 November.




Residents were told that the IRGC’s Ansar Rasoul Commando Unit in Javanrud would conduct military exercises in the mountains until 21 November and that all civilian access to the area was prohibited.




The sources said a military convoy carrying heavy and medium-heavy equipment had been dispatched from the unit’s barracks and deployed around the mountains as the exercises were announced.




The IRGC previously banned civilian access to the area from 2 to 7 October during military exercises and artillery shelling of the Shaho Mountains.




The exercises and shelling take place in an area designated for environmental protection. The Shaho and Kusalan Mountains were granted protected status in 2009 under Resolution No. 303 of the Supreme Council for Environmental Protection and are managed by the Department of Environment.




Environmental activists say the IRGC has built several military bases in the area since 2007, under the pretext of countering the presence of forces affiliated with Kurdish opposition parties.




Military exercises and other military activities have caused fires in parts of the area’s pastures and forests, while the construction of military bases and roads has destroyed further sections despite protests, the activists say.




They add that IRGC forces deliberately set fire to vegetation and pastures around some military bases, with the stated aim of preventing Kurdish opposition forces from using the vegetation as cover to carry out attacks.

The Anarchist Network of “Vancouver Island” (“Victoria”) remembers our comrade Tasha Diamant fondly.

Tasha was a passionate ecological artist, firebrand sneaky actionist, a loving mother, rageful ecofeminist, and matriarch of the Network.

Tasha was an ardent revolutionary mother who fought against patriarchy, hierarchy, and colonization. She was a prolific organizer and consciousness raiser in “Victoria” (Lekwungen), anchoring major in-city supports and disruptions to bolster direct actions against domination in all its forms.

She also spearheaded The Human Body Project to rouse consciousness; in a misogynistic, dissociative society. She at the time did not have words for what she later understood simply as a violent culture, instead using her naked body to share and create space for vulnerability and a process of bearing witness to self participation in estrangement.

These consciousness raising efforts culminated in hundreds of street actions and performances. This work also extended itself into Humans of Fairy Creek, a theatrical series that focused on humanizing the thousands of arrestees in the struggle ignored by the self-appointed hierarchics in the Fairy Creek leadership.

While Tasha herself did not identify as an anarchist, (preferring the label ‘ecofeminist’) she was most often aligned with anti-patriarchal, anti-capitalist, and anti-hierarchical modes of organizing.

Tasha started FreeSkool Victoria in 2022, was involved in the ‘Victoria’ Anarchist Bookfair Collective in 2023, and supporting the People’s Park Palestine liberation encampment on the University of Victoria quad in 2025 through an “Elders” affinity group she started.

Upon connecting with anarchist youths (note from some youths: we playfully called ourselves “strays”) here, she explained:

“This whole time, in my whole life, no one told me the Anarchists were always there. I wish I’d found you all sooner.” When Tasha learned about the anarchist Mujeres Libres (Free Women) of the Spanish Revolution, she lamented she “would’ve surely joined and stood with them.”

Tasha also understood the privatized Victorian city as a collection of open canvasses that ‘ought to be reclaimed from “fuckers,” painting sanctioned murals and unsanctioned guerrilla artworks around the city. She was also a talented and seamless acquirer and redistributor of various goods to poor folks.

Tasha volunteered with William Head on Stage (WHoS, the only prison theatre company in ‘Canada’) for a number of years. She was blacklisted from volunteering at William Head Institution when the administration decided they did not approve of her friendships with incarcerated artists, as well as conducting The Human Body Project outside the prison, after arbitrary and misogynistic police interventions in street demos. Her shortfilm Handcuffed (2020) documents one of these interactions.

Tasha was an underappreciated innovator. She was our sage. She was our comrade. She was often angry. Tasha paved the way for us: one can direct their anger for liberation. We loved her in this anger. She believed (as do we) that her cancer was a result of the daily assault of patriarchal warfare on our bodies and psyches.

We remember you. We carry your torch Tasha.

Tasha’s blog remains up on humanbodyproject.org

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Gull-Masty, Obed to announce new approach to support Inuit children
content:
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami president Natan Obed are set to announce “a new approach to supporting Inuit children,” according to a media advisory from the minister’s department.




The announcement is scheduled for 10:45 a.m. Wednesday at the National Press Theatre in Ottawa.




It will follow a $575-million, five-year funding commitment for the Inuit Child First Initiative in Budget 2026, which was $25 million short of the $600 million ITK requested in its pre-budget submission.







The funding will support the transition to Pirutsiagutiit, a new program that was developed with ITK and the four Inuit treaty organizations.




The program, expected to launch Apr. 1, 2027, 

will transfer responsibilities from Indigenous Services Canada to the treaty organizations or their designates.




The Inuit Child First Initiative provides health, social, educational and other supports to Inuit children and youth. Launched in September 2018, it operates alongside Jordan’s Principle, which provides similar supports to First Nations children.




The program’s future had been uncertain as its funding approached its scheduled end in March 2025. Ottawa extended funding through a one-year commitment while it worked on a replacement.
















In November 2025, Gull-Masty told Nunatsiaq News the initiative would be retooled and made permanent but did not provide a timeline.

title: Milli Savunma Bakanlığı bütçesinde silahlanmada yüzde 229 artış: Askeri sanayi şirketlerinde kârları patlatmaya devam
content:
Dicle Sezen Öz [email protected]

Milli Savunma Bakanlığının (MSB) 2027 bütçesine ilişkin görüşmeler bugün TBMM Plan ve Bütçe Komisyonunda başlıyor. MSB’nin yeni bütçesi, Ankara’da yapılan NATO zirvesinde alınan kararlar, Suudi Arabistan ve Pakistan ile 10 yıl süreyle bağlayıcı olacak şekilde imzalanan Mekke Anlaşması ve Türkiye’nin başta cihatçı HTŞ yönetimindeki Suriye olmak üzere Ortadoğu ve Afrika’da askeri varlığını büyüttüğü bir dönemde görüşülecek.

AKP iktidarı ve askeri sanayi şirketleri yeni siparişler için kapı kapı gezerken, bütçe teklifinde öne çıkan başlık ‘savunma’ ve güvenlik harcamalarındaki rekor artış oldu. Cumhurbaşkanı Yardımcısı Cevdet Yılmaz’ın da bütçe sunumunda belirttiği üzere silah ve mühimmat alımına ayrılan ödenek yüzde 229 oranında artırılıyor.

2026 yılında 822.9 milyar TL olan MSB bütçesi, 2027 teklifinde yüzde 86.2’lik artışla 1 trilyon 532.6 milyar liraya çıkarılıyor. Bu artışın 573.9 milyar lirası mal ve hizmet alımlarından kaynaklanıyor. Bu kalem yüzde 158.2 artışla 936.6 milyar liraya çıkıyor. Yani 2027 bütçesindeki her 100 liranın 61 lirası bu mal ve hizmetlere yani ‘silah ve mühimmata’ gidecek.

Savaş harcamalarındaki artış Savunma Sanayii Destekleme Fonu (SSDF) ve iç güvenlik birimlerini de kapsayan güvenlik bütçesinde de görülüyor. Söz konusu iki kalemin 2.15 trilyon liradan 3.45 trilyon liraya yükselerek merkezi yönetim bütçesinin yüzde 12.7’sine denk gelmesi bekleniyor. Bu toplam içinde doğrudan ‘savunmaya’ ayrılan pay ise yüzde 83.5 artışla 2.2 trilyon liraya çıkacak.

Aselsan, Roketsan, Tusaş, MKE ve Baykar gibi askeri sanayi şirketlerine akan para, genel bütçe dışında tutulan ve Merkez Bankası nezdinde yönetilen SSDF üzerinden sağlanıyor. Teklifin 10. maddesi, silah alımları ve NATO altyapı yatırımlarında bütçe ödenekleriyle birlikte SSDF kaynaklarının da kullanılmasına imkan tanıyor.

Halktan toplanan vergilerin nasıl şirket kasalarına aktığı Sayıştayın son denetim raporlarıyla da belgeleniyor. Sayıştay verilerine göre SSDF’nin geliri 2025’te yüzde 73.8 artışla 374.5 milyar liraya; bu paranın yüzde 99’unun harcandığı ve çoğunluğu silahlara giden mal ve hizmet alım gideri ise 275.2 milyar liraya çıktı.

Bütçenin diğer yüzünde ise iktidarla kol kola olan askeri sanayi şirketlerinin hızla büyüyen kârları var.

Aselsan’ın 2026 yılının ilk dokuz ayındaki net kârı, geçen yılın aynı dönemine göre yüzde 75.1 artarak 15.1 milyar liradan 26.5 milyar liraya kadar yükseldi. Şirketin aynı dönemdeki 151.5 milyar liralık toplam gelirinin yüzde 42’sine denk gelen 63.9 milyar liralık kısmı doğrudan Savunma Sanayii Başkanlığına yapılan satışlardan elde edildi ve elindeki bekleyen sipariş tutarı 30.7 milyar dolara ulaştı.

Baykar 2025 için 2,5 milyar dolar gelir açıklarken, Tusaş’ın üretimden satışları 140.9 milyar lirayı buldu.

Bunlar yalnızca öne çıkan şirketlerin birkaçı. Savunma Sanayii Başkanı Haluk Görgün, geçtiğimiz ay Bursa’da katıldığı bir çalıştayda yıl başından bu yana askeri sanayide 15 milyar dolarlık yeni sözleşme imzalandığını söyledi. Görgün, Aselsan, Roketsan, Tusaş, Havelsan ve STM’nin yurt içindeki alt yüklenicilerine verdiği ve henüz tamamlanmamış siparişlerin tutarının da 13.4 milyar doları aştığını açıkladı.

MSB’ye bütçeden ayrılan bu payın bu denli büyümesinin bir sebebi hiç şüphesiz iktidarın yıl boyu altına imzasını attığı uluslararası anlaşmalar. Son bir yılda askeri sanayi hem yeni iç siparişlerle hem de yeni anlaşmalar ve dış satışlarla yeni pazarlara açıldı. Geçen yılki komisyon görüşmesiyle aynı gün imzalanan 6.5 milyar dolarlık hava savunma paketini, bu yıl ekim ayında Aselsan ile imzalanan 2,46 milyar avroluk hava savunma sözleşmeleri ve mayıs ayında Tusaş ile bağlanan yurt içi Kaan savaş uçağı tedarik anlaşması izledi.

Türkiye, ekim 2025’te Birleşik Krallık’tan 20 Eurofighter savaş uçağı almak için 8 milyar sterline varan bir anlaşmaya imza attı. Mart 2026’da imzalanan eğitim ve destek sözleşmesiyle de BAE Systems ve Rolls-Royce dahil Britanyalı şirketlere iş alanı açıldı. Öte yandan Katar’dan ikinci el Eurofighter alımı için görüşmelerini sürdüren MSB, ekimde Doha’dan satış sözleşmesi taslağını beklediğini bildirdi.

Türkiye’deki askeri sanayi patronlarının bir gözü de dışarıya satışlarda. Bu kapsamda Tusaş, İspanya’nın Airbus liderliğindeki eğitim programı için 30 adet Hürjet, Azerbaycan için ise 14 adet Hürkuş-II üretecek. Türkiye ayrıca Romanya’ya bir adet Hisar sınıfı korvet ve destek paketi satışı için 223 milyon avroluk sözleşme imzaladı.

Aynı süreçte Yemen’in büyük çoğunluğunu kontrol eden Ensarullah hareketine saldırılar düzenleyen Suudi Arabistan ve Pakistan’la imzalanan Mekke Anlaşması, Katar’la geçtiğimiz günlerde yapılan ortak ‘savunma’ mutabakatı, yine Katar, Pakistan ve Endonezya ile Bedir Anlaşması imzalandı.

Bu bütçenin arkasında elbette NATO’ya verilen harcama taahhütleri de var. NATO’nun 2025 Lahey zirvesi’nde üyeler 2035’e kadar milli gelirin en az yüzde 3.5’ini doğrudan savunmaya, yüzde 1.5’ini ise savunma altyapısı ve sanayiye ayırma kararı almıştı. NATO’ya verilen bu söz bütçeye de doğrudan yansıdı.

2027 bütçe gerekçesi Türkiye’nin askeri harcamalarının milli gelire oranını 2026 için yüzde 2.33 olarak tahmin ediyor. İktidar bu oranı 2027’de yüzde 2.85’e, 2028’de yüzde 3.41’e, 2029’da yüzde 3.5’e çıkarmayı hedefliyor.

Türkiye, ayrıca NATO’nun karargah ve altyapı yatırımları için de para ödüyor. Burada ülkenin verdiği pay 2025’te yüzde 4.59 iken bu yıl başından itibaren yüzde 6.3’e çıktı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Fon soruşturmasında ifade veren AKP'li Tayyar: Tera suç örgütünün kumpasıyla karşı karşıyayım
content:
Eski AKP Milletvekili Şamil Tayyar fon vurgunu soruşturması kapsamında "şüpheli" sıfatıyla İstanbul Adliyesi'nde ifade verdi. Tayyar "Alçakça iftira atan Tera suç örgütü yöneticilerinin, fon vurgunuyla mücadelemi akamete uğratmak ve sesimi kısmak için kurguladıkları kumpasın tüm detaylarını yarın yazacağım" dedi.

İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığının yürüttüğü soruşturma kapsamında Çağlayan'daki İstanbul Adliyesi'nde yaklaşık 1.5 saat ifade veren Tayyar, adliye önünde basın mensuplarına açıklama yaparak "Tera suç örgütünün bir kumpasıyla karşı karşıya kaldığımı öğrendim. Onların akıl almaz bazı iddiaları vardı. Savcı Bey de o soruları yöneltti, cevabımızı verdik" dedi.

Tayyar, "Hayatımda görmediğim, tanımadığım, bilmediğim, canlı olarak bile görmediğim, telefonla dahi konuşmadığım insanların benimle ilgili akla hayale gelmeyen çirkin iddiaları. Anlaşılan o ki benim bu fon vurguncularıyla mücadele azmimi kırmak, sesimi kısmak ve bu mücadele sürecini akamete uğratmak için bir kumpas hazırladıklarını görüyorum. Ağır bir iftira ile karşı karşıyayım" ifadelerini kullandı.

Tayyar daha sonra sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı paylaşımda şunları söyledi: "Çağlayan Adliyesi’nden az önce ayrıldım. Tera suç örgütünün kumpasına ilişkin ifademi verdim. Ankara yolundayım. Hayatımda görmediğim, tanımadığım, telefonla dahi görüşmediğim, adlarını operasyonla birlikte ilk kez duyduğum, hiçbir dönemde övücü paylaşımım olmadığı halde alçakça iftira atan Tera suç örgütü yöneticilerinin, fon vurgunuyla mücadelemi akamete uğratmak ve sesimi kısmak için kurguladıkları kumpasın tüm detaylarını yarın yazacağım. Fon mücadelesine omuz veren herkesten istirhamım, asla geri adım atmayın. Bu şeref yoksunları gün yüzü görmesinler. Uzantıları da hesap vermekten kurtulamasınlar."

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Mullin Took Government Plane to Football Game Amid Mass Flight Cancellations
content:
The DHS secretary defended the trip, in which he attended the game in a box with a major DHS contractor.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

As thousands upon thousands of travelers cancelled plans or were stranded at the airport due to the lingering effects of the ground stop on Saturday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took a trip on a government jet to Louisiana to attend a college football game in a private box with a major contractor for his agency.

The New York Post first reported on Tuesday that Mullin took a government plane to attend the Louisiana State University (LSU) home game against University of Texas on Saturday. This was just a day after the Trump administration issued an hours-long nationwide ground stop that affected an estimated 1.5 million travellers, with over 9,200 flights cancelled.

Though Mullin made it to the game, issues for regular travelers persisted on Saturday. Data shows that nearly 6,700 flights on Saturday were cancelled, and over 9,100 delayed, according to FlightAware.

Once at the game, the Post reported, Mullin was hosted in the private box of Ben Bordelon, a major GOP donor and CEO for Louisiana-based Bollinger Shipyards. The company is a major Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contractor; just in July, the department announced it had awarded Bollinger Shipyards with a $2.2 billion contract to construct polar icebreakers for the Coast Guard.

Mullin seemingly confirmed the reporting in an interview with CNBC on Tuesday in which he defended his trip.

He said that he’s required to fly in a government plane and would have “never went if the … airways weren’t completely open, they’[d] been completely open for 21 hours,” even though the ground stop was still having effects at the time, and its cause is still being investigated.

“We’ve still gotta live life, at the same time, we’ve still got family, friends, but we also have work we do every day,” Mullin said.

He also tried to defend the box seats with Bordelon, saying that it was House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) who arranged the tickets for him. OpenSecrets shows that Bordelon has given tens of thousands of dollars to Scalise’s PAC in recent years, as well as numerous other GOP fundraising groups.

“There was never a connection, or never business spoke[n] about that while I was there,” he said of Bordelon. “And like I said, Steve Scalise was who helped me get the tickets.”

The DHS secretary said that he has to pay the government back for the travel and will also pay “fair market value” for the box seats, though it’s unclear to whom those payments would be given.

Mullin’s trip is just one of numerous flight-related scandals in the Trump administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was also recently reported to be using a government jet on a regular basis to attend football games at the University of Florida, as well as for personal trips, with a large security apparatus there to accompany him. The Washington Post noted in that report that officials do reimburse the government for the travel, but at a fraction of the actual cost.

Earlier this year, the Post also reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was using a military jet for trips around the country as he was doing campaign stops for Republican midterm candidates.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign.
