author: Clare Hymer
title: New UK Sanctions on Israeli Groups Will Have No Material Impact, Critics Say
content:
Foreign secretary Ed Miliband has announced UK sanctions against Israeli firms involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, as well as an activist group that blocks aid from entering Gaza.




But the Israeli authorities driving settlement expansion and the denial of aid have not been targeted in the new measures, critics noted.




The 

government said the measures

 against eight construction and property development firms would “disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support further construction in the West Bank”. 




It said that the Tsav 9 group, which has blocked aid crossings into Gaza and set trucks on fire, would also be subject to an asset freeze and ban on its members becoming directors of UK companies. 




Miliband said those who obstruct aid “must be prepared to face the consequences”.




But human rights groups said the sanctions were inadequate and did not target the primary cause of the violations: the Israeli government. 




“Sanctioning a handful of firms involved in illegal settlements is a fraction of what is needed – and targeting one activist group, rather than the Israeli authorities who continue to mastermind the denial of aid to Gaza, is not a serious response to a genocide,” said Kristyan Benedict, Amnesty International UK’s crisis response manager.




Benedict also noted that the 

US already sanctioned Tsav 9 in June 2024, adding that the UK was just “playing catch-up”. 

While the new measures were “a step in the right direction”, they fell “far short of the action international law demands”, he said.




“The UK must impose trade sanctions banning all services, investment and financial assistance linked to Israel’s unlawful occupation, impose targeted sanctions against Israeli officials most implicated in crimes against Palestinians – and ban, with immediate effect, all arms transfers to Israel.”




Huda Ammori, co-founder of banned direct action group Palestine Action, said Miliband was “sanctioning Israeli companies with little to no presence in Britain”, and so it would have “no material impact”. 




“He isn’t sanctioning JCB, 

a British firm

 which destroys Palestinian homes and builds illegal settlements, 

or Elbit [Systems]

, which makes weapons used to enforce the occupation,” she added.




Thomas Bell, acting UK director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The UK should take immediate steps to hold Israeli officials responsible for violations of international law by suspending arms transfers to Israel, suspending the UK-Israel Trade and Partnership Agreement,” and by supporting International Criminal Court cases against Israeli officials.   




The UK’s announcement comes just days before the deadline for tender for the construction of thousands of housing units in the E1 project, which threatens to cut East Jerusalem off from the rest of the West Bank and thereby make a contiguous Palestinian state impossible. 




Miliband said: “My message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.”

author: Mag
title: Klimagipfel der Völker in Antalya zur UN-Klimakonferenz COP31 fordert gemeinsame – soziale – Front gegen ökologische Zerstörung
content:
„

Beim Klimagipfel der Völker in Antalya diskutieren internationale Bewegungen über Naturrechte, Klimagerechtigkeit und Widerstand gegen ökologische Zerstörung. Zum Auftakt wurde auch eine Verbindung zwischen Friedenspolitik und Umweltschutz gefordert.  Als Gegenveranstaltung zur UN-Klimakonferenz COP31 hat am Sonntag im Mimar-Sinan-Kongresszentrum in Antalya der Klimagipfel der Völker begonnen. Bis zum 18. November beraten dort Ökologiebewegungen, Menschenrechtsaktivist:innen und Vertreter:innen gesellschaftlicher Initiativen aus verschiedenen Ländern über gemeinsame Strategien gegen die Klimakrise und die fortschreitende Zerstörung natürlicher Lebensgrundlagen

…“ 

ANF-Meldung vom 15 November 2026

 

 mit Fotos – siehe mehr Informationen:







Klimagipfel der Völker ruft zu gemeinsamem Widerstand gegen Autoritarismus auf




„

Beim Klimagipfel der Völker in Antalya diskutierten Aktivist:innen über politische Repression, akademische Freiheit und autoritäre Entwicklungen. Die Teilnehmenden forderten eine gemeinsame demokratische Gegenbewegung. Der Kampf gegen die Klimakrise lässt sich nicht von der Verteidigung demokratischer Rechte und Freiheiten trennen. Diese Verbindung stand am dritten Tag des Klimagipfels der Völker in Antalya im Mittelpunkt einer Diskussionsveranstaltung über autoritäre Politik, staatliche Repression und gesellschaftlichen Widerstand. Unter dem Motto „Nein zum Faschismus – Siamo Tutti Antifascisti“ tauschten sich Vertreter:innen verschiedener sozialer Bewegungen über ihre Erfahrungen aus und riefen zu einem gemeinsamen Vorgehen gegen die zunehmende Einschränkung demokratischer Handlungsspielräume auf.




Die Veranstaltung fand im Rahmen des alternativen Gipfels zur UN-Klimakonferenz COP31 statt

… 

Bericht von 17. November 2026 bei ANF

 




Alternativer Raum für die Zivilgesellschaft




„

Parallel zu den UN-Verhandlungen findet in Antalya der Peoples’ Climate Summit statt. Ein Volkstribunal verurteilt die Umweltzerstörer. (…) Dieser »Klimagipfel der Völker« versteht sich als internationalistisches Treffen mit der zentralen Forderung, eine basisdemokratische Alternative zum Kapitalismus aufzubauen. Diskutiert wird zur ökologischen Zerstörung, Demokratie, Frieden und zivilgesellschaftlichen Alternativen. Eine starke Kritik am Neoliberalismus und an einer Finanzpolitik, die Kriegen den Vorrang vor Sozialausgaben gibt, durchzieht das Programm. Vertreten sind hier mehr als 130 Organisationen aus rund 30 Ländern, aus Westeuropa unter anderem Oxfam, Medico international, die Rosa-Luxemburg-Stiftung, aber auch viele kleinere Initiativen

…“ 

Artikel von Kio Weck & Aljoscha Hartmann, Antalya, vom 17.11.2026 in ND online

 




COP 31: Die Ausgeschlossenen ergreifen das Wort




„

Weltklimakonferenz in Antalya: Großdemonstration und Gegengipfel von Umweltschützern, Oppositionellen und Gewerkschaftern




Während die UN-Klimakonferenz COP 31 am Sonntag eine eintägige Pause einlegte, erhoben im türkischen Antalya am Wochenende diejenigen ihre Stimme, die vom diplomatischen Theater der Mächtigen ausgeschlossen sind: Betroffene der Klimakrise, Umweltschützer, Vertreter widerständiger lokaler Gemeinschaften aus aller Welt, die Arbeiter- und Gewerkschaftsbewegung sowie Oppositionsparteien aus der Türkei.




Nach unterschiedlichen Angaben beteiligten sich zwischen 5.000 und 10.000 Menschen am Sonnabend an einem Protestmarsch unter dem Motto »Wir verteidigen das Leben« gegen die seit dem 9. November auf dem Expogelände der Mittelmeerstadt laufende COP 31. Das federführende Bündnis »Kräfte Antalyas für Arbeit und Demokratie« kritisierte, dass auf der UN-Konferenz vorwiegend Regierungsvertreter sowie Repräsentanten der fossilen Energiewirtschaft und anderer Großkonzerne zusammenkämen. Die Klimakrise sei eine »Klassenfrage«, deren Lösung nicht in der Ersetzung fossilen durch »grünes« Kapital, sondern in einer demokratischen Planung von Produktion und Ressourcenverwendung liege. »Klimagerechtigkeit wird nicht durch die Gnade des Kapitals, sondern durch den Kampf der Völker errungen«, hieß es in der gemeinsamen Erklärung. (…)




Während Aktivisten lokaler Kämpfe aus verschiedenen Regionen der Türkei am Sonntag in Antalya erneut auf die Straße gingen, begann im dortigen Kongresszentrum ein fünftägiger »Gipfel der Völker«, zu dem sich mehr als 2.000 Teilnehmer angemeldet hatten. 

Dort stellten am Sonntag auch drei Gewerkschaften eine gemeinsame Erklärung vor: DİSK Basın-İş aus dem Presse- und Druckgewerbe, Tümka-İş aus der Papier- und Zellstoffindustrie sowie Dev ­Yapı-İş aus dem Baugewerbe forderten, die Kosten der »grünen« und digitalen Transformation nicht auf die arbeitende Bevölkerung abzuwälzen und Gewerkschaften an allen Entscheidungen über den Umbau der Wirtschaft zu beteiligen. Ihre programmatische Botschaft lautete: »Wenn es nicht sicher ist, ist es nicht ›grün‹. Wenn es keine soziale Sicherheit gibt, ist es nicht gerecht. Ohne Arbeiter gibt es keinen Übergang.«

“ 

Artikel von Nick Brauns in der jungen Welt vom 16.11.2026

 

, siehe







Die DİSK erhebt in Antalya anlässlich der #COP31 die Stimme der türkischen Arbeiterklasse!




„

Die DİSK hat ihre Vorschläge für eine Sozialpolitik im Rahmen eines gerechten Übergangs auf einer Pressekonferenz in Antalya, dem Austragungsort des #COP31-Gipfels, vorgestellt.  (…) Auch Gewerkschafter aus ITUC- und ETUC-Mitgliedsgewerkschaften aus verschiedenen Ländern der Welt waren dabei. Bei der Pressekonferenz, zu der wir Gäste aus 23 Ländern empfingen, hielten Oliver Carriere, Generalsekretär der Fédération des travailleurs du Québec (FTQ), und Rhoda Boateng, Koordinatorin des ITUC-Afrika-Programms für Klimawandel, gerechten Übergang sowie Gesundheit und Sicherheit am Arbeitsplatz, Reden

…“ türk. 

Meldung vom 10. November 2026 mit Fotos

 










Klimakonferenz in Antalya: Laut werden fürs Klima, laut werden gegen die Regierung




„

Umweltgruppen, Gewerkschaften und linke Parteien bringen in Antalya Tausende auf die Straße – zu einer riesigen regierungskritischen Demo.


Die Sorgen im Vorfeld waren groß: Würden die Behörden die Demonstration zum Alternativgipfel der UN-Klimakonferenz COP31 verbieten? Würde die Polizei die Demo gleich auflösen und in gewohnter Härte einschreiten? Würden überhaupt genügend Leute kommen, um ein deutliches Zeichen zu setzen? Am Ende erwiesen sich alle Befürchtungen als grundlos. Zum Auftakt des Alternativgipfels der Zivilgesellschaft zogen Tausende durch das Zentrum von Antalya. Die Veranstalter sprachen von mehr als 10.000 Teilnehmern, die Polizei bestätigte immerhin 7.000 Teilnehmer. Damit erlebte die Türkei eine ihrer größten regierungskritischen Demonstrationen seit Jahren

…“ 

Artikel von Jürgen Gottschlich vom 15.11.2026 in der taz online

 




Türkei: Tausende protestieren am Rande der COP31 in Antalya




„

Die Weltklimakonferenz in der Türkei bietet auch eine seltene Gelegenheit für Kritik am Staatsapparat. Tausende Menschen gehen auf die Straße – auch mit Regenbogenflaggen oder als Eisbär verkleidet. (…)


Die Demonstration war gleichzeitig der Auftakt des sogenannten Gipfels der Völker. Nichtregierungsorganisationen, Klimaaktivisten und andere Vertreter der Zivilgesellschaft veranstalten den „People’s Climate Summit“ bis Mittwoch parallel zur COP31 in Antalya. Dort soll es um die Themen Umweltzerstörung, den Ausstieg aus fossilen Energien und um Demokratie gehen.




Vertreter von Gewerkschaften und der Opposition in Antalya




Beim Protestzug waren neben internationalen Organisationen auch zahlreiche türkische Vereine, Gewerkschaften und Oppositionsparteien vertreten, die die seltene Gelegenheit nutzten, um auf die Situation im Land aufmerksam zu machen. In der Türkei werden vor allem regierungskritische Versammlungen immer wieder verboten. Zuletzt hatten die Behörden beim NATO-Gipfel im Juli in der Hauptstadt Ankara ein umfassendes Demonstrationsverbot verhängt. Hunderte Menschen waren bereits im Vorfeld festgenommen worden

…“ 

Bericht vom 15.11.2026 in DW

 

 mit einigen Fotos




Video: „Klimagipfel der Völker“ als Gegenveranstaltung zur COP31




Video vom 14.11.2026 auf tagesschau.de

 

 




Massendemonstration gegen die COP31 in Antalya: „Kampf gegen die Ausbeutung der Städte und der Natur“




„

Auf Aufruf der „Kräfte für Arbeit und Demokratie in Antalya“ wurde gegen den derzeit in der Stadt stattfindenden COP31-Gipfel mit einem Marsch und einer Kundgebung protestiert. In einer Presseerklärung auf dem Cumhuriyet-Platz hieß es: „Die Lösung der Klimakrise liegt in der demokratischen Planung von Produktion und Ressourcen. Es geht nicht nur darum, fossiles Kapital durch grünes Kapital zu ersetzen, sondern darum, für wen, von wem und zum Nutzen von wem die Energiesysteme umgestaltet werden. Unsere Forderung nach Klimagerechtigkeit richtet sich gegen die Tatsache, dass die Kosten der Umstellung auf die Arbeiterschaft und die Bevölkerung abgewälzt werden, während die Gewinne dem Kapital zugutekommen

.“…“ türk. 

Bericht vom 14. November 2026 in Sendika.org

 







Siehe zuletzt das Dossier zu 

Mesoamerikanische Karawane für Klima und Leben durch 9 Länder zu „Cumbre de los Pueblos“ gegen die COP30 in Belém, Brasilien




Der Beitrag 

Klimagipfel der Völker in Antalya zur UN-Klimakonferenz COP31 fordert gemeinsame – soziale – Front gegen ökologische Zerstörung

 erschien zuerst auf 

LabourNet Germany

.

author: Unknown
title: World of Hurt: Abolitionist Reflections on the Root Causes of Harm
content:
What causes people to harm others? Reactionaries label certain individuals—or, worse, entire demographics—inherently harmful to justify their own efforts to inflict harm via vigilante attacks, policing, and the court system. Others suggest that experiencing harm can lead some to harm others, as suggested by the common catchphrase “Hurt people hurt people.” Here, we examine this popular notion and propose a more useful framework for understanding the root causes of harm.




Today, a ruling class headed by billionaires and aspiring autocrats is making 

the celebration of violence

 central to their narratives and policies, openly campaigning against empathy itself. In this context, the question of what causes harm—and how to interrupt it without reinforcing cycles of hurt and oppression—has become increasingly urgent.







World of Hurt




Abolitionists

 who envision a world without 

police

 or 

prisons

 often face questions about how to address serious forms of interpersonal harm. 

Mutual aid

 and resource redistribution may reduce behaviors that arise as a consequence of lack of access to basic needs. But how can we understand those who seem to hurt others out of cruelty or disregard? If we don’t accept the idea that some people are monsters who must be locked up to keep the rest of us safe, how can we make sense of their actions?




Defenders of the criminal legal system frequently cite rape and abuse to justify prisons and imprisonment. In response, abolitionists have devoted considerable energy to developing 

alternative approaches

 to addressing sexual violence. Groups such as Generation Five have proposed 

principles for responding to child sexual abuse

 through transformative justice frameworks. By focusing on one of the most stigmatized forms of harm, they aim to cut to the root of 

carceral thinking

 in order to reimagine safety and justice.




But creative responses beyond the state are not enough. To end sexual violence, we also need to understand its root causes.




Feminist activists coined the term “

rape culture

” to describe how social norms and institutions enable sexual harm. In addition to these structural effects of gender and power, others argue that past experiences of harm shape the behavior of individuals who go on to harm others. One of the most common ways to articulate this principle appears in the phrase “

Hurt people hurt people

.”




Let’s take a closer look to see where this popular saying came from, how it is used, and its implications for an abolitionist understanding of harm.













The Trajectory of a Slogan




From 

self-help books

 and 

therapist blogs

 to the 

writings of abolitionist activists

, “hurt people hurt people” has become an influential account of the psychology of violence. It suggests that some people harm others not because they are pathological monsters, but because they too are victims whose unresolved trauma shapes their hurtful actions.




The precise origins of the phrase are opaque, but it has been in circulation 

at least since the 1950s

. It seems to have begun trending in the 1990s in therapeutic and pop psychology circles. A popular 1993 Christian self-help book titled 

Hurt People Hurt People

 promised to support readers in healing from painful past relationships “with empathy and biblical insight.” In recent years, this phrase has been repeated by everyone from megachurch pastor Rick Warren to Hollywood actor Andrew Garfield to the stripper con artist character Destiny in the movie 

Hustlers

 to 

the metal band Mudvayne

. It appears most widely in discourse about therapy, self-help, trauma, and religion.




On the surface, “hurt people hurt people” might seem an odd slogan for radical critics of the 

prison industrial complex

. As a maxim of folk wisdom that spans mainstream, religious, feminist, and radical circles, we should consider carefully whether it aligns with our values.




In some ways, it makes sense that abolitionists would find this formulation promising. It humanizes people who cause harm, whereas dehumanizing them paves the way for carceral responses. It attributes the roots of harmful behavior not to inherent depravity, but to contingent circumstances that can be changed. It resonates with the lived experiences of some people who are struggling to heal and to be accountable for hurting others. It seems to offer a hopeful pathway towards a world without sexual violence by intervening in support of those who have been harmed in order to interrupt the cycle.




This compassionate approach to rethinking the causes of violence has inspired abolitionist activists such as 

Mariame Kaba

. In her book 

We Do This ’Til We Free Us: Abolitionist Organizing and Transforming Justice

, she discusses transformative justice alternatives to criminal punishment. Following an instance of harm, she writes, we should first center the immediate needs of a survivor. Next, however, she argues that







We would also focus on the person responsible for the harm—but without disregarding their humanity. This means we have to acknowledge the reality that often it is hurt people who hurt other people. Understanding that harm originates from situations dominated by stress, scarcity, and oppression, one way to prevent violence is to make sure that people have support to get the things they need.







Kaba considers both power structures and individual psychology in responding to violence. Her book proposes a pathway toward the prevention of harm through community support and trauma resolution rather than punishment.




Other abolitionist writers and activists have taken up the phrase. In a chapter on “Healing as Abolitionist Practice,” the authors of 

Thinking Like an Abolitionist to End Sexual Violence in Higher Education

 recount the story of a person who was sexually assaulted by a friend who was himself a survivor of child sexual abuse.




“In reflecting on her trauma,” the authors explain, the young woman interpreted the experience through the lens of “‘hurt people hurt people’—a concept that rings true for her own experiences as someone who has harmed as well.” Having both experienced and caused harm in intimate relationships herself, she decided to turn away from carceral responses. Instead, she pursued a pathway to accountability with the person who had harmed her, intending not to punish him but to reduce the likelihood that he would harm others in the future. The authors cited this framework in their discussions about abolition and sexual violence on college campuses.




Yet despite these positive examples, “hurt people hurt people” poses problems that should prompt abolitionists to reconsider using it. The slogan risks reinforcing victim-blaming and misunderstanding the root causes of harm. Let’s dig deeper and look for an alternative framework to recognize pathways to change while more accurately analyzing the origins of sexual violence.













The Problem with “Hurt People Hurt People”




What’s wrong with the idea that “hurt people hurt people”?




Consider: in general, which people experience the most harm in our society? 

Oppressed people

. Who is primarily responsible for that harm? 

Their oppressors

.




Of course, we know that oppressed people hurt others in many ways. But Black people are not responsible for anti-Black racism; white people, and sometimes other non-Black people, are. Trans people are not responsible for transphobia; cis people are. Posing “hurt people hurt people” as a totalizing explanation risks misrepresenting the root causes of harm and misattributing responsibility for it.




Yes, oppressors themselves have often been hurt in various ways, and are sometimes oppressed along other axes. For instance, white women often perpetuate racial oppression while experiencing gender oppression. There are countless such examples.




But is that what 

leads them

 to hurt others? If so, this framework seems to imply that as we go upwards in 

the pyramid of social power

, to levels where people are less and less oppressed, we should find people who hurt others less and less.




In fact, the opposite is true. To name a single example, Donald Trump’s widely exercised capacity to hurt others exceeds that of almost anyone in human history. However much he may have been hurt by others himself, the harm he causes stems directly from the sense of entitlement that his wealth, whiteness, maleness, US citizenship, and other aspects of privilege have bestowed upon him.




Perhaps, then, we need a more expansive sense of what it means to be “hurt.” From a certain perspective, 

white people are harmed by white supremacy

, which leaves them disconnected from ancestral cultures and land, with a truncated humanity and an inability to relate across lines of difference. Of course, they are hurt by white supremacy differently and far 

less

 severely than non-white people are. Likewise, 

men suffer under patriarchy

—experiencing rigidity, emotional disconnection, shorter lifespans, and greater likelihood of dying in battle—though certainly far 

less

 than women and trans men do. Can the “hurts” that privileged people experience account for their harmful actions?




It’s both accurate and politically strategic to emphasize the stake that 

all

 people have in dismantling systems of oppression, regardless of whether they are privileged or oppressed. If patriarchy is genuinely 

good for men

, if white supremacy is 

in the interest of white people

, then the only basis for men or white people to act against racism or sexism—to act 

against

 their interests—would be altruism or false consciousness. Self-sacrificing altruism alone will not suffice to move large numbers of men and white people to resist patriarchy and white supremacy, but the participation of millions of such people will almost certainly be necessary if we are to dismantle those systems.




The 

well-known words of Lilla Watson and other Aboriginal Australian activists

 bear repeating here: “

If you have come here to help me, you are wasting your time. But if you have come because your liberation is bound up with mine, then let us work together

.” Describing the harms that systems of oppression do to those they privilege—as well as to those they oppress, if unequally—can form one strategy for promoting solidarity. But it may prove more valuable to emphasize, as the above quote does, a positive vision of mutually intertwined liberation.




Still, recognizing that both the privileged and the oppressed are “hurt” by systems of oppression doesn’t necessarily get us any closer to understanding the root causes of harm. It’s inaccurate and offensive to group these vastly different harms under a single generic category of “hurt.” And it makes little sense to attribute responsibility for the oppressive behaviors of members of dominant social groups to the “hurt” they supposedly experience as a consequence of occupying those dominant positions. On the contrary, it seems far more plausible that it is precisely the ways in which such people are 

not

 hurt—their privilege and entitlement—that facilitate their harmful behavior towards others.




These are good reasons to be suspicious of the “hurt people hurt people” framework. Nonetheless, it resonates deeply with many individuals, particularly in the sphere of intimate relationships. Could it still offer a transformative account of the causes of sexual violence?













Beneath the Statistics: How the Criminal Legal System Creates More Harm




Abolitionists reject the idea that some people are inherently, irredeemably bad and therefore deserve punishment and confinement. Instead, we seek to understand the root causes of harmful behavior. If people hurt others because they have themselves been hurt, then harmful behavior emerges from particular circumstances, circumstances that can be changed.




Many “crimes,” such as theft or trespassing, can easily be traced to unmet material needs. To reduce or eliminate these, we need to change our social system to ensure that everyone has access to food, housing, and other basic necessities. But more harmful behaviors such as assault or rape, which can’t be easily explained as people trying to meet core material needs, pose a deeper challenge to abolitionist logics.




Proposing that “hurt people hurt people” offers the hope that by interrupting cycles of harm, we can reduce the likelihood of hurt people in turn hurting others. By promoting healing, resolving trauma, and intervening to prevent harm, we can create a virtuous cycle in which hurt no longer creates more hurt. As fewer people experience sexual violence—the logic goes—fewer people hurt by that violence will hurt others in turn. As the prevalence of rape and abuse diminishes, the perceived need for carceral responses to it will diminish along with it.




Yet once again, the “hurt people hurt people” framing proves problematic when it comes to explaining sexual harm.




At first glance, research into sexual offenders appears to support a connection between experiencing sexual harm and causing it. Sexual violence advocates 

cite a range of studies

 claiming that “perpetrators of child sexual abuse are also often victims of child sexual abuse.

”

 As 

one 2014 study

 concluded, “Sex offenders had more than three times the odds of child sexual abuse, nearly twice the odds of physical abuse, thirteen times the odds of verbal abuse, and more than four times the odds of emotional neglect” relative to men in the general population.




On the surface, this appears to confirm that “hurt people hurt people” when it comes to sexual harm. However, a closer look through an abolitionist lens undermines this conclusion.




According to the criminal legal system’s 

own statistics

, “Rape is the most under-reported crime,” with at least 63% of sexual assaults not reported to police. That’s almost certainly a low figure, given how many survivors don’t define their non-consensual experiences as rape or may not report them on Department of Justice surveys. Additionally, in the minority of experiences of sexual assault that are reported to police, almost none result in convictions and fewer still in imprisonment. According to 

FBI statistics

, “For every 1000 sexual assaults, 50 reports lead to arrests, 28 cases lead to a felony conviction, and only 25 perpetrators are sentenced to incarceration.”




This means that the vast majority of people who commit sexual harm never end up in prison, so never end up in the statistics cited to claim that “hurt people hurt people.”




Who 

actually

 gets sent to prison for sexual offenses? It’s certainly not a representative sample of those who sexually harm others. It’s mostly people who are already vulnerable to the criminal legal system, often due to poverty, racism, and other forms of marginalization.




So when these statistics imply that “perpetrators” (in this case, the tiny percentage of people 

convicted and imprisoned

, not all people who 

commit

 such harms) are themselves disproportionately survivors of sexual abuse, what does that actually tell us?




It tells us that the people who are most likely to be caught up in the criminal legal system are the people who are most likely to be abused. Statistically, 

hurt people are

 

more likely to be hurt by the criminal legal system themselves

 than to hurt others. Consider the enormous proportion of 

incarcerated women who are survivors of partner violence

, whose “crime” was often simply survival.




The reality behind the statistics is that carceral responses are more likely to compound the harms that survivors experience than to prevent future harm or secure “justice.”













The Impact on Survivors




Beyond debates over statistics, there are additional problems with the framework “hurt people hurt people.” Let’s start with the impact it has on survivors themselves.




Consider this account 

from a rape crisis counselor

:







I began to reconsider this idea that “hurt people hurt people” when I worked as a facilitator for support groups of adult male survivors of child sexual abuse. One of the most painful feelings I heard these men express was the fear that they themselves might be doomed to hurt others because of what they’d experienced. This sentiment was frequently shared and widely resonant among the men in my groups. Many of them seemed to have absorbed the narrative that those who commit sexual abuse usually had been subjected to it themselves. They had no desire to hurt anyone; on the contrary, they had an absolute horror of making anyone go through what they had gone through. But they were terrified that somehow, because of what they’d experienced, they were at risk of causing harm to others. Some avoided intimate relationships or raising children because of these fears.







Despite the lingering power of this myth, the research that has been conducted indicates that it isn’t true. 

The National Sexual Violence Resource Center cautions

, “

IT IS RARE

 for victims of child sexual abuse to become perpetrators as adults.” They cite 

a 2015 study

 that concluded, “The widespread belief that sexually abused children are uniquely at risk to become sex offenders was not supported by prospective empirical evidence.”




Yet despite the lack of evidence, this myth remains deeply entrenched, in part due to the influence of the “hurt people hurt people” framework, which is often repeated by well-meaning abolitionists.




This myth inflicts a cruel additional punishment on survivors already burdened by the trauma they have experienced. It builds on the shame that survivors often feel, even when they know that the violence they endured wasn’t their fault. They often feel damaged or broken, and the myth that they are likely to go on to hurt others seems to confirm this. For this reason alone, we should consider the costs of reinforcing this paradigm.




This fear is also distinctly gendered. Female survivors are far less likely than male survivors to internalize the idea that experiencing rape or sexual abuse will lead them to harm others sexually. This is partly due to the social reality that men commit the greatest proportion of sexual violence. But it’s further reinforced by the relative invisibility of male survivors—and particularly for queer men, it’s compounded by the homophobic messaging that associates same-sex love with pedophilia.




Repeating the story that hurt people hurt people turns away from the feminist analysis of rape as an expression of power. In its place, we’re left with a depoliticized take on trauma that ignores how norms of gender and sexuality shape victimization and reinforce stigma.













Harm and Disrupted Empathy




If the framework “hurt people hurt people” does not offer an adequate explanation of the causes of oppression and abuse, what could be a useful alternative?




Here’s a different way that abolitionists might frame the roots of harm:




People with disrupted empathy hurt people.




Empathy here means our ability to perceive, understand, and respond to the feelings of others. It involves entering into another person’s reality, sensing their perspective and their emotions, and reshaping our actions based on that awareness. Empathy is the basis for human connection, a key foundation for relationships and communication. When it is disrupted, it undermines that connection in ways that can lead to harm.




This formulation assumes that all people have an inherent capacity for empathy. It doesn’t describe people as “lacking” empathy; that could imply that some people never had it, can’t attain it, or can’t recover it. Instead, the concept of “disrupted” empathy suggests a propensity that can be regained.




Many different factors shape a person’s capacity for empathy, including past experiences, forms of neurodivergence, cultural norms, and more. This framework emphasizes the social dimensions of empathy, understanding empathy as a mode of relating that is modeled, given and received, learned and practiced over time. In this framing, we can conceive of empathy the way some linguists conceive of language: as an instinct inherent in our species but requiring social connection and learning to unlock and develop.




This conception draws on the abolitionist insight that both the structural and individual changes are necessary if we are to do away with harm. As we work with particular people to help restore their empathetic connection to others, we can also create social structures that reinforce empathy.













Empathy and Sexual Harm




Could this framework provide a more accurate assessment of the impact of sexual violence and similar forms of harm?




In some cases, experiencing sexual harm can disrupt a person’s capacity for empathy. This is most likely to result when the harm occurs in conjunction with other forms of physical and emotional abuse, especially if those are severe forms or take place at an early age. When a person starts out without safe and supportive relationships in which empathy can be modeled and received, that can inhibit the formation of such relationships later in life.




One of the most important components of healing from the trauma of such experiences involves receiving empathy—being believed and taken seriously, having one’s pain validated and grieved. This kind of recognition can form part of a healing journey that can restore disrupted empathy, significantly reducing the possibility that the healing person will harm others.




Often, experiencing sexual harm can 

intensify

 empathy. Many survivors become deeply attuned to the dynamics of consent and more conscientious about their interactions with others. Many become supporters and advocates themselves, transforming their experiences of hurt from liabilities into strengths as they offer empathy to other survivors.




This intensified empathy can feel like a double-edged sword. Sometimes it takes the form of heightened sensitivity to references to sexual assault, which can be dysregulating. It can also show up as becoming a particularly caring friend, a skilled counselor, a determined advocate, or a powerful organizer against violence.




The intensified empathy that can emerge out of experiences of trauma can become a super power, if sometimes an overwhelming one to possess. In touch with their emotions and acutely aware of the pain they experienced, many survivors are particularly attuned to others’ feelings and aware of the ways that they impact others. These qualities make them less likely to cause harm than the average person.




Survivors of sexual violence who fear that their experience may dispose them towards harming others should take heart. It is not the experience of being hurt but a condition of disrupted empathy that leads people to hurt others.




No one can undo what we’ve experienced in the past, but we can take proactive steps to restore empathy. We can actively work to address our own trauma, rebuild a sense of safety and connection, share our experiences with others, and keep listening and learning. In doing so, we can heal ourselves and ensure that the cycle of harm ends with us.













Disrupted Empathy, Oppression, and Entitlement




Experiencing hurt is not the only thing that can disrupt empathy. There are much more common root causes.




Let’s add another layer to our abolitionist analysis of harm:




Oppressive systems that engender entitlement

 

can also disrupt empathy.




Consider patriarchy, a system of oppression that is central to sexual violence. Patriarchy is a system of institutions and social relations that concentrate power for men at the expense of women and others. This system enables men to feel entitled to the labor, bodies, care, and obedience of women and others. Masculinity is defined in part by this sense of entitlement, while empathy is coded as feminine.




The masculine ideal of repressing emotions and remaining impervious to pain cuts off men’s empathy for themselves. This normalizes seeing others as weak and inferior if they feel pain themselves, or if they empathize with the pain of others. Gender norms train men, and all those who aspire to masculine power, into disrupted empathy.




Rape culture feeds on this disrupted empathy. Sexual violence could not exist without disregard for others’ pain and entitlement to others’ bodies. Oppressive gendered power structures bear far more responsibility than “hurt people hurting people” for the disrupted empathy that enables people to cause harm.




A great deal of evidence suggests that sexual violence flourishes in settings or social groups where collective norms support or excuse it. In other words, contexts in which sexual violence often occurs are not simply places that happen to include lots of pathological individuals. All people have a capacity to treat others with respect and consideration or with disregard and contempt. How people choose to treat others depends largely on the norms that predominate in those settings and groups.




It’s not surprising that the settings in which high rates of sexual violence have been documented—such as some fraternity houses, military units, and prisons—are male-dominated environments in which rituals that disrupt empathy are central to social norms. Hazing ceremonies, abusive officers or guards, and dehumanizing language and treatment all model relations devoid of empathy. In such environments, expressing feelings, showing care, and relating to others’ pain can indicate weakness, making someone a target for ridicule, exclusion, and violence. In these mostly single-sex environments where misogynist attitudes predominate, it’s not surprising that participants often direct sexual violence at women, trans and queer people, and others perceived as effeminate.




Another social structure that disrupts empathy is whiteness. Hundreds of years of racist violence and domination could not have taken place without white supremacy, an ideology that numbs its adherents to the pain of those whose humanity it denies. As 

Mab Segrest

 argues in 

Memoir of a Race Traitor

, a key component of white culture and identity established in the era of slavery and persisting to this day is 

anesthesia

, a deliberate repression of sensation and empathy towards racialized people. White supremacy is not just a belief about the superiority of one group defined as a race over another. It’s a claim about who is entitled to land, labor, resources, and bodies.




Sexual violence was central the antebellum economy, as enslavers utilized rape to reproduce the enslaved workforce and increase white intergenerational wealth. White men’s sense of entitlement to the bodies of people of color, particularly women and trans people, persists today in countless forms, from high rates of sexual violence and differential treatment of survivors of color in the criminal legal system to the racist tropes that saturate mainstream pornography.




So long as whiteness persists as a system for distributing power, its disruption of empathy will reinforce cycles of racial and gendered violence.




Yet there is no simple equation between identity and disrupted empathy. It is true that privilege—not having to think about the oppression that others experience—and a lack of shared experience frequently disrupt the empathy of those socialized as men and positioned as white. But there is nothing inherent in any demographic that produces disrupted empathy. Those from dominant groups can be deeply empathetic, and those from oppressed groups experience can experience disrupted empathy as well.




All people are capable of harming others, though patterns of social power distribute those harms unevenly. Developing an analysis of the origins of social harm in disrupted empathy can enable abolitionists to craft effective strategies for responding to it while dismantling the carceral structures that exacerbate its root causes.




While patriarchy and white supremacy form two of the oppressive systems most central to the entitlement and disrupted empathy that drive sexual violence, they are by no means the only ones. The “corrective” rape of lesbian women and the hate-fueled sexual assaults on gay men and trans people reflect the ongoing power of homophobia and transphobia. The persistence of inaccessible spaces throughout much of the American landscape reflects the entitlement many non-disabled people feel to convenience, low costs, or familiarity over disabled people’s ability to participate in public life. The horrific assaults that 

ICE

 and 

the Border Patrol

 are perpetrating against immigrant communities feed on narratives framing immigrants as dangerous outsiders undeserving of empathy.




These oppressive structures—and many others like them—interrupt the basic intuitive feelings of connection and concern we feel towards other people, rendering it possible to concentrate power through artificial social divisions. These structures, far more than individual experiences of hurt, are the root cause of persisting sexual violence and other patterns of harm in our society.













Opposing Empathy to Reinforce Hierarchy




Empathy disrupts oppression; disrupted empathy reinforces oppression. In view of this, it is not surprising that many of the wealthiest and most privileged people in our society today are trying to 

discredit empathy itself

. They want to convince us that selfishness and disregard for others’ suffering—the qualities that have enabled them to amass wealth and power at our expense—are natural and healthy, while connection and solidarity are pernicious.




Elon Musk is leading this charge. In an appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast, the world’s first trillionaire 

claimed

, “The fundamental weakness of Western civilization is empathy.” His rant combined racist anxiety about immigration and changing demographics in “the West” with gendered fears over women’s autonomy and trans people’s existence. As a successful capitalist, it is not surprising that he is promoting competition and economic inequality as desirable for their own sake.




But Elon Musk is not alone. Figures from the Christian Right speak of “

the sin of empathy

,” reframing what is usually seen as a virtue as harmful and citing tolerance for trans people as an example of its “destructive” consequences. Religious critics accuse progressives of deploying “

toxic empathy

” to undermine Biblical morality, citing those who defend reproductive autonomy because they care about pregnant women at least as much as their unborn fetuses. Conservative academics warn that “

suicidal empathy

” subverts logical thought and optimal decision-making, allegedly undermining “Western” society by causing people to accept poor/non-white/Muslim immigration.




Why do MAGA and the far right feel so threatened by empathy today?




Perhaps because their entire program of hierarchy and domination would be undermined if people were fully able to feel and act on the misery that it inflicts on the vast majority of the global population. Perhaps because nationalism, racism, patriarchy, and transphobia could not survive if people from dominant groups considered perspectives and feelings beyond their own. Perhaps because modes of relating based in empathy—such as solidarity and mutual aid—point to the possibility of a way of life beyond capitalism and the state.




Empathy alone won’t suffice to tear down the systems of oppression that confine us, but it’s an essential first step. It connects our responses to interpersonal harm on an individual level to our organizing to transform society on a collective level. It is the keystone of an abolitionist future. That is why it is intolerable to those invested in propping up the ruling order today.













Conclusion: Empathy and Abolition




Abolition requires restoring disrupted empathy. This must go in both directions: it means restoring the empathy that those who have caused harm feel towards those they harmed, while also 

insisting on empathy for people who have caused harm

 as essential to the process of transformation.




By contrast, the core principle of the criminal legal system is the negation of empathy. No one could administer punishments ranging from fines to caging to execution without cutting themselves off from empathy for those they punish. The state’s entire concept of “justice” revolves around perpetually inflicting harm and suppressing empathy. Is it any wonder that our society continues to suffer from forms of behavior stemming from disrupted empathy when one of the chief forces actively disrupting our empathy is the “justice” system itself?




This doesn’t mean that if we simply treated people better and listened to their feelings, no one would hurt anyone. Disrupted empathy isn’t the only cause of harmful behavior, but it is an enabling condition for it. As such, it is a root cause that abolitionists can work to address. And since the primary “solutions” that our criminal legal system offers are explicitly premised on rejecting empathy, this framework offers us a clear basis for rejecting carceral responses.




Let’s let go of the narrative that “hurt people hurt people.” At best, it serves to humanize people who hurt others and to call for responses that interrupt cycles of harm. But it also reinforces hurtful myths, redirects attention from structural to individual factors, and misdiagnoses the root causes of harm.




Instead, let’s tell a broader story about the foundations of social harm that suggests concrete steps we can take to redress it. Focusing on disrupted empathy rather than past experiences of hurt offers a more holistic and accurate account of sexual violence in particular and interpersonal harm in general.




Abolition means more than simply doing away with prisons and police. It requires us to reconnect to our basic capacity to see and feel one another’s humanity. To restore our collective empathy as a culture, we must dismantle the structures of social oppression that have disrupted it.




Those who have been hurt by rape culture, patriarchy, white supremacy, and other harmful systems have a vital role to play in this ongoing struggle. Not because they, as hurt people, are especially likely to hurt others—they aren’t—but because the insights that their experiences offer can equip them to step out of the endless cycles of harm perpetuated by carceral systems and craft a renewed vision of liberation anchored in empathy for all.
















Images courtesy of Frans Masereel. As he put it, “An ideal communism would be, let us say, an anarchic sort of communism.”

author: Alex Nguyen
title: Texas Attorney General Drops Lawsuit Aiming to Ban Muslim Civil Rights Group
content:
The Council on American-Islamic Relations, which has been targeted by Gov. Greg Abbott, called the news “a huge relief.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a lawsuit that sought to ban the country’s largest Muslim civil rights group from operating in Texas, state court records show.

The lawsuit, filed in February, had asked a Collin County judge to declare the Council on American-Islamic Relations a foreign terrorist and transnational criminal organization. It alleged that CAIR was working with the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Sunni Muslim group, to “usurp governmental power and establish dominion through Sharia law.” At the time, CAIR said it was being punished for its opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza.

The petition came after Gov. Greg Abbott slapped the same designation against the two groups and urged Paxton to take legal action against CAIR amid a surge in Republican candidates running anti-Islam campaigns.

Paxton’s office filed a notice of nonsuit Monday, voiding the lawsuit nearly two weeks after a blue wave sunk Paxton’s U.S. Senate bid and swept Abbott out of office. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she will remove the “foreign terrorist organization” label against CAIR.

Shaimaa Zayan, the Austin director of CAIR-Texas, called the lawsuit’s end — which was first reported by Bloomberg Law — a “huge relief.”

“CAIR-Texas faced a huge injustice and continued to operate despite the threats,” Zayan said Tuesday. “We are looking forward to a new chapter in Texas, hopefully where civic life will be flourishing and every voice will be heard in Texas.”

CAIR and its Texas chapter have also cheered Hinojosa’s pledge, which she announced during an interview with The Washington Post.

“Greg Abbott, Ken Paxton, Bo French, and Mayes Middleton staked their political campaigns on shredding the First Amendment to target Texas Muslims, but the people of Texas rejected this un-American bigotry,” the groups added in a statement. “Anti-Muslim hate is no longer an effective political weapon in Texas, and it must no longer have any place in state governance.”

The dropped lawsuit follows a flurry of other lawsuits Paxton’s office has abandoned since the election, including cases against immigrant rights groups as well as the NCAA over transgender athletes.

The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that informs Texans — and engages with them — about public policy, politics, government and statewide issues.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $23,000 in the next 48 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: David Venn
title: RCMP conducts ‘largest drug seizure destined for Nunavut’
content:
In what the RCMP calls “the largest drug seizure destined for Nunavut,” police seized five kilograms of cocaine in southern Canada in August, a news release issued Tuesday says.




As a result, an estimated 50,000 doses (measuring one-tenth of a gram) were prevented from entering the territory, the release said.




“This seizure represents far more than the removal of drugs from the supply chain,” Chief Supt. Kent Pike said in the release. “It represents lives protected, families spared from harm and fewer opportunities for organized crime to profit at the expense of Nunavummiut.”




In February 2026, the police force began investigating an alleged money-laundering and drug-trafficking operation.




In August, officers from Nunavut and the federal Arctic unit executed a search warrant in Ottawa, where they seized the drugs.




The federal Arctic unit works under the Federal Policing Northwest Region, which co-ordinates resources to investigate organized crime in Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, Saskatchewan and Nunavut.




The release did not say if any charges have been laid. It said the investigation is ongoing and that the RCMP will not provide further comment.

author: Daron Letts
title: Two children killed in sliding tragedy in Kimmirut
content:
Kimmirut is in mourning after two young sisters were killed while sliding Sunday afternoon.




Holly Lyta, 8, and Melanie Pootoogook, 5, were struck by a water truck as it was reversing, said Elisapie Pootoogook, the girls’ great aunt Tuesday in a phone interview.




Their father Charlie Pootoogook witnessed the incident, she said.




“I’m having trouble sleeping,” Elisapie Pootoogook said of how she’s handling the tragedy. 

She added that she is very close to her nephew Charlie Pootoogook, who grew up with her in Kinngait.




The girls’ grandparents are planning to head to Kimmirut Friday from Kinngait to support the parents, Elisapie Pootoogook said.




Kimmirut has a population of approximately 400 people.




The community’s school and daycare were closed Monday out of respect for those affected by the girls’ deaths.
















South Baffin MLA David Joanasie, whose riding includes Kimmirut and Kinngait, shared his support for the family Monday in a Facebook post.




“My sincere condolences [go] out to the people of Kimmirut during this difficult time of grief after a sudden tragedy,” he said. 

“We feel for all those who are most impacted by their loss and hope that love and grace surrounds the families and community as a whole. I thank all the responders who help during this hardship.”




The Education Department, in partnership with the Canadian Red Cross, will provide supports,

 he added.




Elisapie Pootoogook and others in the community are holding various fundraisers for the family.




“Donations to the family are also welcome,” she said. “No family should ever have to experience such heartbreaking loss.”




The RCMP did not respond to an interview request as of noon on Tuesday.

author: Clara Saliba
title: Está na hora de falar da pobreza de tempo
content:
Chegamos em novembro. As lojas e praças já estão decoradas para o Natal. No ar, a sensação de que o tempo passa rápido demais, de que nos atropela… Em meio às reflexões de quase fim de ano, reparei que o tempo, desta vez, esteve mais em pauta do que nunca. Afinal, reduzimos a jornada de trabalho e acabamos com a escala 6×1. 




Ainda este ano, em 16 de dezembro, os trabalhadores e trabalhadoras sob o regime CLT terão direito a duas folgas semanais. Também na mesma data, 60 dias após a aprovação da Emenda Constitucional 141, começará a valer o limite de jornada de 42h semanais, que cairá para 40h em dezembro de 2027. A única exceção à lei são os portadores de diploma de ensino superior que recebam mais de duas vezes e meia o teto do Regime Geral da Previdência Social (RGPS) – cerca de R$21 mil mensais. 




Uma conquista e tanto, que colocou no centro do debate público um número que não é monetário. Talvez pela primeira vez na história, falou-se tanto sobre um valor que não vem sempre acompanhado de um cifrão: o tempo das pessoas. 




Sim, tempo é, em certa medida, dinheiro. Sobretudo para a classe trabalhadora, as horas de vida que se gasta trabalhando têm uma relação importante com a possibilidade de pagar as contas ao fim do mês. 




Frequentemente, terceirizamos algumas tarefas porque é mais fácil pagar por elas do que dispor das horas para fazê-las. 




Quem nunca escolheu comer um salgado pronto, no caminho para o trabalho, apenas para poder dormir mais meia hora, e não se preocupar em preparar o café da manhã? Ou contratou uma diarista, para dar conta da faxina que acumulava para o fim de semana? 




Mas essas duas variáveis não são a mesma coisa: ainda que ter tempo nos economize dinheiro – permitindo que nós mesmas realizemos uma série de tarefas em vez de pagar por elas – e que ter dinheiro nos economize tempo – permitindo que contratemos – nem todo o dinheiro do mundo substitui a necessidade de tempo para comer, dormir, ter higiene e socializar, por exemplo. E nem todo o tempo, se não virar dinheiro, nos torna autossuficientes materialmente.




Esse é o raciocínio por trás de uma medida econômica pouco conhecida, e que tem sido explorada pela economia feminista: a pobreza de tempo.  




A economista estadunidense Clair Vickery escreveu sobre isso nos anos 1977. Ela definiu como pobres de tempo as famílias que não teriam uma combinação mínima de tempo para realizar as tarefas de cuidado pessoal e doméstico e dinheiro para comprar bens essenciais. Nessa linha, quem tem menos dinheiro precisa compensar com tempo, e quem tem menos tempo, com dinheiro. Quem não consegue nenhuma combinação suficiente de dinheiro e tempo com o salário que recebe é pobre, mesmo que ganhe mais do que o mínimo da linha de pobreza monetária. 




Nessa pesquisa, ela identificou as mães e pais “solo” como a população mais vulnerável à pobreza de tempo, ainda que essa situação seja mais comum entre as mulheres. Muitas vezes, elas estão sobrecarregadas pelo cuidado dos filhos, acumulando a jornada de trabalho fora com a responsabilidade total por outra(s) pessoa(s). 




Aqui no Brasil, ainda é difícil mensurar a pobreza de tempo, porque nos falta uma variável indispensável dessa equação: saber quantas horas as pessoas gastam por dia em cada atividade, o que é conhecido como pesquisa de “Uso do Tempo”. O que sabemos são quantas horas as pessoas passam trabalhando fora de casa por semana. Sabemos também, em alguma medida, quanto tempo elas gastam em cuidados e afazeres domésticos: 21 horas para as mulheres e 11 para os homens, de acordo com o IBGE, em 2022, ainda que haja fortes indícios de que essa pesquisa erre para baixo. As médias dos outros países da América Latina para mulheres, por exemplo, ficam sempre acima das 30h (para saber mais, vale ler a 

Nota de Política Econômica 64 do Made-USP

). 




Mas, mesmo que seja difícil de medir, 

a pobreza de tempo certamente é experienciada por muitos brasileiros e brasileiras. 




Longas horas no transporte público e jornadas elevadas de trabalho dentro e fora de casa se traduzem em uma qualidade de vida que despenca. 




Soma-se a isso todos os problemas de elevação do custo de vida percebidos desde a pandemia, e o resultado é que nem a renda nem o tempo tem sido suficientes para muitas pessoas, especialmente para as mulheres.




O tamanho da mobilização pela redução da jornada de trabalho foi uma prova disso.

 A aprovação da PEC com unanimidade na Câmara e no Senado não deixou dúvidas: 

no debate público futuro sobre a economia, o tempo também conta, e muito.

 E, nesse sentido, há muitas políticas econômicas que podem aliviar esse tipo de pobreza. O investimento massivo no transporte coletivo de qualidade, por exemplo. Nas políticas de cuidado, como creches públicas, lavanderias comunitárias e 

cuidotecas

. Ou nas de alimentação, como restaurantes populares e mercados ou armazéns solidários. 




Estamos no momento de imaginar o que pautará a agenda econômica dos próximos quatro anos, e a reconquista do nosso tempo não pode ficar de fora do radar dos economistas.

author: Chris Walker
title: Largest Data Centers in US Emit as Much Carbon as Denmark, Study Finds
content:
The largest US data centers use almost 2 percent of US electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A new study published this week suggests that the combined yearly output of carbon dioxide from the largest data centers in the U.S. rivals that of some countries.

The study, which appeared in the journal Nature Sustainability on Monday, finds that the largest data centers in the country release a combined total of 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions per year. That accounts for about 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. — an amount that is greater than the yearly electricity use of Los Angeles and New York City combined.

The study examined 403 facilities in total, finding that their combined carbon emissions were comparable to those of countries the size of Bolivia or Denmark.

Some states’ data centers had larger carbon outputs than others. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio account for half of emissions alone, while other states, such as Oregon, have much smaller carbon emissions, due to a larger portion of electricity being generated through means other than fossil fuels.

According to reporting from The New York Times, much of the researchers’ work amounted to “detective work” due to the lack of federal requirements on public disclosure by these facilities.

“Communities shouldn’t need a team of Harvard researchers to analyze satellite images to understand their environmental impact,” said Gianluca Guidi, the Harvard scientist who led the research team.

Indeed, safeguards against pollution from data centers are limited, in large part due to workarounds that are being allowed by the Trump administration’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), including the use of “islanded” power plants, which are built solely to power data centers and are not part of the electrical grid.

Data centers are also undoing recent progress in reducing pollution in states with larger carbon emissions. In Texas, for example, years of work to lower those rates could be undone if a plan to build hundreds of new data centers (in addition to those that have already been constructed) goes through in the next few years.

Americans appear aware of the problems posed by data centers, including rising electricity prices and environmental concerns. Earlier this month, in midterm elections across the country, voters overwhelmingly passed referenda to bar or regulate the rapid expansion of data centers in their communities.

“Tuesday’s election was a historically bad night for the Republican Party. It might have been even worse for big tech and their plans to spend trillions of dollars building AI data centers,” read one analysis of the election outcomes.

Public opposition to data center expansion likely played a role in Democrats’ “blue wave.” Exit poll data from NBC News found that 56 percent of voters described data centers and artificial intelligence (AI) as “crucial or major factor[s]” in determining their vote.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $23,000 in the next 48 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Labor Notes Staff
title: Stewards Corner: Laying the Foundation for Change in Your Union
content:
Revitalizing a local union may require electing new officers with a different vision. But running for office should not be your first step.




Successful campaigns for union office usually start by organizing against management first, often years in advance of any eventual run.




A group of workers wants to accomplish something—better pay, more control over their conditions on the job, an end to tiered wages or benefits—but their officials, or something about the way their union operates, is in the way. So they begin to change the culture of the union, getting more members involved in building power on the shop floor.




Your ultimate goal, after all, is not just electing new leaders, but building a stronger union. And doing that means involving as many members as possible.




WHERE TO START




The good news is you can begin organizing for change in your union any time. 




“Your campaign should start with workplace fights that involve your co-workers,” says John Pearson, a nurse at Highland Hospital in Oakland, California, and former president of the SEIU Local 1021 chapter there. “You need that type of credibility and trust from people to be able to lead successfully.”




Before running for office, Pearson helped lead a campaign to defend breaks, involving nurses throughout the Alameda County hospital system, which resulted in a big back pay settlement. He also led an effort to save a substance abuse clinic from defunding.




“The word spreads if you’re effective at fighting in the workplace—people know to ask you for help,” says Pearson.




This type of organizing shows members that you have a track record, and that collectively members can make a difference.




The Caucus of Rank-and-File Educators (CORE), which won leadership in the Chicago Teachers Union in 2010, built up strength in campaigns like a fight to stop the school district from closing dozens of neighborhood schools and replacing them with privately run charters. 




“So much of our caucus was really forged in the fight against school closings,” says Norine Gutekanst, who was a third-grade teacher at the time. Caucus members attended school closing hearings and teamed up with community activists to camp out all night in front of threatened schools. The leadership of the union, meanwhile, was absent from the fight.




CORE was already “doing what the union should have been doing,” said Chicago social studies teacher Bill Lamme. “So when the election came, [CORE activists] didn’t say ‘Elect me and I’ll do this.’ They said, ‘This is what we’ve been doing and we’ll keep doing it.’”




ATTEND MEETINGS




If you’re serious about getting involved in and transforming your union, you should be regularly attending union meetings, even if the meetings don’t allow for much debate. Bring other members who share your views. By participating, your group can shake things up.




“The first time you attend a meeting, just listen,” says Ken Paff, longtime national organizer with Teamsters for a Democratic Union. 




“Later on,” Paff says, “you can make a proposal, and organize your group to present it. Talk to members before the meeting; draw them in. Get things out to the members, not only to make your group transparent, but also to make union meetings that way.




“Tell people there will be a motion on the pension plan, or another burning topic. Ask them to come support the motion. Put it out in writing. Get them to sign a petition in support of it.”




In Letter Carriers (NALC) Branch 9 in Minneapolis, a group of members started meeting to talk about how to change the culture of their branch, including its meeting agendas. “We had a president of over 30 years who would just use Robert’s Rules to keep people down,” says letter carrier Chris Pennock.




But the group of reformers kept bringing more members to meetings. Eventually their motions started winning. Pennock got 10 minutes on the agenda to talk about fighting post office closures. It was a small step, but a co-worker told him: “I don’t know if you know how historic that is—I’ve never seen a motion pass that the executive board not only didn’t support but were actively opposed to.”




Their organizing helped lay the basis to run a reform slate; Pennock is now vice president of Branch 9. “Have faith that you can change the culture,” he says.




At the same time, “it’s a mistake to think that meetings are the important thing,” says SEIU Local 1021’s Pearson—especially since most members won’t attend meetings. You want to find other ways to get them involved in the union. 




“Talk to people in the workplace, especially while you’re working, if you can,” advises Pearson.  Some other activities to consider:







Holding classes or discussions on issues the union is not addressing




Getting members to join rallies or picket lines in solidarity with other unions




Organizing a “Vote No” campaign on a subpar contract




Campaigning to change your bylaws to make the union more democratic







BE AN INFORMATION SOURCE




Is your local union run like a small club or clique, with a few insiders making all of the decisions and everyone else wondering what’s going on? Do members feel they don’t have a voice in critical decisions about their jobs, benefits, and contracts?




Members want information, and informed members are more active members. You can start building a campaign for change by becoming an information source. Here are some ideas:







Inform members about the contract and how to enforce it




Take on workplace issues and organize contract enforcement campaigns




Organize short gatherings at lunch or after work to talk about workplace or union issues




Distribute bulletins on workplace and union issues




Hold online or in-person workshops or an educational conference




Use an app like WhatsApp to build communication and spread information among members




Start a Facebook group to share news about your employer and give members a space to communicate with each other 




Start an email and text list to send other members news about your local







Don’t spread rumors or conspiracy theories. Be reliable and provide information that the members can use. Set a positive and constructive tone, especially if you’re using social media. 




Remember, your credibility is your most important asset.




GETTING MEMBERS INVOLVED




A one-person crusade isn’t going to change your local union, and it isn’t what the union needs. You need teammates and helpers if you want to accomplish long-term change.




“Every day you need to ask yourself, ‘Who did I talk to today?’” says Vance Smith of Teamsters Local 135 in Indianapolis. “Get out in the field and have one-on-one, personal conversations.”




Have realistic expectations. Not every member is going to want to become as active as you are.




If someone wants to get involved, start them off with small jobs first, like talking to you about problems where they work or introducing you to other members. Thank them for their efforts and let them know their work is valuable. 




“In every workplace, workers show a range of knowledge about and interest in the union, from A to Z,” says longtime organizer Joe Fahey. Don’t try to move people from A to Z immediately—instead, move them from A to B, and so on.




Once they’ve gotten their feet wet, ask them to do bigger jobs, like passing out a leaflet or standing with you in the parking lot while you do that. Give them options. 




Remember, people’s lives are complicated. If someone doesn’t want to get involved at first, don’t write them off. Stay in contact and ask them again later. You’re building a network here, so cast as wide a net as you can. People can surprise you.




The more members you have working with you, the more work you can get done. Especially in a local that represents multiple workplaces or industries, getting lots of members involved in your campaign can be critical.	










Is It Working?







Here are some of the ways you can tell your organizing is having an effect:







More members are involved in a passive way, like reading a leaflet.




More members are taking a small action step, like wearing a button or signing a petition.




Some members are taking on organizing tasks, like passing out flyers or making phone calls.




Some members are becoming leaders and taking initiative.







If these things aren’t happening, take a step back and re-evaluate your strategy. Are you doing too much yourself? Do you need to reach out to more departments? Do you have the right message?




This advice is drawn from the Labor Notes book 

Democracy Is Power 

by Mike Parker and Martha Gruelle.







This article is excerpted from 

Running for Local Union Office: A Labor Notes Guide.

 Order the book ($20) and find resources including how to be effective at union meetings, a list of labor education programs, and more at 

labornotes.org/runningforoffice

.
