Sharif Jamilenvironmental activist, coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh and board member of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

Bangladesh’s first riverkeeper, Sharif Jamil, shares how poor countries in the Global South are struggling to effectively adapt to climate change as rising sea levels, extreme weather patterns, pollution and more are creating an escalating “humanitarian catastrophe,” while the wealthy impede efforts to reallocate financial resources for adaptation and mitigation. “If you want to protect the planet, if you want to save the planet from global warming, you need climate finance to make all this transition,” says Jamil.

Sharif Jamilenvironmental activist, coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh and board member of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from COP31, the U.N. climate summit, in Antalya, Turkey.

We turn now to how Global South countries at the frontlines of climate change-fueled disasters are demanding more funding and accountability from rich countries during the negotiations here at COP31.

In August, catastrophic floods in mountainous Nepal washed away entire villages, left nearly 7,000 people dead or missing, triggered by the collapse of a Himalayan glacier. Meanwhile, in low-lying Bangladesh, rising sea levels pose an existential threat to tens of millions of Bangladeshis living along the coast. Bangladesh and Nepal are among the most vulnerable to climate change-related disasters, yet together they contribute less than half a percent of global carbon emissions. They’re also among the poorest countries in the world.

The U.N. Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage was created in 2022 to provide financial support to developing nations on the frontlines of climate-fueled disasters, but the fund has fallen far short of what’s needed. In total, the fund already has over 175 requests from developing countries for nearly $3 billion, but rich countries, the most responsible for climate change, have only pledged $820 million to the fund.

For more, we’re joined by Sharif Jamil, environmental activist, coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh, board member of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

It’s great to have you with us.

SHARIF JAMIL: Thank you for having me.

AMY GOODMAN: Why don’t you pick that mic right up? Because it’s noisy here. There are 90,000 people registered over these two weeks of the climate summit, the biggest one yet. Yet, what is being accomplished? And what are you demanding? But I want you to start off by talking about your own country, Bangladesh, the real recipient of, unfortunately, as we can say, the effects of climate change, climate catastrophe.

SHARIF JAMIL: Yes, you are very right. Bangladesh is in the bottom of the Ganges and Brahmaputra River system, and it is the largest active delta in the world. And if you see the demography, it is highly and densely populated country. And as it is delta, so environmental pollution and climate catastrophe are actually creating humanitarian catastrophe there.

So, it’s not like one particular event. There are extreme weather patterns coming up very frequently and more intensely from the Indian Ocean towards the Bay of Bengal. Salinity intrusion are coming to the middle part of the country. Farmers are losing the crop from their farmlands. Fishers are not able to go to the seas or in the oceans to be fishing. So, it’s a lot of livelihood crisis, lot of migration crisis. There are erosions happening. And in the global platform, Bangladesh is also one of the mostly victimized countries in the world under climate catastrophe.

AMY GOODMAN: So, how can what people decide here — I should say, what countries decide here — affect Bangladesh?

SHARIF JAMIL: Well, it’s been discussed a long, long time. And in Paris Agreement, there are some legally binding commitments came up, that the Global North will be providing adequate climate finance. It was not adequate amount that was discussed by then, and still the amount you already told about the Loss and Damage Fund is like peanuts in terms of real need for the Global South. But still, these things are not operationalized since the Paris Agreement.

Even here in COP31, the cover decision came up. Of course, you can get a direction in which way the COP is going heading forward, and you see there is no Belém-Antalya mechanism discussed in the cover decision like that. And there is new things came up with the 1.5-degree threshold overshoot and what the consequences are coming for the countries like us.

AMY GOODMAN: Talk about climate finance. That is a jargon term, but it’s about the most — the countries that are most responsible for climate change paying for the most damaged, poorest countries. What does Bangladesh need? And if Sharif Jamil was in charge, if you were the head of the U.N. climate summit, of course, it would be a different world. But what would you be working for right now?

SHARIF JAMIL: I mean, the U.N. COP process is working to protect the planet, not only Bangladesh. But to protect the planet, you need to actually bring the global temperature threshold below 1.5 degree, or, in other term, you have to come out of fossil fuel, because they are the 80% responsible sector for the global warming.

So, to do the right thing to protect the planet, whatever you want to do, like, adaptation is something for us which you cannot avoid. Whenever there is a crisis, you have to face it. So, adaptation is something you right away need it. But in terms of mitigation, if we don’t do mitigation, if we don’t make the mitigation work program functional, then what will be happening in the future? And, of course, how the transition will be happening?

If you want to bring the fossil fuel transition away from fossil fuel, and if you want to scale up renewable energy, which is very much necessary to protect the planet, then even you need climate finance. So, climate finance is not something you just go and help some other Global South. If you want to protect the planet, if you want to save the planet from global warming, you need climate finance to make all this transition to be happening. Whatever the things are being discussed here, to make it operationalized, you need to institutionalize this thing, and you need proper allocation of finance to let it be happening.

AMY GOODMAN: Can you explain the electrification pledge? “Electrification” is a buzzword here at the U.N. climate summit.

AMY GOODMAN: What does it mean for Bangladesh?

SHARIF JAMIL: That is very interesting. It is not clear to everyone yet here in COP31 space. The COP presidency is pushing for it. It’s an action item. But from the cover decision, we can get it that it is probably coming to the cover discussion.

But 35-35 does not necessarily mean it will expedite the transitioning from fossil fuel, because the end users who can be electrified — as for example, my gas burner can be turned into electricity burner, but that also will increase the demand of electricity. So, the basic question is how you are fueling that electricity, whether you are getting this electricity from renewable sources or not. This is one thing.

Another thing, you can come out with electric vehicles, but in the Global South, how many people can buy, own electric vehicle? You have to focus on the mass traffic transit, how many electric train system you are coming up with, how much mass buses you are coming up with electricity. This is important. And when you are doing it, another thing is very important, which is: Are you considering the social justice, the ecological justice, environmental justice, gender justice and all these things integrated in the 35-35 plan?

AMY GOODMAN: Can I ask you, in this last minute — Bangladesh is now going through massive strikes, people who work in the clothing district shutting down factories, many of those clothes making their way to the United States. You talk about justice. The whole issue of human rights, workers’ rights and climate rights?

SHARIF JAMIL: That’s very much related to the climate rights also, because the climate migrants. We have a very old data that more than a million people are migrated every year from the coastal areas, under river erosion and other environmental crises. So, all these people are coming to the city, and they are working in the garment sector, because our industrialization also did not take place properly. So, these chaoses are also a cumulative impact of all these things. So you cannot put climate issue away from this crisis, as well.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, Sharif Jamil, I want to thank you so much for being with us, environmental activist, coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh and board member of the Waterkeeper Alliance.

Special thanks to our team here in Turkey: Anjali Kamat, Nicole Salazar, Nermeen Shaikh, Tey-Marie Astudillo, Hany Massoud and Denis Moynihan.

Tomorrow on Democracy Now!, here at the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, we’re going to be talking about human rights in Turkey. We’ll also be speaking with a climate scientist, as well as a delegate here at the climate summit.

Oh, and you can tune in, if you live in the United States and Canada, online on Apple, on Amazon Prime, to the Democracy Now! documentary Steal This Story, Please! It begins with a chase scene at the COP summit in Katowice, Poland, chasing a U.S. climate representative. You can check the website StealThisStory.org. I’m Amy Goodman. Thanks so much for joining us.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

title: As U.S. Boycotts U.N. Climate Talks, California Leads State/City Efforts to Combat Climate Crisis
content:
For the second year in a row, the Trump administration has not sent an official delegation to the United Nations’ annual climate change conference, held this year in Antalya, Turkey. But although no federal representatives are present, more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders are participating, including the governor of the fourth-largest economy in the world, California Governor Gavin Newsom. Newsom, a likely candidate for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, has endorsed the Santa Marta Process, a coalition of nations working to develop a global green energy transition.




“The petrostates have made it abundantly clear: Under the current rules of consensus, they are never, ever going to allow COPs to succeed. They’re just not going to sign that agreement. So, essentially, the Santa Marta coalition is making an end run around that, using economic power,” says longtime environmental and climate reporter Mark Hertsgaard.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: NTI vice-president candidates share ambitions
content:
This story was updated on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 1:26 p.m. ET.




Nunatsiaq News reached out to each of the four candidates running to become one of two vice-presidents at Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. in 

its Dec. 14 election

. Here’s what they had to share:




Aaron Aopaloktok Pedersen said three mottos are the heart of his campaign: “Homes we can own, a culture we all share, and money every Inuk can see.”




Pedersen, who is from Cambridge Bay, joined NTI last fall as a housing and homelessness project manager. Since October, he’s served as the chief operating officer of the organization’s 

housing corporation, Igluvut

.




Igluvut will own and operate at least 25 affordable fixed rent apartments after they are constructed under a plan to build over 700 homes with the federal and territorial governments.




Pedersen said he wants to create pathways for renters to become homeowners by helping them access down payments. 

He also wants to support social and cultural programming aimed at youth and elders and introduce annual reports that disclose how NTI spends its money in each community.




Robert Bourassa, from Pangnirtung, has worked in Qikiqtani Inuit Association’s marine and wildlife division since 2018, where he oversees the implementation of impact benefit agreements from protected areas. 
















He also sits on the board of the investment firm Atuqtuarvik Corp., which invests money into Inuit-owned businesses.




“I want to see Inuit prosper,” he told Nunatsiaq News.




He has thought of getting into politics for a long time, he said, mentioning that his grandfather Ipeelee Kilabuk served as a Northwest Territories MLA in the 1970s. 




Bourassa said addressing the housing shortage and improving access to mental health services are his top priorities.




Under the federal budget, Canada pledged $50 billion for Indigenous people over the next decade in sectors like infrastructure, housing and education. Bourassa wants to lobby the government to make sure those funds support housing.




Paul Irngaut, from Igloolik, has been NTI’s vice-president since 2022. 
















He served as acting president after former NTI president Jeremy Tunraluk went on leave in December 2025. Tunraluk ultimately 

resigned

 from the position, triggering a byelection which was held in May. Irngaut threw his hat into the ring to stay in the presidential post, but 

lost

 to Gloria Uluqsi.




“I’ve always worked toward the betterment of Inuit, and I think I have a proven track record with the organization,” Irngaut said.




Last year, he helped oversee NTI’s signing of 

a 

$1.5 billion, 10-year implementation contract

 with the federal government, through which the organization secured $77.6 million per year in funding.




Irngaut wants to strengthen the territory’s fishing industry and create a “marine council” for discussions between Canada’s Department of Fisheries and Oceans and such organizations as the Nunavut Wildlife Management Board and Nunavut Water Board.




“We have to start talking closely with our government before devolution happens,” he said. “It’s important that we have all these things in place so that we can start protecting Inuit rights.”
















Adamee Itorcheak serves as the Qikiqtani Inuit Association’s secretary-treasurer, a role he took leave from earlier this year to serve as NTI’s acting vice-president and, for a short time, acting president in the lead up to the May byelection to fill in during Irgnaut’s bid for president.




He also sits on the board of the non-profit Annauma Community Foundation and the Inuit Broadcasting Corp. He was president of Baffin Fisheries.




Itorcheak said he is focused on encouraging NTI to be more transparent about how it spends money, smarter spending, and revitalizing Inuktikut. He wants to continue the work he was doing under NTI’s $4.3-million education program, which aims to open an all-Inuktikut school.




“We need to make some conscious decisions on how we’re going to preserve our language.”




He also said “Inuit have to be front and centre” at talks about projects of national interest, such as the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link and the Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project.




Correction

: This story has been updated to correct information about Igluvut’s role in regards to the 25 affordable fixed rent apartments, as well as information about Aaron Aopaloktok Pedersen’s role in the plan to build over 700 homes with the federal and territorial governments.

title: Fossil Fuels Are "Undermining Democracy" & Must Be Phased Out: Climate Activist Kumi Naidoo at COP31
content: What will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? We speak to Kumi Naidoo, the president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, which aims to reach a binding agreement for a global transition away from fossil fuels. Currently backed by over 25 countries from the Global South, the intergovernmental process began earlier this year in Santa Marta, Colombia. Meanwhile, at the United Nations, “for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels [in the outcome document]. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol,” says Naidoo. We discuss the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative’s goals, how the oil and gas industry drives global conflict, and the Trump administration’s glaring absence from international action on climate change.

title: Hatice Yakışır: Let these lands finally see peace
content:
The Peace Mothers recently travelled to Ankara to demand peace and held a two-day Peace Vigil. The mothers, who left the city after meeting with Speaker of Parliament Numan Kurtulmuş, reiterated their demands for peace and called for the release of political prisoners.




Hatice Yakışır (76), whose two sons are imprisoned, was among the mothers who travelled to Ankara to demand peace despite her advanced age and health problems. Having endured numerous losses throughout her 76 years while continuing her struggle and determination to live, Hatice Yakışır now spends her days looking at framed photographs of her lost loved ones.




Despite everything, Hatice Yakışır continues to demand peace. She said, "I want to see my children walk through this door," expressing her hope that the peace process will succeed and that she will be reunited with her imprisoned sons.







 







Forced into exile after their village was burned




In 1994, Hatice Yakışır was forced to leave her home after soldiers burned down the hamlet of Xizginos, in the Genç (Darahênî) district of Bingöl (Çewlîg). She first moved to Genç and later to central Amed (Diyarbakır). Hatice Yakışır, a mother of nine, lost her husband, Mehmet Ali Yakışır, after he was detained while attempting to visit his father, who had remained in their burned village. Nothing was heard from him again following his detention.




Following her husband's enforced disappearance, Hatice Yakışır was forced to raise her nine children alone. Despite all the hardships and deprivation she experienced, she continued her struggle to survive.




Lost several relatives in the conflict




Hatice Yakışır's son Cûdî (Mehmet Yakışır) joined the guerrillas in 1998 and was martyred in the Black Sea region in 2018. Another son, Şervan (Yakup Yakışır), was martyred the same year during the resistance against the occupation of Afrin (Efrîn). Her grandson Mahsum Gürkan was martyred in 2016 during the self-government resistance in the Sur district of Amed.




Her son's release was postponed




Hatice Yakışır said that her sons Orhan Yakışır and Talip Yakışır are also imprisoned. She explained that the release of Orhan Yakışır, who was sentenced to 12 years in prison and is held in Sincan Closed Prison, has been postponed three times. His release was postponed twice for three months and once for nine months, preventing him from leaving prison. Hatice Yakışır said that the sentence of her other son, Talip Yakışır, who is imprisoned in Aliağa, Izmir, is due to end in February. She called for an end to human rights violations in prisons.




'I want my children to walk through this door'




Hatice Yakışır described her experiences in the following words: "I have nine children. In 1994, my husband was killed in an unsolved murder. Our village was burned down, and afterwards we were forced to move to Amed. There was nowhere we did not go and nothing we did not endure. We suffered enormously. Despite all these hardships, I raised my children. I raised them with the zakat donations of other people. Today, none of my children are with me. Some are in photographs, others are in prison. I want my children beside me, in this house. I want them to walk through this door."




'Everything is for peace'




Hatice Yakışır said that they had been struggling for peace for years and had travelled to Ankara to express their demands by holding a Peace Vigil.




Hatice Yakışır said: "As mothers, we left our homes and travelled to Ankara to demand peace. I went there so that the prisons would be emptied and no one would have to shed tears anymore. The Leader must be free, and no one should lose their life anymore. This war must end as soon as possible. Neither guerrillas nor soldiers, no one should die anymore. There must be peace so that people can live freely and peacefully in their homes. We travelled a thousand kilometres from here and back. People who saw us there and understood that we had come for peace supported us. There are millions of people throughout this country who want peace and do not want any more tears to be shed."




'These lands must finally see peace'




Hatice Yakışır drew attention to the suffering she had endured and reiterated her demand for peace.




Hatice Yakışır said: "My village was burned down, my husband was killed in an unsolved murder, I lost two of my children, and two are still in prison. As a mother who has experienced all this, I say enough is enough. I am not the only one. Thousands of mothers who have experienced the same suffering want the same thing. We did not get to see peace, but I want our grandchildren and children to experience it. I am 76 years old, and even in this condition, I got up and travelled to Ankara. These lands must finally see peace."

title: Nesrin Akgül: Women are not spectators but architects of peace
content:
Women's direct participation in decision-making mechanisms and their role as founding actors are crucial to achieving a lasting and democratic solution through the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Women emphasise that peace must not be limited to the silencing of weapons or negotiations between political actors. They argue that women must participate in decision-making mechanisms through their own political will if the process is to become rooted in society and achieve lasting results. Questions remain over the extent to which women's demands are reflected in negotiations and political processes, how much representation they have in decision-making mechanisms and whether they are being excluded from the process. Women stress that they must not merely serve as a supporting force but must be actors who make decisions and determine the direction of the process. Equal representation, the establishment of independent women's mechanisms and guarantees for women's participation in concrete decision-making bodies are among the key demands. Women's involvement in the process on the basis of their own demands is considered essential to strengthening the social struggle and establishing peace throughout society.




Free Women's Movement (TJA) activist Nesrin Akgül spoke to ANF about the issue.




'Peace is not merely the silencing of weapons'




Nesrin Akgül said that peace cannot be defined solely as the silencing of weapons and that the conditions which gave rise to the war must be eliminated to build lasting peace. Akgül said: "How do we define the process we call peace? If the forces involved in the war cannot establish common ground, even at a minimal level, the question of how peace can be built becomes a matter of debate. Peace is not an achievement that can be secured simply by silencing weapons. Of course, the greatest devastation caused by war is the loss of human life, and ending that loss is the most valuable achievement. However, this war did not take place between two hegemonic powers. It began when a sovereign state denied the existence of a people and an oppressed people rose up against that denial. A people began a war of self-defence in pursuit of their right to self-determination. This was a war entered into out of necessity, but also by choice. It became a struggle to regain dignity. What gained acceptance was that a people reclaimed their dignity through this struggle. For 52 years, this war continued on the basis of that reality.




It is impossible to envisage how peace can be established without identifying the causes of this war. Abdullah Öcalan has repeatedly stressed this point to the state throughout the process. The issue is not disarmament. The Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) may cease to exist today, but another organisation could emerge tomorrow. The real issue is eliminating the conditions that gave rise to the war. This is the framework within which the peace process must be defined. In other words, we must move from a negative peace process that begins with the silencing of weapons to a positive process of construction that consolidates the elimination of armed conflict. This process can sustain itself through the socialisation of peace and the social reconstruction conceptualised within the Peace and Democratic Society Process. It will acquire a comprehensive character when the state, as a party to peace, becomes responsive to democracy, consolidates peace legislation and moves towards democratic integration."




'Women cannot be defined by their victimhood'




Nesrin Akgül emphasised that women's responsibilities and role in the Peace and Democratic Society Process are decisive. She continued: "It cannot be a coincidence that women are regarded as the most effective force responsible for both silencing weapons and achieving social reconstruction in discussions surrounding the Peace and Democratic Society Process. In every conflict-resolution process, how women will participate has been one of the central questions and challenges. We must ask: Why are women the first to come to mind when peace is mentioned? Let me take that question further: Why are women primarily defined as those who have suffered the most and whose rights have been violated most severely? For women like us, who have waged a struggle for liberation, the identity and historical position from which women's presence in the peace process is defined are even more important.




During this transitional period, many people ask where we, as Kurdish women, stand or will stand in the peace process. We ask ourselves the same question. However, defining Kurdish women primarily through the suffering we have experienced is an incomplete and potentially problematic approach. Why? Because we are a women's movement that has not only paid the price of this war through resistance but has also decided how we want to live and succeeded in building that life.




As women who have waged a liberation struggle, we have a history of becoming guerrillas in the mountains, being captured and imprisoned, and establishing ourselves within political mechanisms in society. As women who resisted throughout this war, we built and institutionalised many things. Through our organisation, we became a distinct and autonomous structure. We achieved these gains through extraordinary acts of courage. We cannot become a party to peace solely on the basis of our victimhood. We want to consolidate our achievements and extend them throughout society. We want to realise the peace process through the political development of women's liberation.




We do not envision peace merely as a means of ending the suffering we have experienced. That would make us passive. We participate in the peace process as subjects of social transformation, and we will continue to do so. Of course, I do not regard these definitions as opposites. Both suffering and resistance are outcomes that emerge through a process. The question is knowing how to transform those outcomes into achievements. We position ourselves as the bearers of the political vision and social will that will build peace. We are women who intervene in the construction of a new social life through our experience of resistance. As women, we are the force that will shape the social and political relations of that new life."




'Women's achievements must lead to social transformation'




Nesrin Akgül said that Kurdish women had achieved significant gains through their struggle, ranging from free and equal relationships and equal representation to establishing their own decision-making mechanisms and challenging male-dominated thinking. She said: "We have extraordinary experiences, but these experiences and achievements have not yet become a force for social transformation. As Kurdish women, we have made gains that were far from easy, from free and equal relationships and the culture of comradeship to equal representation and the establishment of our own decision-making mechanisms. We have developed the capacity to transform men and created practical spaces in which to achieve this. We have numerous areas of success. These have naturally been recognised as achievements of Kurdish women's struggle and resistance. However, we have still not generated sufficient transformative power in society on issues ranging from family relationships and relations between women and men to policies concerning children. One of the conditions necessary for this is the establishment of peace so that the women's movement is no longer criminalised, obstructed or subjected to legal repression. These are all areas of reconstruction that can only be secured through democratic integration. For the state to adopt a democratic approach to integration, it is not enough merely to recognise the legal existence of the Kurdish people, other peoples and identities. Its deeply entrenched patriarchal laws and practices must also change.




Preventing violence against women is important, but so is legally recognising women as equal citizens, guaranteeing their right to make decisions about their own bodies and introducing comprehensive legal arrangements to ensure their equal participation in political and economic decision-making. There must be a legal process that transforms the social and institutional relations that make violence against women possible. Women's access to healthcare, education and public services in their mother tongues must be guaranteed, and the multiple forms of discrimination against women must be legally eliminated. We believe genuine peace can be established through a series of legal arrangements for peace, extending to the creation of autonomous but public courts for women in cases of femicide."




'Women are developing their own peace policy'




Nesrin Akgül said that women were establishing their own organisations and mechanisms to facilitate the transition from negative to positive peace. She also emphasised the importance of bringing women from different backgrounds together and creating opportunities for dialogue.




Nesrin Akgül described the conference "Women Side by Side, Talking About the Future", organised by the Peace and Reconstruction Foundation (BİV), as an important gathering. She said: "To move from the negative peace process we are currently experiencing towards positive peace, we are working to develop our own autonomous forms of organisation and establish the necessary mechanisms. What matters to us is ensuring that this becomes a process encompassing all women through an understanding of the democratic nation. The recent conference organised by BİV, 'Women Side by Side, Talking About the Future', was an important gathering in this regard. Women from all sections of society participated.




It was also important that we wanted to hold this gathering with women representatives from the Justice and Development Party (AKP), which belongs to the political side with which we are negotiating. Although the relevant representatives did not attend the conference, and despite some criticism of their proposed participation, I believe the invitation itself was important. It was a significant call to overcome the divisions created by those in power and the dominant patriarchal political system. Of course, everyone has political grievances and matters that need to be confronted. Everyone would surely acknowledge that Kurdish women, as one of the groups that have paid the highest price, have demands for accountability and confrontation with the state.




However, meaningful confrontation in such processes first requires spaces where people can develop empathy, understand one another and listen to each other face to face. This is what we call dialogue and negotiation. By creating these spaces, we can listen to one another, criticise one another, make ourselves understood and learn tolerance. We can call this the establishment of internal peace. Politics is achieved, above all, through the ability to live together, talk and communicate. Such gatherings therefore acquire meaning not only as expressions of our shared desire for peace but also as spaces where we can discuss how to achieve it. Organising peace as women and succeeding together can make us a leading force."




'We are establishing women's monitoring committees'




Nesrin Akgül stressed that women must not merely observe the process but must actively monitor and implement it. She concluded: "Together with BİV, we are establishing women's monitoring committees, both for women guerrillas who will return from the mountains and to observe, monitor and implement possible steps towards peace. By correctly identifying the needs and priorities of this period, we are coming together as women to develop our own peace policy and the path through which it will be pursued.




The most important need of this period is to believe that we will bring about peace. Notice that I am not saying we should believe peace will come. I am saying we must believe that we will bring peace and build it ourselves. Unfortunately, the negative experiences of the past and the failure to take necessary steps can create a sense of disbelief. This leaves us passive and reduces us to spectators. As women, we will discuss how to build peace and act with confidence in our own collective strength to achieve it."

title: Karayılan: The first step that must be taken is to open the doors of Imrali
content:
Murat Karayılan, Commander of the People's Defence Centre (HSM), talked to Egîd Sîrwan on Stêrk TV about the ongoing political process.




Karayılan said that journalists, politicians and intellectuals must be allowed to visit Imrali.




We publish excerpts of the interview. 




There has been a political process underway in Bakurê Kurdistan (North Kurdistan) for the past two years. During these two years, you have taken numerous steps. Most recently, you withdrew your forces from Bakur and Metîna. The Movement Leadership also issued a statement, declaring that there is no longer any situation that could lead to a risk of confrontation between you and the Turkish state. However, there have been no visible steps taken by the state, and the Peace and Politicisation Commission has still not been put into operation. What is the current situation, and how do you assess the process?




Two days ago, an official statement was issued on behalf of our Movement Leadership. The steps taken, and the results achieved were outlined in that statement. Therefore, there is no need to repeat them here.




In brief, the situation is as follows: From the day the process began until today, we have taken numerous steps. We have done everything necessary to demonstrate that we are determined to advance this strategy, that we have no hesitation in it, and that we genuinely want this Peace and Democratisation Process to move forward.




In contrast, however, very few steps have been taken by the Turkish state or government. The measures necessary to build trust have yet to be implemented. MIT President Ibrahim Kalın spoke at a conference in recent days and said: "This issue has two dimensions. One is the laying down of arms, and the other is democratisation and democratic reforms."




I would therefore ask Mr Ibrahim Kalın: "That is correct, but where is democratisation? Where are the reforms?" Developments in Turkey are moving not towards democratisation, but in the opposite direction. There is repression and a continuing situation of arrests and detentions. So far, nothing has happened that would give us reason to hope that democratisation will take place.




They may say: "First, lay down your arms, and then we will implement reforms." But if they genuinely intend to introduce reforms, there are many things they can do right now, and they should do them. This cannot work through an approach of "You do this first, and then I will do that." The way forward must be opened.




Steps that build trust are necessary 




The issue of trust is extremely important. It cannot be treated as something ordinary or superficial. Concrete steps that inspire confidence are necessary. Turkish state officials sometimes make various statements. They interpret many things according to their own perspective. They present the steps taken by Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] by us as their own achievements and try to portray them to society in that way. However, no steps that would genuinely build trust have been taken so far. These are the circumstances that cause us concern. There is nothing else behind our concerns.




The Turkish state is still pursuing anti-Kurdish policies




We said: "We have made strategic decisions. We are now removing armed struggle from our agenda. We will no longer wage war against Turkey. We will integrate into the Democratic Republic."




Isn't that precisely the purpose of democratic integration? Yet those on the other side are not putting an end to their hostility. They continue to use the language of opposition and enmity. Politics is still being conducted on this basis. Even diplomacy is being pursued on an anti-Kurdish basis.




We say that the Turkish state must abandon its anti-Kurdish stance. On this matter, we have not developed an optimistic assessment. The Turkish state's conduct up to now has given us no reason to form such an assessment. These are the things that create doubt and concern for us.




We are neither inexperienced nor children; we have experience. Our people and our Movement have accumulated historical experience. Leader Apo says: "I neither deceive nor am I deceived." Therefore, it is entirely wrong to portray our concerns as though they stem from some kind of personal reservations. That is not the case, nor is such a thing possible. We are people who have sacrificed ourselves for our people. That is the truth.




Our concern is the future of Leader Apo, our people and Turkey




What concerns us is the future of Leader Apo, our people and Turkey. Leader Apo is the leader of this people, and he is still in prison. How could we not be concerned about that? We do have certain reservations, and that is true. This is because the state has still not taken the steps necessary to build trust. However, everything we have done has been aimed at building trust.




At the theoretical level, we developed a Manifesto. This was not simply the development of a tactical approach! We made a Congress decision. Leader Apo developed the Manifesto for Peace and a Democratic Society. Now all our cadres are receiving training on the basis of this Manifesto.




What did we say at our Congress? "We are dissolving the PKK, abandoning armed struggle and making democratic politics our fundamental approach. However, Leader Apo must lead this process."




So, go ahead and open the way for Leader Apo so that the process can move forward more rapidly. Without this, naturally, it will not progress quickly.




We have always emphasised that Leader Apo must lead the process. If the way is not opened for him to do so, the process cannot move forward in this manner. Some people interpret the slow pace of the process in different ways. But this is the reason: the state is not taking the necessary confidence-building steps. The most important factor in building trust is the state's attitude towards Leader Apo, its attitude towards our people and towards our comrades in prison. There is still hostility in the prisons.




Our steps demonstrate our sincerity




For example, a few days ago, Tuncer Sağlam lost his life in prison. He had cancer, but he was not released, and he died as a martyr. What crime had he committed? He had allegedly engaged in propaganda for the organisation. Yet we have already dissolved the organisation. In other words, the organisation has dissolved itself, and there is a ceasefire process underway. At a time when efforts should be made to develop friendships, a Kurdish politician is arrested on the grounds that he "engaged in propaganda for an illegal organisation". He is not released despite his condition, and he dies as a result. Even though the Forensic Medicine Institute had issued a medical report stating that he should not remain in prison, he was still not released.




It is clear that a fascistic mentality remains in operation. So how can we not be concerned? There is no visible progress here, only rhetoric. What is needed is action, and we have taken action.




Look, let me be clear: we are continuing to take practical steps even now. The steps we have taken previously, as well as those we have taken in recent days, demonstrate just how determined and sincere we are about this process.




Now let the state demonstrate its sincerity as well.




Leader Apo's role must be clearly defined




There is an agenda for the Peace and Politicisation Commission to begin its work in the coming days. Of course, this commission must be officially recognised by the state. In other words, the state needs to make an official announcement. It must also clearly state what Leader Apo's role in this commission will be, and the commission must officially begin its work.




The first step to take is to open the doors of Imrali 




Another issue is what the state or the AKP government is saying. They claim: "Society is not ready for Öcalan's release or freedom." But you are not doing anything to prepare society! Does Turkish society know how beneficial Leader Apo has been to the Turkish state over these past two years? No, it does not.




Why? Because the authorities claim credit for the developments that have taken place, saying, "We did this."




There have been so many developments during this period, and the region is in turmoil. Everyone is preparing for war. Yet Turkey is in a relatively comfortable position under these circumstances, isn't it? Why is it comfortable? Because of this process.




If the work being carried out were accurately communicated to the public, public opinion would change.




The authorities are not doing this themselves, and they are not allowing Leader Apo to do it either. Therefore, as they previously promised, both the commission must be officially established and the doors of Imrali must be opened.




That is the first step that needs to be taken.




Leader Apo must be free. However, the first step that must be taken is to open the doors of Imrali. At the very least, he should be able to speak to the Turkish press and explain his position himself. You are not doing it, so let Leader Apo do it himself.




Some sections of society now ask: "Why do they attach so much importance to the press? Why do they want journalists and intellectuals to come?"




This is the reason.




We want to advance the process. Therefore, Turkish public opinion must also be able to see the truth and be prepared. Making the truth known is an important matter in this regard.




The ball is now in Turkey's court




In short, the Turkish state must take action. I said this once before, but subsequently we took further steps. Therefore, the ball is now entirely in Turkey's court.




We need to see what they are going to do.




We have fulfilled everything that was within our power during this period. As stated in the declaration issued by the Movement Leadership, the situation is now such that the Turkish state or the Turkish military can no longer claim that there is a threat against them from the PKK or the Apoist Movement. For this reason, it is now up to them to take the necessary steps.




Naturally, the fundamental issue is Leader Apo's freedom. However, before that, Leader Apo's working conditions must be improved, the commission must be officially established and journalists, politicians and intellectuals must be allowed to visit Imrali.




In other words, conditions must be created that will enable Leader Apo to lead the process. Creating these conditions is essential.

title: Two Revolutionary Guards killed, two others wounded in YRK actions
content:
The Press Center of the East Kurdistan Defense Units (YRK) issued a statement announcing the details of two actions they carried out in the cities of Bane and Serdeşt in Rojhilat (East Kurdistan).




The YRK stated that two actions had been conducted in central Serdeşt and the Bane region on November 15 and 16. Both actions were carried out in memory of Dersim Behar.




Dersim Behar, a member of the YRK, fell a martyr during clashes that followed an ambush by Iranian forces in Serdeşt region on the night of November 11.




According to the statement, specialized and professional YRK teams targeted a base of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in central Serdeşt on November 15. The base commander and one Revolutionary Guard were killed, while two other Revolutionary Guards were wounded.




On the other hand, another YRK unit killed an officer affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in Bane at 3:10 p.m. on November 16.




The YRK stated that both actions had been carried out to honor Dersim Behar’s memory and avenge her death.




The statement stressed that the YRK would respond to any attacks against its forces, defend itself within the framework of legitimate self-defense and deliver the necessary response at the appropriate time and place.

title: Triple lesbicidio de Barracas: llega el veredicto y movilizan a Tribunales para exigir que se reconozca el crimen de odio
content:
Foto: Ariel Gutraich / Archivo Agencia Presentes.




A más de dos años del ataque incendiario en una habitación de una pensión de Barracas, este miércoles 18 de noviembre se conocerá el veredicto del juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas. La Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más convoca a concentrarse desde las 9 frente al Palacio de Tribunales para exigir que la sentencia contra Justo Fernando Barrientos reconozca el ataque como un crimen de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género. 

La fiscalía y las querellas solicitaron prisión perpetua, mientras que la defensa pidió la absolución del acusado y, subsidiariamente, que se descarten los agravantes. El proceso busca establecer la responsabilidad penal por el ataque que terminó con la vida de Andrea Amarante, Pamela Cobbas y Roxana Figueroa y dejó gravemente herida a Sofía Castro Riglos.

 Por ANRed.







Este miércoles 18 de noviembre se conocerá el veredicto del juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas. 

La Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más convoca a concentrarse desde las 9 frente al Palacio de Tribunales para exigir que la sentencia contra Justo Fernando Barrientos reconozca el ataque como un crimen de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género

. La fiscalía y las querellas solicitaron prisión perpetua, mientras que la defensa pidió la absolución del acusado.




La audiencia ante el Tribunal Oral en lo Criminal y Correccional N° 5 comenzará a las 9:30 con las respuestas de las acusaciones a los planteos de la defensa y las últimas palabras del imputado. La lectura del veredicto está prevista para las 11. 

La convocatoria invita a organizaciones, activistas y a toda la comunidad a acompañar la jornada y reclamar justicia por Andrea Amarante, Pamela Cobbas y Roxana Figueroa, además de justicia y reparación para Sofía Castro Riglos, única sobreviviente del ataque

.




Imagen: archivo Perycia.




El hecho ocurrió durante la madrugada del 6 de mayo de 2024, en una habitación de una pensión ubicada en la calle Olavarría al 1600, en el barrio porteño de Barracas. Allí vivían las cuatro mujeres lesbianas, que compartían un espacio habitacional en un contexto de precariedad económica y habitacional. Según la acusación, Barrientos, vecino del lugar que había protagonizado episodios previos de hostigamiento y amenazas, arrojó un artefacto incendiario contra la habitación. Como consecuencia del ataque, Andrea, Pamela y Roxana murieron, mientras que Sofía sobrevivió con graves secuelas.




Durante el juicio oral, que comenzó el 18 de mayo de este año, las querellas y la fiscalía sostuvieron que el ataque estuvo motivado por el odio hacia la orientación sexual de las víctimas. Los testimonios de vecinas y allegadas reconstruyeron las situaciones de hostigamiento que atravesaban las mujeres, mientras que las pericias de bomberos y especialistas apuntaron a que el incendio fue intencional. 

Las acusaciones solicitaron prisión perpetua y reclamaron que se contemplen los agravantes de odio por orientación sexual y de género, junto con los restantes agravantes penales

.




Imagen: archivo Enfant Terrible.




Una de las particularidades del proceso fue la participación de 

una querella colectiva impulsada por la Federación Argentina LGBT (FALGBT+)

, que representa a la comunidad en el juicio. Su intervención constituye un antecedente inédito en un debate judicial de estas características y fue posible luego de que la Cámara de Casación habilitara su incorporación, tras anteriores rechazos durante la etapa de instrucción.




Por su parte, la defensa de Barrientos, encabezada por 

Ricardo Antonio Richiello

, pidió la absolución por el beneficio de la duda y cuestionó las pruebas testimoniales y periciales presentadas durante el debate. De manera subsidiaria, solicitó que se descarte la aplicación de los agravantes de odio y violencia de género y que, en caso de una condena, se considere una figura penal menos grave. También cuestionó la constitucionalidad de la prisión perpetua y las medidas de reparación económica reclamadas para Sofía.




Imagen: Agencia Presentes.




Desde la Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más remarcaron que el reclamo excede la determinación de la responsabilidad penal del acusado: «Exigimos que la causa se nombre como lesbicidio y que la sentencia contemple el agravante de odio por orientación sexual e identidad de género, además de la violencia de género».




En el comunicado difundido ante la instancia decisiva del proceso, la organización sostuvo: «

Nombrar el lesbicidio es dar cuenta de una violencia con su propia historia, su propia lógica y sus propias víctimas. Lo sabemos y lo repetimos: lo que no se nombra, no existe, y la impunidad sólo genera más violencia

».




La concentración de este miércoles buscará que el tribunal reconozca judicialmente el carácter lesboodiante del ataque y que la sentencia contemple las medidas de justicia y reparación reclamadas. «¡Por existencias lésbicas sin violencia ni agresión! ¡Lesbicidios nunca más!», expresaron desde la Coordinadora, que cerró la convocatoria con las consignas: «¡Justicia para Andrea, Pamela y Roxana! ¡Justicia y reparación para Sofía! Como dijimos con Pepa Gaitán: ¡Justicia es que no vuelva a pasar!».

title: Pisa, depositi di esplosivi: la città sempre più esposta ai rischi della guerra
content:
Due nuovi depositi di munizioni a San Giusto, un hangar da 40 milioni e un aeroporto che ogni anno accoglie quasi sei milioni di passeggeri. Chi garantisce la sicurezza della popolazione?




Un’interessante inchiesta condotta dal 

Movimento No Base.

 




All’interno dell’aeroporto militare di Pisa vogliono realizzare due nuovi depositi destinati allo stoccaggio di esplosivi e munizionamento. Non si tratta di un’ipotesi o di un progetto ancora indefinito. A confermarlo è il capitolato speciale d’appalto dell’Aeronautica Militare, che descrive nel dettaglio le opere previste, le loro finalità e i costi.




Il progetto prevede la costruzione di due riservette di tipo igloo, strutture in cemento armato destinate alla conservazione di materiale esplosivo, accompagnate da bastionature di protezione, una tettoia per lo stoccaggio temporaneo degli esplosivi, una recinzione perimetrale con cancello carrabile elettrificato e un locale uffici. L’importo a base di gara è di oltre 5,5 milioni di euro. Il 28 ottobre 2026 l’appalto è stato aggiudicato per un impegno complessivo indicato in oltre 6,1 milioni di euro. Secondo la documentazione progettuale resa pubblica da Diritti in Comune, ciascuna delle due strutture sarebbe dimensionata per una capacità indicativa di dieci tonnellate di esplosivo netto equivalente, per un totale iniziale di venti tonnellate. La stessa documentazione segnala inoltre la possibilità di predisporre in futuro altre quattro riservette, che porterebbero la capacità complessiva potenziale a sessanta tonnellate.




Ma il dato che più dovrebbe richiamare l’attenzione della cittadinanza non è soltanto la quantità di materiale che potrà essere conservata. È la funzione che queste strutture sono chiamate a svolgere. Il capitolato spiega infatti che la necessità di stoccare munizionamento e materiali esplosivi, indicati con la denominazione 

HOT CARGO

, deriva da esigenze operative direttamente collegate all’attività di volo e alla presenza di un 

Air Terminal Operation Centre

 della JMOU Italia. Non siamo quindi davanti a un intervento edilizio generico all’interno di un’area militare: l’obiettivo dichiarato è dotare lo scalo di una nuova capacità di deposito e gestione di munizionamento ed esplosivi funzionale alle attività militari, anche a quelle connesse ai teatri di guerra.




È questo passaggio che rende il progetto particolarmente rilevante per Pisa. La città ospita la 46ª Brigata Aerea, uno dei principali reparti italiani per il trasporto militare di personale, mezzi e materiali. L’aeroporto militare costituisce una componente essenziale del sistema infrastrutturale della Difesa, ma si trova anche al centro di un contesto urbano densamente abitato e condivide lo spazio aeroportuale con lo scalo civile Galileo Galilei. La realizzazione dei depositi aggiunge dunque una funzione nuova e significativa a un’infrastruttura che già svolge un ruolo militare rilevante.




Un aeroporto, due funzioni, milioni di passeggeri




C’è un elemento che rende la vicenda pisana particolarmente delicata e che non può essere lasciato sullo sfondo: l’aeroporto militare non è un’infrastruttura separata dalla vita civile della città. La gestione dello scalo civile è affidata a Toscana Aeroporti, società il cui presidente è 

Marco Carrai

, che ricopre anche l’incarico di console onorario dello Stato di Israele per Toscana, Emilia-Romagna e Lombardia. Il sedime e le infrastrutture militari fanno invece capo all’Aeronautica Militare. Le due funzioni convivono nello stesso sistema aeroportuale.




Nel 2025 lo scalo ha registrato quasi sei milioni di passeggeri. A questi numeri si aggiungono le centinaia di lavoratrici e lavoratori che ogni giorno operano nei servizi aeroportuali, nella movimentazione delle merci, nella manutenzione, nella sicurezza e nelle attività connesse allo scalo. Intorno all’aeroporto si trovano inoltre quartieri abitati da decine di migliaia di persone, a partire da San Giusto e San Marco. 

Ma non ci sono soltanto le abitazioni e le infrastrutture aeroportuali: nelle vicinanze si sviluppano alcune delle principali arterie di comunicazione della città e dell’intera area pisana, come la via Aurelia e la superstrada Firenze-Pisa-Livorno (Fi-Pi-Li), percorse quotidianamente da un intenso traffico di automobili, mezzi pesanti e lavoratori pendolari. A queste si aggiunge la rete ferroviaria che converge sulla stazione di Pisa Centrale, uno dei principali nodi ferroviari della Toscana, attraversato ogni giorno da treni regionali e a lunga percorrenza.




È questa la specificità che dovrebbe essere al centro di ogni valutazione: 

la realizzazione di depositi per esplosivi e munizionamento avviene all’interno di un aeroporto nel quale transitano ogni anno milioni di passeggeri e che è inserito in un tessuto urbano abitato, attraversato da strade ad alta intensità di traffico e da importanti collegamenti ferroviari

. Non basta quindi richiamare genericamente il rispetto delle norme tecniche previste per i depositi militari. 




Le documentazioni e gli studi pubblicamente individuati finora sul tema delle distanze di sicurezza e della pericolosità dei depositi militari fanno riferimento a contesti aeroportuali esclusivamente militari, nei quali non è presente un traffico civile di passeggeri paragonabile a quello del Galilei.




La questione non può essere risolta limitandosi a dire che le riservette saranno costruite secondo le prescrizioni tecniche. Occorre sapere quali scenari incidentali siano stati considerati, quali distanze di sicurezza siano state calcolate e rispetto a quali elementi territoriali, quali aree siano interessate dalle eventuali conseguenze di un incidente e quali procedure siano previste per proteggere passeggeri, lavoratori e abitanti. 

Sono state considerate anche la via Aurelia, la Fi-Pi-Li e le linee ferroviarie che attraversano l’area pisana?

 È necessario conoscere inoltre come siano state valutate le operazioni di movimentazione e trasporto del materiale esplosivo, dentro e fuori il sedime aeroportuale.




La sicurezza di un deposito non riguarda soltanto la sua struttura: riguarda anche ciò che si trova intorno, le attività che si svolgono nelle vicinanze e le persone che potrebbero essere coinvolte.




La domanda politica è inevitabile: 

chi ha valutato il rischio per la popolazione e in quale sede queste valutazioni sono state discusse?

 Il Comune di Pisa e la Regione Toscana sono stati informati del progetto? Hanno ricevuto la documentazione relativa alla sicurezza e alle eventuali ricadute sui quartieri? Esiste una valutazione specifica delle interferenze con il traffico civile e con le infrastrutture stradali e ferroviarie? Quali piani di emergenza sono stati predisposti?




Non è accettabile che una trasformazione di questa portata venga considerata una faccenda esclusivamente interna all’organizzazione militare. Quando un’infrastruttura destinata alla conservazione di esplosivi viene realizzata in un aeroporto frequentato da milioni di persone, la sicurezza dei cittadini diventa una questione prioritaria.




Non soltanto depositi: i 40 milioni per il nuovo hangar militare




I nuovi depositi non sono l’unico investimento che negli ultimi anni ha riguardato il rafforzamento delle infrastrutture militari all’interno dell’aeroporto pisano. Un altro progetto, già denunciato da Una Città in Comune, riguarda la costruzione di un nuovo grande hangar militare, per il quale il Ministero della Difesa aveva previsto uno stanziamento di circa 40 milioni di euro nel triennio 2024-2026.




L’aviorimessa è destinata a ospitare velivoli da trasporto militare come i C-130J e i C-27J, aerei utilizzati per la movimentazione di personale, mezzi e materiali. Si tratta di una struttura che rafforza le capacità operative e logistiche della 46ª Brigata Aerea e, più in generale, il ruolo dell’aeroporto pisano nel sistema del trasporto militare.




La vicenda ha avuto ulteriori sviluppi amministrativi: nel 2026 risultano pubblicati nuovi interventi relativi al completamento dell’Hangar GEA. Per questo non è corretto presentare il progetto come definitivamente cancellato o tuttora fermo senza ricostruire l’intero iter. Resta però il dato politico e finanziario: un investimento di decine di milioni di euro per potenziare le infrastrutture militari dello scalo, che si aggiunge oggi alla realizzazione dei depositi per esplosivi e munizionamento.




Eppure, mentre si discute di investimenti, appalti e necessità operative, resta in secondo piano la questione di come queste trasformazioni si inseriscano in uno scalo utilizzato quotidianamente dalla popolazione civile. La domanda non è soltanto quanto costino queste opere, ma quale modello di aeroporto e quale ruolo per la città si stiano costruendo.




Il rafforzamento dell’hub militare toscano




Per comprendere il significato degli interventi bisogna allargare lo sguardo. I nuovi depositi e il progetto dell’hangar non compaiono in un territorio privo di infrastrutture militari e logistiche, ma si inseriscono in un processo più ampio di rafforzamento delle capacità strategiche della costa toscana. Pisa, Livorno e l’area di Camp Darby sono nodi di un sistema nel quale trasporto militare, logistica, infrastrutture portuali, collegamenti ferroviari e attività industriali si trovano sempre più strettamente connessi.




Un documento particolarmente utile per comprendere questa trasformazione è la proposta di istituzione della Zona Logistica Semplificata della Regione Toscana, elaborata nel novembre 2024. La proposta descrive una struttura logistica policentrica, nella quale i porti di Livorno, Piombino, Marina di Carrara e Portoferraio vengono messi in relazione con l’Interporto Toscano Amerigo Vespucci di Guasticce, l’Interporto di Prato e l’aeroporto di Pisa, individuato come nodo di prossimità e di completamento funzionale. Il documento insiste sulla necessità di integrare i diversi poli infrastrutturali attraverso collegamenti stradali, ferroviari e intermodali, costruendo una piattaforma logistica capace di collegare la costa con i principali corridoi nazionali e internazionali.




Quella proposta riguarda la logistica e lo sviluppo economico regionale ma descrive una trasformazione territoriale fondamentale anche quando si analizzano le infrastrutture della Difesa: la crescente integrazione tra aeroporti, porti, interporti, reti ferroviarie e piattaforme di movimentazione delle merci. In un territorio attraversato da infrastrutture militari e da nodi strategici per la mobilità di materiali e mezzi, la distinzione tra funzioni civili e militari diventa un tema politico centrale. Le infrastrutture civili possono infatti assumere anche funzioni di interesse strategico e militare, secondo logiche di duplice uso, senza per questo diventare automaticamente infrastrutture militari.




È in questo contesto che va letto il rafforzamento dell’aeroporto pisano. La realizzazione dei depositi non è un episodio isolato, ma un ulteriore tassello nella crescita delle capacità operative e logistiche dello scalo. A quali missioni e flussi queste strutture dovranno servire? A quali interessi rispondono?




Il quadro che emerge è quello di un 

hub militare toscano

 che non coincide con una singola base, ma si costruisce attraverso la connessione di più infrastrutture: l’aeroporto militare di Pisa, Camp Darby, il porto di Livorno, i collegamenti ferroviari e stradali, il sistema dei Navicelli e le reti industriali e tecnologiche presenti sul territorio. È una trasformazione che va osservata nella sua dimensione complessiva, perché il rafforzamento di un nodo accresce le possibilità operative dell’intero sistema.




Le risorse per la guerra, le risorse sottratte alla vita quotidiana




C’è infine una questione economica e sociale che non può essere separata da quella territoriale. Mentre si investono milioni di euro per nuove infrastrutture destinate a esplosivi, munizionamento e trasporto militare, le condizioni materiali di una parte crescente della popolazione continuano a peggiorare. Il costo degli affitti, delle bollette, dei generi alimentari e dei trasporti pesa sui bilanci familiari; i salari faticano a tenere il passo con il costo della vita; i servizi pubblici, dalla sanità alla scuola, attraversano una condizione di difficoltà che si traduce in liste d’attesa, carenze di personale e maggiori costi a carico delle famiglie.




Le scelte di spesa esprimono delle priorità politiche e oggi la crescita delle risorse destinate alla difesa e agli armamenti avviene in un contesto nel quale viene chiesto alla popolazione di accettare vincoli, sacrifici e ridimensionamenti della spesa sociale.




Per il Movimento No Base, questa direzione pone una questione che riguarda il modello di sviluppo e il ruolo assegnato ai territori. La Toscana viene progressivamente organizzata come una piattaforma nella quale logistica, infrastrutture, ricerca, industria e capacità militari possono concorrere a sostenere una proiezione strategica che supera ampiamente i confini regionali.




La questione riguarda anche la collocazione dell’Italia dentro gli equilibri militari internazionali e la crescente dipendenza dalle strategie della NATO e degli Stati Uniti. Quando infrastrutture, risorse pubbliche e territori vengono messi a disposizione di una crescente capacità di mobilitazione militare, le comunità locali rischiano di subire decisioni assunte altrove, pagandone pesantemente le conseguenze.




La città deve decidere




I nuovi depositi di esplosivi, insieme al progetto del nuovo hangar militare, pongono dunque una questione di contrapposizione tra esigenze del complesso militare industriale e bisogni sociali della cittadinanza. Riguardano anche livelli macro della vivibilità come la sicurezza collettiva, la trasparenza amministrativa, l’utilizzo delle risorse pubbliche e il futuro di un intento territorio.




Per il Movimento No Base, il progetto dei depositi va fermato.




La questione riguarda la direzione che sta prendendo il territorio e il ruolo che la Toscana viene chiamata a svolgere dentro la crescente economia di guerra. Di fronte a investimenti militari che aumentano e a una pressione sempre più forte per destinare risorse alla difesa, la priorità crescente della popolazione e’ la tutela delle persone, il rafforzamento dei servizi pubblici, la qualità del lavoro, la sicurezza dei quartieri e la possibilità per le comunità di decidere nei luoghi in cui vivono.




Un aeroporto che accoglie quasi sei milioni di passeggeri all’anno non può essere considerato una piattaforma operativa della Difesa.

La sicurezza della popolazione non può essere una variabile subordinata alle esigenze delle loro guerre!
