In 1868 he wrote, “thanks to a dialectics put in the service of a method more often metaphysical than scientific (which it is necessary to avoid confusing with the historical and objective method of Karl Marx), Proudhon has discovered in the social world some laws that observation confirms more from day to day; it is, however, incontestable that hypothesis still plays an infinitely more considerable role in the works of that thinker and that often he has concluded a priori or from insufficient observations: witness the conclusions of his last works relative to the social role of strikes and trades-unions, and those relative to the tendencies of modern production towards association and thus towards the collective appropriation of land and the large instruments of labor, two phenomena of which Proudhon has misunderstood the immense scope from the point of view of the organization of the future, and that he condemned even in the name of reason and logic, while Marx, already well before 1848, in the name of observation and history, considers them the two principal elements of the solution of the social problem. The majority of the writers of Liberté have made the defects of Proudhon their own by sacrificing, so to speak absolutely, his scientific side” (De Paepe 2014). It is unclear how De Paepe, who was six when The Poverty of Philosophy was published, acquired knowledge of Marx’s critique of Proudhon. He may have found an old copy of the book. Or perhaps he learnt this information from conversations with Marx and Eccarius at the conference and Marx’s critical obituary of Proudhon, which was published in February 1865 within Der Social-Demokrat (MECW 20, 26-33).

7It is not known how Cafiero first read the Communist Manifesto. One obvious source is Bakunin, who owned a German copy and his own Russian translation of it. Cafiero arrived at Bakunin’s on 20 May 1872 and then read aloud to Bakunin the first part of his letter to Engels on 31 May and the rest on 3 June. It was then sent to Engels on 19 June from Milan, one day after he had left Switzerland (Eckhardt 2016, 223-25). This was enough time in which to read the Manifesto, but I do not know if Cafiero had the required language skills. He definitely read Italian, English, and French to a high level. I have been unable to find evidence that he read German or Russian. This is indirectly supported by the fact that he first read Marx’s Capital in its French translation and not the German original. Bakunin could have read out the Manifesto to Cafiero by translating it in real time as he spoke, but there is no direct evidence that this happened. It has been suggested that the edition of the Manifesto that Cafiero read was the December 1871 English edition published by the American paper Woodhull & Claflin’s Weekly under the title German Communism – Manifesto of the German Communist Party. This is because it would explain why Cafiero referred to the originally titled Manifesto of the Communist Party as the “Manifesto of the German Communist Party” in the letter (Eckhardt 2016, 224, 518n167). Engels had mentioned the publication of this translation in a 15 February 1872 letter to Wilhelm Liebknecht (MECW 44, 319). On 17 March Engels complained to Friedrich Sorge, who lived in the United States, about the quality of the recent translations and asked him to send over “50 copies of the issue of Woodhull & Claflin's which contains the translation of the Communist Manifesto, and 50-100 of the issues of the Socialiste with the French translation” (ibid, 343, 643n440). Engels could have forwarded one of these new copies, or the previous one he owned, to Cafiero. Previously when Engels had sent documents to Cafiero he wrote a letter informing him that they were on their way (ibid, 171). No such letter for the Manifesto has been found. If Engels sent Cafiero a copy it was probably attached to the lost letter that was written between 29 February and 9 March (Eckhardt 2016, 225). It should also be kept in mind that Bakunin referred to the Manifesto as “the famous manifesto of the German Communists” in the unsent October 1872 letter to the editors of La Liberté and his 1873 book Statism and Anarchy (Bakunin 1973, 252; Bakunin 1990, 146). As a result, Bakunin could potentially have also been the reason why Cafiero used this phrase.

8Engels privately complained about this distortion of his and Marx’s ideas in a few letters. See MECW 49, 34-6, 59-63, 197; MECW 50, 163-65, 264-67.

9It is unclear why this is the case. In the preface they claim that “the present memoir, ‘God and the State,’ is really a fragment of a letter or report. Composed in the same manner as most of Bakunin's other writings, it has the same literary fault, lack of proportion; moreover it breaks off abruptly: we have searched in vain to discover the end of the manuscript” (Bakunin 1970, 6). But this account was later contradicted by Guillaume, who had originally provided Reclus with the relevant manuscripts. He complained in 1908, “that last assertion is incomprehensible to me, for the end of the manuscript (pages 248-340) was found, along with the part published by Reclus and Cafiero, in the case passed by me to Élisée Reclus; that case also contained pages 139-148, which Reclus and Cafiero have not included, a proof of pages 139-148, and a proof of pages 149-210; the second of these proofs bore corrections of style and some deletions in the hand of Reclus and in one other hand; I find it still more difficult to explain, in view of that circumstance, that the editors of 1882 could have called this piece “a fragment from a letter or report.” This little literary artifice — for that is probably what it is — was not necessary to make the reader appreciate the high value of those pages” (Guillaume, 2016).

author: MissyRedaktion
title: Der neue Medienpass
content:
Wir verbünden uns mit GoodImpact, Krautreporter, Übermedien und Surplus und launchen den Medienpass, mit dem du auf alle digitalen Inhalte von allen fünf Publikationen zugreifen. Das haben wir vor:

Gemeinsam mit GoodImpact, Krautreporter, Übermedien und Surplus launchen wir den neuen Medienpass. Dieser erlaubt dir, unbegrenzt auf alle digitalen Inhalte von allen fünf Publikationen zugreifen.

im Probe-Pass: 90 Tage lang als Jahrespass: 365 Tage lang

Und das für nur 15 Euro im Monat!

Fernab großer Verlage gibt es im deutschsprachigen Raum eine vielfältige, unabhängige Medienlandschaft – mit vielen tollen Inhalten.

Das Problem: Bisher bedeutete jedes neue Angebot auch ein weiteres Abo. Mehrere unabhängige Medien zu lesen und zu unterstützen, geht schnell ins Geld. Auf Dauer wird das schlicht zu teuer und zwingt zur Qual der Wahl. Das Ergebnis: Du verpasst spannenden Content bei anderen – und wir viele Leser*innen!

Das ändern wir jetzt: Mit dem Medienpass kannst du für einen günstigen Preis deinen Horizont erweitern und fünf unabhängige Medien supporten. Denn in Zeiten von Desinformation, KI-Slop und aufgeheizten Diskursen braucht es deren kritische Berichterstattung ganz besonders!

Mit dem Medienpass hast du Zugang zu den Themen, Expertisen und Perspektiven von fünf Medien, die sich für kritische Berichterstattung, verlässliche Fakten und eine starke Demokratie engagieren.

Der Medienpass kostet einmalig 180€ für ein Jahr oder 53€ für 90 Tage – das sind nur 15 € im Monat und über 50% preiswerter als die jeweiligen Einzelabos der fünf Medien kombiniert. (Wenn dir das zu viel ist: Wir freuen uns auch sehr, wenn du ein reguläres Missy Online-Abo für 5€/Monat abschließt.)

Uns kennst du ja schon <3 Wir stehen seit 18 Jahren für queeren und intersektionalen Feminismus in Pop, Kultur und Politik. Die Missy erscheint alle zwei Monate in Print und Online. Unser Online-Angebot umfasst zusätzlich mehr als 4000 feministische Texte zu Pop, Kultur und Politik sowie den Pissy Podcast.

Die Plattformen berichten seit 2010 konstruktiv über gute Ideen und Lösungen. Getragen wird ihre Arbeit aktuell von ca. 6.000 Menschen, die uns durch eine Good Membership und freiwillige Beiträge unterstützen.

Das genossenschaftliche Online-Magazin wird von über 15.000 Mitgliedern getragen. Die Redaktion berichtet seit 2014 ohne Drama und tiefgründig über Bildungspolitik, Klima und weitere aktuelle Themen.

Seit zehn Jahren ist das Team die Instanz für Medienkritik. Getragen wird das Online-Magazin von 7.000 Abonnent:innen.

Surplus ist das Wirtschaftsmagazin, das sich um die Interessen der großen Mehrheit und nicht der Reichsten dreht. Täglich veröffentlicht Surplus Texte, wöchentlich Video- und Podcastformate und zweimonatlich ein digitales sowie gedrucktes Magazin.

Bestehende Abos werden angerechnet Wenn du bereits ein Missy Online-Abo hast (oder auch ein Abo bei einer der anderen Medien), wird dir dieses angerechnet. Das System erkennt nämlich deine e-Mail Adresse wieder. Das heißt: Du musst für Abos, die du schon hast, nicht doppelt zahlen!

Der Medienpass ist kein Abo Die Laufzeit vom Medienpass ist ein Jahr. Es gibt keine automatische Verlängerung. Und wenn du dir noch nicht ganz sicher bist: Mit dem Probe-Pass kannst du 90 Tage lang testen, ob dir der Medienpass taugt.

Erstmal nur für jetzt Das Angebot ist zeitlich befristet und endet am 6. Januar 2027

Faire Verteilung Alle Einnahmen werden gerecht zwischen den fünf Medien aufgeteilt. Jedes Medium bleibt absolut eigenständig.

We <3 Community Statt (vermeintlich) gegeneinander zu konkurrieren, bieten wir euch diesen Pass gemeinsam an. Wir wollen miteinander statt gegeneinander gegen den Rechtsruck kämpfen!

Dein Medienpass unterstützt unseren feministischen und unabhängigen Journalismus und hilft dabei, Missy zu erhalten. Danke für deinen Support, wir wissen ihn sehr zu schätzen! <3

Übrigens: Den Medienpass kann man auch als Geschenk-Pass für jemand anderen kaufen. Stichwort Weihnachten. Just saying ;)

author: Jake Bittle
title: Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects
content:
After years of negotiation, Congress is on the cusp of passing a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill that would make it far easier to build power plants and electric transmission lines in the United States. The bill was negotiated by a bipartisan group of senators including Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse, a noted climate hawk, and Republican Mike Lee, an opponent of environmental regulation. It has picked up support from 

clean

 

energy

 

advocates

 because it would promote more transmission lines to carry renewable power to cities, speed up review for solar and wind projects, and stop presidents from cancelling offshore wind farms. It has also been endorsed by many 

conservative

, 

business

, and 

fossil fuel

 groups, who say it would cut down on environmental red tape and speed up natural gas pipelines.




The bill has 

divided the climate movement

, separating groups focused on 

decarbonization

 from those focused on endangered species protection and environmental justice, but the most influential opposition has come from tribal nations. The bill would weaken a historic preservation law that tribes often use to protect cultural and religious sites from development, and numerous prominent Indigenous nations and organizations have said it harms tribal sovereignty.




While the bill cleared a procedural hurdle in the Senate last week, it remains unclear whether it will pass there or in the House. The negotiators who framed the bill say they believe they 

have the votes

, but a number of Democrats in both chambers have opposed the bill. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, has 

criticized

 what he called the bill’s “failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.” Nevada senator Catherine Cortez Masto, who voted to advance the bill, has said she won’t 

ultimately vote to pass it

, saying she “cannot ignore the concerns” of tribes in her state.




“Projects affecting tribal governments before were already fast-tracked, but now this allows for a super fast track,” said John Bathke, a member of the Navajo Nation, a former historic preservation officer for the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Reservation, and now a professor of Indigenous studies at San Diego City College.




The 1966 National Historic Preservation Act, passed in the wake of nationwide urban renewal efforts that demolished many old buildings, requires the federal government to consider the effect of construction projects on historic and cultural properties. (Most intact objects or properties that are more than 50 years old and have some kind of historical, cultural, or religious significance qualify under the law.) When you’re building a solar farm or a transmission line, that is a big undertaking: The area of review can extend for as much as 5 miles away from the project itself, and major transmission lines can be hundreds of miles long. Even if a project is visible a few miles away when you’re standing in a historic area, that still counts as a potential effect.




While tribal nations have control over infrastructure projects on their reservations, many tribes have cultural, religious, and political claims over areas that are outside their reservation boundaries. The historic preservation law is one of the only tools they have to stop or alter construction projects that might desecrate sacred territories or religious sites. 




“Even though a lot of these projects aren’t on reservation land, it’s part of their traditional homeland, it’s part of their spiritual landscape,” said Bathke. “That land still belongs to them and they belong to that land.”




Tribal nations have used this law to limit energy projects that they say would harm their sacred territories. In perhaps the best-known example, the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation 

sued the federal government

 in 2010 over its approval of a 6,000-acre solar farm on federal land in California, one of the first such projects in the United States. The tribe argued that the project would destroy religious sites and buried remains and that the government had rubber-stamped it after just a few meetings. A court sided with the tribe and the solar developer nixed the project, moving to build on private farmland instead. (Bathke was the tribe’s historic preservation officer — the tribal official who helps with historic reviews — during the solar dispute.)




Supporters of clean energy development have long sought to reform the law. They argue that historic preservation review has become a far more sweeping and burdensome process than the authors of the law intended, and that clean energy projects are affected more than any other type of construction. The onus is heaviest for transmission lines — in some cases, the area under review can extend to hundreds of square miles, and entire rivers or valleys can be considered historic sites. Since transmission wires can be seen from miles away, it’s hard to eliminate all visual impacts associated with building them. 




“As written, [the historic preservation law] is a modest procedural check on hasty decisionmaking. … In practice, it has grown into a substantive burden on building infrastructure of all kinds,” write Ben Schifman and Aiden Mackenzie, two research analysts at the Institute for Progress, in a 

report on how the law affects energy development

. The Institute for Progress has been a leading advocate for reforming the law and for the bipartisan permitting bill. 




To illustrate their argument, Schifman and Mackenzie cite the example of SunZia, an $11 billion transmission line that carries wind energy west from New Mexico to California. The project took two decades to complete. The line had to secure permits from multiple state power regulators, but it also had to undergo a historic review process that covered an area twice the size of Delaware. Among many other things, the government had to consider whether being able to see the transmission line in the distance would harm the historic characteristics of thousands of different sites across multiple states. 




While the government undertook this review, a coalition of tribes in the area protested the process. One of their main arguments centered on the San Pedro River Valley, a landform in Arizona that is sacred to the Apache, O’odham, Hopi, and Zuni peoples. The tribes wanted the government to declare the entire valley a historic zone, which could have required SunZia to reroute its wires. The government declined to give the valley that designation, arguing that the tribes had not identified the issue early enough in the review process. The Tohono O’odham and the San Carlos Apache tribes along with a group of environmental nonprofits then sued to stop the line. They failed to halt construction before the wires joined the grid, but the case is still ongoing, and a court could still force the developer to alter the project if the tribes win. 




Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Mike Lee of Utah listen during a hearing on reforming the National Historic Preservation Act. The two senators are part of a bipartisan group behind the permitting reform bill moving through Congress.
 

Photo by Alex Wong / Getty Images




The initial version of the permitting bill limited the scope of the historic review process in several ways in an apparent attempt to avoid future SunZias. It made consultation with tribes effectively optional, allowing the federal government to move ahead with projects in cases where a tribe’s designated historic preservation official took too long to identify important sites. It outlined a definition for “traditional religious or cultural importance,” which had previously been open-ended under federal law. It narrowed the definition of a “visual” impact, requiring that such impacts “direct[ly]” and “significantly diminish” the historic value of a place; this standard is subjective, but it would likely exclude things like being able to see a wind turbine on the horizon. It also prohibited judges from halting construction work on projects if they find a flaw in a historic preservation analysis, as happened in the Quechan Tribe wind farm case; instead, judges could only order the federal government to redo its analysis as construction continued. 




These provisions provoked an immediate outcry from several tribal nations and Indigenous groups, who said it would threaten tribal sovereignty. A coalition of several major tribal groups, including the National Congress of American Indians, 

said that the bill

 was in “deep conflict with federal trust and treaty obligations” and that Senate negotiators were “proposing to facilitate the demolition of our heritage.”




Some lawmakers who support the bill expressed regret about their failure to incorporate Native interests.




 “We didn’t bring the tribes along on this … we could have done better on it in retrospect,” said Republican senator Alan Armstrong, who represents Oklahoma, 

in an interview

 with Punchbowl News.




Negotiators amended the bill earlier this month to address these concerns. The bill now makes tribal consultation mandatory throughout the historic review process, which isn’t the case under current law. It also prevents the government from taking over the historic review process when tribal officials are slow to respond. These changes are significant given that the Trump administration is 

already trying to weaken

 the historic review process through executive action. The administration’s rulemaking could limit the historic review process even if the permitting bill doesn’t pass. 




The tribes and tribal organizations that opposed the first version of the bill say these changes are nowhere near enough. Their primary areas of concern, including the limited definition of visual effects and the ban on injunctions, are still in the new version.




“While this amendment addresses select concerns, the authors ask Indian Country to be grateful Washington chose to take away fewer of our rights in the name of ‘progress,’” said Ira Matt, the head of the the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers and a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. He also said the bill erodes “protections we have spent decades fighting to secure” and that those supporting it had demonstrated a “fundamental failure to understand and respect Tribal sovereignty.” 




The Kayenta Solar Plant in the Navajo Nation is the first tribally-built and owned solar facility in the United States. Tribes that support the permitting bill say it would help attract investment for energy projects on tribal lands.
 

Jim West / UCG / Universal Images Group via Getty Images




It’s unlikely that lawmakers will strip the historic preservation section altogether. Many of the most suitable areas for clean energy development are on federal land in the west. In order to build enough clean energy to replace fossil fuels, developers will likely have to build projects that pass near tribal cultural sites. In that light, the bill’s historic preservation reform represents the biggest win for clean energy companies since the passage of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, which subsidized wind and solar construction and has since been largely repealed. 




Some tribal nations believe they themselves will benefit from the bill’s effort to speed up energy permitting. A few tribes have endorsed the bill, most of them tribes that have significant coal and oil resources. The Apsáalooke (Crow) tribe, whose reservation covers 2 million acres in Montana, 

told Senate negotiators last month

 that the bill could deliver “a predictable regulatory environment” and greater investment certainty” for “energy-producing tribes.” The tribe has significant coal reserves and has historically been a large coal producer, but its production has declined in recent years. The National Tribal Energy Association, which represents a number of fossil-fuel producing tribes, has also endorsed the bill. 




The bill will also strengthen the investment case for solar and wind on tribal lands, said Anthony Walters, a member of the Cherokee Nation and the vice president for government relations at the Alliance for Tribal Clean Energy, which helps tribes develop renewable energy. Walters says the main constraint that many tribes face is getting access to capital, and speedy environmental reviews and more transmission lines would make it easier for tribes to attract the money they need. 




Even so, he said the economic benefits of that development could never outweigh the potential destruction of sites that tribes hold sacred.




“The bill would help clean energy development projects across the board, so tribes would see the benefit of that,” he said. “But on the whole, right, we can’t do that at the expense of all the processes that tribes use to protect their interests. It’s a big trade-off.”




This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects

 on Nov 17, 2026.

content:
Berî nîvroya îro Sêşemê 17/11/2026, rêzdar Nêçîrvan Barzanî, Serokê Herêma Kurdistanê, pêşwaziyê li xatûna Reem Al-Abali Radovan, Wezîra Federal a Hevkariya Aborî û Geşepêdanê ya Almanyayê û şandeya pê re kir, ku ji hejmarek endamên Parlamentoya Almanyayê û berpirsên wezaretê û birêz karbirêkerê Balyozxaneya Almanyayê li Bexdayê pêk hatibû. author: EDRi
title: Open Letter: EDRi warns of EU’s undemocratic attempt to introduce surveillance in satellite-based communications
content:
The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union are currently negotiating two laws to regulate communications service providers, including satellite-based ones. In both laws, the Commission has sneakily attempted to attribute itself the possibility to impose intrusive surveillance, notably data retention and interception obligations, on those satellite operators through opaque procedures. EDRi and its members warns against these unchecked powers and asks the Parliament and the Council to stand for fundamental rights and the EU’s principles for good law-making.

EDRi and members concerned about attempt to introduce unlawful data retention obligations

EDRi and its members are writing to the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union to express their serious concerns about the attempt to introduce unlawful data retention obligations through EU authorisation procedures for satellite operators under the Digital Networks Act (DNA) and Mobile Satellite Services (MSS) Regulation proposals.

In short, the Commission could impose data retention and interception obligations on satellite operators and define their modalities through a comitology procedure, which is shrouded in secrecy. The discretionary powers granted to the Commission are therefore far-reaching, bypass essential EU democratic processes, and may have grave implications for the rights to privacy and data protection.

The introduction of data retention obligations in the DNA and the MSS are also wholly inappropriate as the Commission is currently assessing the impacts of data retention as part of a wider process to determine the need for a new EU framework or not. Furthermore, it is settled case-law by the Court of Justice of the European Union that the general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data is a serious interference with fundamental rights, and is incompatible with EU law as a preventive measure for combatting crime.

author: WoMin
title: Women Unite to Defend the Congo Basin Against Extractivism – A Call for Climate Justice at COP31
content:
As world leaders gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), taking place from 9–20 November 2026, women from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the Republic of Congo and Cameroon are raising an urgent message: there can be no climate justice without defending the Congo Basin, protecting community territories and recognising the leadership of women on the frontlines of environmental struggles.




The Congo Basin is one of the world’s most important ecological treasures, acting as the “

second lungs

 of the Earth”, after the Amazon, which is being decimated. Spanning over four million square kilometres across six countries, its forests, rivers and peatlands play a vital role in regulating the global climate, protecting biodiversity and sustaining millions of people. For Indigenous Peoples and local communities, the forest is not simply a natural resource; it is their home, heritage, identity and source of life.




Yet this vital ecosystem faces growing threats from mining, logging, oil and gas extraction, deforestation and expanding infrastructure. Across the Congo Basin, rising demand for minerals is increasing pressure on forests and community territories.




Recent investigations have 

documented

 mining concessions overlapping with community forests in the DRC, gold-mining-related 

forest destruction and water pollution

 in the Republic of Congo, and 

concerns over the impacts

 of the Lobé-Kribi iron-ore project on forests and livelihoods in Cameroon.




This exposes a growing contradiction: while governments promote renewable energy as a solution to the climate crisis, the extraction of minerals needed for the energy transition can create new threats to forests, water resources and the communities that depend on them.




For women in the Congo Basin, this is not an abstract debate. It means polluted rivers, disappearing food sources, loss of agricultural land and declining access to forests.




Women on the frontlines expose the cost of extractivism




To strengthen collective resistance, women and community organisations from the DRC, the Republic of Congo and Cameroon came together for a 

cross-border solidarity exchange

 to share stories of resistance, expose the impacts of extractivism and develop strategies to defend the Congo Basin.




Over three days, organisations including 

Centre d’Encadrement pour la Promotion de la Femme et la jeune fille

 (CEPF), 

Dynamique des femmes pour le développement

 (DYFED), 

Green Development Advocates

 (GDA), and the Association pour le Respect des Droit des population autochtones et du développement rural et du Droit de l’homme (ARPA2DH) 

shared their experiences and struggles. Testimonies from women in Lessoukou, Mayoko, Mangi, Bongonde and Bandzonko revealed the devastating impacts of mining and forest exploitation.




In Lessoukou, 17 of the community’s 24 villages are reportedly occupied by mining companies, threatening access to ancestral lands and traditional livelihoods. Élisé Matsanga, an Indigenous woman from Lessoukou, shared:







“

Agriculture once enabled us to feed our families and send our children to school. Today, because of corporate activities and the loss of access to our lands, we can no longer farm as we used to. We have lost our livelihoods

.”







In Mangi, Tshopo Province, Nyota described how communities are excluded from decisions affecting their territories while rivers become increasingly polluted.







“

We are forced to walk up to three kilometres to find safe drinking water, and sometimes even our children have no choice but to drink polluted water. Our lands, forests and rivers are our sources of livelihood, yet we watch helplessly as they are destroyed

.”







In Bandzonko, Republic of Congo, Odile, the village chief, 

described how mining pollution

 has forced women to walk up to 15 kilometres in search of water, exposing families to serious health risks. In Bongonde, Équateur Province, Annie Mboyo, a community woman, 

highlighted the disappearance

 of mushrooms, caterpillars, wild fruits and fish, resources that have traditionally sustained community food systems. Meanwhile, in Mayoko, Oko Jeanine, another community woman, denounced the lack of consultation and the destruction of agricultural fields by mining companies.







“

These lands belong to us. They are our heritage, our livelihoods and our identity. How can companies demand that we obtain permits to cultivate our own land while they extract minerals without consulting us?

”







These testimonies reveal that extractivism is not only rapidly destroying forests and ecosystems; it is also undermining women’s rights, food sovereignty, safety and dignity. Indigenous women face additional discrimination, land dispossession and heightened exposure to gender-based violence.




Beyond climate promises: communities demand accountability




As COP31 comes to a close, African women’s experiences bring urgency to discussions on the transition to clean energy and forest protection.




One prominent initiative on the table in this round of negotiations is the 

proposed 35-by-35 electrification pledge

, which aims to increase electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035. While this ambition supports the transition to cleaner energy, it also raises questions about growing mineral demand and the environmental and social costs of extraction.




COP31’s 

focus on stewarding forests, oceans and biodiversity

 is equally important for the Congo Basin. Protecting these ecosystems must mean more than recognising their role in regulating the global climate; it must also mean defending the rights, livelihoods and territories of the Indigenous Peoples and local communities who depend on them.




There can be no green transition that sacrifices the territories, livelihoods and rights of the people who protect our forests. Women on the frontlines are calling for a just transition that guarantees Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), upholds the Right to Say NO, protects community forests and ensures meaningful participation in decisions affecting their territories.




The question for COP31 is not simply how quickly the world can transition to cleaner energy, but whose lands, resources and livelihoods will pay the price?




The women of the Congo Basin remind world leaders that there can be no climate justice without protecting forests, respecting community rights and recognising women’s leadership.










(WoMin staff attending COP31 in Turkey. Picture: WoMin)










From solidarity to collective action




Beyond sharing experiences, participants at the cross-border exchange developed a common action plan to strengthen women’s leadership and community resistance. Priorities included mapping iron ore activities and impacts, strengthening knowledge of legal protections, promoting the Right to Say NO and FPIC, improving risk and safety strategies, and building advocacy.




One immediate commitment was to launch a collective advocacy action demanding access to safe drinking water for communities affected by extractive activities. These commitments demonstrate that women are not simply victims of environmental destruction. They are organisers, knowledge holders, defenders of territories and leaders of alternatives that place life, collective care and ecological sustainability at the centre.




Defending the Congo Basin is defending life




The cross-border exchange reaffirmed that protecting the Congo Basin cannot be separated from protecting the rights of the women, Indigenous Peoples and communities who have safeguarded these territories for generations.




As world leaders deliberate over climate solutions at COP31, the voices of women from the Congo Basin must not remain on the margins of global climate discussions. United across borders, these women and communities show that collective power and solidarity can challenge extractivism and defend the forests, territories, and livelihoods of present and future generations. Defending the Congo Basin 

is

 defending life, dignity and the future of our planet.

author: Priyanka Sharma
title: Africa on the Map, But Still Off the Table
content:
On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a non-binding resolution that might initially appear to belong to the relatively technical world of cartography. The resolution, “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa,” was introduced by Togo on behalf of the African Group and adopted by 164 countries, with one country voting against and six abstaining.




In presenting the resolution, Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey argued that maps are not merely technical tools: their repeated use in schools, the media and digital platforms shapes how people understand and visualise the world. The African Group argued that the Mercator projection, designed for specific purposes—especially maritime navigation—had become a general-purpose image of the world that visually minimises Africa and other regions near the Equator.




The delegation framed the initiative around scientific and educational accuracy, cognitive justice, historical memory and the equal dignity of peoples. It also stressed what the resolution would not do: condemn the Mercator projection, impose a single map for every use, alter borders or take a position on territorial claims. Instead, it encouraged the use of projections such as Equal Earth when comparing the relative areas of continents, alongside better teaching about the strengths and limitations of different projections.




The resolution encourages the use of equal-area map projections, including Equal Earth, particularly when the relative size of regions matters. It also highlights the implications of existing representations for geographical and cartographic literacy. Importantly, however, it does not replace the Mercator projection, redraw international borders or alter the legal status of any territory. So why does a map matter? And why now?




These questions are more significant than the technical debate over which projection should be used. The UN resolution opens a much larger question about who has historically possessed the authority to represent the world, whose knowledge becomes universal knowledge, and what happens when previously marginalised actors begin to challenge that authority.




Mercator Map versus Equal Earth (wikicommons)




The map is not the territory—but it shapes how the territory is imagined




Gerardus Mercator’s famous projection was first published in 1569. It was developed primarily as a tool for maritime navigation, as its preservation of angles and constant compass bearings made it particularly useful for sailors plotting routes across oceans. The projection was never intended to provide an accurate comparison of the relative size of continents. Its distortion, however, has had a long afterlife.




Because the Mercator projection increasingly enlarges landmasses as they move away from the Equator, Greenland can appear comparable in size to Africa, despite Africa being approximately fourteen times larger.There is therefore an important distinction to make. Mercator was not invented as a deliberate attempt to make Africa smaller. Its original purpose was navigational. The political question emerges from what happened afterwards: how a projection designed for a particular technical purpose became normalised as a general image of the world.




A cartographic choice made for navigation became, through repetition, an educational and cultural convention. Maps entered classrooms, atlases, newspapers, television graphics, websites and digital platforms. In doing so, they did more than provide geographical information. They participated in producing a particular visual imagination of the world. This is where cartography becomes political. Can a two-dimensional map ever be neutral?




From geographical distortion to cognitive hierarchy




The significance of the new 

UN resolution

 therefore lies less in replacing one map with another than in recognising that representation itself has consequences. The resolution’s language is striking. It connects cartographic representation to education, perception and collective understanding, framing the correction of historical distortions as a matter of equitable representation. The UN Office of the Special Adviser on Africa has presented the initiative as an African-led effort to challenge the symbolic minimisation of the continent. But the tension remains.




If representation contributes to how societies imagine the world, then correcting representation can be understood as a form of cognitive or epistemic intervention. Yet cognitive correction is not the same thing as material transformation. Africa does not become politically more powerful because it appears larger on a classroom wall. Its borders do not change. Its economies do not automatically become less dependent on external capital. Its resources do not cease to be sites of extraction. Conflicts do not become more visible merely because the continent is represented more proportionately. This is precisely where the politics of the map becomes interesting. What does it mean to correct the image of Africa while leaving many of the structures that have historically shaped Africa’s position in the international system intact?




Why Africa, and why now?




The timing of the resolution is important. It comes amid a broader period in which African states have increasingly sought greater authority over how African histories, identities and political interests are represented internationally. In March 2026, for example, Ghana led a separate UN initiative recognising the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement as the “gravest crime against humanity”. That resolution was adopted by 123 votes to three, with 52 abstentions.




These initiatives are different in substance. One concerns historical enslavement; the other concerns cartographic representation. Yet they can be read together as part of a broader struggle over who gets to define historical knowledge and the terms of recognition within international institutions. This is not simply a demand to be represented more accurately. It is also a demand to participate in determining what counts as accuracy. That distinction matters.




For centuries, knowledge about Africa was frequently produced through institutions, categories and intellectual frameworks located outside the continent. Colonial cartography did not merely describe territories; it participated in ordering them. Colonial knowledge systems classified populations, territories and resources in ways that made them legible to imperial administration.




The contemporary map is not identical to the colonial map. Nor should Mercator’s projection itself be treated as a colonial conspiracy. But the history of mapping reminds us that knowledge and power have rarely been entirely separate.The question today is therefore not simply whether Africa has been drawn at the wrong scale. It is whether Africa is increasingly claiming the authority to participate in drawing the conceptual map of the world.




The paradox of symbolic recognition




Here lies the deeper paradox. The international system can recognise that Africa has been visually underrepresented while continuing to struggle with the structural inequalities that shape Africa’s position within that same system. The map can be corrected much more easily than the hierarchy. A classroom can replace one projection with another in an afternoon. Changing the global distribution of economic power, institutional representation and access to capital—and changing who controls natural resources or sets the terms of international decision-making—is considerably more difficult. I describe this gap as moral fragmentation.




By moral fragmentation, I mean a condition in which international actors can converge around the recognition of a particular historical or representational injustice while remaining divided—or unwilling to act collectively—on the deeper structures through which inequality is reproduced. The map provides a particularly revealing example. The African Union has also called for permanent African representation on the UN Security Council. This demand raises a related question: how should the continent’s political weight and interests be represented within global institutions?




There is now remarkably broad agreement that the relative size of Africa should not be visually distorted when size is what a map is intended to communicate. Yet there is no equivalent consensus about what a more equitable international political and economic order should look like. The correction of representation therefore raises an uncomfortable question: Can an international system correct the image of inequality without confronting the structures that produce inequality?




The politics of the classroom




The emphasis on education in the resolution deserves particular attention. The UN initiative is not only about producing a different image for diplomats or cartographers. It explicitly engages with educational and geographical literacy.




That matters because maps enter political consciousness long before most people encounter international relations as an academic discipline. Children learn the world through images. They learn which countries appear large, which appear small, which regions dominate the page, and which are visually peripheral. They learn spatial hierarchies before they necessarily have the vocabulary to question them.




This does not mean that seeing Africa at its correct relative scale automatically produces anti-racist or anti-colonial consciousness. That would be another form of determinism. But it does mean that representational choices form part of the environment in which political knowledge is produced. The classroom is therefore not politically neutral simply because the lesson is called geography.The question is not whether a map determines what a child thinks. It is whether repeated representations contribute to what becomes familiar, normal and imaginable.




The United States and the politics of disagreement




The vote itself adds another layer to the story. The United States was the only country to vote against the resolution, while Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained. It would be tempting to interpret the American vote as evidence that Washington rejects the principle of more equitable representation of Africa. The vote alone, however, cannot establish that. The United States did offer an explicit explanation: its representative argued that the resolution formed part of what 

Washington characterised as a wider ideological project

, pointing specifically to references to reparations and “cognitive justice”.




The US delegation described resolutions of this kind as distractions from issues it considered more directly connected to international peace, prosperity and good relations, and argued that they undermined the UN’s credibility. This provides evidence for interpreting the vote: the objection was not presented as a technical disagreement over the mathematics of map projections, but as opposition to the resolution’s wider political framing. It does not, however, establish every motive behind the vote or mean that the United States opposed all efforts to improve cartographic accuracy.




The contrast is revealing: Togo presented accurate representation as a matter of dignity and educational fairness, while the United States treated the 

resolution’s links to reparations

 and cognitive justice as evidence of ideological overreach. Several delegations supporting the resolution emphasised that it should not be understood as changing borders, sovereignty or territorial claims. Mexico, for example, supported the resolution while stressing that different projections serve different purposes and that no single projection can represent every property of the Earth without distortion.




This disagreement is important because it prevents the debate from becoming a simplistic opposition between a supposedly enlightened South and an obstructive North. Politics are more complicated.




The real question is not whether one map is universally “correct”. Every projection involves choices and compromises. The question is who gets to decide which compromises are appropriate, for which purposes, and whose historical experience informs those decisions.




From correcting the map to questioning the world it represents




Perhaps the most provocative aspect of the resolution is therefore not that Africa will appear larger. It is that an African-led initiative has successfully placed a seemingly technical question of cartography onto the agenda of the world’s principal multilateral institution.  For a long time, Africa has frequently appeared in international discourse as an object of knowledge: a continent to be mapped, measured, developed, secured, rescued or extracted from. The “Correct the Map” initiative reverses that relationship, at least symbolically. Africa is not simply being represented; it is intervening in the politics of representation.




But symbolic intervention has limits. If the correction ends with a different image on the classroom wall, the transformation remains incomplete. The more difficult task is to ask what else must be corrected: whose knowledge is treated as authoritative, whose histories receive institutional recognition, who controls resources, who sets the terms of development, whose voices shape international institutions, and who gets to define what constitutes justice.




The danger is that the international system becomes very good at recognising injustice symbolically while becoming considerably less willing to redistribute power materially. That is the contradiction at the heart of the new map. A larger Africa on the map is not necessarily a more powerful Africa in the world. That is precisely why the map matters. The point of correcting it should not be to make Africa look bigger. It should be to make visible the question of why Africa has so often been made to matter less.




–




This article was first published by 

ROAPE

.

The post 

Africa on the Map, But Still Off the Table

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

title: Mass grave discovered in Harasta
content:
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) has reported that the remains of six people have been recovered from a mass grave in Harasta. According to SOHR, 28 mass graves containing the remains of 231 people have been discovered across Syria since the beginning of 2026.




The mass grave was discovered in the Al-Ajami neighbourhood of Harasta, in the Damascus countryside, an area that was heavily damaged during the war, according to SOHR.




The remains of six people were found during clearance work to remove rubble from destroyed buildings. SOHR said forensic experts were examining the remains in an effort to identify the victims and notify their families.




According to SOHR, a total of 28 mass graves have been uncovered across Syria since the beginning of 2026, containing the remains of 231 people.
