author: CMI Argentina
title: Pauny no se presentó a la audiencia y crece la incertidumbre sobre la continuidad de los 450 empleados de su planta de Córdoba
content:
Pauny, la fábrica de tractores, debía presentar un plan para afrontar la deuda salarial y reactivar la producción en la fábrica de Las Varillas. Lucas Sarmiento, titular de la UOM San Francisco, aseguró que adeuda dos meses de sueldos.







La crisis de Pauny sumó un nuevo capítulo este jueves, luego de que la empresa no se presentara a la audiencia convocada por la Secretaría de Trabajo de Córdoba para abordar la deuda salarial con sus empleados y la paralización de la actividad productiva en la planta de Las Varillas.




En diálogo con Cadena 3, Lucas Sarmiento, secretario general de la Unión Obrera Metalúrgica (UOM) de San Francisco, cuestionó la decisión de la firma y rechazó los argumentos expuestos en un comunicado empresarial, en el que se responsabilizó a los trabajadores por las dificultades para retomar la actividad.




La audiencia tenía como objetivo que la empresa presentara un plan para afrontar las obligaciones salariales pendientes y una propuesta productiva que permitiera reactivar la fábrica, prácticamente paralizada desde hace entre tres y cinco meses.




“Los trabajadores están acá en planta esperando justamente una propuesta de la patronal para reactivar rápidamente la empresa. Eso no sucede”, sostuvo Sarmiento.







Sarmiento precisó que Pauny tiene alrededor de 450 trabajadores directos y que la deuda con el personal no se limita a los últimos dos meses de salarios impagos: “Están adeudando los últimos dos meses completos, pero no es solamente eso. Los trabajadores fueron tomando deuda a lo largo de este año y del año pasado porque la empresa fue pagando a destiempo”, explicó.




Uno de los puntos más cuestionamientos del sindicato es la intención de la empresa de desprenderse de 150 trabajadores mediante un plan de retiros voluntarios o desvinculaciones, con el pago de parte de las indemnizaciones en 12 cuotas.




“Es ilógico que la empresa plantee un plan de retiro voluntario cuando ni siquiera junta la plata para pagar la deuda que tiene con los trabajadores”, afirmó Sarmiento.




El dirigente también puso en duda la capacidad de la firma para afrontar esos compromisos y mencionó la situación financiera de Pauny. Según los datos que dijo haber consultado en la Central de Deudores del Banco Central, la compañía registra obligaciones con distintas entidades bancarias por más de 50 millones de dólares y 206 cheques rechazados en los últimos 15 días, por un monto superior a los $1.500 millones.




“¿Con qué van a pagar? ¿Con cheques? ¿Quién va a aceptar cheques de Pauny? Es una locura lo que está haciendo la empresa”, cuestionó.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Fresh Off Electoral Defeat on Iran War, Trump Floats New Military Front in Cuba
content:
The Trump administration’s fuel blockade has already been likened to an act of war by critics.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump said this week that he wants to “get Cuba done” before his term is over, casually saying that he is considering opening yet another military front in a country whose civilian population is already being killed and starved by his sweeping sanctions campaign.

When asked by conservative talk show host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday whether or not he would use military force in Cuba, Trump said he “would certainly consider” a military campaign on the small island nation.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave, yeah,” said Trump.

“We have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco,” Trump went on. “Because Marco’s parents are from — Marco Rubio, his parents are from Cuba, as you probably know and he would love to do that. So we’re watching it very closely. It’s doing very poorly, it’s essentially a failed place, nation, whatever you want to call it, it’s failed. And we’re watching it. I would like to be able to do it.”

The suggestion to open a new military front comes despite voters delivering Trump and the Republicans a historic loss in last week’s midterm elections, due in large part to his failed war on Iran.

Cuba is indeed “doing very poorly” due in large part to the U.S.’s decades-old sanctions regime. The U.S. has held an embargo prohibiting U.S. businesses and citizens from conducting trade with Cuba since the 1960s, which had already had severe deleterious effects on the country.

Trump’s severe escalation in the sanctions regime, including the fuel embargo, is currently killing even more people in Cuba. As of June, childhood cancer survival rates in the country had declined from 85 percent to 65 percent since Trump’s sanctions were imposed, with medicine supplies reaching critically low levels. Infant mortality also doubled in that time, to 9.9 per 1,000 births, compounding on the existing effects of U.S. sanctions; according to an analysis this April by the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR), the U.S.’s sanctions regime caused 1,800 excess deaths of infants between 2017 and 2025.

“The Trump policy of ‘maximum pressure’ on Cuba has killed a lot of babies — and, although we don’t yet have data for the last few months, it’s highly likely that more babies are dying now, and at an even higher rate than last year as a result of the current U.S. fuel blockade targeting Cuba,” said CEPR report coauthor Alexander Main at the time.

The U.S.’s fuel blockade, meanwhile, has led to numerous near-total or total blackouts across Cuba this year, leaving Cubans literally in the dark as they clamor for basic food and medicine supplies. Experts have said that the blockade is akin to an act of war.

The Trump administration has not shown any signs of letting up on Cuba. Just last week, Rubio and the Trump administration instituted yet another wave of sanctions targeting Cuba. Trump and Rubio have openly called for regime change. Two weeks ago, Rubio issued an open call on X for people to open a “discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA” if they seek change in Cuba, in concert with the CIA’s Cuba task force set up earlier this year.

In remarks on Monday, Trump said, on Cuba, that he “imagine[s] it will fall fairly soon.” The same day, Rubio criticized the Cuban “regime” and said that the U.S.’s goal is for Cubans to “wake up and realize that there is no future on the path they are on right now.”

title: La inflación de octubre fue del 2,2 por ciento y suma 26,3 en el año
content:
La inflación de octubre volvió a superar el 2% y alcanzó el 2,2%, según informó el Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos (INDEC). Con este resultado, el Índice de Precios al Consumidor (IPC) acumuló un incremento del 26,3% en los primeros diez meses de 2026 y del 33,1% en los últimos doce meses.







El dato de octubre fue el más alto desde abril, cuando la inflación había alcanzado el 2,6%. Además, se ubicó 0,3 puntos porcentuales por encima del registro de septiembre y terminó superando las previsiones de analistas y consultoras privadas.




El mayor aumento se registró en vivienda, agua, electricidad, gas y otros combustibles, con una suba del 4,2%, impulsada principalmente por el incremento del gas. Le siguieron Recreación y cultura, con el 3,3%, y Bienes y servicios varios, con el 2,3%. Las tres divisiones se ubicaron por encima del promedio general.




En tanto, prendas de vestir y calzado aumentó un 2,2%; Transporte, un 2,1%; y Comunicación y Alimentos y bebidas no alcohólicas, un 2% en ambos casos. Por debajo del nivel general quedaron Salud (1,8%), Restaurantes y hoteles (1,5%), Equipamiento y mantenimiento del hogar (1,4%), Educación (1,3%) y Bebidas alcohólicas y tabaco (0,8%).




En la división por regiones, tres jurisdicciones superaron el índice nacional: la región Pampeana registró una inflación del 2,6%, la Patagonia del 2,5% y Cuyo del 2,3%.




Por otra parte, el informe del INDEC detalló que los precios estacionales tuvieron el mayor incremento, con un 5,5%, mientras que los precios regulados subieron un 2,9%. La inflación núcleo, que excluye los componentes estacionales y regulados, fue del 1,5%.




De esta manera, el índice continúa con una dinámica de subas y bajas que se observa desde julio, cuando había sido del 2,1%. En agosto llegó al 1,7%, el registro más bajo del año, mientras que marzo continúa siendo el mes de mayor inflación, con un 3,4%.

author: labor4pal
title: Trump Subpoenas Teachers Union for Info on Pro-Palestine Students (The Intercept)
content:
The expansive subpoena asked the American Federation of Teachers headquarters for information related to a vandalism case against Michigan students.

Activists gather at a pro-Palestine encampment at the University of Michigan’s campus on April 24, 2024, in Ann Arbor, Michigan.Photo: Adam J. Dewey/Anadolu via Getty Images

The Trump administration quietly broadened its crackdown on campus pro-Palestine protests over the summer, moving to ensnare one of the largest unions in the country in a case revolving around alleged incidents of vandalism.

The national headquarters of the American Federation of Teachers, or AFT, received a grand jury subpoena in August as part of an ongoing federal investigation into protests at the University of Michigan. Twelve pro-Palestine activists have been charged with felonies in the case.

The subpoena against the AFT, which has not been previously reported and was obtained by The Intercept, shows the administration casting a wider net in its investigation into student protesters than was previously known.

“They’re using this language around conspiracy and trying to draw in all of these different organizations.”

The Graduate Employees’ Organization, or GEO, an AFT local at the university, also received a notice to provide information and testimony to a grand jury around the same time, according to a copy of the previously unreported subpoena obtained by The Intercept.

The effort to draw a powerful, liberal union into a case that revolves around spray-painting charges represents a dramatic escalation in Donald Trump’s war on the left.

“They’re using this language around conspiracy and trying to draw in all of these different organizations that are taking stances against fascism, against the government, and anything that’s counter to their ideology,” said Natalie Chen, who serves as GEO’s communications director. “This is perhaps another ‘in’ for them to broaden their attack

As pro-Palestine protests swept campuses across the country in 2024 and widespread demonstration broke out against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this year, the Trump administration has sought to paint left-of-center protest, nonprofit work, and labor organizing as a nefarious far-left conspiracy, even labeling some activists and groups as terrorists.

Critics of the administration’s crackdown on Palestine solidarity and protests against ICE see moves like the ones against AFT and GEO as part of an effort to silence dissent.

“Historically, federal grand jury subpoenas have been used against social movements and political dissent to gather information, to isolate individuals, and of course to try and prosecute people,” said Xavier de Janon, executive director of the National Lawyers Guild. “What is different in politicized cases is the extent of people and places that get subpoenaed, which many people see clearly goes way beyond what they’re supposedly trying to prosecute.”

Activists at the University of Michigan said the effort to extract information about students from the union was an attempt to further target pro-Palestine protesters and their relationships with labor organizers.

“What is different in politicized cases is the extent of people and places that get subpoenaed.”

The grand jury subpoenas came as part of a case that has seen a dozen protesters become caught up in serious federal charges against the students, dubbed “the Michigan 12.” They allege that protesters committed illegal acts like vandalism as part of a pressure campaign seeking to push university officials to divest school holdings tied to the Israeli genocide in Palestine.

The subpoenas against the GEO and AFT were requested by federal prosecutor Margaret Smith with assistance from FBI agent Kara Phipps — two federal officials deeply enmeshed in the investigation into the Michigan 12. (The Department of Justice declined to comment for this story.)

The subpoenas were issued as the GEO was already reeling after its president, Hiab Teshome, was charged with felony embezzlement by local prosecutors working in conjunction with the University of Michigan Police Department.

Authorities alleged that Teshome, who was a bargaining team member in the middle of intense contract negotiations between the union and the school, misused organizational funds to purchase laptops for a campus club.

In a statement, the GEO called the charges meritless and characterized them as an attempt to limit protected union activity. Teshome was later cleared of any wrongdoing by the university’s student government, and the charges against her were thrown out by a judge.

Federal prosecutors issued the subpoenas the same day the charges against Teshome were dismissed, leaving activists little time to regroup.

Although GEO is not mentioned in the federal indictment against protesters, the AFT chapter is a prominent member of the Tahrir coalition, a pro-Palestine student collective that is referenced repeatedly in federal filings and characterized by prosecutors as having ties with defendants.

The scope of the information requested of the unions by the federal government is broad. GEO and AFT are being compelled, according to the subpoenas, to surrender information including complete membership rolls, payroll records on officers, reimbursement policies, audit reports, and all transcribed minutes on membership and executive board meetings of the University of Michigan local since January 2023.

The American Federation of Teachers has more than 1.7 million members and more than 3,000 local chapters.

After receiving the subpoena, GEO immediately obtained attorneys and filed a motion to quash the order. The national office of the AFT, however, has not publicly acknowledged receiving the directive or stated whether it intends to comply. (AFT did not respond to requests for comment about the subpoenas, including whether the union would be complying.)

Teshome, the GEO president, believes that the subpoena against the AFT may be an attempt by the federal government to circumvent the local union and force the national organization to comply.

“GEO has taken the stance that we will do everything in our power to protect the data and the information of our membership,” Teshome said. “I think that this is a strategy that the federal government is using in order to try to actually receive the information that they are trying to get by usurping us as a local union and going instead to AFT national.”

Additionally, Teshome likened the GEO’s case to similar surveillance activities conducted by federal agents against trade unionists in Minnesota as part of the Trump White House’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, a presidential directive that attempts to criminalize leftist political organizations.

“All of the repression we are seeing across the country is the federal government’s attack on anyone who has political thought,” Teshome said. “Michigan is no different than all of these other cases in that we are one of the testing grounds for NSPM-7 and how much oppression can be applied through the federal government in order to demobilize and disorganize.

author: Chris Walker
title: Poll: Most US Voters Want a Popular Vote Model for Picking Future Presidents
content:
Democrats in several states have indicated support for the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

New polling demonstrates that a majority of registered voters in the United States support changing the method through which presidents are selected.

Currently, the Electoral College is the mechanism used to pick presidents. Each state receives electoral votes equal to its number of congressional representatives — the number of House districts in the state plus its two Senate seats. These electors are directed by their states to vote for a presidential candidate following an election.

For most states, their entire slate of electors is given to the presidential candidate who won the most votes in their state. To win the presidency, a candidate must receive a majority of the tallied Electoral College votes, which is currently 270.

Due to significant population differences among states that are not accurately reflected in the Electoral College, the model can sometimes choose a presidential winner who did not win the popular vote among voters nationwide. Indeed, there have been five elections in U.S. history — including two elections since 2000 — in which the popular vote winner did not end up becoming president.

The post-midterm Economist/YouGov poll, conducted November 9-11, asked respondents whether they favored keeping the Electoral College or preferred to replace it with a popular vote system. Among registered voters, 51 percent said they wanted presidents to be selected through a popular vote, while only 28 percent said they wanted to keep the current system in place. Another 21 percent said they were unsure.

According to the poll, one in five registered voters (22 percent) have either heard of the Electoral College but don’t know how it works, or have never heard of it at all. It’s possible that a large segment of this population of voters would also support a popular vote model if they learned more about the undemocratic way in which the Electoral College functions.

With the results of the midterms flipping several state governments to Democratic Party control, there now exists a real opportunity for lawmakers to implement a popular vote system.

Complete abolition of the Electoral College would require a constitutional amendment. But advocates for a plan called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact say the rules of the Electoral College can actually be used to create a popular vote system.

Per the Constitution, each state determines for itself how its electors are chosen. If the compact was implemented, states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes would direct their electors to the candidate who won the majority of votes nationwide, rather than the candidate who won the majority of votes in their state.

The compact doesn’t kick in until states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes sign on. As it stands right now, just 48 electoral votes are needed for the compact to go into effect.

In this month’s midterm elections, Democrats won new trifecta governments (e.g., states in which Democrats have control of the state legislature and governor’s office) in Wisconsin, Michigan, Nevada, Arizona, and Pennsylvania. Each of those states has yet to back the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact — but if they do, they would represent more than enough of the remaining electoral votes needed to put it in place.

Lawmakers from those states have indicated that they are planning to pursue that route or are open to the idea of doing so.

Even if those states pass the compact, there’s one more hurdle: Article I Section 10 of the Constitution also requires Congress to approve most interstate compacts. That means the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress must pass a resolution to approve the idea — and that a filibuster by Republicans in the Senate could block it.

That is, unless Democrats change rules in that chamber to limit how and when a filibuster can occur, a matter that is presently dividing members of the party.

title: 19-летнего анархиста Дмитрия Сюткина приговорили к 9 годам заключения
content:
19-летнего анархиста Дмитрия Сюткина приговорили к 9 годам заключения по «террористическим» статьям. В то же время в суд поступило новое дело против него — о госизмене.

Центральный окружной военный суд в Екатеринбурге вынес приговор 19-летнему уральскому анархисту Дмитрию Сюткину — 9 лет заключения. Об этом он сам сообщил в письме, которое его собеседница получила 13 ноября.

Неизвестно, когда именно был оглашен этот приговор — карточка дела на сайте ЦОВС до сих пор не опубликована, даже в обезличенном виде. Известно только, что Сюткина обвиняли сразу по семи уголовным статьям: «подготовка к теракту» (часть 1 статьи 30 УК, часть 1 статьи 205 УК), «cклонение к террористической деятельности иного лица» (часть 1.1 статьи 205.1 УК), «публичное оправдание терроризма» (часть 2 статьи 205.2 УК), «участие в террористическом сообществе» (часть 2 статьи 205.4 УК), «участие в террористической организации» (часть 2 статьи 205.5 УК), незаконное хранение и незаконное изготовление взрывчатки (часть 1 статьи 222.1 УК и часть 1 статьи 223.1 УК).

Как заметили «Огни свободы», 9 ноября в Свердловский областной суд поступило еще одно уголовное дело против Сюткина — «о государственной измене» (275 УК). Первое заседание назначено уже на 23 ноября. Дела по этой статье всегда рассматриваются российскими судами в закрытом режиме, без слушателей.

Что известно о преследовании Сюткина

Впервые Диму задержали в возрасте 16 лет в 2023 году из-за поста, посвященного сбору на адвоката для одного из поджигателей военкомата. Тогда подростка опросили и отпустили.

Вскоре с ним связался «куратор» из Сибирского батальона, который предложил Диме «помощь с выездом за границу». Сначала подросток отказался, но через какое-то время передумал. «Куратор» дал ему ссылку на второго «куратора» — уже из «Русского добровольческого корпуса», а тот попросил Диму передать неизвестным коктейли Молотова. На месте встречи подростка встретили сотрудники ФСБ.

До ареста Дима жил в городе Серов и учился в колледже на логиста. Он вел телеграм-канал «Вольная родина», где продвигал идеи анархизма и уральского сепаратизма.

Дима сохраняет бодрость и хорошее настроение. И оно станет только лучше, если вы поддержите его письмом! К тому же совсем скоро, 28 ноября, Диме исполняется 20 лет — и это уже второй его день рождения в заключении

author: Joseph Lee
title: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
content:
The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and 

protest

, with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a longstanding pattern of exclusion from international negotiations. 




This year’s gathering in Antalya, Turkey, is billed as an “implementation” conference 

focused less on sweeping new pledges

 than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes COP31, which started November 9, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action.




“It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.”




Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on 400 million acres in tropical forest countries, provide 

$1.8 billion in funding

, and respect rights to free, prior, and informed consent in the energy transition. 




Despite those pledges, funds have been 

slow to reach affected communities

 and Indigenous land defenders say their rights and 

lives remain under constant threat

. Porokwa said that he feels that responsibility to address climate change continues to fall on smaller countries and Indigenous peoples. 




The stakes have been particularly stark over the last year. In Nepal, massive floods and landslides in August killed more than 1,500 people and destroyed entire villages. In Canada, a 

historic wildfire season

 saw millions of acres burned, causing thousands of evacuations. And in Indonesia, wildfire smoke alone has 

caused thousands of deaths

 and led to school closures and other emergency measures across Southeast Asia.




“The recent large-scale mountainside collapse on the border of Nepal and Tibet should serve as a wake-up call to the global community,” said Biswash Chepang, who is a founder of the Institute for Indigenous Affairs and Development in Nepal.




Climate-driven threats to Indigenous peoples and their lands continue to mount as a historically powerful 

El Niño

 threatens to drive famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes across the globe.










Read Next




























DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects













Joseph Lee

 



















The conference comes in the wake of a recent United Nations report that said it will be virtually 

impossible to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees

, the goal set under the landmark 

2015 Paris Agreement

. Indigenous delegates find that reality particularly frustrating because they see it as a direct result of decision makers ignoring their knowledge and 

all the ways

 their 

stewardship has been proven

 to 

benefit the environment and climate

. 




“For over 30 years we have brought Indigenous knowledges and sciences to these negotiations,” Māori activist Quack Pirihi said in an opening statement on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. “Yet emissions continue to rise, putting 1.5 degrees C beyond reach.”




While the work of reducing emissions and protecting Indigenous rights in the energy transition continues, securing funding for nations and communities most impacted by climate disasters is also a priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved $21.6 million for Nepal — its first disbursement and less than 1 percent of the nearly $5 billion in damage the country sustained. But the process to receive and administer those funds is 

ongoing

, and Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster. Their push comes as wealthy countries face renewed scrutiny over climate-finance pledges they have failed to deliver.




“Loss and damage is not simply a question of humanitarian assistance,” Chepang said. “It is also a question of climate responsibility, historical emissions, equity, and the right of affected communities to recover with dignity.” 




Indigenous peoples also hope to hold polluters to account. Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, is attending COP31 in part to highlight the landmark climate case her father Mike Smith led against major emitters in New Zealand. The case, which uses Māori customary law, has been 

blocked

 by the national government.




Despite the logistical, financial, and political hurdles of attending an event like COP, Ranson said there is value in global spaces. “I think that with the geopolitical moment that we’re in, with the rise of the far right and fascism and war, and the struggles that Indigenous peoples are facing across the globe, it’s a really important place for us to be able to come together to connect, to strengthen our solidarity,” Ranson said. 




As negotiations continue through November 20, Indigenous advocates will continue their push for all the discussions to lead to tangible actions. “Now I think it is not time only to talk about the commitment,” Porokwa said. “It is time to change the commitment into practice.”




This story was originally published by 

Grist

 with the headline 

Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action

 on Nov 13, 2026.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: John Amagoalik squares off with GN in court over home-care funding
content:
Nunavut Chief Justice Susan Cooper reserved her decision after hearing lawyers for John Amagoalik argue the territorial government should pay for his private medical care in Iqaluit while government lawyers argued it shouldn’t.




Lawyers for the man many consider the “Father of Nunavut” were in civil court Friday, trying to secure emergency funding to allow him to receive medical care in Iqaluit while 

a lawsuit

 he brought against the Nunavut government proceeds.




At issue is the retired politician’s request for approximately $16,000 a month to pay for private support care workers and housing.




Amagoalik says he needs that money so he can live with his wife and family in Iqaluit instead of at a long-term care facility in Ottawa, where he had been living for a year and a half until he returned North in August.




Nunavut’s Health Department has declined the request, saying it’s outside the government’s 

legislative authority

 to provide the amount of in-home care Amagoalik needs to stay in Nunavut.




Last month, Amagoalik, 79, 

filed an application

 for a judicial review of the Health Department’s decision, which the court will consider at a later date.




The department has so far offered to cover two hours a week of private support care for Amagoalik, which his lawyer Dougald E. Brown said is unacceptable. He currently receives up to 10 hours of care a day.
















“This is for an individual who is described in the plan of care as medically fragile,” Brown told Cooper in an Iqaluit courtroom Friday morning. “That is not a scenario that ends well. Mr. Amagoalik would be left vulnerable, and at risk of serious, adverse medical consequences – and I say this candidly – death.”




Brown cited sections of the territory’s Hospital Insurance and Health and Social Services Administration Act and its Boards of Management Dissolution Amendment Act, which he said appear to give the department the authority to fund his care and housing.




Brown told the judge “it is clear” the Health Department does have the legislative authority to grant Amagoalik’s request.




The way the Government of Nunavut has chosen to handle Amagoalik’s pleas for help infringe upon his Charter of Rights and Freedoms rights, Brown said.




Since the 1970s, Amagoalik had lived in Iqaluit with his family, until a surgery resulted in him being sent to the care home in February 2025.




Amagoalik has described his life at Embassy West as lonely and says he was unsatisfied with the care he was receiving.
















He cannot and will not return to Embassy West in Ottawa, Brown told the judge.




“A return to Embassy West is not a Charter-compliant option,” he said. “John Amagoalik already experienced life at Embassy West to be psychologically distressing and painful.”




In the afternoon, lawyers for the government took their turn.




“How public dollars are spent and the delivery of public health care is for the legislative assembly” to decide, not the courts, said Craig Boyer, a lawyer for the GN.




Exercising discretion in a way that goes against values in the Charter is not the same as infringing upon someone’s Charter rights, he also said.
















“[The Charter] does not provide an unqualified right to healthcare,” he said.




Using that logic, Iqaluit’s hospital would not be considered Charter-compliant, because some higher levels of care, such as certain kinds of cancer treatments, aren’t available there, Boyer said.




Brown, Amagoalik’s lawyer, said however they are “not asking for a restructuring” of the government’s home-care program delivery. Rather, they want the court to assess the reasonableness of the Health Department’s decision not to fund Amagoalik’s home care.




Cooper did not say when she will give a decision on Amagoalik’s application.

author: Lisa Sorg
title: Critics Slam Department of the Interior’s New Strategic Plan for Public Lands
content:
They say data center developers, mining firms, and energy companies could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The U.S. Department of the Interior could transfer swaths of public lands to state, local and tribal governments through sales or land swaps, according to the agency’s new strategic plan.

Critics are concerned that many states, cities and counties can’t afford to maintain the lands, and would sell them to private interests — the first step toward a wholesale privatization of lands that have belonged to Americans for more than 150 years.

“This is the biggest attack we’ve ever seen on public lands,” said Kate Groetzinger, communications director for the nonprofit Center for Western Priorities.

The Interior Department did not respond to requests for comment.

The agency manages more than 500 million acres of land in addition to 3.2 billion acres of offshore resources and 700 million acres of underground minerals. All told, the department manages 20 percent of the country’s lands, from national parks to wildlife refuges.

Data center developers, mining firms and energy companies — all favored industries of the Trump administration — could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts for their environmentally harmful operations, critics say.

The plan says Interior “will work to decrease the size of the federal estate” through the sales. That will allow the department to “focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands,” according to the plan, with some of the sales proceeds going back to “the purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes.”

The plan also says the agency will “consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies.” Interior has already lost more than 17 percent of its workforce under the second Trump administration.

In the plan’s introduction, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote that the agency will streamline environmental reviews and expedite leasing and permitting for energy companies. Nowhere in the plan does the agency mention wind or solar power. The first goal outlined in the plan is “Increase American Prosperity,” and the opening pages feature pictures of an oil rig and an offshore oil operation.

“Together, we can simplify processes and remove red tape that creates drudgery for our team members and impedes progress,” Burgum wrote. “We can bring forward new ideas and better ways of working. For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence.”

Burgum has made millions of dollars off investments in artificial intelligence, powered by data centers, ProPublica reported Nov. 6.

The plan doesn’t specifically identify data centers as potential customers to purchase federal property, but the White House previously asked Bureau of Land Management state offices to identify lands that would be appropriate for these uses.

Last June, BLM approved an AI data center on 81 acres of public land near Boulder City, Nevada. The builder had received federal approval in 2023 to construct a solar farm, but amended its application to include a data center.

A federal judge has halted the project because BLM did not conduct a new environmental analysis but rather used the previous one for the solar project, a likely violation of the National Environmental Policy Act.

Energy and mining interests have long sought — and received — access to the oil, gas and minerals beneath public lands via leases. The new Interior plan would allow BLM to sell or transfer those properties outright to agencies that could then resell them.

The plan runs from fiscal year 2026 to 2030. However, the Trump administration has already begun planning to offload some public lands in particular.

This September, the Forest Service, which is under the U.S. Department of Agriculture, issued a permit to Pitkin County in Colorado to manage a section of the White River National Forest that contains the Maroon Bells Scenic Area, the gateway to stunning burgundy peaks where hundreds of thousands of recreators visit annually. Critics see this move as a trial run for public land transfers.

In Alaska, the federal government is expected to soon open 28 million acres to new development and land ownership, according to the Juneau Independent.

Last March the Forest Service officially transferred a sacred indigenous site to Resolution Copper, a mining company.

BLM needs congressional approval to sell public parcels over 2,500 acres. However, federal law contains loopholes, Groetzinger said. The sales, for example, must serve the national interest, which can be broadly interpreted. The plan lays the foundation for that claim by repeatedly justifying future sales on national security grounds.

Not only does the Interior Department propose shrinking its current inventory of public lands, but the plan also forecloses the possibility of buying more. Instead of using the Land and Water Conservation Fund to purchase additional acreage, the agency says it will “shift its investment focus” to buying recreational and conservation easements on privately owned lands.

The Land and Water Conservation Fund protects thousands of parks, natural areas, historic sites and other projects nationwide from private development. “That’s an important function of the fund,” Groetzinger said. “For them to not use any of those funds to buy new land is just unprecedented.”

Jayson O’Neill is a spokesman for Save Our Parks and lives in Montana, where recreation and tourism driven by access to public lands and waters is critical for the local economy. “We need somebody that actually understands how important this is to the economic viability of our communities and also our way of life,” O’Neill said. “Instead they’re literally calling to give away federal public lands and public resources to industry.”

Inside Climate News reporter Jake Bolster contributed reporting.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

However, the policy faced legal challenges from three transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons, including one transgender woman and two transgender men. Their attorneys argued that the new restrictions would force the end of treatments that the Bureau of Prisons had provided to people with gender dysphoria since 1992.

The policy could affect nearly 1,000 incarcerated people in federal custody. The lawsuit raises questions about whether the government can discontinue established medical treatments for incarcerated people and what constitutional protections apply to people in its custody.

A lower federal court blocked the administration from enforcing the policy. The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause that ruling and allow the restrictions to take effect while the case continued. On October 21, the Supreme Court rejected the emergency request in an unsigned order. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas stated that they would have granted the request. The decision leaves the lower court’s order in place, preventing the administration from immediately enforcing the restrictions.

However, the Supreme Court’s decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine whether the administration’s policy is constitutional. The legal challenge will continue in the lower courts.

The case highlights the challenges transgender people face when seeking health care in settings where the government controls their medical decisions. Incarcerated people depend on prison authorities for access to doctors, medication, and other necessary services so when a policy restricts particular treatment, people in custody may have limited options for obtaining care independently.

Although the ruling does not end the case, it prevents the Trump administration from immediately implementing the restrictions while the legal proceedings continue. The outcome of the lawsuit will have important consequences for transgender people in federal prisons if the restrictions are placed and as the case moves forward, it shows the importance of questioning how government policies affect vulnerable populations and how government decisions apply to people whose freedom and access to healthcare are already limited.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide Calls on ICC to Arrest Trump, Rubio Over Gaza
content:
The alliance accused Trump and Rubio of aiding and abetting “genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in Gaza.”

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A delegation of U.S. taxpayers and human rights attorneys has called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to issue arrest warrants for President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their role in the genocide in Gaza.

On Wednesday, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG) delivered evidence against Trump and Rubio at the Hague, the headquarters of the ICC in the Netherlands, calling for their arrests for “aiding and abetting Israel in the commission of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in Gaza.”

The organization announced its submission to the ICC at a press conference at the Hague on Wednesday.

Individuals and organizations working with the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide collected evidence for nearly a year, including sworn affidavits from doctors who worked in Gaza, firsthand eyewitness testimonies, and whistleblower accounts related to U.S. military, financial, and diplomatic support for Israel throughout the course of the three-year genocide in Gaza.

The submission to the Office of the Prosecutor includes testimony of medical professionals who treated victims of 2,000-pound bombs and victims of shootings at distribution sites of the U.S. and Israel-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation — and notes that the Trump administration lifted a hold on 2,000-pound bombs, with Trump personally confirming the release of these bombs in early 2025. Rubio, the document states, also “approved or facilitated major arms transfers” including “large quantities of 2,000-pound bomb bodies or penetrator warheads,” while “waiving or compressing congressional review.” In addition, Rubio “participated in, funded, or defended” activities of the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, even after Médecins Sans Frontières, the UN, USAID, and other organizations warned that the foundation was involved in “mass casualties, hunger, and aid-site danger.”

Seth Donnelly, co-founder of TAAG, introduced Wednesday’s press conference, explaining that the organization had attempted to utilize the U.S. court system to stop the government’s participation in the genocide — but that the U.S. court system “has proven incapable again, and again, and again, from addressing this crime,” forcing them to turn to the ICC.

“It is not enough to wait for elections, or to vote them out,” Donnelly said, of U.S. government officials including Trump and Rubio. “Those responsible for grave crimes against humanity, including genocide, must be prosecuted — even if they are the most powerful officials in the world.”

Lawyers working with TAAG spoke at the press conference, explaining that the evidence submitted demonstrates that Trump and Rubio “knowingly supplied, released, expedited, and protected the transfer of weapons to Israel after repeated warnings that those weapons were being used to cause mass civilian deaths, destruction, starvation, displacement, and to create conditions that made life virtually impossible in Gaza.”

Trump and Rubio’s attempts to dismantle the ICC were also addressed at the press conference. The Trump administration has “withdrawn from international human rights mechanisms and sought to undermine institutions” that aim to hold the powerful to account, argued Palestinian American human rights lawyer and TAAG member Huwaida Arraf.

Francesca Albanese, human rights expert and UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, also spoke at the press conference, saying, “This administration’s attack on the ICC, on UNRWA, and the United Nations as a whole reveal an ambition to entrench global hegemony and extinguish the possibility of justice, not just in Palestine — everywhere.”

Albanese decried Trump’s celebration of the so-called ceasefire, during which the Israeli military has killed more than a thousand Palestinians in Gaza, and his creation of the “Board of Peace,” which, she says, “revives imperial ambitions and colonial tones while securing conditions for Palestine’s continued erasure and Israel’s impunity.”

“Let us be clear: the genocide of the Palestinian people would not have been possible without the unwavering support of the United States,” Albanese said.

author: Andrés
title: Explosión en Remedios de Escalada por negligencia y precarización de METROGAS
content:
Foto: Nico Kobane




En trabajos con una tuneladora, Exgadet SA, una empresa tercerizada de Metrogas, rompió un caño de gas. En lugar de activar  los protocolos de seguridad, llamaron a METROGAS. La cuadrilla de la empresa se acercó al lugar y convino en seguir con el trabajo. El gas se acumuló y la explosión voló en pedazos toda la esquina. 21 personas fueron traladadas, 8 ya fueron dadas de alta. 6 permanecen en estado de gravedad en el Hospital Evita, 5 son empleados de Exgadet. Y 7 quedaron en observación. Hay un muerto y dos desaparecidos. Se demoraron a dos administrativos no jerárquicos y se está realizando la investigación administrativa. Pasadas las dos de la mañana lograron obturar el caño y se apagó el fuego. 

Por ANRed.




Foto: Nico Kobane




Los trabajos los estaban realizando este mediodía (13.11.26) en el centro de Lanús, luego de que vecinos sintieran durante días el permanente olor a gas. Con una tuneladora, la empresa EXGADET SA rompió un caño de gas. Llamaron a METROGAS, acudió la cuadrilla, dijo que estaba controlada, pero poco después estalló luego de que el gas se hubiera acumulado, provocando heridas en más de 30 personas, que fueron trasladadas en su mayoría al Hospital Evita, en Lanús.




«Hubo una violación en los protocolos de emergencia. En este momento METROGAS está realizando los cortes al Este, Oeste, Norte y Sur. Por eso en este momento la llama ha disminuido, aunque deben cortar aún sobre la calle Iberlucea. Por el momento, la fiscal ordenó la detención de dos personas jerárquicas de METROGAS. No han disipado con líneas de agua el gas que se fue derramando. La empresa METROGAS decidió mantener en reserva, a pesar de que vecinos dijeran que percibían desde ayer el olor a gas.», testimonIó desde el lugar Claudio Arale, director de Defensa Civil de Lanús.




Foto: Nico Kobane




Hay personas con quemaduras y politraumatizadas por la explosión. 5 cinco obreros de la empresa tercerizada Exgadet S.A. (tercerizada de Metrogas), tienen quemaduras y lesiones de gravedad, entre los que contamos un muerto y dos desaparecidos.




Ante una falla en los protocolos de actuación, la justicia deberá determinar qué sucedió. En el lugar está establecido un comando de operaciones y gracias a los cuarteles de bomberos hermanos ya está todo controlado.




Foto: Nico Kobane




Desde hace días, los vecinos venían avisando sobre el fuerte olor a gas en la zona. Nuevamente, los trabajadores, comerciantes y vecinos son víctimas de la negligencia de las empresas, del gobierno nacional, del provincial y del municipal, que tercerizan trabajos de alto riesgo sin garantizar la adecuada seguridad.




Varias dotaciones de bomberos siguen intervininedo para disminuir las llamas.




Los suministros de gas y luz se encuentran cortados.




Casas, comercios, escuelas y bibliotecas de la zona fueron evacuados.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Nvidia Scandal Has Exposed “How Precarious the Governance of This AI Truly Is”
content:
Tech critic Paris Marx and Professor Ramesh Srinivasan discuss the centrality of Nvidia to the whole AI industry.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries.

Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk.

We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: We begin today’s show looking at the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as the CEO of Nvidia, one of the world’s most powerful companies. Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips have powered much of the artificial intelligence boom. Huang cultivated close ties to President Trump and is credited with helping to shape U.S. policies around artificial intelligence and rules around the export of advanced AI chips.

Huang’s resignation came days after reports emerged he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of spying for Beijing and helping China obtain advanced Nvidia chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. The Information news outlet reports Alice Huang helped route at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with the woman. Later, published reports revealed he also had affairs with two employees at Nvidia, including with a senior executive who reported to him.

Nvidia has announced its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, would serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

On Thursday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche took questions about Nvidia.

REPORTER: When did the Justice Department learn, with regard to Nvidia, that Alice Huang might be a suspected Chinese asset? And there’s been concerns raised that the Commerce Department was giving favoritism to Nvidia and Megaspeed, which is Alice Huang’s company. Do you share the concerns that maybe the Commerce Department was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network that Alice Huang was involved in?

ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE: Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said and that I don’t know to be true. So, you assume that DOJ learns that she is, in fact, a spy. I’m not — nobody said that. I certainly haven’t said that. And I don’t — all I said a minute ago, and all that I think I will say, is that, of course, DOJ is investigating or looking at it. So, there’s no — there’s no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice or by me or by Director Patel around who she is or is not.

I don’t have concerns with the Commerce Department. I don’t. We have a good relationship with the Commerce Department. I’ve read some of the stories, which, you know, are sourced or not sourced, and so I don’t have any — but, no, I don’t have — the answer to your question is, no, I don’t have any — I don’t have any concerns.

AMY GOODMAN: On Capitol Hill, Republican and Democratic lawmakers are calling for probes into Nvidia’s actions and the Trump administration’s policies regarding chip exports to China. Republican Senator Tim Scott, the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has requested Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify. Democratic lawmakers Ron Wyden of Oregon and Richard Neal of Massachusetts are investigating the Trump administration’s decision to allow Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.

For more on Nvidia and questions about the concentration of power in the AI industry, we’re joined now by two guests. In Toronto, Canada, we’re joined by Paris Marx, a tech critic and host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast. He writes the Disconnect newsletter, author of the book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires. And in Germany, we’re joined by Ramesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA and host of the podcast Utopias.

Paris Marx and Ramesh Srinivasan, welcome back to Democracy Now! Professor Srinivasan, let’s begin with you. What should we understand about what has just taken place? And talk about the centrality of Nvidia to the whole AI bubble, to the whole AI industry.

RAMESH SRINIVASAN: Right. Thank you so much for having me, Amy.

AI is not magic. It comes from the planet, and the technologies that produce it often return to the planet as electronic waste. It’s powered by water, energy sources, labor and our data, and those come from us, from the planet itself. Right? So, what has occurred is this astonishing technology that reduces life to data and numbers, and reduces intelligence to pattern recognition, has been — has now been governed and run by just a few people on the planet, mainly men, and men that you’ve discussed, you know, commonly on Democracy Now!, who were there at the inauguration and so on.

So, now when we have soap opera sorts of moments, like Mr. Jensen Huang being connected to, you know, this Chinese — potential Chinese spy, various affairs and so on, you can see how precarious the governance of this AI truly is, because the administration has completely handed the keys to this incredibly powerful technology, that feeds off of all of us and the planet, to basically a few people, and they can do what they want — their vagaries, their mishaps, their corruption in certain cases, their gluttony. That is what is being accumulated more and more.

So, the story of AI is a story that’s tied to data centers — right? — which you cover all the time, which are, you know, computing and so on, much like server farms in the past. They’re tied to chips, and that’s very key to this story, the Nvidia chips, or superchips, that were originally used in the context of gaming and now were applied to artificial intelligence and large language models. But it also comes from all of our data, and then the screens and systems that determine and shape our lives.

So, this is a technology that is harvested, extracted from our planet and all of us to create potentially trillions of dollars of valuation, which might be a massive bubble — and we can talk about that — with returning almost next to nothing for the rest of us, other than anxiety, insecurity and deep concerns. The technology doesn’t have to go in that direction, but that’s the direction the Trump administration has taken it.

And I think it’s incredibly notable that it’s the China — it’s the China scare yet again, just like we saw with Huawei, just like we saw with COVID. It’s the China scare that’s forcing all of this action and this spectacle and this controversy, rather than the real conditions of AI, which are disenfranchising and robbing people of many aspects of their futures.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, if you could continue, talking about what is the role of Nvidia when it comes to, overall, fueling so much? And explain the issue of the ban on these — on these superchips, why they’re so significant, what kind of monopoly Nvidia has on this, and why you believe he is so close to President Trump, who didn’t want him to resign.

PARIS MARX: Absolutely. Great to join you this morning, Amy.

You know, Nvidia is key to this AI market. You know, it controls about 90% or so of the chips that go into, you know, all these data centers that are powering the AI boom that we have seen occurring now for the past few years, right? And as a result of that, Nvidia has become one of the most valued companies, and for a while has been, you know, the most valuable publicly traded company on the planet, which is just staggering to imagine, right? You know, it went from kind of just, you know, a regular old tech company, you know, not particularly notable — sure, it made some graphics cards for gamers — to being now one of the key companies that, as you say, you know, is so important for what so many other companies are doing.

And it’s not just the fact that it creates these chips — right? — these chips that are just essential to, you know, the generative AI workloads behind ChatGPT and the image generators and those sorts of things, but because Nvidia has made so much money for the past number of years, it has also become a major investor, plowing more than $120 billion into other AI companies across the economy, across the United States, around the world, which has meant that now there are all these companies that not just depend on Nvidia’s chips, but also depend on Nvidia’s financing. You know, I’m sure you’ve been talking on the show about the upcoming Anthropic IPO, you know, Anthropic looking to go public. It is expecting about $10 billion from Nvidia as part of its public offering. And so, Nvidia has been really key here.

And because of that, you know, because Nvidia was valued at something like more than $5 trillion until recently, it’s no surprise, then, that Jensen Huang has become very close with Donald Trump, right? It’s a very valuable company. It is a company that makes the technology that is very important to the broader AI boom that has been kind of lifting the U.S. economy and the U.S. stock market — right? — because of the investment, not just in all these AI products, but in all these data centers that, you know, have been being built across the country, as well. And so, Jensen Huang has become a major adviser to Donald Trump on AI policy and has certainly been pushing him to weaken the restrictions on, you know, basically, his ability to sell these chips to China.

And I think now in light of these revelations, there are questions as to whether, you know, that is kind of a firmly held belief that Jensen Huang had because there was obviously, you know, as someone who runs a major company, a big market opportunity in selling those chips to China, or whether there was influence on his thoughts, you know, from Alice Huang. And I think those are questions that we don’t have answered yet, but certainly is probably, you know, what some of these lawmakers are hoping to try to get more insight into by having Jensen Huang come speak to congresspeople.

AMY GOODMAN: Paris Marx, in your book, you quote one investor who describes Nvidia as “the central bank of AI.” And there are many descriptions of how Huang is really the conduit from the other tech billionaire bros to reaching President Trump and making the demands that they want.

PARIS MARX: Absolutely. You know, as I was mentioning, when we look at Nvidia, it is not just a company that is selling all these chips. It is a company that has gone to a lot of these other AI and data center companies and made sure that they had investment, sure, so that they could, you know, grow, expand their businesses, what have you, but also that they — so that they could then buy more Nvidia chips from Nvidia, right? So, it’s kind of like a circular financing scheme, where Nvidia gives it the money to operate, and then they buy the chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia makes more money in that way, right? So the money comes back to Nvidia all the time.

And then, of course, linked with that is it has also used that money to try to support companies that were in difficult situations. So, for example, a company called CoreWeave, that creates data centers to power AI and kind of sells that computing power to these AI companies, has been in trouble, on and off, for a number of years, and Nvidia has often been there to support that company when it has been in dire straits. And it’s not the only one like that.

And so, of course, you know, linked to that, Jensen Huang has developed this really close relationship with Donald Trump. You know, we saw this just the other day, just yesterday, after Jensen Huang resigned, and, you know, Donald Trump came out and said that he was talking to Jensen and, you know, that things are difficult, and, you know, basically, had this really kind of personal relationship to him, seems to be someone who he really trusts. And as a result of that, I’m sure that Donald Trump has been open when Jensen Huang has been discussing AI and tech policy with him.

And, of course, Jensen has been pushing to make sure that there is not regulation of AI products, in the way that your other guest has been talking about, you know, is really necessary, but then, on top of that, again, trying to weaken these restrictions on the ability to sell chips to China. And, of course, you know, the U.S. government’s concern and many lawmakers’ concern there is that by selling those chips, because they are some of the — because they are the most advanced chips that are out there, that if they get sold to China, you know, China will not just be able — Chinese companies will not just be able to use them to power their own AI products, but that there’s a concern that, you know, Chinese companies will be able to kind of reverse-engineer the technology and then have a big kind of leap in their — in their kind of chip-making capabilities, essentially.

AMY GOODMAN: In October of last year, Jensen Huang spoke to the media about whether China should have access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

JENSEN HUANG: The China market is large, and it’s a vibrant, vibrant market with a lot of developers. And those developers create AI technology that’s exported from China all over the world. And so, to the extent that American tech stack can run and operate those AI models, it’s good for the United States and around the world.

REPORTER: So, would you want the Blackwell to be sold in China?

JENSEN HUANG: I hope so. I hope so. But that’s a decision for President Trump to make.

AMY GOODMAN: So, Professor Ramesh Srinivasan, if you can explain what he is saying there? And also, this whole issue of the so-called Chinese spy, what evidence do we have of this? Is it other competing companies saying this? Is there a big division within the U.S. government in the intelligence community who had informed Trump of this months and months ago?

RAMESH SRINIVASAN: Right. It’s not clear what the evidence is as of this point. You could even see in the story, in the introduction to this story, that even the Attorney General Todd Blanche is, you know, very elusive and vague in his comments about, you know, what is — what exactly occurred here.

But I do think it’s very important to note a couple things that were already mentioned here. First of all, the AI industry, there’s incredible amount of concern that this is an overspeculated bubble. That’s because many of the revenues are occurring in the circular way that your other guest just described. So the revenues seem to be inflated here.

And talking about China, as we actually discussed before, Amy, back, you know, about almost two years ago, Chinese models around AI are performing nearly as well as the top American so-called frontier models. I mean, the question of what we’re building all these models for is a worthwhile question, I think a big elephant in the room. But they’re doing it at a fraction of the cost. So, we have to really consider what’s occurring here and what’s really occurring here, right?

So, the president’s response around all these concerns is often to say that the economy is super healthy. And when he says that, what he’s talking about — Trump, I’m saying — is he’s talking about the S&P 500. But the vast majority of people in America and around the world do not have large amounts of investment capital. Investment capital is how people make money, but there’s a deep amount of concern that these — this is not going to actually produce the type of revenues that even legitimate it for investors.

But what about the rest of us, as workers, as consumers? AI is being pushed out as a technology of replacement, not a technology to augment or expand or help us, you know, create together. It’s not a telescope. It’s not, you know, a microscope. It’s not what Steve Jobs once famously called a “bicycle for the mind.” It’s being — it’s using us. It’s surveilling us. It’s turning us into data. It’s turning life and intelligence into patterns to replace us, to read, write, speak for us. In fact, a CEO in Big Tech told me recently, because I’m from Silicon Valley and I have friends in that industry, “Hey, Ramesh, you don’t even have to do this interview with Democracy Now! Very soon, an AI can do that for you, and better than you.” What does that even mean? So, this is what’s at play here.

And so, this has been cast, as I alluded to earlier, as some sort of flat, you know, geopolitical battle between the U.S. and China, when, in reality, what we need is cooperation between the two nations, and, most importantly, outside of the elites in those two nations, governance by stakeholders, not just in the Global South and around the planet, where I’m part of a Global South AI alliance, but also from workers, consumers and so on, to ensure that a technology that uses patterns to predict the present and construct the future is a technology that’s applied to the right domains. And no one, at the end of the day, has been paid for their data. None of us have equity in any of these companies, but these companies are feeding off us to potentially replace us. And that’s what I would call a parasitic technology. But it doesn’t have to go in that direction.

AMY GOODMAN: Ramesh, can you show us your hands? AI models are notoriously bad at generating the correct number of fingers. I’m only kidding. OK, Paris Marx, Paris, this was from Bloomberg. You have Bloomberg in — let’s see, says, “Jefferies Financial Group Inc.’s Chris Wood said the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom will be massive capital destruction in the U.S.” Do you see that coming now?

PARIS MARX: It’s hard to say when exactly that would come. You know, I think that there are multiple moments over the past few years where it looked like, you know, maybe — maybe the bubble is going to start bursting, and then, you know, it has continued. I think that it is facing a serious threat in this moment, and not just because of the resignation of Jensen Huang from Nvidia.

And to be clear, you know, Nvidia was a company that was really like Jensen Huang’s fiefdom. You know, it was not set up to have a lot of kind of people who could easily take over from him if he were to leave the company. You know, a number of his family members are also executives within the company. And so, you know, I think that there’s real concern about what this is going to mean for Nvidia’s future — right? — as such a key player in the AI market, you know, again, one of the most valuable companies in the world, supplying the key technology that these companies need, but also providing a lot of financing to other companies.

But we’ve also been seeing, through this year, a lot of major companies kind of pulling back on their generative AI spending, because they’re finding they’re not getting the return on investment from what they’re doing there. There was just a report at the end of October from an analyst at Apollo called Torsten Slok, and he basically looked at the S&P 500 to see, you know, whether companies had really been benefiting from this rollout of generative AI, and found that with the big seven tech companies, you could clearly see an increase in profit margins and in revenue per employee, you know, from rolling out generative AI products, but for those other 493 companies within the S&P 500, he did not see, you know, kind of like a notable difference or that generative AI had really benefited them.

So, there are growing questions there about the economic benefits of actually using this technology, not to mention, you know, kind of the many social harms that your other guest was talking about that need to be addressed and reined in. And so, you know, there are already — there’s already kind of skepticism and questions about all the money that has been put into these AI models, into these data centers in order to power them, whether they’re actually going to be as useful or whether the market for them is actually going to be as big as the companies are promising. And so, on top of those existing concerns, now these issues at Nvidia are kind of adding on top of that, which means that there is a potential kind of greater risk there, you know, of a collapse of some sort coming in the near future. But I certainly wouldn’t want to go as far as to call that this is the moment that it’s all going to happen.

AMY GOODMAN: And, Paris Marx, as you look down on us in the United States from Toronto, and across, of course, at Alaska, I wanted to get your comment on the midterms. You’ve written extensively about the anti-data center movement in the United States. It certainly fueled a lot of people, might have driven a lot of people to the polls. If you can also talk about the possibility of Democrats investigating tech CEOs? And, of course, right now we have the demand of Democrats and Republicans to investigate Jensen Huang.

PARIS MARX: Yeah, I would love to see it. Let’s bring on more investigations of the tech CEOs. Start with Jensen, and we can go from there.

But I do think that the midterms were not just a repudiation of the Republican Party and Donald Trump, but also of these tech CEOs that have been wielding so much power over, you know, our societies collectively for such a long period of time. And especially it feels like they really took this to a new level with what they’ve been doing the past few years — right? — not just the rollout of this generative AI technology that, as I was saying, is not as beneficial as they promised, but also had a lot of negative social and environmental consequences that came along with it, but then, paired with that, trying to push these massive hyperscale data centers into so many communities across the United States and around the world.

And so, what we saw is voters really push back against that. You know, so many races in the United States had a data center component to them. And if we look at key states like, say, Texas or Georgia or Ohio, we can see that data centers were really consequential in the battles that played out there, and that Democratic lawmakers recognized that, you know, going against data centers, promising moratoriums, was going to win the votes.

I think now the question is where this goes from here, right? Are we actually going to see those Democrats follow through on those promises? Is the pressure going to keep up? Or is the tech industry, which I’m sure it is, you know, about to pivot at this moment, hiring a ton of lobbyists to try to find a way to shape some of what Democrats are going to try to do, try to shape that kind of tech regulation, data center regulation agenda to make sure it’s not going to be as biting as it might otherwise appear? And so, I think that’s what I’ll be watching, you know, going forward, how this is going to play out.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, Paris Marx, I want to thank you for being with us, author of Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, speaking to us from Toronto, and Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA, today speaking to us from Germany. Thanks so much, both, for being with us.

Coming up, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Gaza has killed at least six people, including a surgeon. We’ll speak to Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, who volunteered at Nasser and worked with Dr. Abu Shaira. Stay with us.

AMY GOODMAN: “Garden” by Nicolás Jaar.
